explanations.a: Correct — proportional abundance is the count of species i divided by the total individuals counted, so all p_i sum to 1 across the community.
explanations.b: Subtracting counts produces a number with no proportional meaning and can even go negative.
explanations.c: Inverting the ratio gives a number greater than 1 for any species with fewer individuals than the total, which cannot be a proportion.
explanations.d: Multiplying by richness S has no basis in the definition and would not yield values that sum to 1.

questions.prompt: A 100-individual plot has one species at n=91 and nine other species at n=1 each, so S=10. Which statement best describes this community?

options.text: It is maximally diverse because it has 10 species
It behaves functionally close to a monoculture despite S=10, because evenness is very low
Richness and evenness must always move together, so this scenario is impossible
N is undefined because the counts are unequal

explanations.a: Species count alone does not mean high diversity in the functional sense; a heavily dominated community is not what most people mean by 'diverse'.
explanations.b: Correct — with p_dominant = 0.91, one species accounts for nearly all individuals, so ecologically the plot behaves almost like a single-species stand with rare stragglers.
explanations.c: Richness and evenness are independent axes by design; this scenario (high S, very low evenness) is a standard illustration of that independence.
explanations.d: N is simply the sum of all individuals (91+9x1=100) and is always defined regardless of how unequal the counts are.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for correctly building an abundance table from raw field counts, from first to last.

items.text: Identify and count individuals of each species encountered in the sample
Sum all counts to get total individuals N
Divide each species' count n_i by N to get relative abundance p_i
Check that all p_i values sum to 1.00 as an arithmetic check

questions.explanation: You must first tally each species (s1), then total the tally to get N (s2), then divide each species count by that total to get p_i (s3), and finally verify the proportions sum to 1.00 as a sanity check before computing any diversity index from them (s4).

lessons.label: The Shannon Index

sections.heading: Borrowed from signal engineering, not born in ecology
sections.body: The formula H' = -Sigma p_i * ln(p_i) did not start as an ecology tool. Claude Shannon introduced it in his 1948 paper 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' (Bell System Technical Journal) to measure the uncertainty, or information content, of a message source — a channel that could emit many symbols with low probability each is 'more uncertain' per symbol than one dominated by a few common symbols. Ecologists imported the same math because a community is structurally the same problem: species play the role of symbols, and p_i is the probability that the next individual you sample belongs to species i. Ramon Margalef's 1958 paper 'Information Theory in Ecology' made the connection explicit and popularized H' as a community diversity statistic, with Robert MacArthur applying closely related information measures to bird communities around the same period. H' is frequently mislabeled the 'Shannon-Weaver index' in ecological writing, crediting Warren Weaver — who co-authored the 1949 book 'The Mathematical Theory of Communication' with Shannon, expanding on his 1948 paper for a general audience, but did not create the entropy formula itself and had no hand in its ecological application.

sections.heading: Computing it by hand
sections.body: For each species compute p_i, then p_i * ln(p_i) (a negative number since 0 < p_i < 1), sum those products, and negate the sum. Using natural log (ln) is the ecological convention, though log base 2 or log10 appear in some papers — H' values are NOT comparable across studies unless the log base matches, since switching base rescales H' by a constant factor. Most real communities land H' approximately 1.5 to 3.5 when computed in ln; values near 0 indicate a single-species stand, and values climbing past 4 typically require dozens of well-represented species, which is rare outside hyperdiverse systems like tropical arthropod assemblages.

sections.heading: Turning H' back into something interpretable: evenness and effective number
sections.body: H' by itself is hard to feel intuitively — is 2.1 'good'? Two conversions fix that. Pielou's evenness, J = H' / ln(S), rescales H' by the maximum possible value it could take at that richness (achieved when all p_i are equal), producing a 0-to-1 evenness score independent of S. Separately, the effective number of species is e^H' (Hill number of order 1, covered next lesson) — it answers 'how many EQUALLY abundant species would produce this same H'?', turning an awkward log-scale number into a species count that is directly comparable across sites.

lessons.workedExample: Five species with p_i = 0.48, 0.31, 0.12, 0.06, 0.03 (the prairie quadrat from the previous lesson). Compute p_i*ln(p_i) for each: 0.48*ln(0.48)=0.48*(-0.734)=-0.352; 0.31*ln(0.31)=0.31*(-1.171)=-0.363; 0.12*ln(0.12)=0.12*(-2.120)=-0.254; 0.06*ln(0.06)=0.06*(-2.813)=-0.169; 0.03*ln(0.03)=0.03*(-3.507)=-0.105. Sum = -1.243, so H' = 1.243. Max possible at S=5 is ln(5)=1.609, so Pielou's J = 1.243/1.609 = 0.77 — fairly even given the dominance skew. Effective number = e^1.243 = 3.47, meaning this 5-species, grass-dominated plot behaves diversity-wise like about 3.5 equally common species.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask students to walk through an H' calculation by hand because it is the single fastest way to catch someone who pasted numbers into software without understanding what the index means. A weak answer states 'H' = 1.24' with no sense of what that number implies. A strong answer explains that H' rewards both more species AND more even distribution among them, converts H' to Pielou's J or the effective number to make the value interpretable, and — critically — states which log base was used, since a judge who spots an uncredited base-10 value being compared to a base-e literature value has found a real analytical error.

questions.prompt: The Shannon index H' was originally developed for what purpose before ecologists adopted it?

options.text: Measuring genetic mutation rates
Quantifying the information/uncertainty content of a communication signal
Estimating population growth rates
Calculating species-area curves

explanations.a: H' has no connection to mutation rates; that is a population-genetics concept unrelated to Shannon's 1948 work.
explanations.b: Correct — Claude Shannon introduced the formula in his 1948 information theory paper to quantify the uncertainty of symbols emitted by a communication source, later imported into ecology by Ramon Margalef in 1958.
explanations.c: Population growth rates are handled by demographic models (e.g., exponential/logistic growth), not information theory.
explanations.d: Species-area curves (S = cA^z) are a separate, unrelated relationship covered later in this unit.

questions.prompt: A study reports H' = 3.9 computed with log base 2, and a student wants to compare it to their own H' = 2.1 computed with natural log (ln). What is the problem?

options.text: There is no problem; H' values are always directly comparable
H' values computed with different log bases are on different scales and cannot be directly compared without converting
H' can only be computed with base 10, so both values are invalid
The comparison is fine as long as both communities have the same richness S

explanations.a: Different log bases rescale H' by a constant multiplicative factor, so treating the two values as equivalent overstates or understates the actual diversity difference.
explanations.b: Correct — switching log base changes the units of H', so a base-2 value and a base-e (ln) value must be converted to the same base before comparison.
explanations.c: Base 10 is one valid convention among several (ln is the most common in ecology); no single base is 'required'.
explanations.d: Matching richness S does not fix a log-base mismatch; the base affects the scale of H' regardless of S.

questions.prompt: What does Pielou's evenness J = H'/ln(S) represent?

options.text: The total number of individuals sampled
H' rescaled by its maximum possible value at that richness, giving a 0-to-1 evenness score
The number of species not detected in the sample
The square of the Shannon index

explanations.a: J is a ratio derived from H' and S, not a raw individual count.
explanations.b: Correct — ln(S) is the maximum H' achievable at that richness (when all species are equally abundant), so dividing H' by it produces a normalized 0-to-1 evenness measure independent of S.
explanations.c: J says nothing about undetected species; that is the domain of estimators like Chao1, covered in a later lesson.
explanations.d: J is a ratio, not a squared quantity; squaring H' has no defined ecological meaning here.

questions.prompt: A community has H' = 1.386 (natural log). What is its effective number of species, e^H', and roughly what does that number mean?

options.text: e^1.386 ≈ 4, meaning the community behaves like 4 equally abundant species
e^1.386 ≈ 1.386, meaning nothing further can be said
e^1.386 ≈ 0.25, meaning the community is 25% diverse
e^1.386 is undefined because H' is a logarithmic quantity

explanations.a: Correct — e^1.386 ≈ 4.0; the effective number of species converts the log-scale H' into a count-scale answer to 'how many equally common species would give this same H'?'.
explanations.b: Exponentiating is not the identity function; e^1.386 is not equal to 1.386 itself.
explanations.c: There is no '% diverse' interpretation of H'; e^H' yields a species count, not a percentage.
explanations.d: H' being computed via logarithms does not make it non-invertible; exponentiating it is exactly how the effective number is obtained.

lessons.label: Simpson, Dominance, and Hill Numbers

sections.heading: Simpson's index: the probability two random individuals match
sections.body: Edward Simpson introduced D = Sigma p_i^2 in 1949 as the probability that two individuals drawn at random from the community, with replacement, belong to the same species. Because it squares each proportion before summing, D is dominated by whichever species has the largest p_i — a single abundant species contributes p^2 to the sum in a way rare species barely can (a species at p=0.01 contributes only 0.0001, while one at p=0.5 contributes 0.25, 2500 times more). D therefore rises toward 1 as dominance increases and falls toward 0 as the community becomes more even, which is the opposite direction from how 'diversity' should read, so two transforms are standard: 1-D (Gini-Simpson index, probability the two individuals differ) and 1/D (Simpson's reciprocal), both of which increase with diversity.

sections.heading: Why Simpson and Shannon disagree on what matters
sections.body: Simpson's squaring means it is driven almost entirely by common species — adding or removing a rare singleton barely moves D. Shannon's H' uses p_i * ln(p_i) rather than p_i^2, a gentler weighting that keeps rare species mathematically 'louder' relative to their abundance. Practically: if a community loses one abundant species, D changes sharply while H' also drops, but if it loses several rare singletons, H' drops noticeably (fewer terms in the sum, small evenness shift) while D barely moves. This is why field ecologists often report both — Simpson answers 'how dominated is this community?' and Shannon answers 'how much information does species identity carry?', including the signal from rare taxa that Simpson discounts.

sections.heading: Hill numbers: one family, one dial
sections.body: Lou Jost's 2006 paper 'Entropy and Diversity' (Oikos) reframed richness, Shannon, and Simpson as three points on a single continuum: the Hill number of order q, qD = (Sigma p_i^q)^(1/(1-q)). Order q controls how much weight rare species get. At q=0, rare and common species count equally and qD = S, plain richness. At q=1 (the limit as q approaches 1), qD = e^H', the Shannon effective number from the last lesson. At q=2, qD = 1/D, Simpson's reciprocal. All three are 'effective number of species' on the same scale, which is precisely why Jost argued that comparing raw H' or D values between studies is misleading — only Hill numbers with a stated q are directly comparable, and a claim like 'diversity doubled' is meaningless unless q is specified, since doubling at q=0 (twice the species) is a very different claim from doubling at q=2 (twice the effective number weighted toward dominant species).

lessons.workedExample: The prairie plot from earlier lessons: p = 0.48, 0.31, 0.12, 0.06, 0.03, S = 5, H' = 1.243. Simpson's D = 0.48^2+0.31^2+0.12^2+0.06^2+0.03^2 = 0.2304+0.0961+0.0144+0.0036+0.0009 = 0.3454. So 1-D = 0.655 (65.5% chance two random individuals differ), and 1/D = 2.90. Hill numbers: q=0 gives 0D=5; q=1 gives 1D=e^1.243=3.47; q=2 gives 2D=1/D=2.90. The steady decline from 5 to 3.47 to 2.90 as q rises shows the community's effective diversity shrinking as rare species get discounted — exactly what you'd expect from a plot where two grasses hold 79% of individuals.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on Simpson-versus-Shannon because it tests whether a student understands that 'diversity' is not one number but a family of related measures with different sensitivities. A weak answer reports both D and H' without connecting them or explaining the discrepancy when they diverge. A strong answer explains that Simpson (via squaring) is dominance-driven and nearly blind to rare species, that Shannon weights rare species more, and — best of all — frames both as special cases of Hill numbers (q=2 and q≈1), showing they understand the unifying structure rather than treating each index as an isolated formula to memorize.

questions.prompt: Simpson's D = Sigma p_i^2 is best interpreted as what?

options.text: The probability that two randomly drawn individuals belong to the same species
The total number of species in the community
The average abundance per species
The log of the total individuals sampled

explanations.a: Correct — Edward Simpson (1949) defined D as the probability that two individuals drawn at random from the community (with replacement) are the same species, which is why squaring each p_i and summing gives that probability.
explanations.b: That is species richness S, a completely different and much simpler count-based quantity.
explanations.c: Average abundance per species would be N/S, not a sum of squared proportions.
explanations.d: D involves no logarithms at all; that is a feature of the Shannon index, not Simpson's.

questions.prompt: Why is Simpson's D much less sensitive to rare species than Shannon's H'?

options.text: Because D ignores species with fewer than 10 individuals by definition
Because squaring small p_i values (as D does) makes their contribution tiny, while H' uses p_i*ln(p_i), which weights rare species more heavily
Because D and H' are mathematically identical, so this premise is false
Because H' is computed only from the most abundant species

explanations.a: D has no built-in abundance cutoff; it simply weights all species by p_i^2, which naturally shrinks small values rather than excluding them.
explanations.b: Correct — a rare species with p=0.01 contributes only 0.0001 to D's sum but contributes a proportionally larger term to H's sum via p*ln(p), so rare species carry more weight in Shannon's index than in Simpson's.
explanations.c: D and H' are different formulas with different weighting behavior; they are not identical, which is exactly why ecologists report both.
explanations.d: H' sums over every species in the community, not only the most abundant one; excluding rare species would defeat its purpose.

questions.prompt: According to Jost (2006), the Hill number at q=2, given by (Sigma p_i^2)^(1/(1-2)), simplifies to which familiar quantity?

options.text: Species richness, S
The Shannon effective number, e^H'
Simpson's reciprocal, 1/D
Pielou's evenness, J

explanations.a: Richness is the q=0 Hill number, not q=2; at q=0 rare and common species count equally.
explanations.b: The Shannon effective number is the q=1 Hill number (the limiting case as q approaches 1), not q=2.
explanations.c: Correct — at q=2 the Hill number formula reduces to (Sigma p_i^2)^(-1), i.e., 1/D, Simpson's reciprocal, showing D is just one point on the Hill number continuum.
explanations.d: Pielou's J is a separate evenness ratio (H'/ln S), not a point on the Hill number curve at all.

questions.prompt: Match each Hill number order q to the classic diversity index it equals.

right.text: Species richness, S
Shannon effective number, e^H'
Simpson's reciprocal, 1/D

questions.explanation: Jost's (2006) Hill number framework unifies the three classic indices as one family: q=0 weights all species equally regardless of abundance, giving plain richness S; q=1 (the limiting case) equals the Shannon effective number e^H'; and q=2 equals Simpson's reciprocal 1/D, which is dominated by the most abundant species.

questions.prompt: A researcher says 'Site B has double the diversity of Site A.' Why is this claim incomplete without more information, per the Hill number framework?

options.text: It isn't incomplete; 'diversity' means the same thing at every Hill number order
Because doubling at q=0 (twice the species) is a very different claim from doubling at q=2 (twice the effective number weighted toward dominant species), so the order q must be stated
Because diversity can never be compared numerically between two sites
Because Hill numbers only apply to plant communities, not general ecological sites

explanations.a: Different Hill number orders weight rare versus common species very differently, so 'diversity' is not a single fixed quantity across orders.
explanations.b: Correct — Jost's argument is precisely that comparisons like 'doubled' are only meaningful once q is specified, since low-q comparisons emphasize rare species while high-q comparisons emphasize dominant ones.
explanations.c: Numerical comparison is possible and routine; the issue is specificity (which q), not impossibility.
explanations.d: Hill numbers are a general mathematical framework applicable to any community data, not restricted to plants.

lessons.label: Sampling Effort, Rarefaction, and Unseen Species

sections.heading: The accumulation curve: richness is a function of effort, not a fixed number
sections.body: Plot cumulative species detected against cumulative individuals (or samples, or traps, or hours) and you get a species-accumulation curve: steep at first, since every early individual is likely a new species, then flattening as the easy species get found and only rare ones remain to add. A curve that is still climbing steeply at the end of a survey is a direct signal that undersampling occurred — richness has not been measured, only a lower bound on it has. Because effort drives the curve's shape, comparing raw S between a site sampled with 50 individuals and one sampled with 500 is not a comparison of communities, it is largely a comparison of effort; the 500-individual site will almost always report higher S even if the underlying community is less diverse.

sections.heading: Rarefaction and coverage-based standardization fix the comparison
sections.body: Rarefaction resamples the larger dataset down to the smaller sample size (or a common lower N) many times, averaging the resulting S at that common effort — producing a fair, apples-to-apples richness estimate at equal sampling. Its limitation is that it discards information from the larger sample past the rarefaction point. Anne Chao and Lou Jost's 2012 refinement, coverage-based standardization (Ecology), instead equalizes samples by their estimated sample completeness (coverage — the proportion of the total community's individuals that belong to already-detected species) rather than by raw count, which handles cases where equal N still represents very unequal completeness across two communities with different rarity structures.

sections.heading: Estimating what you didn't see: Chao1 and the jackknife
sections.body: Two workhorse nonparametric estimators infer undetected richness from the shape of the rare end of the abundance distribution. Chao1 (Anne Chao, 1984) uses only singletons (f1, species observed exactly once) and doubletons (f2, species observed exactly twice): S_Chao1 = S_obs + f1^2 / (2*f2). The logic is that a community with many singletons relative to doubletons is one where many more species are likely present but undetected; when f2 = 0 the bias-corrected variant S_obs + f1(f1-1)/(2(f2+1)) avoids dividing by zero. The first-order jackknife (Burnham and Overton, 1978) instead uses incidence across n samples: S_jack1 = S_obs + f1*(n-1)/n, where f1 here is the number of species found in exactly one sample. Both estimators are lower bounds on true richness, not guarantees — they extrapolate from the same rare-species signal an accumulation curve's unclosed tail already warns you about.

lessons.workedExample: A pitfall-trap survey after 5 trap-nights yields 8 species with individual counts 15, 10, 6, 4, 2, 1, 1, 1 (N=40), and the accumulation curve is still rising steeply. Here f1 (singletons, count=1) = 3 and f2 (doubletons, count=2) = 1. Chao1 = 8 + 3^2/(2*1) = 8 + 4.5 = 12.5, roughly 12-13 species estimated versus 8 observed — a 50-60% gap suggesting the trap-night count should roughly double before richness claims are trustworthy. If a second site sampled to 200 individuals reports S_obs=15 with a flat curve, comparing 8 (rising curve) to 15 (flat curve) directly would wrongly conclude Site 2 is richer, when Site 1 is simply undersampled.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about sampling effort because comparing unequal-effort richness counts is the single most common statistical error in student ecology projects — 'we found more species at Site A' often just means 'we sampled Site A longer.' A weak answer reports raw S values from different sample sizes as if they were comparable. A strong answer shows the accumulation curve, states whether it has flattened, and either rarefies both sites to a common N or cites a Chao1/jackknife estimate acknowledging how many species likely went undetected — demonstrating they understand richness as effort-dependent rather than as a fixed property waiting to be read off.

questions.prompt: A species-accumulation curve is still climbing steeply at the end of a survey. What does this indicate?

options.text: The community has been fully sampled and richness is accurately known
The survey is undersampled and true richness is likely higher than observed
The community has unusually low evenness
The Shannon index must be recalculated using a different log base

explanations.a: A fully sampled community would show a flattening (asymptoting) curve, not continued steep climbing.
explanations.b: Correct — a steeply rising curve at the end of sampling means new species are still being found at a high rate, so observed S is a lower bound and more effort would likely add more species.
explanations.c: Evenness is a separate property (how abundances are distributed) unrelated to whether the accumulation curve has flattened.
explanations.d: Log base choice affects H' calculation, not accumulation curve shape; the two are unrelated.

questions.prompt: Why is it invalid to directly compare raw species richness S between a site sampled with 50 individuals and a site sampled with 500 individuals?

options.text: It is valid; richness is always independent of sample size
Because larger samples almost always detect more species regardless of true community diversity, so the comparison conflates effort with diversity
Because Simpson's D cannot be computed from unequal sample sizes
Because species richness can only be measured with camera traps

explanations.a: Richness is strongly sample-size dependent, especially early on the accumulation curve; treating it as size-independent is the core error this lesson addresses.
explanations.b: Correct — more individuals sampled means more chances to encounter rare species, so the 500-individual site will tend to show higher S purely from effort, not necessarily from being a richer community.
explanations.c: Simpson's D can be computed from any abundance table regardless of size; that isn't the issue with comparing S directly.
explanations.d: Richness can be measured with any consistent sampling method (quadrats, traps, transects, nets); camera traps are not required.

questions.prompt: Rarefaction addresses the unequal-effort comparison problem by doing what?

options.text: Resampling the larger dataset down to a common smaller sample size and averaging the resulting richness
Multiplying the smaller sample's richness by the ratio of sample sizes
Discarding the larger dataset entirely and using only the smaller one's raw S
Recomputing Shannon's H' in place of species richness

explanations.a: Correct — rarefaction repeatedly subsamples the larger dataset down to a common N (matching the smaller sample) and averages the resulting richness, producing a fair comparison at equal effort.
explanations.b: Richness does not scale linearly with sample size (accumulation curves are concave, not linear), so a simple ratio multiplication is not how rarefaction works and would be mathematically wrong.
explanations.c: Rarefaction uses the larger dataset's actual composition to simulate smaller samples; it doesn't discard it, it resamples from it.
explanations.d: Rarefaction is specifically a richness-standardization technique; it does not substitute in a different index like H'.

questions.prompt: In the Chao1 richness estimator S_Chao1 = S_obs + f1^2/(2*f2), what do f1 and f2 represent?

options.text: f1 is the number of singleton species (observed once), f2 is the number of doubleton species (observed twice)
f1 is total individuals, f2 is total species
f1 and f2 are arbitrary tuning constants with no ecological meaning
f1 is the sample area, f2 is the number of trap-nights

explanations.a: Correct — Chao's (1984) estimator uses the count of singletons (species detected exactly once) and doubletons (species detected exactly twice) as signals of how many more species likely remain undetected.
explanations.b: Total individuals is N and total species is S_obs, both distinct quantities already used elsewhere in the formula.
explanations.c: f1 and f2 are directly counted from the abundance data (rarity counts), not arbitrary constants.
explanations.d: Neither f1 nor f2 refers to sampling area or effort directly; they are species counts drawn from the observed abundance distribution.

questions.prompt: A trap survey has S_obs = 8, with f1 (singletons) = 3 and f2 (doubletons) = 1. What is the Chao1 estimate of total richness?

explanations.a: Correct — applying the formula: 8 + (3^2)/(2*1) = 8 + 9/2 = 8 + 4.5 = 12.5, suggesting roughly 4-5 additional undetected species beyond the 8 observed.
explanations.b: This divides f1 by f2 directly instead of squaring f1 and dividing by 2*f2, which is not the Chao1 formula.
explanations.c: The estimated undetected richness is added to S_obs, not subtracted; subtracting would imply fewer species exist than observed, which is not the estimator's logic.
explanations.d: Multiplying S_obs by the f1/f2 ratio has no basis in the Chao1 formula and wildly overstates the estimate.

lessons.label: Species-Area Relationships

sections.heading: S = cA^z: one of ecology's most reliable empirical laws
sections.body: Plot species richness S against sampled area A across nested plots of increasing size — a 1 m2 quadrat, then 10 m2, then 100 m2, then a hectare — and richness climbs in a strikingly consistent curved pattern: fast at small areas, decelerating at large ones, described by the power function S = cA^z. Olof Arrhenius first formalized the relationship in 1921 from Swedish plant plots, and Frank Preston's influential 1962 papers ('The Canonical Distribution of Commonness and Rarity,' Ecology) connected it to the lognormal species-abundance distribution, arguing the power law falls out naturally once you accept that abundance is lognormally distributed and rarer species are undersampled at small area. The relationship holds across taxa and scales from square meters to continents, which is part of why it is treated as a near-law rather than a curiosity.

sections.heading: Fitting it: why ecologists work in log-log space
sections.body: Taking logs of both sides linearizes the power function: log(S) = log(c) + z*log(A). Plotted as log(S) versus log(A), the relationship becomes a straight line with slope z and intercept log(c), which is why species-area data is almost always fit as a log-log linear regression rather than a curved nonlinear fit — it is easier to fit, easier to compare across studies (z values are directly comparable slopes), and easier to spot outliers or deviations from power-law behavior. The constant c is the richness predicted at A=1 (whatever unit area is used), so its value depends on units and is rarely compared across studies directly; z, the slope, is the number that carries the ecological meaning.

sections.heading: Two regimes of z, and what they say about isolation
sections.body: The magnitude of z differs systematically between two sampling contexts. For nested mainland samples — plots of increasing size within one continuous, non-isolated landscape — z typically falls around 0.15 to 0.25, because species just outside a small plot are usually still reachable by dispersal from nearby habitat, so richness climbs gently with area. For true islands (or habitat 'islands' — isolated fragments, mountaintops, lakes) z runs higher, roughly 0.25 to 0.35, a pattern central to Robert MacArthur and E.O. Wilson's 1967 Theory of Island Biogeography: isolation itself, not just area, limits colonization, so richness is more area-sensitive (steeper z) once dispersal is constrained by a barrier. A z value well outside these bands is itself informative — it can flag that 'nested' plots were not actually nested, or that the habitat behaves ecologically more like an island than continuous land.

lessons.workedExample: Nested plots of native shrubland: 1 m2 -> 5 species, 10 m2 -> 8 species, 100 m2 -> 14 species, 1000 m2 -> 23 species. Log-log regression of log10(S) on log10(A) gives roughly log10(S) = 0.69 + 0.22*log10(A) (c=10^0.69=4.9, z=0.22) -- a nested-mainland z, as expected for contiguous plots on one hillside. Now suppose habitat clearing shrinks the surrounding shrubland from 1000 m2 to 250 m2 (a 75% area loss). Using S=cA^z: S_before=4.9*1000^0.22=4.9*4.57=22.4 (matching the ~23 observed), S_after=4.9*250^0.22=4.9*3.37=16.5 -- predicting roughly a 26% richness loss from a 75% area loss, illustrating why species loss lags habitat loss but is far from negligible.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges lean on species-area relationships because they connect a clean statistical fit to a policy-relevant claim — habitat loss causes species loss, but not 1-to-1. A weak answer states 'smaller area means fewer species' with no quantification. A strong answer fits log(S) vs log(A), reports both c and z, states which regime (mainland-nested vs. island) the z value falls into and whether that matches the sampling design, and uses the fitted power law to predict a specific richness change from a specific area change — showing they can move from a regression line to a testable ecological prediction, which is exactly the skill fragmentation and reserve-design questions later in this track will demand.

questions.prompt: Why do ecologists typically fit species-area data as log(S) versus log(A) rather than S versus A directly?

options.text: Because the power function S = cA^z becomes a straight line in log-log space, making it easy to fit with linear regression and compare slopes across studies
Because area can only be measured on a logarithmic scale
Because richness cannot be counted at large spatial scales
Because log transformation eliminates the need for replicate plots

explanations.a: Correct — taking logs of S = cA^z gives log(S) = log(c) + z*log(A), a linear equation in log(A), so a simple linear regression on logged data directly yields z as the slope, which is far easier to fit and compare than a curved nonlinear fit.
explanations.b: Area is measured in ordinary linear units (m2, hectares); the log transform is applied afterward purely for fitting convenience, not because area is inherently logarithmic.
explanations.c: Richness can be counted at any scale with appropriate sampling methods; that is unrelated to why log-log fitting is used.
explanations.d: Replicate plots are still needed for a reliable regression regardless of whether the data is logged; the transform doesn't remove that requirement.

questions.prompt: In S = cA^z fit via log-log regression, what does the slope z represent, and roughly what range does it take for true islands versus nested mainland plots?

options.text: z is the intercept; islands run 0.05-0.10, mainland runs 0.40-0.50
z is the power-law exponent (regression slope); mainland nested samples run about 0.15-0.25, true islands run higher, about 0.25-0.35
z is always exactly 1.0 regardless of context
z represents total species richness at the largest sampled area

explanations.a: This reverses the actual pattern; islands have the higher z range, not the lower one, and z is the slope of the log-log line, not the intercept.
explanations.b: Correct — z is the regression slope in log-log space; nested mainland samples typically show z around 0.15-0.25 (gentle area-sensitivity, since dispersal from nearby habitat softens the effect of area alone), while isolated islands show steeper z, about 0.25-0.35, per MacArthur and Wilson's 1967 island biogeography framework.
explanations.c: z varies by ecological context and is essentially never exactly 1.0 in real data; a z of 1.0 would imply richness scales linearly with area, which is not the observed power-law pattern.
explanations.d: Total richness at the largest area is simply the observed S value at that A; z is a separate slope parameter describing the rate of increase, not a richness count.

questions.prompt: Robert MacArthur and E.O. Wilson's 1967 Theory of Island Biogeography explains why island z values run higher than mainland z values by pointing to what factor?

options.text: Islands have more fertile soil than mainland habitats
Isolation itself limits colonization, making richness more sensitive to area once dispersal is constrained by a barrier
Islands are always sampled with smaller plot sizes
Island species have higher mutation rates

explanations.a: Soil fertility is not the mechanism MacArthur and Wilson proposed; their framework centers on colonization and extinction dynamics driven by isolation and area.
explanations.b: Correct — because islands are isolated, colonization is dispersal-limited, so a species absent from a small island is less likely to be 'just outside' and reachable the way it would be in continuous mainland habitat, making richness more steeply area-dependent (higher z).
explanations.c: Plot size choice is a sampling decision unrelated to the underlying biogeographic mechanism MacArthur and Wilson described.
explanations.d: Mutation rate is a genetics concept unrelated to the colonization-extinction dynamics of island biogeography theory.

questions.prompt: Using a fitted relationship S = 2.75*A^0.27, roughly how much does richness fall when area shrinks from 1000 m2 to 250 m2 (a 75% area reduction)?

options.text: Richness falls by roughly 75%, matching the area loss exactly
Richness falls by roughly 30%, considerably less than the 75% area loss
Richness is unaffected by area changes under a power-law model
Richness falls to zero once any area is lost

explanations.a: A power-law relationship with z < 1 (as is always observed) means richness loss is always proportionally smaller than area loss, not equal to it.
explanations.b: Correct — S_before = 2.75*1000^0.27 ≈ 17.8 and S_after = 2.75*250^0.27 ≈ 12.2, a drop of about 31%, illustrating the well-known pattern that species loss lags habitat area loss but is still substantial.
explanations.c: The entire point of S=cA^z is that richness DOES change with area, just not linearly; treating it as unaffected contradicts the model itself.
explanations.d: A power law with z < 1 predicts gradual decline, never an abrupt collapse to zero from a single area reduction of this magnitude.

lessons.label: Rank-Abundance Plots and Comparing Communities

sections.heading: Reading a Whittaker plot: slope is evenness, shape is process
sections.body: A rank-abundance (Whittaker) plot ranks species from most to least abundant on the x-axis and plots log(abundance) on the y-axis. A steep downward slope means a few species dominate and most are rare (low evenness); a shallow, nearly flat slope means abundances are similar across species (high evenness) — so the plot makes the single number Pielou's J represents visually obvious. Robert Whittaker used these plots in the 1960s-70s to argue that the overall curve SHAPE, not just its slope, carries information about the ecological process assembling the community. Four canonical shapes recur: the geometric series (a straight line on the log plot, produced when dominant species preempt a fixed fraction of remaining resources — niche preemption, common in harsh or early-successional habitats), Fisher's log-series (proposed by Ronald Fisher, A. Steven Corbet, and C. B. Williams in 1943, fitted to Corbet's Malayan butterfly collections and, separately in the same paper, to Williams' moth catches from a light trap at Rothamsted in England — common when one factor limits many rare species similarly), Preston's lognormal (an S-shaped curve, expected in large, mature, well-sampled communities where many independent factors govern abundance), and MacArthur's broken-stick (1957, the flattest, most even shape, from randomly dividing a fixed resource among species — rarely fits real data but serves as a null-model benchmark for 'maximum plausible evenness').

sections.heading: Whittaker's alpha, beta, and gamma: diversity has a spatial structure
sections.body: In his 1960 paper on the Siskiyou Mountains ('Vegetation of the Siskiyou Mountains, Oregon and California,' Ecological Monographs), Whittaker partitioned diversity across scales: alpha diversity is richness within one site or habitat; gamma diversity is total richness across a whole region or set of sites combined; beta diversity is the turnover between them — how different the sites' species composition is from one another. The original multiplicative relationship is gamma = alpha(mean) * beta, so beta can be read as 'how many distinct community types' the region contains beyond one average site's worth of species. High beta means sites are compositionally distinct (species turn over sharply across the landscape); low beta means most sites look alike.

sections.heading: Quantifying beta: similarity indices
sections.body: Beta diversity is usually operationalized by comparing two sites directly. On presence/absence data, Jaccard's index J = a/(a+b+c) and the Sorensen (or Bray-Curtis presence/absence) index Cs = 2a/(2a+b+c) both use a = species shared, b and c = species unique to each site — Sorensen weights shared species more heavily (the factor of 2), so it is typically less conservative than Jaccard, and the two are mathematically related (Cs = 2J/(1+J)). When abundance data (not just presence) is available, the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, BC = Sigma|x_i - y_i| / Sigma(x_i + y_i), is standard — it ranges 0 (identical abundance profiles) to 1 (no species shared) and is far more informative than presence/absence alone since two sites can share every species yet still be very different if relative abundances diverge sharply.

lessons.workedExample: Site A (dry ridge): 8 species detected. Site B (moist ravine): 11 species, sharing 5 species with Site A. Jaccard: a=5 shared, b=3 unique to A, c=6 unique to B; J = 5/(5+3+6) = 5/14 = 0.36. Sorensen: Cs = 2*5/(2*5+3+6) = 10/19 = 0.53 -- noticeably higher than Jaccard, as expected since Sorensen upweights the shared species. If instead full abundance counts are used and the two sites' relative-abundance profiles for the 5 shared species differ sharply (e.g., a dominant fern at Site B is rare at Site A), Bray-Curtis dissimilarity would run well above the (1-Cs) presence/absence estimate, capturing a compositional difference that simple species overlap alone misses.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask students to interpret a rank-abundance plot, not just report H' or D, because reading the plot's shape tests whether the student can connect a statistical pattern to a candidate ecological mechanism. A weak answer identifies only the slope ('site A is more even than site B'). A strong answer names the likely underlying process — a near-straight log-linear line suggesting niche preemption (geometric series), an S-curve suggesting a mature, multi-factor-limited community (lognormal) — and, when comparing two sites, correctly distinguishes alpha (within-site), beta (turnover), and gamma (regional) diversity rather than conflating 'more species at one site' with 'more diverse region.'

questions.prompt: On a Whittaker rank-abundance plot (species ranked on x-axis, log abundance on y-axis), what does a steep downward slope indicate?

options.text: High evenness — abundances are similar across species
Low evenness — a few species dominate while most are rare
High species richness regardless of abundance distribution
That the community was undersampled

explanations.a: High evenness produces a shallow, nearly flat slope, since abundances are similar across ranks — the opposite of a steep slope.
explanations.b: Correct — a steep slope means abundance drops sharply from the most common to the next-ranked species, the visual signature of dominance and low evenness.
explanations.c: Slope reflects the abundance distribution's shape, not the total count of species (richness), which is simply how many points appear on the x-axis.
explanations.d: Undersampling shows up in a species-accumulation curve, not directly in a rank-abundance plot's slope.

questions.prompt: Match each rank-abundance curve shape to the ecological process or origin classically associated with it.

left.text: Geometric series (straight line on log plot)

right.text: Niche preemption — dominant species claim a fixed fraction of remaining resources
One limiting factor governing many rare species similarly (1943, Corbet's Malayan butterfly collections)
Many independent factors governing abundance in a large, mature community
Resources randomly divided among species — a null-model benchmark for maximum evenness

questions.explanation: Whittaker's four canonical shapes each imply a different assembly process: the geometric series comes from niche preemption; the 1943 log-series of Fisher, Corbet, and Williams was fitted to Corbet's Malayan butterfly collections (and, in the same paper, to Williams' English light-trap moth catches from Rothamsted), a pattern read as one limiting factor acting similarly on many rare species; Preston's lognormal S-curve is expected when many independent factors jointly govern abundance in large, well-sampled communities; and MacArthur's 1957 broken-stick model, the most even of all, represents resources split at random and serves mainly as a null-model benchmark rather than a common real-world fit.

questions.prompt: Under Whittaker's (1960) framework, if gamma is the total regional richness and alpha is the average within-site richness, what does beta diversity represent?

options.text: The turnover in species composition between sites — how distinct the sites are from one another
The total number of individuals sampled across the region
The evenness of the most diverse single site
A synonym for species richness at the regional scale

explanations.a: Correct — beta diversity captures compositional turnover between sites; under the multiplicative relationship gamma = alpha(mean)*beta, a high beta means sites differ sharply in which species they contain, beyond what any one average site would show.
explanations.b: Total individuals sampled (N, summed regionally) is a distinct quantity unrelated to the alpha/beta/gamma partition, which concerns richness and composition, not raw counts.
explanations.c: Evenness at one site is a separate property (e.g., Pielou's J), not what beta diversity measures.
explanations.d: Gamma, not beta, is the regional richness term; beta specifically measures the turnover/difference between sites, not a richness count itself.

questions.prompt: Two sites share 5 species; Site A has 3 species unique to it, Site B has 6 species unique to it. What is the Jaccard similarity, J = a/(a+b+c)?

explanations.a: Correct — with a=5 (shared), b=3 (unique to A), c=6 (unique to B), Jaccard = 5/(5+3+6) = 5/14 ≈ 0.36.
explanations.b: This divides shared species by (a+b) only, omitting c entirely, which is not the Jaccard formula.
explanations.c: 10/19 is the Sorensen formula's result (2a/(2a+b+c) = 10/19 ≈ 0.53), not Jaccard's — Sorensen upweights shared species with a factor of 2 in both numerator and denominator.
explanations.d: This omits b from the denominator (5/(5+6)+... miscount), which does not match the defined Jaccard formula using all three counts a, b, and c.

questions.prompt: Why is Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, computed from abundance data, often more informative than a presence/absence index like Jaccard for comparing two communities?

options.text: Because two sites can share every species yet still differ greatly if their relative abundances diverge, a difference presence/absence data cannot detect
Because Bray-Curtis does not require any species identification, only counts
Because Jaccard can only be computed for exactly two sites, while Bray-Curtis works for any number
Because presence/absence data is always less accurate to collect than abundance data

explanations.a: Correct — presence/absence indices treat 'species present' as a binary match regardless of how common it is at each site, so a dominant species at one site that is rare at another looks identical to Jaccard but produces a large Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, capturing a real compositional difference.
explanations.b: Bray-Curtis still requires identifying species to attach counts to; it is not identification-free, only richer than presence/absence in the information it uses.
explanations.c: Both Jaccard and Bray-Curtis are pairwise indices by standard definition, extendable to multiple sites via pairwise matrices in the same way; that is not the distinguishing factor here.
explanations.d: Data collection accuracy depends on field method, not on which index is later computed from it; this is not a real distinction between the two indices.

lessons.label: Exponential and Geometric Growth

sections.heading: Continuous growth: dN/dt = rN
sections.body: When resources are effectively unlimited, a population's growth rate at any instant is proportional to the number of individuals already present: dN/dt = rN, where r is the intrinsic (per-capita) rate of increase — births minus deaths per individual per unit time. Solving this differential equation gives N_t = N_0 e^(rt): population size rises along a J-shaped curve that accelerates forever. A convenient way to characterize how fast that acceleration happens is doubling time, t_d = ln(2)/r — the time for N to double regardless of the current population size, because growth is proportional, not additive. A yeast culture with r = 0.6/hour doubles roughly every 1.16 hours; the same math describes an invasive plant spreading unchecked across open habitat in its first seasons.

sections.heading: The discrete analogue: geometric growth
sections.body: Many organisms — annual plants, univoltine insects, most temperate fish — don't reproduce continuously; they breed in discrete, non-overlapping generations. For these, the geometric model applies: N_t+1 = λN_t, so N_t = N_0 λ^t, where λ is the finite rate of increase (the multiplier per generation). λ > 1 means growth, λ = 1 means stasis, λ < 1 means decline. Because λ is a discrete-time analogue of continuous e^r, the two are related by r = ln(λ), or λ = e^r. A population with λ = 1.15 per year (15% annual increase) has r = ln(1.15) ≈ 0.14 — the two frameworks describe the same trajectory measured on different clocks, and choosing between them depends on whether the organism's generations overlap.

sections.heading: Reading growth on a semi-log plot
sections.body: Because N_t = N_0 e^(rt), taking the natural log of both sides gives ln(N_t) = ln(N_0) + rt — a straight line whose slope is r. This is the standard trick for extracting r from real count data: plot ln(count) against time and fit a regression line; the slope is the per-capita growth rate, and a genuinely straight line is itself evidence that growth is exponential (constant per-capita rate) rather than slowing or accelerating. Duckweed (Lemna minor) frond counts, a common classroom system, typically double every 2–4 days under good light and nutrients; bacterial or yeast optical-density time series behave the same way during log phase. A classic field case is the ring-necked pheasants introduced to Washington's Protection Island in 1937: a founding group of 8 birds, released onto an island with no predators and abundant food, grew to roughly 1,900 within about five years, tracking a near-exponential curve before the population outstripped its food supply. The reason doubling time stays constant regardless of N is visible directly in the math: differentiating N_t = N_0 e^(rt) gives dN/dt = rN, so the proportional growth rate r is the same whether N is 20 or 20,000 — only the absolute number of new individuals added per day scales up.

lessons.workedExample: A student counts duckweed fronds every day: N_0 = 20 on day 0, rising to 41, 79, 162, and 331 by day 4. Plotting ln(N) against day gives points at 3.00, 3.71, 4.37, 5.09, 5.80 — a nearly straight line. Linear regression yields a slope of about 0.70/day, so r ≈ 0.70, giving a doubling time of ln(2)/0.70 ≈ 0.99 days, matching the observed near-daily doubling. Projecting forward with N_t = 20e^(0.70t) predicts about 1,334 fronds by day 6 — useful for planning when the culture will overcrowd its tray, and a check on whether the population is still in unconstrained exponential phase or has started to bend toward a ceiling.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes exponential/geometric growth to see whether a student can move from a table of counts to a mechanistic parameter, not just a trend line. A weak answer says 'the population went up fast' or fits a generic best-fit curve in spreadsheet software without knowing what it means. A strong answer log-transforms the counts, explains that a straight line on that transformed plot is the signature of constant per-capita growth, reports r (or λ) with units, and states the doubling time — then correctly flags when the assumption breaks (data curving off the line signals resource limitation, i.e., the population is leaving exponential phase for logistic phase).

questions.prompt: A population has an intrinsic growth rate r = 0.35 per day. Approximately how long does it take to double?

options.text: About 0.35 days
About 2 days
About 3.5 days
It cannot double under exponential growth

explanations.a: This confuses r itself with the doubling time; r is a rate, not a duration.
explanations.b: Correct — doubling time is ln(2)/r = 0.693/0.35 ≈ 1.98 days, roughly 2 days.
explanations.c: This overshoots; ln(2) ≈ 0.693, not 1, so the doubling time is a bit under 2 days, not 3.5.
explanations.d: Exponential growth by definition doubles repeatedly; doubling time is one of its defining properties.

questions.prompt: An annual plant population has a finite rate of increase λ = 1.2 per generation. What is the equivalent continuous-time intrinsic rate r?

explanations.a: λ and r are related but not numerically equal; this just restates λ.
explanations.b: λ − 1 is not the correct conversion; the relationship is logarithmic, not linear.
explanations.c: Correct — since λ = e^r, r = ln(λ) = ln(1.2) ≈ 0.182 per generation.
explanations.d: This inverts the relationship; e^(1.2) would convert an r of 1.2 back into a λ, not the other way around.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for estimating r from a raw series of population counts over time.

items.text: Record population size (N) at each sampling time
Take the natural log of each N value
Plot ln(N) against time and check for a straight-line pattern
Fit a regression line and read off its slope
Report the slope as the estimate of r

questions.explanation: You must first have raw counts, log-transform them, visually confirm linearity (evidence of constant per-capita growth), then fit a regression whose slope is the numerical estimate of r.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its meaning in growth models.

right.text: Intrinsic (continuous, per-capita) growth rate
Finite rate of increase per discrete generation
ln(2)/r, time for N to double
Estimate of r from real count data

questions.explanation: r is the continuous per-capita rate underlying dN/dt = rN; λ is its discrete-generation counterpart in N_t+1 = λN_t; doubling time follows directly from r; and the slope of ln(N) vs. time is how r is actually estimated from data.

lessons.label: Logistic Growth and Carrying Capacity

sections.heading: Adding a ceiling: dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K)
sections.body: Exponential growth assumes resources never run out; the logistic model relaxes that by multiplying the exponential term by (1 − N/K), where K is the carrying capacity — the population size an environment can sustain indefinitely. When N is small relative to K, (1 − N/K) is close to 1 and growth looks nearly exponential; as N approaches K, the term shrinks toward zero and growth stalls. The result is the classic S-shaped (sigmoid) curve: slow start, accelerating middle, decelerating approach to a plateau at K. Differentiating shows that the absolute growth rate dN/dt is maximized exactly at N = K/2 — the population's fastest growth, in individuals added per unit time, happens at the curve's inflection point, halfway to capacity, not at the top.

sections.heading: From theory to data: Gause and Pearl & Reed
sections.body: Georgyi Gause's 1934 laboratory cultures of the ciliate Paramecium, grown in fixed daily rations of bacteria in test tubes, produced textbook logistic curves — population size climbed, then leveled off near a stable density once food renewal capped further growth, giving early quantitative support for the model. A more consequential — and more cautionary — application came from Raymond Pearl and Lowell Reed, who in 1920 fit a logistic curve to U.S. census data from 1790–1910 and projected an upper asymptote around 197 million people, approached only asymptotically and never exactly reached. The U.S. population blew past 197 million by 1967, decades ahead of schedule, because K itself was never fixed: agricultural technology, energy use, trade, and immigration kept raising the ceiling the model assumed was constant.

sections.heading: Why the logistic model is a starting point, not the answer
sections.body: Three standard criticisms follow directly from the Pearl & Reed failure. First, time lags: reproduction and maturation take time, so populations often overshoot K before feedback catches up, producing oscillations or crashes rather than a smooth approach — a modification G. Evelyn Hutchinson formalized with a time-delay term. Second, K is rarely fixed: it moves with climate, technology, competitors, and resource pulses, so treating it as a constant misses real ecological and social change. Third, most field populations don't sit calmly at a stable K at all; predation, disease, weather, and dispersal keep them below or oscillating around it far more often than textbook S-curves suggest. Despite this, the K/2 maximum-growth result underlies real management practice: fisheries and wildlife managers set maximum sustainable yield targets by trying to hold harvested populations near K/2, where surplus production is highest.

lessons.workedExample: A wildlife manager models a deer population with r = 0.3/year and K = 1,000 in a reserve. Using dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), growth is fastest at N = 500 (K/2): dN/dt = 0.3 × 500 × (1 − 0.5) = 75 deer/year, versus only dN/dt = 0.3 × 900 × 0.1 = 27 deer/year near N = 900. If the goal is maximum sustainable harvest, the manager should keep the herd near 500, not let it grow toward 1,000 — harvesting too conservatively (letting N approach K) actually shrinks the sustainable annual surplus, the same logic fisheries biologists use to set maximum-sustainable-yield quotas.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on logistic growth because the model's most quoted number — carrying capacity — is also its most fragile assumption, and testing whether a student knows that is a fast way to separate memorized formula from real understanding. A weak answer states dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K) and stops. A strong answer explains why growth peaks at K/2 rather than at K, can name a real case (Gause's Paramecium fitting the curve, Pearl & Reed's population projection missing it) and articulate specifically why the miss happened — K was assumed static when it wasn't — rather than vaguely saying 'the model was wrong.'

questions.prompt: Under the logistic model dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), at what population size is the absolute growth rate (individuals added per unit time) maximized?

options.text: N = K
N = K/2
N = 2K

explanations.a: At N = K, (1 − N/K) = 0, so growth rate is zero, not maximal — this is the plateau, not the peak.
explanations.b: Correct — differentiating dN/dt with respect to N and setting the result to zero shows the maximum occurs at N = K/2, the curve's inflection point.
explanations.c: At N near 0, the population is too small in absolute terms for growth to be at its numerical maximum, even though the per-capita rate is highest there.
explanations.d: N cannot exceed K under this model's assumptions in a meaningful sustained way, and growth rate would be negative there regardless.

questions.prompt: Pearl and Reed's 1920 logistic projection of the U.S. population badly underestimated actual growth by the late 1960s. What was the main reason?

options.text: They used the wrong value of r
Carrying capacity K was assumed fixed but actually rose with technology, agriculture, and immigration
The U.S. population actually followed exponential, not logistic, growth the whole time
Census data before 1910 was fabricated

explanations.a: The fitted r was not the core problem; the deeper flaw was the assumption baked into K, not the growth-rate parameter.
explanations.b: Correct — the model treated K as a fixed asymptote (~197 million), but real carrying capacity kept rising as technology and resource use expanded, so actual population overtook the projected ceiling decades early.
explanations.c: The U.S. population did slow relative to pure exponential growth at times; the failure was specifically that the assumed ceiling was too low and static, not that logistic growth was entirely the wrong shape.
explanations.d: There is no basis for this; the projection failure is a well-documented modeling issue, not a data-fabrication issue.

questions.prompt: Order the phases of a logistic growth curve from earliest to latest as N rises from near zero toward K.

items.text: Slow start: N small, growth resembles early exponential phase
Accelerating growth as N increases but is still well below K
Inflection point at N = K/2, maximum absolute growth rate
Decelerating growth as N approaches K
Plateau near K, growth rate approaches zero

questions.explanation: The logistic curve moves from a slow, near-exponential start, through accelerating then peak growth at the K/2 inflection point, into decelerating growth, and finally levels off near the carrying capacity.

questions.prompt: Match each standard criticism of the logistic model to its description.

right.text: Reproductive/maturation delays cause overshoot and oscillation instead of smooth leveling
Carrying capacity shifts with climate, technology, or resource pulses rather than staying constant
Predation, disease, and weather usually keep real populations below or fluctuating around K, not resting on it

questions.explanation: Time lags produce overshoot/oscillation, a moving K undermines the fixed-asymptote assumption (as in the Pearl & Reed case), and most field populations are held below or bounced around K by outside forces rather than resting stably on it.

lessons.label: Density Dependence vs Density Independence

sections.heading: Two very different ways populations get pushed around
sections.body: Density-dependent factors change their impact per individual as population density changes — usually acting as brakes that intensify as N rises. Intraspecific competition for food or breeding sites, crowding stress that suppresses reproduction, disease that spreads faster when contact rates are higher, and territoriality that caps the number of breeding spots all get proportionally worse as density increases, pulling per-capita growth back down toward zero. Density-independent factors, by contrast, kill or displace a roughly fixed proportion of the population regardless of how crowded it is: a hard freeze, a wildfire, or a flood removes about the same fraction of a sparse population as a dense one. Both matter, but they predict different things — density dependence can, in principle, stabilize a population near an equilibrium, while density-independent shocks just move N around unpredictably.

sections.heading: The Allee effect: when low density is also dangerous
sections.body: Named for Warder Clyde Allee, whose 1930s studies documented benefits of aggregation in animals, the Allee effect describes populations whose per-capita growth rate actually declines at low density instead of rising, because sparse individuals struggle to find mates, lose the benefits of group defense or cooperative foraging, or suffer more inbreeding. A component Allee effect affects one fitness trait (e.g., mating success); a demographic Allee effect drags overall growth rate negative below a critical threshold, creating an extinction vortex that density-dependent models alone don't predict.

sections.heading: The Nicholson vs. Andrewartha and Birch dispute — and key-factor analysis as referee
sections.body: A.J. Nicholson argued from the 1930s through the 1950s, based on lab experiments with sheep blowflies (Lucilia cuprina), that populations are regulated — held near a long-term equilibrium — by density-dependent competition, and that this negative feedback was essentially necessary for persistence. H.G. Andrewartha and L.C. Birch countered in their 1954 book The Distribution and Abundance of Animals, using field data on Australian thrips (Thrips imaginis) showing abundance tracking weather fluctuations far more tightly than any density-dependent signal; they argued populations are often merely limited by resources and climate, rarely staying near an equilibrium long enough for regulation to be the dominant story. The dispute wasn't fully resolved by argument — it pushed ecologists toward key-factor analysis, developed by R.F. Morris (1959) and refined by G.C. Varley and G.R. Gradwell (1960) on multi-year life-table data for pests like the winter moth, which statistically identifies which single mortality factor's year-to-year variation (its k-value) best explains total generation-to-generation mortality, letting data rather than theory decide which forces dominate a given system.

lessons.workedExample: A herd of 200 elk in a valley experiences two pressures in the same winter: forage competition (density-dependent) reduces calf survival more sharply as herd size grows — at 200 elk, 70% of calves survive; if the herd were 400, competition for browse might drop that to 40%. Separately, an unusually severe ice storm (density-independent) kills roughly 15% of all elk that winter regardless of whether the herd was 200 or 400. A researcher distinguishing these needs multi-year data: the competition effect should track herd size across years, while the ice-storm effect should track winter severity and hit small and large herds proportionally the same — exactly the kind of pattern key-factor analysis is built to tease apart from a life-table time series.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about density dependence versus independence to test whether a student can classify a real pressure on their study population correctly, because the classification changes what a manager should do about it — density-dependent pressures respond to reducing crowding, density-independent ones don't. A weak answer lists definitions with no example. A strong answer picks a specific pressure in their own project, explains whether its impact per individual should scale with density or not, and — if pushed — can describe how a multi-year life-table comparison (the logic behind key-factor analysis) would distinguish the two rather than just asserting one.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a density-INDEPENDENT source of mortality?

options.text: A wildfire that burns through a habitat regardless of population size
Competition for nesting territories that intensifies as more birds crowd in
A disease that spreads faster because more individuals are in close contact
Starvation from overgrazing as a herd grows too large for its range

explanations.a: Correct — a wildfire removes roughly the same proportion of a population whether it is sparse or dense, the hallmark of a density-independent factor.
explanations.b: Territoriality intensifies with crowding, so its impact scales with density — this is density-dependent.
explanations.c: Disease transmission scaling with contact rate is a textbook density-dependent mechanism.
explanations.d: Overgrazing worsens as herd size grows relative to the range, making this density-dependent, not independent.

questions.prompt: In an Allee effect, what happens to per-capita growth rate at low population density?

options.text: It rises, since there is less competition for resources
It falls, because mate-finding, group defense, or cooperative foraging break down
It stays constant regardless of density
It becomes undefined below a certain N

explanations.a: This is the standard density-dependent expectation (less competition helps at low N) — the Allee effect is specifically the exception to that pattern.
explanations.b: Correct — an Allee effect means per-capita growth declines at low density because sparse individuals struggle to find mates or lose cooperative benefits, the opposite of the usual density-dependent expectation.
explanations.c: The whole point of the Allee effect is that growth rate is NOT constant at low density — it drops.
explanations.d: Growth rate remains a defined (negative) quantity below the Allee threshold; it does not become mathematically undefined.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or research group to their position or contribution in the population-regulation debate.

right.text: Argued density-dependent competition regulates populations, based on blowfly experiments
Argued weather (density-independent) often dominates, based on Australian thrips field data
Developed key-factor analysis to identify which mortality factor drives generation-to-generation change

questions.explanation: Nicholson's blowfly work supported density-dependent regulation; Andrewartha and Birch's thrips data supported a bigger role for weather; Varley and Gradwell's key-factor analysis gave ecologists a statistical tool to settle which factor matters most in a given case.

questions.prompt: What did Andrewartha and Birch's study of Thrips imaginis in South Australia mainly show?

options.text: Thrips abundance tracked weather conditions more closely than any density-dependent signal
Thrips populations were perfectly regulated by intraspecific competition
Thrips showed a strong Allee effect at low density
Thrips abundance was unrelated to any environmental variable

explanations.a: Correct — their field data showed thrips abundance fluctuating in step with weather, which they used to argue density-independent factors were often the dominant driver, not tight density-dependent regulation.
explanations.b: This is the opposite of their conclusion; they argued against strong, consistent density-dependent regulation in this system.
explanations.c: Their thrips study was about weather-driven abundance, not about mate-finding or cooperative breakdown at low density.
explanations.d: Their entire point was that abundance WAS strongly related to an environmental variable — weather — just not to density.

lessons.label: Life Tables and Survivorship Curves

sections.heading: Building a cohort life table
sections.body: A life table tracks a group of same-age individuals (a cohort) through life, recording, for each age interval x: l_x, the proportion of the original cohort still alive at the start of age x (l_0 = 1.0 by definition); d_x, the number dying during that interval; q_x = d_x divided by the number alive at the start of the interval, the age-specific mortality rate; and e_x, life expectancy — the average number of further age-intervals an individual alive at age x can expect to live. A cohort (dynamic) life table follows one real cohort from birth to the last death, which is accurate but slow — it can take a species' full lifespan to collect. A static (time-specific) life table instead samples the age distribution of a whole population at one moment and assumes each age class reflects what a single cohort would experience over time — fast to build, but only valid if the population's birth and death rates have been roughly stable across the years those age classes were born into.

sections.heading: A classic dataset: Deevey's Dall sheep
sections.body: Edward Deevey's influential 1947 paper compiled life tables for several species to make survivorship curves comparable, most famously using Adolph Murie's data on Dall mountain sheep (Ovis dalli) from Mount McKinley (Denali), aged from horn growth rings on several hundred skulls found in the field. The pattern showed relatively low mortality through most of adulthood, with a smaller mortality bump in the first year (predation and harsh winters on lambs) and a sharp spike in old age as animals became too weak to survive winter — a mixed but broadly Type I-leaning shape that made the dataset a standard classroom example ever since.

sections.heading: Plotting survivorship: Type I, II, and III
sections.body: Survivorship curves plot log10(l_x) against age, because a log scale turns a constant mortality rate into a straight line and makes differing patterns visually distinct. Type I curves stay high through most of the lifespan and drop steeply only near maximum age — heavy investment in few offspring with strong parental care, typical of large mammals and humans in low-mortality settings. Type II curves are roughly straight lines on the log plot, meaning a constant mortality risk at every age — seen in many birds and some rodents. Type III curves crash almost immediately, with the small fraction that survives early life then facing much lower risk — the pattern for oysters, most fish, and most plants, which produce enormous numbers of offspring but invest nothing per individual. Few species are purebred examples: many fish and amphibians are Type III as larvae and shift toward Type I or II as surviving adults, so a single label often describes only part of a life cycle.

lessons.workedExample: A simplified life table modeled on the Dall sheep pattern starts a cohort of 1,000 lambs: 801 survive to age 1 (d_0 = 199, q_0 ≈ 0.20, reflecting lamb mortality), then losses stay low through midlife — roughly 734 alive at age 5, 670 at age 8 — before mortality accelerates sharply, dropping to about 120 by age 12 as animals reach old age. Plotting log10(l_x): log10(1.0) = 0 at birth, log10(0.801) ≈ −0.10 at age 1, only easing to log10(0.12) ≈ −0.92 by age 12 — a curve that stays fairly flat in the log domain through the middle years, then bends sharply downward at the end, the visual signature Deevey used to classify this dataset as closer to Type I than Type II or III.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about life tables because building one forces a student to be explicit about a cohort's fate rather than reporting a vague impression of 'high mortality.' A weak answer describes a survivorship curve shape without having computed l_x, q_x, or e_x from actual counts, or builds a static table from a single snapshot without acknowledging the assumption that birth/death rates were stable across cohorts. A strong answer shows the arithmetic (deaths divided by starting number, per interval), states which curve type the pattern approximates and why, and — if the data is a static rather than cohort table — flags that limitation unprompted.

questions.prompt: In a life table, if 500 individuals are alive at the start of age interval x and 100 of them die during that interval, what is q_x?

explanations.a: 100 is d_x, the raw number of deaths, not the mortality rate q_x.
explanations.b: Correct — q_x = d_x / (number alive at start of interval) = 100/500 = 0.2, a 20% mortality rate for that interval.
explanations.c: 400 is the number of survivors at the end of the interval, not the mortality rate.
explanations.d: This inverts the ratio (500/100); q_x must be a proportion between 0 and 1.

questions.prompt: What key assumption does a static (time-specific) life table make that a cohort (dynamic) life table does not need to make?

options.text: That the species reproduces only once
That birth and death rates have been roughly stable across the years the sampled age classes were born into
That the population has no predators
That all individuals in the population are the same age

explanations.a: Semelparity vs. iteroparity is a separate life-history property, unrelated to the cohort/static distinction.
explanations.b: Correct — a static table infers a cohort's fate from a single snapshot of a population's current age structure, which only works if conditions (and thus birth/death rates) were roughly constant across the years represented by that age structure.
explanations.c: Predator presence is not the distinguishing assumption; both table types can be built for populations with predators.
explanations.d: A static table specifically requires a range of ages present at once, the opposite of everyone being the same age.

questions.prompt: Match each survivorship curve type to its description.

right.text: High survival through most of life, steep drop only near maximum age (e.g., large mammals with parental care)
Roughly constant mortality risk at every age, a straight line on a log survivorship plot (e.g., many birds)
Massive early mortality, low risk for the few survivors thereafter (e.g., oysters, most fish and plants)

questions.explanation: Type I curves stay high then crash late; Type II curves are constant-risk straight lines on a log plot; Type III curves crash early, leaving few survivors who then face low ongoing risk.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for constructing a cohort life table from raw age-at-death data.

items.text: Determine the age at death for every individual in the cohort
Tally the number of deaths (d_x) in each age interval
Compute the number surviving to the start of each interval (l_x, as a proportion of the starting cohort)
Compute the mortality rate for each interval (q_x = d_x / number alive at interval start)
Plot log10(l_x) against age to classify the survivorship curve

questions.explanation: You need raw ages at death first, then tally deaths per interval, derive the running survivorship proportion, compute the interval mortality rate from those two, and only then plot the log-transformed survivorship curve to classify its type.

lessons.label: Age Structure and Population Projection

sections.heading: Age pyramids as a forecast, not just a snapshot
sections.body: An age-structure pyramid stacks the number (or percentage) of individuals in each age class, usually split by sex for human populations. An expanding pyramid has a broad base of young individuals tapering to a narrow top — Niger, with a very young age structure, is a textbook modern example — and predicts continued growth even if birth rates fell today, because so many individuals are still entering reproductive age. A stable pyramid has roughly even bars across age classes, predicting a population near replacement. A contracting pyramid is top-heavy, narrow at the base — Japan and Italy are current examples — and predicts population decline as a shrinking cohort of young people replaces a larger cohort of older ones. The shape alone, independent of total population size, tells you the near-term trajectory.

sections.heading: Fecundity schedules and the net reproductive rate
sections.body: Pairing survivorship (l_x) with a fecundity schedule (m_x, the average number of offspring produced by an individual at age x) yields the net reproductive rate, R0 = Σ (l_x · m_x) — the expected number of offspring an individual produces over its entire lifetime, accounting for the chance of surviving to each reproductive age. R0 > 1 means each generation is larger than the last (population growing); R0 = 1 means each generation exactly replaces itself; R0 < 1 means decline. Generation time, T, is the mean age at which mothers give birth, and Lotka's classic approximation links R0 and T to the continuous growth rate: r ≈ ln(R0)/T. This means two populations can have identical R0 but very different growth rates in real time if their generation times differ — the same lifetime output compressed into a short generation compounds faster than the same output spread across a long one.

sections.heading: The Leslie matrix: structure predicts trajectory, not just total N
sections.body: P.H. Leslie's 1945 matrix model formalizes age-structured projection: an age-structured population is written as a vector n(t), and a matrix L — with age-specific fecundities across the top row and age-specific survival probabilities on the subdiagonal — projects it forward one time step via n(t+1) = L·n(t). Repeated multiplication drives the population toward a stable age distribution, in which every age class grows at the same rate: the matrix's dominant eigenvalue, which equals λ. The practical payoff is that total population size alone doesn't determine trajectory — two populations with identical N but different age structures behave differently. This produces demographic momentum: a population weighted toward reproductive-age individuals keeps growing for years or decades even after fertility instantly drops to replacement level, purely because so many people are still moving through their childbearing years — a major reason population projections for many developing countries kept rising well after fertility rates fell.

lessons.workedExample: A small population is tracked in three age classes with l_x (survival to that age) and m_x (offspring per individual at that age): age 0, l_0 = 1.0, m_0 = 0; age 1, l_1 = 0.5, m_1 = 2.0; age 2, l_2 = 0.2, m_2 = 3.0. R0 = Σ l_x m_x = (1.0×0) + (0.5×2.0) + (0.2×3.0) = 0 + 1.0 + 0.6 = 1.6, meaning each individual replaces itself with 1.6 offspring on average — the population is growing.
