Generation time T ≈ Σ(x·l_x·m_x)/R0 = [(1×1.0) + (2×0.6)]/1.6 = 2.2/1.6 ≈ 1.375. Applying r ≈ ln(R0)/T = ln(1.6)/1.375 ≈ 0.47/1.375 ≈ 0.34 gives an estimated continuous growth rate — all derived from just two per-age columns of data.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes age structure and R0 because it is the cleanest way to test whether a student understands that population trajectory depends on more than a single number N. A weak answer reports total population size and a growth rate with no mention of age composition. A strong answer explains why two populations of equal size can have opposite trajectories based on pyramid shape, correctly computes R0 from l_x and m_x, and can explain demographic momentum — why a population can keep growing for a generation even after birth rates fall to replacement, because of who is already alive and at what age.

questions.prompt: A population has R0 = 1.6. What does this mean?

options.text: The population grew by 1.6% last year
Each individual, on average, produces 1.6 offspring over its lifetime, so the population is growing
The population's carrying capacity is 1.6 times its current size
1.6 generations pass per calendar year

explanations.a: R0 is a per-generation lifetime reproductive output, not an annual percentage growth rate.
explanations.b: Correct — R0 = Σ l_x m_x is the expected lifetime number of offspring per individual; a value above 1 means each generation is larger than the last.
explanations.c: R0 says nothing directly about carrying capacity; it is a demographic replacement statistic, not a resource-ceiling estimate.
explanations.d: R0 is not a measure of generation frequency per year; that would relate to generation time T, a separate quantity.

questions.prompt: Two countries have identical current total populations but different age pyramids: Country A is expanding (broad young base), Country B is contracting (top-heavy). What does this predict?

options.text: Both will follow identical population trajectories since total N is the same
Country A will likely keep growing while Country B will likely decline, even before comparing birth rates
Country B will grow faster because it has more older, established individuals
Age structure has no predictive value beyond current total population

explanations.a: This is exactly the misconception age-structure analysis corrects — identical N with different structures predicts different futures.
explanations.b: Correct — a young, broad-based pyramid predicts continued growth (more individuals entering reproductive age), while a top-heavy pyramid predicts decline, independent of matching total population sizes.
explanations.c: More older individuals near or past reproductive age predicts slower growth or decline, not faster growth.
explanations.d: Age structure is specifically valuable because it predicts trajectory beyond what total N alone can tell you.

questions.prompt: Match each age-pyramid shape to its demographic prediction.

right.text: Continued population growth as young cohorts reach reproductive age
Population size holding near replacement level
Population decline as a smaller young cohort replaces a larger older one

questions.explanation: A broad-based pyramid predicts growth, an even pyramid predicts stability, and a top-heavy pyramid predicts decline — the shape alone forecasts the trend independent of current total size.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of projecting a population forward one time step using a Leslie matrix.

items.text: Build the age-structured population vector n(t), listing individuals in each age class
Build the Leslie matrix L, with age-specific fecundities in the top row and survival probabilities on the subdiagonal
Multiply n(t) by L to obtain n(t+1)
Repeat the multiplication over successive time steps
Observe the population converge toward a stable age distribution growing at rate λ

questions.explanation: Projection requires the current age-structured vector and the matrix of fecundities/survival probabilities, then repeated matrix multiplication, which drives the population toward the stable age distribution defined by the matrix's dominant eigenvalue λ.

lessons.label: Life History Strategies

sections.heading: r-selection and K-selection
sections.body: Robert MacArthur and E.O. Wilson introduced r- and K-selection in their 1967 book The Theory of Island Biogeography, later extended by Eric Pianka in 1970: the idea that the two parameters of the logistic equation, r and K, describe not just growth curves but selective regimes. In unstable, disturbed, or uncrowded environments, selection favors r-selected traits — early maturity, many small offspring, little parental investment, rapid population growth — think dandelions, weedy annuals, and most insects. In stable, crowded environments near carrying capacity, selection favors K-selected traits — slow maturity, few large offspring, heavy parental investment, strong competitive ability — think elephants, oaks, and albatross. A closely related axis is semelparity versus iteroparity: semelparous species reproduce once and die (Pacific salmon, the century plant Agave, periodical cicadas, most annual plants), while iteroparous species reproduce repeatedly across a lifespan (most mammals, birds, and perennial plants).

sections.heading: The offspring size-number tradeoff and Grime's CSR triangle
sections.body: Because reproductive investment is finite, organisms face an offspring size-number tradeoff, formalized by Smith and Fretwell in 1974: a fixed reproductive budget can fund many small offspring (each with higher individual mortality risk but more attempts) or few large offspring (each with better survival odds but fewer chances). Philip Grime extended this thinking to plants in 1977 with the CSR triangle, classifying species along two independent axes — stress and disturbance — into three primary strategies: Competitors (C) thrive under low stress and low disturbance through fast growth and aggressive resource capture (e.g., stinging nettle); Stress-tolerators (S) persist under high stress with slow growth and resource conservation (e.g., alpine plants, lichens); and Ruderals (R) exploit high-disturbance, low-stress conditions with rapid life cycles and heavy seed output (e.g., weeds colonizing bare, disturbed ground).

sections.heading: Why r/K is now considered an oversimplification
sections.body: Despite its staying power in textbooks, r/K selection has largely fallen out of favor among working ecologists, because it forces life-history variation onto a single axis when empirical tests kept finding that real traits don't cluster as predicted — many species combine 'r' traits with 'K' traits in ways the framework can't accommodate. The dominant replacement is the fast-slow life-history continuum, built directly from demographic trade-off data rather than from proximity to carrying capacity: work by Andrew Read and Paul Harvey (1989) and Daniel Promislow and Paul Harvey's widely cited 1990 paper 'Living Fast and Dying Young' showed mammal life histories line up along a single empirical axis from fast (early maturity, short lifespan, high fecundity, high mortality — shrews, mice) to slow (late maturity, long lifespan, low fecundity — elephants, whales), later extended across thousands of species by Jon Bielby and colleagues in 2007. Stephen Stearns' 1992 book The Evolution of Life Histories helped formalize the underlying trade-off logic — survival traded against reproduction — that now grounds this approach, a clear case of a simple, intuitive textbook dichotomy being superseded by data-driven demographic analysis.

lessons.workedExample: Two small mammals illustrate why fast-slow fits better than r/K alone: a meadow vole matures at about 6 weeks, can produce 5+ litters a year, and rarely lives past 12 months — squarely 'fast.' A naked mole rat matures around 1-2 years, produces far fewer pups per litter, but can live 30 years in captivity — squarely 'slow' — yet it also lives in large, crowded, resource-limited underground colonies, an environment r/K theory would predict favors K-selected traits like large, well-provisioned offspring, which mole rats don't produce. Placing both species on the fast-slow continuum (using actual trade-off data: age at maturity, litter size, and mortality rate) explains the pattern without needing the vole's habitat to be 'unstable' or the mole rat's to be 'stable near K.'
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge raises r/K selection specifically to see whether a student is repeating a simplified textbook dichotomy or actually knows its limits, because this is one of the clearest cases in ecology where the popular version and the current scientific consensus have diverged. A weak answer defines r- and K-selected species and stops there as if the theory were settled. A strong answer can do that AND explain why ecologists mostly moved to the fast-slow life-history continuum — grounded in real demographic trade-offs (age at maturity, fecundity, mortality) rather than a species' proximity to carrying capacity — and can name the shift as evidence they've engaged with primary literature, not just a syllabus summary.

questions.prompt: Which pair of traits is most characteristic of a K-selected species under the MacArthur and Wilson framework?

options.text: Early maturity and many small offspring with little parental care
Slow maturity, few large offspring, and heavy parental investment
A single reproductive event followed by death
Rapid colonization of disturbed, uncrowded habitat

explanations.a: This describes r-selected traits, favored in unstable or uncrowded environments, not K-selected ones.
explanations.b: Correct — K-selected traits fit stable, crowded environments near carrying capacity: slow maturity, few well-provisioned offspring, strong parental investment and competitive ability.
explanations.c: Semelparity (one reproductive bout then death) is a separate axis from r/K and can occur in either r- or K-leaning species.
explanations.d: Rapid colonization of disturbed habitat is the r-selected pattern, the opposite of K-selection.

questions.prompt: What did Promislow and Harvey's 1990 'Living Fast and Dying Young' analysis mainly demonstrate?

options.text: That r/K selection perfectly predicts every mammal's life history
That mammal life histories line up along a single empirical fast-to-slow demographic axis, based on actual trade-off data
That carrying capacity is the main driver of offspring size in mammals
That semelparity is more common than iteroparity in mammals

explanations.a: Their work is part of what challenged rather than confirmed r/K as a full predictive framework.
explanations.b: Correct — their analysis, building on Read and Harvey (1989), showed mammal life histories align along a fast-slow continuum grounded in maturity age, fecundity, and mortality data, largely superseding r/K as the working model.
explanations.c: Their framework is built on demographic trade-offs, not on proximity to a carrying capacity value.
explanations.d: Most mammals are iteroparous, and this was not the focus or finding of their analysis.

questions.prompt: Match each Grime CSR strategy to its defining condition and example.

right.text: Low stress, low disturbance; fast growth and aggressive resource capture (e.g., stinging nettle)
High stress, low disturbance; slow growth and resource conservation (e.g., alpine plants, lichens)
Low stress, high disturbance; rapid life cycle and heavy seed output (e.g., weeds on bare ground)

questions.explanation: Grime's triangle sorts plant strategies by stress and disturbance level: competitors dominate benign, stable conditions; stress-tolerators persist under chronic stress; ruderals exploit disturbed but otherwise favorable conditions.

questions.prompt: Order these life-history framework developments chronologically, earliest to most recent.

items.text: MacArthur and Wilson introduce r- and K-selection (Theory of Island Biogeography)
Pianka extends r/K selection theory
Smith and Fretwell formalize the offspring size-number tradeoff
Grime proposes the CSR triangle for plant strategies
Promislow and Harvey show mammal life histories fit a fast-slow continuum

questions.explanation: r/K selection (1967) came first, was extended by Pianka (1970), followed by the Smith-Fretwell offspring tradeoff model (1974), Grime's CSR triangle (1977), and finally the fast-slow continuum work of Promislow and Harvey (1990), which came to supersede r/K as the dominant framework.

units.label: Species Interactions, Food Webs, and Energy Flow

lessons.label: Competition and Coexistence

sections.heading: Gause and the exclusion principle
sections.body: In 1934 the Russian ecologist Georgy Gause grew two species of the ciliate Paramecium, P. caudatum and P. aurelia, on a fixed bacterial food supply. Grown alone, each species reached a stable population. Grown together in the same tube, P. aurelia reproduced faster and drove P. caudatum to local extinction within about three weeks. From this Gause proposed the competitive exclusion principle: two species with identical resource requirements cannot coexist indefinitely in the same niche, because even a small growth-rate advantage compounds until the weaker competitor is eliminated. Tellingly, when Gause instead paired P. aurelia with a third species, P. bursaria, the two coexisted — P. bursaria fed on bacteria settled at the bottom of the tube while P. aurelia fed on bacteria suspended in the broth, a spatial split in resource use.

sections.heading: Lotka-Volterra isoclines and four outcomes
sections.body: Alfred Lotka and Vito Volterra formalized competition with paired logistic equations, each species' growth reduced by its own crowding plus the crowding effect of the other (weighted by a competition coefficient, alpha). Plotting each species' zero-growth isocline on the same graph yields four possible outcomes depending on where the isoclines cross relative to each species' own carrying capacity: species 1 always wins, species 2 always wins, unstable coexistence where whichever species starts more numerous wins (founder control), or stable coexistence where each species limits itself more than it limits its rival.

sections.heading: Two escape routes: partitioning and displacement
sections.body: Real communities usually avoid strict exclusion through niche differentiation. Robert MacArthur's 1958 study of five Dendroica warbler species in Maine spruce forests found that although all five ate insects in the same trees, each foraged in a different vertical and structural zone — Cape May warblers at the outer top branches, Bay-breasted lower and closer to the trunk — reducing overlap enough for coexistence. Character displacement pushes divergence further: on natural selection, competing species evolve to differ more where they co-occur than where they live apart. Peter and Rosemary Grant's long-term study of Darwin's finches on Daphne Major documented this directly — when the large-beaked Geospiza magnirostris arrived and a severe drought hit in 2004-2005, medium ground finches (G. fortis) with the largest beaks, which competed most directly with the newcomer for large seeds, died disproportionately, shifting the population's average beak depth measurably smaller within a single generation.

lessons.workedExample: A student sets up two protist cultures, Species A and B, each alone growing to a stable 500 cells/mL. Mixed together on the same bacterial food, Species A climbs to 600 cells/mL while B declines to zero by day 18 — textbook Gause-style exclusion. The student then asks whether A and B could coexist by adding a second food type available only near the surface. If B specializes on the surface resource, resource partitioning could let both persist, the same logic MacArthur found in warblers dividing tree canopy zones instead of dividing food type.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing a competition project is checking whether the student understands that exclusion is not automatic doom but a prediction that depends on whether niches actually overlap. A weak answer says 'the two species compete so one dies out.' A strong answer names the mechanism — identical resource requirements plus a growth-rate or efficiency edge compound over generations — and can point to a specific axis (space, time, diet, foraging height) along which the species in their own project might partition resources, citing something like MacArthur's warblers or the Grants' finches as the template for how real systems dodge Gause's prediction.

questions.prompt: In Gause's Paramecium experiments, what allowed P. aurelia and P. bursaria to coexist when P. aurelia and P. caudatum could not?

options.text: P. bursaria fed at the bottom of the tube while P. aurelia fed in suspension
P. bursaria reproduced too slowly to compete at all
The two species were genetically identical
P. aurelia switched to eating P. bursaria directly

explanations.a: Correct — the spatial split in where each species fed on bacteria meant their realized niches did not fully overlap, avoiding exclusion.
explanations.b: Slow reproduction alone would still lead to exclusion under identical resource use, not coexistence.
explanations.c: Genetic identity is irrelevant here and was not the case; niche separation, not genetics, explains coexistence.
explanations.d: This was a competition experiment for shared bacterial food, not a predator-prey relationship.

questions.prompt: On a Lotka-Volterra competition isocline diagram, which condition produces stable coexistence?

options.text: Each species limits its own growth more than it limits its competitor's
Each species limits its competitor more than it limits itself
The two isoclines are parallel and never cross
One species has zero carrying capacity

explanations.a: Correct — strong intraspecific self-limitation relative to interspecific effects is exactly what produces a stable interior equilibrium where both isoclines cross.
explanations.b: This configuration produces the unstable, founder-control outcome, not stable coexistence.
explanations.c: Parallel non-crossing isoclines mean one species always excludes the other; there is no interior equilibrium.
explanations.d: A zero carrying capacity means that species cannot persist under any condition, not coexistence.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or research team to their contribution to competition theory.

right.text: Formalized competition with paired logistic equations and isoclines
Documented character displacement in Galápagos finch beak depth
Showed warblers partitioning foraging zones within the same trees
Demonstrated competitive exclusion in Paramecium cultures

questions.explanation: Gause ran the Paramecium exclusion experiments, MacArthur documented warbler foraging-zone partitioning, the Grants tracked finch beak-depth character displacement on Daphne Major, and Lotka and Volterra built the mathematical isocline model.

questions.prompt: What triggered the measurable shift toward smaller beak depth in Geospiza fortis on Daphne Major documented by the Grants?

options.text: A 2004-2005 drought combined with new competition from the larger Geospiza magnirostris
A volcanic eruption that destroyed all large seeds permanently
Direct predation by G. magnirostris on G. fortis
Human-introduced pesticides affecting beak development

explanations.a: Correct — drought reduced seed availability while the arrival of the large-beaked G. magnirostris intensified competition for large seeds, so large-beaked G. fortis individuals died disproportionately.
explanations.b: No volcanic eruption drove this event; it was drought plus a new competitor.
explanations.c: G. magnirostris competed for seeds with G. fortis rather than preying on it directly.
explanations.d: Pesticides were not implicated; the mechanism was resource competition under drought stress.

lessons.label: Predation, Herbivory, and Cycles

sections.heading: Coupled oscillations and the quarter-period lag
sections.body: The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model links two populations: prey grow exponentially minus losses to predation, predators grow from consumed prey minus a constant death rate. Solved together, the pair does not settle to equilibrium but cycles — and the predator peak consistently lags the prey peak by about a quarter of the cycle's period, because predators keep multiplying on abundant prey even after prey have started declining, until predator numbers finally overtake the depleted prey and crash. This quarter-period lag is the model's signature fingerprint, and hunting for it in real population data is how ecologists test whether a cycle looks predator-driven.

sections.heading: The lynx-hare cycle and the Kluane experiments
sections.body: The best-known real-world case is the snowshoe hare and Canada lynx, whose roughly 9-to-10-year cycle is documented in Hudson's Bay Company fur-trapping ledgers stretching back to the early 1800s. For decades ecologists debated whether the cycle was driven by predation, by food shortage (hares overbrowsing willow and stunting their own food supply), or both. Charles Krebs, Rudy Boutin, and colleagues resolved much of this with a large factorial field experiment at Kluane Lake, Yukon, in the 1980s-90s: they added supplemental food, excluded predators with electric fencing, and did both together across replicated plots. Predator exclusion alone roughly doubled hare density and food addition alone roughly tripled it; the two combined raised it about elevenfold — far more than an additive effect — showing predation and food limitation interact rather than acting independently.

sections.heading: Functional responses and spatial refuges
sections.body: C.S. Holling's 1959 work on small mammals eating pine sawfly cocoons described three functional-response shapes: Type I, consumption rising linearly with prey density (typical of filter feeders); Type II, consumption decelerating and saturating because handling time limits each predator (the most common pattern, and destabilizing at low prey density since predators can't respond fast enough); and Type III, a sigmoid curve where predators switch to or learn a prey type only once it's common, which can stabilize prey at low densities. Carl Huffaker's 1958 orange-mite experiments showed a second stabilizing ingredient: on a simple flat array of oranges, the predatory mite Typhlodromus always found and exterminated its prey, crashing the whole system. Only when Huffaker added mazes of partial barriers and distant patches — giving prey mites scattered refuges and dispersal routes the predator couldn't track as fast — did the two mite populations sustain multiple oscillations instead of collapsing.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher modeling a Type II functional response for a ladybug eating aphids finds attack rate a = 0.5/hour and handling time h = 0.1 hour per aphid. At low aphid density (10/m²), consumption rate is roughly a·N/(1+a·h·N) = 5/(1+0.5) = 3.3 aphids/hour. At high density (200/m²), it saturates near 1/h = 10 aphids/hour regardless of how many more aphids are added — the ladybug simply cannot process prey faster once handling time dominates, which is exactly why Type II responses fail to check fast-growing prey outbreaks at high density.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing a predator-prey project want to know whether the student can distinguish a real driver from a coincidental pattern. A weak answer says 'predators control prey population size.' A strong answer specifies which functional response applies, names the quarter-period lag as the testable Lotka-Volterra signature, and — if citing the lynx-hare cycle — knows the Kluane result that food and predation interact multiplicatively rather than pick one cause and ignore the other. Citing Huffaker's mites to explain why spatial structure matters for persistence signals real command of the mechanism, not just the vocabulary.

questions.prompt: In the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model, how does the predator population peak relate to the prey population peak?

options.text: The predator peak occurs about a quarter-period after the prey peak
The predator and prey peaks always occur simultaneously
The predator peak always occurs before the prey peak
There is no consistent phase relationship between the two peaks

explanations.a: Correct — predators keep increasing on abundant prey even as prey begin declining, so the predator peak trails the prey peak by roughly a quarter cycle.
explanations.b: Simultaneous peaks would mean no time lag in the predator's numerical response, which the model does not produce.
explanations.c: A predator peak before the prey peak would require predators to anticipate prey abundance, which contradicts the model's lagged response.
explanations.d: The quarter-period lag is a consistent, predictable feature of the coupled equations, not a random relationship.

questions.prompt: What was the key finding of the Kluane Lake factorial experiment on snowshoe hares?

options.text: Food addition and predator exclusion combined raised hare density far more than either alone
Predators had no measurable effect on hare density
Food supply alone fully explained the hare cycle
Hare density was unaffected by any experimental manipulation

explanations.a: Correct — food and predator exclusion together raised hare density roughly elevenfold versus about twofold for predator exclusion alone and threefold for food addition alone, showing the two factors interact.
explanations.b: Predator exclusion alone substantially raised hare density, so predators clearly mattered.
explanations.c: Food alone raised density only about threefold, far short of the combined-treatment effect, so food alone does not fully explain the cycle.
explanations.d: Both single treatments and the combined treatment produced large, measurable increases in hare density.

questions.prompt: Match each Holling functional response type to its defining shape.

right.text: Consumption rises linearly with prey density
Consumption decelerates and saturates due to handling time
Sigmoid curve from prey switching or predator learning at low density

questions.explanation: Type I rises linearly (typical of filter feeders), Type II saturates because handling time caps intake per predator, and Type III is sigmoid because predators need prey to become common before switching to or learning that prey type.

questions.prompt: In Huffaker's orange-mite mesocosm experiments, what allowed the predator-prey mite system to sustain multiple oscillations instead of crashing?

options.text: Adding spatial barriers and distant patches that gave prey mites dispersal refuges
Removing all predatory mites from the system entirely
Feeding both mite species an artificial diet instead of oranges
Keeping the oranges in a single simple flat array with no barriers

explanations.a: Correct — mazes of partial barriers and scattered distant patches let prey mites disperse to refuges the predator could not track as quickly, sustaining oscillations across the system.
explanations.b: The experiment kept predators present; removing them would eliminate the predator-prey dynamic being studied.
explanations.c: The mites fed on real oranges, not an artificial diet; the manipulated variable was spatial structure.
explanations.d: The simple flat array without barriers was the original setup that let the predator find and exterminate prey quickly, crashing the system.

lessons.label: Mutualism, Parasitism, and Symbiosis

sections.heading: Mutualisms that structure whole ecosystems
sections.body: Mutualism is a plus-plus interaction, and several forms of it underwrite entire terrestrial food webs. Roughly 80-90% of land plant species form mycorrhizal partnerships, fungal networks that thread through roots and soil, trading phosphorus and water the fungus scavenges for sugars the plant photosynthesizes; arbuscular mycorrhizae, found in about 70% of plant species, penetrate root cells directly, while ectomycorrhizae wrap around roots without entering them, dominant in temperate forest trees like oaks and pines. Pollination and seed dispersal add two more mutualist economies — a bee gets nectar, a plant gets pollen moved; a bird gets fruit pulp, a plant gets its seed carried away from parent-plant competition and pathogens. Cleaning symbioses work the same plus-plus logic in reverse: at a cleaning station, a cleaner wrasse (Labroides dimidiatus) removes parasites from a client fish's skin and gills, gaining food while the client gains parasite removal, and both species treat the station as a recognizable, repeatedly visited location.

sections.heading: Why mutualisms are unstable without enforcement
sections.body: Mutualism looks cooperative, but each partner is still an individual selected to maximize its own payoff, which creates room for cheating — taking the benefit while shirking the cost. A legume-rhizobium root nodule can host bacterial strains that take the plant's sugar but fix little or no nitrogen in return. Toby Kiers and colleagues showed in a 2003 Nature paper that soybean plants sanction those cheating rhizobia directly: nodules with underperforming bacteria get less oxygen and fewer resources, stunting the cheater's own reproduction inside that nodule. Nectar-robbing insects that bite through a flower's base to reach nectar without contacting the anthers are the plant-side mirror image. Without sanctions, policing, or repeated-encounter reputation effects like the cleaning-station model, natural selection favors cheats that take the payoff without paying the cost, so persistent mutualisms generally carry some enforcement mechanism.

sections.heading: Host-parasite dynamics: R0 and myxomatosis
sections.body: Parasitism is a plus-minus interaction tracked with R0, the average number of new infections one infected host produces in a fully susceptible population; R0 above 1 means the parasite spreads, below 1 it fades out. The classic evolutionary case is myxomatosis, a poxvirus deliberately released in Australia in 1950 to control invasive European rabbits. The original strain killed over 99% of infected rabbits, but because mosquitoes transmit the virus only from rabbits still alive to be bitten, ultra-lethal strains that killed hosts too fast before transmission were outcompeted by intermediate-virulence strains that kept hosts alive longer. Within about a decade, field surveys by Frank Fenner and Francis Ratcliffe documented both a shift toward those moderate-virulence viral strains (grade III, still lethal but slower) and rising genetic resistance in the rabbit population — a textbook case of virulence and resistance coevolving in opposite, converging directions.

lessons.workedExample: A student sampling oak seedlings finds 92% have visibly colonized root tips consistent with ectomycorrhizal fungi, and wants to test whether the fungus benefits the tree. Growing paired seedlings in sterilized versus fungus-inoculated soil, the inoculated group shows 40% greater root biomass and higher leaf phosphorus after 8 weeks — a controlled demonstration of the mutualism's plus-plus payoff, rather than assuming colonization itself proves benefit.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing mutualism wants proof the student understands it as a balance of costs and benefits between two independent evolutionary interests, not a fuzzy notion of cooperation. A weak answer describes only the benefit each side gets. A strong answer can also explain why the relationship doesn't collapse to cheating — naming an enforcement mechanism like rhizobial sanctions — and, for a parasite project, can define R0 and connect the myxomatosis case's virulence decline to the specific transmission constraint (mosquitoes need a living host) that made lower virulence favored by selection.

questions.prompt: Approximately what fraction of land plant species form mycorrhizal associations?

options.text: About 10%
Roughly 50%
Essentially 100%, with no exceptions

explanations.a: Correct — roughly 80-90% of land plant species form mycorrhizal partnerships, mostly arbuscular mycorrhizae plus a smaller ectomycorrhizal fraction in many trees.
explanations.b: 10% dramatically understates how widespread mycorrhizal associations are among land plants.
explanations.c: 50% is still well below the documented majority of plant species forming these partnerships.
explanations.d: Some plant families, notably Brassicaceae like mustards and cabbages, do not form mycorrhizae, so it is not universal.

questions.prompt: How do soybean plants sanction cheating rhizobia that fix little or no nitrogen, per Kiers et al.'s 2003 findings?

options.text: By reducing oxygen and resource supply to the underperforming nodule
By actively killing all rhizobia in every nodule
By dropping the entire root system
Plants have no way to detect or respond to cheating rhizobia

explanations.a: Correct — nodules hosting underperforming, low-fixing rhizobia receive reduced oxygen and resources, limiting the cheating bacteria's own reproduction within that nodule.
explanations.b: Sanctions target specific underperforming nodules, not a blanket kill of all rhizobia including cooperative ones.
explanations.c: Dropping the whole root system would be self-destructive and is not the documented mechanism.
explanations.d: The 2003 Nature paper specifically demonstrated that plants can and do detect and sanction low-performing nodules.

questions.prompt: Why did myxomatosis virulence decline in Australian rabbits within about a decade of the 1950 release?

options.text: Mosquito transmission requires a living host, so intermediate-virulence strains that kept rabbits alive longer spread better
The virus was deliberately re-engineered by scientists to be less lethal
Rabbits developed complete immunity within the first year
Virulence increased rather than decreased over that period

explanations.a: Correct — since mosquitoes only transmit the virus from living rabbits, ultra-lethal strains that killed hosts too fast were outcompeted by intermediate-virulence strains, which selection favored.
explanations.b: The virulence shift was an evolutionary outcome of natural selection on the virus population, not deliberate re-engineering.
explanations.c: Resistance rose gradually over roughly a decade alongside virulence decline, not as complete first-year immunity.
explanations.d: Field surveys documented a decline in virulence toward intermediate grades, not an increase.

questions.prompt: Match each symbiosis example to the mutualist benefit exchanged.

right.text: Phosphorus and water for sugars
Parasite removal for a food source
Nectar for pollen transport
Fruit pulp for seed transport away from the parent plant

questions.explanation: Mycorrhizae trade fungal-scavenged phosphorus and water for plant sugars, cleaner wrasses trade parasite removal for food, bees trade pollen transport for nectar, and dispersers trade seed transport for fruit pulp.

lessons.label: Food Webs, Keystones, and Cascades

sections.heading: Food webs as testable hypotheses, not diagrams
sections.body: A food web maps trophic levels — primary producers, primary consumers, secondary consumers, and so on — connected by feeding links, and two structural properties matter for how it behaves: connectance, the fraction of all possible feeding links that actually exist, and omnivory, species feeding at more than one trophic level, which is common enough (foxes eating both rabbits and berries) that real webs are messier than the clean pyramid diagrams suggest. Crucially, every arrow in a food-web diagram is a claim about who eats whom, and that claim needs evidence. Gut-content analysis (dissecting or flushing a stomach to identify prey fragments) only captures a recent meal and misses soft-bodied or fully digested prey. Stable isotope analysis is the modern complement: nitrogen-15 becomes enriched relative to nitrogen-14 by about 3-4 per mil with each trophic step, so measuring an organism's tissue δ15N estimates its trophic position even when no one ever watched it eat.

sections.heading: Paine's 1966 experiment and the keystone concept
sections.body: Robert Paine tested food-web structure directly rather than just drawing it. At Mukkaw Bay, Washington, in 1963-66, he repeatedly removed the predatory sea star Pisaster ochraceus from experimental rocky-shore plots while leaving paired control plots untouched. Within the removal plots, the mussel Mytilus californianus, freed from its main predator, spread and monopolized space, competitively excluding barnacles, algae, and other species; local diversity collapsed from about 15 species down to 8. Paine's 1969 follow-up paper coined the term keystone species for a predator whose impact on community structure is disproportionately large relative to its own abundance or biomass — remove the keystone and the whole arch of the community structure falls.

sections.heading: Otters, urchins, kelp, and the top-down/bottom-up debate
sections.body: James Estes and John Palmisano documented a parallel trophic cascade in the North Pacific in 1974: where sea otters were present, they kept sea urchin populations low, allowing kelp forests to flourish; where otters had been hunted out by the fur trade, urchins irrupted and grazed kelp down to barren rock. Both cases are top-down control, predators regulating community structure from above. But ecologists have long argued over how general this is. Hairston, Smith, and Slobodkin's 1960 'green world' hypothesis asked why herbivores don't strip the planet bare, and answered that predators keep herbivore numbers below what plant productivity could otherwise support — a three-trophic-level, top-down argument. Critics countered with bottom-up control: nutrient and light availability set the ceiling on plant productivity first, and that ceiling constrains everything above it. Most modern food-web ecologists now treat top-down and bottom-up forces as simultaneous, with their relative strength shifting by ecosystem type and productivity level, rather than picking one as universally dominant.

lessons.workedExample: A student modeling a local pond food web assumes largemouth bass eat only smaller fish, based on visual observation. Gut-content sampling of 20 bass finds fish fragments in only 6 stomachs, with the rest containing crayfish and insect larvae — revealing omnivory the diagram missed. Running stable isotope analysis on bass muscle tissue gives a δ15N value about 6.8 per mil higher than the pond's algae baseline, roughly two trophic steps up (at ~3.4 per mil enrichment per step), independently confirming the bass sit at the third trophic level rather than the fourth a purely fish-eating diet would suggest.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probing a food-web or cascade project want evidence the student treats trophic links as claims to be tested, not assumptions to be drawn. A weak answer presents a diagram with arrows and no method behind them. A strong answer names how each link was established — gut contents, isotopes, or direct observation — and, for a keystone or cascade claim, can describe the actual manipulation (removal, exclusion) that distinguishes a keystone effect from mere correlation, the way Paine's removal plots did against untouched controls, rather than just asserting a species is 'important.'

questions.prompt: What did Robert Paine's 1963-66 Pisaster removal experiment at Mukkaw Bay demonstrate?

options.text: Removing the sea star let mussels dominate space and local diversity dropped from about 15 to 8 species
Sea stars had no measurable effect on the rocky-shore community
Mussel removal caused sea star populations to collapse
Diversity increased when Pisaster was removed

explanations.a: Correct — with Pisaster removed, Mytilus californianus monopolized space and competitively excluded other species, and diversity fell from about 15 to 8 species.
explanations.b: The removal plots diverged sharply from paired controls, demonstrating a strong, measurable predator effect.
explanations.c: The manipulation removed sea stars, not mussels; mussels were the species that then expanded.
explanations.d: Diversity decreased, not increased, once the keystone predator was removed and mussels dominated space.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much does an organism's tissue δ15N value increase with each trophic step, and why is that useful?

options.text: About 3-4 per mil, letting ecologists estimate trophic position from tissue chemistry
About 50 per mil, making it useless for distinguishing nearby trophic levels
0 per mil, since nitrogen isotopes do not change across trophic levels
It decreases by 3-4 per mil with each trophic step

explanations.a: Correct — the roughly 3-4 per mil enrichment per trophic step is consistent enough to back-calculate an organism's approximate trophic position from a tissue sample.
explanations.b: A 50 per mil step would be implausibly large and would not match the well-documented small stepwise enrichment.
explanations.c: There is a real, measurable enrichment per trophic step; it is not zero.
explanations.d: δ15N is enriched, not depleted, at higher trophic levels, since lighter nitrogen-14 is preferentially excreted.

questions.prompt: What is the central claim of the Hairston, Smith, and Slobodkin (1960) 'green world' hypothesis?

options.text: Predators keep herbivore populations below what plant productivity could otherwise support
Herbivores are limited entirely by nutrient availability in plants, with no predator role
Plants are limited only by sunlight and never by consumers
The world appears green because herbivores have gone extinct globally

explanations.a: Correct — HSS argued the world stays green because predators (top-down control) suppress herbivore numbers below the level at which they would strip vegetation.
explanations.b: This describes a purely bottom-up view, which HSS's hypothesis argued against by emphasizing predator control.
explanations.c: HSS's argument centers on consumer (herbivore and predator) dynamics, not solely sunlight limitation on plants.
explanations.d: Herbivores clearly still exist; the hypothesis explains why they don't consume all available vegetation, not their extinction.

questions.prompt: Order the events of the sea otter-urchin-kelp trophic cascade as it unfolds when otters are removed by hunting.

items.text: Sea otters are hunted out of a coastal area
Sea urchin populations irrupt without their main predator
Urchins graze kelp forests down to barren rock
Kelp-dependent species lose their habitat

questions.explanation: Otter removal releases urchins from predation, urchin populations explode, they overgraze kelp into barrens, and the cascade finally strips habitat from species that depended on the kelp forest structure.

lessons.label: Energy Flow and Productivity

sections.heading: GPP, NPP, and NEP: three different questions
sections.body: Gross primary production (GPP) is the total energy an ecosystem's autotrophs capture through photosynthesis. Net primary production (NPP) is what's left after subtracting the autotrophs' own respiration (Ra): NPP = GPP - Ra, and it's what's actually available to be eaten, stored, or decomposed. Net ecosystem production (NEP) goes one layer further, subtracting heterotroph respiration (Rh) too: NEP = GPP - Ra - Rh, telling you whether the whole ecosystem is a net carbon sink or source over a given period. These are genuinely different quantities — a forest can have high GPP but low NEP if decomposers are respiring nearly as much carbon as producers fix, which matters enormously for questions like whether a given ecosystem is offsetting or contributing to atmospheric carbon.

sections.heading: Lindeman's trophic-dynamic paper and the 10% rule
sections.body: Raymond Lindeman's 1942 paper 'The Trophic-Dynamic Aspect of Ecology,' built on his data from Cedar Bog Lake, Minnesota, was the first to formalize energy flow through trophic levels quantitatively, tracking how much energy moved from producers to primary consumers to secondary consumers. From data like his came the popularized '10% rule' — roughly a tenth of the energy at one trophic level ends up incorporated into the next, the rest lost to respiration, movement, heat, and undigested material. The real empirically measured range across ecosystems runs much wider, roughly 2% to 20% depending on the taxa involved (ectotherms like fish are typically more efficient than endotherms, which burn substantial energy on metabolic heat), so the 10% figure is a convenient average, not a hard law, and a strong project cites a measured transfer efficiency rather than assuming 10%.

sections.heading: Pyramids, and how NPP is actually measured
sections.body: Because energy is lost at every transfer, a pyramid of energy is always upright, each level holding less than the one below it. A pyramid of numbers or biomass, though, can invert: in open ocean ecosystems, phytoplankton biomass at any instant can be lower than the zooplankton biomass grazing on it, because phytoplankton turn over (reproduce and get eaten) so fast that a small standing stock still supports a much larger, longer-lived consumer biomass. NPP itself is measured with several concrete methods depending on the system: the harvest method clips, dries, and weighs plant biomass in known plot areas over time for terrestrial systems; the light-and-dark bottle method incubates water samples in clear versus opaque bottles and tracks dissolved oxygen change to back out photosynthesis versus respiration in aquatic systems; and chlorophyll-a concentration, measured by water-sample fluorescence or satellite ocean-color sensors, serves as a fast proxy for phytoplankton biomass across huge areas. None of these methods is 'the' 10% rule in action directly — they're what makes any transfer-efficiency number possible to calculate at all.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures a pond's GPP using light and dark bottles: the light bottle gains 2.4 mg O2/L over 24 hours (net photosynthesis), the dark bottle loses 0.9 mg O2/L (respiration alone). GPP = net photosynthesis + respiration = 2.4 + 0.9 = 3.3 mg O2/L. Converting O2 to carbon fixed and comparing it to the zooplankton biomass sampled by net tow the following week, the student finds a transfer efficiency of about 6% from phytoplankton to zooplankton — below the textbook 10%, which the student reports honestly rather than rounding up to match the rule.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing an energy-flow project wants to see the 10% rule treated as an approximation grounded in a real measurement, not memorized dogma. A weak answer states 'only 10% of energy transfers to the next level' with no idea where that number comes from. A strong answer names the actual method used to estimate production — harvest, light/dark bottle, or chlorophyll-a — reports whatever efficiency the data actually gave (even if it's 4% or 18%), and can explain in one sentence why ectotherms and endotherms differ in typical transfer efficiency.

questions.prompt: How is net ecosystem production (NEP) defined?

options.text: GPP minus autotroph respiration minus heterotroph respiration
GPP plus autotroph respiration
NPP divided by the number of trophic levels
Total biomass at the top trophic level

explanations.a: Correct — NEP = GPP - Ra - Rh, subtracting both autotroph and heterotroph respiration to find the ecosystem's net carbon balance.
explanations.b: Adding respiration rather than subtracting it would overstate net production and doesn't match the standard definition.
explanations.c: NEP is not a per-trophic-level average; it's a whole-ecosystem carbon balance calculation.
explanations.d: Top-level biomass reflects accumulated transfers, not the ecosystem-wide production-versus-respiration balance NEP measures.

questions.prompt: What is the empirically measured range of energy transfer efficiency between trophic levels, and how does the '10% rule' relate to it?

options.text: Roughly 2-20%, with 10% as a convenient average rather than a fixed law
Exactly 10% in every ecosystem ever measured
Roughly 50-90%, making the 10% rule a severe underestimate
0%, since no energy transfers between trophic levels

explanations.a: Correct — real measured efficiencies range roughly 2% to 20% depending on the taxa, with 10% serving as a rough average rather than a strict rule.
explanations.b: Real ecosystems show substantial variation around 10%, not a fixed universal value.
explanations.c: 50-90% is far above any measured trophic transfer efficiency in real ecosystems.
explanations.d: Energy clearly does transfer between trophic levels; that's what supports every consumer population.

questions.prompt: Why can a pyramid of biomass be inverted in open ocean ecosystems even though the pyramid of energy never inverts?

options.text: Phytoplankton turn over so fast that a small standing biomass can support larger, longer-lived consumer biomass
Energy actually flows backward from zooplankton to phytoplankton in the ocean
Ocean phytoplankton do not photosynthesize
Zooplankton produce more energy than they consume

explanations.a: Correct — fast phytoplankton turnover means a small instantaneous standing stock can still flow enough energy to sustain a larger standing biomass of slower-turnover zooplankton.
explanations.b: Energy still flows from producers to consumers, in the normal direction; only the biomass snapshot can invert due to turnover rates.
explanations.c: Phytoplankton are the ocean's primary producers and do photosynthesize; that's the whole basis of the food web.
explanations.d: Consumers always lose energy relative to what they take in through respiration; they cannot net-produce more energy than consumed.

questions.prompt: Match each NPP measurement method to what it directly measures.

right.text: Dried plant biomass clipped from known plot areas over time
Dissolved oxygen change in clear versus opaque water samples
A fast proxy for phytoplankton biomass via fluorescence or satellite ocean color

questions.explanation: The harvest method weighs clipped and dried terrestrial plant biomass, the light/dark bottle method tracks oxygen change to separate photosynthesis from respiration in water, and chlorophyll-a measurement proxies phytoplankton biomass rapidly over large areas.

lessons.label: Decomposition and Nutrient Cycling

sections.heading: Three cycles, one big structural difference
sections.body: Carbon cycles between atmospheric CO2, living biomass via photosynthesis, and back to the atmosphere via respiration and decomposition, with slower geological storage in rock and fossil fuel. Nitrogen has more steps because atmospheric N2 is nearly inert: nitrogen fixation converts it to usable ammonium, done biologically by bacteria like Rhizobium in legume root nodules and free-living Azotobacter, plus a small amount by lightning; nitrification then oxidizes ammonium to nitrite and on to nitrate, carried out by Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter; and denitrification, mainly by Pseudomonas under low-oxygen conditions, converts nitrate back to N2 gas, closing the loop. Phosphorus is the odd one out: it has no significant gaseous phase, entering ecosystems only through the slow weathering of phosphate-bearing rock, which is why phosphorus is so often the limiting nutrient in soils and freshwater systems where nitrogen is comparatively abundant.

sections.heading: Decomposers as the return path, made measurable
sections.body: Fungi and bacteria do the chemical breakdown of dead organic matter, while detritivores like earthworms, millipedes, and isopods physically fragment litter first, increasing the surface area microbes can act on — the two groups work in sequence, not competition. Decomposition rate is commonly measured with litterbags: known masses of leaf litter sealed in mesh bags of a set pore size are buried or laid on the soil surface, then retrieved at intervals and reweighed, with mass loss typically fit to Olson's 1963 exponential decay model, M(t) = M0·e^(-kt), where k is the decomposition rate constant. The Tea Bag Index, developed by Judith Keuskamp and colleagues in 2013, standardizes this further using mass-produced green tea and rooibos tea bags as a labile-versus-recalcitrant litter pair: comparing their mass loss after roughly 90 days yields both a decomposition rate k and a stabilization factor S, the fraction of the labile material that resists breakdown, letting sites across the globe be compared on identical litter.

sections.heading: Hubbard Brook: the whole-ecosystem proof
sections.body: The clearest demonstration that vegetation actively retains nutrients, rather than nutrients simply cycling on their own, came from the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest in New Hampshire. In 1965-66, F. Herbert Bormann and Gene Likens clear-cut an entire watershed (Watershed 2) and applied herbicide to prevent regrowth for several years, while a neighboring untouched watershed served as the control, both instrumented with stream gauges to measure nutrient export. Stream nitrate concentrations in the deforested watershed rose roughly fortyfold above the control, at times exceeding U.S. drinking-water standards, along with sharply increased loss of calcium and other cations. With no living roots left to take up nitrate and no canopy to intercept and use nutrients, nitrification proceeded unchecked and the watershed simply flushed its capital away in stream water — a controlled, whole-ecosystem experiment that remains the reference case for how intact vegetation regulates nutrient retention.

lessons.workedExample: A student burying litterbags of oak leaves (initial mass 10.0 g) at a forest site retrieves them at 30, 60, and 90 days, finding masses of 8.1 g, 6.7 g, and 5.5 g. Fitting M(t) = M0·e^(-kt) gives k ≈ 0.0067/day (about 2.4/year). Running the same site with Tea Bag Index rooibos and green tea bags for 90 days gives k = 0.011/day and stabilization factor S = 0.35, meaning about 35% of the labile tea fraction resisted decomposition — letting the student compare their local oak-litter result against the globally standardized tea benchmark rather than an uncalibrated one-off number.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing decomposition or nutrient cycling wants a measurable process, not a diagram with arrows labeled 'decomposition happens here.' A weak answer describes the nitrogen or carbon cycle from memory with no method for measuring any step. A strong answer names a concrete technique — litterbags with a fitted decay constant k, the Tea Bag Index's k and S, or soil respiration flux — and, if discussing whole-ecosystem nutrient loss, can explain why Hubbard Brook's Watershed 2 nitrate spike happened mechanistically (no living roots to take up nitrate, no canopy uptake) rather than just citing 'deforestation causes nutrient loss.'

questions.prompt: Why does phosphorus behave differently from carbon and nitrogen in ecosystem cycling?

options.text: Phosphorus has no significant gaseous phase and enters ecosystems mainly through rock weathering
Phosphorus is always more abundant than nitrogen in soils
Phosphorus cycles exclusively through the atmosphere like nitrogen
Phosphorus is fixed by bacteria the same way nitrogen is

explanations.a: Correct — with no gaseous form, phosphorus enters ecosystems only via slow rock weathering, making it a frequent limiting nutrient.
explanations.b: Phosphorus is often the scarcer, limiting nutrient precisely because it lacks nitrogen's atmospheric replenishment route.
explanations.c: Unlike nitrogen, phosphorus has no atmospheric gas phase to cycle through at all.
explanations.d: Biological nitrogen fixation converts atmospheric N2; there is no phosphorus equivalent since phosphorus isn't atmospheric.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the nitrogen cycle from atmospheric N2 to its return back to N2 gas.

items.text: Nitrogen fixation converts N2 to ammonium
Nitrification oxidizes ammonium to nitrite then nitrate
Plants and microbes assimilate nitrate or ammonium
Denitrification converts nitrate back to N2 gas

questions.explanation: Fixation makes atmospheric nitrogen biologically usable as ammonium, nitrification oxidizes it stepwise to nitrate, organisms assimilate it into biomass, and denitrification under low-oxygen conditions returns nitrate to atmospheric N2, closing the cycle.

questions.prompt: What did the Hubbard Brook Watershed 2 clear-cut experiment find in stream water after deforestation?

options.text: Stream nitrate concentrations rose roughly fortyfold above the control watershed
Nutrient export was unchanged compared to the control watershed
Nitrate concentrations dropped to nearly zero
Only phosphorus levels changed, with nitrogen unaffected

explanations.a: Correct — with no living roots to take up nitrate and no canopy uptake, stream nitrate rose roughly fortyfold above the control, at times exceeding drinking-water standards.
explanations.b: The deforested watershed diverged sharply from the untouched control in nutrient export.
explanations.c: Nitrate rose dramatically rather than dropping, since nitrification proceeded unchecked without plant uptake.
explanations.d: Calcium and other cations were also lost at increased rates alongside the nitrate spike, not nitrogen alone.

questions.prompt: Match each nutrient-cycling measurement technique to what it produces.

right.text: A site-specific decay constant k from reweighed leaf litter over time
A globally standardized decay rate k and stabilization factor S
Whole-watershed nutrient export measured in stream water

questions.explanation: Litterbags yield a local decay constant from mass loss, the Tea Bag Index standardizes this into a globally comparable k and stabilization factor S using uniform tea litter, and Hubbard Brook's stream gauges measured whole-ecosystem nutrient export directly.

lessons.label: Clements vs Gleason: Is a Community a Thing?

sections.heading: Clements: the community as superorganism
sections.body: In 1916's Plant Succession, Frederic Clements argued that a plant community develops like a single organism: it is born (pioneer colonization of bare ground), grows through predictable seral stages, and matures into a stable 'climax' determined entirely by regional climate. Push a prairie back with fire or plow it, and Clements predicted it would retrace the same sequence of stages back to the same climax — succession was deterministic and convergent, and the community itself was a real, bounded, quasi-organismal unit worth naming and studying as such.

sections.heading: Gleason: communities as coincidence
sections.body: Henry Gleason's 1926 'individualistic hypothesis' (elaborating ideas he'd floated since 1917) rejected the superorganism outright. Each species, he argued, is distributed according to its own physiological tolerances and dispersal ability, responding independently to gradients of moisture, light, and temperature. A 'community' is simply the set of species whose tolerance ranges happen to overlap at a given point in space — a statistical coincidence, not a bounded, repeatable unit. Change the starting conditions or the seed rain and you get a different assemblage, not a return to one true climax.

sections.heading: Whittaker's gradient analysis settles the empirical question
sections.body: The dispute stayed largely rhetorical until Robert Whittaker's Great Smoky Mountains gradient analysis (1956) and Curtis and McIntosh's companion Wisconsin continuum study (1951). Plotting species' abundances against measured environmental gradients (elevation, moisture), Whittaker found no sharp community boundaries — species turned over continuously and individually along the gradient, each peaking at its own optimum, overlapping broadly with neighbors on both sides. This 'continuum concept' delivered empirical support for Gleason's individualistic view over Clements's discrete, superorganismal zones, and became the standard picture in community ecology textbooks by the 1970s.

sections.heading: Still unresolved
sections.body: The debate didn't fully close, it relocated. Alternative stable states theory (Lewontin 1969; Holling 1973; formalized by Beisner, Haydon & Cuddington 2003) revived a Clementsian-flavored claim that some systems really do snap between a small number of discrete, self-reinforcing configurations rather than sliding continuously — closer to Clements's basins of attraction than Gleason's smooth gradient. A concrete example: shallow lakes can flip from a clear-water state, dominated by rooted macrophytes that stabilize sediment and starve algae of nutrients, to a turbid, algae-dominated state once nutrient loading (mainly phosphorus runoff) crosses a threshold — the plants collapse, sediment resuspends, and light drops too low for macrophytes to recover even if nutrient inputs are later cut, because the turbid state is self-reinforcing. Restoration ecology inherits the fight directly: if there is no single true climax to restore to, what counts as a legitimate 'reference' target for a restored wetland or prairie remains a live, practically consequential argument, not a settled textbook fact.

lessons.workedExample: A student proposes restoring an abandoned Midwest farm field to 'its natural prairie state.' A Clementsian design assumes one predictable climax and plants a single fixed species mix, expecting convergence regardless of starting conditions. A Gleasonian design instead treats the outcome as contingent: soil legacy, seed bank, and which species arrive first (priority effects) will shape a somewhat different assemblage each time, so the student tracks multiple reference sites across a moisture gradient rather than one 'ideal' target community, and reports a range of acceptable end states instead of a single pass/fail community type.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'is your restored or studied plot converging toward a defined community, or did you just measure whatever species happened to be there?' because the question exposes whether the student understands communities as contested constructs rather than obvious natural units. A weak answer treats 'the community' as self-evidently real and complete once species are listed. A strong answer names the tension explicitly — deterministic climax versus individualistic co-occurrence — and explains which framework their sampling design and conclusions actually assume, especially if they invoke a 'reference' or 'target' state.

questions.prompt: Clements's model of succession predicted that after disturbance, a plant community would:

options.text: Follow one of many possible paths depending on which species arrived first
Converge deterministically back to a single climate-determined climax
Never recover to anything resembling its prior state
Be replaced permanently by whichever species has the broadest tolerance range

explanations.a: That path-dependent, contingent view is closer to Gleason's individualistic hypothesis, not Clements's.
explanations.b: Correct — Clements treated succession as organismal development toward one predictable, climate-set climax, regardless of the disturbance's starting point.
explanations.c: Clements's model was explicitly about predictable recovery, not permanent non-recovery.
explanations.d: This describes competitive dominance, not Clements's climate-determinism argument.

questions.prompt: What did Whittaker's gradient analyses in the Great Smoky Mountains find?

options.text: Sharp, discrete boundaries between plant communities matching Clements's zones
Species abundances turning over continuously and individually along environmental gradients
No relationship between species distribution and elevation or moisture
That all species in a community shared identical tolerance ranges

explanations.a: This is what Whittaker's data argued against, not for.
explanations.b: Correct — species peaked at individual optima and overlapped broadly rather than forming sharp community boundaries, supporting Gleason's continuum concept.
explanations.c: Whittaker explicitly plotted abundance against gradients like elevation and moisture; a relationship is exactly what he found.
explanations.d: Individual, non-identical tolerance ranges are the whole point of the continuum result.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their core contribution to the community-concept debate.

right.text: Superorganism model with deterministic climax
Individualistic hypothesis of chance co-occurrence
Empirical gradient analysis showing continuous species turnover
Early formalization of alternative stable states

questions.explanation: Clements proposed the superorganism/climax model; Gleason countered with the individualistic hypothesis; Whittaker's Smoky Mountains gradient study (with Curtis and McIntosh's companion Wisconsin work) empirically supported Gleason; Holling's 1973 resilience paper helped formalize alternative stable states.

questions.prompt: Why does the restoration-ecology 'reference target' debate connect back to Clements vs. Gleason?

options.text: It doesn't — restoration ecology is unrelated to this historical debate
Because if there is no single true climax, choosing one 'correct' restoration target is itself a contested claim about how communities work
Because Clements personally designed the first restoration projects
Because Gleason proved that restoration is always impossible

explanations.a: The connection is direct and is why the debate is still practically consequential today.
explanations.b: Correct — a Clementsian view licenses one fixed reference community; a Gleasonian/contingent view implies a range of acceptable outcomes, making 'the' correct target a live theoretical choice.
explanations.c: Clements died in 1945, well before modern restoration ecology as a discipline existed.
explanations.d: Gleason's hypothesis is about how communities assemble, not a claim that restoration cannot succeed.

lessons.label: Tansley, Lindeman, and the Ecosystem Idea

sections.heading: Tansley's 1935 rebuttal coins a word
sections.body: British botanist Arthur Tansley coined 'ecosystem' in his 1935 paper 'The Use and Abuse of Vegetational Concepts and Terms' — and he coined it as a deliberate corrective, not a neutral label. Tansley was attacking the Clementsian language of communities as quasi-organisms with something like collective purpose, which he considered mystical and untestable. His alternative: define the unit as the whole physical system — organisms plus the abiotic factors (soil, climate, nutrients) they exchange matter and energy with — something you could, in principle, measure with the tools of physics and chemistry rather than argue about with organismal metaphors.

sections.heading: Lindeman's trophic-dynamic paper and a rocky path to print
sections.body: Raymond Lindeman turned Tansley's abstract unit into a quantitative research program. Working on Cedar Bog Lake, Minnesota, Lindeman's 1942 paper 'The Trophic-Dynamic Aspect of Ecology' modeled an ecosystem as energy flowing through trophic levels — producers to herbivores to carnivores — with each transfer losing most of the energy as heat, an idea building on Elton's 1927 pyramid of numbers and Juday's productivity work. The paper was initially rejected by peer reviewers at Ecology as too speculative; it was published in 1942 only after limnologist G. Evelyn Hutchinson, Lindeman's colleague at Yale, intervened on its behalf. Lindeman never saw it in print — he died of a liver ailment in 1942 at age 26, before the issue appeared.

sections.heading: The Odums build energy flow into a program
sections.body: Brothers Eugene and Howard T. Odum turned Lindeman's framework into a full research tradition. Howard Odum's 1957 study of Silver Springs, Florida, was the first attempt to measure the complete energy budget of a real ecosystem — quantifying gross production, respiration, and energy loss at each trophic step in kilocalories per square meter per year — and Eugene Odum's Fundamentals of Ecology (1953) popularized ecosystem energetics as the organizing framework for the entire discipline, cementing 'ecosystem' as ecology's central unit of analysis for decades.

sections.heading: The critique: systems ecology over-promised
sections.body: By the 1970s-80s, critics argued the systems-ecology program had overreached. Large computer-modeling efforts like the International Biological Programme's biome studies aimed to simulate whole ecosystems predictively, but the models proved too complex to validate and often failed to predict real dynamics better than simpler approaches — a critique articulated by ecologists including Simon Levin and later reviewed critically by figures such as Donald Strong. The energy-flow framework survived as a genuinely useful accounting tool, but the more ambitious claim — that whole ecosystems behave as predictable, deterministic systems analogous to physical circuits — did not hold up, foreshadowing later debates over whether communities are as orderly as their founders hoped.

lessons.workedExample: A student measures a small farm pond as an ecosystem: they quantify phytoplankton production (grams of carbon fixed per square meter per day), then zooplankton biomass, then fish biomass, following Lindeman's trophic-level logic directly. Applying his roughly 10% trophic transfer efficiency as a first estimate, if phytoplankton fix 200 g C/m²/yr, zooplankton production should be on the rough order of 20 g C/m²/yr and fish production on the order of 2 g C/m²/yr — a testable prediction the student can then check against actual net production measured at each level, exactly the kind of quantitative energy-budget question Lindeman's paper made askable for the first time.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'why measure energy flow instead of just species lists?' is testing whether a student knows that the ecosystem concept was a specific, argued-for methodological choice — Tansley rejecting organismal mysticism, Lindeman making it quantifiable — not the obvious default unit of ecology. A weak answer says 'ecosystems are what ecologists study.' A strong answer explains that energy, unlike species identity, is conserved and transfers in measurable, comparable units across very different systems, which is exactly why Lindeman's framework could travel from a single Minnesota bog to Silver Springs to global carbon-cycle science.

questions.prompt: What was Tansley's main objection to Clementsian community language that motivated coining 'ecosystem' in 1935?

options.text: It ignored abiotic factors like soil and climate entirely
It treated communities as quasi-organisms with collective purpose, which he saw as untestable mysticism
It was too focused on measurable energy flow
It failed to name individual species

explanations.a: Tansley's alternative unit explicitly included abiotic factors; his objection was about the organismal metaphor, not a lack of abiotic focus.
explanations.b: Correct — Tansley wanted a physically definable unit (organisms plus their abiotic environment) instead of Clements's organismal, purpose-laden community metaphor.
explanations.c: Measurable energy flow came later with Lindeman; Tansley's 1935 objection targeted vitalist community language.
explanations.d: Naming species was never the issue in this dispute.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the development of the ecosystem-energetics tradition.

items.text: Tansley coins 'ecosystem' as an alternative to organismal community language
Lindeman's trophic-dynamic paper on Cedar Bog Lake is published after Hutchinson's intervention
Eugene Odum's Fundamentals of Ecology popularizes ecosystem energetics
Howard Odum measures the full energy budget of Silver Springs

questions.explanation: Tansley's term (1935) preceded Lindeman's quantitative trophic-dynamic model (1942), which preceded Eugene Odum's 1953 textbook synthesis, which preceded Howard Odum's 1957 Silver Springs energy-budget study.

questions.prompt: What happened to Raymond Lindeman's landmark 1942 paper before publication?

options.text: It was accepted immediately without revision
It was rejected by peer reviewers as too speculative and published only after Hutchinson intervened
It was published posthumously decades after his death
It was co-authored with Eugene Odum

explanations.a: The paper actually faced reviewer rejection first.
explanations.b: Correct — Ecology's reviewers initially rejected it as overly speculative; G. Evelyn Hutchinson intervened, and it appeared in 1942, the same year Lindeman died at 26.
explanations.c: It was published in 1942, the same year he died, not decades later.
explanations.d: It was solo-authored by Lindeman; the Odums built on it afterward.

questions.prompt: The critique of systems ecology that emerged by the 1970s-80s mainly argued that:

options.text: Energy-flow accounting was entirely useless and should be abandoned
Ambitious whole-ecosystem computer models proved too complex to validate and often failed to outpredict simpler approaches
Tansley's original ecosystem concept had been forgotten by ecologists
Lindeman's trophic levels were mathematically impossible to define

explanations.a: The critique targeted predictive overreach, not the basic accounting usefulness of energy-flow measurement, which survived.
explanations.b: Correct — large IBP-era biome simulation models overpromised deterministic, predictive power that the complexity of real ecosystems didn't support.
explanations.c: The concept remained central; the critique was about how far its predictive ambitions could be pushed, not whether it was used.
explanations.d: Trophic levels remained a workable, widely used accounting framework despite the critique.

lessons.label: The Experiments That Changed the Field

sections.heading: Paine's starfish and Connell's barnacles
sections.body: Robert Paine's 1963-66 removal experiment at Mukkaw Bay, Washington, hand-pulled the predatory sea star Pisaster ochraceus from marked rocky-shore plots and left paired control plots untouched. Over the next several years of continued monitoring, the mussel Mytilus californianus that Pisaster normally kept in check progressively overgrew the barnacles that recruited first and monopolized space, and species richness in cleared plots crashed from about 15 species to 8. Falsification would have been no change in richness after removal; the result launched the term 'keystone species' (Paine, 1969). Joseph Connell's 1961 barnacle transplant on Scotland's Isle of Cumbrae tested why Chthamalus stellatus lives only in the high intertidal while Balanus balanoides dominates lower down: Connell transplanted Chthamalus larvae into the low zone and, critically, removed Balanus from half those plots. Chthamalus survived fine low down only where Balanus was excluded — proving its fundamental niche is broader than its realized niche, which competitive exclusion by Balanus compresses upward.

sections.heading: Park's flipping beetles and Simberloff-Wilson's islands
sections.body: Thomas Park's Tribolium flour-beetle experiments (1940s-54) pitted T. castaneum against T. confusum in controlled flour microcosms across combinations of temperature and humidity. Rather than one species always winning, outcomes flipped: T. castaneum won reliably in hot-humid conditions, T. confusum in cold-dry conditions, with genuinely probabilistic outcomes at intermediate settings — a direct challenge to any simple competitive-exclusion rule that ignores environmental context. E.O. Wilson and Daniel Simberloff's 1969 mangrove-island defaunation in the Florida Keys fumigated small red-mangrove islands with methyl bromide to kill every resident arthropod, then monitored recolonization against unfumigated controls. Species number rebounded to near pre-defaunation levels within about a year, a direct test of MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium theory; falsification would have been recolonization to a permanently different richness or no recovery at all.

sections.heading: Hubbard Brook: a whole watershed as the experimental unit
sections.body: F. Herbert Bormann and Gene Likens's Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest study (New Hampshire, beginning 1963) clear-cut Watershed 2 and applied herbicide for several years to block regrowth, comparing stream chemistry against an unmanipulated reference watershed. Nitrate export in stream water rose roughly 40-fold or more compared to the reference watershed, and net water yield increased substantially, demonstrating that intact vegetation actively retains nutrients rather than passively sitting atop them. The paired-watershed design, still running today, made an entire forested catchment the experimental and control unit — falsification would have been no measurable change in stream nutrient export after clear-cutting.

lessons.workedExample: A student designing a mini-Paine experiment on a local rocky shore removes a mid-shore predatory whelk from ten marked 1 m² plots weekly for eight weeks, leaving ten unmanipulated plots as controls, and censuses percent cover of the dominant competitor (a mussel or barnacle) biweekly in both. If the manipulated plots show a competitor cover increase the control plots don't, that is evidence for a keystone effect; if cover tracks similarly in both regardless of removal, the whelk is not keystone at that site — mirroring exactly the control-versus-manipulation logic Paine used, just at a scale a team can execute in a season.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'what was your control, and what result would have proven you wrong?' because these five studies are the field's canonical answer to that question, and a student who can't name an analogous control/falsification pair for their own project hasn't designed a real experiment. A weak answer describes what was observed without a paired comparison. A strong answer explicitly names what would have falsified the hypothesis — exactly as Paine's unchanged control plots, or Wilson and Simberloff's failure-to-recolonize scenario, would have — showing the student understands manipulation experiments as tests, not demonstrations.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher(s) to the experiment they ran.

right.text: Pisaster removal from rocky-shore plots
Chthamalus/Balanus transplant and removal
Tribolium competition across temperature/humidity
Mangrove-island defaunation by fumigation
Hubbard Brook watershed clear-cut

questions.explanation: Paine removed Pisaster; Connell transplanted and manipulated barnacle competitors; Park varied climate conditions for Tribolium beetles; Simberloff and Wilson fumigated mangrove islands; Bormann and Likens clear-cut a Hubbard Brook watershed.

questions.prompt: What did Connell's barnacle transplant demonstrate about Chthamalus stellatus?

options.text: It cannot physiologically survive in the low intertidal under any conditions
Its realized niche is narrower than its fundamental niche because Balanus excludes it from the low intertidal
It outcompetes Balanus wherever the two overlap
Temperature alone determines its distribution, independent of competition

explanations.a: Chthamalus survived fine in the low zone when Balanus was experimentally removed, disproving a pure physiological limit.
explanations.b: Correct — Chthamalus could physiologically tolerate the low intertidal (its fundamental niche) but was normally excluded there by Balanus, so its realized niche is the narrower, high-intertidal zone.
explanations.c: The opposite is true — Balanus outcompetes Chthamalus in the low zone under normal conditions.
explanations.d: The experiment specifically isolated competition, not temperature, as the limiting factor by removing Balanus.
