questions.prompt: What made Thomas Park's Tribolium results significant for competition theory?

options.text: T. castaneum always won regardless of conditions
Competitive outcomes flipped depending on temperature and humidity, showing outcomes are context-dependent and sometimes probabilistic
The two species could never coexist under any tested condition
Competition had no measurable effect on either species' population

explanations.a: T. castaneum won reliably only in hot-humid conditions; T. confusum won in cold-dry conditions.
explanations.b: Correct — the reversal of winners across environmental conditions, with probabilistic outcomes at intermediate settings, challenged simple universal competitive-exclusion predictions.
explanations.c: Coexistence outcomes and winner identity both varied by condition rather than being uniformly impossible.
explanations.d: One species reliably displaced the other under most tested conditions; competition had strong measurable effects.

questions.prompt: What result would have falsified the Hubbard Brook hypothesis that vegetation actively retains ecosystem nutrients?

options.text: Stream nitrate export rising sharply after clear-cutting
Stream nutrient export showing no measurable change after clear-cutting, relative to the reference watershed
The reference watershed showing changes identical to the clear-cut one
Both b and c

explanations.a: This is the actual observed result supporting the hypothesis, not a falsifying one.
explanations.b: No change in the clear-cut watershed relative to reference would falsify the hypothesis, but it isn't the only falsifying scenario listed.
explanations.c: The reference watershed changing identically to the treatment would also undercut the causal claim, but it isn't the only correct option.
explanations.d: Correct — either no differential change in the clear-cut watershed, or the untouched reference watershed mirroring the clear-cut one, would undermine the causal claim that vegetation removal drives nutrient loss.

lessons.label: Island Biogeography and the SLOSS War

sections.heading: MacArthur and Wilson's equilibrium model
sections.body: Robert MacArthur and E.O. Wilson's The Theory of Island Biogeography (1967) proposed that the number of species on an island reflects a dynamic equilibrium, not a fixed list. Immigration rate falls as more species accumulate (fewer new colonists remain to arrive), while extinction rate rises with species number (more species competing for the same resources, plus smaller populations per species). Island area sets the extinction curve — larger islands hold larger, more resistant populations — and isolation sets the immigration curve — closer islands receive more colonists. The intersection of these two curves predicts an equilibrium species number S*, with species composition continuously turning over even while richness stays roughly constant, a genuinely novel, testable claim confirmed by Simberloff and Wilson's mangrove-defaunation recolonization data.

sections.heading: From real islands to habitat fragments
sections.body: Conservation biologists in the 1970s extended the model metaphorically: a forest fragment surrounded by cleared land is an 'island' in a sea of unsuitable habitat, so its expected richness should likewise depend on fragment area and isolation from other forest. This move was influential but contested from the start, since habitat fragments differ from true islands in obvious ways — edges are porous to seed and animal movement, and the surrounding 'sea' is not lifeless ocean.

sections.heading: The SLOSS fight
sections.body: Jared Diamond's 1975 paper in Biological Conservation drew geometric reserve-design rules directly from island biogeography — among them, that a single large reserve conserves more species than several small reserves of the same total area (the 'SL' side of SLOSS: Single Large Or Several Small). Daniel Simberloff and Lawrence Abele's 1976 rebuttal in Science argued Diamond's rules rested on unsupported extrapolation: several small reserves can capture more total beta diversity (distinct habitat types and species turnover between fragments) and provide insurance against a single reserve being wiped out by fire or disease, and no consistent empirical pattern favored SL over SS. The dispute ran through the late 1970s-80s without a clean resolution, largely because the answer depends on the specific taxa and landscape.

sections.heading: What long-term fragmentation experiments actually show
sections.body: The Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project (BDFFP), begun by Thomas Lovejoy near Manaus, Brazil, in 1979, tracked real forest fragments of controlled size for decades, finding pronounced edge effects (increased tree mortality, altered microclimate) penetrating up to 100+ meters into fragments. Nick Haddad and colleagues' 2015 synthesis in Science Advances, pooling seven long-term fragmentation experiments including BDFFP, found habitat fragments lost 13-75% of their species over time, with edge effects reducing biodiversity by roughly half within edge-affected zones. The synthesis didn't crown SL or SS the winner; it showed fragmentation itself, independent of that debate, degrades ecosystems through edge and isolation effects that neither original camp had fully modeled.

lessons.workedExample: A county wildlife agency has 400 hectares to set aside near a shrinking wetland bird population and must choose one 400-hectare reserve versus four 100-hectare reserves. Applying MacArthur-Wilson logic favors the single large reserve for area-sensitive species with big home ranges (lower extinction risk from small population size). Applying the Simberloff-Abele critique favors the four smaller reserves if the wetlands differ in vegetation type (higher combined beta diversity) and if a single large reserve is more exposed to one catastrophic event like a levee failure. A strong student proposal names both effects, then makes a case grounded in the specific species' area requirements and each site's habitat heterogeneity rather than citing 'SLOSS theory' as if it hands over one universal answer.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes SLOSS because it's the clearest case in conservation biology where a mathematically elegant theory (MacArthur-Wilson) generated a plausible-sounding practical rule (Diamond's) that turned out to be empirically unresolved. A weak answer cites 'island biogeography theory' to justify a reserve-design choice as if the science settled it. A strong answer explains that the SL-versus-SS answer is taxon- and landscape-dependent, cites Simberloff and Abele's rebuttal by name, and grounds their own recommendation in area-sensitivity and beta-diversity evidence specific to their system rather than a universal rule.

questions.prompt: In MacArthur and Wilson's equilibrium model, what does island isolation (distance from the mainland) primarily determine?

options.text: The extinction rate curve
The immigration rate curve
The total number of trophic levels
Soil nutrient availability

explanations.a: Extinction rate is primarily set by island area, which governs population size and resource availability.
explanations.b: Correct — more isolated islands receive fewer colonists per unit time, lowering the immigration curve and shifting equilibrium richness downward.
explanations.c: Trophic structure is not a direct output of the immigration-extinction equilibrium model.
explanations.d: Soil nutrients are not a variable in MacArthur and Wilson's model.

questions.prompt: What was the core claim of Simberloff and Abele's 1976 rebuttal to Diamond's reserve-design rules?

options.text: Reserve size is completely irrelevant to species richness
Diamond's single-large-preferred rules were unsupported extrapolations, and several small reserves can capture more beta diversity
Island biogeography theory should never be applied to any conservation question
Large reserves are always inferior to small reserves
Fragmentation has no measurable effect on species loss

explanations.a: Simberloff and Abele did not claim size is irrelevant; they challenged a specific universal ranking of SL over SS.
explanations.b: Correct — they argued the geometric SL-preferred rules lacked empirical support and that several small reserves could conserve more total diversity via habitat heterogeneity.
explanations.c: Their critique targeted overextension of specific rules, not the entire theoretical framework.
explanations.d: They argued the answer is context-dependent, not that small reserves always win.
explanations.e: This wasn't their claim at all; fragmentation effects came later from BDFFP and Haddad's synthesis.

questions.prompt: According to Haddad et al.'s 2015 synthesis of long-term fragmentation experiments, what range of species loss did habitat fragments show?

options.text: 100% in every fragment studied
No measurable species loss

explanations.a: This underestimates the losses reported across the seven pooled long-term experiments.
explanations.b: Correct — the synthesis found fragments lost 13-75% of species, with edge effects roughly halving biodiversity in edge-affected zones.
explanations.c: Total extinction was not the finding; losses were substantial but partial and variable.
explanations.d: The whole point of the synthesis was documenting substantial, measurable species loss from fragmentation.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the island biogeography and SLOSS timeline.

items.text: MacArthur and Wilson publish The Theory of Island Biogeography
Diamond proposes geometric reserve-design rules based on island biogeography
Simberloff and Abele publish their rebuttal in Science
Haddad et al. publish the multi-experiment fragmentation synthesis

questions.explanation: MacArthur and Wilson's 1967 theory came first, Diamond's 1975 reserve rules followed, Simberloff and Abele's 1976 rebuttal came next, and Haddad's 2015 synthesis of decades of fragmentation data came last.

lessons.label: Does Diversity Beget Stability?

sections.heading: The founding intuition
sections.body: Charles Elton's Ecology of Invasions by Animals and Plants (1958) argued that species-rich communities resist invasion and collapse better than simple ones, reasoning informally from cases like species-poor agricultural monocultures suffering severe pest outbreaks. Robert MacArthur's 1955 paper made a related but sharper claim: a food web with more links offers more alternate pathways for energy to flow if one species declines, so more connections should mean more stability. Both were intuitive, widely repeated, and — crucially — untested mathematically.

sections.heading: May's mathematical counterpunch
sections.body: Robert May's 1972 Nature paper 'Will a Large Complex System Be Stable?' tested the intuition with random-matrix models of interacting species. May found the opposite of Elton and MacArthur's expectation: as the number of species, the connectance (fraction of possible links realized), and the average interaction strength all increase, a randomly assembled system becomes generically less locally stable, not more — small perturbations are more likely to grow rather than damp out. This was a genuine shock to the field, since it showed the beloved diversity-stability intuition had no automatic mathematical basis and real ecosystems must be organized non-randomly (through weak-interaction patterns, modularity, or other structure) to persist at all.

sections.heading: Tilman's grassland test
sections.body: David Tilman's long-term Cedar Creek Ecosystem Science Reserve plots in Minnesota offered a rare empirical resolution. During the severe 1987-88 Midwest drought, Tilman and Downing (1994, Nature) found that plots planted with more plant species showed a smaller relative drop in total productivity and recovered to pre-drought biomass faster than species-poor plots — the first strong field evidence tying diversity to a real measure of aggregate ecosystem stability under an actual stress event, not a model.

sections.heading: The sampling-effect critique and where things stand
sections.body: Michael Huston's 1997 critique argued that diversity-productivity results like Tilman's could be an artifact of the 'sampling effect' — more-diverse plots are simply more likely to randomly include one highly productive species by chance, so the plot-level result reflects which species happen to be present, not diversity acting causally through complementary resource use. The critique forced better-designed experiments (including manipulating species identity, not just number) and sharpened a separate distinction: diversity can stabilize the aggregate (total community biomass or productivity) through the portfolio effect — different species respond asynchronously to the same stress, so their fluctuations partly cancel out — even while individual population sizes remain just as variable or more so. Current consensus, reinforced by large meta-analyses such as Cardinale et al. (2012), supports diversity generally stabilizing aggregate ecosystem function via this portfolio/insurance mechanism, while acknowledging both the sampling-effect confound and that stability at the population level is a distinct, separately contested question.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares total plant biomass variability across a growing season in a 2-species prairie plot versus a 16-species plot at a local restoration site. If the 16-species plot's total biomass fluctuates less week to week even though individual species within it rise and fall more (because a drought-tolerant species compensates when a moisture-loving one dips), that is a portfolio effect at the aggregate level — precisely the pattern Tilman documented. The student should also check whether the 16-species plot's high performance is being driven by one dominant, highly productive species (a sampling effect, per Huston) rather than true complementarity, by comparing observed biomass to what monocultures of each species alone would predict.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'more diverse compared to what, and stability of what exactly?' because the diversity-stability question is one ecology got mathematically wrong before getting it empirically right, and vague answers repeat Elton's 1958 intuition without knowing it was later overturned by May and only partly rescued by Tilman. A weak answer says 'diversity increases stability' as an unexamined law. A strong answer distinguishes aggregate stability from population-level stability, names the portfolio/insurance mechanism, and flags the sampling-effect confound as something their own experimental design needs to rule out.

questions.prompt: What did Robert May's 1972 random-matrix models find about complex ecological systems?

options.text: Greater species number, connectance, and interaction strength generically increase stability
Greater species number, connectance, and interaction strength generically decrease local stability
Complexity has no effect on stability under any conditions
Only interaction strength affects stability, not species number or connectance

explanations.a: This is what Elton and MacArthur's intuition predicted, but the opposite of what May's math actually showed.
explanations.b: Correct — May's models showed randomly assembled complex systems are generically less stable, contradicting the earlier diversity-begets-stability intuition and implying real ecosystems must be non-randomly structured to persist.
explanations.c: May's result was specifically that complexity does affect stability — negatively, in random assemblages.
explanations.d: May's model varied all three factors together and found each contributed to destabilization.

questions.prompt: What did Tilman and Downing's 1994 Cedar Creek study measure to test diversity-stability during the 1987-88 drought?

options.text: The number of species that went locally extinct in each plot
The relative decline and recovery rate of total plot productivity across a diversity gradient
Soil pH before and after the drought
The genetic diversity within a single dominant species

explanations.a: The key measured variable was aggregate productivity change, not extinction counts.
explanations.b: Correct — more diverse plots showed a smaller relative drop in total productivity and recovered faster, the core empirical result linking diversity to aggregate stability.
explanations.c: Soil pH was not the measured stability variable in this study.
explanations.d: The study varied plant species number across plots, not within-species genetic diversity.

questions.prompt: Huston's 'sampling effect' critique argues that diversity-productivity results might actually be explained by:

options.text: More diverse plots being more likely to randomly contain one highly productive species, rather than diversity itself causing higher productivity through complementarity
Diverse plots always having worse soil quality
Random measurement error that increases with plot size
A statistical impossibility in Tilman's original design

explanations.a: Correct — this is Huston's core point: a diverse plot is more likely to include a highly productive species by chance, producing a spurious diversity-productivity link unless species identity effects are controlled for.
explanations.b: Soil quality differences were not Huston's proposed confound.
explanations.c: The critique is about a real biological confound (species composition), not measurement error.
explanations.d: Huston's critique was a methodological/interpretive challenge, not a claim that the design was statistically impossible.

questions.prompt: What key distinction does the portfolio/insurance effect concept clarify in the diversity-stability debate?

options.text: That aggregate community properties can be stabilized by diversity even while individual population sizes remain highly variable
That diversity always stabilizes every individual population equally
That diversity has no relationship to stability at any level
That only May's mathematical models are relevant to real ecosystems

explanations.a: Correct — asynchronous species responses can cancel out at the aggregate level (total biomass or productivity) even though individual populations still fluctuate, distinguishing aggregate stability from population-level stability.
explanations.b: The portfolio effect specifically does not claim individual populations become more stable; it operates at the aggregate level.
explanations.c: The concept explains a specific mechanism by which diversity does relate to stability, at the aggregate level.
explanations.d: Both May's models and Tilman's field data remain relevant; the portfolio effect concept builds on and reconciles them, not replaces one with the other.

lessons.label: Neutral Theory and Community Assembly Rules

sections.heading: Hubbell's provocative assumption
sections.body: Stephen Hubbell's The Unified Neutral Theory of Biodiversity and Biogeography (2001) built a model of community structure on a deliberately shocking assumption: that all individuals of all competing species in a given trophic guild are ecologically equivalent — identical per-capita birth, death, dispersal, and (at longer timescales) speciation probabilities, with community dynamics driven purely by random ecological drift, migration, and speciation rather than niche differences. Applied to real data, especially tropical forest plots like Barro Colorado Island in Panama, Hubbell's zero-sum multinomial model reproduced observed species-abundance distributions and species-area relationships strikingly well.

sections.heading: Why a 'wrong' assumption fitting so well was provocative
sections.body: The provocation was epistemological, not just empirical: for decades, niche theory held that coexisting species must differ in resource use or the competitively superior one would exclude the rest, so realistic abundance patterns were assumed to require niche differentiation as an ingredient. Hubbell's model got comparably realistic patterns while assuming the opposite — no niche differences at all — which forced ecologists to confront an uncomfortable possibility: commonly observed abundance and diversity patterns might simply not be sensitive enough to distinguish niche-structured communities from neutrally drifting ones, undermining the evidentiary basis for a great deal of niche-based inference built on pattern-matching alone.

sections.heading: Assembly rules versus the null-model rebuttal
sections.body: A parallel, earlier fight over community structure had already previewed this tension. Jared Diamond's 1975 study of bird distributions across New Guinea's Bismarck Archipelago proposed 'assembly rules' — checkerboard distributions in which certain species pairs never co-occur on the same island — attributing these patterns to interspecific competitive exclusion. Edward Connor and Daniel Simberloff's 1979 rebuttal built explicit null models (randomizations preserving row and column totals of the presence-absence matrix) and showed many of Diamond's checkerboards were statistically indistinguishable from patterns expected by chance colonization and biogeographic constraint alone, without invoking competition at all. Joseph Connell's 1980 'ghost of competition past' paper sharpened the difficulty further: even real historical competition can leave no detectable present-day signature once species have evolved apart or one competitor has gone locally extinct, so a present-day snapshot showing no overlap cannot cleanly distinguish ongoing competition, past competition, or no competition ever having occurred.

sections.heading: The modern niche-neutral synthesis
sections.body: Rather than crowning a winner, the field largely converged on treating neutral theory as an indispensable null model: a rigorous baseline against which departures attributable to real niche differentiation can be statistically measured, as argued in influential syntheses like Adler, HilleRisLambers, and Levine's 2007 'A niche for neutrality.' Most real communities appear to show both — stochastic neutral-like dynamics operating alongside genuine niche differences — with the interesting scientific question shifting from 'which theory is right' to 'how much of this specific pattern is drift versus selection, and at what spatial and temporal scale.'

lessons.workedExample: A student studying tree species abundance in a local woodland plot fits both a neutral (zero-sum multinomial) model and a niche-based resource-partitioning model to their species-abundance data. If both models predict the observed abundance curve almost equally well, that is not evidence the woodland lacks niche differentiation — it replicates exactly the ambiguity Hubbell's results exposed, and the student needs a different kind of test (for example, tracking whether species' recruitment success depends on soil-moisture microsites, a niche-specific prediction neutral theory does not make) rather than relying on abundance-pattern fit alone.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how would you tell a neutral process from a niche-based one in your data?' because Hubbell's result is famous precisely for showing that abundance-pattern fit alone often cannot answer this question, and many student projects unknowingly rely on exactly that weak kind of evidence. A weak answer treats a good model fit to abundance data as proof of the underlying mechanism. A strong answer names the niche-neutral ambiguity directly, cites the assembly-rules/null-model precedent, and proposes an independent test — like a manipulation or trait-specific prediction — that could actually discriminate between the two processes.

questions.prompt: What core assumption defines Hubbell's neutral theory of biodiversity?

options.text: Species differ dramatically in resource-use efficiency, driving all community patterns
All individuals within a trophically similar guild have identical per-capita demographic rates, regardless of species identity
Species abundance is determined entirely by predator population size
Only the most competitively dominant species can persist in any community

explanations.a: This describes classic niche theory, the opposite of neutral theory's core assumption.
explanations.b: Correct — neutral theory's defining, deliberately provocative assumption is ecological equivalence: identical birth, death, dispersal, and speciation probabilities across species within a guild.
explanations.c: Predator-driven abundance is not the mechanism neutral theory proposes; it relies on drift, migration, and speciation.
explanations.d: Neutral theory explicitly rejects competitive dominance as the organizing mechanism of community structure.

questions.prompt: Why was it scientifically provocative that Hubbell's neutral model fit real tropical forest abundance data so well?

options.text: It proved competition never occurs in any ecological community
It suggested commonly used abundance patterns may not reliably distinguish niche-structured from neutrally-drifting communities
It showed that all tropical forests have identical species lists
It disproved the existence of speciation

explanations.a: Neutral theory's fit to data doesn't prove competition is absent; it raises a question about what abundance patterns can and cannot demonstrate.
explanations.b: Correct — a model assuming zero niche differentiation matching real data as well as niche-based models challenged the assumption that pattern-fit alone validates a niche-based mechanism.
explanations.c: The model addressed abundance distributions and diversity patterns, not identical species composition across sites.
explanations.d: Speciation is an explicit component of Hubbell's model, not something it disproves.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or pair to their contribution to the assembly-rules debate.

right.text: Proposed checkerboard 'assembly rules' from New Guinea bird data
Rebutted assembly rules using randomization null models
Coined 'ghost of competition past'
Proposed the unified neutral theory of biodiversity

questions.explanation: Diamond proposed competition-driven assembly rules from Bismarck Archipelago birds; Connor and Simberloff rebutted them with null-model randomizations; Connell's 1980 paper coined 'ghost of competition past'; Hubbell proposed neutral theory in 2001.

questions.prompt: What does the 'ghost of competition past' concept caution against?

options.text: Assuming that a present-day lack of species overlap proves competition is currently occurring, when it could instead reflect past competition or no competition at all
Ever studying historical ecological processes
Using null models in community ecology
Applying neutral theory to any dataset

explanations.a: Correct — Connell's point is that present-day non-overlap is ambiguous evidence: it is consistent with ongoing competition, historical competition with no current signature, or no competition ever having occurred.
explanations.b: The concept encourages more careful historical reasoning, not avoiding it.
explanations.c: Null models are a tool used to address exactly this kind of ambiguity, not something the concept warns against.
explanations.d: Neutral theory application is a separate methodological question from this specific inferential caution.

lessons.label: Live Controversies and How to Talk About Them

sections.heading: Hurlbert and the pseudoreplication problem
sections.body: Stuart Hurlbert's 1984 paper 'Pseudoreplication and the Design of Ecological Field Experiments' (Ecological Monographs) named a design flaw that was already everywhere: treating repeated measurements from a single, unreplicated treatment unit as if they were independent replicates for statistical testing — for instance, sampling one fertilized plot ten times and one control plot ten times, then running a t-test as if there were ten true replicates per treatment rather than one. Hurlbert's review of published field studies found a substantial share used designs with this flaw, and the paper reshaped how ecological experiments are designed and reviewed. The underlying problem — small sample sizes, non-independent replicates, and consequent effect-size inflation or false positives — remains an active concern in ecology's ongoing replication-crisis conversations, alongside newer worries about publication bias favoring large, novel effects.

sections.heading: The insect-decline debate
sections.body: Caspar Hallmann and colleagues' 2017 PLOS ONE study, using 27 years of malaise-trap data from German nature reserves collected largely by amateur entomologists in the Krefeld Entomological Society, reported a 76% decline in total flying insect biomass between 1989 and 2016 (up to 82% at midsummer peaks). The finding drew wide public alarm but also methodological pushback: critics flagged inconsistent trap placement and site turnover over the study period, uncontrolled surrounding land-use change, and weather-driven year-to-year variability that a non-random sample of sites cannot fully separate from a true trend. A later broader meta-analysis, van Klink et al. (2020, Science), found terrestrial insect abundance declining overall but freshwater insects increasing in the same period — complicating any single global narrative and illustrating that both the size and even the direction of 'the' insect decline depend heavily on habitat type and methodology.

sections.heading: Scaling and data-bias disputes
sections.body: Two further live disputes: whether results from small, controlled microcosms and mesocosms (bottle or tank experiments testing diversity-stability or predator-prey dynamics) generalize to real landscapes, where dispersal, spatial heterogeneity, and interaction-web complexity operate at scales no tank can capture; and whether open biodiversity databases like GBIF and NEON, despite their scale, carry systematic sampling bias toward accessible, roadside, and already well-studied sites and toward charismatic, easily identified taxa — meaning apparent global patterns in these databases may partly reflect where and what ecologists chose to sample, not just where organisms actually are.

sections.heading: How to talk about an unresolved debate
sections.body: In judge Q&A, naming a live controversy well means stating both positions accurately, citing the specific evidence on each side, and naming what evidence would actually settle it — without declaring a winner the field hasn't declared. For the insect-decline debate, that means citing Hallmann's 76% figure and its site-consistency critique together, and naming standardized, randomized long-term trapping across land-use gradients as the kind of study that would resolve the disagreement, rather than asserting insects are (or are not) collapsing.

lessons.workedExample: A judge asks a student presenting pollinator survey data: 'Is the global insect decline real?' A weak answer says 'yes, insects have declined 76% according to a 2017 study' as settled fact. A strong answer says: 'Hallmann et al. 2017 found a 76% biomass decline in German reserves, but critics noted the sites weren't a fixed, randomized panel over the 27 years, and van Klink's 2020 global meta-analysis found terrestrial declines but freshwater increases — so the pattern isn't uniform. My own trap data from one site over one season can't resolve that; it can only say whether this local site matches the terrestrial-decline direction.' The second answer cites the real evidence on both sides and correctly scopes what the student's own data can and cannot claim.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges specifically probe live, unresolved debates to test whether a student can distinguish 'what the evidence shows' from 'what I wish the evidence showed,' since science-fair projects are especially prone to overclaiming a clean answer to a genuinely open question. A weak answer picks a side and states it as consensus. A strong answer names the competing evidence with real citations, states what specific study design would settle the disagreement, and is explicit about how far their own project's evidence actually reaches — which is exactly the discipline Hurlbert's pseudoreplication critique demands of everyone's experimental claims, including a judge's own.

questions.prompt: Pseudoreplication, as defined by Hurlbert (1984), occurs when:

options.text: A study has too many true experimental replicates
Repeated non-independent measurements from a single treatment unit are treated statistically as independent replicates
A researcher fails to report any statistics at all
Two different treatments are compared using a t-test

explanations.a: Pseudoreplication is a problem of too few true replicates disguised as many, not too many real ones.
explanations.b: Correct — this is Hurlbert's core definition: samples that are not statistically independent get treated as if they were, inflating apparent sample size and statistical confidence.
explanations.c: The problem specifically concerns how statistics are applied, not their absence.
explanations.d: A t-test itself is not the problem; using it on non-independent samples masquerading as independent replicates is.

questions.prompt: What decline did Hallmann et al. (2017) report in flying insect biomass across German nature reserves from 1989-2016?

options.text: About 10%
About 76%
About 25%
No measurable decline

explanations.a: This substantially understates the study's reported figure.
explanations.b: Correct — the study reported a roughly 76% decline in seasonal mean flying insect biomass, up to 82% at midsummer peaks.
explanations.c: This understates the reported figure by a wide margin.
explanations.d: The study's central, widely publicized finding was a large measured decline, not an absence of one.

questions.prompt: What did van Klink et al.'s 2020 meta-analysis add to the insect-decline debate?

options.text: It confirmed Hallmann's exact 76% figure applies globally
It found terrestrial insects declining but freshwater insects increasing, complicating a single global narrative
It found insect populations were stable worldwide with no trend
It focused exclusively on German nature reserves like the original study

explanations.a: The meta-analysis found more mixed, habitat-dependent results rather than confirming one uniform global figure.
explanations.b: Correct — the divergent trend between terrestrial decline and freshwater increase shows the pattern depends heavily on habitat type, undercutting a single simple global insect-decline narrative.
explanations.c: The analysis found real trends, just not a uniform single-direction global trend.
explanations.d: It was a broader global meta-analysis pooling many studies, not limited to the original German reserve sites.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest way for a student to answer a judge's question about an unresolved ecological debate?

options.text: Pick whichever side sounds more dramatic and state it as settled fact
State both positions with their supporting evidence, name what study would resolve the disagreement, and scope what the student's own data can claim
Avoid the question entirely by saying the topic is too controversial to discuss
Cite only the most recent paper regardless of its methodology

explanations.a: Overclaiming a settled answer to a genuinely open question is exactly the failure mode judges are testing for.
explanations.b: Correct — accurately representing both sides, naming the evidence that would settle the debate, and being precise about the limits of the student's own evidence demonstrates real scientific judgment.
explanations.c: Avoiding the question entirely forfeits the chance to demonstrate understanding of the debate's structure.
explanations.d: Recency alone doesn't establish methodological quality; a strong answer weighs evidence, not just publication date.

units.label: Reading Evidence and Designing a Field Study

lessons.label: Correlation vs Causation in Field Data

sections.heading: Gradients Bundle Their Causes
sections.body: A single urban-to-rural transect can look like a clean natural experiment: sample bird richness at eight points from downtown to remote forest, and richness climbs steadily outward. But every step along that transect changes many things at once - impervious surface, canopy cover, nighttime light, traffic noise, soil compaction from foot traffic, and management regime (mowed lawns vs unmanaged woodlot) all shift together. This is the classic problem field ecologists confront: an observational gradient is a bundle of confounded variables, not a controlled lever on one cause. Mark McDonnell and Steward Pickett's 1990 Ecology paper on urban-rural gradients, later tested empirically along a New York City-to-Litchfield County, Connecticut forest gradient, helped formalize this design - but also its central limitation. A correlation between distance-from-city and species richness cannot, by itself, say which co-varying factor (noise? light? patch size?) is doing the causal work.

sections.heading: Two Routes Toward Real Causal Evidence
sections.body: When you cannot randomly assign 'urban' to a forest, two designs get you closer to causal claims than raw correlation. A natural experiment exploits an event nobody controlled - a hurricane, a dam removal, a wildfire - that hits some sites and spares comparable others, approximating random assignment after the fact. A Before-After-Control-Impact (BACI) design goes further, measuring both impact and reference sites before and after a change, so the causal claim rests on the difference-in-differences rather than a single after-the-fact snapshot. Allan Stewart-Oaten, William W. Murdoch, and Keith Parker formalized this logic in a 1986 Ecology paper responding to weak impact-assessment designs common through the 1970s: a control site's own before-after change tells you what would have happened anyway, so subtracting it out isolates the impact's effect.

sections.heading: Dose-Response as the Strongest Non-Manipulative Evidence
sections.body: The strongest correlational evidence is a monotonic dose-response relationship across many gradient points, ideally checked against a true experiment. David Schindler's Experimental Lakes Area program in Ontario supplied the gold standard: rather than only correlating lake phosphorus with algal blooms across many lakes, his team artificially fertilized whole lakes with phosphorus starting in the early 1970s, reported in a landmark 1974 Science paper, and watched blooms appear on cue, then subside when fertilization stopped - turning a suggestive correlation into a demonstrated cause. Field ecologists without lake-scale budgets settle for the next best thing: sampling many points across a continuous gradient rather than just two extremes, and checking whether the response tracks the presumed cause in a dose-dependent, not merely present-or-absent, way.

lessons.workedExample: A team samples bird richness at two sites - a downtown plaza and a forest 20 km away - finding 6 vs 22 species, and concludes noise reduces richness. But the two sites also differ in canopy cover (5% vs 90%), patch size (0.1 ha vs 40 ha), and light pollution, any of which could explain the gap. A stronger design samples richness at 10 sites spanning a continuous percent-impervious-surface gradient (5% to 95%), measures canopy cover and patch size at each site as covariates, and tests whether richness declines in a dose-dependent way with the gradient after statistically accounting for canopy and patch size - or pairs the gradient with a true experiment, such as broadcasting recorded traffic noise into otherwise quiet forest plots and comparing nest success to silent controls.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'what else changed along your gradient' because it is the fastest way to tell whether a student understands confounding or just ran a two-point comparison and called it causal. A weak answer restates the correlation ('richness was higher away from downtown') as if that settles the question. A strong answer names the specific covariates that moved together with the presumed cause - canopy cover, patch size, light - explains which ones were measured and controlled for, and is honest about which could not be ruled out. Citing Schindler's whole-lake fertilization experiments as the causal gold standard, and explaining why a field project cannot fully replicate that control, shows real understanding of the correlation-causation gap.

questions.prompt: A student finds bird richness is higher in rural forest sites than downtown sites and concludes noise reduces richness. What is the main flaw in this conclusion?

options.text: The sample size is too small to test anything
Noise, light, canopy cover, and patch size all differ at once, so any of them could explain the pattern
Birds are not a valid indicator taxon
The study never stated a hypothesis

explanations.a: Small sample size would weaken statistical power, but even a huge sample of just two site-types would remain confounded - the problem is design, not n.
explanations.b: Correct - this is confounding: several variables change together along the gradient, so the correlation cannot be attributed to noise specifically.
explanations.c: Species richness in a well-studied taxon like birds is a reasonable response variable; that is not the flaw here.
explanations.d: The hypothesis is clear (noise reduces richness); the flaw is that other variables changed along with noise.

questions.prompt: What does a BACI design measure that a single after-the-impact comparison cannot?

options.text: Whether the impact site had higher richness before the study began
The change at the impact site relative to the change at a reference site over the same before/after period
The exact species responsible for any decline
Statistical significance without needing any replication

explanations.a: That is only the 'before' half of the design; BACI's power comes from comparing changes, not a single time point.
explanations.b: Correct - subtracting the reference site's own before-after change isolates what the impact actually caused, per Stewart-Oaten, Murdoch, and Parker (1986).
explanations.c: BACI tests whether an impact had an effect on a measured response; it does not by itself identify causal species-level mechanisms.
explanations.d: BACI still requires adequate replication of impact and reference sites; it does not remove that requirement.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description.

right.text: Exploits an uncontrolled event that hits some sites but spares comparable others, approximating random assignment after the fact
Compares before/after change at both impact and reference sites so the reference's own change can be subtracted out
A variable that changes together with the presumed cause, making it impossible to attribute a correlation to one factor alone

questions.explanation: A natural experiment substitutes an uncontrolled event for random assignment; a BACI design isolates an effect by differencing before/after change at impact vs reference sites; a confound is any co-varying factor that could equally explain an observed correlation.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of implementing a BACI study.

items.text: Select impact site(s) where the disturbance or change will occur
Select comparable reference/control site(s) unaffected by the change
Sample both impact and reference sites BEFORE the change occurs
Let the change or disturbance occur at the impact site only
Sample both impact and reference sites AFTER the change, then compare the before-after difference at impact vs reference

questions.explanation: BACI's causal logic requires both site types to be identified and sampled before the change, so that the impact site's after-change shift can be compared against the reference site's own before-after shift, isolating the effect of the disturbance itself.

lessons.label: Pseudoreplication and Independence

sections.heading: Hurlbert's 1984 Warning
sections.body: Stuart Hurlbert's Ecological Monographs paper 'Pseudoreplication and the Design of Ecological Field Experiments' is among the most-cited methods papers in the field for a reason: it showed that a large fraction of published field experiments treated non-independent measurements as if they were independent replicates, inflating confidence far beyond what the data supported. Hurlbert defined pseudoreplication as using inferential statistics to test a treatment effect when either treatments are not truly replicated - though samples within them may be numerous - or when the replicates used in the analysis are not statistically independent of one another. The fix is not more samples; it is recognizing which unit in the design the treatment was actually applied to.

sections.heading: Three Flavors
sections.body: Simple pseudoreplication: one plot per treatment (one shaded, one sunny), with many quadrats sampled inside each and treated in the analysis as if every quadrat were an independent replicate of 'shade' vs 'sun' - in truth, every quadrat in the shaded plot shares that plot's soil, microclimate, and history, so they are correlated subsamples, not independent replicates of the treatment. Temporal pseudoreplication: sampling the same plots repeatedly over time - weekly for a season - and treating each date as an independent data point, when repeated measures on the same units are autocorrelated. Sacrificial pseudoreplication: true replicate plots exist, but the replication gets discarded before analysis - for example, pooling all quadrats across five replicate plots per treatment into a single number per treatment, throwing away the very structure that would let the treatment be tested properly.

sections.heading: Fixing the Shade-vs-Sun Design
sections.body: The design of one shaded plot and one sunny plot, each with 20 quadrats, has a true n of 1 per treatment - the quadrats are subsamples, not replicates. The fix is to replicate the treatment spatially: for example, five shaded and five sunny plots scattered across the site, interspersed rather than clustered, so that shade is not confounded with whatever else varies from one corner of the site to another - Hurlbert's interspersion principle. Analysis then respects the true unit: average the 20 quadrats to one value per plot, giving a genuine n of 5 per treatment, or fit a mixed-effects model with plot as a random effect so quadrat-level variation cannot masquerade as extra degrees of freedom.

lessons.workedExample: The original design - 1 shaded plot, 1 sunny plot, 20 quadrats each - gets analyzed as a t-test on 40 quadrats (df=38) and reports p=0.01, appearing highly significant. But the true replication is n=1 per treatment: any difference between the two plots could be due to shade, or equally to some other unmeasured difference between those two particular plots (drainage, prior land use), and the test cannot tell them apart. The fix: five shaded and five sunny plots interspersed across the site, 20 quadrats sampled within each plot as before, then quadrats averaged to one cover value per plot before testing - a paired or two-sample test on 5 vs 5 plot means, or a mixed model with plot as a random effect.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'what was your true n' because it is the single fastest way to expose pseudoreplication, and it is the most common flaw in student ecology projects. A weak answer says 'n=40, we had 20 quadrats per treatment' without noticing all 20 came from one plot. A strong answer says 'our true replicate is the plot, not the quadrat; we had n=5 plots per treatment, and quadrats were subsamples we averaged within each plot before testing.' The distinction matters because pseudoreplicated designs report false confidence - a real p=0.01 from n=1 per treatment says almost nothing about the treatment itself.

questions.prompt: A team samples the same 3 plots every week for 10 weeks and analyzes all 30 weekly measurements as 30 independent data points. What type of pseudoreplication is this?

options.text: Simple pseudoreplication
Temporal pseudoreplication
Sacrificial pseudoreplication
This is not pseudoreplication because 30 is a large sample

explanations.a: Simple pseudoreplication is about unreplicated treatments with many within-plot subsamples, not repeated visits to the same units over time.
explanations.b: Correct - repeated measurements on the same 3 plots over time are autocorrelated, so treating all 30 as independent inflates the true sample size.
explanations.c: Sacrificial pseudoreplication involves discarding existing true replication by pooling, which is not what happened here.
explanations.d: A large count of measurements does not create independence; the true replicate count is still 3 plots, regardless of how many times each was visited.

questions.prompt: One shaded plot and one sunny plot are each sampled with 20 quadrats, and a t-test is run treating this as n=40. What is the core problem?

options.text: 20 quadrats per plot is too few to average reliably
The quadrats are subsamples of a true n of 1 plot per treatment, so treatment is confounded with whichever plot happened to be chosen
Quadrats should never be used in field ecology
The t-test is the wrong statistical test for continuous cover data

explanations.a: 20 is a reasonable number of subsamples per plot; the problem is treating them as independent replicates of the treatment, not their quantity.
explanations.b: Correct - this is simple pseudoreplication: quadrats share the plot's soil and microclimate, so they cannot substitute for independent replicate plots.
explanations.c: Quadrats are a standard and useful subsampling tool; the issue is only how they are analyzed relative to true replication.
explanations.d: A t-test is an appropriate test for two-group comparisons of continuous data; the flaw here is the unit of analysis, not the test family.

questions.prompt: Match each pseudoreplication type to its example.

right.text: One plot per treatment, with many quadrats inside it treated as independent replicates
The same experimental units sampled repeatedly over time, with each time point treated as an independent data point
True replicate plots exist but are pooled into a single value per treatment before analysis, discarding the replication

questions.explanation: All three, defined in Hurlbert (1984), share the same root cause - inferential statistics applied to units that are not independent replicates of the treatment - but differ in whether the non-independence comes from unreplicated plots, repeated time points, or discarded existing replication.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to fix the broken shade-vs-sun design (1 shaded plot, 1 sunny plot, 20 quadrats each).

items.text: Identify the true experimental unit: the plot, not the quadrat
Add spatially interspersed replicate plots per treatment (e.g., 5 shaded, 5 sunny)
Collect quadrat subsamples within each plot, as before
Average the quadrats within each plot, or fit a model with plot as a random effect
Analyze at the plot level (n=5 per treatment), not the quadrat level (n=100)

questions.explanation: Fixing pseudoreplication starts with correctly identifying the unit the treatment was applied to, then adding real replication of that unit, and finally analyzing at that unit's level rather than at the level of its subsamples.

lessons.label: Variability, Controls, and Statistical Power

sections.heading: Natural Variability Is the Bar Your Effect Must Clear
sections.body: Field measurements - plant cover, insect counts, soil moisture - vary hugely from quadrat to quadrat, plot to plot, and year to year, driven by microtopography, patchy resource distribution, and stochastic colonization. This natural noise is not a nuisance to wish away; it is the baseline against which any experimental effect has to be detected. The coefficient of variation (CV = standard deviation divided by the mean) for herbaceous plant cover in quadrat-scale field surveys commonly runs 25-40%, and can be higher still for animal counts. Any effect a study hopes to detect must be large relative to that noise, or the study needs enough replicates to average the noise down - which is exactly what a power calculation quantifies before a single quadrat is sampled.

sections.heading: Reducing Noise Before Adding Sample Size
sections.body: Three tools shrink apparent variability without necessarily adding replicates. A control shares every condition with the treatment except the one manipulated, so any difference can be attributed to that manipulation. Blocking groups replicates into similar clusters - by soil type, by slope position - and randomizes treatment within each block, a design R.A. Fisher formalized in the 1920s-30s at Rothamsted Experimental Station; it removes a known source of variation from the error term, so the treatment effect stands out against a smaller residual noise. Interspersion, Hurlbert's term, scatters treatment and control units throughout the site rather than clustering them, so an unmeasured spatial gradient cannot masquerade as a treatment effect.

sections.heading: Computing a Minimum Detectable Effect Before You Collect Data
sections.body: Before going to the field, a planned sample size can be checked against the effect a study hopes to detect using a standard rule of thumb, sometimes called Lehr's equation: n per group is approximately 16 x (CV/effect)^2 for 80% power at alpha=0.05, two-sided (documented in van Belle, Statistical Rules of Thumb, 2002). Run backward, n=3 quadrats per treatment with a typical CV of 30% can only reliably detect an effect around 30% x sqrt(16/3), roughly 69% - nowhere near a realistic 15% difference many field manipulations actually produce. That gap is exactly why so many small pilot studies report 'no significant difference,' and why that result alone proves nothing about whether a real effect exists. Randall Peterman's 1990 analysis in the Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences found exactly this pattern in published fisheries and field ecology studies: many reported 'no significant effect' results turned out to be underpowered rather than genuinely null, once someone went back and checked the sample sizes against the effect sizes those studies could actually detect.

lessons.workedExample: A student expects a 15% increase in leaf-litter decomposition under a nutrient treatment and knows the quadrat-level CV for litter mass loss runs about 30%, typical for field decomposition-bag studies. Using n ≈ 16(CV/effect)^2 = 16 x (0.30/0.15)^2 = 16 x 4 = 64, roughly 64 litter bags per treatment are needed for 80% power. With only 3 bags per treatment planned - a common shortcut under time pressure - the same formula rearranged gives a minimum detectable effect of CV x sqrt(16/n) = 0.30 x sqrt(16/3) ≈ 0.30 x 2.31 ≈ 69%: unless the true effect is roughly 4.5 times the size hoped for, the study is very likely to conclude 'no difference' even if a real 15% effect exists.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about sample size and power because it separates students who picked n=3 because that fit in a weekend from students who checked whether n=3 could ever have detected their hypothesized effect. A weak answer says 'we didn't have time for more replicates.' A strong answer names the CV used, states the minimum detectable effect that sample size could actually find, and is honest that a null result at n=3 does not refute a real 15% effect - it simply lacked the power to see it. That distinction, between 'no effect' and 'not enough data to detect an effect,' is exactly what separates a defensible negative result from an uninterpretable one.

questions.prompt: Why can't natural spatial and temporal variability in field data just be ignored when planning a study?

options.text: It's a minor issue that rounding in the final report resolves
It sets the baseline noise level that any real treatment effect must be distinguished from, which determines how many replicates are needed
It only matters for animal studies, not plant studies
Statistical software adjusts for it automatically regardless of sample size

explanations.a: Rounding does not address variability; it can only obscure it further.
explanations.b: Correct - natural variability is the noise floor an effect must rise above, and it directly determines the sample size a study needs to reliably detect that effect.
explanations.c: Both plant and animal field data show substantial natural variability; neither is exempt.
explanations.d: No software can compensate for an underpowered design; the sample size itself has to be adequate.

questions.prompt: Using n ≈ 16(CV/effect)^2, with CV=30% and a target of detecting a 15% difference at 80% power, roughly how many replicates per group are needed?

explanations.a: 3 replicates would only detect an effect of roughly 69%, far larger than the 15% target - this option confuses the achievable effect with the needed sample size.
explanations.b: 16 is the constant in the formula (from z-values at alpha=0.05, power=0.80), not the answer to the calculation.
explanations.c: Correct - 16 x (0.30/0.15)^2 = 16 x 4 = 64 replicates per group.
explanations.d: 240 overshoots the calculation; it would correspond to a much smaller CV/effect ratio than the one given.

questions.prompt: Blocking replicates by soil type and randomizing treatment within each block increases statistical power mainly by

options.text: Increasing the true sample size
Removing a known source of variation from the error term, making the treatment effect easier to detect
Making the p-value threshold less strict
Eliminating the need for a control group

explanations.a: Blocking does not add replicates; it groups the existing ones more informatively.
explanations.b: Correct - blocking, formalized by R.A. Fisher, isolates a known source of variance (soil type) so it no longer inflates the residual error the treatment effect is judged against.
explanations.c: Blocking changes the design, not the significance threshold itself.
explanations.d: A control remains necessary within a blocked design; blocking and controls address different problems.

questions.prompt: Match each design tool to what it does.

right.text: Shares every condition with the treatment except the manipulated variable, isolating that variable's effect
Groups replicates by a known source of variation and randomizes treatment within each group
Scatters treatment and reference units across the site so unmeasured spatial gradients cannot mimic a treatment effect

questions.explanation: A control isolates the manipulated variable, blocking removes a known variance source from the error term, and interspersion prevents an unmeasured spatial gradient from being confounded with treatment - three distinct ways of raising a study's power without simply adding more replicates.

lessons.label: Error Bars and Confidence Intervals

sections.heading: SD, SE, and CI Answer Different Questions
sections.body: Standard deviation describes the spread of individual observations around the mean - how variable a single quadrat's cover value is. Standard error of the mean (SE = SD divided by the square root of n) describes how precisely the mean itself is known, and shrinks as sample size grows even though the underlying spread of individuals does not. A 95% confidence interval, roughly mean plus or minus 1.96 x SE for a large, normally-distributed sample, is a range constructed so that if the whole sampling process were repeated many times, about 95% of such intervals would contain the true population mean. Plotting error bars without labeling which of the three is shown - a surprisingly common practice - makes a figure impossible to interpret honestly, since SD, SE, and 95% CI bars can look identical on a graph but differ substantially in width.

sections.heading: The Overlap Rule Is Not What Most Students Think
sections.body: Geoffrey Cumming and Sue Finch's widely cited 2005 American Psychologist paper, 'Inference by Eye,' showed that intuitions about error-bar overlap are routinely wrong. The SE-bar rule runs opposite to what most students assume: for n≥10 and roughly equal sample sizes, two means only reach p≈0.05 once their SE bars are SEPARATED by a gap of about one bar-arm, so SE bars that overlap at all usually mean the difference is not significant. For 95% CIs the caution runs the other way: two 95% CIs can overlap substantially, up to about 50% of their length, and the difference between the means can still be significant. So 'the bars touch' rules out neither significance nor non-significance for either bar type - the only safe move is to state which interval was plotted and run the actual test.

sections.heading: When There's No Simple Formula: Bootstrap CIs
sections.body: Some ecological statistics have no straightforward analytic standard error. Shannon diversity (H') is a nonlinear function of proportional abundances, and although approximate formulas exist (Hutcheson, 1970), they perform poorly with small or uneven samples. Mark-recapture population estimates, such as the Lincoln-Petersen estimator N = (M x C) / R, have a skewed sampling distribution, especially with few recaptures. For both, ecologists commonly use the bootstrap, introduced by Bradley Efron in 1979: resample the raw data with replacement thousands of times, recompute the statistic on each resample, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of that distribution as an empirical 95% CI that does not assume normality. The logic behind this is simpler than it sounds: resampling the observed data with replacement treats that one sample as a stand-in for the whole population, so each resample is like drawing a new 'what if we'd sampled slightly differently' dataset. Recomputing the statistic on thousands of these resamples produces a distribution of plausible values, and the spread of that distribution approximates how much the statistic would actually vary if the real sampling process were repeated - which is exactly what a standard error or confidence interval is supposed to capture, without needing a formula for it.

lessons.workedExample: In a stream fish study, 50 fish are marked (M) and released; a second sample of 40 fish (C) includes 8 marked recaptures (R). The Lincoln-Petersen estimate is N = M x C / R = 50 x 40 / 8 = 250 fish. With only 8 recaptures the sampling distribution of N is skewed, so rather than reporting N plus or minus a symmetric SE, the team bootstraps: resample the 40 second-catch fish with replacement 10,000 times, recompute N each time, and report the empirical 95% CI as the 2.5th-97.5th percentile range - for example, roughly 165 to 410 fish, a wide, asymmetric interval that a naive symmetric SE bar would have hidden entirely.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'is that SD or SE' because it is the fastest tell for whether a student understands their own error bars, and asking 'why 250 fish' invites an explanation of why a mark-recapture estimate needs a bootstrap rather than a textbook SE. A weak answer cannot say which interval is plotted, or treats bar overlap as a significance test by itself. A strong answer names the interval, states in one sentence what it means, and explains why a nonlinear statistic like N or H' needed resampling rather than a formula - showing they understand the estimate's uncertainty, not just its point value.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes standard deviation (SD) from standard error (SE)?

options.text: SD describes the precision of the mean; SE describes the spread of individual observations
SD describes the spread of individual observations; SE describes the precision of the estimated mean and shrinks as n grows
They are identical statistics with different names
SE is always larger than SD, regardless of sample size

explanations.a: This reverses the two definitions.
explanations.b: Correct - SD is a property of the data's spread and does not shrink with n; SE = SD/sqrt(n) describes how precisely the sample mean estimates the true mean and does shrink as n grows.
explanations.c: SD and SE are related but distinct: SE is derived from SD divided by the square root of n.
explanations.d: Because SE = SD/sqrt(n) and n is at least 1, SE is always less than or equal to SD, not larger.

questions.prompt: Two group means are plotted with 95% CI error bars that overlap by about 30% of their length. What can be concluded?

options.text: The difference is definitely not significant, because the CIs overlap
The difference could still be statistically significant; overlapping 95% CIs do not rule out p<0.05, so the actual test must be run
The difference is definitely significant, because the CIs are wide
SD bars would necessarily show the opposite result

explanations.a: This is the common but incorrect assumption Cumming and Finch (2005) warned against - 95% CIs can overlap by up to roughly 50% and the difference can still be significant.
explanations.b: Correct - overlap alone does not determine significance for 95% CIs; the appropriate statistical test is needed to know for certain.
explanations.c: Bar width alone does not establish significance either; only the actual test does.
explanations.d: SD bars are not a significance test at all - they show spread of individuals, not precision of the mean - so this claim doesn't follow from anything stated.

questions.prompt: Why do ecologists often bootstrap a confidence interval for Shannon diversity (H') or a Lincoln-Petersen population estimate instead of using a textbook standard-error formula?

options.text: Bootstrapping is required by scientific journals for any statistic
Both statistics are nonlinear functions of counts with skewed or poorly-approximated sampling distributions, so resampling gives a more reliable interval than an analytic formula
Textbook SE formulas do not exist for any ecological statistic
Bootstrapping always produces a narrower interval than the true one

explanations.a: There is no blanket journal requirement to bootstrap every statistic; the choice is driven by the statistic's properties.
explanations.b: Correct - H' and Lincoln-Petersen N are nonlinear functions of counts whose sampling distributions are not well approximated by simple normal-theory formulas, especially at small or uneven sample sizes.
explanations.c: Approximate analytic formulas do exist (e.g., Hutcheson 1970 for H'); the issue is that they perform poorly in common field conditions, not that they don't exist.
explanations.d: Bootstrap intervals reflect the true sampling variability of the statistic and are often wider, not narrower, than a naive symmetric interval would suggest.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of the bootstrap procedure used to get a 95% CI for a mark-recapture population estimate.

items.text: Start with the original capture/recapture data
Resample the data with replacement to create one bootstrap sample of the same size
Recompute the statistic (e.g., N via Lincoln-Petersen) on that resample
Repeat the resampling and recomputation thousands of times to build a distribution of the statistic
Take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of that distribution as the 95% CI

questions.explanation: The bootstrap builds an empirical sampling distribution by repeatedly resampling the original data with replacement and recomputing the statistic each time, then reads the confidence interval directly off the percentiles of that distribution rather than assuming a normal shape.

lessons.label: Choosing and Reading the Right Analysis

sections.heading: Matching the Test to the Design
sections.body: The test should follow from how many groups are compared and what type the data are, not from which test a student already knows. Two independent groups with roughly normal, continuous data call for a two-sample t-test; when normality is doubtful, common with skewed field counts, or samples are small, the nonparametric Mann-Whitney U test (Henry Mann and Donald Whitney, 1947) compares ranks instead of means and makes no distributional assumption. Three or more groups extend the same logic: one-way ANOVA for roughly normal data, or the Kruskal-Wallis test (William Kruskal and W. Allen Wallis, 1952) - effectively ANOVA run on ranks - when they are not. Paired before-after measurements on the same units, the same 10 plots sampled pre- and post-treatment, need a paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test, which uses within-plot differences and is far more powerful than treating before and after as two independent groups.

sections.heading: Counts, Tables, and Gradients
sections.body: Count data in contingency tables - species present or absent across habitat types - call for a chi-square test of independence or, preferred by many ecological statisticians such as John McDonald in his Handbook of Biological Statistics, the G-test, a log-likelihood-ratio test that behaves better with small expected counts. Continuous gradients, richness against elevation, call for correlation or regression, not a t-test. Raw abundance counts are rarely normal: they are often zero-inflated, many quadrats with a true zero, and overdispersed, variance exceeding the mean, which breaks the assumptions of ordinary Poisson regression; ecologists instead fit negative binomial models, which add an extra dispersion parameter tracing back to Greenwood and Yule's 1920 formulation, or zero-inflated models when a large fraction of sites truly have none of the organism.

sections.heading: What a p-value Says, and the Cost of Testing Many Species
sections.body: A p-value is the probability of seeing data this extreme or more, if the null hypothesis were exactly true - not the probability the null is true, and not the probability the result is due to chance, two of the misreadings the American Statistical Association explicitly warned against in its 2016 statement (Wasserstein and Lazar). Testing many things compounds the risk: run 12 separate t-tests, one per species, at alpha=0.05 each, and even if nothing truly differs, the chance of at least one false positive is 1 minus 0.95 to the 12th power, about 46%. A Bonferroni correction, dividing alpha by the number of tests, here 0.05/12 ≈ 0.0042, or a false-discovery-rate procedure (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) keeps that inflation in check.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares insect abundance on 12 tree species using 12 separate two-sample t-tests, each at alpha=0.05, and reports 'red maple showed significantly higher abundance (p=0.03).' Even if none of the 12 species truly differ, the chance that at least one test comes back significant by chance alone is 1 - 0.95^12 ≈ 46%, nearly a coin flip. Applying a Bonferroni correction, the threshold for any single test becomes 0.05/12 ≈ 0.0042, and the red-maple result (p=0.03) no longer clears that bar - it was very likely a false positive produced by testing too many species at once, not a real difference in insect preference.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'why that test' and 'did you correct for testing 12 species' because these two questions instantly reveal whether a project's statistics were chosen to fit the data or borrowed because it was the only test the student had heard of. A weak answer says 'I used a t-test because that's what we learned in class,' regardless of whether the data were counts, paired, or tested repeatedly across many groups. A strong answer names the actual structure of the data, paired or not, count table or gradient, more than two groups, tested many times, explains why that structure demands a particular test, and states plainly what the resulting p-value does and does not mean.

questions.prompt: Match each data/design situation to the test that fits it.

left.text: Three or more groups, roughly normal data
Before-after measurements on the same units
Count data in a table (habitat x present/absent)

right.text: Mann-Whitney U test
One-way ANOVA
Paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Chi-square or G-test

questions.explanation: Test choice follows from the data structure: rank-based tests replace their normal-theory counterparts when normality fails, paired tests exploit within-unit differences for before-after data, and contingency-table counts need chi-square or the G-test rather than a test built for continuous means.

questions.prompt: A student counts beetles in 40 quadrats and finds many quadrats with zero beetles and a variance far larger than the mean. Which model handles this data best?

options.text: Ordinary linear regression
Standard Poisson regression, since ecological counts are always Poisson-distributed
A negative binomial or zero-inflated model, which account for overdispersion and excess zeros
A paired t-test

explanations.a: Linear regression assumes normally distributed, continuous residuals, which count data with many zeros violate.
explanations.b: Standard Poisson regression assumes variance equals the mean; when variance far exceeds the mean (overdispersion), Poisson standard errors are too small and results look falsely significant.
explanations.c: Correct - negative binomial models add a dispersion parameter to handle variance exceeding the mean, and zero-inflated models explicitly separate structural zeros from count variation, matching this data's described pattern.
explanations.d: A paired t-test addresses matched before-after sampling, not the distributional shape of count data.

questions.prompt: What does a p-value of 0.03 actually mean?

options.text: There is a 3% chance the null hypothesis is true
There is a 97% chance the treatment worked
If the null hypothesis were exactly true, there is a 3% chance of seeing data this extreme or more, by chance alone
The effect size is 3%

explanations.a: A p-value is not the probability the null hypothesis is true; that would require different (Bayesian) reasoning entirely.
explanations.b: The p-value says nothing directly about the probability the treatment worked.
explanations.c: Correct - this is the formal definition, and confusing it with the probability the null is true is one of the misinterpretations the ASA's 2016 statement specifically flagged.
explanations.d: A p-value reflects statistical evidence against the null, not the magnitude of any effect - effect size is a separate quantity entirely.

questions.prompt: A student runs 12 separate t-tests, one per species, at alpha=0.05 each. If none of the 12 species truly differ, roughly what is the chance at least one test comes back significant by chance alone?

explanations.a: 5% is the per-test error rate, not the combined chance across all 12 independent tests.
explanations.b: 12% would undercount the compounding effect of running 12 separate tests at 5% each.
explanations.c: Correct - the chance of at least one false positive across 12 independent tests is 1 - (0.95)^12 ≈ 0.46, about 46%.
explanations.d: The chance is high but not certain; some fraction of repeated trials would show no false positives among the 12.

lessons.label: Designing and Defending a Science-Fair Ecology Project

sections.heading: Write the Whole Chain Before You Touch the Field
sections.body: A defensible ecology project states, in writing, before any data collection: a specific question, a hypothesis with a predicted direction - not 'soil moisture affects ant density' but 'ant nest density will be higher in drier, well-drained plots' - the design and replication that will test it, with the true experimental unit identified per Hurlbert's independence standard, an effort budget appropriate to the taxon, and the analysis that will be run on the resulting data. This ordering matters: deciding the analysis after seeing the data invites cherry-picking whichever test gives a significant result, while a plan written in advance functions like the preregistration now standard across much of experimental science - Brian Nosek and colleagues' 2018 PNAS paper, 'The Preregistration Revolution,' formalized this argument.

sections.heading: Effort Budgets and the Detectability Problem
sections.body: Field ecology measures effort in comparable units so different sites or nights can be fairly compared: trap-nights, the number of traps multiplied by the number of nights they were set, for mammal or insect trapping, so a site sampled with 10 traps for 3 nights (30 trap-nights) can be compared to one with 5 traps for 6 nights (also 30 trap-nights) on equal footing, reporting captures per 100 trap-nights. A separate and often-missed issue is detectability: a species can be present but simply not detected on a given visit, so raw counts underestimate true occurrence. Darryl MacKenzie and colleagues' 2002 Ecology paper on occupancy modeling formalized this by using repeated visits to the same sites to separate 'truly absent' from 'present but missed' - a distinction most student projects never address.

sections.heading: The Logbook and the Judge's Questions
sections.body: A dated logbook recording exact locations, weather, time, and any deviation from the plan is what turns a project from a story into evidence, letting a judge check whether the analysis plan really was written before the data came in. The questions that reliably sink ecology projects are predictable: What was your true replicate - the plot or the subsample? How did you handle detectability - did you visit sites more than once? What confounds ride along with your gradient? What result would have falsified your hypothesis - can you state it plainly? And what would you change with one more season? A team that can answer all five without notes has actually done the science; one that cannot has collected data without a design.

lessons.workedExample: Question: does soil moisture affect ant nest density on a hillside? Hypothesis (directional): nest density will be higher in drier, upper-slope plots than in wetter, lower-slope plots. Design: 6 upper-slope and 6 lower-slope plots (12 true replicates), interspersed across three separate hillsides to avoid confounding slope with hillside identity. Effort budget: each plot searched for one person-hour, plus 5 pitfall-trap-nights per plot (5 traps x 1 night) for confirmation, with each plot visited twice to check detectability. Analysis plan, written before data collection: a Mann-Whitney U test comparing nest counts per plot between upper and lower slope, alpha=0.05. Falsification: if median nest density is equal or higher on the wet, lower-slope plots, the hypothesis is rejected.
lessons.judgeFraming: The five rehearsed questions above are the judging rubric in miniature. Judges ask this exact cluster because together they test whether a project has a real design or just a data set. A weak team answers each question by describing what was measured; a strong team answers by explaining what decision each answer would have changed - what they would have concluded if detectability had been low, or if the confound they identified had gone the other way. The falsification question is the sharpest test of all: a hypothesis that could not have been proven wrong by any realistic result was never actually tested, no matter how much data was collected around it.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of planning an ecology project, before touching the field.

items.text: State a specific, answerable question
Write a hypothesis with a predicted direction
Design the replication scheme, identifying the true experimental unit and how many are needed
Set the effort budget (e.g., trap-nights, quadrat count, visits per site for detectability)
Write the analysis plan that will be applied to the resulting data
