questions.explanation: A defensible plan moves from a concrete question to a directional hypothesis to a replication design to a matched effort budget, and finally locks in the analysis before any data exist - so the analysis cannot be chosen to fit whatever pattern shows up.

questions.prompt: A trapping effort of 10 traps for 3 nights at Site A and 5 traps for 6 nights at Site B both equal how many trap-nights, making capture rates comparable between the two sites?

explanations.a: 15 doesn't match either site's trap x night product.
explanations.b: 20 doesn't match either site's trap x night product.
explanations.c: Correct - 10 traps x 3 nights = 30, and 5 traps x 6 nights = 30, so both sites represent equal sampling effort despite different trap counts and durations.
explanations.d: 60 would double either site's actual effort.

questions.prompt: Why does visiting each site more than once matter for detectability?

options.text: It doesn't matter; one visit is always enough
Repeated visits let a study distinguish a species that is truly absent from one that is present but was missed on a given visit, following the occupancy-modeling logic of MacKenzie et al. (2002)
It only matters for plant surveys, not animal surveys
It eliminates the need for a stated hypothesis

explanations.a: A single visit cannot separate true absence from a missed detection, which is exactly the gap occupancy modeling was designed to close.
explanations.b: Correct - repeated visits generate a detection history per site, allowing 'never detected' to be split into 'truly absent' and 'present but undetected.'
explanations.c: Detectability is a general sampling issue and applies at least as strongly to mobile or cryptic animal taxa as to plants.
explanations.d: Detectability is a data-quality issue independent of whether a hypothesis has been stated.

questions.prompt: What makes a hypothesis falsifiable in a defensible ecology project?

options.text: It is phrased as a question
It states a predicted direction specific enough that some realistic result would count as contradicting it
It references a well-known ecologist
It is written after the data are collected

explanations.a: A question alone doesn't commit to a testable prediction; a hypothesis needs a stated, directional claim.
explanations.b: Correct - falsifiability requires naming, in advance, a realistic outcome that would count as evidence against the hypothesis.
explanations.c: Citing a researcher lends context but does not itself make a claim testable.
explanations.d: Writing the hypothesis after seeing the data undermines falsifiability entirely, since the claim can simply be tailored to match what was found.

lessons.label: What Counts as a Population

sections.heading: Two ways to draw the boundary
sections.body: Ecologists delimit a population in one of two ways, and they don't always agree. Geographic delimitation draws a boundary around a place — the fish in this lake, the deer on this island — and treats anyone inside as one population regardless of how much they actually interbreed. Genetic (panmictic) delimitation instead asks where random mating actually breaks down: sample individuals across space, genotype them at neutral markers, and look for a drop in gene flow (rising FST, isolation-by-distance) that marks a real reproductive boundary. The two can disagree sharply. Yellowstone's grizzly bears occupy one contiguous geographic range but split into genetically distinguishable subunits because females rarely disperse far; wood frogs breeding in separate vernal pools 200 m apart can be nearly panmictic if males range widely between ponds. A study that picks the wrong boundary is measuring the wrong thing before it collects a single count.

sections.heading: Open, closed, and why every estimator cares
sections.body: A closed population has no births, deaths, immigration, or emigration during the study window; an open one has some or all of these. Closure is not a detail — it is the load-bearing assumption behind the classic mark-recapture estimators. The Lincoln-Peterson estimator and the closed-population models formalized by Otis and colleagues (1978) only return an unbiased N if no one enters or leaves between the mark and recapture occasions; violate closure and the estimate silently drifts, usually upward — a real overestimate — because marked animals lost to death, emigration, or tag loss deflate the recapture count relative to the total catches, inflating N-hat. Choosing a short enough sampling window, or switching to an open-population model (Jolly-Seber) that explicitly estimates survival and recruitment, is how field ecologists manage this rather than pretend it away.

sections.heading: Census size N versus effective size Ne
sections.body: N counts heads. Effective population size Ne is the size of an idealized, randomly mating population that would lose genetic diversity at the same rate as the real one — and it is almost always much smaller than N. Frankham's 1995 review of 192 Ne/N estimates across 102 species found a median ratio near 0.10. The gap comes from three drivers: skewed reproductive success (a few males siring most offspring collapses Ne per Wright's variance-effective formula), fluctuating N over time (Ne is dominated by the harmonic mean, so one bottleneck year suppresses it for generations), and unequal sex ratio, where Ne = 4NmNf/(Nm+Nf). Northern elephant seals crashed to as few as 20 individuals by the 1890s and rebounded to over 200,000 by the late 20th century — but genetic surveys confirm this: Bonnell and Selander (1974) found no allozyme variation, and Hoelzel et al. (1993) found only two mtDNA control-region haplotypes versus 23 in the southern elephant seal, because the bottleneck's tiny Ne, not today's huge N, set the ceiling on diversity.

lessons.workedExample: A red deer herd has 55 adults: 5 harem-holding stags and 50 hinds, typical of the heavily skewed mating system Clutton-Brock documented on Rum. Census size N = 55. Effective size uses Ne = 4NmNf/(Nm+Nf) = (4 × 5 × 50)/(5+50) = 1000/55 ≈ 18.2. So Ne/N ≈ 0.33 here — better than the cross-species median because only sex ratio is skewed, not also variance in siring success within the 5 stags (which would push Ne lower still) or a historical bottleneck (which would push it lower via the harmonic mean across years).
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks how a student defined their study population because it is the single fastest way to catch a design flaw: a student who sampled one pond and calls it 'the population' without checking dispersal, or who reports N from a headcount and treats it as a proxy for genetic diversity, has skipped a real decision. A strong answer names the boundary criterion used (geographic convenience vs. evidence of restricted gene flow) and, if genetics or extinction risk is part of the claim, distinguishes N from Ne rather than using them interchangeably. A weak answer treats 'population' as self-evident.

questions.prompt: Across Frankham's 1995 review of wild species, the median ratio of effective size to census size (Ne/N) was closest to:

explanations.a: This would mean almost all individuals contribute equally to the next generation's gene pool, which is far higher than what field data show.
explanations.b: Even a moderate ratio like this is well above what Frankham's cross-species compilation found; skew, fluctuation, and sex-ratio effects push the real median much lower.
explanations.c: Correct — Frankham (1995) found a median near 0.10 across 192 estimates from 102 species, meaning effective size is typically an order of magnitude smaller than census size.
explanations.d: This is lower than the typical finding; ratios this small are seen mainly in species with extreme bottlenecks or extreme reproductive skew, not as the general median.

questions.prompt: A closed-population mark-recapture estimate is applied to a site where animals are actually emigrating between the mark and recapture occasions. What happens to the population estimate?

options.text: It remains unbiased because emigration affects Ne, not N
It becomes biased, because the closure assumption underlying the estimator has been violated
It becomes biased only if immigration also occurs
It is unaffected as long as births and deaths are zero

explanations.a: Ne is a separate genetic concept; emigration directly violates the demographic closure assumption the estimator itself depends on, biasing N.
explanations.b: Correct — closed-population estimators like Lincoln-Peterson assume no entries or exits between occasions; emigration alone breaks that assumption and biases the estimate.
explanations.c: Emigration alone is sufficient to violate closure; immigration is a separate, additional violation, not a requirement for bias to appear.
explanations.d: Births and deaths are only two of the four BIDE terms; emigration alone still breaks closure regardless of B and D.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its correct description.

right.text: Boundary drawn by physical location regardless of measured interbreeding
Boundary drawn where gene flow measurably declines
No births, deaths, immigration, or emigration during the study window
Size of an idealized randomly-mating population losing diversity at the same rate as the real one

questions.explanation: Geographic delimitation uses place; genetic delimitation uses measured gene flow; closure is the no-entry/no-exit assumption behind mark-recapture math; Ne is the genetically effective, not headcount, size of a population.

questions.prompt: Why did northern elephant seals retain almost no measurable allozyme genetic variation even after recovering to over 200,000 individuals?

options.text: Because their current census size N is still too small to matter
Because the historical bottleneck of roughly 20 individuals set a low Ne that constrains diversity for many generations, regardless of today's N
Because elephant seals reproduce asexually
Because Ne always equals N in marine mammals

explanations.a: 200,000 is a large census size; the problem is not present-day N but the genetic legacy of a past bottleneck.
explanations.b: Correct — Ne is dominated by the harmonic mean of past population sizes, so a severe historical bottleneck (about 20 individuals in the 1890s) suppresses genetic diversity long after N has rebounded.
explanations.c: Elephant seals are sexually reproducing mammals; asexuality is not relevant here.
explanations.d: Ne/N ratios of 1 would be unusual in any species and are not a general rule for marine mammals.

lessons.label: The BIDE Equation and Growth Currencies

sections.heading: One accounting identity underlies every population model
sections.body: Strip away every complication in population ecology and one bookkeeping statement remains true by definition: N(t+1) = N(t) + B − D + I − E, where B and D are the births and deaths during the interval and I and E are immigrants and emigrants. Graeme Caughley formalized this BIDE framework in his 1977 text Analysis of Vertebrate Populations, and it is not a model of anything — it is an accounting identity, true whether the population is growing, crashing, or stable, because it simply tallies everyone who entered or left. Every growth model you will meet later (exponential, logistic, matrix, integral projection) is really a set of assumptions bolted onto this same identity about how B, D, I, and E depend on N, age, density, or time.

sections.heading: Per-capita rates and two currencies for the same growth
sections.body: Raw counts of B and D depend on population size, so ecologists convert to per-capita rates: b = B/N (births per individual per unit time) and d = D/N (deaths per individual per unit time). For a closed population (I = E = 0), the instantaneous per-capita growth rate is r = b − d, the intrinsic rate of increase used in continuous-time exponential growth. A second currency describes the same change in discrete steps: the finite rate of increase λ = N(t+1)/N(t), a per-step multiplier. The two are related by r = ln(λ), because continuous exponential growth over one unit of time compounds to exactly the same ratio a discrete multiplier produces. λ > 1 means growth, λ = 1 stability, λ < 1 decline — matching r > 0, r = 0, r < 0.

sections.heading: Where the unit mismatch bites
sections.body: Both r and λ are only meaningful attached to a time step, and the single most common student error is silently changing that step mid-calculation. λ compounds multiplicatively across steps — λ over a decade is (λ_annual)^10, not λ_annual × 10 — while r compounds additively in the exponent, so r_annual = 12 × r_monthly holds exactly for the continuous model, but the equivalent move for λ (λ_annual = 12 × λ_monthly) is wrong; the correct conversion is λ_annual = (λ_monthly)^12. Mixing a per-day r estimated from lab bacterial growth with a per-year t in a formula built for one time base produces answers off by orders of magnitude, and it is invisible unless you write the units next to every rate.

lessons.workedExample: A team monitoring a 500-animal population over one year counts B = 60 births, D = 40 deaths, I = 10 immigrants, E = 5 emigrants. BIDE gives N(t+1) = 500 + 60 − 40 + 10 − 5 = 525, so λ = 525/500 = 1.05 and r_total = ln(1.05) ≈ 0.0488 per year (this r reflects all four terms combined). If the team instead wants the intrinsic rate from births and deaths alone, b = 60/500 = 0.12 and d = 40/500 = 0.08, giving r = b − d = 0.04 per year — noticeably different from 0.0488 because immigration and emigration are folded into λ but excluded from the birth-death-only r. Reporting one when the question asked for the other is the exact error a careful judge listens for.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks a student to state their population's growth rate is testing whether the student knows which currency they measured and which time step it is attached to. A strong answer states r or λ with explicit units ('r = 0.04 per year, from births and deaths only, excluding migration') and can convert between them correctly on the spot. A weak answer gives a bare number, conflates r with λ, or — the classic tell — reports an annual rate but multiplies it by 12 to get a decade figure instead of exponentiating, revealing the identity was memorized, not understood.

questions.prompt: In the BIDE equation N(t+1) = N(t) + B − D + I − E, what kind of statement is this?

options.text: A testable hypothesis about density dependence
An accounting identity that is true by definition, regardless of the mechanisms driving B, D, I, E
A model that only applies to closed populations
An approximation valid only for exponential growth

explanations.a: It makes no claim about density dependence or any mechanism; it is a bookkeeping tally of who entered and left.
explanations.b: Correct — BIDE simply counts every individual added or removed during the interval, so it holds regardless of what growth model is layered on top of it.
explanations.c: It applies to open populations too; I and E are included precisely to handle migration, and are just zero for closed populations.
explanations.d: It underlies exponential, logistic, and every other growth model equally; it is not itself an approximation.

questions.prompt: A population has λ_monthly = 1.02. What is λ_annual?

explanations.a: λ compounds multiplicatively across steps, not additively by multiplication of the rate itself; this treats λ like an additive rate and overshoots hugely.
explanations.b: Correct — λ is a per-step multiplier, so 12 monthly steps compound as λ_monthly raised to the 12th power, giving about 1.268, a 26.8% annual increase.
explanations.c: Adding a count of time steps to a multiplicative rate has no mathematical basis.
explanations.d: Dividing λ by the number of steps is the wrong direction and the wrong operation for a compounding multiplier.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to correctly convert a births-and-deaths-only census into an intrinsic growth rate r for one year, given N(t)=500, B=60, D=40.

items.text: Compute per-capita birth rate b = B/N = 60/500 = 0.12
Compute per-capita death rate d = D/N = 40/500 = 0.08
Subtract: r = b − d = 0.04 per year
Report r with its explicit time unit (per year) and note migration was excluded

questions.explanation: b and d must each be computed as rates before they can be subtracted to get r, and the final step of attaching the time unit and scope (births/deaths only) is what prevents the value from being misread or misapplied later.

questions.prompt: Why is r = ln(λ) the correct relationship between the two growth currencies, rather than r = λ − 1?

options.text: Because λ is defined as a percentage and r is not
Because continuous exponential growth at rate r over one time unit compounds to exactly the same ratio as the discrete multiplier λ, and e^r = λ is that equality, so r = ln(λ)
Because r and λ measure different populations
r = λ − 1 is in fact the correct relationship for all cases

explanations.a: λ and r are both dimensionless-per-time rates in different mathematical forms (multiplicative vs. exponential), not a percentage-vs-non-percentage distinction.
explanations.b: Correct — the continuous model N(t+1) = N(t)e^r must equal the discrete model N(t+1) = N(t)λ for the same interval, forcing e^r = λ and therefore r = ln(λ).
explanations.c: They describe the same population over the same interval, just in two different mathematical forms.
explanations.d: r = λ − 1 is only a close approximation when λ is near 1 (slow growth); it diverges from the true r = ln(λ) as growth gets faster.

lessons.label: Density, Abundance, and Spatial Dispersion

sections.heading: Two densities, and why the denominator matters
sections.body: Crude density is N divided by total area — every hectare of the study site, occupied or not. Ecological (specific) density, a distinction Eugene Odum emphasized, divides N by only the area of habitat actually usable by the species: the wetland patches within a landscape, not the surrounding farmland. A deer population reported as '2 per km²' across a whole county sounds sparse; the same deer reported per km² of actual forest cover might be 15 per km², a number that predicts browsing pressure and competition far better. Which density to report is a judgment call that changes the biological conclusion, not just the units.

sections.heading: Diagnosing dispersion with numbers, not eyeballs
sections.body: Individuals in space fall into three patterns — random, uniform, or clumped — and telling them apart by looking at a map is unreliable; the standard is a quantitative test on quadrat counts. Under a random (Poisson) distribution, the variance equals the mean, so the ratio s²/x̄ = 1 is the null expectation. A ratio above 1 signals clumping (individuals attract, or respond to shared clumped resources); a ratio below 1 signals uniform spacing (individuals repel, as in territorial birds). A second, more robust tool is Morisita's index of dispersion, Id = n·[Σxi(xi−1)] / [N(N−1)], computed across n quadrats with counts xi summing to N: Id = 1 matches random, Id > 1 clumped, Id < 1 uniform, and it is less sensitive to quadrat size than the raw variance-to-mean ratio.

sections.heading: The negative binomial and why clumping punishes your sample size
sections.body: When counts are clumped, the Poisson distribution underestimates variance badly, so ecologists fit the negative binomial distribution instead, whose variance is mean + mean²/k. The parameter k is inversely tied to aggregation: small k (near 0) means severe clumping, and as k → ∞ the negative binomial converges back to the Poisson. L. R. Taylor's 1961 Nature paper formalized the same idea as a power law, variance = a·mean^b, with b near 2 typical of strongly aggregated insects and b near 1 typical of near-random distributions — a relationship now called Taylor's Power Law and confirmed across hundreds of species. The practical consequence is blunt: clumped distributions inflate the variance of any count-based abundance estimate, so a clumped population needs many more quadrats than a random one to pin down N to the same precision — sampling a few quadrats and extrapolating will badly underestimate the true uncertainty.

lessons.workedExample: A student counts aphids in 10 randomly placed 0.25 m² quadrats on a bean field: counts are 2, 3, 45, 1, 50, 2, 0, 48, 1, 3 (total N = 155, mean x̄ = 15.5). The variance is large (s² ≈ 495) because three quadrats landed on infested clusters and seven landed on nearly bare plants — s²/x̄ ≈ 32, far above 1, confirming strong clumping rather than random dispersion. Fitting a negative binomial gives a small k (roughly 0.5–1), consistent with aphid colonies founded by a few winged migrants that then reproduce clonally in place. Because of this clumping, the same 10-quadrat sample used for a randomly dispersed insect would give a much tighter, more trustworthy estimate of mean density than it does here.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes dispersion because 'my organism was clumped/random/uniform' is a claim that is either backed by a variance-to-mean ratio or Morisita's index, or it is just a guess from staring at a map. A strong answer reports the actual ratio or index value and connects it to a mechanism (shared resource patches, territoriality, clonal spread) rather than describing the pattern. It also recognizes the downstream consequence: a clumped population needs a larger or stratified sample to estimate density with the same confidence as a random one, and a student who increased quadrat number after finding s²/x̄ » 1 is showing real statistical judgment, not just following a protocol.

questions.prompt: A researcher finds s²/x̄ = 4.2 for quadrat counts of a shrub species. What does this indicate?

options.text: Uniform dispersion, because the ratio is above 1
Random (Poisson) dispersion, since any ratio above 1 is within sampling noise of 1
Clumped dispersion, since variance substantially exceeds the mean
The result is uninterpretable without knowing quadrat size

explanations.a: Uniform dispersion produces a ratio below 1, from repelled/evenly-spaced individuals, the opposite of this result.
explanations.b: The Poisson null expectation is a ratio of exactly 1; 4.2 is far enough above 1 to indicate real aggregation, not noise.
explanations.c: Correct — a variance-to-mean ratio well above 1 is the signature of clumped (aggregated) dispersion.
explanations.d: Quadrat size can affect the magnitude of the ratio, but a ratio this far above 1 already signals clumping under standard practice.

questions.prompt: In the negative binomial distribution (variance = mean + mean²/k), what does a very small value of k indicate?

options.text: Near-random (Poisson-like) dispersion
Severe clumping/aggregation
Perfectly uniform dispersion
That the mean must also be small

explanations.a: Poisson-like behavior corresponds to k approaching infinity, not a small k.
explanations.b: Correct — small k inflates the mean²/k term, producing high variance relative to the mean, the signature of strong aggregation.
explanations.c: Uniform dispersion has variance below the mean, which the negative binomial (variance ≥ mean) cannot represent at all.
explanations.d: k and the mean are independent parameters; a small k says nothing about the mean's magnitude.

questions.prompt: Taylor's Power Law (1961) describes variance as a·mean^b. A value of b close to 2 across many insect datasets indicates:

options.text: Strong, consistent spatial aggregation
Uniform spacing driven by territoriality
That sampling error dominates over any real spatial pattern
That density and dispersion are unrelated

explanations.a: Correct — Taylor found b near 2 was typical of strongly aggregated species, a pattern that held across hundreds of species when he compiled it.
explanations.b: Uniform spacing corresponds to variance growing more slowly than the mean, i.e., b closer to or below 1, not near 2.
explanations.c: Taylor's Power Law describes a real, repeatable biological relationship between variance and mean, not sampling artifact.
explanations.d: The whole point of the power law is that variance and mean are systematically related via the exponent b, which itself reflects the degree of aggregation.

questions.prompt: Match each dispersion pattern to its variance-to-mean signature.

right.text: s²/x̄ = 1
s²/x̄ < 1
s²/x̄ > 1

questions.explanation: Poisson (random) dispersion sets variance equal to the mean by definition; repulsion among individuals (uniform) suppresses variance below the mean; attraction or shared clumped resources (clumped) inflates variance above the mean.

lessons.label: Age, Stage, and Size Structure

sections.heading: When age is the wrong currency
sections.body: Human-style age structure — count everyone by birth year — assumes age reliably predicts survival and reproduction. For many organisms it does not. A 2-year-old oak and a 200-year-old oak both have a chronological age, but what predicts an oak's fecundity and mortality risk is its size and canopy position, not its age; two oaks the same age growing in shade versus full sun can differ by orders of magnitude in reproductive output. Fish, most insects, and many plants are classified by life-cycle stage (egg, larva, juvenile, reproductive adult) or by size class instead, because stage or size tracks the biology that matters while age is either unmeasurable or biologically uninformative. The tradeoff is that stage and size classes are drawn by the researcher, not given by nature — a study using five size bins and one using ten will produce different-looking structures from the same population, so the classification scheme itself needs to be reported and justified, not treated as a neutral measurement.

sections.heading: Ageing methods that generate real data
sections.body: Where age can be measured, it usually comes from counting growth increments laid down in hard tissue. Fish otoliths (ear stones) accumulate annual rings readable much like tree rings, a method pioneered on plaice by Reibisch in 1899 and still central to fisheries stock assessment today. Mammal age is commonly read from cementum annuli — annual growth layers in tooth root cementum, first developed systematically for pinnipeds and ungulates in the mid-20th century and still the standard for aging deer, seals, and carnivores from a single extracted tooth. Tree age comes from ring counts via dendrochronology, a field A. E. Douglass established in the early 1900s using cross-dated ring-width patterns. Insects usually lack annual rings, but larvae passing through discrete instars obey Dyar's Law (1890): head-capsule width increases by a roughly constant ratio, often near 1.4, at each molt, letting a single head-capsule measurement assign an insect to its instar.

sections.heading: Reading a pyramid past its shape
sections.body: An age or stage pyramid's overall shape — expanding (broad base, many juveniles), stationary (roughly even bars), or contracting (narrow base) — gives a first-pass read on whether a population is growing, stable, or declining. But the shape name is only the headline; the data underneath carries more information. Percent juveniles quantifies recruitment intensity rather than just its presence. A missing or thin bar at a specific age — a cohort gap — flags a single bad recruitment year, a signal fisheries stock assessments use routinely to detect a year-class failure caused by a poor spawning season or a bad larval survival year, distinct from a gradually declining trend.

lessons.workedExample: A fisheries team ages 200 walleye from otolith sections and builds an age pyramid. Ages 1–3 are well represented (roughly 15% of the sample each), but age-4 fish make up under 2% of the sample — a sharp cohort gap — while ages 5–7 recover to 8–10% each. Read only by overall shape, the pyramid looks 'expanding' and healthy. Read for the gap, it reveals that four years ago a single poor spawning season (perhaps a cold, high-flow spring that scoured nests) produced almost no surviving recruits, a signal that will predict a temporary dip in the fishable population four years from now, once today's strong young cohorts have not yet grown large enough to replace the missing one.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees an age or size pyramid in a project display is checking whether the student read it or just labeled it. Naming the shape ('expanding pyramid') is the minimum; a strong answer goes further, quantifying percent juveniles, pointing to any cohort gaps, and proposing a specific cause (a bad recruitment year, a size-selective harvest) rather than a vague 'the population is growing.' It is also a chance to catch overconfidence in the classification itself — a student who used size classes should be able to defend where the size-bin boundaries came from and admit that a different binning could shift the picture.

questions.prompt: Why do ecologists often classify plants and many insects by size or stage rather than chronological age?

options.text: Because size and stage are always easier to measure than age in every organism
Because for these organisms, survival and reproduction track size or life stage much more closely than they track chronological age
Because age structure is only defined for vertebrates
Because size classes require no researcher judgment, unlike age

explanations.a: Measurability varies by taxon and method; the deeper reason is biological relevance, not universal ease of measurement.
explanations.b: Correct — an oak's fecundity and mortality risk depend on its size and light environment far more than on its age in years, so size or stage is the biologically meaningful currency.
explanations.c: Age structure can be applied to any organism where age is measurable; the issue is whether age is the biologically informative variable, not taxonomic restriction.
explanations.d: Size and stage bins are chosen by the researcher just as age bins are, and different binning choices can change the resulting structure.

questions.prompt: Match each taxon to the structure it commonly used to determine age.

right.text: Otolith annual rings
Tooth cementum annuli
Dendrochronological ring counts
Head-capsule width and instar count (Dyar's Law)

questions.explanation: Fish age is read from otolith rings, mammals from tooth cementum annuli, trees from ring counts (dendrochronology), and insect larvae from instar stage inferred via Dyar's Law's head-capsule scaling.

questions.prompt: A walleye age pyramid shows a sharp dip at age-4 while ages 1–3 and 5–7 are all well represented. What does this cohort gap most likely indicate?

options.text: A steady long-term population decline
A single poor recruitment year roughly four years before sampling
That age-4 fish are systematically undercounted by the otolith method
That the population has an unusually low overall growth rate

explanations.a: A steady decline would thin every younger age class progressively, not produce a sharp dip isolated to one cohort with normal classes on both sides.
explanations.b: Correct — a narrow dip at one specific age, with normal representation before and after, is the classic signature of one bad spawning or larval-survival year for that single cohort.
explanations.c: There is no stated evidence of a method-specific bias against age-4 fish; otolith aging works the same way at every age.
explanations.d: An isolated single-age dip does not indicate a general property like overall growth rate, which would show up as a broader pattern, not a single missing cohort.

questions.prompt: Dyar's Law (1890) describes what regularity in insect larval development?

options.text: Head-capsule width increases by a roughly constant ratio at each successive molt
Every insect species has exactly five instars
Larval body mass doubles at a fixed calendar interval regardless of temperature
Instar number is unrelated to head-capsule size

explanations.a: Correct — Dyar's Law states that head-capsule width scales by a roughly constant ratio (often near 1.4) at each molt, letting instar be inferred from a single measurement.
explanations.b: Instar counts vary substantially among insect species/orders; Dyar's Law describes a scaling pattern, not a fixed count of instars.
explanations.c: The law concerns a geometric scaling of a hard structure across molts, not a calendar-based mass-doubling rule.
explanations.d: The entire utility of Dyar's Law is that head-capsule size and instar are tightly related, which is the opposite of this claim.

lessons.label: Sex Ratio, Mating System, and Two-Sex Demography

sections.heading: Three sex ratios, measured at three different moments
sections.body: 'Sex ratio' hides which life stage was counted. The primary sex ratio is the ratio at fertilization/conception, before any stage-specific mortality has acted. The secondary sex ratio is the ratio at birth or hatching, after any embryonic mortality that differs by sex. The tertiary sex ratio is the ratio among sexually mature adults, after further sex-biased mortality across juvenile life. These can diverge substantially: human secondary sex ratio runs roughly 105 males per 100 females, but male mortality outpaces female mortality at nearly every life stage, so the tertiary ratio at reproductive age drifts back toward parity and then past it in older cohorts. A fourth, situational measure — the operational sex ratio (OSR), the ratio of sexually active, mate-seeking males to receptive females at a given moment — was formalized by Emlen and Oring in their influential 1977 Science paper connecting OSR to the intensity of sexual selection and mating-system evolution.

sections.heading: Why 1:1 is the evolutionary default
sections.body: R. A. Fisher's 1930 argument (The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection) explains why most sexually reproducing species hover near a 1:1 secondary sex ratio despite no obvious ecological reason to do so. If one sex becomes rare, each individual of that rare sex has, on average, more mates and more offspring than an individual of the common sex, so parents genetically predisposed to produce the rarer sex leave more grandoffspring. This frequency-dependent advantage pushes the ratio back toward equality — a self-correcting mechanism now called Fisher's principle, and one of the earliest clean examples of frequency-dependent natural selection identified.

sections.heading: Why models go female-only, and when that assumption breaks
sections.body: Most population projection models (Leslie matrices, life tables) track only the female half of the population and assume male availability never limits reproduction — reasonable in species where a small number of males can fertilize many females and mating is easy to find, so B is well predicted by female fecundity and survival alone, with no separate male bookkeeping needed. That assumption fails under a highly skewed operational sex ratio (very few receptive females relative to searching males, or vice versa), under strict monogamy where each female needs one specific available male, and under Allee effects in small populations where mate-finding itself becomes unreliable. The standard fix is a two-sex model using a harmonic-mean birth function: births are made a function of the harmonic mean of male and female numbers rather than female number alone, because the harmonic mean is disproportionately dragged down by whichever sex is scarcer, correctly capturing mate limitation in a way a female-only model cannot.

lessons.workedExample: A reintroduced condor population has 40 females but only 6 breeding-age males after a die-off skewed toward males lost to lead poisoning near carcasses. A female-only model would use only the 40 females to project births, implicitly assuming 6 males can service all of them without limitation — plausible for a highly polygynous species, less so if pairing is largely monogamous, as it is in condors. A two-sex harmonic-mean birth function instead computes 2·(40×6)/(40+6) ≈ 10.4 as the effective breeding-pair currency, sharply lower than 40, correctly predicting that male scarcity — not female number — is now the bottleneck limiting how fast the population can recover.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes sex-ratio assumptions because 'we assumed a 1:1 sex ratio' or 'we modeled females only' are convenience choices with real consequences, and a fair-goer should know why they made them. A strong answer distinguishes primary/secondary/tertiary ratios when relevant, cites Fisher's principle as the reason 1:1 is a sensible default rather than an arbitrary guess, and — if the study organism has a skewed or monogamous mating system — flags that a female-only model would understate mate limitation and describes (even qualitatively) the two-sex fix. A weak answer treats sex ratio as a fixed fact rather than a life-stage-dependent, mechanism-driven quantity.

questions.prompt: Match each sex-ratio term to the life stage or context at which it is measured.

right.text: At fertilization/conception
At birth or hatching
Among sexually mature adults
Ratio of sexually active, mate-seeking males to receptive females at a given moment

questions.explanation: Primary is measured at fertilization, secondary at birth/hatching, tertiary among reproductive-age adults, and OSR is the situational ratio of currently mate-seeking individuals that Emlen and Oring (1977) tied to sexual-selection intensity.

questions.prompt: According to Fisher's principle (1930), what restores a population's sex ratio toward 1:1 when one sex becomes rare?

options.text: Rare-sex individuals gain higher average reproductive success, so parents predisposed to produce that sex leave more descendants — a frequency-dependent selective advantage
Predators preferentially remove the more common sex
Environmental temperature automatically corrects the ratio in all species
Population size itself has no effect on sex ratio evolution

explanations.a: Correct — when one sex is rarer, each of its individuals has more available mates on average, so genes favoring production of the rare sex spread, pulling the ratio back toward parity.
explanations.b: Fisher's argument is about differential reproductive opportunity from rarity, not a predation mechanism.
explanations.c: Temperature-dependent sex determination exists in some reptiles but is not the general mechanism Fisher described, which applies far more broadly.
explanations.d: Fisher's principle is precisely a population-size/frequency-dependent effect; it is central, not absent.

questions.prompt: Most population projection models track only females and assume male availability never limits births. Under which condition does this assumption most clearly break down?

options.text: When the species is highly polygynous with abundant males
When the operational sex ratio becomes highly skewed, mating is strictly monogamous, or the population is small enough for Allee-type mate limitation
When female survival is high
When the population is at carrying capacity

explanations.a: Abundant males relative to females is exactly the scenario where the female-only assumption holds up well, not where it breaks.
explanations.b: Correct — a skewed OSR, strict monogamy, or small-population mate limitation are the conditions under which male availability, not just female fecundity, starts to cap the birth rate.
explanations.c: High female survival does not by itself create male mate limitation; it says nothing about male availability.
explanations.d: Carrying capacity relates to density dependence generally, not specifically to whether male scarcity limits mating.

questions.prompt: Why does a two-sex model use the harmonic mean of male and female numbers, rather than the arithmetic mean, in its birth function?

options.text: The harmonic mean is easier to compute
The harmonic mean is disproportionately pulled down by whichever sex is scarcer, correctly representing mate limitation
The harmonic mean always equals the arithmetic mean when sexes are unequal
The harmonic mean ignores sex ratio entirely

explanations.a: Computational ease is not the biological justification; the harmonic mean is chosen for its mathematical behavior under imbalance.
explanations.b: Correct — the harmonic mean is sensitive to the smaller of the two values, so a scarce sex sharply reduces the harmonic mean even if the other sex is abundant, matching how mate limitation actually works.
explanations.c: The harmonic mean is strictly less than or equal to the arithmetic mean, and the two diverge more, not less, as the two numbers become unequal.
explanations.d: The entire reason to use it is that it is sensitive to sex-ratio imbalance, the opposite of ignoring it.

lessons.label: Life-History Timing: Generation Time and Reproductive Schedule

sections.heading: One big bet or many small ones
sections.body: Semelparous organisms reproduce exactly once, investing everything, then die: Pacific salmon that spawn a single time upriver, the century plant (Agave) that flowers once after years of growth, and periodical cicadas emerging synchronously after 13 or 17 years underground. Iteroparous organisms reproduce repeatedly across multiple seasons, spreading the bet: most mammals, birds, and perennial plants. Lamont Cole's 1954 paper 'The Population Consequences of Life History Phenomena' posed a puzzle now called Cole's paradox: adding just one extra iteroparous reproductive event should, by his simple algebra, confer almost as much of a growth-rate advantage as an entire additional semelparous reproductive episode, which seemed to predict iteroparity should almost always win. Later work (notably Charnov and Schaffer, 1973) resolved the paradox by showing Cole's model ignored adult versus juvenile survival differences — once survival costs of repeated breeding are included, semelparity's advantage in high-juvenile-mortality environments reappears.

sections.heading: Age at first reproduction sets the clock
sections.body: Age at first reproduction, α, is the age at which an individual begins contributing to B. It varies enormously: a mouse can breed at 6 weeks, an African elephant rarely before 10-12 years, a female loggerhead sea turtle not until 20-30 years old. α matters beyond biology trivia because population growth rate r is disproportionately sensitive to changes in the age at which reproduction starts: shaving years off α raises r more steeply than an equivalent proportional gain in fecundity does, because every year removed from the front of the reproductive schedule compounds through survivorship for the rest of the cohort's life. That asymmetry is the same one underlying Cole's paradox in the previous section — one extra early breeding event is worth disproportionately more than raw offspring counts suggest — and it is why the R0-versus-T tradeoff in the next section hinges on timing, not just lifetime totals.

sections.heading: Two definitions of generation time, and why the choice matters
sections.body: Generation time T is often loosely defined as 'time between generations,' but demographers use two distinct formal versions. Cohort generation time Tc is the mean age of mothers when their offspring are born, weighted by survivorship and fecundity across a single cohort's life table: Tc = Σ(x·lx·mx) / Σ(lx·mx), where x is age, lx is survivorship to age x, and mx is fecundity at age x. A second, population-level definition treats T as the mean age of reproducing parents in a stable-age-distribution population, connected to the net reproductive rate R0 (offspring per individual per lifetime) and r by the approximation r ≈ ln(R0)/T. The two definitions can differ when survivorship and fecundity schedules are irregular, and picking the wrong one changes the r estimate you back out.

lessons.workedExample: Two hypothetical fish populations both have a net reproductive rate R0 = 2 (each fish replaces itself twice per lifetime). Population A has cohort generation time Tc = 2 years (fast-maturing, short-lived); population B has Tc = 10 years (slow-maturing, long-lived). Using r ≈ ln(R0)/T: population A gets r ≈ ln(2)/2 ≈ 0.347 per year, population B gets r ≈ ln(2)/10 ≈ 0.069 per year — a five-fold difference in growth rate from identical lifetime reproductive output, purely because A turns generations over five times faster. A depleted population of type A can rebuild in a few years; a depleted population of type B, even with the same R0, needs a decade or more, which is exactly why slow-maturing species like sharks and sea turtles recover so much slower from overharvest than short-generation species with comparable R0.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about generation time when a student claims a population 'can bounce back' or 'is vulnerable to decline,' because R0 alone is a misleading predictor of recovery speed — T is often the dominant lever. A strong answer distinguishes R0 (how much a generation replaces itself) from T (how long a generation takes) and can explain, even with a rough number, why a species with late age at first reproduction recovers slowly even with a healthy R0. A weak answer cites only R0, or uses 'generation time' as a vague phrase without stating which definition (cohort Tc vs. stable-population T) it means, which matters when the two would give different numeric answers for an irregular life table.

questions.prompt: What is Cole's paradox (1954)?

options.text: The observation that semelparous species always outcompete iteroparous ones

The finding that, in a simplified model, adding one iteroparous reproductive event yields nearly as much growth-rate benefit as an entire extra semelparous episode, seeming to predict iteroparity should almost always be favored
The claim that generation time has no effect on population growth rate
A paradox about why sex ratios deviate from 1:1

explanations.a: The paradox runs the opposite direction — it seemed to favor iteroparity too strongly, not semelparity.
explanations.b: Correct — Cole's simplified algebra suggested one extra iteroparous breeding bout was worth almost as much as an entire extra semelparous reproductive episode, a result later shown to ignore survival costs.
explanations.c: The paradox is precisely about how reproductive scheduling affects growth rate, not a claim that it's irrelevant.
explanations.d: This concerns semelparity/iteroparity and reproductive scheduling, unrelated to sex-ratio evolution.

questions.prompt: What resolved Cole's paradox, according to later work by Charnov and Schaffer (1973)?

options.text: Including the survival cost differences between juveniles and reproducing adults, which restores semelparity's advantage under high juvenile mortality
Showing that Cole's original math contained an arithmetic error unrelated to biology
Proving that generation time is irrelevant to the paradox
Demonstrating that semelparity does not actually exist in nature

explanations.a: Correct — Cole's original model omitted survival differences between juveniles and breeding adults; accounting for these costs of repeated breeding restores semelparity's advantage in high-juvenile-mortality settings.
explanations.b: The resolution was biological (an omitted survival term), not a simple arithmetic correction.
explanations.c: Generation time and survival scheduling are central to the resolution, not irrelevant.
explanations.d: Semelparity is well documented (salmon, agave, periodical cicadas); the paradox concerned when it is favored, not whether it exists.

questions.prompt: Two populations both have R0 = 2, but population A has Tc = 2 years and population B has Tc = 10 years. Using r ≈ ln(R0)/T, which statement is correct?

options.text: Population A has a growth rate about five times higher than population B
Both populations have identical growth rates because R0 is the same
Population B grows faster because it lives longer
Growth rate cannot be estimated without knowing population size

explanations.a: Correct — r_A ≈ ln(2)/2 ≈ 0.347/yr and r_B ≈ ln(2)/10 ≈ 0.069/yr, roughly a five-fold difference despite equal R0, because T sets how fast that lifetime output is realized per year.
explanations.b: R0 being equal does not make r equal; r also depends on T, which differs five-fold here.
explanations.c: Longer generation time slows, not speeds, the per-year growth rate for a given R0.
explanations.d: r ≈ ln(R0)/T is a rate independent of absolute population size; N is not needed for this estimate.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compute cohort generation time Tc from life-table data.

items.text: For each age x, obtain survivorship lx and fecundity mx from the life table
Compute the product x·lx·mx for each age x
Sum x·lx·mx across all ages to get the numerator, and sum lx·mx across all ages to get the denominator
Divide the numerator by the denominator to obtain Tc

questions.explanation: Tc = Σ(x·lx·mx)/Σ(lx·mx) requires first gathering lx and mx per age, forming the weighted product per age, summing both the weighted and unweighted totals across ages, and finally dividing to get the survivorship-and-fecundity-weighted mean maternal age.

lessons.label: Discrete vs Continuous Time, and Doubling Time

sections.heading: Two clocks for the same kind of growth
sections.body: Geometric growth, N_t = N_0·λ^t, describes populations that reproduce in discrete pulses — a single annual breeding season, non-overlapping generations, a step every t = 1, 2, 3 units. Exponential growth, N_t = N_0·e^(rt), describes populations that reproduce continuously, with births and deaths happening at every instant rather than in one synchronized burst. The two are mathematically compatible: when λ = e^r, they predict identical population sizes at every whole time step, so for many textbook purposes they are used interchangeably. They diverge in what they claim is happening between those steps. A population of once-a-year breeders (say, an annual plant or a bird with a single spring clutch) genuinely jumps in a step function — flat, then a pulse, then flat again — and modeling it as smoothly exponential misrepresents the within-year pattern even though the year-to-year endpoints match.

sections.heading: Which one to use is a biology question, not a math preference
sections.body: The right choice follows the organism's actual reproductive schedule. Species with sharply seasonal, synchronized breeding (most temperate birds, many insects with one generation per year, annual plants) are naturally geometric — population size only truly changes at the pulse. Species with year-round or highly overlapping reproduction (bacteria dividing continuously, many tropical species, most large mammals with staggered birth timing across a population) are better approximated as exponential, since new individuals are entering continuously rather than all at once. Using the wrong form does not just introduce rounding error; it changes what a mid-interval prediction means — a geometric model has nothing meaningful to say about month 6 of an annual cycle, while an exponential model asserts a specific, and possibly false, smooth trajectory through that point.

sections.heading: Doubling time and where students lose the units
sections.body: Doubling time, td = ln(2)/r, answers 'how long until N doubles' directly from the instantaneous rate r. It scales across many orders of magnitude of r: Escherichia coli growing under ideal lab conditions can divide roughly every 20 minutes, an extraordinarily high r that yields a doubling time of about 20 minutes; a slow-reproducing species like the African elephant, with r on the order of 0.02-0.06 per year, has a doubling time of roughly 12-35 years. The formula itself never changes, but the time unit attached to r absolutely must match the unit you want td reported in — using a per-day r estimated from a bacterial culture in a formula meant to output years, or vice versa, without converting first, produces an answer wrong by a factor of 365. This exact per-day-versus-per-year mismatch, layered on top of the earlier λ-versus-r confusion, is the single most common arithmetic error in student population-growth calculations.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares two organisms: E. coli with r = 0.033 per minute (consistent with a roughly 20-minute doubling time) and African elephants with r = 0.04 per year. For E. coli, td = ln(2)/0.033 ≈ 21 minutes — matching known lab growth rates. For elephants, td = ln(2)/0.04 ≈ 17.3 years. If the student instead plugged the bacterial r (per minute) directly into a calculation meant to output years without converting, they would compute a nonsensical doubling time of a fraction of a year for a population that, physically, cannot double that fast — a clear signal that time units were dropped somewhere in the algebra rather than an actual biological finding.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'how did you decide between geometric and exponential growth' to check whether the model choice was matched to the organism's actual breeding biology or just copied from a template. A strong answer names the organism's reproductive timing (pulsed annual breeding vs. continuous reproduction) as the deciding factor and can compute a doubling time with units carried through correctly. A weak answer uses exponential growth by default without considering whether the species breeds in discrete pulses, or reports a doubling time with a suspiciously implausible magnitude that reveals a dropped or mismatched time unit rather than a real result.

questions.prompt: Which organism is best modeled with geometric growth (N_t = N_0·λ^t) rather than continuous exponential growth?

options.text: A bacterial culture dividing continuously in a chemostat
An annual plant with one synchronized seed-set pulse per year
A large mammal population with births staggered evenly across the year
Any population, since geometric and exponential growth are always fully interchangeable

explanations.a: Continuous division with no synchronized pulse is the textbook case for the exponential (continuous-time) model, not geometric.
explanations.b: Correct — a single synchronized annual reproductive pulse is exactly the discrete, non-overlapping-generation pattern geometric growth was built to describe.
explanations.c: Staggered, spread-out births across the year are better approximated as continuous reproduction, favoring the exponential model.
explanations.d: They agree only at matching whole time steps when λ = e^r; between steps they describe different underlying processes (pulsed vs. continuous), so the choice matters biologically.

questions.prompt: A population has r = 0.04 per year. Its doubling time td = ln(2)/r is closest to:

options.text: 0.4 years
1.7 years
17.3 years
173 years

explanations.a: This is off by roughly two orders of magnitude — likely from misplacing a decimal in ln(2)/0.04.
explanations.b: This is about a tenth of the correct value; ln(2) ≈ 0.693, and 0.693/0.04 is much larger than 1.7.
explanations.c: Correct — ln(2) ≈ 0.693, and 0.693/0.04 ≈ 17.3 years, consistent with slow-reproducing large mammals like elephants.
explanations.d: This overshoots by a factor of 10; check the division of 0.693 by 0.04 directly.

questions.prompt: A student has r = 0.033 per minute for E. coli but needs a doubling time in hours. What must they do before applying td = ln(2)/r?

options.text: Nothing — the formula works regardless of the time unit attached to r
Convert r to a per-hour rate (or compute td in minutes first and then convert minutes to hours) so the output unit matches r's time base
Multiply r by 60 and call that the doubling time directly
Use λ instead of r, since λ has no time unit

explanations.a: The formula's output inherits whatever time unit r is expressed in; skipping conversion produces an answer in the wrong unit, not a unit-free universal answer.
explanations.b: Correct — td = ln(2)/r comes out in whatever time unit r uses, so to report hours the student must either convert r to per-hour first or convert the resulting per-minute td into hours afterward.
explanations.c: Multiplying r by 60 does not compute a doubling time at all; it conflates a unit-conversion step with the doubling-time formula itself.
explanations.d: λ is also tied to a specific time step (whatever step defines N_t/N_t-1) and is not unit-free; switching to λ does not avoid the unit problem.

questions.prompt: Under what condition do the geometric model N_t = N_0·λ^t and the exponential model N_t = N_0·e^(rt) predict exactly the same population size at every whole time step?

options.text: Only when the population is at carrying capacity
When λ = e^r (equivalently, r = ln λ)
Only for populations with 1:1 sex ratios
Never — the two models are mathematically incompatible

explanations.a: Carrying capacity concerns logistic growth and density dependence, which is unrelated to this specific equivalence.
explanations.b: Correct — setting λ equal to e^r makes the two formulas produce identical values of N_t at every integer time step, even though they represent different within-step processes.
explanations.c: Sex ratio does not enter into this purely mathematical relationship between λ and r.
explanations.d: They are compatible at matching time steps under the r = ln(λ) relationship; they only diverge in their claims about what happens between steps.

units.label: Life Tables, Survivorship, and Fecundity Schedules

lessons.label: Building a Cohort Life Table

sections.heading: Tracking one generation from birth to the last death
sections.body: A cohort (or horizontal) life table follows a single group of individuals born at roughly the same time and records how many survive to each subsequent age class until none remain. This is the design behind Joseph Connell's 1970 study of the barnacle Balanus glandula on rocky shores at San Juan Island, Washington: he marked and followed a settling cohort on a fixed patch of substrate, censusing survivors at fixed intervals. The table has five core columns. nx is the number alive at the start of age interval x. lx is survivorship — the proportion of the ORIGINAL cohort (n0) still alive at age x, calculated as nx / n0, so l0 always equals 1.0. dx is the number dying during interval x, nx minus nx+1. qx is the age-specific mortality rate: the fraction of those alive AT THE START of interval x that die during it.

sections.heading: The denominator trap: qx is a rate, lx is a proportion
sections.body: The single most common construction error is computing qx as dx / n0 (deaths divided by the original cohort size) instead of dx / nx (deaths divided by the number alive at the start of that specific interval). The two columns answer different questions. lx asks 'what fraction of everyone who started has made it this far' — a running, monotonically non-increasing proportion of the founding cohort. qx asks 'of those still alive right now, what fraction die before the next census' — a fresh probability recalculated each interval against a shrinking denominator. Confusing the two silently deflates qx in later age classes, making old-age mortality look artificially mild, because a shrinking nx is being divided by the large, fixed n0 instead of itself.

sections.heading: Life expectancy closes the table
sections.body: The ex column, life expectancy, requires an intermediate: Lx, the average number alive during interval x (typically (nx + nx+1)/2), and Tx, the sum of Lx from age x to the oldest age recorded. Then ex = Tx / nx. This is why e0, expectancy at birth, is usually lower than e1 in species with heavy early mortality: it is averaged across everyone, including those who die almost immediately, dragging the mean down even though survivors who clear that first hurdle can expect to live much longer. Continuing the barnacle cohort: L0 = (n0 + n1)/2 = (1000 + 200)/2 = 600, and L1 = (n1 + n2)/2 = (200 + 150)/2 = 175. If the cohort ends at age 2 with n2 = 150, T0 = L0 + L1 = 775, so e0 = T0 / n0 = 775/1000 = 0.775 years. T1 = L1 = 175, so e1 = T1 / n1 = 175/200 = 0.875 years — higher than e0, exactly because e0 is dragged down by the settlement die-off that e1's survivors have already escaped.

lessons.workedExample: A barnacle cohort settles with n0 = 1000 recruits. After year 1, n1 = 200 (dx0 = 800, so q0 = 800/1000 = 0.80). After year 2, n2 = 150 (dx1 = 50, so q1 = 50/200 = 0.25, NOT 50/1000 = 0.05). A student who divides by n0 throughout would report q1 as 0.05 and conclude mortality eased dramatically after settlement, when survivors actually still face a 25% chance of dying in year two — the true story is a brutal settlement bottleneck followed by only moderately improved odds, not near-safety.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'walk me through how you calculated qx' because the lx-vs-qx denominator swap is the single most diagnostic error in a life-table poster — it reveals whether a student understands what each column represents or just filled in a template. A weak answer says 'I divided deaths by the total' without specifying which total. A strong answer states explicitly that qx uses nx (the survivors entering that interval) as its denominator because it is a conditional probability, while lx uses n0 because it is a cumulative proportion of the founding cohort — and can explain why swapping them would make late-life mortality look artificially low.

questions.prompt: In a cohort life table, qx (age-specific mortality rate) should be calculated as:

options.text: dx divided by n0, the original cohort size
dx divided by nx, the number alive at the start of interval x
nx divided by n0
dx divided by Tx

explanations.a: Dividing by n0 turns qx into a proportion of the founding cohort, not a conditional probability of dying during that interval — it deflates mortality rates in later age classes.
explanations.b: Correct — qx is the probability of dying during interval x GIVEN you were alive at its start, so the denominator must be nx, the survivors entering that interval.
explanations.c: nx / n0 is the definition of lx, survivorship, not qx.
explanations.d: Tx (total future life-years from age x) is used to calculate life expectancy ex, not the mortality rate qx.

questions.prompt: In Connell's barnacle cohort study, why does e0 (life expectancy at birth) tend to be lower than e1 (expectancy at age 1) when settlement mortality is heavy?

options.text: Older barnacles reproduce more, which mathematically raises ex
e0 averages in the many individuals that die almost immediately after settling, pulling the mean down
e1 is calculated from a larger n0 than e0
Life expectancy always increases with age in every species

explanations.a: Reproduction (mx) is a separate schedule and does not enter the ex calculation.
explanations.b: Correct — e0 is dragged down by the large mass of settlers that die in the first interval; barnacles that survive that bottleneck are averaged only among themselves for e1, raising the mean.
explanations.c: n0 is the same founding cohort for the whole table; it is not recalculated per age class.
explanations.d: This is only true for species with steep early mortality (like Type III survivors); in many species with rising late-life mortality, ex eventually declines with age.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to build a cohort life table from raw census counts.

items.text: Record nx, the number alive at the start of each age interval
Compute lx = nx / n0 for each age class
Compute dx = nx − nx+1 for each interval
Compute qx = dx / nx for each interval
Compute Lx, Tx, and ex to get life expectancy

questions.explanation: You must first have nx (raw survivor counts) before lx can be derived from it; dx falls out of consecutive nx values; qx needs dx and the corresponding nx; and ex is the final derived column, built from Lx and Tx which themselves depend on the nx sequence.

questions.prompt: Match each life-table column to its correct definition.

right.text: Proportion of the ORIGINAL cohort surviving to age x
Number of individuals dying during interval x
Probability of dying during interval x, given alive at its start
Average remaining lifespan for an individual reaching age x

questions.explanation: lx = nx/n0 is cumulative survivorship from birth; dx = nx − nx+1 counts deaths within the interval; qx = dx/nx is the interval's conditional mortality probability; ex = Tx/nx is life expectancy remaining at age x.

lessons.label: Static Life Tables and Their Assumptions

sections.heading: A snapshot instead of a movie
sections.body: A cohort life table needs years or decades of following one generation, which is impossible for long-lived or hard-to-track animals. The static (or time-specific, or vertical) life table shortcuts this by sampling a cross-section of the population at a single point in time — either the age structure of everyone alive right now, or, more commonly, the ages at death of everyone who died recently. From that snapshot you back out an lx column by counting how many of the sampled individuals reached at least age x, then applying the same dx, qx, ex machinery as a cohort table.

sections.heading: The assumption that makes the shortcut work — and when it breaks
sections.body: The static method is only valid if the population is stationary: constant size, constant age-specific birth and death rates, year after year, so that this year's 5-year-olds experienced the same mortality schedule as last year's did. If the population is actually growing, young age classes are numerically inflated relative to what a true cohort would show, which can manufacture an apparent dx that is NEGATIVE — more individuals appear to be alive at an older age class than at the younger one immediately before it, an artifact rather than biology. A declining population biases the other direction, understating survivorship of young animals because fewer of them were ever born into the sample. Either way, ex estimates from a non-stationary population are systematically biased, not just noisy.

sections.heading: Deevey's Dall sheep and its skull-collection bias
sections.body: Edward Deevey's landmark 1947 review, 'Life Tables for Natural Populations of Animals,' popularized Adolph Murie's data on Dall mountain sheep (Ovis dalli) skulls collected in Mount McKinley National Park (now Denali), published in Murie's 1944 report The Wolves of Mount McKinley. Because sheep horns grow in visible annual rings, Murie could age each skull at death, and Deevey assembled these into a static life table showing a roughly Type I curve — high survivorship through middle age, then a steep late-life mortality rise. But the method assumes skulls are found in proportion to actual deaths across all ages, and modern critiques note this is unlikely: skulls of animals that died of predation, exposure, or accident in accessible terrain are recovered unevenly, small or fragile skulls (younger animals) may degrade or be overlooked, and searcher effort was not randomized across the landscape. The lesson generalizes: any static table built from opportunistically found remains inherits the biases of how those remains were found, not just the biology of dying.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a park ranger ages 100 Dall sheep skulls found over several years: 5 died as lambs (age 0-1), 10 at age 1-2, and so on up through old age, with a cluster of deaths concentrated around age 9-13 reflecting late-life mortality. Deevey's static table treats this as if it were a single cohort's death record, computing lx as the fraction of the 100 skulls that died at age x or later. If lamb skulls are actually under-recovered in the field (small, quickly scattered by scavengers) relative to the true lamb death rate, the resulting table will UNDER-estimate early mortality and correspondingly overstate e0, making the population look hardier at birth than it really is.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'is your age-at-death sample actually a fair record of who died?' is testing whether the student understands that a static life table is not free data — it substitutes a strong assumption (stationarity, or unbiased recovery of remains) for years of fieldwork a cohort table would require. A strong answer names the stationary-population assumption explicitly and can describe what a growing or shrinking population would do to the table (negative dx, biased ex), and ideally cites the Dall sheep skull-collection critique as a concrete case of recovery bias. A weak answer treats the static table as interchangeable with a cohort table with no caveat at all.

questions.prompt: What key assumption must hold for a static (time-specific) life table to give an unbiased estimate of survivorship?

options.text: The population must be growing exponentially
The population must be stationary — constant size and constant age-specific vital rates over time
Every individual must be marked and recaptured
The species must reproduce only once per lifetime

explanations.a: A growing population violates the stationarity assumption and biases the static table (e.g., inflated apparent survivorship of young age classes).
explanations.b: Correct — a static table substitutes a snapshot of ages at death (or ages alive) for true cohort tracking, and this substitution is only valid if birth and death rates have been constant long enough that today's snapshot resembles what a real cohort would show.
explanations.c: Mark-recapture is a data-collection method associated with cohort tables, not a requirement for static tables, which typically use unmarked skeletal or standing-age-structure data.
explanations.d: Semelparity (reproducing once) is irrelevant to whether the stationarity assumption for a static table holds.

questions.prompt: A static life table built from a rapidly GROWING population is most likely to produce which artifact?

options.text: A negative dx value in some age interval, because young age classes are numerically inflated relative to a true cohort
Perfectly accurate lx values regardless of growth rate
An underestimate of survivorship in the oldest age classes only
No effect on the table, since dx is always calculated from raw counts

explanations.a: Correct — in a growing population, each successive birth cohort is larger than the one before, so young age classes in the snapshot are overrepresented relative to what constant-rate cohort tracking would show, which can make an older age class appear to have MORE survivors than a younger one, an impossible negative dx.
explanations.b: Population growth systematically biases static-table estimates; it is the central limitation of the method.
explanations.c: The bias appears in the young/old ratio broadly, not exclusively in the oldest classes.
explanations.d: dx is calculated from the (biased) nx sequence, so growth-driven bias propagates directly into dx.

questions.prompt: Deevey's 1947 static life table for Dall mountain sheep was built from what underlying data source?

options.text: Radio-collar tracking of a single marked cohort over 15 years
Aged skulls (via horn annual rings) collected opportunistically in Mount McKinley National Park by Adolph Murie
Zoo records of captive-bred sheep
A standing census of live sheep counted by age from a single helicopter survey

explanations.a: Radio-collar cohort tracking would make this a cohort (horizontal) table, not the static table Deevey actually constructed from field-collected remains.
explanations.b: Correct — Murie's 1944 report used horn-ring aging of skulls found across the range to reconstruct age at death, which Deevey compiled into the widely cited static life table.
explanations.c: The data came from a wild, free-ranging population in the field, not captive records.
explanations.d: The source was aged remains (skulls), not a live standing-age census.

questions.prompt: What is the main modern critique of Deevey's Dall sheep skull data?

options.text: Horn rings do not actually correlate with age at all
Skull recovery in the field is likely uneven across ages and terrain, so the sample may not represent true population-wide mortality
The sheep population was captive, not wild, so the data is irrelevant to natural mortality
Deevey used the wrong formula for lx

explanations.a: Horn annual rings are a well-established and reliable aging method in bovids; that is not the critique.
explanations.b: Correct — opportunistic skull recovery is not a random sample of deaths: fragile young skulls may be scattered or overlooked, and recovery effort was not standardized across the landscape, so the resulting age-at-death distribution can misrepresent true mortality schedules.
explanations.c: The sheep were wild, free-ranging animals in Denali; captivity is not the issue.
explanations.d: The formula (lx from age-at-death counts) is standard; the critique concerns the representativeness of the underlying sample, not the arithmetic.

lessons.label: Survivorship Curves Done Properly

sections.heading: Why log10, not raw lx
sections.body: Plotting raw lx against age produces a curve whose shape is hard to read quantitatively: a constant mortality RATE produces a curve that decelerates visually even though the underlying risk per unit time never changes, because each interval's deaths are a constant fraction of an ever-shrinking number alive. Plotting log10(lx) against age fixes this: under a constant mortality rate, log10(lx) declines in a straight line, and the SLOPE of that line is directly proportional to the mortality rate itself. A steepening slope means mortality is rising with age; a flattening slope means it is easing. This log transform is why survivorship curves are conventionally drawn on a log y-axis — it converts an eyeball impression into a readable rate.

sections.heading: Pearl's typology as a continuum, not three boxes
sections.body: Raymond Pearl proposed the Type I/II/III scheme in the 1920s (developed across his work on Drosophila and other populations, consolidated by 1928). Type I is convex: low mortality through youth and middle age, a steep late-life plunge — the classic pattern of large mammals with parental care and few predators, humans in developed nations being the textbook case. Type II is a straight diagonal line on the log plot: constant mortality risk at every age, independent of how old you already are. Type III is concave: catastrophic mortality immediately after birth or hatching, with the rare survivors then facing low, roughly constant risk. Almost nothing is purely one type. These are end members of a continuum, and most real curves are composites.

sections.heading: Reading mixed and real curves
sections.body: Many species show a STEPPED curve: a steep Type III-like drop during a vulnerable larval or juvenile phase, followed by a much flatter, Type I-like segment once individuals clear that bottleneck — a marine invertebrate with planktonic larvae is the classic case, since the larval stage suffers over 99% mortality while post-settlement adults can be comparatively long-lived. The American oyster (Crassostrea virginica) is a canonical near-Type III curve: enormous larval and spat mortality, then a much gentler slope among established adults. Hydra, the freshwater cnidarian studied by Laurence Slobodkin in the 1960s, is the textbook near-Type II example: under lab conditions its mortality risk stays roughly constant across observed ages, giving a straight diagonal log-lx line, consistent with negligible senescence. Modern human populations in wealthy nations are strongly Type I, but pre-industrial and historical human populations show a more stepped curve with substantial infant and childhood mortality before the Type I late-life plunge.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher tracks a cohort of 10,000 oyster larvae. By the end of the free-swimming larval stage only 40 remain (lx = 0.004), a catastrophic drop reflecting predation and failure to find suitable settlement substrate. Of those 40 settled spat, 30 survive to reproductive adulthood two years later (lx = 0.003) — a much gentler decline. Plotted on log10(lx), the first segment is an almost vertical cliff and the second segment is nearly flat, producing a visibly Type III curve overall: the steep early drop dominates the shape even though adult mortality afterward is mild.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'why did you plot log survivorship instead of raw survivorship?' because it tests whether a student understands the log transform is doing real analytical work, not just following a convention. A strong answer explains that slope on the log plot equals mortality rate, so a straight line means constant risk (Type II) and a bend signals changing risk with age — and can point to a specific bend or cliff in their own data and name what life stage causes it. A weak answer says 'that's just how the textbook draws it' without connecting the transform to what the slope means.

questions.prompt: Why are survivorship curves conventionally plotted as log10(lx) versus age rather than raw lx versus age?

options.text: Because raw lx values are always negative and cannot be plotted directly
Because under a constant mortality rate, log10(lx) declines linearly, so the slope directly reads as the mortality rate
Because log plots are required by convention with no analytical benefit
Because it converts survivorship into a probability distribution

explanations.a: lx values are proportions between 0 and 1, always non-negative; that is not the reason for the log transform.
explanations.b: Correct — a constant per-capita mortality rate produces exponential decline in lx, which becomes a straight line only once you take the log; the slope of that line is then directly proportional to the mortality rate.
explanations.c: The transform has a specific mathematical payoff (turning rate into slope), it is not an arbitrary stylistic choice.
explanations.d: lx is already a proportion of the founding cohort; the log transform changes how it's visualized, not its statistical nature.

questions.prompt: A survivorship curve that is a straight diagonal line on a log10(lx)-vs-age plot indicates:

options.text: Mortality rate is constant across all ages (Type II)
Mortality is concentrated entirely in early life (Type III)
Mortality is concentrated entirely in late life (Type I)
The population is not stationary

explanations.a: Correct — a constant slope on the log plot means a constant rate of decline in log-survivorship, which is the definition of a constant mortality rate: Type II, as seen in Slobodkin's Hydra data.
explanations.b: Type III produces a steep early drop followed by a flatter segment — a bend, not a single constant slope.
explanations.c: Type I produces a shallow early slope that steepens with age — also a bend, not a constant slope.
explanations.d: Curve shape reflects the mortality schedule, not the stationarity assumption used in building static tables.

questions.prompt: Which organism is the canonical example of a near-Type III survivorship curve, driven by catastrophic larval mortality?

options.text: Hydra
Humans in developed nations
American oyster (Crassostrea virginica)
Dall mountain sheep

explanations.a: Hydra is the canonical near-Type II example: roughly constant mortality risk across observed ages, per Slobodkin's studies.
explanations.b: Humans in wealthy nations are the canonical Type I example: low early mortality, steep late-life decline.
explanations.c: Correct — the oyster loses the overwhelming majority of individuals during the planktonic larval stage, then shows much gentler mortality among settled adults, the defining Type III pattern.
explanations.d: Dall sheep (Deevey's data) are closer to Type I: relatively good survivorship through middle age with a late-life mortality rise.
