questions.prompt: Match each survivorship pattern to the example organism most associated with it.

left.text: Type II (constant mortality risk, straight diagonal)
Stepped curve (Type III early, then Type I-like)

right.text: Humans in developed nations
Hydra (Slobodkin's studies)
American oyster larvae/spat
Marine invertebrate with a vulnerable planktonic larval stage but long-lived settled adults

questions.explanation: Humans in wealthy nations show a sharp late-life mortality plunge (Type I); Hydra shows roughly constant risk at every age (Type II); the oyster loses nearly all individuals as larvae then declines gently as adults (Type III); many marine invertebrates combine a steep larval bottleneck with a flat adult segment, the stepped composite curve.

lessons.label: Fecundity Schedules and Net Reproductive Rate

sections.heading: Adding a birth column to the death table
sections.body: A life table's lx, dx, and qx columns describe only mortality. To capture reproduction you add mx, the age-specific fecundity schedule: the average number of (typically female) offspring produced per surviving female during age interval x. Convention restricts mx to female offspring because most demographic models of sexually reproducing populations track only the female half — the number of daughters born to daughters is what determines whether the female lineage replaces itself, and this side-steps having to model variable male mating success separately. mx is usually near zero before an age-of-first-reproduction threshold, rises through a peak reproductive age range, and tapers or drops off with senescence or menopause-like decline.

sections.heading: The lxmx product and R0
sections.body: Multiplying lx by mx at each age gives the expected number of (female) offspring produced by an average NEWBORN female during that specific age interval — it discounts raw fecundity by the probability of even surviving to reproduce at that age. Summing lxmx across every age class gives R0, the net reproductive rate: the total expected number of daughters a newborn female will produce over her entire lifetime, accounting realistically for the chance she dies before reaching each reproductive age. R0 = 1.0 means exact replacement — each female exactly replaces herself with one daughter on average, so the population is (in the long run, given a stable age structure) neither growing nor shrinking. R0 greater than 1 signals growth; R0 less than 1 signals decline toward extinction of that lineage.

sections.heading: The r ≈ ln(R0)/T shortcut and where it breaks
sections.body: R0 alone doesn't say how FAST a population is growing per unit time, because it says nothing about generation length. The commonly used approximation converts R0 into an annual-scale intrinsic growth rate: r ≈ ln(R0) / T, where T is the generation time (often approximated as the mean age of mothers at reproduction, weighted by lxmx). This is a genuine approximation, not the exact solution — it assumes reproduction is effectively concentrated at a single generation time T rather than spread across many ages. It works reasonably well for species with a short, tight reproductive window, but it systematically misestimates r for long-lived species whose reproduction is spread across many years, because a single T cannot capture the real variance in when offspring are produced; a more accurate r for those species requires the full Euler-Lotka equation.

lessons.workedExample: A vole population's life table gives: age 0, lx = 1.0, mx = 0; age 1, lx = 0.5, mx = 3.0 (so lxmx = 1.5); age 2, lx = 0.2, mx = 4.0 (lxmx = 0.8); age 3, lx = 0.05, mx = 2.0 (lxmx = 0.1). R0 = 1.5 + 0.8 + 0.1 = 2.4 daughters per newborn female over her lifetime — clearly above replacement. The weighted mean generation time T = (1×1.5 + 2×0.8 + 3×0.1) / 2.4 ≈ 1.42 years. Then r ≈ ln(2.4) / 1.42 ≈ 0.875 / 1.42 ≈ 0.62 per year, meaning this population is approximated to grow roughly 62% per year under these vital rates if they held constant — consistent with voles' famously fast population cycles.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what does an R0 of exactly 1 mean, and is it the same as zero population growth right now?' to test whether a student separates lifetime replacement (R0) from the population's current growth trajectory (r) and its stable age structure. A strong answer states R0 = 1 means each female replaces herself exactly, over a full generation, and can explain that r ≈ ln(R0)/T is only an approximation valid when reproduction clusters near one generation time — and can name that long-lived species with spread-out breeding (whales, oaks, humans) break the approximation. A weak answer treats R0 and r as interchangeable numbers with the same units.

questions.prompt: What does R0 = 1.0 mean for a population?

options.text: The population is growing at 100% per generation
Each female exactly replaces herself with one daughter on average over her lifetime — exact replacement
No individual in the population reproduces
Mortality rate equals fecundity rate at every single age

explanations.a: R0 = 1.0 is replacement, not growth; growth requires R0 > 1.
explanations.b: Correct — R0 is the sum of lxmx across all ages, the expected lifetime number of daughters per newborn female, so R0 = 1.0 means exact one-for-one replacement.
explanations.c: R0 = 1.0 requires substantial reproduction; it is R0 = 0 that would indicate no reproduction at all.
explanations.d: R0 aggregates lxmx across the whole lifespan; it says nothing about lx and mx being equal at each specific age.

questions.prompt: Why is the lxmx product, rather than mx alone, used to compute expected lifetime offspring?

options.text: lxmx corrects for inflation in offspring counts across years
lxmx discounts raw fecundity at age x by the probability that a newborn female even survives to reach age x
mx alone is always larger than lxmx so it overstates growth
lxmx is only used when the population is declining

explanations.a: There is no inflation adjustment involved; this is a survival-weighting concept, not an economic one.
explanations.b: Correct — mx alone assumes the female already survived to age x, but a newborn female might die before ever reaching that age; multiplying by lx (probability of surviving to age x) gives the realistic expected contribution of that age class to lifetime output.
explanations.c: lxmx is always less than or equal to mx since lx is a proportion ≤ 1; it does not overstate anything.
explanations.d: lxmx is used universally in computing R0, regardless of whether the population is growing or declining.

questions.prompt: The approximation r ≈ ln(R0)/T is most likely to give a misleading estimate of the true intrinsic growth rate for which kind of species?

options.text: A species with a short, tightly synchronized breeding season concentrated at one age
A long-lived species whose reproduction is spread across many years of adult life
Any species with R0 exactly equal to 1
A species with no juvenile mortality at all

explanations.a: This is exactly the case where the approximation works best, because reproduction really is well-summarized by a single generation time T.
explanations.b: Correct — the approximation collapses the whole mx schedule into one number T, which breaks down when reproduction is genuinely spread across many ages with different survival weights; the exact Euler-Lotka equation is needed for accuracy there.
explanations.c: R0 = 1 does not by itself determine whether the approximation is accurate; that depends on how spread out reproduction is across ages, not on the value of R0.
explanations.d: Absence of juvenile mortality does not address whether reproduction is concentrated or spread across ages, which is what drives the approximation's error.

lessons.label: The Euler-Lotka Equation

sections.heading: The exact definition of r
sections.body: Leonhard Euler worked out the mathematics of age-structured population growth in 1760, and Alfred Lotka independently rediscovered and formalized it for demography between 1907 and the early 1920s, giving the result its modern joint name. The Euler-Lotka equation states: the sum, across every age x, of e^(−rx) × lx × mx must equal exactly 1. Here r is the intrinsic rate of increase — the same r from exponential growth, N(t) = N0 e^(rt) — and e^(−rx) is a discount factor that down-weights offspring produced late in life relative to offspring produced early, because early offspring start reproducing themselves sooner and so contribute more to compounding growth. Unlike the r ≈ ln(R0)/T shortcut, this is not an approximation — it is the exact condition r must satisfy given a population's full lx and mx schedules.

sections.heading: Why you solve it by iteration, not algebra
sections.body: Because r sits inside an exponent and is summed across every age class with a different lx and mx weight, the equation generally cannot be rearranged to isolate r algebraically once there are more than one or two age classes contributing to reproduction. In practice ecologists solve for r numerically: plug in a guess for r, compute the sum, see whether it lands above or below 1, and adjust the guess — this is exactly what a spreadsheet's goal-seek or solver function automates, converging on the r value that drives the weighted sum to 1.0. This is a case where a real research tool (numerical root-finding) stands in for a closed-form formula, because none exists for the general case.

sections.heading: The stable age distribution as a consequence
sections.body: A remarkable output of the Euler-Lotka framework is that ANY age-structured population experiencing constant lx and mx schedules will converge, regardless of its starting age structure, toward a fixed proportional breakdown across age classes called the stable age distribution — for instance, always settling toward roughly 40% age-0, 25% age-1, 20% age-2 and so on, for that specific lx/mx regime. A population artificially perturbed away from this ratio (say, after a mass die-off that disproportionately killed juveniles, or a pulse of immigrants skewed toward one age) will oscillate for a few generations as the disturbance echoes forward through the age classes, then damp back down and re-converge on the same stable proportions, so long as the underlying vital rates stay constant. This is why wildlife managers are cautious about reading short-term post-disturbance age counts as if they reflect the population's long-run trajectory — the transient wobble is a mathematical echo, not new biology.

lessons.workedExample: A biologist has lx/mx data for a beetle: age 1, lx = 1.0, mx = 2; age 2, lx = 0.4, mx = 5; age 3, lx = 0.1, mx = 3. Guessing r = 0.5: e^(−0.5)(1.0)(2) + e^(−1.0)(0.4)(5) + e^(−1.5)(0.1)(3) = 1.213 + 0.736 + 0.067 = 2.02, well above 1, so r = 0.5 is too low (too little discounting). Trying r = 1.1: e^(−1.1)(1.0)(2) + e^(−2.2)(0.4)(5) + e^(−3.3)(0.1)(3) = 0.666 + 0.222 + 0.011 = 0.898, now just under 1. Interpolating between these brackets and refining lands r ≈ 1.0-1.05 per generation, the value that drives the weighted sum to exactly 1.0 — this bracket-and-refine process is precisely what a spreadsheet solver automates.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the Euler-Lotka equation to see whether a student can explain why r must be solved numerically rather than treat it as a plug-and-chug formula, and why it differs from the ln(R0)/T shortcut used elsewhere in their own project. A strong answer explains the exponential discount term e^(−rx) directly — early reproduction compounds, so it is weighted more heavily than late reproduction — and can say they solved for r via iteration or a spreadsheet solver rather than claiming a closed-form answer exists. A weak answer cannot explain what the equation is actually solving for, or conflates it with the simple R0 sum.

questions.prompt: In the Euler-Lotka equation, Σ e^(−rx) lx mx = 1, what does the e^(−rx) term accomplish?

options.text: It converts mx from a raw count into a probability
It discounts offspring produced late in life more heavily than offspring produced early, since early offspring compound growth sooner
It corrects lx for sampling bias
It has no mathematical function beyond making the equation look more precise

explanations.a: mx already represents an average count of offspring per female; the exponential term does not touch its units.
explanations.b: Correct — offspring born early in a female's life themselves have time to reproduce sooner, compounding the population's growth more than offspring born late; the discount factor e^(−rx) captures that asymmetric contribution to r.
explanations.c: lx is a survivorship value computed from the life table directly; the exponential term is unrelated to sampling correction.
explanations.d: The term is doing essential mathematical work — it is what makes solving for r require iteration rather than simple summation.

questions.prompt: Why is the Euler-Lotka equation typically solved by numerical iteration (e.g., spreadsheet goal-seek) rather than by algebraic rearrangement?

options.text: Because ecologists prefer computers to hand calculation for aesthetic reasons
Because r appears inside an exponent summed across multiple age classes with different lx, mx weights, so it generally cannot be isolated algebraically
Because the equation has no unique solution
Because lx and mx are unknown until r is found

explanations.a: Iteration is a mathematical necessity here, not a stylistic preference.
explanations.b: Correct — with more than a couple of contributing age classes, r cannot generally be isolated in closed form from a sum of exponential terms, so ecologists bracket and refine a numeric guess until the weighted sum equals 1.
explanations.c: For a fixed lx/mx schedule the equation does have a unique real solution for r; the issue is only that it must be found numerically, not that it doesn't exist.
explanations.d: lx and mx are known life-table inputs measured beforehand; r is the single unknown being solved for.

questions.prompt: A population is perturbed away from its stable age distribution by a die-off that disproportionately kills juveniles. Assuming lx and mx schedules stay constant afterward, what happens?

options.text: The age structure permanently locks into the new, juvenile-poor distribution
The population's age structure oscillates for a few generations and then converges back to the same stable age distribution
r immediately becomes negative and stays negative forever
The stable age distribution itself shifts to match the new post-disturbance ratios

explanations.a: Constant vital rates pull the age structure back toward the same stable distribution; the perturbation does not permanently reset it.
explanations.b: Correct — the stable age distribution is a mathematical attractor determined by lx and mx; any perturbation to the age structure damps out over a few generations as the disturbance echoes through the age classes, converging back on the original stable proportions.
explanations.c: A single age-structure disturbance does not by itself change r, which is determined by the (unchanged) lx and mx schedules.
explanations.d: The stable age distribution is a property of the vital-rate schedules themselves, not of any particular starting or perturbed age structure.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to numerically solve the Euler-Lotka equation for r using a guess-and-refine (goal-seek) approach.

items.text: Compile the full lx and mx schedule across all reproductive ages
Pick an initial guess value for r
Compute Σ e^(−rx) lx mx using that guess
Compare the sum to 1; if too high, increase r, if too low, decrease r
Repeat until the sum converges to 1, and report that r as the intrinsic rate of increase

questions.explanation: You need the lx/mx data before any guess can be evaluated; a starting guess for r is required to compute the weighted sum; comparing that sum to the target of 1 tells you which direction to adjust r; and the process repeats until convergence, at which point the converged r is the answer.

lessons.label: Reproductive Value and the Cost of Reproduction

sections.heading: Fisher's question: which age class matters most to fitness?
sections.body: R. A. Fisher introduced reproductive value in his 1930 book The Genetical Theory of Natural Selection, asking a sharper question than 'how many offspring total': at each specific age, how much does an individual of that age contribute, on average, to the future of the population, counting both offspring it will produce itself AND offspring its future descendants will produce? Reproductive value vx sums, over every remaining age class x' from now to the end of life, the discounted expected future offspring — weighted by (lx'/lx), the probability of surviving from the current age to that future age, and by mx', fecundity at that future age. A newborn (age 0) has a reproductive value scaled to 1.0 by convention; every other age is expressed relative to that baseline.

sections.heading: Why vx peaks near first reproduction, not at birth
sections.body: Intuition suggests a newborn, with its whole life of reproduction ahead, should have the HIGHEST reproductive value — but this is usually wrong. A newborn's future reproduction is still discounted by all the mortality risk it must survive before reaching reproductive age, and that risk is often steep (recall Type III-leaning juvenile mortality). An individual that has JUST reached the age of first reproduction has already cleared that juvenile mortality gauntlet — the discounting from lx'/lx starts fresh from a survivor's vantage point — while still having its full reproductive lifespan ahead. This is why vx characteristically rises from birth, peaks around the age of first reproduction, and then declines through the reproductive years and senescence as fewer future breeding opportunities remain.

sections.heading: The cost of reproduction and unequal demographic impact
sections.body: David Lack's 1947 clutch-size argument reframed a puzzle: why don't birds lay more eggs than they do, if more offspring should always be favored? Lack proposed that clutch size is under stabilizing selection, tuned to the number of chicks parents can successfully feed and raise, because overextending trades current reproduction against parental survival and future reproductive opportunity — the cost of reproduction. This trade-off has been measured directly in long-term individually-monitored populations: Tim Clutton-Brock and colleagues' work on Soay sheep on St Kilda and red deer on the Isle of Rum showed that females who bred in a given year had measurably reduced survival and reduced fecundity the following year compared to females that skipped breeding, especially under harsh winters or high population density. Because reproductive value is concentrated in the age classes around first reproduction and peak breeding, removing a prime-age breeding adult from a population removes far more expected future offspring than removing a juvenile with low survival odds ahead of it — which is why wildlife managers weight harvest quotas and conservation priorities by age class rather than treating every individual as demographically equal.

lessons.workedExample: In a red deer population on Rum, a hind's reproductive value is low at birth (large fraction of calves die before age 1), rises steeply through the juvenile years, and peaks around age 3-4, just after first calving age — a hind that age has survived the juvenile bottleneck and has most of her breeding lifespan ahead. Clutton-Brock's long-term data showed hinds that successfully raised a calf in a given year were less likely to conceive and calve successfully the following year, and in hard winters had elevated mortality themselves, compared to hinds that failed to breed or skipped a year — a direct, measured survival cost of reproduction consistent with Lack's trade-off logic.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'why would removing one 3-year-old breeding female matter more than removing three newborns?' to test whether a student grasps that reproductive value, not raw headcount, is what predicts demographic impact. A strong answer explains that vx peaks near first reproduction because that age class has both cleared the juvenile mortality gauntlet AND retains its full future breeding potential, and can cite the Soay sheep or red deer cost-of-reproduction data as direct evidence that breeding trades off against survival. A weak answer treats every individual, regardless of age, as contributing equally to population growth.

questions.prompt: Reproductive value vx typically peaks at what point in a species' life, rather than at birth?

options.text: At the very oldest recorded age, just before death
Around the age of first reproduction, once the individual has survived juvenile mortality but retains its full breeding future
It peaks at birth and declines monotonically thereafter in every species
It is constant across all ages by definition

explanations.a: The oldest ages have little or no future reproduction left, so vx is typically low there, not at its peak.
explanations.b: Correct — a newborn's expected future reproduction is still discounted by the steep mortality risk it must survive to reach breeding age; an individual that has just reached first-reproduction age has already cleared that risk while retaining its whole reproductive future, which is why vx characteristically peaks there.
explanations.c: This describes a monotonic decline, which fails to capture the initial RISE from birth to peak reproductive value that is typical.
explanations.d: vx varies substantially across ages precisely because it tracks changing survival probability and remaining reproductive opportunity.

questions.prompt: David Lack's 1947 clutch-size argument proposed that bird clutch sizes are:

options.text: Maximized without limit, since more eggs is always better for fitness
Under stabilizing selection, tuned to the number of chicks parents can successfully raise, trading off against parental survival and future reproduction
Entirely determined by egg-laying physiology with no role for natural selection
Random with respect to fitness

explanations.a: Lack's whole point was to explain why clutch size is NOT maximized — overextending has costs.
explanations.b: Correct — Lack argued clutch size is tuned by selection to the brood size parents can successfully feed and fledge, because raising more chicks than that trades off against the parents' own survival and future reproductive opportunities, the cost of reproduction.
explanations.c: Lack's argument is explicitly an adaptive, selection-driven explanation, not a claim that physiology alone determines clutch size.
explanations.d: Lack proposed a specific fitness-optimizing mechanism, the opposite of a random pattern.

questions.prompt: Long-term studies of Soay sheep and red deer (Clutton-Brock and colleagues) demonstrated a cost of reproduction by showing that:

options.text: Females that bred in a given year had reduced survival and/or reduced fecundity the following year compared to females that skipped breeding
Breeding females always had higher survival than non-breeding females
Clutch or litter size had no relationship to parental survival
Only male reproductive success was measured, with no data on females

explanations.a: Correct — individually monitored hinds and ewes that successfully bred showed measurable survival and future-fecundity costs relative to non-breeders, especially in harsh winters, providing direct field evidence for the cost of reproduction.
explanations.b: The studies found the opposite pattern for breeders under harsh conditions: reduced survival relative to non-breeders, not higher.
explanations.c: The core finding was precisely a negative relationship between reproductive effort and subsequent parental survival/fecundity.
explanations.d: These were long-term studies of individually monitored females (ewes and hinds) tracking their own survival and fecundity across years.

questions.prompt: Why does removing a prime-age breeding adult typically have a larger demographic impact on a population than removing a juvenile?

options.text: Because juveniles never contribute to reproductive value under any circumstances

Because prime-age breeders have high reproductive value — they have cleared juvenile mortality risk and retain substantial future reproduction — while a juvenile's expected future contribution is discounted by the mortality it still must survive
Because juveniles are always more numerous, which makes their removal irrelevant regardless of biology
There is no difference in demographic impact between age classes

explanations.a: Juveniles do have positive reproductive value (assuming lx > 0), just typically lower than the age classes around first reproduction because of the mortality risk still ahead of them.
explanations.b: Correct — reproductive value concentrates around the age of first reproduction and peak breeding, so removing an individual from that age class removes more expected future offspring (both direct and via descendants) than removing a juvenile whose future is still heavily discounted by survival risk.
explanations.c: Relative abundance is a separate consideration from the per-capita reproductive-value argument driving differential demographic impact.
explanations.d: This is the misconception the reproductive-value framework directly corrects: age classes are not demographically interchangeable.

units.label: Estimating Numbers and Rates in the Field

lessons.label: Mark-Recapture Beyond Lincoln-Petersen

sections.heading: From a simple ratio to a bias-corrected estimator
sections.body: The idea traces to C.G.J. Petersen's 1896 plaice-tagging work in Danish waters and Frederick Lincoln's 1930 use of banded-duck recoveries to estimate continental waterfowl numbers. The logic: mark n1 animals, release them, later take a second sample of n2 animals, and count how many (m2) are already marked. If marked animals mix randomly, the marked fraction in the second sample should equal the marked fraction in the whole population, giving the naive Lincoln-Petersen index N-hat = n1*n2/m2. The catch is that 1/m2 is a convex function, so by Jensen's inequality E[n1*n2/m2] overshoots the true N whenever m2 is small relative to n1 and n2 — the estimator is upward-biased exactly when data are sparse, which is often. Chapman's 1951 correction fixes this by adding 1 to each count before dividing: N-hat = ((n1+1)(n2+1)/(m2+1)) - 1. This nearly-unbiased estimator converges to the naive ratio as m2 grows large, but pulls the estimate down substantially when recaptures are few.

sections.heading: Variance and how precise the estimate really is
sections.body: Precision, not just the point estimate, is what a defensible number needs. Seber's variance formula for the Chapman estimator is Var(N-hat) = [(n1+1)(n2+1)(n1-m2)(n2-m2)] / [(m2+1)^2(m2+2)]. Because m2 sits in the denominator raised to roughly the third power, doubling the number of recaptures shrinks the variance far faster than doubling either sample size alone — because m2 carries outsized leverage on variance, effort spent increasing the overlap between the two samples (and thus m2) buys more precision per unit effort than effort spent simply expanding either sample in isolation. A 95% CI is then N-hat plus or minus 1.96 times the square root of that variance.

sections.heading: The four assumptions, and why behavior breaks them asymmetrically
sections.body: Closed-population mark-recapture rests on four assumptions: the population is closed between samples (no births, deaths, immigration, or emigration); no marks are lost or become unreadable; every individual has equal catchability regardless of mark status; and marks are recorded without error. Violations of equal catchability are the most insidious because they bias in opposite directions. Trap-happy behavior — animals drawn back to bait or a familiar trap, as documented in many small-mammal studies — inflates m2 relative to what random mixing predicts, which shrinks N-hat below the true population size. Trap-shy behavior — animals that learn to avoid a trap after a bad first experience — deflates m2, inflating N-hat above the truth. Program CAPTURE and later closed-capture models (Otis et al. 1978) build in a behavioral-response parameter precisely to detect and correct for this.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher live-traps 50 deer mice (n1=50), marks and releases them, then traps again a week later, catching 40 mice (n2=40) of which 10 carry marks (m2=10). The naive Lincoln-Petersen index gives N-hat = 50*40/10 = 200. Chapman's estimator gives N-hat = (51*41/11) - 1 = 190.1 - 1 ≈ 189 — noticeably lower, as expected when m2 is small. Plugging into the variance formula: Var = (51*41*40*30)/(121*12) ≈ 1728, so SE ≈ 41.6 and the 95% CI runs roughly from 107 to 271 — wide enough that the researcher cannot distinguish a population of 150 from one of 250 without more recaptures.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees 'we used mark-recapture' wants to know whether the student understands why the raw ratio is untrustworthy, not just that a formula exists. A strong answer names Chapman's correction, explains that it matters most when recaptures are few, and reports a confidence interval rather than a bare point estimate. An even stronger answer anticipates which assumption is most likely broken in their specific system — for instance, that bait-based traps risk trap-happy bias — and states the direction that bias pushes the estimate. A weak answer recites n1*n2/m2 with no variance and no discussion of what could make it wrong.

questions.prompt: Why is the naive Lincoln-Petersen ratio n1*n2/m2 upward-biased when m2 is small?

options.text: Because m2 appears in the denominator and 1/m2 is a convex function, so its expected value overshoots the true ratio
Because n1 and n2 are always undercounted in the field
Because marked animals are always easier to see than unmarked ones
Because the formula assumes the population is growing between samples

explanations.a: Correct — by Jensen's inequality, the expectation of a convex function like 1/m2 exceeds the function of the expectation, so small, noisy m2 values push the average estimate above the true N.
explanations.b: Undercounting n1 or n2 would bias the estimate but is not the specific mathematical reason the ratio is biased at small m2.
explanations.c: Visibility of marks is a data-quality assumption (marks recorded correctly), not the source of the statistical bias in the ratio itself.
explanations.d: The Lincoln-Petersen ratio assumes a closed population, not growth; growth would violate an assumption but is not why the ratio itself is mathematically biased.

questions.prompt: A trapping study uses strongly scented bait. Some animals become 'trap-happy,' returning to the bait after first capture. How does this bias the Chapman N-hat?

options.text: It inflates m2 relative to random mixing, biasing N-hat downward (underestimate)
It has no effect because Chapman's correction removes all behavioral bias
It deflates m2, biasing N-hat upward (overestimate)
It only affects the variance, not the point estimate

explanations.a: Correct — trap-happy individuals are recaptured more often than random mixing predicts, inflating m2, which drives N-hat below the true population size.
explanations.b: Chapman's correction fixes the small-sample bias of the ratio itself; it does not correct violations of the equal-catchability assumption.
explanations.c: This describes trap-shy behavior, the opposite case, which deflates m2 and inflates N-hat.
explanations.d: Behavioral bias in m2 shifts the expected value of N-hat, not just its spread, because m2 sits in the numerator's structure of the estimator.

questions.prompt: Match each mark-recapture assumption violation to its typical consequence.

left.text: Population is not closed (deaths/immigration occur between samples)
Marks fall off or fade before the second sample
A field technician misreads unmarked animals as marked

right.text: N-hat is biased upward because effective m2 is deflated
N-hat no longer estimates a single well-defined population size
N-hat is biased upward because true marked animals are miscounted as unmarked
N-hat is biased downward because m2 is artificially inflated

questions.explanation: An open population means N itself changes between samples, so a single N-hat is not well defined. Trap-shy animals reduce recaptures, deflating m2 and inflating N-hat. Lost marks make marked animals look unmarked, which also deflates the effective m2 and inflates N-hat. A technician who over-counts marked animals inflates m2, biasing N-hat downward.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a standard two-sample Chapman mark-recapture study, from first to last.

items.text: Capture and individually mark n1 animals, then release them
Allow time for marked animals to redistribute randomly through the population
Take a second sample of n2 animals and record m2, the number already marked
Compute N-hat with the Chapman correction and its variance
Report N-hat with a confidence interval and check assumption violations

questions.explanation: Marking and release must come first, followed by a mixing period so marked individuals are no longer clumped in one location, then the second sample yields m2, from which the bias-corrected estimate and its variance are computed, and finally the result should be reported with uncertainty and assumption checks rather than a bare number.

lessons.label: Open-Population Models: Jolly-Seber and CJS

sections.heading: Why closed models fail once the population itself is changing
sections.body: Lincoln-Petersen and its relatives assume the population is closed between the two samples — no births, deaths, immigration, or emigration. Real field seasons rarely hold still that long. George Jolly and George Seber independently published, in 1965, a framework built for exactly this: many trapping occasions spread across a season or years, each producing a capture history like 0-1-0-1-1 (not caught, caught, not caught, caught, caught) for every individual ever marked. The Jolly-Seber (JS) model uses the pattern of when each animal appears and disappears from the record to simultaneously estimate apparent survival (phi, the probability an animal already in the population is still alive and present at the next occasion), recapture probability (p), and the number of new animals entering the population (births plus immigration) between occasions — which together let it estimate total abundance at each occasion, not just at one moment.

sections.heading: CJS: dropping abundance to sharpen survival
sections.body: The Cormack-Jolly-Seber (CJS) model, built from Richard Cormack's 1964 paper alongside Jolly and Seber's work, conditions on each animal's first capture and asks only what happens afterward, discarding the entry-process part of JS. That trade lets CJS estimate phi and p cleanly without needing to model recruitment, which is why it became the default tool for survival studies in banding and telemetry programs. The crucial reframe is that phi is apparent survival, not true survival: an animal that permanently emigrates out of the study area is statistically indistinguishable from one that died, so 'not seen again' silently blends mortality and emigration. This matters for any conclusion drawn from banding data — a low phi in a fragmented landscape could mean a real survival problem or just animals moving off the grid.

sections.heading: The robust design and estimating software
sections.body: Kenneth Pollock's 1982 robust design combines both worlds: primary periods (say, each year) are treated as open, while several secondary occasions within each primary period (a week of trapping) are treated as closed. This nested structure lets researchers borrow the abundance precision of closed models within a season while tracking survival and temporary emigration across seasons with an open model — and it can separately estimate the probability an animal temporarily leaves and returns, something neither pure JS nor pure CJS can do alone. Fitting these models by hand is impractical; Gary White's program MARK (Colorado State University, first released in 1998) and its R interface RMark became the standard tools, letting researchers specify which parameters vary by time, group, or covariate and compare models by AIC.

lessons.workedExample: A team CJS-marks 200 salamanders at a vernal pool and resamples monthly for five months, building a capture history for each individual (e.g., 10110 for one caught in months 1, 3, and 4). Fitting a CJS model in RMark against the pooled histories yields phi ≈ 0.82 per month and p ≈ 0.55. A naive reading might call this a healthy population, but because phi is apparent survival, a nearby ephemeral wetland connected by a wet-season corridor could be pulling animals out of the study grid — the same 0.82 could reflect true survival of 0.95 with 13% permanent emigration, or true survival of 0.82 with none. Distinguishing the two requires either fencing the study area or a spatial/robust design that tracks where 'missing' animals actually go.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because 'we didn't recapture it, so it died' is the single most common inferential error in field ecology projects, and open-population models exist specifically to prevent it. A strong answer explains that phi is apparent survival that conflates mortality with permanent emigration, names CJS or Jolly-Seber by which parameter it estimates, and can say why abundance requires the fuller JS model while a pure survival question only needs CJS. A weak answer treats 'recapture rate' as if it were survival, with no acknowledgment that an unmarked or unseen animal could simply be alive elsewhere.

questions.prompt: What does the Cormack-Jolly-Seber (CJS) model estimate that the Jolly-Seber (JS) model also estimates but goes beyond?

options.text: CJS estimates the same things as JS but also estimates new entrants (births/immigration) to give total abundance
JS additionally estimates the number of new entrants to the population, allowing abundance estimation, which CJS does not attempt
CJS and JS are identical models with different names
JS only works on closed populations, while CJS only works on open populations

explanations.a: This reverses the relationship — CJS is the reduced model that drops the entry process, not the fuller one.
explanations.b: Correct — JS models both survival/recapture and the entry of new animals, which is what lets it estimate abundance at each occasion; CJS conditions on first capture and estimates only phi and p.
explanations.c: They share machinery but differ in what they estimate: JS gives abundance and recruitment in addition to phi and p, CJS gives only phi and p.
explanations.d: Both are open-population models; the closed-population assumption belongs to Lincoln-Petersen/Chapman-style estimators, not to either of these.

questions.prompt: A CJS model estimates apparent survival phi = 0.80 per season for a marked bird population. Why is 'apparent' the operative word?

options.text: Because phi conflates true mortality with permanent emigration out of the study area — an animal that leaves looks identical to one that died
Because phi is always an overestimate of true survival
Because CJS cannot distinguish adults from juveniles
Because 0.80 is not a valid probability

explanations.a: Correct — CJS infers phi purely from resighting patterns, so it cannot tell death apart from permanent emigration; both produce the same signature of 'never seen again.'
explanations.b: Apparent survival is a lower bound on true survival (since emigration only adds to the 'disappeared' pool), not systematically an overestimate.
explanations.c: Age structure can be modeled as a covariate in CJS, but that is unrelated to why phi is called 'apparent.'
explanations.d: 0.80 is a perfectly valid probability; the issue is what the parameter represents, not its numeric validity.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it represents in open-population capture-recapture models.

right.text: Probability of detecting/recapturing an animal that is present, at a given occasion
Apparent survival probability between consecutive occasions
Nested design with closed secondary occasions inside open primary periods
Software used to fit capture-recapture models via maximum likelihood and compare them by AIC

questions.explanation: Phi is apparent survival between occasions, p is recapture/detection probability given presence, the robust design nests closed secondary sampling within open primary periods to gain both precision and survival estimation, and program MARK (with its RMark interface) is the standard software for fitting these likelihood-based models.

questions.prompt: Order the historical development of these mark-recapture approaches from earliest to most recent.

items.text: Petersen's two-sample tagging ratio for plaice (1896)
Cormack's survival-estimation approach (1964) merged with Jolly and Seber's open-population model (1965)
Chapman's bias-corrected two-sample estimator (1951)
Pollock's robust design combining closed and open sampling (1982)

questions.explanation: Petersen's original two-sample ratio (1896) came first, Chapman's bias correction to that same two-sample approach followed in 1951, the open-population Cormack-Jolly-Seber framework arrived in 1964-1965, and Pollock's robust design, which nests closed sampling inside an open framework, was published in 1982.

lessons.label: Removal, Depletion, and Catch-Per-Unit-Effort

sections.heading: Depletion as its own experiment: the Leslie-Davis regression
sections.body: P.H. Leslie and D.H.S. Davis's 1939 study of Norway rat populations introduced a method that needs no marking at all: repeatedly remove animals from a closed area and watch the catch rate fall as the population is drawn down. Plot catch-per-unit-effort (CPUE) for each removal pass against the cumulative catch already taken before that pass. If every remaining individual has the same constant probability of capture per unit effort, the points fall on a straight line with a negative slope: CPUE declines linearly as fewer animals remain to be caught. Because CPUE should reach zero exactly when no animals are left, extrapolating that line to its x-intercept — the cumulative catch at which CPUE would hit zero — gives N-hat, the estimated initial population size, without ever needing a second, independent sample.

sections.heading: The three-pass electrofishing standard
sections.body: Stream-fish crews rarely fit a full regression by hand; they use a simpler cousin. Calvin Zippin's 1958 maximum-likelihood removal estimator generalizes the depletion regression to any number of removal passes through a blocked-off stream reach, computing N-hat directly from the pattern of catches under the same constant-catchability assumption. Stream-fish crews settled on exactly three passes (C1, C2, C3) as the practical field standard for state and federal stream surveys because it balances statistical adequacy against the real cost of repeatedly shocking, netting, and processing fish in a reach — a design choice that trades precision for feasibility, much like every method in this unit.

sections.heading: When the constant-catchability assumption breaks
sections.body: Both methods stand or fall on one assumption: that each individual's probability of capture per pass stays constant across passes. Two field realities routinely violate it. Learned avoidance — fish that survive the first electrofishing pass retreating deeper under cover, or rats that become wary of a trap-and-remove routine — lowers catchability specifically in later passes. Gear saturation, where a crew's dip nets or holding buckets cannot keep pace with a genuinely dense first-pass catch, has a similar effect at high density. Either way, catches fall off faster across passes than the true population decline would predict, so the regression line (or the Zippin likelihood) reaches its zero-catch point after removing fewer animals than are actually present — the classic signature of these violations is a removal estimate biased low, understating true abundance, a problem documented repeatedly in electrofishing-efficiency studies comparing removal estimates to independently marked populations.

lessons.workedExample: A crew blocks off a 100-meter reach and electrofishes it three times for brook trout, catching C1=45, C2=20, C3=9 (74 fish total). Cumulative catch before each pass is K1=0, K2=45, K3=65. Plotting CPUE (here, catch per pass since effort is held constant) against K gives points (0,45), (45,20), (65,9); the fitted regression line has a slope of roughly -0.55 and an x-intercept near 81, so N-hat ≈ 81 fish were present in the reach, of which the crew caught 74 (roughly 91% efficiency). If instead catchability dropped after pass one because surviving trout retreated under undercut banks, the later catches (20, 9) would fall faster than constant catchability predicts, pulling the x-intercept — and thus N-hat — down toward the observed catch of 74, understating the true population.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about depletion methods to see whether a student understands that the estimate comes entirely from the shape of the decline, not from an independent check — which makes the constant-catchability assumption load-bearing in a way mark-recapture's closure assumption is not. A strong answer can state that catch should fall linearly against cumulative catch under constant catchability, name a real reason it might not (fish hiding after the first shock, gear saturation at high density), and correctly say this biases the estimate low, not high. A weak answer reports three catch numbers and a total with no acknowledgment that fewer fish caught on later passes could mean either a smaller population or a violated assumption.

questions.prompt: In the Leslie-Davis depletion method, what quantity is plotted on each axis, and what does the x-intercept estimate?

options.text: CPUE on the y-axis, cumulative catch on the x-axis; the x-intercept estimates N-hat, the initial population size
Cumulative catch on the y-axis, time on the x-axis; the x-intercept estimates capture probability
Number of passes on the y-axis, CPUE on the x-axis; the x-intercept estimates survival rate
CPUE on the y-axis, number of observers on the x-axis; the x-intercept estimates detection probability

explanations.a: Correct — plotting catch-per-unit-effort against cumulative prior catch produces a declining line whose x-intercept is the cumulative catch at which CPUE would reach zero, i.e., the estimated total initial population.
explanations.b: Cumulative catch against time does not isolate the depletion signal the way CPUE against cumulative catch does, and its intercept has no such interpretation.
explanations.c: The method does not plot number of passes on an axis, nor does it estimate survival rate.
explanations.d: Detection probability is estimated by occupancy models, not by the depletion regression's x-intercept.

questions.prompt: After pass one of a three-pass electrofishing survey, surviving fish retreat under undercut banks and become harder to shock. What does this learned-avoidance effect do to the removal estimate of N?

options.text: Biases N-hat low, because later catches fall faster than constant catchability would predict, so the depletion curve reaches zero catch too soon
Biases N-hat high, because avoidance behavior adds extra individuals to the population
Has no effect, since the Zippin estimator automatically corrects for behavioral change
Only affects the variance of the estimate, not its expected value

explanations.a: Correct — declining catchability after the first pass makes later catches drop faster than true depletion of the population would, so the model concludes the population is exhausted before it actually is, understating N.
explanations.b: Avoidance behavior changes catchability, not the actual number of fish present, and it pulls the estimate down, not up.
explanations.c: The Zippin estimator assumes constant catchability across passes; it has no built-in correction for behavioral change and will be biased if that assumption fails.
explanations.d: This is a bias in the expected value of the estimator (a systematic underestimate), not merely added noise around a correct value.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in removal/depletion estimation.

right.text: Introduced the CPUE-vs-cumulative-catch regression method for closed-population removal
Developed the maximum-likelihood removal estimator used for standard multi-pass electrofishing
The catch rate per unit sampling effort, used as a proxy for remaining density
A high-density field condition where crews cannot process all catchable individuals, lowering effective catchability

questions.explanation: Leslie and Davis originated the CPUE-versus-cumulative-catch regression approach; Zippin later formalized a maximum-likelihood version standard for multi-pass electrofishing; CPUE is the catch-rate proxy for density both methods rely on; and gear saturation is one of the two named causes (with learned avoidance) of a constant-catchability violation.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a three-pass electrofishing depletion survey.

items.text: Block off both ends of the stream reach to enforce closure
Electrofish the reach and record the pass-1 catch (C1)
Electrofish again without releasing prior catch, recording pass-2 catch (C2)
Electrofish a third time, recording pass-3 catch (C3)
Fit the removal estimator to C1, C2, C3 to obtain N-hat

questions.explanation: Closure must be enforced first by blocking the reach, then three successive electrofishing passes are conducted with previously caught fish held out of the water (not released back), and only after all three catches are recorded is the removal estimator fit to compute N-hat.

lessons.label: Distance Sampling and Line Transects

sections.heading: The problem: detectability falls off with distance
sections.body: Walk a transect counting every bird you see or hear, and you will always undercount density, because detection probability is never uniform — an observer catches nearly everything within a few meters and progressively less as distance grows. Simply dividing 'animals counted' by 'area searched' therefore always underestimates true density, and the underestimate gets worse in denser cover or for quieter species. Steve Buckland and colleagues formalized the fix in their 1993 book Distance Sampling and its expanded 2001 edition: instead of pretending detection is perfect out to some arbitrary boundary, record the perpendicular distance x from the transect line to every detected animal, then use those distances to model detectability directly.

sections.heading: The detection function and effective strip width
sections.body: The recorded distances let you fit a detection function g(x) — the probability of detecting an animal given it is at perpendicular distance x from the line — typically a half-normal or hazard-rate curve, constrained so that g(0)=1: an animal sitting directly on the line is assumed to be detected with certainty. Integrating g(x) out to a truncation distance w gives the effective strip width (ESW), essentially the width of a strip in which detection is perfect that would yield the same number of detections as the true, imperfect-detection search actually did. Density then follows as D = n / (2*L*ESW), where n is the number of detections and L is total transect length — the factor of 2 accounts for the strip extending on both sides of the line. Program DISTANCE, developed by Buckland's group at the University of St. Andrews, is the standard software for fitting and comparing candidate detection functions.

sections.heading: Assumptions and the two most common field failures
sections.body: Three design assumptions underpin the whole method: transect lines are placed randomly (or systematically with a random start) with respect to where animals actually are; animals are detected at their original location, before they move in response to the observer; and distances are measured accurately. Two field habits routinely break these. First, distance heaping — observers who estimate rather than measure distances tend to round to convenient values, especially zero, creating an artificial spike right at the line that distorts the fitted g(x) and biases density. Second, running transects along roads or established trails for logistical ease violates random placement outright, since many species are either drawn to edges and open travel corridors or actively avoid human-associated routes — either way, the transect no longer samples a representative slice of the landscape.

lessons.workedExample: A team surveys grassland sparrow density using four 5-km line transects (L = 20,000 m total), recording the perpendicular distance to every bird detected and truncating at w=100 m to drop the long, unreliable tail. Fitting a half-normal detection function in program DISTANCE to n=160 detections yields an effective strip width of ESW=45 m. Density is then D = n / (2*L*ESW) = 160 / (2*20,000*45) ≈ 0.89 birds per hectare — about 89 birds per 100 hectares of grassland. A naive count-and-divide approach using the full 200 m strip (100 m each side) as if detection were perfect would instead give D = 160/(2*20,000*100) ≈ 0.40 birds/ha, understating true density by more than half because it ignores that most of those 200 m were never searched with certainty.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe distance sampling to check whether a student understands that the method's entire value is modeling imperfect detection rather than assuming it away. A strong answer explains that g(0)=1 is an assumption, not a given, and can name a concrete way it gets violated — heaping distances at zero, or laying a transect along a trail that animals either favor or avoid. A student who says 'we counted everything within 50 meters' without discussing a detection function or effective strip width has not actually done distance sampling, just an uncorrected strip count, and a sharp judge will ask exactly that distinction.

questions.prompt: What does g(0)=1 mean in a line-transect distance sampling model?

options.text: An animal located exactly on the transect line is assumed to be detected with certainty
Zero animals were detected on the transect
The detection function has no width
The effective strip width equals zero

explanations.a: Correct — g(0)=1 is the key assumption that anchors the detection function: perfect detectability right on the line, from which detectability is modeled to decline with distance.
explanations.b: This confuses the notation for the detection function g(x) with a count of zero detections; they are unrelated.
explanations.c: The detection function's width is described by the truncation distance w and effective strip width, not by the value g(0).
explanations.d: g(0)=1 is an assumption about detectability at distance zero, not a statement about the size of the effective strip width, which is typically much less than the truncation width.

questions.prompt: A field crew estimates distances by eye rather than measuring them, and many recorded distances end up rounded to exactly 0 m ('heaping'). What is the main consequence for the density estimate?

options.text: It distorts the shape of the fitted detection function near the line, which biases the estimated effective strip width and density
It has no effect since program DISTANCE ignores distances of exactly zero
It only affects transect length, not density
It automatically triggers use of the hazard-rate model instead of half-normal

explanations.a: Correct — an artificial spike of detections at distance zero misrepresents the true shape of g(x) near the line, which propagates into a biased effective strip width and therefore a biased density estimate.
explanations.b: DISTANCE uses all recorded distances including zeros to fit the detection function; it does not discard them.
explanations.c: Heaping is a measurement-error problem affecting the distance data used to fit g(x), not a change to the physical transect length walked.
explanations.d: Choosing between half-normal and hazard-rate models is a model-selection decision (often by AIC), not an automatic response to data heaping.

questions.prompt: Match each distance-sampling term to its definition.

right.text: The probability of detecting an animal given its perpendicular distance from the line
The width of a perfect-detection strip that would yield the same number of detections as the real survey
The maximum perpendicular distance beyond which detections are discarded from the analysis
The design assumption that ensures the sampled area is representative of where animals actually occur

questions.explanation: g(x) is the detection function itself; effective strip width is the integral of g(x) reinterpreted as a perfect-detection strip; the truncation distance sets the outer boundary for which distances are analyzed; and random (or systematic-random) line placement is what makes the sampled strip representative of the study area.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a line-transect distance sampling analysis.

items.text: Randomly place transect lines across the study area
Walk each transect, recording the perpendicular distance to every detected animal
Fit a candidate detection function g(x) to the recorded distances
Integrate g(x) to obtain the effective strip width
Compute density as D = n / (2*L*ESW)

questions.explanation: Random line placement must be established before data collection, distances are then recorded during the walk, a detection function is fit to those distances afterward, its integral gives the effective strip width, and only then can density be computed from detections, transect length, and effective strip width.

lessons.label: Occupancy Modeling and Imperfect Detection

sections.heading: The false-absence problem
sections.body: For elusive species, the question is often simpler than abundance: is this species present at this site at all? But a single visit that fails to detect a species does not mean the species is absent — it may simply have been missed. Darryl MacKenzie and colleagues formalized this in a landmark 2002 Ecology paper, 'Estimating Site Occupancy Rates When Detection Probabilities Are Less Than One.' Their core point: naive occupancy — the raw proportion of surveyed sites where the species was ever seen — is always a downward-biased estimate of true occupancy psi, because some occupied sites will show up as all-zero simply due to imperfect detection. The size of that bias grows as per-visit detection probability p shrinks, which is exactly the regime cryptic, nocturnal, or low-density species live in.

sections.heading: Separating psi from p with repeat visits
sections.body: The fix is to visit each site multiple times within a short window assumed closed to changes in true occupancy status, recording a detection history like 1-0-1 (detected, missed, detected) for each site. A history containing even one detection proves the site is occupied and reveals something about p. A history of all zeros is ambiguous — it could be an unoccupied site or an occupied site where detection failed on every visit — but maximum likelihood can still apportion probability correctly, because the rate of partial-detection histories across all sites pins down p, and that estimated p tells you how likely an all-zero history is to be a false absence versus a true one. The output is two separate parameters: psi, true occupancy probability, and p, per-visit detection probability, rather than one confounded number.

sections.heading: Where this gets used, and the tools behind it
sections.body: Camera-trap grids are the most common application: a species like a bobcat or fisher might be caught on camera during only 2 of 10 deployment nights at a truly occupied site, so any single-night survey would badly undercount presence. Acoustic recorders extend the same logic to species detected by sound rather than sight — bat call detectors and passive owl recorders feed into occupancy analyses in exactly the same repeat-visit framework, treating each recording night as one 'visit.' Programs built for this include MacKenzie and Hines's dedicated software PRESENCE and the R package unmarked (Fiske and Chandler, 2011), both of which fit the maximum-likelihood model directly from detection-history matrices and let covariates (habitat type, recorder type, moon phase) be added to either psi or p.

lessons.workedExample: A camera-trap grid of 30 sites runs for 5 survey occasions each, targeting bobcats. Twelve of the 30 sites record at least one bobcat photo, giving a naive occupancy of 12/30 = 0.40. Fitting MacKenzie's occupancy model estimates per-occasion detection probability p ≈ 0.30. At a truly occupied site, the probability of at least one detection across 5 occasions is 1 - (1-0.30)^5 ≈ 1 - 0.168 = 0.832 — meaning even occupied sites have a 16.8% chance of a false, all-zero history. Correcting for this, psi-hat = naive occupancy / 0.832 ≈ 0.40 / 0.832 ≈ 0.48: true occupancy is estimated at 48% of sites, noticeably higher than the raw 40% count suggests.
lessons.judgeFraming: This concept separates students who ran a real occupancy analysis from those who reported a raw detection rate and called it presence data. A judge probing here wants the student to say, unprompted, that a single visit per site cannot distinguish absence from non-detection, and that repeat visits within a closed window are what make psi and p separately estimable. A strong answer can walk through why an all-zero detection history is ambiguous rather than conclusive. A weak answer treats 'we didn't see it on the camera' as equivalent to 'it wasn't there,' with no accounting for detection probability at all.

questions.prompt: Why does naive occupancy (the raw fraction of sites with at least one detection) underestimate true occupancy psi?

options.text: Because some truly occupied sites will, by chance, produce an all-zero detection history when detection probability is less than 1
Because observers tend to overcount detections at unoccupied sites
Because psi is mathematically defined to always exceed any observed proportion
Because camera traps have a higher false-positive than false-negative rate

explanations.a: Correct — with imperfect per-visit detection, some occupied sites will fail to register any detection across all visits, producing false absences that pull naive occupancy below true psi.
explanations.b: Overcounting at unoccupied sites (false positives) is a different, generally rarer problem and is not the mechanism MacKenzie's model addresses.
explanations.c: There is no such definitional guarantee; the bias arises specifically from imperfect detection, and with p=1 naive occupancy would equal true psi.
explanations.d: This describes a hypothetical detector error-rate asymmetry, not the general reason naive occupancy is biased, which applies to any imperfect detection method, not just cameras.

questions.prompt: A site has the detection history 0-0-0 across three visits. What can an occupancy model conclude about this site?

options.text: The site is definitely unoccupied
The history is ambiguous — the site could be truly unoccupied or occupied with three consecutive missed detections — and the model uses the estimated p to weigh each possibility
The site must be occupied, since three visits is enough to guarantee detection
The history should be discarded from the analysis

explanations.a: This is exactly the naive-occupancy error the model is built to avoid — an all-zero history does not prove absence when detection is imperfect.
explanations.b: Correct — an all-zero history is consistent with both 'truly unoccupied' and 'occupied but never detected,' and the likelihood uses the estimated detection probability p (informed by other sites' partial histories) to weigh these possibilities correctly.
explanations.c: Three visits only guarantee detection if p=1; with p<1 there is always some chance of missing an occupied site across a finite number of visits.
explanations.d: All-zero histories carry real information (they help estimate psi given the estimated p) and are retained, not discarded, in the likelihood.

questions.prompt: Match each occupancy-modeling term or source to what it represents.

right.text: True probability that a site is occupied by the species
Per-visit probability of detecting the species given the site is occupied
The foundational paper establishing the repeat-visit maximum-likelihood occupancy framework
Software commonly used to fit occupancy models to detection-history data

questions.explanation: Psi is true occupancy probability, p is per-visit detection probability given occupancy, MacKenzie et al. (2002) established the maximum-likelihood repeat-visit framework that separates the two, and PRESENCE and the R package unmarked are the standard tools for fitting these models.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of an occupancy-modeling camera-trap study.

items.text: Deploy cameras at a network of sites across the study area
Leave cameras running for multiple survey occasions per site within a closed window
Compile a detection history (e.g., 1-0-1) for each site
Fit the maximum-likelihood occupancy model to estimate psi and p jointly
Report corrected occupancy psi-hat instead of the naive detection proportion

questions.explanation: Cameras must first be deployed across sites, then run across multiple occasions within a period short enough that occupancy status is assumed unchanged, after which detection histories are compiled per site, the model is fit to jointly estimate psi and p, and the corrected psi-hat — not the naive proportion of sites with detections — is reported.

lessons.label: Indices, Long-Term Monitoring, and Effort Correction

sections.heading: Why most long-term data are indices, not counts
sections.body: Mark-recapture, distance sampling, and occupancy models all demand more effort per site than a decades-long, continent-wide program can afford at every stop. Instead, the great long-running monitoring programs collect an index — a number that is assumed to track true abundance N without claiming to equal it. The North American Breeding Bird Survey (BBS), begun in 1966 by Chandler Robbins at the USGS Patuxent lab, sends volunteers along fixed 24.5-mile roadside routes, stopping every half mile for a standardized 3-minute point count, 50 stops per route, once a year. The Christmas Bird Count (CBC), started by ornithologist Frank Chapman in 1900 as an alternative to a traditional Christmas 'side hunt,' has volunteers tally every bird seen or heard within a 15-mile-diameter circle in a single day — now the longest-running citizen-science survey in North America. Neither program estimates a true population size; both track a relative index over time and space.

sections.heading: The load-bearing assumption, and correcting effort
sections.body: Every index-based inference rests on one assumption: index is proportional to true abundance, Index = q*N, where q is a constant of proportionality (catchability, detectability, or effort-scaled effort per unit). If q genuinely holds constant, a rising index means a rising population, full stop. But q is rarely constant on its own, so these programs correct what they can measure: BBS and CBC track observer identity and experience, because a skilled observer detects and identifies more birds per stop than a novice, and a change in observer on a route can look like a population change if uncorrected — modern analyses (following the mixed-model approach of Sauer and Link, among others) include observer as a covariate for exactly this reason. Light-trap and pheromone-trap insect monitoring faces its own version: bulb type (mercury vapor versus LED), trap placement, and even moon phase change effective catchability, so long series that span a bulb-technology switch need calibration overlap periods before the two eras can be compared directly.

sections.heading: Hyperstability: when the index lies about a collapsing stock
sections.body: Fisheries catch-per-unit-effort (CPUE) is the sharpest cautionary case, because getting the index wrong there has driven real collapses. Hyperstability, a term popularized by Ray Hilborn and Carl Walters in their 1992 text Quantitative Fisheries Stock Assessment, occurs when catch rates stay misleadingly high even as true biomass falls, because schooling fish continue to aggregate in dense patches and improving technology (sonar, GPS-marked hotspots) lets a shrinking fleet keep finding and fishing those patches efficiently — catchability q rises even as N falls, masking the decline in the very index meant to track it. The Atlantic cod collapse off Newfoundland is the textbook example: commercial CPUE stayed relatively strong through the years leading up to the 1992 moratorium, even as the spawning stock had already crashed, because fishers were still finding the last aggregations.

lessons.workedExample: A groundfish stock's true biomass falls from 100,000 tons to 20,000 tons over ten years — an 80% real decline. If catchability q were constant, CPUE should also drop by 80%. Instead, because the fleet adopted sonar and the remaining fish stayed schooled in dense patches, recorded CPUE falls only from 50 kg/hour to 40 kg/hour — just a 20% apparent decline. A manager reading CPUE alone would conclude the stock lost a fifth of its size, when it actually lost four-fifths; the index has become hyperstable and is actively concealing the collapse it was supposed to warn about.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes index data to see whether a student treats 'the numbers went up' as proof of a real trend or checks the proportionality assumption first. A strong answer names the specific assumption (index proportional to N with constant q), can cite BBS or CBC's decades-long effort-standardization practices as the ordinary way this is defended, and can explain hyperstability as the case where q itself rises, hiding a real decline inside a flat or rising index. A weak answer plots an index over time and reads a population trend directly off it with no discussion of what could make the index diverge from true abundance.

questions.prompt: What is the load-bearing assumption behind treating an abundance index (like BBS counts or fisheries CPUE) as a proxy for true population size N?

options.text: Index = q*N, where q (catchability/detectability) stays constant over the period being compared
The index equals N exactly at every time point
Observer identity never needs to be recorded
Sample size must exceed 1,000 individuals for the index to be valid

explanations.a: Correct — the entire inferential chain from 'the index changed' to 'the population changed' depends on q staying constant, so that changes in Index are driven only by changes in N.
explanations.b: Indices are explicitly not claimed to equal N; they are a relative measure assumed proportional to N, not identical to it.
explanations.c: Observer identity is exactly what programs like BBS DO track, precisely because it can alter q and needs to be accounted for, not ignored.
explanations.d: There is no fixed minimum sample size that makes an index valid; validity depends on the proportionality assumption holding, not on a raw count threshold.

questions.prompt: In the Atlantic cod fishery prior to the 1992 moratorium, why did CPUE stay relatively high even as the spawning stock had already collapsed?

options.text: Hyperstability: cod remained aggregated in dense schools, and improving technology let the fleet keep finding and exploiting those patches, so catchability rose as true abundance fell
Cod biomass had not actually declined; the moratorium was a precautionary overreaction
CPUE is mathematically incapable of declining in a fishery
Fishing effort was reduced to zero before the moratorium, so CPUE could not fall

explanations.a: Correct — this is the textbook hyperstability case: schooling behavior plus improving detection technology kept catch rates deceptively high while the underlying stock had already crashed.
explanations.b: The spawning stock biomass had genuinely collapsed by the time of the 1992 moratorium; independent stock assessments, not just CPUE, documented the decline.
explanations.c: CPUE can and does decline in fisheries; hyperstability describes cases where it declines less than true abundance, not cases where it cannot decline at all.
explanations.d: Effort was not reduced to zero before the moratorium; the fleet continued fishing, which is precisely what let CPUE stay artificially high by targeting remaining aggregations.

questions.prompt: Match each long-term monitoring program or concept to its description.

right.text: Volunteer roadside routes with standardized 3-minute point counts, begun 1966
Single-day circle counts begun in 1900, the longest-running citizen-science survey
Catch rates stay high while true abundance falls, because catchability itself increases
A bulb-type change (e.g., mercury vapor to LED) alters catchability partway through a long insect-trapping series

questions.explanation: BBS is the standardized roadside point-count survey begun in 1966; CBC is the single-day circle count begun in 1900; hyperstability is the phenomenon where rising catchability masks a true decline in abundance; and technology drift describes how equipment changes mid-series (like light-trap bulbs) alter catchability and require calibration before eras can be compared.

questions.prompt: Order these steps for correctly interpreting a long-term abundance index before drawing a population-trend conclusion.

items.text: Confirm the sampling protocol (effort, method, timing) was held constant or is documented across years
Check for changes in observer identity, skill, or equipment technology across the series
Assess whether catchability q could plausibly have changed independent of true abundance N
Apply available corrections (observer covariates, calibration overlap periods) where possible
Interpret the trend in the corrected index as evidence about the trend in N

questions.explanation: Sound interpretation starts by confirming the protocol's consistency, then checking for known sources of catchability drift like observer or equipment changes, reasoning about whether q could be moving independent of N (as in hyperstability), applying whatever corrections are available, and only then reading a population trend off the corrected index rather than the raw one.

lessons.label: Designing a Feasible Single-Species Study

sections.heading: Matching the organism's generation time to the project's calendar
sections.body: The single biggest design decision in a student population-ecology project is choosing an organism whose biology fits the time available, not the other way around. Daphnia magna reaches reproductive maturity in roughly 6-10 days at 20°C and reproduces asexually by parthenogenesis, so a 6-week study window can span five or six full generations — enough to see real population dynamics, not just one cohort aging in place. Duckweed (Lemna) can double its frond count in as little as 1-4 days under good light and nutrients, making it one of the fastest options for growth-rate work. Tribolium flour beetles, made famous by Thomas Park's competitive-exclusion experiments in the 1940s-50s, take about 3-4 weeks egg-to-adult — slower than Daphnia but still tractable, and easy to rear in flour alone. Isopods, pond snails, and mealworms (Tenebrio molitor) sit at the slower end, with generation times of months rather than weeks, and are better suited to measuring individual growth or behavior than to tracking several full population generations in one fair season.

sections.heading: Sizing the study before running it: pilot data and power
sections.body: A study with too few replicates cannot detect a real effect even when one exists, and a student rarely has budget to guess. A short pilot run — a handful of replicate containers tracked for one or two time-steps — gives an estimate of the response variable's natural variability (its standard deviation), which is the missing ingredient in any sample-size calculation. Statistical power, formalized by Jacob Cohen's 1988 conventions, is the probability of correctly detecting a real effect of a given size; the field standard is 80% power at alpha=0.05. Plugging pilot variance and a target effect size (say, a 30% shift in population size between treatments) into the standard two-sample formula, n = 2*(z-alpha/2 + z-beta)^2 * sigma^2 / delta^2, converts vague hopes ('we'll run a few jars') into a specific, defensible replicate count.

sections.heading: Marking methods, permits, and what actually fits a 6-12 week window
sections.body: Even fast-reproducing invertebrates need a plan for individual identification if the question is about survival or movement rather than raw counts — a dot of enamel paint on an isopod's exoskeleton or a distinct container label per cohort are typical low-cost options; vertebrate work (fish fin clips, bird bands, PIT tags) carries far heavier requirements, including institutional animal-care review, and is rarely feasible for a student project on this timeline. Under Society for Science's International Science and Engineering Fair rules, any study involving live vertebrate animals requires prior review comparable to an Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC), while most invertebrate work — Daphnia, Tribolium, duckweed, isopods, snails, mealworms — faces a lighter Scientific Review Committee check focused on humane handling rather than full IACUC oversight. Given all these constraints together, a realistic 6-12 week single-species study lands on roughly 10-30 replicate microcosms per treatment group, an organism with a generation time of days to a few weeks, and a sampling interval set to catch at least 3-4 full generations.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to test whether a fertilizer runoff concentration affects Daphnia population growth. A one-week pilot with 5 jars gives a day-14 population count of mean=45, SD=12. Targeting an 80%-power test at alpha=0.05 to detect a 30% shift (delta=13.5) between treatment and control: n = 2*(1.96+0.84)^2*(12)^2/(13.5)^2 = 2*7.84*144/182.25 ≈ 12.4, rounding up to 13 replicate jars per group, 26 total. With a 6-10 day Daphnia generation time, a 6-week study spans roughly 5-6 generations, sampled weekly — enough to see the population respond to the treatment rather than just capturing one static snapshot.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe study design because it is the single clearest signal of whether a project was planned or improvised. A strong answer explains why the organism was chosen relative to the project's timeline (generation time versus weeks available), can state that a pilot study supplied the variance estimate behind the sample size, and names the target power and effect size rather than an arbitrary replicate count picked for convenience. A weak answer says 'we used 10 jars because that's what fit on the shelf' with no connection between sample size, variability, and the effect the student was actually trying to detect.

questions.prompt: Why is a pilot study necessary before calculating the sample size (number of replicates) for a population study?
