options.text: It provides an estimate of the response variable's variability (standard deviation), which the sample-size formula requires
It is required by ISEF rules regardless of the study design
It replaces the need for a control group
It guarantees the main study will find a significant result

explanations.a: Correct — the sample-size formula needs an estimate of sigma (variability) to convert a target effect size and desired power into a specific number of replicates; a pilot is the practical way to get that estimate.
explanations.b: Pilot studies are good practice but are not a blanket ISEF requirement; the requirement being described here is statistical, not regulatory.
explanations.c: A pilot study estimates variance; it does not substitute for a control group in the main experiment.
explanations.d: Power analysis increases the probability of detecting a true effect at the chosen sample size; it cannot guarantee significance, since that also depends on whether a real effect exists.

questions.prompt: A student wants to study multi-generational population dynamics within a 6-week science fair window. Which organism choice best matches this timeline?

options.text: Daphnia magna, with a generation time of roughly 6-10 days
A deer mouse population, with a generation time of roughly 2 months
Any organism works equally well as long as replicate count is high
A songbird population, since banding data are easy to collect

explanations.a: Correct — Daphnia's short generation time lets a 6-week study span roughly five to six generations, enough to observe real population-level dynamics rather than a single cohort.
explanations.b: A 2-month deer mouse generation time would allow barely more than two generations in 6 weeks, and vertebrate work also triggers much heavier ethical/permit requirements unsuited to a short student project.
explanations.c: Replicate count addresses precision, not whether the study window captures enough generations to see population-level change; organism choice independently constrains what is observable in a fixed timeframe.
explanations.d: Songbird banding requires federal banding permits and vastly longer generation times, making it infeasible for a 6-12 week single-species study.

questions.prompt: Match each study organism to its approximate generation time.

right.text: 1-4 days (frond doubling time)
6-10 days
3-4 weeks
Roughly 3 months, egg to adult

questions.explanation: Duckweed can double its frond count in 1-4 days under good conditions, Daphnia reaches reproductive maturity in about 6-10 days, Tribolium flour beetles take roughly 3-4 weeks egg-to-adult, and mealworms take around 3 months to complete a full life cycle, making them the slowest of the four for a short study window.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of designing a feasible single-species population study.

items.text: Choose a study organism whose generation time fits the available project timeline
Run a short pilot to estimate variability in the response variable
Use pilot variance, a target effect size, and desired power to calculate required replicate number
Confirm marking method and any required ethics/permit review for the chosen organism
Run the full study with the calculated sample size and appropriate sampling interval

questions.explanation: Organism choice constrained by the available timeline must come first, followed by a pilot to estimate variance, then a power-based sample-size calculation using that variance, confirmation of marking method and ethics/permit requirements appropriate to the organism, and finally the full study run at the calculated sample size and sampling interval.

units.label: Reading and Interpreting Population Time Series

lessons.label: Fitting Growth Models to Real Data

sections.heading: Linearize first: ln(N) against time
sections.body: Exponential growth, N_t = N_0 e^(rt), looks intimidating to fit until you take the natural log of both sides: ln(N_t) = ln(N_0) + rt. That is a straight line in t, so ordinary least-squares regression of ln(count) against time hands you r directly as the slope, with the intercept giving ln(N_0). This is the first move on almost any real count series — a founding population, an invasive species in its early lag-free phase, a recovering fishery — because it converts a nonlinear fitting problem into arithmetic a spreadsheet can do, and because the residuals from that line immediately show you where growth stopped being exponential.

sections.heading: Discrete models: logistic and Ricker
sections.body: Continuous logistic growth, dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), has a discrete-time cousin ecologists actually fit to yearly census data: the Ricker model, N_(t+1) = N_t·e^(r(1 − N_t/K)), which Bill Ricker introduced in 1954 for Pacific salmon stock-recruitment (Journal of the Fisheries Research Board of Canada, 559–623). The Ricker model linearizes too: ln(N_(t+1)/N_t) = r − (r/K)N_t is a straight-line regression of per-capita growth against N_t, whose intercept estimates r and whose slope estimates −r/K, so K falls out as intercept/(−slope). Nonlinear least squares or maximum likelihood on the untransformed data gives the same estimates with better-behaved error structure, and either way you bootstrap the residuals to get honest confidence intervals rather than reporting a bare point estimate.

sections.heading: The θ-logistic and why K refuses to pin down
sections.body: Gilpin and Ayala (1973, PNAS 70:3590) generalized the logistic by adding a shape parameter: dN/dt = rN(1 − (N/K)^θ). At θ = 1 this is the ordinary logistic; θ > 1 delays the onset of crowding until N is close to K, θ < 1 makes crowding bite early. The extra parameter is genuinely useful for describing how density dependence curves — but it is also where short field series break down. Most real time series never sit near K for long, so the data constrain the product-like combination of r, K, and θ far better than they constrain K alone: a wide range of K values, paired with compensating θ and r, fit the observed trajectory almost equally well. This is a flat ridge in the likelihood surface, not a sampling-size fluke, and it means a single point estimate of K from a 15-year series should always be reported with its confidence interval, not as a fact.

lessons.workedExample: In 1944, 29 reindeer (24 females, 5 males) were released on St. Matthew Island, a predator-free, 332-km² island in the Bering Sea (Klein 1968, Journal of Wildlife Management 32:350–367). Fitting ln(N) against time on the early censuses gives r ≈ 0.30–0.35/year, consistent with near-exponential growth once the founders established. By summer 1963 the herd reached about 6,000. A naive logistic or Ricker fit using only the 1944–1963 data would read that leveling as approach to K and estimate K somewhere in the low thousands — but the population was not approaching a stable carrying capacity, it was overshooting the island's actual sustainable winter lichen forage. That winter (1963-64) the herd collapsed from starvation on the overgrazed lichen range; when researchers returned to the island in 1966, only 42 animals remained. The lesson: a model that fits the rising limb beautifully can still be pointing at the wrong K, because the data never sampled the true equilibrium region.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks "how did you get r and K from your counts?" is checking whether you understand that a fitted parameter is only as good as the data's coverage of the relevant range. A weak answer reports K as a single number pulled from a curve-fit with no sense of its uncertainty. A strong answer explains the linearization used, states the confidence interval on K (not just r), and can say in plain terms why a short or rising-only series leaves K poorly identified — ideally naming the flat-likelihood-ridge problem, which signals the student fit the model rather than just running a built-in solver on it.

questions.prompt: Plotting ln(N_t) against t and fitting a straight line estimates which parameter as the slope?

options.text: The carrying capacity K
The intrinsic growth rate r
The initial population size N_0
The shape parameter θ

explanations.a: K never appears in the pure exponential model at all, so this line cannot estimate it.
explanations.b: Correct — ln(N_t) = ln(N_0) + rt is linear in t with slope r, which is exactly why ecologists log-transform counts before fitting exponential growth.
explanations.c: N_0 is recovered from the intercept (as ln N_0), not the slope.
explanations.d: θ only appears in the θ-logistic extension, not in the plain exponential model this question describes.

questions.prompt: Why is K typically poorly identified when the θ-logistic or Ricker model is fit to a short (10-20 year) field time series?

options.text: Because the equations are mathematically unsolvable for K
Because the population rarely stays near K long enough for the data to constrain it, producing a flat likelihood ridge
Because K is not a real biological quantity
Because software cannot fit more than two parameters at once

explanations.a: The equations are perfectly solvable; the problem is statistical identifiability, not algebra.
explanations.b: Correct — when observed abundances mostly sit well below K, many (K, θ, r) combinations fit the rising trajectory almost equally well, so the estimate of K carries a very wide confidence interval.
explanations.c: K is a real, meaningful quantity (the density a habitat can sustain); the issue is estimating it precisely from limited data, not its existence.
explanations.d: Modern software fits many-parameter models routinely; the limitation is the information content of the data, not computational capacity.

questions.prompt: Match each growth model to the person(s)/year most associated with introducing it to ecology.

right.text: Ricker, 1954
Gilpin and Ayala, 1973

questions.explanation: Ricker introduced the discrete stock-recruitment model in 1954 for Pacific salmon; Gilpin and Ayala added the θ shape parameter to the logistic in 1973 using data from laboratory Drosophila populations.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for fitting a Ricker model to a raw yearly count series and getting an honest K estimate.

items.text: Compute per-capita growth ln(N_(t+1)/N_t) for each consecutive pair of counts
Regress that per-capita growth against N_t
Read r from the intercept and K from intercept/(-slope)
Bootstrap the residuals to build a confidence interval around the K estimate

questions.explanation: You must first construct the per-capita growth series, then regress it against N_t, then extract point estimates of r and K from the fitted line, and only then quantify the uncertainty around those estimates by resampling — reporting K without step 4 hides how poorly it may be constrained.

lessons.label: Detecting Density Dependence

sections.heading: The standard test
sections.body: The textbook way to ask "is this population regulated by its own density?" is to compute the per-capita growth rate, ln(N_(t+1)/N_t), for every consecutive pair of censuses and regress it against N_t (or ln N_t). If growth slows as density rises, the regression slope should be negative and significantly different from zero; a slope indistinguishable from zero is read as evidence of density-independent (exponential-like) dynamics. This is the workhorse test built into most intro ecology courses, and it is genuinely the right first move — the trouble is entirely in how easy it is to get a "significant" negative slope for the wrong reason.

sections.heading: Two biases that manufacture density dependence
sections.body: The first is regression to the mean: if N_t happens to be high in a given year partly because of ordinary sampling noise, the next count is likely to look lower just by chance, independent of any real biological regulation — Francis Galton flagged this statistical artifact (1886) decades before ecologists imported the problem. The second, more insidious for field data, is measurement error in N_t itself: because N_t appears in both the denominator of the growth-rate response and as the predictor, any counting error in N_t creates a built-in negative correlation between them even when the true population is a pure random walk with no density dependence at all. Freckleton, Watkinson, Green, and Sutherland (2006, Journal of Animal Ecology 75:837–851) showed with simulated and real census data that this census-error bias inflates false-positive detection of density dependence substantially, and that the effect gets worse, not better, as observation error grows.

sections.heading: Fixes: Bulmer's test and randomization
sections.body: Bulmer (1975, Biometrics) proposed the first formal test built specifically around this problem: a statistic based on the reciprocal of the von Neumann ratio, evaluated against the distribution expected under a pure random-walk null, plus a second version explicitly built to stay robust when measurement error is superimposed on the true series. Later work — Dennis and Taper (1994, Ecological Monographs) built a likelihood-ratio test comparing a density-dependent discrete logistic model against a random-walk null, with the null distribution obtained by parametric bootstrap rather than assumed analytically. Randomization approaches in the same spirit shuffle or resample the observed series thousands of times to build an empirical null distribution for the regression slope, which sidesteps the analytic assumptions that make the naive test's p-values untrustworthy in the first place.

lessons.workedExample: A 15-year sweep-net survey of a grasshopper population, with roughly 25% counting error per visit (insects missed in dense grass), gives a naive regression of per-capita growth on N_t with slope −0.42 and p = 0.03 — textbook "significant" density dependence. A randomization test that shuffles the observed abundance values 2,000 times and re-runs the same regression on each shuffled series finds that about 30% of the shuffled (biologically meaningless) series also produce a slope at least that negative, purely from the measurement-error structure baked into the data. The naive p-value of 0.03 was computed under a null that ignored census error; the honest randomization-based p-value is closer to 0.30, and the claim of density dependence does not survive.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this because "I regressed growth on density and got a significant slope" is the single most common overclaim in a student population project, and it is nearly always vulnerable to exactly the artifact above. A weak answer treats the naive regression's p-value as the final word. A strong answer names the measurement-error problem specifically, describes how counting error was estimated or bounded (repeat counts, detection-probability correction, a randomization null), and can say what would change the conclusion — showing the student understands the test can lie to you even when it's coded correctly.

questions.prompt: In the standard density-dependence test, what is regressed against N_t?

options.text: The per-capita growth rate ln(N_(t+1)/N_t)
The raw count N_(t+1)
Time t
Carrying capacity K

explanations.a: Correct — a negative slope of per-capita growth against N_t is the signature the test looks for.
explanations.b: Regressing the raw next count against N_t does not isolate per-capita growth and is not the standard test.
explanations.c: Regressing against time is the exponential-growth linearization from a different lesson, not the density-dependence test.
explanations.d: K is a parameter to be estimated, not a variable you regress against in this test.

questions.prompt: Why does measurement error in N_t create a spurious negative slope even when the true population follows a random walk with no density dependence?

options.text: Because N_t appears in both the response ratio and the predictor, so its error term is correlated with itself across the regression
Because measurement error always underestimates population size
Because random walks have no variance
Because software rounds small numbers down

explanations.a: Correct — this shared-term structure is exactly what Freckleton et al. (2006) identified: an inflated N_t due to error tends to be followed by a growth-rate estimate that looks artificially low, and vice versa, manufacturing a negative slope from noise alone.
explanations.b: Measurement error can go either direction; systematic underestimation is not the mechanism behind this bias.
explanations.c: Random walks have nonzero variance by definition; that variance is exactly what the test is trying to distinguish from true density dependence.
explanations.d: This is not a rounding artifact; it is a structural statistical bias from shared measurement error.

questions.prompt: Match each method to what it was specifically designed to address.

right.text: Staying robust when measurement error is superimposed on the true series
Comparing a density-dependent model against a random-walk null via parametric bootstrap
Building an empirical null distribution for the regression slope without analytic assumptions

questions.explanation: Bulmer's second test was explicitly constructed to tolerate superimposed measurement error; Dennis and Taper built a likelihood-ratio framework with a parametric-bootstrap null; randomization methods generate an empirical null by resampling the actual data rather than relying on distributional assumptions.

lessons.label: Process Error vs Observation Error

sections.heading: Two different sources of "noise" in a count series
sections.body: Every population time series bounces around, but the bounce comes from two entirely different places that get lumped together if you are not careful. Process error is real: the population itself actually grew or shrank by a random amount because births, deaths, and movement are stochastic events happening to real organisms. Observation error is not biological at all — it is the gap between the true population size and what your survey method recorded, from missed individuals, double-counts, or an imperfect detection probability. A series with N_t = 500 one year and 420 the next could reflect a genuine 16% decline, or a stable population that a hastier survey undercounted, or some mix of both — and you cannot tell which from the raw numbers alone.

sections.heading: Why conflating them is dangerous
sections.body: Treating all the variance in a series as process error inflates two things that matter for real decisions: apparent density dependence (as covered in the previous lesson, observation error alone manufactures a negative growth-density slope) and estimated extinction risk, because a viability analysis that mistakes counting noise for true demographic volatility will overstate how likely a population is to crash. The fix that state-space models provide is structural, not statistical sleight of hand: they explicitly separate a hidden "true state" process model (how the real population evolves, with its own process-error variance) from an observation model (how the true state maps to what you measured, with its own observation-error variance), and estimate both variances jointly rather than pretending one is zero. Dennis, Ponciano, Lele, Taper, and Staples (2006, Ecological Monographs 76:323–341) built exactly this framework for testing density dependence while separately estimating process noise and observation error from a single time series.

sections.heading: Demographic vs environmental stochasticity
sections.body: Process error itself splits further. Demographic stochasticity is the variance from each individual's birth and death being a coin flip — averaged across N independent individuals, this variance in per-capita growth scales as roughly 1/N, so it swamps a population of 8 individuals and is nearly irrelevant to a population of 8,000. Environmental stochasticity is variance in the vital rates themselves — a drought year, a harsh winter — that hits every individual in the population simultaneously and correlately, so it does not shrink as N grows. Lande (1993, American Naturalist 142:911–927) formalized why this distinction matters for extinction risk: because demographic stochasticity's effect vanishes as 1/N while environmental stochasticity's does not, small populations face both risks acutely while environmental stochasticity alone dominates the extinction time for populations of any moderate size.

lessons.workedExample: A biologist censuses a salamander pond population by dip-netting for 30 minutes each spring, detecting roughly 60% of individuals present (estimated from a mark-recapture side-study). Raw counts go 45, 30, 52, 28 over four years — a series that looks wildly unstable, even cyclic. Fitting a state-space model that separately estimates observation error (from the known 60% detection rate and its sampling variance) and process error attributes most of that swing to observation noise: the estimated true population is closer to 75, 70, 82, 68 — still variable, but far less erratic, and no longer flirting with the appearance of a boom-bust cycle. Reporting the raw counts as "the population" would have overstated both its volatility and its extinction risk.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "how do you know that's real population change and not just how you counted them?" because it is the fastest way to tell whether a student treated their count data as gospel or as a noisy measurement of something hidden. A weak answer has no separate handle on detection probability and cannot say whether the swings in the graph are biology or method. A strong answer names a concrete source of observation error specific to their method (net efficiency, observer fatigue, weather-dependent activity), ideally with an estimated detection rate, and explains — even qualitatively — how that would change the true-population estimate relative to the raw counts.

questions.prompt: A population census shows large year-to-year swings. What is the key diagnostic question for separating process error from observation error?

options.text: Whether the swings are large or small in absolute terms
Whether the swings reflect true changes in the population or gaps between true size and what the survey method detected
Whether the population is a mammal or an insect
Whether the study lasted more than five years

explanations.a: Magnitude alone does not tell you the source — both process and observation error can produce large or small swings.
explanations.b: Correct — process error is real biological change; observation error is the gap between true size and what the method recorded, and only that distinction resolves what the swings mean.
explanations.c: Taxon does not determine which error source dominates; both mammals and insects can have either.
explanations.d: Study length affects how precisely you can estimate the variances, but it is not itself the diagnostic question.

questions.prompt: Demographic stochasticity's contribution to variance in per-capita growth rate scales approximately as:

options.text: 1/N, so it matters most when N is small
N, so it grows with population size
It is constant regardless of N
N², so it dominates in large populations

explanations.a: Correct — because it comes from averaging independent birth/death events across N individuals, demographic stochasticity's variance shrinks roughly as 1/N and is only a major risk factor for small populations.
explanations.b: This describes the opposite relationship; demographic variance shrinks, not grows, with N.
explanations.c: Environmental stochasticity is the one that stays roughly constant regardless of N, not demographic stochasticity.
explanations.d: No standard population model gives demographic stochasticity this scaling; it would make large populations riskier than small ones, which contradicts observed extinction patterns.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its defining property.

right.text: Real change in the population from stochastic births/deaths/movement
Gap between true population size and what the survey method recorded
Variance from individual-level chance events, scaling as roughly 1/N
Variance from shared conditions (drought, harsh winter) affecting all individuals alike, not shrinking with N

questions.explanation: Process error and observation error are the two top-level sources of noise in a count series; demographic and environmental stochasticity are the two components of process error, distinguished by whether their variance scales down with population size.

questions.prompt: What is the structural fix state-space models provide for the process/observation error problem?

options.text: They increase the sample size by interpolating extra data points
They jointly estimate a hidden true-state process model and a separate observation model, each with its own variance
They eliminate the need for any statistical model of the population
They replace field counts with laboratory data

explanations.a: State-space models do not fabricate data points; they use the observed series to estimate two linked but distinct variance components.
explanations.b: Correct — this is exactly the separation Dennis et al. (2006) built: a process model for the true (hidden) population dynamics and an observation model linking it to the measured counts, with both variances estimated from the same series.
explanations.c: State-space models are themselves statistical models; they do not remove the need for one.
explanations.d: They are fit to field time-series data, not a substitute for it.

lessons.label: Variability, Autocorrelation, and Noise Color

sections.heading: CV as a stability metric
sections.body: The simplest way to compare how "stable" two populations are over time is the coefficient of variation of abundance, CV = SD/mean, calculated across the years of a series. It is unitless, so a 5,000-individual deer population and a 50-individual salamander population can be compared directly, and low CV is the standard shorthand for a well-regulated or buffered population while high CV flags either weak regulation or a noisy environment. The catch is that CV alone cannot tell you why a population is variable — a high CV could come from strong density independence, from a genuinely turbulent environment, or, as the next section covers, from the temporal structure of environmental noise itself rather than its raw magnitude.

sections.heading: Noise color: why autocorrelation matters as much as variance
sections.body: Environmental noise is not always "white" (independent from year to year) — it can be reddened, meaning good years cluster with good years and bad years cluster with bad years, a positive autocorrelation across time. Steele (1985, Nature) generalized that terrestrial systems tend toward white environmental noise while marine systems run redder, and later work (Vasseur and Yodzis, 2004, Ecology) showed the reddening itself, independent of total variance, changes population dynamics: red noise filtered through a population's own dynamics can produce multi-year runs of consecutive good or bad years that look, to the naked eye, exactly like a cycle. This matters because a population with modest year-to-year variance but strongly autocorrelated environmental drivers can produce a time series that seems to show regular booms and busts with no periodic mechanism behind it at all — the pattern is a statistical property of the noise, not evidence of an oscillator.

sections.heading: The evidentiary bar for calling something a cycle
sections.body: This is why claiming a "population cycle" from a short series is a common overreach. The canonical real cycle — the roughly 9.6-year period in Canada lynx fur-return records compiled by the Hudson's Bay Company and analyzed by Elton and Nicholson (1942, Journal of Animal Ecology 11:215–244) — is convincing precisely because the record runs from 1821 to the 1930s, spanning well over ten full periods, and because decades of subsequent field and experimental work (predator-prey coupling with snowshoe hares) supplied a mechanism. A student series showing three peaks over 12 years has shown, at most, two intervals — nowhere near enough to distinguish a true periodic process from a single lucky run of red noise. The honest bar for calling something a cycle is: several repeated periods (not two or three data points that happen to look regular) plus an independently supported mechanism, not a peak count and an eyeball fit to a sine wave.

lessons.workedExample: A 12-year deer count shows apparent 4-year peaks: high in years 1, 5, and 9. That is only two intervals — a coin flip could produce two similarly spaced peaks by chance from red noise alone. Simulating a purely random-walk population driven by autocorrelated (red) environmental noise with the same overall variance as the real series, and no density dependence or periodicity built in, produces "apparent 4-year peaks" in roughly one out of every four simulated runs just from the noise structure. Compare this to the lynx series: Elton and Nicholson's Hudson's Bay Company record spans over a century, showing more than ten repetitions of the ~9.6-year period, and the mechanism (lynx numbers tracking snowshoe hare abundance with a lag) is independently documented. Two peaks and a plausible story is not the same evidentiary weight as ten repetitions and a mechanism.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe cycle claims hard because "my population has a cycle" is a strong causal-sounding claim that a short student dataset almost never earns. A weak answer points at two or three peaks on a graph and calls it periodic. A strong answer either has enough repeated periods to make the claim statistically credible, or — more realistically for a science-fair timeline — explicitly says the data cannot yet distinguish a real cycle from red-noise autocorrelation and names what additional years or mechanism would be needed to make the case, which shows more scientific maturity than a confident wrong claim.

questions.prompt: What does a low coefficient of variation (CV) of abundance indicate about a population, and what can it NOT tell you on its own?

options.text: It indicates relative stability, but cannot by itself tell you whether that stability comes from strong regulation or simply a calm environment
It indicates the population is at carrying capacity
It indicates the population is cyclic
It indicates the census method has no observation error

explanations.a: Correct — CV is a summary of relative fluctuation magnitude only; it says nothing about the mechanism (regulation vs. quiet environment) or the temporal structure of that fluctuation.
explanations.b: CV describes variability, not the absolute abundance relative to any carrying capacity.
explanations.c: A low CV says fluctuations are small on average; it says nothing about whether they repeat periodically.
explanations.d: CV is computed from whatever counts you have, whether or not they include observation error; it does not diagnose or rule out that error.

questions.prompt: "Red" (positively autocorrelated) environmental noise can, on its own, produce which of the following in a population time series?

options.text: Multi-year runs of consecutive good or bad years that resemble a cycle, with no periodic mechanism present
A perfectly constant population size
Zero variance in abundance
Guaranteed extinction within five years

explanations.a: Correct — because good and bad years cluster together under red noise, the resulting series can show apparent multi-year runs or pseudo-cycles even though nothing periodic is actually driving the population.
explanations.b: Red noise still has real variance from year to year; it does not produce constancy.
explanations.c: Reddening changes the temporal correlation structure of variance, not its magnitude, and does not zero it out.
explanations.d: Red noise changes dynamics and can affect extinction risk, but does not guarantee extinction on any fixed timeline.

questions.prompt: Order these from weakest to strongest evidence that an observed pattern in a population series is a true periodic cycle rather than red-noise variability.

items.text: Two or three peaks in a 10-15 year student dataset, no proposed mechanism
A regular period recurring across roughly five to six intervals in a multi-decade dataset
The same recurring period across many decades, plus an independently documented driving mechanism (e.g., a coupled predator-prey relationship)

questions.explanation: A couple of peaks with no mechanism is the weakest possible evidence for periodicity; several repeated intervals over decades strengthens the case considerably; and a long, many-times-repeated period paired with an independently supported mechanism (as with the lynx-hare system) is the strongest evidentiary bar.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher(s)/finding to the correct description.

right.text: Compiled and analyzed Hudson's Bay Company fur records showing a ~9.6-year lynx cycle
Showed terrestrial environmental noise tends to be white while marine noise tends to be reddened

questions.explanation: Steele's 1985 Nature paper contrasted the spectral color of terrestrial versus marine environmental variability; Elton and Nicholson's 1942 analysis of Hudson's Bay Company fur returns established the classic ~9.6-year lynx cycle spanning over a century of records.

lessons.label: Model Comparison and Honest Uncertainty

sections.heading: AIC, BIC, and the small-sample correction
sections.body: When several models could plausibly describe a count series — exponential (1 parameter, r), logistic (2 parameters, r and K), Ricker with a θ shape term (3-4 parameters) — you cannot just pick whichever fits best, because a model with more parameters can always fit the observed points more closely, even if it is capturing noise rather than signal. The Akaike Information Criterion, AIC = −2ln(L) + 2k, and the Bayesian Information Criterion, BIC = −2ln(L) + k·ln(n), both penalize extra parameters (k), with BIC penalizing more heavily as sample size n grows. For the small n typical of field ecology (a 10-20 year series), the standard fix is AICc, the small-sample-corrected AIC (Burnham and Anderson), which adds a further penalty term that grows sharply as n approaches k — precisely because ordinary AIC badly underpenalizes extra parameters when there is little data to estimate them from.

sections.heading: Why a 10-point series cannot support a 4-parameter model
sections.body: This is not a rule of thumb to be waived for a compelling-looking fit: a rough working guideline used in model-selection practice is that you need on the order of several times more data points than free parameters before a fitted model's parameter estimates are trustworthy, and well below that ratio AICc's correction term dominates and effectively refuses to prefer the complex model regardless of its raw likelihood. A 10-year count series fit with a 4-parameter θ-logistic-with-observation-error model is fitting nearly one parameter per data point — the model can trace the observed wiggles almost exactly, but the fitted r, K, and θ have essentially no ability to generalize to a year not in the sample, and the same wiggly trajectory can usually be matched by several very different parameter combinations.

sections.heading: Bootstrapped CIs and prediction intervals, not point forecasts
sections.body: Because a single fitted r or K is a point estimate drawn from one noisy realization of the population's history, the honest next step is bootstrapping: resampling the residuals (or, for autocorrelated series, resampling in contiguous blocks to preserve the temporal correlation structure) and refitting the model hundreds or thousands of times to build an empirical confidence interval around each parameter. The single most common gap in student projects is stopping there and reporting a bare forecast — "the population will be 340 in five years." A defensible forecast is a prediction interval: propagating the parameter uncertainty (and, ideally, process-error variance) forward through the model to report a range, such as "between roughly 210 and 510 individuals, with 340 as the central estimate," because a point forecast implies a confidence the underlying data never earned.

lessons.workedExample: A student has 10 years of pond turtle counts and compares three models: exponential (k=1), logistic (k=2), and θ-logistic (k=4). Raw log-likelihoods favor the θ-logistic — it traces the observed ups and downs almost perfectly. But AICc, computed with the small-sample correction for n=10, penalizes the θ-logistic so heavily that the logistic model has the lowest (best) AICc despite its slightly worse raw fit; the 4-parameter model is judged to be overfitting. The student then bootstraps 2,000 resampled residual series through the logistic fit and gets r = 0.14 (95% CI: 0.05-0.24) and K = 180 (95% CI: 130-310). A five-year-ahead forecast propagated through those bootstrap replicates gives a prediction interval of roughly 95-260 individuals rather than a single number like "170."
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about model choice and forecast confidence because reporting a bare number ("my model predicts 340 in 2030") is the fastest tell that a student never grappled with how much uncertainty their small dataset actually carries. A weak answer picks the model with the best-looking fit line and reports one forecast number. A strong answer explains why a simpler model was chosen over a more flexible one given the sample size (ideally citing AICc rather than raw AIC), and reports a range — a bootstrapped confidence interval on the parameters and, better still, a prediction interval on the forecast — rather than a single confident-sounding value.

questions.prompt: Why is AICc (small-sample-corrected AIC) preferred over ordinary AIC for a 10-15 year population time series?

options.text: AICc is always numerically smaller than AIC, so it always favors more complex models
Ordinary AIC underpenalizes extra parameters when the sample size is small relative to the number of parameters, so AICc adds a correction that grows as n approaches k
AICc does not require computing a likelihood
AICc is only valid for exponential growth models

explanations.a: AICc is not simply smaller; it is a larger (more conservative) penalty than AIC specifically to counteract overfitting risk in small samples.
explanations.b: Correct — the correction term is designed to grow sharply as sample size n gets close to parameter count k, which is exactly the regime a 10-20 year field series sits in.
explanations.c: AICc still requires a fitted likelihood; it modifies the penalty term, not the likelihood computation itself.
explanations.d: AICc applies to any model comparison problem, not specifically to exponential growth.

questions.prompt: A student reports "the model predicts the population will be exactly 340 individuals in 2030." What is the main problem with this statement?

options.text: It is a point forecast that hides the parameter and process uncertainty; a prediction interval should be reported instead
340 is not a whole number of turtles
Forecasts should never be stated in numbers
The year 2030 is too far in the future for any model to ever be used

explanations.a: Correct — a bare point forecast implies a precision the fitted model, with its parameter uncertainty and process noise, cannot actually deliver; the honest statement is a range.
explanations.b: 340 is a perfectly fine whole number; the issue is the false precision of a single value, not its format.
explanations.c: Numeric forecasts are fine and expected — the fix is reporting them as an interval, not avoiding numbers.
explanations.d: Distance into the future affects how wide the interval should be, but it does not make forecasting invalid outright.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it does.

right.text: Penalizes extra parameters using a fixed penalty of 2 per parameter
Penalizes extra parameters more heavily as sample size n grows, via a ln(n) term
Resamples residuals (or blocks, for autocorrelated data) and refits repeatedly to build empirical parameter confidence intervals
Propagates parameter and process uncertainty forward to report a range for a future forecast, not a single value

questions.explanation: AIC uses a flat 2k penalty; BIC's penalty scales with ln(n), so it punishes complexity more as data accumulate; bootstrapping resampled residuals is how empirical confidence intervals on fitted parameters are typically built; a prediction interval is the forward-propagated range that should replace a bare point forecast.

questions.prompt: Order the steps in a defensible model-comparison and forecasting workflow.

items.text: Fit exponential, logistic, and Ricker models to the same count series
Compare AICc across the fitted models to select the best-supported one given the sample size
Bootstrap residuals to obtain confidence intervals on the selected model's parameters
Propagate that uncertainty forward to report a prediction interval, not a point forecast

questions.explanation: You must first fit the candidate models, then use AICc (not raw likelihood) to select among them given the sample size, then quantify parameter uncertainty via bootstrapping, and only then propagate that uncertainty into an honest forecast range.

lessons.label: Correlation, Causation, and Confounds in Population Data

sections.heading: Pseudoreplication: repeated counts are not independent replicates
sections.body: Hurlbert (1984, Ecological Monographs 54:187–211) named and formalized a problem that runs through nearly every observational population study: pseudoreplication is treating measurements that are not statistically independent as if they were independent replicates in an inferential test. Surveying at counting one site every year for twenty years gives you twenty data points, but it does not give you twenty independent tests of whether, say, predator density drives prey decline at that site — the site's soil, microclimate, and history are shared across every one of those years, so autocorrelated conditions, not independent trials, generate the pattern. Hurlbert's survey of 176 published ecological field experiments found 27% suffered from pseudoreplication, rising to 48% among studies that used inferential statistics at all — a rate that should make any student pause before treating a single site's time series as proof of a general mechanism.

sections.heading: Confounded covariates
sections.body: Even setting pseudoreplication aside, a correlational time series is routinely haunted by confounding: a third variable that drives both the predictor and the outcome you are studying, making them move together without either one causing the other. The classic case in population ecology is weather: a cold, harsh winter can simultaneously suppress predator hunting success and reduce food-plant growth, so predator abundance and prey food supply end up correlated across years purely because both track the same climate signal, not because one drives the other. A correlation between predator numbers and prey decline, observed only at one site over one stretch of years, cannot distinguish "predators caused the decline," "weather caused both," and "prey decline caused predators to leave" — all three produce the same correlational signature.

sections.heading: What manipulative experiments buy you
sections.body: This is exactly why manipulative field experiments carry more inferential weight than any correlational series, however long. Krebs, Boutin, Boonstra, Sinclair, Smith, Dale, Martin, and Turkington (1995, Science 269:1112–1117) ran an eight-year factorial experiment on snowshoe hares in the Kluane region of the Yukon: nine 1-km² blocks, with electric fences excluding mammalian predators on some blocks (while allowing avian predators through), supplemental alfalfa-pellet food added to others, and both manipulations combined on others, against unmanipulated controls. Because the manipulations were assigned by the experimenters rather than observed as they happened to occur, the result was not just correlational: predator exclusion alone roughly doubled hare density during the cyclic peak and decline, food addition alone roughly tripled it, and the combined treatment produced an 11-fold increase relative to controls — a result no amount of watching an unmanipulated, weather-confounded time series could have delivered with the same certainty.

lessons.workedExample: A student observes 15 years of fox and vole counts at one field site and finds a strong negative correlation: high fox years line up with low vole years. They conclude fox predation regulates the vole population. But the site had unusually snowy winters in the same years foxes were scarce, and snow cover independently boosts vole survival by insulating their subnivean burrows — so the true driver could be weather affecting both species independently, not fox predation at all, and the fifteen years are also pseudoreplicated (one site, autocorrelated conditions) rather than fifteen independent trials. The Kluane hare experiment shows the fix: Krebs and colleagues did not wait to see if predator and food levels happened to vary together — they built the fence and added the food themselves, on replicated blocks, which is what let them attribute the 11-fold density increase to predation and food specifically rather than to whatever the weather happened to do that decade.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges lean hard on this because "my two variables were correlated over N years" is the most common causal overreach in a population-ecology fair project, and it is usually fixable with one sentence the student hasn't said yet. A weak answer treats a correlation from one site's time series as proof of mechanism. A strong answer names a specific plausible confound (usually weather) that could produce the same pattern without the claimed causal link, acknowledges that repeated counts at one site are not independent replicates, and — if the project allows it — describes what a manipulation (even a small-scale exclusion or supplementation) would need to look like to actually test the causal claim.

questions.prompt: According to Hurlbert (1984), what is pseudoreplication?

options.text: Using inferential statistics on data where treatments are not replicated or the replicates are not statistically independent
Making a typo when copying data into a spreadsheet
Running the same experiment twice to confirm the result
Using too small a sample size

explanations.a: Correct — this is Hurlbert's definition; the core issue is that the statistical test assumes independence the data do not actually have, most often because repeated measures share the same site or history.
explanations.b: Pseudoreplication is a structural design and analysis issue, not a data-entry error.
explanations.c: Genuine replication for confirmation is good practice; pseudoreplication is the opposite — treating non-independent measures as if they were replicates.
explanations.d: A small sample can be a separate problem, but pseudoreplication specifically concerns non-independence, not merely low n.

questions.prompt: Why can a confound like weather make predator abundance and prey food supply appear correlated without either causing the other?

options.text: Because weather independently affects both variables at the same time, so they move together without a direct causal link between them
Because weather always increases predator numbers
Because correlational data always overstate variance
Because weather has no effect on animal populations

explanations.a: Correct — a shared external driver hitting both variables at once produces exactly the correlational pattern you would expect from direct causation, without any causal arrow between the two variables themselves.
explanations.b: Weather's effect direction varies by species and condition; the general mechanism is shared influence, not a fixed direction.
explanations.c: This is not a statement about variance; the confound issue is about causal misattribution.
explanations.d: Weather routinely affects population variables; the point of this lesson is precisely that it does, which is what makes it a dangerous confound.

questions.prompt: Match each treatment in the Kluane snowshoe hare experiment (Krebs et al. 1995) to its approximate effect on hare density relative to controls.

left.text: Predator exclusion plus food addition combined

right.text: Roughly doubled density
Roughly tripled density
Roughly 11-fold increase in density

questions.explanation: In the eight-year Kluane factorial experiment, predator exclusion alone roughly doubled hare density during the cyclic peak and decline, food addition alone roughly tripled it, and the two combined produced an 11-fold increase — a result that let the researchers attribute density changes to specific manipulated causes rather than to correlated, unmanipulated conditions.

questions.prompt: Order these study designs from weakest to strongest for establishing that predators cause prey decline.

items.text: A negative correlation between predator and prey counts at one site over several years
The same correlation observed independently across several unconnected sites
A manipulative experiment with replicated predator-exclusion and control plots

questions.explanation: A single-site correlation is the weakest evidence because it is both pseudoreplicated and vulnerable to confounds like weather; replicating the correlation across independent sites strengthens the case somewhat by ruling out site-specific quirks; but only a manipulative experiment with true replication, like the Kluane predator-exclusion plots, can isolate the causal effect of predation from confounding variables.

units.label: Landmark Work and Open Debates in Population Ecology

lessons.label: The Logistic Curve: Verhulst, Pearl, and the Backlash

sections.heading: Verhulst's forgotten equation
sections.body: The Belgian mathematician Pierre-François Verhulst derived the logistic equation in 1838, adding a self-limiting term to Malthus's exponential growth model: dN/dt = rN(1 - N/K). Growth slows as population size N approaches a ceiling K, the carrying capacity. Verhulst even fit it to French and Belgian census data, but the work was largely ignored for eighty years — there was no mechanism offered for why K should exist, and no way to measure it independently of the growth curve itself.

sections.heading: Pearl and Reed's confident rediscovery
sections.body: Biologist Raymond Pearl and mathematician Lowell Reed re-derived the same equation independently in 1920, unaware of Verhulst, and published "On the Rate of Growth of the Population of the United States since 1790 and its Mathematical Representation." Fitting the curve to a century of US census figures, they projected an asymptote near 197 million people. Pearl went further, growing Drosophila melanogaster in half-pint milk bottles with a fixed daily food ration and watching the fly counts trace a near-perfect S-curve as the culture filled its bottle — visible, countable proof, he argued, that the same law governed a jar of flies and a nation.

sections.heading: The critique: K is fitted, not measured
sections.body: The forecast collapsed on contact with reality. US population passed 197 million by 1967 and kept climbing past 330 million by 2020, showing no sign of leveling off — immigration, medicine, and agriculture had moved the ceiling Pearl treated as fixed. The deeper statistical critique came from William Feller in 1940, who showed that three free parameters (r, K, and the curve's inflection point) let the logistic fit almost any smoothly rising S-shaped dataset regardless of the true underlying biology, so a good fit is weak evidence the mechanism is real. Ecologist Frederick E. Smith extended the challenge in 1963, using his own Daphnia magna population data to show that the logistic's fixed inflection point doesn't match how real populations grow, and proposed a revised three-parameter growth model in its place. K, critics concluded, is a curve-fitting parameter recovered after the fact, not a biological quantity a field ecologist can go out and independently measure before a population reaches it.

sections.heading: Why it survives anyway
sections.body: Despite the failed forecast, the logistic remains the entry point for population ecology because it is the simplest model that produces density-dependent slowing, and it underlies later tools like the Ricker and Beverton-Holt fisheries models and the r/K selection framework. Students should hold both facts at once: it is pedagogically essential and empirically fragile as a predictive tool.

lessons.workedExample: Pearl fit the 1790-1910 US census (roughly 3.9 million to 92 million) to a logistic curve and solved for K algebraically from three equally spaced census points, getting K ≈ 197,274,000 with an inflection near 1914. The curve tracked the data closely through 1950. But it had no mechanism for antibiotics, the Green Revolution, or post-1965 immigration reform — all of which raised the effective ceiling. By 1967 the US had already exceeded Pearl's predicted maximum; by 2020 the population (~331 million) was 68% above it. The lesson is not that Pearl calculated carelessly — his algebra was correct — but that a three-parameter fit to fifty years of data cannot see a ceiling that itself moves.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a student fit a logistic curve to their own data (bacteria in a flask, yeast in broth, a classroom population game) will ask: "How do you know K is a real biological limit and not just wherever your curve happened to level off?" A weak answer restates that the R-squared is high. A strong answer names the fitting problem directly — cites that Pearl's own 197-million forecast was wrong within two generations because conditions that set K changed — and proposes an independent check, such as directly measuring the limiting resource (food, space, oxygen) rather than trusting the curve's asymptote alone.

questions.prompt: Pearl and Reed's 1920 logistic fit to US census data projected a population ceiling of about 197 million. What happened to that prediction?

options.text: The US population leveled off almost exactly at 197 million as predicted
The US population exceeded 197 million by 1967 and kept growing past 330 million with no sign of a ceiling
The prediction was correct but only for the eastern states
Census data after 1920 was too unreliable to test the prediction

explanations.a: The population blew past 197 million decades before 2000 and never leveled off near that figure.
explanations.b: Correct — the US passed 197 million by 1967 and reached roughly 331 million by 2020, about 68% above the projected ceiling, because factors like immigration policy and agricultural yield shifted K over time.
explanations.c: The census data are national totals; the failure was in the model's assumption of a fixed ceiling, not a regional artifact.
explanations.d: Census methodology was reasonably consistent across the 20th century; the mismatch is a modeling failure, not a data-quality issue.

questions.prompt: William Feller's 1940 critique of the logistic model centered on which problem?

options.text: The equation cannot produce an S-shaped curve at all
With three free parameters, the logistic can be fit to almost any smoothly rising S-curve, so a good fit does not confirm the underlying mechanism
The logistic only applies to insects, never to vertebrates
Verhulst's original 1838 derivation contained an algebra error

explanations.a: The logistic reliably produces an S-curve; that was never in dispute.
explanations.b: Correct — Feller showed the curve's flexibility (via r, K, and the inflection point) lets it match many datasets that arise from different underlying processes, so fit quality alone cannot validate the biology.
explanations.c: The logistic has been fit to organisms from bacteria to whales to human census data; taxonomic scope was not Feller's objection.
explanations.d: Feller's critique was statistical/philosophical about parameter fitting, not a correction of Verhulst's math.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their contribution to the logistic-curve story.

right.text: First derived the logistic equation (1838), largely ignored for decades
Fit the curve to US census and Drosophila bottle cultures, forecast a 197-million ceiling
Showed the model's flexible parameters can fit many S-curves regardless of true mechanism
Used his own Daphnia magna data to propose a revised growth model, showing the logistic's fixed inflection point doesn't fit real population curves

questions.explanation: Verhulst originated the equation; Pearl and Reed revived and popularized it with the flawed census forecast and Drosophila cultures; Feller attacked its statistical fitting logic; Smith used his own Daphnia magna data to show the logistic's fixed inflection point doesn't fit real population curves and proposed a new model.

questions.prompt: Why does the logistic model still appear throughout population ecology despite its failed 1920 forecast?

options.text: Because the 197-million prediction was later shown to be correct after all
Because it is the simplest model producing density-dependent slowing and underlies later tools like the Ricker model and r/K selection theory
Because Feller's and Smith's critiques were later retracted
Because no population has ever grown exponentially, so the logistic is the only valid growth model

explanations.a: The prediction was wrong and stayed wrong; the US population never returned toward 197 million.
explanations.b: Correct — its simplicity and its role as a foundation for later fisheries and life-history models keep it central pedagogically even though it is a weak predictive tool on its own.
explanations.c: Both critiques stand in the literature; they were not retracted, only accommodated by treating the logistic as a heuristic rather than a precise forecasting tool.
explanations.d: Exponential growth does occur, especially at low density or short timescales; the logistic is used because it adds realism, not because exponential growth is impossible.

lessons.label: The Great Density-Dependence Debate

sections.heading: Nicholson: populations are regulated by competition
sections.body: Australian entomologist A. J. Nicholson argued in "The Balance of Animal Populations" (1933) that populations are held near an equilibrium by density-dependent factors — mechanisms whose intensity rises as crowding rises, chiefly intraspecific competition for a limiting resource. He tested this directly with laboratory cultures of the sheep blowfly Lucilia cuprina (published 1954), feeding larvae a fixed daily protein ration. As adult flies became crowded, larval food per capita fell, egg production crashed, and the population cycled in sharp boom-bust oscillations driven by a lag between resource scarcity and its effect on reproduction. To Nicholson this was regulation in action: a negative feedback loop that, given enough time, would always pull numbers back toward a bound.

sections.heading: Andrewartha and Birch: weather, not balance
sections.body: H. G. Andrewartha and L. C. Birch rejected the whole framing in their 1954 book "The Distribution and Abundance of Animals." Drawing on decades of counts of Thrips imaginis, a tiny insect that swarms on Australian rose blossoms, they showed abundance tracked rainfall and temperature far more tightly than any density-dependent signal, and argued most populations rarely stay near a resource ceiling long enough for competition to matter — weather resets things first. They distrusted the very idea of a "balance of nature," seeing it as an unproven assumption smuggled into ecology rather than a demonstrated fact.

sections.heading: The 1957 collision
sections.body: The dispute came to a head at the 1957 Cold Spring Harbor Symposium on Quantitative Biology ("Population Studies: Animal Ecology and Demography"), where Nicholson and the Andrewartha-Birch camp presented competing frameworks to the same room. Neither side converted the other; contemporaries described the exchange as a genuine impasse rather than a resolved debate, and it set the terms — density-dependent regulation versus density-independent, weather-driven limitation — that structured population ecology for the following decades.

sections.heading: The modern partial resolution
sections.body: Later work reframed the argument rather than declaring a winner. Both processes operate: weather and other density-independent factors set the ceiling and cause much of the year-to-year noise, while density-dependent regulation acts to pull populations back toward bounds — but often only intermittently, in occasional bad years, or at spatial scales and time spans too long for a typical multi-year study to detect. A short dataset can look purely density-independent simply because the regulating event (a crash from overcrowding, a disease outbreak) has not yet occurred within the observation window. The lesson for a science-fair project: absence of a density-dependence signal in three years of data is not evidence it doesn't exist.

lessons.workedExample: Nicholson's blowfly cultures held larval food constant at a fixed daily ration while adults bred freely. Egg output tracked available protein per larva; when adult numbers surged, larvae starved and the next generation's adult count crashed 2-3 generations later because of the larval-to-adult development lag, producing a sawtooth cycle Nicholson read as textbook density dependence. Andrewartha and Birch's Thrips imaginis counts, gathered from South Australian rose gardens across multiple decades, instead correlated tightly with spring temperature and rainfall — years of favorable weather produced huge swarms regardless of how crowded the previous generation had been, with no clear ceiling effect. Both datasets were real and carefully collected; they described genuinely different systems (a resource-capped lab culture versus a wild population rarely near any resource limit), which is exactly why the argument could not be settled by declaring one dataset wrong.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes this debate because it is the cleanest test of whether a student understands that a clean correlation with weather does not rule out regulation, and a demonstrated feedback loop in a cage does not prove the same species is regulated the same way in the wild. A weak answer picks a side ("populations are regulated" or "it's all weather") as if the question were settled in 1954. A strong answer says both mechanisms operate, that regulation can be intermittent and easy to miss in a short study, and can point to the 1957 Cold Spring Harbor symposium as the moment the field had to admit the two camps were talking about genuinely different timescales and systems rather than one being simply wrong.

questions.prompt: In Nicholson's blowfly (Lucilia cuprina) cultures, what caused the sawtooth population cycles he observed?

options.text: Random seasonal temperature swings in the lab
A lag between larval food scarcity from crowding and its delayed effect on adult egg production
Predators introduced partway through the experiment
A gradual decline in fly fertility with each generation

explanations.a: The cultures were kept in controlled lab conditions; temperature swings were not the driver Nicholson identified.
explanations.b: Correct — a fixed daily protein ration meant crowding reduced food per larva, which suppressed the following generation's adult egg output with a time lag, producing the boom-bust cycle.
explanations.c: The cultures were closed systems without predators; the dynamic was purely intraspecific competition for larval food.
explanations.d: Nicholson's model relied on density-dependent food limitation, not an intrinsic decline in fertility over generations.

questions.prompt: What did Andrewartha and Birch's Thrips imaginis data show that challenged Nicholson's framework?

options.text: Thrips abundance tracked temperature and rainfall closely, with populations rarely staying near a resource ceiling long enough for competition to dominate
Thrips populations were perfectly stable year to year regardless of weather
Thrips showed the same sawtooth cycling Nicholson found in blowflies
Thrips populations were controlled entirely by an introduced predator

explanations.a: Correct — abundance on Australian rose blossoms correlated strongly with spring rainfall and temperature, supporting a density-independent, weather-driven view of limitation rather than resource-based regulation.
explanations.b: Their data showed strong year-to-year swings tied to weather, not stability.
explanations.c: Their long-term Thrips record did not show the regulated sawtooth pattern Nicholson found in his caged blowflies; that contrast was the whole point of the disagreement.
explanations.d: No predator-driven mechanism was the basis of the Andrewartha-Birch argument; weather variables were.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the density-dependence debate chronologically.

items.text: Nicholson publishes "The Balance of Animal Populations," arguing for density-dependent regulation
Andrewartha and Birch publish "The Distribution and Abundance of Animals," using Thrips imaginis data to argue for weather-driven, density-independent limitation
The Cold Spring Harbor Symposium brings the two camps into direct confrontation
Later ecologists propose a partial resolution: regulation exists but acts intermittently, often invisible in short studies

questions.explanation: Nicholson's 1933 theoretical paper (later backed by the 1954 blowfly data) came first, Andrewartha and Birch's 1954 book directly challenged it, the 1957 Cold Spring Harbor Symposium staged the public collision, and the modern synthesis recognizing both mechanisms as real but operating on different timescales came afterward.

questions.prompt: Why can a 3-year field study fail to detect density dependence even in a population that IS regulated?

options.text: Because density dependence is a statistical illusion that never actually exists in nature
Because regulating events (like a crowding-driven crash) may occur only intermittently, at intervals or spatial scales longer than a short study can capture
Because density dependence only affects insects, never vertebrates
Because a 3-year study always has too few individuals to count accurately

explanations.a: Nicholson's blowfly cultures demonstrated a real, repeatable density-dependent mechanism; it is not merely a statistical artifact.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the modern partial resolution: regulation can be real but sporadic, so a short observation window can catch only the density-independent noise and miss the rarer regulating event.
explanations.c: Density dependence has been documented across insects, birds, mammals, and fish; it is not taxonomically restricted.
explanations.d: The problem is temporal/spatial scale of the regulating process, not simply small sample size within a given year.

lessons.label: Cycles: Lynx, Hares, and the Kluane Experiment

sections.heading: A fur-trade archive becomes ecological data
sections.body: Charles Elton and Mary Nicholson's 1942 paper "The Ten-Year Cycle in Numbers of the Lynx in Canada" mined nearly a century of Hudson's Bay Company pelt-purchase records to reconstruct boreal Canada's famous roughly 10-year snowshoe hare and Canada lynx cycle: hare numbers surge, lynx (their main predator) follow with a lag of a year or two, then both crash. It remains one of the longest continuous wildlife abundance records ever assembled, but the source carries a built-in artifact — pelt counts reflect trapper effort and fur prices, not just true animal abundance, so a slump in trapping during a hard winter or a market downturn can masquerade as a population crash, and vice versa. Later reconstructions using independent methods (snow tracking, live trapping) confirmed the cycle is real, but the fur data alone cannot be taken as a precise abundance index.

sections.heading: Two candidate drivers, tested in the field
sections.body: For decades the debate was whether the cycle was driven primarily bottom-up (hares crash because they exhaust their winter browse) or top-down (hares crash because predators, having built up during the hare peak, overwhelm the declining population). Charles Krebs and colleagues' Kluane Boreal Forest Ecosystem Project, run in Canada's southwestern Yukon from 1986 to 1996, tested both directly across nine 1 km² experimental blocks: some had supplemental food (rabbit chow) added year-round, some were fenced with electric predator exclosures, some had both, and some served as unmanipulated controls.

sections.heading: Neither factor alone, both together
sections.body: The results were decisive against either single-cause story. Predator exclusion alone roughly doubled hare density during the cyclic peak and decline; food addition alone roughly tripled it. But the two treatments combined — food added AND predators excluded — produced an 11-fold increase in hare density relative to controls, far more than the two individual effects summed. Predation risk was suppressing how much hares fed (they were spending energy staying vigilant and avoiding food-rich but exposed patches), so removing predators let them fully exploit the added food, and the two forces amplified each other rather than acting independently. The cycle, Krebs concluded, is driven by an interaction between food and predation, not by either factor in isolation.

sections.heading: An open puzzle: fading cycles in Europe
sections.body: A parallel and still-unresolved case is the collapse of multi-year vole cycles across parts of northern Europe since the late 1980s. Cornulier and colleagues (2013, Science) compiled vole time series from many sites and found a continent-scale dampening of cycle amplitude tied to reduced winter population growth, consistent with a shared climatic driver — likely warmer, less snow-insulated winters disrupting the subnivean conditions voles depend on — though the underlying regulatory processes have not disappeared and cycles have partially recovered at some sites in more recent years. It stands as an open reminder that even a textbook-strength population cycle is not guaranteed to be permanent.

lessons.workedExample: In the Kluane experiment's food + predator-exclosure blocks, hare density during the 1990s peak reached roughly 11 times that of unmanipulated control blocks — far beyond the roughly 2-fold effect of excluding predators alone or the roughly 3-fold effect of adding food alone. The nonadditive result (11 is much larger than 2+3=5, let alone what either factor achieved alone) is the key data point: it shows the two pressures were not simply stacking, they were interacting, because fear of predation was itself suppressing how much food hares would eat even when food was abundant. A study that manipulated only one variable — say, only fencing out predators — would have concluded predation is a moderate but not dominant factor, missing the much larger interactive effect entirely.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about the Kluane experiment because it is the clearest illustration in population ecology of why factorial design (manipulating two variables both separately and together) matters — a single-factor experiment would have badly underestimated the true effect. A weak answer says "food and predators both affect hares." A strong answer names the actual multipliers (roughly 2x, 3x, and 11x combined), explains the interaction mechanism (predation risk suppresses foraging even when food is present), and can extend the reasoning to their own project: did they test factors in combination, or only one at a time?

questions.prompt: What key artifact limits the Hudson's Bay Company fur-return records used by Elton and Nicholson to reconstruct the lynx-hare cycle?

options.text: The records only cover a five-year span, too short to show a cycle
Pelt counts reflect trapper effort and fur market prices as well as true animal abundance
The company only recorded lynx, never hares
The records were destroyed and had to be estimated from memory

explanations.a: The fur-return archive spans nearly a century, which is what makes it so valuable despite its flaws.
explanations.b: Correct — a drop in pelts sold can reflect fewer trappers going out or falling fur prices rather than fewer animals, so the record is a proxy confounded with human economic behavior.
explanations.c: The records include both species, which is what allowed Elton and Nicholson to compare their cycles and lags in the first place.
explanations.d: The Hudson's Bay Company kept detailed purchase ledgers; the issue is what the ledgers measure, not their survival.

questions.prompt: In the Kluane experiment, what was the approximate hare density increase in blocks that received BOTH food addition and predator exclusion, relative to controls?

options.text: About 2-fold, the same as predator exclusion alone
About 5-fold, the simple sum of the individual treatment effects
About 11-fold, far exceeding the sum of the individual effects
No measurable increase over controls

explanations.a: 2-fold was the effect of predator exclusion alone, not the combined treatment.
explanations.b: 5-fold would be the simple additive prediction (roughly 2 + 3); the actual combined result was much larger, which is the key finding.
explanations.c: Correct — the combined treatment produced roughly an 11-fold increase, showing food and predation interact rather than act independently on hare density.
explanations.d: Both single-factor treatments already produced substantial increases, and the combined treatment produced the largest effect of all.

questions.prompt: What does the nonadditive Kluane result (11-fold combined vs. roughly 2-fold and 3-fold individually) reveal about the mechanism driving the hare cycle?

options.text: Predation risk was suppressing how fully hares exploited available food, so removing predators let added food have a much larger effect
Food and predation act on completely separate, non-interacting hare subpopulations
Predation had no real effect on hare density in any treatment
The experiment was flawed because the treatments should have produced only additive effects

explanations.a: Correct — hares under predation risk avoid exposed, food-rich patches or spend energy on vigilance; removing that risk lets them fully use added food, producing a synergistic rather than additive combined effect.
explanations.b: The whole point of the nonadditive result is that the two factors interact within the same hares, not that they act on separate groups.
explanations.c: Predator exclusion alone roughly doubled hare density, showing predation clearly mattered on its own.
explanations.d: A synergistic (nonadditive) result is a real and informative biological finding, not evidence of experimental flaw.

questions.prompt: Match each study or record to what it primarily demonstrated.

right.text: Reconstructed a ~10-year hare-lynx cycle from historical trapping records, with abundance confounded by trapper economics
Showed food and predator-exclusion treatments interact synergistically, producing an 11-fold combined effect on hare density
Documented a continent-scale dampening of vole population cycle amplitude since the late 1980s, an unresolved puzzle

questions.explanation: Elton and Nicholson's fur-record analysis established the classic cycle but with a data-quality caveat; Krebs' factorial field experiment identified the food-predation interaction driving it; Cornulier's compilation showed a related rodent cycle fading across Europe for reasons still being investigated.

lessons.label: Laboratory Populations: Gause, Park, Huffaker

sections.heading: Gause: logistic curves and competitive exclusion in a test tube
sections.body: Soviet biologist Georgy Gause published "The Struggle for Existence" in 1934, growing the protist Paramecium caudatum alone in nutrient broth and finding its numbers traced a textbook logistic curve as it exhausted its bacterial food supply. He then cultured P. caudatum together with the smaller, faster-reproducing P. aurelia in the same tube: every time, P. aurelia won and P. caudatum was driven locally extinct, never coexisting stably. This became the empirical anchor for the competitive exclusion principle — two species with sufficiently similar resource requirements cannot indefinitely share one limiting resource in one homogeneous space.

sections.heading: Park: outcomes depend on climate and chance, not fixed superiority
sections.body: Thomas Park's flour-beetle experiments (Tribolium confusum versus T. castaneum, published through the 1940s-50s) complicated the tidy exclusion story. Pitting the two species against each other in jars of flour under different combinations of temperature and humidity, Park found the "winner" flipped depending on climate: T. confusum tended to win in cool, dry conditions and T. castaneum in warm, humid ones. Crucially, even within a single fixed climate treatment, the outcome was not perfectly predictable — repeated replicate jars sometimes produced different winners, showing that early demographic chance (which larvae survived cannibalism, which eggs hatched first) could tip an otherwise even contest. Competitive outcomes, Park showed, are conditional and partly stochastic, not fixed properties of two species.

sections.heading: Huffaker: predator-prey persistence needs space
sections.body: Carl Huffaker's 1958 mite experiments addressed a different failure mode: simple predator-prey systems in a small, uniform arena tend to go extinct fast, as the predator (Typhlodromus occidentalis) simply hunts down every last prey mite (the six-spotted mite, Eotetranychus sexmaculatus) and then itself starves. In a small, homogeneous tray of oranges, that is exactly what happened — one boom-bust cycle and both species were gone. Huffaker then built a far more complex "universe": a large array of oranges partially masked with wax paper, interspersed with rubber balls as dispersal obstacles and Vaseline barriers slowing mite movement, giving prey scattered refuges and travel time to recolonize empty patches before predators arrived. In that spatially structured arena, predator and prey coexisted through several oscillation cycles rather than collapsing after one.

sections.heading: What microcosms can and cannot tell you
sections.body: All three systems triggered the same ongoing argument: a bottle, jar, or orange array strips away spatial heterogeneity, immigration, and multi-species complexity that dampen extinction risk in real landscapes, so a lab result (competitive exclusion, chance-dependent outcomes, predator-driven collapse) shows what CAN happen under controlled conditions, not what always DOES happen in the field. Huffaker's own result makes the point for spatial structure specifically: the mechanism he needed to add — refuges and dispersal barriers — is exactly the kind of real-world complexity a simple cage removes by design.

lessons.workedExample: Huffaker's first, simple setup used a single tray of oranges (partly covered so only exposed rind was edible) — prey mites established, predator mites found them quickly, and the predator-prey system crashed within roughly one oscillation as the predator ate itself out of food.
