explanations.b: Correct — environmental filtering selects for one narrow strategy suited to local conditions, producing trait convergence among survivors.
explanations.c: Biotic filtering via limiting similarity typically produces the opposite pattern — trait divergence, not convergence.
explanations.d: Convergence significantly tighter than a null-model random draw indicates a real filtering process, not randomness.

questions.prompt: Why is defining the regional species pool from the observed local community a circularity trap?

options.text: It makes the pool too large to analyze statistically
It bakes the filtering outcome into the baseline, so any detected convergence or divergence becomes an artifact of pool definition rather than evidence of a real process
It violates rules about sample size in null models
Regional pools cannot include plant species, only animals

explanations.a: The trap is about validity of inference, not computational size.
explanations.b: Correct — if the pool already excludes poor dispersers or environmental misfits because it was built from what's locally observed, the comparison no longer tests an independent hypothesis.
explanations.c: This is a methodological/independence issue, not a sample-size rule.
explanations.d: The trap applies equally to any taxon; it is not taxon-restricted.

questions.prompt: The 'limiting similarity' principle (MacArthur & Levins 1967) predicts that coexisting species competing for a shared limited resource will tend to:

options.text: Become more similar to each other in resource-use traits over time
Diverge in resource-use traits, reducing competitive overlap
Go locally extinct together
Show no trait pattern related to competition

explanations.a: Convergence under strong competition for the same resource would intensify exclusion, not stabilize coexistence.
explanations.b: Correct — species too similar in resource use for the same limiting resource tend to exclude one another, so surviving coexisting species are pushed toward divergence (overdispersion) in relevant traits.
explanations.c: Limiting similarity describes trait sorting among persisting species, not necessarily co-extinction.
explanations.d: The principle specifically predicts a trait pattern — divergence — as a signature of competitive sorting.

lessons.label: Interaction Networks: Food Webs, Mutualistic Webs, and Indirect Effects

sections.heading: Describing a web as a network, not a list
sections.body: Once a community has more than a few species, its interactions are best described as a network: nodes are species, edges are interactions (who eats whom, who pollinates whom). Three summary statistics let ecologists compare webs of different sizes objectively. Connectance, C = L/S², is the fraction of all possible links (S² for S species, allowing cannibalism and reciprocal links) that are actually realized — a sparse web might have C around 0.05, a dense one above 0.3; the well-studied Ythan Estuary food web, for example, has been measured at roughly 90 species with a connectance near 0.06, a benchmark real value ecologists cite when judging whether another web is unusually sparse or dense. Linkage density, L/S, is the average number of links per species, a measure of how connected a typical species is. Modularity measures whether the network breaks into semi-isolated clusters (modules) of tightly interacting species with weak links between clusters, versus one uniformly interconnected mass.

sections.heading: Nestedness in mutualistic webs
sections.body: Jordi Bascompte, Pedro Jordano, Carlos Melián, and Jens Olesen (2003, PNAS) analyzed 52 plant-pollinator and plant-frugivore mutualistic networks and found them consistently and strongly nested: specialist species interact with a subset of the partners that generalist species interact with, rather than each specialist claiming its own exclusive partner. Picture the interaction matrix sorted from most- to least-connected species on each axis — a nested web forms a triangular, staircase-like block of filled cells rather than a scattered diagonal. This structure matters functionally: nested webs are more robust to random species loss (redundant generalist links buffer the system) but can be more vulnerable to the loss of the most-connected hub species, since specialists depend disproportionately on those same generalist partners.

sections.heading: Indirect effects: no direct link required
sections.body: Not every important interaction is a drawn edge. Robert Holt (1977) formalized apparent competition: two prey species that never interact directly can still suppress each other if they share a common predator, because an increase in prey A supports more predators, which then depredate more of prey B — the same mathematical signature as resource competition, but mediated entirely through a shared enemy rather than a shared resource. More generally, trophic cascades propagate indirect effects down exploitative chains (predator suppresses herbivore, herbivore release lets plants recover), and removing a species can raise, not lower, a competitor's abundance if that competitor was being suppressed by a predator the removed species also fed — apparent competition and cascades both illustrate why single-link thinking (X eats Y, done) systematically misses real community dynamics.

lessons.workedExample: A rangeland has two grasshopper species, A and B, that never compete for the same grass and show no measurable direct interaction. Both are eaten by the same generalist bird predator. When species A's population booms after a wet spring, the local bird population grows in response (functional and numerical response), and the resulting extra predation pressure lands on both grasshopper species — species B's population crashes even though A and B share no resource and never meet. A field experiment excluding birds from half the plots would show B recovering only where predators are excluded, confirming apparent competition (Holt 1977) rather than a phantom direct interaction between A and B.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on indirect effects because the single most common conceptual gap in student food-web projects is assuming every important relationship must be a drawn arrow. A strong answer can describe a mechanism — apparent competition via a shared predator, or a trophic cascade — where removing species X changes species Z's abundance despite no direct link between them, and can propose a manipulation (a predator-exclusion or removal experiment) that would distinguish direct from indirect causation. A weak answer treats network diagrams as complete descriptions of causality just because two species share no edge.

questions.prompt: Two prey species share no resource and never physically interact, but an increase in one causes a decline in the other because both are eaten by the same predator. This is:

options.text: Exploitative competition
Apparent competition (Holt 1977)
Mutualism
Ecosystem engineering

explanations.a: Exploitative competition requires a shared limiting resource, which is explicitly absent here.
explanations.b: Correct — apparent competition, formalized by Robert Holt (1977), produces a competition-like negative effect between two species mediated entirely by a shared predator, with no direct link or shared resource.
explanations.c: Mutualism requires a positive interaction between the two species, the opposite of what's described.
explanations.d: No physical habitat modification is involved; this is a trophic, not structural, mechanism.

questions.prompt: Connectance is calculated as:

options.text: L/S, the number of links divided by the number of species
L/S², the number of realized links divided by all possible links
S/L, species count divided by link count
The number of trophic levels in the web

explanations.a: L/S is linkage density, a related but distinct statistic (average links per species), not connectance.
explanations.b: Correct — connectance C = L/S² measures what fraction of all theoretically possible pairwise links are actually realized in the observed web.
explanations.c: This inverts the ratio and does not correspond to any standard network statistic used for food webs.
explanations.d: Trophic level count describes vertical structure, unrelated to the connectance calculation.

questions.prompt: Bascompte et al.'s (2003) analysis of plant-pollinator networks found they were strongly:

options.text: Random, with no detectable structure
Nested — specialists interact with subsets of the partners generalists use
Perfectly modular, with no overlap between clusters
One-to-one, each specialist paired with one exclusive partner

explanations.a: The study specifically found strong, non-random structure across 52 networks, not randomness.
explanations.b: Correct — nestedness means specialist species' partner sets are largely subsets of generalist species' broader partner sets, forming a triangular interaction-matrix pattern.
explanations.c: Nestedness and high modularity are largely alternative structures; mutualistic networks were found to be nested, not sharply modular.
explanations.d: Strict one-to-one exclusive pairing is the opposite of the redundant, overlapping structure nestedness describes.

questions.prompt: Match each network statistic or concept to its definition.

right.text: Fraction of all possible links that are realized (L/S²)
Average number of links per species (L/S)
Degree to which the network splits into semi-isolated clusters
Specialists' partners form subsets of generalists' partners

questions.explanation: Connectance = L/S² (fraction of possible links realized); linkage density = L/S (average links per species); modularity measures cluster structure; nestedness (Bascompte et al. 2003) describes the specialist-within-generalist partner pattern typical of mutualistic webs.

lessons.label: Trophic Structure and Cascades Across Communities

sections.heading: Why is the world green?
sections.body: Nelson Hairston, Frederick Smith, and Lawrence Slobodkin published a short but hugely influential 1960 paper in American Naturalist posing a deceptively simple question: if herbivores could eat all available plant matter, the world should be mostly bare — yet it is visibly green. Their answer, the HSS hypothesis, argued that herbivores are themselves held below the level where they would deplete vegetation by predation from carnivores — top-down control cascading through three trophic levels. This was a foundational claim that predators regulate plant abundance indirectly, and it launched decades of debate about whether communities are controlled from the top (predators limiting herbivores, herbivores releasing plants) or from the bottom (resource/productivity limiting plants, which limits everything above).

sections.heading: Productivity sets chain length: the Oksanen model
sections.body: Lauri Oksanen, Stephen Fretwell, Juan Arruda, and Pekka Niemelä (1981) extended HSS with the exploitation ecosystems hypothesis: whether top-down control operates at all depends on how many trophic levels the local primary productivity can support. At very low productivity, only plants persist (herbivores can't be supported, so nothing controls plants but resources — bottom-up). At moderate productivity, herbivores appear and suppress plants (still bottom-up limited plants, but herbivores are now resource-limited). At higher productivity, predators appear and suppress herbivores, releasing plants — three-level, top-down HSS-style control. Each added trophic level flips the sign of control on the level below it, so food-chain length itself is not fixed but predicted by the site's productivity. This theoretical link between productivity and cascade strength is borne out empirically: Jonathan Shurin and colleagues' (2002) cross-system meta-analysis found cascade strength ranked lake and marine benthic systems strongest, streams moderate, and terrestrial systems and marine plankton weakest of all — despite marine plankton being aquatic.

sections.heading: Where cascades are strong, and why: the cross-system meta-analysis
sections.body: Jonathan Shurin and colleagues (2002, Ecology Letters) meta-analyzed trophic cascade strength across many published studies spanning lakes, marine benthic systems, marine plankton, streams, and terrestrial systems, and found a striking four-tier gradient: cascades were strongest in lake and marine benthic (e.g., rocky intertidal, kelp forest) systems (mean effect size around 0.4-0.45), moderate in stream (lotic) systems (around 0.25), and weakest in terrestrial systems and marine plankton alike (around 0.08-0.12), with planktonic marine systems the single lowest category of all. The explanation students should be able to give centers on three factors. First, body-size ratios: aquatic predators are often vastly larger than their algal/phytoplankton prey, allowing near-total consumption, while terrestrial predators and plants are closer in relative processing constraints. Second, plant defenses: terrestrial plants invest heavily in structural and chemical defenses (lignin, tannins, thorns) that blunt herbivore impact regardless of predation pressure, while aquatic algae are largely undefended. Third, edibility: a much larger fraction of aquatic primary producer biomass is edible and nutritious (thin-walled algal cells) compared to terrestrial biomass, which is dominated by structural, low-nutrient tissue like wood and cellulose. Marine plankton systems are the exception to the 'aquatic means strong' pattern: fast phytoplankton turnover and grazer compensation there make cascades weak despite the system being aquatic.

lessons.workedExample: A class compares two systems: a rocky-intertidal kelp bed where sea otters prey on urchins, and a nearby oak woodland where coyotes prey on deer. Removing otters lets urchins overgraze kelp into 'urchin barrens' within a couple of growing seasons — a strong, fast cascade, consistent with Shurin et al.'s benthic-marine finding, driven by large predator-to-prey body ratios and undefended, fully edible kelp tissue. Removing coyotes, by contrast, produces a much weaker, slower shift in oak seedling recruitment, because deer browsing pressure is buffered by oak chemical/structural defenses (tannins, bark) and because much of the woodland's plant biomass (trunk wood) was never edible to deer in the first place — illustrating why terrestrial cascades in Shurin's meta-analysis were among the weakest categories, on par with planktonic marine systems.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'why would/wouldn't you expect a cascade in your system?' because predicting cascade strength from first principles (not just hoping to find one) is what separates a mechanistic understanding from pattern-matching. A strong answer names the relevant factor — body-size ratio, plant defense investment, or edible-biomass fraction — and connects it to whether the system is aquatic or terrestrial, citing the Shurin et al. (2002) cross-system gradient. A weak answer asserts 'predators control everything' as a universal law without engaging why HSS's own logic (via Oksanen) predicts cascades should appear only above a certain productivity threshold and be system-dependent in strength.

questions.prompt: Hairston, Smith, and Slobodkin's (1960) 'why is the world green' argument proposed that herbivores are kept below plant-depleting levels by:

options.text: Limited plant productivity alone (bottom-up control)
Predation from carnivores (top-down control)
Disease limiting herbivore reproduction
Herbivore migration out of productive areas

explanations.a: HSS's central claim was the opposite of pure bottom-up limitation for herbivores — they argued predators, not resources, hold herbivores down.
explanations.b: Correct — HSS proposed that carnivores suppress herbivores below the level that would deplete vegetation, a top-down control cascading through three trophic levels.
explanations.c: Disease was not the mechanism HSS proposed; their argument centered on predation.
explanations.d: Migration is not part of the HSS mechanism.

questions.prompt: According to Oksanen et al.'s (1981) exploitation ecosystems hypothesis, what determines whether a system has 2 or 3 functional trophic levels of control?

options.text: Latitude alone
Primary productivity, which determines how many trophic levels can be supported
The presence of any predator species, regardless of productivity
Soil pH

explanations.a: Latitude can correlate with productivity but is not the mechanism itself in the model.
explanations.b: Correct — Oksanen's model predicts food-chain length and which trophic level controls the one below it as a function of site productivity, with each added level flipping the control direction below it.
explanations.c: A predator's mere presence does not guarantee top-down control if productivity cannot sustain the additional trophic level's full effect.
explanations.d: Soil pH is not a variable in the exploitation ecosystems hypothesis.

questions.prompt: Order these ecosystem types from strongest to weakest average trophic cascade strength, per Shurin et al. (2002).

items.text: Marine benthic / lake systems
Stream (lotic) systems
Terrestrial and marine plankton systems

questions.explanation: Shurin et al. (2002) found cascades strongest in lake and marine benthic systems, moderate in stream systems, and weakest in terrestrial and marine plankton systems, with planktonic marine the single lowest of all.

questions.prompt: Which factor best explains why terrestrial trophic cascades tend to be weaker than aquatic ones?

options.text: Terrestrial predators are always rarer than aquatic predators
Terrestrial plants invest heavily in structural/chemical defenses and much of their biomass (wood, cellulose) is low-nutrient and inedible
Terrestrial food webs have no indirect effects
Terrestrial herbivores reproduce more slowly than aquatic herbivores in all cases

explanations.a: Predator rarity is not the general explanation offered for the terrestrial-aquatic cascade-strength gap.
explanations.b: Correct — heavy investment in structural/chemical defenses and a large fraction of low-nutrient, inedible biomass (wood, cellulose) blunt herbivore impact on terrestrial plants regardless of predation pressure, weakening the cascade.
explanations.c: Indirect effects (apparent competition, cascades) occur in terrestrial systems too; they are simply weaker on average, not absent.
explanations.d: Herbivore reproductive rate is not the primary factor Shurin et al. identify; body-size ratios, defenses, and edibility are.

lessons.label: Community Structure in Space and Time

sections.heading: Zonation: two forces bracket a band
sections.body: The rocky intertidal shore is the classic teaching system for spatial community structure because its bands are visible and their causes are experimentally proven. Joseph Connell's 1961 study of two barnacle species on the Scottish coast, Chthamalus stellatus and Balanus balanoides, showed that Chthamalus's upper limit is set by physical stress — desiccation and heat during low tide, which it tolerates and Balanus does not — while its lower limit is set by competition: Balanus, competitively superior for space lower on the shore where both could physically survive, out-grows and smothers Chthamalus. Removing Balanus experimentally let Chthamalus persist much lower than it does naturally. The general pattern this established, later confirmed across many rocky shores, is that upper community boundaries are usually physiologically/abiotically set, while lower boundaries are usually biotically set by competition or predation.

sections.heading: Vertical layering beyond the shore
sections.body: The same stratification logic recurs wherever a strong vertical gradient exists. A temperate forest divides into canopy, subcanopy, shrub, and herb/litter layers, each hosting largely distinct bird and insect assemblages sorted by light availability and structural habitat. A lake divides vertically by light and temperature: the epilimnion (warm, mixed, photosynthetic) sits above the thermocline, which sits above the cold, dark hypolimnion, and phytoplankton, zooplankton, and fish distributions track this thermal layering closely, especially once summer stratification sets in. In a typical temperate dimictic lake this layering is concrete, not abstract: the epilimnion commonly runs 20-25°C and 0-5 m deep in summer, the thermocline drops sharply across roughly 5-10 m, and the hypolimnion below settles near 4-10°C, cold and often oxygen-depleted enough that many fish avoid it even though it is nutrient-rich.

sections.heading: Turnover in time, and the grain problem
sections.body: Communities also restructure across time. Seasonal turnover and phenological aspection — the term for the seasonal parade of a temperate community's dominant visible life forms, spring ephemeral wildflowers giving way to summer grasses giving way to autumn asters — mean a single-season snapshot systematically undercounts true community membership. Finally, whatever the axis, what a community 'looks like' structurally depends on the sampling grain (the size of each sampling unit) and extent (the total area/time covered) relative to the scale of underlying spatial autocorrelation — how similar nearby points tend to be. Grain much finer than the patch size of real structure reads as noise; grain much coarser than it blurs real mosaic structure into an apparent smooth gradient; only grain matched to the true patch scale reveals the actual mosaic or gradient pattern.

lessons.workedExample: A team samples salt-marsh vegetation with 0.25 m² quadrats along a 100 m transect from creek edge to upland. At this fine grain they detect sharp mosaic patches of Spartina alterniflora versus bare pannes, each just a meter or two across. When they resample the same transect using 20 m segments averaged together, the same landscape now reads as one smooth elevation gradient from tall Spartina to short Spartina to upland shrub, with the panne patches invisible — the underlying ecology didn't change, but coarsening the grain past the patch scale converted real mosaic structure into an apparent gradient, a direct illustration of why grain and extent must be reported alongside any claim about community pattern.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe sampling grain because it is the most common hidden confound in student vegetation and community-structure projects — two teams can sample the identical hillside and report contradictory 'patterns' purely because one used 1 m² plots and the other used 50 m transects. A strong answer states the grain and extent used, explains what scale of real structure that choice can and cannot detect, and — for zonation claims specifically — separates the abiotic driver of an upper boundary from the biotic driver of a lower one, citing the Connell logic. A weak answer describes a band on a shore or graph as simply 'the zone' without asking what set each edge.

questions.prompt: In Connell's (1961) barnacle study, what set the UPPER limit of Chthamalus stellatus's zone on the shore?

options.text: Competition from Balanus balanoides
Physical stress — desiccation and heat during low tide exposure
Predation by shore birds
Availability of planktonic larvae

explanations.a: Competition from Balanus set the LOWER limit, not the upper limit, of Chthamalus's zone.
explanations.b: Correct — the upper boundary was set by Chthamalus's own physiological tolerance limit for desiccation/heat stress during low tide.
explanations.c: Bird predation was not the mechanism Connell identified for the upper-limit boundary.
explanations.d: Larval supply affects colonization broadly but was not the specific mechanism shown to set the upper zonation edge.

questions.prompt: The general pattern from rocky-intertidal zonation studies is that upper community boundaries tend to be set by ___, while lower boundaries tend to be set by ___.

options.text: competition; abiotic/physical stress
abiotic/physical stress; competition or predation
predation; dispersal limitation
tidal current; sediment type

explanations.a: This reverses the established pattern from Connell's work and subsequent studies.
explanations.b: Correct — upper limits are typically set by physiological tolerance to abiotic stress (desiccation, heat), while lower limits are typically set by biotic interactions (competition, predation) where physical conditions would otherwise allow persistence.
explanations.c: Predation can matter but dispersal limitation is not the standard mechanism cited for lower zonation boundaries in this classic pattern.
explanations.d: Tidal current and sediment type are not the mechanisms Connell's barnacle work identified.

questions.prompt: Match each spatial/temporal concept to its description.

right.text: The seasonal parade of a community's dominant visible life forms
The size of each individual sampling unit
The total area or time span covered by sampling
The tendency for nearby points to be more similar than distant ones

questions.explanation: Phenological aspection describes seasonal turnover in dominant visible life forms; grain is the size of each sampling unit; extent is the total sampled area/time; spatial autocorrelation describes how similarity decays with distance, which interacts with grain choice to determine whether structure reads as pattern or noise.

questions.prompt: A team resamples a patchy marsh landscape using much coarser quadrats than the true patch size and now sees a smooth gradient instead of the mosaic detected at fine grain. This is best explained by:

options.text: The vegetation actually changed between samplings
Coarsening the grain past the true patch scale blurred real mosaic structure into an apparent smooth gradient
The species were misidentified the second time
Phenological aspection caused the shift

explanations.a: Nothing in the scenario indicates real ecological change between the two samplings — only the sampling grain changed.
explanations.b: Correct — when sampling grain is much coarser than the scale of real spatial structure, fine mosaic patchiness gets averaged out and appears as a smooth gradient, even though the underlying ecology is unchanged.
explanations.c: Misidentification is not indicated or the relevant mechanism here.
explanations.d: Aspection concerns seasonal (temporal) turnover, not a spatial grain-resolution artifact.

lessons.label: Designing a Community Survey: Effort, Grain, and Standardization

sections.heading: Nesting your plots to separate scales of variation
sections.body: A single transect confounds two questions ecologists usually want kept apart: how much does composition vary within one patch, versus between patches across a landscape? Hierarchical (nested) sampling designs — subplots nested inside plots nested inside sites, often several replicate sites per habitat type — let a variance-components analysis partition total variation into within-site and between-site terms, which is exactly what Robert Whittaker formalized when he distinguished alpha (within-site), beta (turnover between sites), and gamma (regional total) diversity in his 1960 Siskiyou Mountains vegetation survey (Ecological Monographs, covering Oregon and California) and refined conceptually in his 1972 review paper in Taxon. Skipping the nesting collapses that distinction: a single 1 m2 quadrat per site cannot tell you whether a rare species is patchily distributed within a site or genuinely restricted to certain sites, and it leaves beta diversity — often the more ecologically interesting number — impossible to estimate at all.

sections.heading: Rarefaction: sample-based versus individual-based
sections.body: Raw species counts are not comparable across sites sampled with unequal effort — more individuals or more samples almost mechanically finds more species. Rarefaction, developed originally by Howard Sanders in 1968 for marine benthic surveys and later corrected for bias by Stuart Hurlbert in 1971, standardizes this by resampling. Individual-based rarefaction randomly subsamples individuals down to a common number and asks how many species remain; sample-based rarefaction instead resamples whole plots or traps, which better reflects real survey effort because it preserves spatial aggregation (a rare species clumped in one plot behaves differently than one individual randomly drawn). Sample-based curves rise more slowly and sit below individual-based curves for the same total N, so mixing the two methods when comparing sites is a common, quietly serious error.

sections.heading: Coverage-based standardization and taxonomic resolution
sections.body: Chao and Jost (2012) showed that even rarefaction to equal sample size is not always fair, because two sites at the same sample size can have very different sample completeness (the fraction of the community's individuals belonging to species already detected). Their fix, coverage-based rarefaction and extrapolation, standardizes to equal sample coverage — estimated from the ratio of singletons to total individuals via the Good-Turing estimator — rather than equal n, and it can extrapolate curves beyond the observed data using the estimated asymptotic richness. Finally, taxonomic resolution is itself a design choice with consequences: identifying every specimen to species is expensive, so many arthropod and soil surveys use morphospecies (sorted by external features without formal names) or even family-level identification. Coarser resolution systematically deflates richness estimates and can reverse diversity rankings between sites, so the resolution must be fixed in advance and reported, not chosen post hoc to fit a hoped-for result.

lessons.workedExample: Two forest plots are surveyed for ground beetles: Plot A gets 20 pitfall traps run for 10 days (200 trap-days, 340 individuals, 28 species), Plot B gets 8 traps run for 10 days (80 trap-days, 150 individuals, 24 species). Naively, Plot A looks more diverse. Individual-based rarefaction to 150 individuals shows Plot A drops to about 22 species — lower than Plot B's observed 24 — because Plot B's community is more even. Coverage-based rarefaction (Chao & Jost 2012) standardizing both to 90% sample coverage confirms Plot B has the higher true richness, reversing the naive ranking entirely.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees two bar charts of raw species counts and asks 'did you standardize effort?' is testing whether the student understands that richness is an artifact of sampling until proven otherwise. A weak answer says 'we sampled both sites the same way'; a strong answer names the actual standardization method — sample-based or coverage-based rarefaction — and explains why equal trap-days is not the same as equal sample coverage when abundances differ. The strongest answers also flag their taxonomic resolution (species vs. morphospecies) as a stated limitation rather than an afterthought, since a judge who catches an unstated resolution shift between site comparisons will treat the whole richness comparison as unreliable.

questions.prompt: Why does sample-based rarefaction typically produce a lower species accumulation curve than individual-based rarefaction at the same total abundance?

options.text: Sample-based rarefaction always uses fewer total individuals
It resamples whole plots, preserving spatial clumping of species rather than treating individuals as independently drawn
It only counts the most common species
It requires coverage-based correction first

explanations.a: Both methods can be standardized to the same total individuals; the difference is in what unit is randomly drawn, not the total.
explanations.b: Correct — because a rare species clumped into one plot only enters the resample when that whole plot is drawn, spatial aggregation slows the accumulation curve compared to drawing individuals independently.
explanations.c: Both methods count all species detected in the resampled units; neither excludes rare species by design.
explanations.d: Coverage-based standardization is a separate, additional correction (Chao & Jost 2012), not a prerequisite for sample-based rarefaction.

questions.prompt: What quantity does Chao and Jost's (2012) coverage-based rarefaction standardize sites to, instead of equal sample size?

options.text: Equal number of singleton species
Equal estimated sample completeness (coverage)
Equal number of plots regardless of individuals caught
Equal taxonomic resolution only

explanations.a: Singletons are used to estimate coverage via the Good-Turing estimator, but they are not themselves the standardized quantity.
explanations.b: Correct — coverage is the estimated fraction of the community's individuals belonging to already-detected species; standardizing to equal coverage compares sites at equal completeness rather than equal raw n.
explanations.c: Equal plot number is a design choice, not what coverage-based rarefaction statistically standardizes for.
explanations.d: Taxonomic resolution is a separate design decision made before sampling; coverage-based rarefaction is a statistical correction applied to abundance data.

questions.prompt: Match each sampling/analysis concept to what it is used for.

right.text: Separating within-site from between-site variation (alpha vs. beta diversity)
Comparing richness fairly when sites differ in sample completeness
A cheaper taxonomic resolution that can deflate richness estimates

questions.explanation: Nested designs partition variance across spatial scales; coverage-based rarefaction (Chao & Jost 2012) fairly compares sites of unequal completeness; morphospecies sorting trades taxonomic precision for cost, which can bias richness comparisons if applied inconsistently.

questions.prompt: A student compares beetle richness at two sites using species counts from unequal total trap-days, without any rarefaction. What is the main problem?

options.text: There is no problem if both sites used pitfall traps
Higher effort at one site will tend to inflate its apparent richness regardless of true diversity
Pitfall traps cannot catch beetles
Richness comparisons require identical weather at both sites

explanations.a: Using the same trap type does not fix unequal effort; effort itself (trap-days, individuals caught) drives richness up mechanically.
explanations.b: Correct — more sampling effort finds more species almost by construction, so raw counts confound true diversity with survey effort unless standardized by rarefaction.
explanations.c: Pitfall traps are a standard, effective method for ground beetles; that is not the issue here.
explanations.d: Weather can add noise but is not the systematic bias that unequal effort introduces into raw richness counts.

lessons.label: Imperfect Detection and Occupancy Modelling

sections.heading: The problem: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence
sections.body: Most survey methods have a detection probability p strictly less than 1 — a bird can be present and silent, a salamander can be under a log you didn't flip, a camera trap can miss an animal that walked outside its detection cone. If you treat a single survey's non-detection as a confirmed absence, your naive occupancy estimate (fraction of sites with at least one detection) is biased low, and the bias is worst for rare or cryptic species — exactly the species community ecologists most need accurate occupancy for, since they drive rarity-weighted diversity metrics and conservation triage. In datasets with moderate per-visit detection probability, ignoring imperfect detection can understate true occupancy by tens of percentage points, easily enough to flip a monitored site from apparently 'declining' to actually 'stable.'

sections.heading: MacKenzie's fix: repeat visits separate p from psi
sections.body: MacKenzie et al. (2002, Ecology, 'Estimating site occupancy rates when detection probabilities are less than one') formalized the solution: visit each site multiple times within a period short enough that true occupancy state does not change (the closure assumption), and record a detection history per site, like 1-0-1 across three visits. Because a species detected on visit 1 and 3 but not visit 2 must have been present the whole time, the pattern of detections and non-detections across repeat visits lets a likelihood model simultaneously estimate detection probability p and true occupancy psi, rather than confusing the two. The model can also fold in covariates — vegetation density affecting p, elevation affecting psi — so the two processes can respond to entirely different variables. A widely cited rule of thumb is that 3-5 repeat visits are enough to estimate p reasonably well when detection probability per visit is moderate (roughly 0.3-0.7); lower per-visit p needs more visits to pin down psi precisely.

sections.heading: Scaling up to whole communities
sections.body: Multi-species (community) occupancy models extend the single-species framework hierarchically: each species gets its own psi and p, but these are drawn from a shared community-level distribution, which lets data-poor rare species borrow statistical strength from data-rich common ones. This approach, developed further by Dorazio and Royle (2005) and widely used in camera-trap and bird-point-count studies since, can even estimate the richness of species never detected at all, by including an augmented set of all-zero pseudo-species in the model. It turns a community species list from a fixed count of what was seen into a modeled estimate of what is actually there.

lessons.workedExample: A team surveys 20 ponds for a cryptic treefrog by visiting each pond 4 times over 3 weeks. Naive occupancy (any detection at any visit) is 9/20 = 0.45. Detection histories show the frog was often missed on individual visits (e.g., site 7's history is 0-1-0-1), and a MacKenzie occupancy model estimates per-visit detection probability p = 0.35 and true occupancy psi = 0.68 — meaning the naive count understates true occupancy by 23 percentage points, because at p = 0.35 a truly occupied site has roughly a 0.65^4 ≈ 18% chance of showing zero detections across all 4 visits and being wrongly scored absent.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes detection probability because it is the single most common silent error in student field surveys: a species list built from one pass through a site is treated as a ground-truth community, when it is really a lower bound. A weak answer insists 'we didn't see it, so it wasn't there.' A strong answer says something like 'we visited each site four times, built detection histories, and used an occupancy model to separate the chance we missed a present species from the chance it was truly absent' — showing the student understands that p and psi are two different numbers that a single visit cannot disentangle.

questions.prompt: Why does naive occupancy (fraction of sites with at least one detection) underestimate true occupancy when detection probability p < 1?

options.text: Because sites can be truly occupied but yield zero detections across all visits by chance
Because occupancy models always overcorrect low values
Because naive occupancy double-counts detections
Because p only matters for common species

explanations.a: Correct — with p < 1, a truly present species has a nonzero probability of being missed on every single visit, so some occupied sites get scored as absent, biasing the naive estimate downward.
explanations.b: The correction moves the naive estimate up toward the true value based on the observed detection pattern; it is not a blanket overcorrection.
explanations.c: Naive occupancy undercounts, it does not double-count; the issue is missed detections, not duplicated ones.
explanations.d: Imperfect detection biases occupancy estimates for any species with p < 1, and the effect is proportionally worse for rare or cryptic species, not restricted to common ones.

questions.prompt: What key assumption does the MacKenzie et al. (2002) repeat-visit design require to validly separate p from psi?

options.text: All sites must have identical habitat
Population closure — true occupancy state does not change across the repeat visits
Every visit must use a different observer
Detection probability must equal 1 on at least one visit

explanations.a: Habitat can vary between sites and is often modeled as a covariate on psi; identical habitat is not required.
explanations.b: Correct — closure means a site's true occupancy state (present or absent) stays fixed across the repeat-visit window, so any variation in detection across visits reflects p, not a real change in occupancy.
explanations.c: Using different observers is not required and can even add unmodeled variation in detection.
explanations.d: The whole point of the model is to estimate p even when it never reaches 1 on any visit.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a single-species occupancy survey and analysis, from field design to final estimate.

items.text: Select sites and define the closure period (short enough that occupancy won't change)
Visit each site multiple times within that period, recording detection/non-detection each visit
Build a detection history (e.g., 1-0-1) for every site
Fit a likelihood model estimating p and psi jointly from the detection histories

questions.explanation: Occupancy design starts with choosing sites and a closure period, then repeat visits generate the raw detection/non-detection data, which is compiled into per-site detection histories, and only then is the MacKenzie-style model fit to jointly estimate detection probability and true occupancy.

questions.prompt: What does a multi-species (community) occupancy model gain by modeling all species' psi and p as drawn from a shared community-level distribution?

options.text: It eliminates the need for repeat visits
Rare, data-poor species borrow statistical strength from common, data-rich species, improving estimates for rarities
It guarantees p = 1 for all species
It removes the closure assumption entirely

explanations.a: Community occupancy models still require repeat-visit detection histories per site for each species; that requirement doesn't go away.
explanations.b: Correct — the hierarchical structure lets information from commonly detected species inform the parameter estimates for rare species that individually have too little data to estimate p and psi reliably alone.
explanations.c: The model still estimates p as a parameter that can be well below 1; it does not force perfect detection.
explanations.d: Closure within the repeat-visit window is still required for each species modeled; the community structure changes how strength is shared across species, not the closure assumption.

lessons.label: Manipulative Field Experiments: Removals, Exclosures, and Transplants

sections.heading: The toolkit: removals, exclosures, transplants, density series
sections.body: Correlation between two species' abundances does not show interaction; community ecologists manipulate the community directly. Species-removal experiments physically remove a target species from plots and track how competitors or prey respond — Connell's 1961 barnacle removals on the Scottish coast, pulling Balanus off rocks to see Chthamalus expand downward into the lower shore zone it is normally excluded from, is the founding example of this design. Exclosures use cages, fences, or sticky tanglefoot rings around plant stems to keep out a size class of consumer (herbivore or predator) while a paired open control gets the same disturbance without the exclusion. Reciprocal transplant experiments move organisms across an environmental gradient (elevation, soil type, latitude) in both directions to separate genetic from environmental causes of a trait or performance difference. Density-series designs plant or stock a target species at several fixed densities to fit a functional response curve rather than just comparing present versus absent.

sections.heading: Press versus pulse, and why the distinction matters
sections.body: Bender, Case, and Gilpin (1984, Ecology) formalized a crucial distinction: a pulse experiment removes or adds a species briefly and tracks the transient recovery trajectory, revealing short-term interaction strengths and return times; a press experiment holds a perturbation constant indefinitely (permanently reduced density, sustained exclusion) and measures the new equilibrium, which can look completely different from the pulse's short-term signal because indirect effects propagating through the food web need time to reach steady state. A predator whose pulse removal shows little effect on a basal resource can show a strong press effect once mesopredator release cascades through several links — so a one-time pulse study risks badly underestimating a species' true community role if the system has slow indirect pathways.

sections.heading: Cage artifacts: the silent confound
sections.body: Any physical exclosure changes more than access — mesh shades light, alters airflow and temperature, can create a perching or nesting structure, and its edges create a boundary effect where excluded consumers concentrate their pressure. The mandatory control is a 'cage control': a structure identical to the real cage (same mesh, same shading, same posts) but with an opening that lets the target consumer through, isolating the caging artifact from the biological effect. Studies that skip cage controls and just compare caged versus fully open plots cannot distinguish 'herbivory suppressed this plant' from 'shade suppressed this plant.' Edge effects are managed by using a buffer zone and sampling only the plot interior, since consumer pressure is often disproportionately high right at a cage boundary.

lessons.workedExample: A team studies whether deer herbivory suppresses tree seedling diversity in a forest understory. They set up three plot types: full exclosure (deer-proof fence), cage control (same fence design with a deer-sized gap cut in one side), and open control (no fence). After two growing seasons, full exclosures have 3.2x the seedling density of open plots — but the cage control also shows a 1.4x increase over open plots, revealing that roughly a third of the apparent 'herbivory effect' was actually a shading/microclimate artifact of the fence structure itself. Reporting only exclosure-versus-open would have overstated deer impact by that same margin.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'what was your control for the cage itself?' because it is the fastest way to tell whether a caging experiment is trustworthy. A weak answer treats caged-versus-open as the whole design and has no answer for shading or microclimate effects. A strong answer names the cage control explicitly, reports how much of the effect it absorbed, and can also say whether the manipulation was press or pulse — because a judge who understands Bender, Case, and Gilpin (1984) knows a one-week pulse removal and a full-season press exclosure are answering different questions, and will ask which one the student's hypothesis actually required.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a 'cage control' in an herbivore exclosure experiment?

options.text: To exclude a different, larger predator
To isolate physical artifacts of the caging structure (shading, microclimate) from the biological effect of excluding the consumer
To double the sample size
To replace the need for an open control entirely

explanations.a: A cage control uses the same structure as the real exclosure, just with an opening allowing the same target consumer through; it isn't targeting a different species.
explanations.b: Correct — the cage control has identical mesh, shading, and structure but lets the target consumer access the plot, so any difference between cage control and open control reveals the caging artifact rather than the herbivory/predation effect.
explanations.c: It's an additional treatment needed for a valid comparison, not simply a replicate added for statistical power.
explanations.d: A full design needs all three: full exclosure, cage control, and open control — the cage control does not replace the open control, it supplements it.

questions.prompt: According to Bender, Case, and Gilpin (1984), why might a pulse experiment underestimate a predator's true long-term community role compared to a press experiment?

options.text: Pulse experiments use larger sample sizes
Indirect effects propagating through multiple food-web links take time to reach a new equilibrium that a brief pulse can't capture
Press experiments always use higher predator densities
Pulse experiments cannot be replicated

explanations.a: Sample size is a separate design parameter unrelated to the press/pulse distinction.
explanations.b: Correct — a pulse captures only the short-term transient response, while sustained (press) removal allows slower indirect pathways, like trophic cascades, to fully play out and reach a new equilibrium that can look very different from the initial pulse response.
explanations.c: Press versus pulse describes duration of the perturbation, not the density or intensity applied.
explanations.d: Pulse experiments can absolutely be replicated across plots; replicability is not what distinguishes the two designs.

questions.prompt: Match each experimental design to its primary purpose.

right.text: Tests how a competitor or prey responds when a target species is physically taken out
Separates genetic from environmental causes of trait differences across a gradient
Fits a functional-response curve across multiple fixed densities rather than presence/absence

questions.explanation: Removal experiments (like Connell's 1961 barnacle work) isolate a species' effect on others by taking it out; reciprocal transplants move organisms both directions across a gradient to separate genotype from environment; density-series designs vary stocking density to characterize a dose-response rather than a binary comparison.

questions.prompt: Connell's 1961 barnacle removal experiment on the Scottish coast is a founding example of which design?

options.text: Reciprocal transplant across an elevation gradient
Species-removal experiment testing competitive exclusion
Whole-lake predator addition
Passive acoustic monitoring

explanations.a: Connell's experiment removed Balanus from plots rather than transplanting organisms across a gradient; it tested a competitive interaction, not genotype-by-environment effects.
explanations.b: Correct — Connell physically removed the competitively dominant barnacle Balanus balanoides from rocks and observed Chthamalus stellatus expand into the freed space, demonstrating competitive exclusion in the field.
explanations.c: Whole-lake manipulations are a distinct, much larger-scale ecosystem experiment design, not what Connell used.
explanations.d: Passive acoustic monitoring is a modern sampling technique unrelated to Connell's intertidal removal design.

lessons.label: Mesocosms, Microcosms, and Natural Experiments

sections.heading: Microcosms: maximum control, minimum realism
sections.body: The realism-control tradeoff sits at the center of experimental community ecology. At the controlled end, G.F. Gause grew Paramecium in test tubes in the 1930s and watched one species competitively exclude another under constant conditions, founding the whole tradition of protist microcosm experiments. Lawler and Morin (1993) extended this logic to build multi-species protist food chains in laboratory microcosms, manipulating chain length to test how it affected population stability and dynamics — work only possible because generation times of hours let you run dozens of population cycles in weeks. The tradeoff: a test tube has no spatial structure, no seasonal cycle, and a handful of species, so results generalize to real ponds only cautiously.

sections.heading: Mesocosms and assembly experiments scale up realism
sections.body: Mesocosms — outdoor tanks or cattle-tank ponds — add real weather, more species, and more spatial structure while keeping replication and manipulation. Wilbur's classic 1972 Ecology paper used replicated pond tanks to manipulate the density and combination of Ambystoma salamander larvae and Rana tadpoles, showing that competition and predation interacted to structure amphibian larval communities in ways no single-factor lab study could reveal. Drake (1991) used a similar aquatic-microcosm approach to test assembly rules directly: by introducing the same regional species pool in different sequences, he showed that the order species arrive in — not just which species are present — determines which community forms, a priority effect that is invisible in any single-timepoint field survey.

sections.heading: Carpenter's critique and the whole-ecosystem alternative
sections.body: Stephen Carpenter's influential 1996 Ecology paper, 'Microcosm experiments have limited relevance for community and ecosystem ecology,' argued that bottle- and tank-scale experiments systematically miss processes that only operate at landscape scale — nutrient spiraling across a watershed, fish migration, multi-year lags in whole-lake trophic cascades — so a microcosm result can be internally valid yet fail to predict what happens in the real system it is meant to model. His alternative is whole-ecosystem manipulation: the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest clear-cut study (Bormann and Likens, beginning in the 1960s-70s) removed all vegetation from an entire watershed and measured a roughly 40-fold increase in stream nitrate export, a result no lab microcosm could have produced because it depends on real hydrology and real soil at real scale. Similarly, whole-lake predator-addition experiments — adding piscivores to entire experimental lakes and tracking cascades down to phytoplankton — have shown trophic cascade strengths and time lags that bottle experiments consistently underestimate.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher wants to know whether adding a top predator triggers a trophic cascade to algae. A microcosm version — predatory copepods added to 2-liter jars with algae and grazers — shows a cascade within 5 days: algae biomass roughly doubles when grazers are suppressed. Carpenter's critique predicts this understates the real effect, and a whole-lake predator addition (fish stocked into an entire experimental lake, tracked over 2-3 years) confirms it: the whole-lake cascade takes months to develop as fish redistribute grazing pressure spatially, but ultimately produces a larger and more persistent shift in water clarity than the jar experiment predicted, because the lake's spatial refuges and multi-year zooplankton generation turnover cannot exist in a 2-liter jar.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'would this work in a jar' or 'why a tank and not a real pond' to test whether a student has actually thought about scale, not just about control. A weak answer defends the microcosm purely on convenience ('it was easier to replicate'). A strong answer names the specific process the microcosm cannot capture — Carpenter's point about landscape-scale nutrient flow or multi-year lags — and explains what result from Wilbur-style mesocosms or a Hubbard-Brook-style whole-ecosystem study would be needed to validate the microcosm finding, showing the student sees replication and realism as a spectrum with a real cost at each end, not a binary of 'controlled' versus 'sloppy.'

questions.prompt: What was the central argument of Carpenter's 1996 critique of microcosm experiments?

options.text: Microcosms are never internally valid
Microcosms systematically miss landscape-scale and multi-year processes, so results may not predict whole-ecosystem behavior
Microcosms should replace all field experiments
Microcosms are too expensive to replicate

explanations.a: Carpenter did not question internal validity (whether the manipulation caused the observed effect within the microcosm); his concern was external validity at ecosystem scale.
explanations.b: Correct — Carpenter argued small-scale, short-duration microcosms cannot capture processes like watershed nutrient spiraling, fish migration, or multi-year trophic cascade lags, limiting how far their conclusions generalize.
explanations.c: Carpenter argued for the value of whole-ecosystem manipulations as a complement, not for eliminating field experiments generally, and microcosms remain useful for other questions.
explanations.d: Cost was not Carpenter's argument; his point was about scale-dependent ecological processes being absent from small vessels, not expense.

questions.prompt: In Drake's (1991) assembly-sequence experiments, what key finding distinguished them from a standard species-removal experiment?

options.text: The order in which species were introduced from the same pool determined which community assembled — a priority effect
Removing species always produced the same final community
Only predator identity mattered, not sequence
Assembly sequence had no measurable effect on outcome

explanations.a: Correct — Drake introduced the same regional species pool in different sequences into aquatic microcosms and found different final community compositions, demonstrating that arrival order (a priority effect), not just species identity, shapes community assembly.
explanations.b: This describes the opposite finding; species-removal experiments test the effect of taking a species out, and Drake's result was that order of addition, not just presence, mattered.
explanations.c: Drake's design varied introduction sequence across the whole species pool, not just predator identity.
explanations.d: The whole point of the finding was that sequence had a strong, measurable effect on which community formed.

questions.prompt: Match each study/system to what it demonstrated.

right.text: Competitive exclusion under fully controlled lab conditions
Density and species combination interact to structure larval amphibian communities
Whole-watershed vegetation removal massively increased stream nitrate export

questions.explanation: Gause's test-tube Paramecium work established competitive exclusion; Wilbur's replicated pond tanks showed density and species combination jointly shape amphibian larval community structure; the Hubbard Brook whole-watershed clear-cut demonstrated a landscape-scale nutrient-export effect no microcosm could reproduce.

questions.prompt: Order these systems from lowest to highest ecological realism (least to most like the real, whole ecosystem being studied).

items.text: Test-tube protist microcosm (Gause-style)
Outdoor cattle-tank pond mesocosm (Wilbur-style)
Whole-lake or whole-watershed manipulation (Hubbard Brook-style)

questions.explanation: Test-tube microcosms offer the most control but the least realism (no weather, minimal spatial structure); outdoor tank mesocosms add real weather and more species while retaining replication; whole-ecosystem manipulations have the least experimental control but capture landscape-scale hydrology, migration, and multi-year dynamics that smaller systems cannot.

lessons.label: Trait and Phylogenetic Data for Community Analysis

sections.heading: From a species list to a trait matrix
sections.body: A species list alone treats every taxon as ecologically interchangeable, which throws away information community ecologists actually want: how species function. Functional trait ecology instead pairs each species with standardized, measurable traits chosen because they predict resource use — specific leaf area (SLA, leaf area per unit dry mass, cm2/g) as a proxy for growth rate and light-capture strategy, seed mass as a proxy for dispersal and stress tolerance, body size and gape width in animals as a proxy for prey size range and trophic position, and wood density as a proxy for drought and mechanical-damage resistance in trees. These traits are measured with standardized protocols (Pérez-Harguindeguy et al.'s widely used handbook) precisely so that values are comparable across studies and sites, not just internally consistent within one dataset.

sections.heading: Summarizing trait distributions across a community
sections.body: Once every species in a plot has trait values, two families of metrics summarize the community. Community-weighted mean (CWM) trait value averages each trait across species, weighting each by its relative abundance, producing one number per plot per trait — useful for tracking a directional shift, like community mean SLA rising after nitrogen fertilization. Functional dispersion (FDis, Laliberté and Legendre 2010) instead measures spread: the mean distance of each species from the abundance-weighted centroid of the community in multivariate trait space, capturing whether the community is functionally narrow (species clustered near the same strategy) or broad. Rao's quadratic entropy, a related and older index, sums pairwise trait dissimilarity weighted by relative abundance and is mathematically closely related to FDis; both increase when a community holds a wider spread of ecological strategies, not just more species.

sections.heading: Phylogenetic structure and its contested meaning
sections.body: Webb, Ackerly, McPeek, and Donoghue's landmark 2002 review formalized how to ask the same clustering-versus-spreading question using a phylogeny instead of traits: the Net Relatedness Index (NRI) and Nearest Taxon Index (NTI) compare the observed mean phylogenetic distance among co-occurring species to a null distribution generated by randomly drawing species from the regional pool. Phylogenetic clustering (species more closely related than expected) was originally interpreted as evidence of environmental filtering selecting for a shared ancestral trait; phylogenetic overdispersion (less related than expected) was read as evidence of competitive exclusion among close relatives sharing similar niches. This interpretation faced a sharp correction: because trait evolution is not always conserved along the phylogeny (a trait can evolve convergently or reverse), the same ecological process can produce either pattern depending on how the relevant trait actually maps onto the tree — meaning NRI/NTI values alone cannot uniquely diagnose whether filtering or competition produced them, and must be paired with the actual functional traits believed to drive the interaction.

lessons.workedExample: A grassland plot has three co-dominant species with SLA values of 12, 14, and 40 cm2/g and relative abundances of 40%, 40%, and 20%. The community-weighted mean SLA is (12×0.4)+(14×0.4)+(40×0.2) = 18.4 cm2/g, dominated by the two low-SLA species. Functional dispersion is high despite the low CWM, because the third species sits far from the other two in trait space — a single abundance-weighted mean would miss that this community actually spans two very different resource-use strategies, which FDis or Rao's Q correctly flags but CWM alone hides.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who sees a phylogenetic clustering result and asks 'so is that filtering or competition?' is testing whether the student has absorbed the post-Webb-et-al. correction, not just the original 2002 framework. A weak answer states the pattern (clustered or overdispersed) and stops, treating it as a self-explanatory diagnosis of process. A strong answer explains that the same NRI/NTI pattern is ambiguous without knowing whether the trait driving the interaction is phylogenetically conserved, and names what additional evidence (a measured functional trait, an experimental manipulation) would be needed to actually distinguish habitat filtering from competitive exclusion.

questions.prompt: What does a high functional dispersion (FDis) value indicate about a community, that a community-weighted mean (CWM) cannot capture on its own?

options.text: The total number of species present
How spread out species are across trait space around the abundance-weighted centroid, regardless of the mean trait value
The exact abundance of the rarest species
The phylogenetic age of the community

explanations.a: FDis is about trait spread, not species count; a species-poor community can have high or low FDis depending on how different those few species are.
explanations.b: Correct — FDis measures the average distance of species from the community's trait centroid, so two communities can share the same CWM but differ hugely in FDis if one has all species near the mean and the other has species spread far in opposite directions.
explanations.c: FDis is a community-level summary and doesn't isolate any single species' abundance.
explanations.d: FDis is a trait-space metric, not a phylogenetic one; phylogenetic spread is captured by separate metrics like NRI/NTI.

questions.prompt: Webb et al. (2002) originally interpreted phylogenetic clustering (co-occurring species more closely related than expected by chance) as evidence for which process?

options.text: Competitive exclusion of close relatives
Environmental/habitat filtering for a shared ancestral trait
Random dispersal with no ecological signal
Convergent evolution unrelated to the environment

explanations.a: Competitive exclusion of close relatives was the interpretation originally attached to phylogenetic overdispersion (less related than expected), the opposite pattern.
explanations.b: Correct — clustering was read as environmental filtering selecting for a trait shared by close relatives due to phylogenetic conservatism, causing related species to co-occur more than chance would predict.
explanations.c: The whole premise of the null-model comparison is to detect signal beyond random assembly; clustering is specifically a deviation from that random expectation.
explanations.d: Convergent evolution across distant relatives would tend to work against clustering, not explain it, since it makes unrelated species trait-similar.

questions.prompt: What is the main criticism of using NRI/NTI patterns alone to identify whether habitat filtering or competition structured a community?

options.text: NRI/NTI cannot be computed without a fossil record
The same ecological process can produce either clustering or overdispersion depending on whether the relevant trait is phylogenetically conserved
NRI/NTI only work for animal communities
Null models are never available for phylogenetic data

explanations.a: NRI/NTI are computed from a phylogeny and observed co-occurrence data plus a null model; a fossil record is not required.
explanations.b: Correct — if the trait driving competition or filtering is not conserved along the phylogeny (it evolved convergently, for instance), the resulting community pattern will not map cleanly onto clustering-equals-filtering or overdispersion-equals-competition, making the pattern ambiguous about process without independent trait data.
explanations.c: NRI/NTI are applied broadly across plants, animals, and microbes wherever a phylogeny and community data exist.
explanations.d: Null models (random draws from the regional species pool) are precisely what NRI/NTI are built on; they are readily available, not the limiting factor.

questions.prompt: Match each trait to the ecological property it is commonly used as a proxy for.

right.text: Growth rate and light-capture strategy
Dispersal ability and stress tolerance
Drought and mechanical-damage resistance
Prey size range and trophic position

questions.explanation: SLA (leaf area per dry mass) proxies growth rate and light capture; seed mass proxies dispersal and stress tolerance; wood density proxies drought and mechanical resistance; gape width in animals proxies the range of prey sizes a predator can consume, and thus trophic position.

lessons.label: Modern Community Sampling: eDNA, Camera Traps, and Acoustics

sections.heading: eDNA metabarcoding: power and its hidden biases
sections.body: Environmental DNA (eDNA) metabarcoding detects a whole community from shed cells, mucus, or feces in a water or soil sample: DNA is extracted, a short marker region (commonly 12S or COI for animals, ITS or 18S for other groups) is PCR-amplified using 'universal' primers, and the resulting mixed pool is sequenced and sorted into taxonomic units. The first hidden bias is primer choice — no primer amplifies every taxon with equal efficiency, so the same water sample run with different primer sets produces measurably different community compositions, and taxa with primer-binding-site mismatches can drop out entirely or be systematically underrepresented. The second is the reference-database gap: a sequence can only be assigned to a species if that species (or a close relative) is already in the database, so metabarcoding surveys of poorly studied groups or regions routinely return a large fraction of reads that can only be classified to genus or family.

sections.heading: OTUs, ASVs, and the compositional-data trap
sections.body: Raw sequences are clustered into units for analysis: Operational Taxonomic Units (OTUs) group sequences by a similarity threshold, commonly 97%, blurring closely related species together but tolerant of sequencing error; Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs), the newer standard, resolve exact sequence differences without an arbitrary threshold, giving finer taxonomic resolution but potentially splitting one species into several variants if it carries natural intragenomic variation. The single most important rule for interpreting either output is that read counts are compositional, not absolute abundances: because a fixed total number of sequencing reads is divided among however many species are present in a sample, an increase in reads from one species mechanically decreases the reads assigned to every other species even if their real-world abundances didn't change, and PCR amplification bias further decouples read proportion from starting DNA quantity. Treating read counts as if they were biomass or density is a common and serious misinterpretation.

sections.heading: Camera traps and acoustic monitoring: their own error structure
sections.body: Camera-trap arrays estimate community composition and activity through motion-triggered images, but each camera's true sampling unit is its detection zone — a fixed cone of distance and angle — so images of the same individual walking past twice must be filtered by an independence interval (commonly 30-60 minutes between images of the same species at the same camera) to avoid treating one visit as multiple independent detections. Passive acoustic monitoring extends the same logic to sound-producing species (birds, bats, frogs, insects), recording continuously and relying on automated classifiers to identify species from spectrograms. These classifiers introduce their own error matrix: false positives (misclassifying a similar-sounding species) inflate apparent richness, while false negatives (missing calls in noisy or overlapping recordings) deflate it, and both errors propagate directly into the community species matrix unless validated against a human-verified subset — mirroring the same detection-probability problem occupancy modeling was built to solve.

lessons.workedExample: A watershed eDNA survey for fish uses 12S primers and returns 40,000 reads across 15 taxa. One rare native minnow makes up only 200 of those reads (0.5%), while an invasive carp makes up 28,000 (70%). A student concludes the carp population is roughly 140 times larger than the minnow population — but because reads are compositional, a heavy PCR amplification bias toward carp DNA (documented for many 12S primer sets) could produce that same read ratio even if the minnow and carp populations were numerically similar; the correct claim is only that carp DNA was far more heavily represented in the amplified pool, not that carp are 140 times more abundant in the stream.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge who asks 'is that read count an abundance?' is checking for the single most common eDNA misinterpretation in student projects. A weak answer treats a rise in read percentage as a rise in population size. A strong answer states plainly that metabarcoding reads are compositional and PCR-biased, so they support relative presence/detection claims and cautious within-species-across-samples trend comparisons at best, not cross-species abundance comparisons — and a student who also names their independence interval for camera-trap data, or their classifier's validated false-positive rate for acoustic data, is showing the same detection-error discipline across every modern sampling method they used, not just eDNA.

questions.prompt: Why is it a mistake to interpret eDNA metabarcoding read counts as direct measures of species abundance?

options.text: eDNA cannot detect fish species at all
Reads are compositional (a fixed total split among taxa) and subject to PCR amplification bias, so read proportion does not track real abundance
eDNA only works in terrestrial habitats
Reads always equal exactly the number of individuals sampled

explanations.a: eDNA is a well-established method for detecting fish and other aquatic taxa from shed DNA; detection is not the issue here.
explanations.b: Correct — since a fixed pool of sequencing reads is divided among whatever taxa are present, one species' read share can rise or fall without any real abundance change, and primers do not amplify all taxa with equal efficiency, further decoupling reads from true DNA quantity.
explanations.c: eDNA metabarcoding is used in both aquatic and terrestrial/soil systems; it is not restricted to land.
explanations.d: Read counts are a function of sequencing depth, PCR efficiency, and primer bias, not a direct one-to-one count of individuals.

questions.prompt: What is the key practical difference between OTU clustering and ASV resolution of amplicon sequences?

options.text: OTUs use an arbitrary similarity threshold (commonly 97%), while ASVs resolve exact sequence variants without that threshold
ASVs require no reference database at all
OTUs can only be used for plant species
ASVs always produce fewer taxonomic units than OTUs

explanations.a: Correct — OTU clustering groups sequences within a similarity threshold (often 97%) which can blur closely related species together, while ASVs distinguish exact sequence differences, giving finer resolution but sometimes splitting a single species with natural variation into multiple variants.
explanations.b: Both OTU and ASV pipelines still need a reference database to assign taxonomic identity to the resulting sequence clusters or variants.
explanations.c: OTU clustering is a general amplicon-sequencing method applied across animals, plants, fungi, and microbes.
explanations.d: ASVs can produce more units than OTUs in some cases, since a single species' natural intragenomic variation can be split into multiple distinct ASVs rather than merged as one OTU.

questions.prompt: Why do camera-trap studies apply an 'independence interval' (e.g., 30-60 minutes) between images of the same species at the same camera?

options.text: To conserve battery life on the camera
To avoid counting repeated images of the same individual passing by as multiple independent detection events
Because animals cannot be photographed twice in one day
To match the primer amplification cycle length

explanations.a: Battery management is a separate hardware concern unrelated to the statistical purpose of the independence interval.
explanations.b: Correct — without an independence interval, one animal lingering or repeatedly passing the camera would be recorded as several separate detections, artificially inflating apparent detection frequency and activity estimates for that species.
explanations.c: Animals can and do trigger cameras multiple times in a day; the interval exists precisely because that is common and needs to be filtered.
explanations.d: PCR amplification cycles are relevant to eDNA methods, not to camera-trap image timing.

questions.prompt: Match each modern sampling method to its characteristic source of error discussed in this lesson.

right.text: Primer bias and reference-database gaps distort which taxa are detected and identified
Repeated images of one individual can be miscounted as multiple detections without an independence interval
Automated classifiers introduce false positives and false negatives from similar-sounding calls or overlapping noise

questions.explanation: eDNA's main error sources are primer amplification bias and gaps in reference databases; camera traps need an independence interval to avoid overcounting repeat visits by the same individual; acoustic monitoring depends on automated classifiers whose false-positive and false-negative rates directly distort the resulting species matrix.

units.label: Reading Community Data: Composition, Ordination, and Gradients

lessons.label: Beta Diversity: Partitioning Variation Across Sites

sections.heading: Whittaker's multiplicative beta
sections.body: Robert Whittaker coined beta diversity in 1960 studying vegetation zones on Oregon's Siskiyou Mountains. His original formulation is multiplicative: beta = gamma / alpha, where gamma is total regional richness and alpha is mean local (within-site) richness. A beta of 3 means the region holds three times as many species as a typical site, i.e., sites are turning over species at a rate of 3x. Because beta here is a ratio, it is unitless and can be compared across studies with wildly different absolute richness. But multiplicative beta has an awkward floor: it equals 1 only when every site holds every species, and it has no fixed ceiling, which makes the number hard to interpret intuitively without a reference community.

sections.heading: Additive partitioning as an alternative
sections.body: Lande (1996) and later Veech et al. (2002) popularized additive partitioning: gamma = alpha + beta, so beta is expressed in the same species-count units as alpha and gamma, and can itself be partitioned hierarchically (within-site, among-site, among-region) the way variance is partitioned in ANOVA. This makes additive beta directly comparable to alpha in a way multiplicative beta is not, at the cost of losing the clean ratio interpretation.

sections.heading: Baselga's turnover-nestedness split
sections.body: Andres Baselga (2010, Global Ecology and Biogeography) showed that a single beta number conflates two distinct processes and decomposed Sorensen-based beta diversity into two additive components: turnover (species replacement — some species are swapped for others of similar number) and nestedness-resultant richness difference (poorer sites are subsets of richer ones, with no replacement at all). Two site pairs can post an identical overall beta while one pair is pure turnover (different species, same richness) and the other is pure nestedness (a species-poor site is a strict subset of a species-rich one) — ecologically opposite stories that the total beta number alone erases. Baselga's decomposition (beta.SOR = beta.SIM + beta.SNE) lets a researcher say which process dominates.

sections.heading: Beta is mathematically bounded by alpha and effort
sections.body: Beta diversity is not a free-floating signal of biology alone: it is mathematically constrained by alpha diversity and sampling effort. When alpha is small relative to gamma, beta is forced to be large almost by arithmetic, and undersampled sites inflate apparent turnover because rare species are missed unevenly across sites, manufacturing artificial dissimilarity. This is why beta comparisons across studies with different sample sizes or site richness are suspect unless standardized (e.g., via rarefaction) first.
