lessons.judgeFraming: A judge brings up the Yellowstone wolves specifically because it is the cascade story every student has already heard, and testing whether a student can separate the well-supported classic cases (Paine, Estes) from the overclaimed popular one reveals real scientific literacy. A weak answer retells the wolves-fixed-the-rivers narrative as settled fact. A strong answer names Paine's controlled removal and Estes's cross-island comparison as the rigorous baseline, then explains specifically why Yellowstone is weaker evidence — no control area, confounded by elk culling and drought, patchy results — citing Mech's or Marshall et al.'s critique rather than just asserting skepticism.

questions.prompt: In Paine's 1963-66 Mukkaw Bay experiment, what happened to species richness after Pisaster removal?

options.text: It increased, from about 8 to 15 species
It fell, from about 15 to 8 species, as Mytilus mussels monopolized space
It stayed the same as the control plot
All species went locally extinct within a month

explanations.a: This is backwards — richness fell after removal, not rose.
explanations.b: Correct — with its main predator gone, the mussel Mytilus californianus outcompeted other species for space, collapsing richness from roughly 15 to about 8 species.
explanations.c: The removal plot diverged sharply from the untouched control, which stayed diverse.
explanations.d: The effect was a reduction in richness through competitive exclusion by mussels, not total extinction.

questions.prompt: Match each study/finding to its system.

right.text: Pisaster removal collapses rocky-shore diversity as Mytilus overgrows space
Sea otter presence/absence predicts urchin barrens vs. kelp forests across Aleutian islands
Contested cascade: willow/aspen recovery claims confounded by elk culling and drought

questions.explanation: Paine's sea star removal and Estes/Palmisano's otter-urchin-kelp comparison are the well-supported classic keystone/cascade cases; the Yellowstone wolf cascade is the actively debated, more confounded case.

questions.prompt: What is the core critique that David Mech and Marshall et al. (2013) raise about the popular Yellowstone wolf cascade narrative?

options.text: Wolves were never actually reintroduced to Yellowstone
Willow/aspen recovery was patchy and coincided with confounders like elk culling and drought, so wolves are not shown to be the single cause
Elk populations increased after wolf reintroduction
Trophic cascades never occur in terrestrial ecosystems

explanations.a: Wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone in 1995; that part is not disputed.
explanations.b: Correct — the critique is about confounding and inconsistent evidence, not about whether wolves exist or had any effect at all.
explanations.c: Elk numbers generally declined after reintroduction; that is not the disputed part of the story.
explanations.d: Terrestrial cascades do occur elsewhere; the critique is specific to the strength of evidence in this particular case.

questions.prompt: What does Paine's 1969 concept of 'keystone species' describe?

options.text: The single most abundant species in a community
A species whose effect on community structure is disproportionately large relative to its abundance or biomass
Any species at the top of a food web
A species that only affects its own population size

explanations.a: Abundance is the opposite of the point — Pisaster was not the most abundant species, but had an outsized effect.
explanations.b: Correct — Paine's definition centers on disproportionate impact relative to abundance, like a keystone holding up an arch despite being one stone among many.
explanations.c: Trophic position alone doesn't make a species a keystone; the disproportionate impact is what matters.
explanations.d: Keystone species by definition restructure the whole community, not just their own numbers.

lessons.label: Island Biogeography and the SLOSS War

sections.heading: A dynamic equilibrium, not a fixed species list
sections.body: Robert MacArthur and E.O. Wilson's equilibrium theory of island biogeography, sketched in a 1963 paper and expanded in their 1967 book, proposed that the number of species on an island is set by a balance between two rates rather than by a fixed 'carrying capacity list.' Immigration rate falls as an island fills up and as distance from the mainland source pool increases (farther islands get fewer colonizing propagules). Extinction rate rises as island area shrinks (smaller islands support smaller, more extinction-prone populations). Where the two curves cross is a dynamic equilibrium species number — species richness stays roughly constant over time even though the actual species present keep turning over, a process they called turnover.

sections.heading: Simberloff and Wilson test it with real defaunation
sections.body: The theory made falsifiable predictions, and Daniel Simberloff and Wilson tested one directly: in 1969, they fumigated several small mangrove islets in the Florida Keys with methyl bromide, killing every arthropod, then monitored recolonization. Within about a year, species richness on each islet returned close to its pre-fumigation number — support for an equilibrium — even though the specific species composition differed from before, exactly the turnover the model predicted. This was one of the first true manipulative tests of a large-scale biogeographic theory and made island biogeography testable rather than just descriptive.

sections.heading: The SLOSS fight: Diamond's rules vs. the rebuttal
sections.body: The theory's applied stakes came from reserve design: given a fixed total area, is it better to have a Single Large or Several Small reserves (SLOSS)? Jared Diamond's 1975 paper proposed a set of geometric design rules for reserves drawn from island biogeography — bigger is better, closer to a source pool is better, one large reserve beats several small ones of the same total area because large reserves hold larger, less extinction-prone populations. Simberloff and Lawrence Abele's sharp 1976 rebuttal argued the theory was being overextended: several small reserves scattered across different habitat types can capture more total species (including habitat specialists absent from any single large block) and provide insurance against a single catastrophe (disease, fire) wiping out the whole population at once. The fight was as much about scientific overreach — turning an elegant equilibrium model into prescriptive land-use policy — as about the biology itself.

sections.heading: What survived and what didn't
sections.body: No universal SLOSS answer emerged, and that is the actual resolution: the better design depends on species' dispersal ability, habitat heterogeneity across the small reserves, and whether the reserves are close enough for individuals to move between them (functioning as one large connected population) or isolated. The area-extinction and distance-immigration relationships from MacArthur-Wilson held up well empirically and remain foundational; the simple prescriptive 'one big reserve always wins' rule did not survive scrutiny. Modern conservation planning treats SLOSS as a case-by-case tradeoff analysis, often folded into metapopulation theory, rather than a settled rule.

lessons.workedExample: Picture two islands 2 km² and 20 km² at the same distance from a mainland. MacArthur-Wilson predicts the 20 km² island reaches equilibrium at a higher species number because its larger populations have lower extinction rates — this held up in real data (e.g., West Indian island surveys). Now picture instead ten 2 km² reserves scattered across a mainland at different distances and in different habitat types (wetland, forest, grassland) versus one 20 km² reserve in a single habitat. Simberloff and Abele's point: the ten small reserves might collect species from three habitat types the one large reserve never touches, so total species count across the network can exceed the single large reserve — the SLOSS answer flips once habitat heterogeneity, not just area, is in play.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge raises SLOSS because it's the textbook example of a clean theory colliding with messy real-world tradeoffs, and it tests whether a student can hold two true things at once. A weak answer picks a side ('big reserves are better') as if it were settled. A strong answer explains that MacArthur-Wilson's area/distance relationships are well-supported, that Diamond tried to turn them into a design rule, that Simberloff and Abele showed habitat heterogeneity and disease-risk considerations break the simple rule, and that the real answer is 'it depends on dispersal and habitat variation' — showing they understand the difference between a validated mechanism and an overextended policy claim built on it.

questions.prompt: According to MacArthur and Wilson's equilibrium theory, why do smaller islands support fewer species at equilibrium?

options.text: Smaller islands have lower immigration rates only
Smaller islands support smaller populations, which have higher extinction rates
Smaller islands are always farther from the mainland
Smaller islands have no equilibrium at all

explanations.a: Area primarily drives extinction rate in the model; distance (not area) primarily drives immigration rate.
explanations.b: Correct — smaller area means smaller populations, and smaller populations are more vulnerable to stochastic extinction, raising the extinction curve and lowering the equilibrium species number.
explanations.c: Area and distance are independent variables in the model; smaller islands are not necessarily farther away.
explanations.d: The model predicts every island reaches SOME equilibrium; smaller ones just reach a lower one.

questions.prompt: What did Simberloff and Wilson's 1969 mangrove islet fumigation experiment show?

options.text: Species richness never recovered after defaunation
Richness returned close to pre-fumigation levels within about a year, with turnover in which species were present
Only the exact same species that were killed returned
Islets closer to shore had lower richness than distant ones

explanations.a: Richness did recover, supporting the equilibrium prediction.
explanations.b: Correct — species number rebounded to near pre-fumigation levels while composition differed, directly demonstrating the predicted turnover at equilibrium.
explanations.c: Composition changed even as total richness recovered — that turnover was the key finding.
explanations.d: The general immigration-distance relationship predicts the opposite: closer islets should get more immigrants.

questions.prompt: Match each figure/finding to their role in the SLOSS debate.

right.text: Proposed reserve design rules favoring one large reserve over several small ones of equal total area
Argued several small reserves can capture more species via habitat heterogeneity and reduce catastrophe risk
Treats SLOSS as a case-by-case tradeoff depending on dispersal ability and habitat variation, not a fixed rule

questions.explanation: Diamond proposed prescriptive design rules from island biogeography; Simberloff and Abele rebutted the single-large-reserve prescription; the field ultimately settled on context-dependent tradeoff analysis.

questions.prompt: Order these milestones in island biogeography and the SLOSS debate.

items.text: MacArthur and Wilson publish the equilibrium theory of island biogeography
Simberloff and Wilson fumigate mangrove islets to test turnover
Diamond proposes reserve design rules based on the theory
Simberloff and Abele rebut the single-large-reserve prescription

questions.explanation: The theory (1963/1967) preceded its empirical test (1969), which preceded its application to reserve design (Diamond, 1975) and the subsequent rebuttal (Simberloff & Abele, 1976).

lessons.label: The Null Model Wars: Diamond vs Connor and Simberloff

sections.heading: Diamond's assembly rules from New Guinea birds
sections.body: Surveying bird distributions across the Bismarck Archipelago near New Guinea, Jared Diamond noticed that certain species combinations never co-occurred on the same island even though each species individually occupied many islands, while other combinations were common. In his 1975 paper he proposed a set of 'assembly rules' to explain this: competitively similar species form checkerboard distributions (never sharing an island), some combinations are effectively 'forbidden' by competitive exclusion, and the observed community structure on any given island reflects the outcome of interspecific competition filtering which species can coexist. This reframed community composition itself — not just individual species' niches — as something competition actively shapes.

sections.heading: Connor and Simberloff's null-model rebuttal
sections.body: Edward Connor and Daniel Simberloff's 1979 paper attacked the inference, not the pattern. Their argument: Diamond had no explicit null model — no baseline of what species co-occurrence would look like if species were distributed at random with respect to each other, subject only to each species' known total number of island occurrences and each island's known total species count. When Connor and Simberloff built randomized communities respecting those same row and column totals (a randomization now called the fixed-fixed algorithm), checkerboard-like patterns and 'forbidden' combinations appeared anyway, as a statistical byproduct of some species being common and some islands being species-rich, with no competition required. Pattern alone, they argued, cannot distinguish competition from chance.

sections.heading: What the fight was actually about
sections.body: The substantive disagreement was methodological, not personal: what counts as a legitimate null community against which to test for a nonrandom signature? Diamond's camp argued some of Connor and Simberloff's randomizations were too permissive, allowing biologically impossible communities (e.g., an island with more species than ever actually observed there) that biased the test toward finding no pattern. Connor and Simberloff countered that Diamond's 'assembly rules' were largely unfalsifiable post hoc pattern-matching — any co-occurrence pattern could be relabeled as an assembly rule after the fact. Both sides had a real point: null-model choice matters enormously, and vague verbal theories resist rejection.

sections.heading: Gotelli and Graves: turning a fight into a method
sections.body: Nicholas Gotelli and Gary Graves' influential 1996 book Null Models in Ecology (building on their and others' work through the late 1980s-90s) systematized the dispute into standard practice: define the null hypothesis explicitly, choose a randomization algorithm whose constraints are justified by the biology (which row/column totals should and shouldn't be held fixed), and report an explicit test statistic like the C-score alongside a simulated null distribution — rather than eyeballing 'this looks nonrandom.' What began as an acrimonious two-paper feud became the field's default toolkit: today almost no co-occurrence claim in community ecology is published without an explicit null-model comparison, a direct legacy of the Diamond-Connor-Simberloff exchange.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose 20 islands and 15 bird species, where species A and species B are never found together. Diamond's approach: point to this checkerboard and infer competitive exclusion between A and B. Connor and Simberloff's approach: build 1,000 randomized species-by-island matrices that preserve each species' total number of islands occupied and each island's total species count, then ask how often A-B co-occurrence is zero purely by chance. If A occurs on only 2 of 20 islands and B on only 3, a zero overlap is unsurprising by chance alone — no competition needed to explain it. Only if the observed non-overlap is rarer than, say, 95% of randomized matrices does the pattern support a competitive-exclusion claim.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge brings up the null-model wars to test whether a student understands that 'the pattern looks nonrandom' is not itself evidence — you need a null model to know what random would even look like. A weak answer says Diamond found forbidden combinations caused by competition, full stop. A strong answer explains that Connor and Simberloff showed the same patterns emerge from randomizations with no competition, that the real fight was over which randomization constraints are biologically defensible, and that this dispute is exactly why any co-occurrence claim in a modern project needs an explicit simulated null distribution, not just a visual impression of nonrandomness.

questions.prompt: What was Diamond's core claim from the 1975 New Guinea/Bismarck bird survey?

options.text: Bird species distributions across islands were essentially random
Certain species combinations never co-occur ('checkerboards'), reflecting competitive assembly rules
Island area had no effect on which species were present
All bird species on the islands were competitively equivalent

explanations.a: Diamond's whole point was that the pattern looked nonrandom, not random.
explanations.b: Correct — Diamond identified checkerboard distributions and 'forbidden' species combinations and attributed them to interspecific competition shaping community assembly.
explanations.c: Diamond's assembly rules were about competitive co-occurrence patterns, not primarily area effects.
explanations.d: Diamond's argument specifically required competitive differences between species, not equivalence.

questions.prompt: What was Connor and Simberloff's (1979) central methodological objection to Diamond's assembly rules?

options.text: Diamond's bird survey data were fabricated
Diamond had no explicit null model, so his 'nonrandom' patterns could arise from chance alone given each species' and island's totals
Competition cannot occur between bird species
Islands cannot be used to study community assembly

explanations.a: The objection was about inference and methodology, not data fabrication.
explanations.b: Correct — their randomization approach, holding species and island totals fixed, produced similar checkerboard patterns without any competition, showing pattern alone doesn't prove competition caused it.
explanations.c: They did not deny competition could occur, only that the pattern alone proved it.
explanations.d: Their method itself used island data; they were not objecting to islands as a study system.

questions.prompt: Match each contribution to its source.

right.text: Proposed competitive assembly rules from checkerboard bird distributions
Showed randomizations without competition reproduce the same checkerboard patterns
Systematized null-model practice with explicit statistics like the C-score

questions.explanation: Diamond proposed the pattern-based assembly rules; Connor and Simberloff showed the pattern doesn't require competition; Gotelli and Graves later formalized rigorous null-model methodology for the field.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a proper null-model test for competitive exclusion, as the field settled on after this dispute.

items.text: Record the observed co-occurrence pattern (e.g., species A and B never share an island)
Define a randomization algorithm with biologically justified constraints (e.g., fix species and island totals)
Generate many randomized community matrices under that null model
Compare the observed pattern's statistic to the simulated null distribution to test significance

questions.explanation: Rigorous null-model testing starts from the observed pattern, requires an explicit and justified randomization scheme, generates a null distribution via simulation, and only then tests whether the observed pattern is statistically unusual relative to chance.

lessons.label: Neutral Theory vs Niche Theory

sections.heading: A deliberately unrealistic assumption
sections.body: Stephen Hubbell's 2001 book The Unified Neutral Theory of Biodiversity and Biogeography proposed something niche theory treats as almost heretical: that individuals of different species within the same trophic level are, for modeling purposes, per-capita ecologically equivalent — identical in birth rate, death rate, and dispersal ability. Species abundances then drift over time purely through random birth-death-immigration events (ecological drift), analogous to genetic drift in population genetics, and community structure is shaped mainly by dispersal limitation — how far propagules realistically travel — rather than by fine-tuned niche differences between species.

sections.heading: Theta, m, and the biodiversity number
sections.body: The theory formalizes this with two key parameters: theta, the 'fundamental biodiversity number,' which governs the rate at which new species arise (via speciation or immigration from a wider metacommunity) into the local community, and m, the immigration rate connecting a local community to that regional source pool. From just these parameters, Hubbell derived predicted species-abundance distributions (how many species are rare vs. common) and species-area relationships. Remarkably, when fit to real data — most famously the fully mapped, continuously censused 50-hectare forest plot on Barro Colorado Island, Panama, tracking roughly 300 tree species and hundreds of thousands of individual stems — neutral theory's predicted abundance curves matched the observed data strikingly well, rivaling or beating niche-based models on the same metric.

sections.heading: The core critiques
sections.body: Robert Ricklefs and James Clark, among others, raised a sharp methodological objection: fitting a species-abundance distribution is a weak test, because very different underlying mechanisms — including many niche-based models — can produce statistically similar abundance curves. A model matching one summary statistic doesn't mean its mechanism (true ecological equivalence) is correct. The equivalence assumption is also directly falsified by decades of niche research: species obviously differ in shade tolerance, drought tolerance, seed size, and dozens of other traits that predictably affect performance, so treating them as interchangeable is a known simplification, not a discovered truth. Critics argued Hubbell had built a good null model, not a good description of nature.

sections.heading: The modern synthesis: different processes at different scales
sections.body: Rather than declaring a winner, the field has largely converged on a scale-dependent view: niche differences likely dominate at fine spatial scales and among functionally dissimilar species (a drought-tolerant pine versus a shade-tolerant maple), while dispersal limitation and drift can dominate among functionally similar, co-occurring competitors (many similar tropical tree species that are hard to functionally distinguish) — the situation Hubbell was originally modeling. Neutral theory's lasting contribution is less 'species really are equivalent' and more that it gave the field a rigorous null model: any niche-based explanation now has to demonstrate it does better than pure drift and dispersal limitation, a bar neutral theory itself set.

lessons.workedExample: On the Barro Colorado Island plot, hundreds of tree species show the classic 'hollow curve' abundance pattern: a few species with thousands of individuals, many species with just a handful. Hubbell's neutral model, tuned with a single theta value estimated from the data, reproduces this hollow-curve shape closely using no species-specific traits at all — every species obeys the same per-capita birth/death/dispersal rules. A niche modeler responds: fit a resource-partitioning model with per-species drought and shade tolerance parameters, and it can match the same curve just as well, or better, once enough parameters are added. The stalemate is exactly Ricklefs's point — the abundance curve alone cannot referee between the two mechanisms; you need independent data, like tracking which species die during a drought year, to tell them apart.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about neutral theory to see whether a student understands the difference between a model fitting data and a model's mechanism being true. A weak answer says neutral theory proved species don't matter. A strong answer explains that Hubbell's theta/m framework fit the Barro Colorado Island abundance data remarkably well, that Ricklefs and Clark showed abundance-curve fits are a weak test because niche models can match the same curve, and that the field's real conclusion is scale-dependent: niche differences matter more among dissimilar species, drift and dispersal matter more among similar competitors — not a clean win for either side.

questions.prompt: What is the core assumption of Hubbell's unified neutral theory?

options.text: Different species have wildly different birth, death, and dispersal rates
Individuals of different species at the same trophic level are per-capita ecologically equivalent
Species abundances are entirely determined by resource partitioning
Dispersal has no effect on community composition

explanations.a: This is the niche-theory assumption neutral theory explicitly rejects for modeling purposes.
explanations.b: Correct — neutral theory's defining, deliberately simplified assumption is per-capita equivalence among co-trophic-level species, with community structure arising from drift and dispersal limitation instead.
explanations.c: Resource partitioning is a niche-theory mechanism, not a neutral-theory one.
explanations.d: Dispersal limitation is actually central to neutral theory's predictions.

questions.prompt: What is Ricklefs's and Clark's main critique of neutral theory's empirical support?

options.text: The Barro Colorado Island data were collected incorrectly
Fitting a species-abundance distribution is a weak test because different mechanisms, including niche-based ones, can produce similar curves
Neutral theory makes no testable predictions at all
Tree species do not have measurable trait differences

explanations.a: The critique is methodological about inference, not about data collection quality.
explanations.b: Correct — matching an abundance curve doesn't uniquely confirm the equivalence mechanism, since niche-based models with enough parameters can match the same curve.
explanations.c: Neutral theory does make quantitative predictions (theta, m, abundance/species-area curves); the critique is about what a good fit actually proves.
explanations.d: Tree species clearly differ in traits like drought and shade tolerance — this is part of the critique, not something it denies.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its role in neutral theory.

right.text: The fundamental biodiversity number governing the rate new species enter the local community
The immigration rate connecting the local community to the regional metacommunity
The 50-hectare fully mapped forest census used to empirically test the theory's predicted abundance curves

questions.explanation: Theta and m are the theory's two core parameters, and the Barro Colorado Island plot is the famous long-term dataset used to test whether neutral theory's predictions matched observed tropical tree abundances.

questions.prompt: What is the modern, scale-dependent resolution between niche theory and neutral theory?

options.text: Niche theory has been fully abandoned in favor of neutral theory
Neutral theory has been fully disproven and discarded
Niche differences likely dominate among functionally dissimilar species, while drift and dispersal limitation can dominate among functionally similar competitors
The two theories make identical predictions in all cases and cannot be distinguished

explanations.a: Niche theory remains well-supported, especially for functionally distinct species; it has not been abandoned.
explanations.b: Neutral theory remains a useful and influential null model, not a discarded idea.
explanations.c: Correct — the field's current view is that the two mechanisms operate at different scales and among different sets of species, rather than one being universally correct.
explanations.d: The theories can be distinguished with the right data (e.g., trait-performance links, drought responses); they are not empirically identical in all situations.

lessons.label: Does Diversity Beget Stability? An Open Question

sections.heading: An old intuition, and a mathematical shock
sections.body: Charles Elton and, later, Robert MacArthur argued mid-century that diverse communities should be more stable — more species and more feeding links, the reasoning went, should buffer a community against invasion, disease, or the loss of any one species, since alternative pathways and predators pick up the slack. This was intuitive and widely accepted until Robert May's 1972 paper used random-matrix mathematics to show the opposite: modeling communities as randomly connected sets of interacting species, May found that as the number of species, the connectance (fraction of possible links realized), and interaction strength all increased, the mathematical probability that the system returns to equilibrium after a small perturbation actually falls. Complexity, in May's random model, destabilizes rather than stabilizes — a direct contradiction of the Elton-MacArthur intuition.

sections.heading: Tilman's Cedar Creek drought test
sections.body: David Tilman's long-term plots at Cedar Creek Ecosystem Science Reserve in Minnesota gave the debate real field data. Tilman and Downing's 1994 Nature analysis found that plots with more plant species lost proportionally less biomass and recovered faster than species-poor plots after the 1987-88 drought — empirical support for diversity conferring stability, seemingly contradicting May's math. The resolution to the apparent contradiction: May modeled RANDOMLY structured interactions, while real communities are shaped by selection and coevolution into non-random, often more stable configurations — so May's result is a statement about generic complex systems, not a universal law about real ecological communities.

sections.heading: The Tilman-Huston fight over mechanism
sections.body: A sharp methodological dispute followed. Tilman initially attributed the diversity-productivity/stability link to complementarity — different species using resources in different ways (rooting depth, phenology, nutrient needs) so a diverse plot uses the total resource pool more completely and consistently. Michael Huston and others countered that much of the effect could instead be a statistical artifact: the sampling effect (also called the selection effect) — a diverse plot has a higher chance of containing at least one highly productive or stress-tolerant species by chance alone, and that one species, not diversity-driven complementarity, could be doing most of the work. Distinguishing the two mechanisms required new experimental designs, not just more diversity plots.

sections.heading: Loreau-Hector's partition and stability's many meanings
sections.body: Michel Loreau and Andy Hector's influential 2001 Nature paper provided the statistical fix: an additive partitioning method that decomposes a biodiversity experiment's total yield into a complementarity effect and a selection effect from the same dataset, rather than treating them as competing all-or-nothing hypotheses. Applied across the pan-European BIODEPTH experiment, both effects were often present simultaneously, with complementarity typically the larger contributor — vindicating part of Tilman's original claim while validating Huston's methodological critique. Separately, Anthony Ives and Stephen Carpenter's influential 2007 Science review made a related but different point: 'stability' itself is not one thing — resistance (resisting change), resilience (returning to equilibrium quickly), variability (year-to-year fluctuation), and persistence (avoiding extinction) are at least four or five distinct, sometimes independently varying properties, and a study claiming diversity 'promotes stability' has to specify which one it measured.

lessons.workedExample: Imagine two 9 m² Cedar Creek plots during the 1988 drought: Plot A has 1 species (a shallow-rooted grass), Plot B has 16 species including deep-rooted legumes, forbs, and grasses. Plot A loses 60% of its biomass because its single strategy fails uniformly when topsoil dries out. Plot B loses only 25%, because different species access water at different soil depths (complementarity) — but a skeptic asks: did Plot B do better only because it happened to contain one exceptionally drought-tolerant legume (selection effect), and the other 15 species were irrelevant? Loreau and Hector's partitioning method statistically separates these two possibilities using the same yield data, rather than requiring a separate experiment to adjudicate the Tilman-Huston dispute.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge raises this debate because 'diversity causes stability' is a claim students repeat without knowing it survived a serious mathematical challenge and a real methodological fight. A weak answer states the Elton-MacArthur intuition as settled fact. A strong answer can explain May's 1972 destabilization result, why it doesn't contradict Tilman's Cedar Creek drought data (random vs. real community structure), the difference between complementarity and the sampling/selection effect in the Tilman-Huston dispute, and — the sophisticated move — that Ives and Carpenter showed 'stability' has multiple distinct meanings, so any claim needs to specify resistance, resilience, or variability rather than 'stability' in the abstract.

questions.prompt: What did Robert May's 1972 random-matrix analysis find about complexity and stability?

options.text: Increasing species number, connectance, and interaction strength increases the probability a random system returns to equilibrium
Increasing species number, connectance, and interaction strength decreases the probability a random system returns to equilibrium
Complexity has no mathematical relationship to stability
Real ecosystems are always unstable regardless of diversity

explanations.a: This was the older Elton-MacArthur intuition, which May's math directly contradicted for randomly structured systems.
explanations.b: Correct — May showed that in randomly connected model communities, more species, more connections, and stronger interactions mathematically reduce the likelihood of returning to equilibrium after perturbation.
explanations.c: May's whole result was establishing a clear (negative) mathematical relationship.
explanations.d: May's model was about random systems specifically; it did not claim all real ecosystems are unstable.

questions.prompt: How is Tilman's Cedar Creek drought finding (diverse plots more resistant) reconciled with May's destabilization result?

options.text: Tilman's data were later shown to be fraudulent
May modeled randomly structured interactions, while real communities are shaped by selection into non-random, often more stable configurations
May's result only applies to plant communities, not animal ones
There is no real conflict because May also found diversity increases stability

explanations.a: The Cedar Creek data have held up as a major long-term ecological dataset.
explanations.b: Correct — May's mathematics describes generic randomly-assembled systems, while real communities' non-random structure (shaped by evolution and ecological filtering) can behave very differently, resolving the apparent contradiction.
explanations.c: May's random-matrix model was general, not restricted to a taxonomic group.
explanations.d: May's original finding was that complexity destabilizes random systems, the opposite direction from Tilman's empirical result — that is exactly the tension needing reconciliation.

questions.prompt: Match each mechanism/effect to its description in the Tilman-Huston dispute.

right.text: Different species partition resources differently, so a diverse plot uses the total resource pool more fully and consistently
A diverse plot is statistically more likely to contain one highly productive species by chance, which drives most of the outcome

questions.explanation: Complementarity is a true diversity-driven mechanism from resource partitioning; the sampling/selection effect is a statistical artifact where diversity merely raises the odds of including one strong performer.

questions.prompt: Order these developments in the diversity-stability debate chronologically.

items.text: Elton and MacArthur propose diversity stabilizes communities
May's random-matrix analysis shows complexity destabilizes randomly structured model systems
Tilman's Cedar Creek drought data show diverse plots losing less biomass
Loreau and Hector publish an additive method partitioning complementarity from selection effects

questions.explanation: The Elton-MacArthur intuition came first, May's 1972 mathematical challenge followed, Tilman's empirical drought data came from the late 1980s, and Loreau and Hector's statistical resolution came in 2001.

questions.prompt: What is the key point of Ives and Carpenter's 2007 review regarding the phrase 'diversity promotes stability'?

options.text: Stability is a single, well-defined measurement, so the phrase is always precise
'Stability' actually refers to several distinct properties (e.g., resistance, resilience, variability, persistence), so claims must specify which one is meant
Diversity has been proven to have no effect on any stability measure
Only resilience matters in ecology; other stability measures are irrelevant

explanations.a: This is exactly the assumption Ives and Carpenter's review challenges as too imprecise.
explanations.b: Correct — resistance, resilience, variability, and persistence are distinct, sometimes independently varying properties, so a diversity-stability claim is incomplete without specifying which measure was tested.
explanations.c: Their point was about definitional precision, not a blanket denial of any diversity effect.
explanations.d: They argued for recognizing multiple distinct stability measures, not privileging one over the rest.

lessons.label: Competition Theory Foundations

sections.heading: Gause's flasks: exclusion made visible
sections.body: In 1934 Georgy Gause published The Struggle for Existence, reporting Paramecium experiments that turned Darwinian competition into a laboratory curve. Grown alone in oat-broth tubes, both Paramecium aurelia and Paramecium caudatum settled onto their own logistic growth curves. Grown together, P. aurelia's faster division rate let it out-consume the shared bacterial food, and P. caudatum's population declined toward zero within about two to three weeks — one competitor always lost. But when Gause paired P. caudatum with P. bursaria instead, both persisted indefinitely, because P. bursaria fed mostly at the bottom of the tube and P. caudatum higher up, splitting the resource by microhabitat. The two outcomes together produced the competitive exclusion principle (also called Gause's Law): two species competing for the identical limiting resource in a stable, homogeneous environment cannot coexist indefinitely — one drives the other locally extinct unless some difference lets them partition the resource.

sections.heading: Putting numbers on it: Lotka-Volterra competition
sections.body: Alfred Lotka and Vito Volterra independently extended the logistic equation to two competitors around 1926-1932. Species 1's growth becomes dN1/dt = r1N1(K1 - N1 - alpha12*N2)/K1, where alpha12 converts each individual of species 2 into its equivalent crowding effect on species 1 (and alpha21 does the reverse for species 2). When alpha12 is greater than 1, one individual of species 2 suppresses species 1 more than one of species 1's own kind would — interspecific competition outweighs intraspecific. Competition coefficients like alpha12 are typically estimated with de Wit replacement-series experiments: growing each species alone and in fixed-ratio mixtures at constant total density, then backing out alpha from how much the mixture yield of each species falls short of its monoculture yield.

sections.heading: Isoclines and the four outcomes
sections.body: Plotting each species' zero-growth isocline (the line where dN/dt = 0) on N1-vs-N2 axes reveals four qualitative outcomes depending on where the isoclines cross relative to each species' own carrying capacity. If species 1's isocline lies entirely outside species 2's, species 1 always wins. If reversed, species 2 always wins. If the isoclines cross with each species' isocline outside its own K on the far axis (interspecific effects exceed intraspecific effects for both), the crossing point is an unstable saddle — a priority effect where whichever species starts more abundant excludes the other. Only when each species suppresses itself more than it suppresses its rival (intraspecific > interspecific competition, alpha12 and alpha21 both less than 1) does the crossing point become a stable equilibrium — genuine coexistence.

lessons.workedExample: Set K1 = K2 = 100. Case A: alpha12 = 0.4, alpha21 = 0.3 (both < 1, self-limitation dominates) — isoclines cross at a stable point, both species persist near equilibrium. Case B: alpha12 = 1.5, alpha21 = 1.8 (both > 1, each species hurts its rival more than itself) — the crossing point is unstable; starting with 60 of species 1 and 20 of species 2 drives species 2 extinct, but starting with 20 and 60 reverses the outcome. Same equations, same carrying capacities — only the alphas decide whether you get robust coexistence or a coin-flip priority effect.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe competition models to see whether a student understands that 'they compete for the same thing' is not an endpoint but a starting hypothesis that predicts a specific, falsifiable outcome. A weak answer says two species 'compete so one wins.' A strong answer names which regime the data suggest — whether intraspecific effects exceed interspecific ones — and explains that this is testable by comparing a species' response to its own crowding versus a rival's crowding, not just by watching who is more abundant at the end.

questions.prompt: In Gause's experiments, what allowed Paramecium caudatum to coexist with P. bursaria but not with P. aurelia?

options.text: P. bursaria fed in a different part of the tube, reducing direct resource overlap
P. bursaria reproduced more slowly, so it never competed
P. aurelia and P. caudatum were the same species
The tubes with P. bursaria had double the food supply

explanations.a: Correct — P. bursaria fed mainly at the tube bottom while P. caudatum fed higher up, spatially partitioning the shared bacterial resource enough to avoid full competitive overlap.
explanations.b: Reproductive rate differences drive exclusion (as with P. aurelia), not coexistence by themselves; the key was habitat partitioning, not slow growth.
explanations.c: They are three distinct species; the exclusion outcome with P. aurelia depended on shared resource use, not taxonomic identity.
explanations.d: Gause controlled food supply across trials; the coexistence outcome came from niche separation, not extra food.

questions.prompt: In the Lotka-Volterra competition model, stable coexistence at the isocline intersection requires which condition?

options.text: alpha12 and alpha21 both greater than 1
alpha12 and alpha21 both less than 1
r1 must equal r2
K1 must equal K2

explanations.a: Both alphas greater than 1 means each species suppresses its rival more than itself — this produces the unstable priority-effect saddle, not stable coexistence.
explanations.b: Correct — when each species limits itself more than it limits its competitor, the shared equilibrium is stable and both persist.
explanations.c: Intrinsic growth rates affect how fast equilibrium is approached but not whether the equilibrium is stable.
explanations.d: Carrying capacities can differ between species; stability depends on the competition coefficients, not on K1 equaling K2.

questions.prompt: What does a 'priority effect' mean in the Lotka-Volterra framework?

options.text: The species with the higher intrinsic growth rate always wins
Whichever species starts more abundant tends to exclude the other
Both species always coexist regardless of starting numbers
The species with the larger body size always wins

explanations.a: Growth rate is not what determines outcome at an unstable saddle; initial abundance is.
explanations.b: Correct — at an unstable equilibrium (both alphas > 1), the outcome is history-dependent: initial numbers determine which species is excluded.
explanations.c: Coexistence requires the stable case (both alphas < 1); priority effects arise specifically when that condition fails.
explanations.d: Body size is not a term in the Lotka-Volterra competition equations.

questions.prompt: Match each isocline configuration to its predicted outcome.

right.text: Species 1 always excludes species 2
Stable coexistence
Unstable priority effect

questions.explanation: One isocline entirely outside the other means one species always wins regardless of starting density. Crossing isoclines with both intraspecific effects dominant (alphas < 1) give a stable joint equilibrium. Crossing isoclines with both interspecific effects dominant (alphas > 1) give an unstable saddle where the starting condition decides the winner.

questions.prompt: Order the historical/logical steps that build up to the competitive exclusion principle.

items.text: Lotka and Volterra independently derive coupled logistic equations for two competitors
Gause grows P. aurelia and P. caudatum together and observes one competitor's extinction
Gause grows P. caudatum and P. bursaria together and observes stable coexistence via microhabitat partitioning
The competitive exclusion principle is generalized: identical-niche competitors cannot coexist indefinitely

questions.explanation: The mathematical framework (Lotka-Volterra) predates and structures Gause's empirical tests; his exclusion result with P. aurelia/caudatum and his coexistence result with P. caudatum/bursaria together were generalized into the competitive exclusion principle.

lessons.label: Resource Competition and the R* Rule

sections.heading: R* replaces the competition coefficient with a measured number
sections.body: David Tilman's resource-ratio theory, developed through the 1970s-80s and formalized in his 1982 book Resource Competition and Community Structure, reframes competition mechanistically instead of phenomenologically. Rather than fitting an abstract alpha coefficient, Tilman asks: at what resource concentration does a species' population growth exactly equal its death rate, so net growth is zero? Call that concentration R*. A species that can persist down to a lower R* keeps growing and drawing the resource down even after its rival's population has stopped growing and started declining from starvation or dilution. The R* rule follows directly: on a single limiting resource, in a stable environment, the species with the lowest R* wins — it depletes the resource to a level too low for any competitor to maintain positive growth. This is mechanistically the same conclusion as competitive exclusion, but now it comes with a testable, measurable number rather than an inferred coefficient.

sections.heading: ZNGIs and consumption vectors for two resources
sections.body: With two essential resources, Tilman plots each species' zero-net-growth isocline (ZNGI) — the combination of resource 1 and resource 2 concentrations at which that species exactly breaks even — on resource-1-vs-resource-2 axes. Where the ZNGIs cross, and only if each species' consumption vector (the ratio in which it draws down the two resources) points more steeply toward the resource it is relatively more limited by, a stable coexistence point exists: each species locally depletes the resource that most limits itself, indirectly benefiting its competitor.

sections.heading: The diatom chemostats that made the theory famous
sections.body: Tilman's strongest evidence came from freshwater diatoms Asterionella formosa and Cyclotella meneghiniana grown in silicate-and-phosphate-limited chemostats in the late 1970s-80s. He first measured each species' R* for silicate and for phosphate separately, then predicted competitive outcomes under different resource-supply ratios purely from those pre-measured R* values — and the chemostat trials matched the predictions, including a coexistence zone where the two resource ratios favored different species. That successful a priori prediction (measure R* first, then predict the winner, then test) is what elevated R* theory beyond curve-fitting. Field confirmation has been far harder: terrestrial systems have many co-varying resources (nitrogen, light, water, multiple soil nutrients), diffuse and indirect competition, herbivory, and disturbance, so isolating a single limiting resource and measuring true R* in situ is rarely feasible outside controlled microbial or algal chemostats.

lessons.workedExample: Two algae compete for phosphate in a chemostat with fixed dilution rate. Species X's population stops net growth at 0.5 micromolar phosphate (R*X = 0.5); species Y needs 1.2 micromolar to break even (R*Y = 1.2). Started together, X keeps consuming phosphate below 1.2 micromolar, so Y's growth rate goes negative there and Y's population declines while X persists near 0.5 micromolar. Tilman's Asterionella/Cyclotella system worked exactly this way for silicate: Asterionella's lower silicate R* let it competitively exclude Cyclotella under silicate-limited supply, while the ranking flipped under phosphate limitation, matching pre-measured R* values without any free-fitted parameters.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on R* theory to test whether a student can distinguish a measured mechanistic prediction from a fitted correlation. A weak answer says 'the species with more resources wins.' A strong answer explains that R* is measured independently (via monoculture growth-vs-death curves) before the competition trial, so the two-species outcome is a genuine prediction, not a post hoc fit — and can explain why this rigor is achievable in a chemostat but not in a field plot with a dozen co-limiting factors.

questions.prompt: What does R* represent for a given species and resource?

options.text: The maximum resource concentration the species can tolerate before dying
The resource concentration at which the species' population growth rate exactly equals zero
The total amount of resource the species consumes per day
The resource concentration that maximizes the species' growth rate

explanations.a: R* is not a tolerance ceiling; it is the break-even floor where births balance deaths.
explanations.b: Correct — R* is the resource concentration at which growth rate equals death rate, the break-even point below which the population declines.
explanations.c: Consumption rate is a separate parameter from R*; R* is defined by population growth, not consumption volume.
explanations.d: Maximum growth occurs at high resource levels, not at R*, which is specifically the low-resource break-even point.

questions.prompt: On a single limiting resource in a stable environment, the R* rule predicts that:

options.text: The species with the highest R* wins because it needs more resource
The species with the lowest R* wins by depleting the resource below its competitors' break-even point
Both species always coexist regardless of R* values
The outcome depends only on which species starts more abundant

explanations.a: A high R* means the species needs more resource just to break even — a competitive disadvantage, not an advantage.
explanations.b: Correct — the lowest-R* species can persist and keep depleting the resource even after competitors' growth has turned negative, driving exclusion.
explanations.c: Coexistence on a single limiting resource is not predicted by R* theory; it requires multiple resources with crossing ZNGIs.
explanations.d: Unlike the Lotka-Volterra priority-effect case, single-resource R* competition is not starting-density dependent — the lower-R* species wins deterministically.

questions.prompt: Why has R* theory been much harder to confirm in terrestrial field systems than in Tilman's diatom chemostats?

options.text: Terrestrial plants do not compete for resources at all
Field systems have multiple co-varying resources, indirect competition, herbivory, and disturbance that make isolating and measuring a single true R* difficult
R* theory only applies to aquatic organisms by definition
Terrestrial soils lack any limiting nutrients

explanations.a: Terrestrial plants clearly compete for light, water, and nutrients; the issue is measurement, not absence of competition.
explanations.b: Correct — chemostats let researchers control one resource precisely; field systems confound many resources plus non-competitive processes, making clean R* measurement rare.
explanations.c: R* theory is general to any resource-limited system; it is just empirically easier to test in controlled microbial/algal setups.
explanations.d: Terrestrial soils commonly have limiting nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus); the difficulty is isolating one as the sole driver.

questions.prompt: Match each term from resource-ratio theory to its correct description.

right.text: Zero-net-growth isocline: combinations of two resources where a species exactly breaks even
The ratio in which a species draws down two resources as it grows
The single-resource break-even concentration for a species

questions.explanation: R* is the single-resource break-even point; when two resources are considered jointly, the set of break-even combinations forms the ZNGI, and the consumption vector describes how a species depletes the two resources relative to each other, which together determine whether stable two-resource coexistence is possible.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of Tilman's diatom chemostat test of R* theory.

items.text: Measure each diatom species' R* for silicate and phosphate separately in monoculture
Use the measured R* values to predict which species should win under given resource-supply ratios
Grow both diatom species together under those same resource-supply ratios
Compare the observed competitive outcome to the a priori R* prediction

questions.explanation: R* theory's strength was measuring R* independently first, generating a genuine advance prediction, then testing that prediction in two-species competition — the sequence that distinguishes a real test from post hoc curve-fitting.

lessons.label: Limiting Similarity and Character Displacement

sections.heading: How different is different enough? The d/w ratio
sections.body: If competitive exclusion punishes niche overlap, how similar can two coexisting species be before one is doomed? Robert MacArthur and Richard Levins tackled this in 1967 with a limiting-similarity model: species' resource use along a niche axis (say, prey size) is treated as a bell curve of width w (niche breadth), and d is the distance between two species' curve centers. Their models suggested coexistence requires d/w to exceed some threshold — often cited near 1 to 1.5 depending on the model's assumptions about competition strength and environmental noise — below which competitive overlap becomes too strong for stable coexistence. The appeal was a single dimensionless ratio that seemed to predict a minimum spacing along any resource axis.

sections.heading: Hutchinson's 1.3 and the finch beaks
sections.body: G. Evelyn Hutchinson's 1959 paper 'Homage to Santa Rosalia' proposed, from surveying body-size and mouth-part ratios in congeneric species pairs (weasels, sunfish, and others), that coexisting close relatives commonly differ by a size ratio around 1.3 — quickly dubbed the 'Hutchinson ratio.' Peter and Rosemary Grant's long-term Galapagos work on Daphne Major gave this idea its most celebrated confirmation: when the larger-beaked Geospiza magnirostris colonized the island and a severe 2004-05 drought collapsed the shared seed supply, medium ground finches (Geospiza fortis) with beak depths overlapping magnirostris suffered much higher mortality than smaller-beaked fortis, driving a rapid, measurable shift in the fortis beak-depth distribution — character displacement caught happening in real time, published by the Grants in Science in 2006. Caribbean Anolis lizards provide a parallel, non-size-ratio example: island communities repeatedly evolve the same set of habitat 'ecomorphs' (crown-giant, trunk-ground, twig, and others) partitioning perch height and diameter, independently on different islands.

sections.heading: Simberloff and Boecklen's demolition of the numerology
sections.body: Daniel Simberloff and William Boecklen's 1981 paper 'Santa Rosalia Reconsidered' subjected published size-ratio datasets to a null-model test: if you generate random assemblages of species from the same regional pool without any competition, do you get size ratios clustering around 1.3 anyway? Often, yes — many of the celebrated size-ratio patterns were statistically indistinguishable from random assortment, especially once researchers controlled for the tendency to selectively report or exclude 'messy' data points. The lesson generalized well beyond finches: a pattern consistent with limiting similarity is not evidence for it unless it beats an explicit null model of no competition.

lessons.workedExample: A science-fair project measures beak depths across six sympatric finch species and finds ratios between adjacent species averaging 1.28 — close to Hutchinson's 1.3. Presented alone, this looks like textbook confirmation. But following Simberloff and Boecklen's method, the student instead draws 1,000 random six-species subsets from the full regional finch pool and computes the same ratio statistic for each. If the observed 1.28 falls within the middle of that random distribution (not in its extreme tail), the 'confirmation' evaporates — the ratio is unremarkable under pure chance. Only a ratio that sits outside, say, the top 5 percent of randomized outcomes supports limiting similarity over the null.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe limiting similarity because it is the textbook case where a pattern-matching claim ('the ratio is near 1.3, so competition shaped it') can look rigorous while being statistically empty. A weak answer reports the ratio and stops. A strong answer explicitly compares the observed pattern to a null model built from the same species pool without competition — echoing exactly the Simberloff and Boecklen critique — and can also cite the Grants' Daphne Major work as an example where the mechanism (differential mortality tied to a resource bottleneck) was demonstrated directly rather than inferred from a static ratio.

questions.prompt: In MacArthur and Levins' limiting-similarity model, what do d and w represent?

options.text: d is population density and w is carrying capacity
d is the distance between two species' niche centers and w is niche breadth
d is dispersal distance and w is wing length
d is death rate and w is water availability

explanations.a: Density and carrying capacity are Lotka-Volterra terms, not the limiting-similarity ratio's components.
explanations.b: Correct — d/w measures how far apart two species' resource-use curves sit relative to how broad each curve is, predicting a minimum spacing for stable coexistence.
explanations.c: Dispersal and wing length are not part of this niche-overlap framework.
explanations.d: Death rate and water availability are not the quantities MacArthur and Levins modeled here.

questions.prompt: What did the Grants document on Daphne Major following the arrival of Geospiza magnirostris and the 2004-05 drought?

options.text: Geospiza fortis and magnirostris merged into a single interbreeding population
Medium-beaked fortis individuals overlapping magnirostris in beak depth suffered higher mortality, shifting the fortis population toward smaller beaks
Both species went extinct on the island
Beak depth in both species increased identically, with no divergence

explanations.a: The species remained distinct; competitive mortality, not hybridization, drove the observed change.
explanations.b: Correct — during the seed-supply collapse, fortis individuals with beak depths closest to magnirostris competed poorly for the same large seeds and died at higher rates, shifting the surviving population toward smaller beaks: character displacement observed directly.
explanations.c: Both species persisted on Daphne Major; the drought caused a mortality event, not extinction.
explanations.d: The key result was divergence, not identical parallel change, between the two species' beak depths.

questions.prompt: What was the core method Simberloff and Boecklen (1981) used to challenge the 1.3 size-ratio claim?

options.text: They re-measured all the original specimens with more precise calipers
They compared observed size ratios against ratios generated by random null-model assemblages drawn from the same species pool
They argued competition never occurs in nature
They proposed a new, larger universal ratio to replace 1.3

explanations.a: Their critique was statistical, about whether the pattern beat chance, not about measurement precision.
explanations.b: Correct — by generating randomized species assemblages without competition and comparing the resulting size-ratio distribution to the real data, they showed many published 1.3-like patterns were not distinguishable from chance.
explanations.c: They did not deny competition occurs; they challenged a specific numerological claim about a universal ratio.
explanations.d: They did not propose a replacement constant; they showed the search for any universal constant was often statistically unsupported.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher(s) or study to their contribution to limiting-similarity theory.

right.text: Proposed the d/w niche-overlap threshold model
Proposed the ~1.3 body-size ratio among coexisting congeners
Documented real-time character displacement in Darwin's finch beak depth
Showed many size-ratio patterns are statistically indistinguishable from random null models

questions.explanation: MacArthur and Levins built the theoretical d/w ratio; Hutchinson proposed the empirical 1.3 constant; the Grants provided the strongest direct field demonstration of character displacement in action; Simberloff and Boecklen showed the broader size-ratio literature often failed a proper null-model test.

questions.prompt: Order the historical development of limiting-similarity theory from proposal to critique.

items.text: Hutchinson proposes the ~1.3 size-ratio pattern from surveyed congener pairs
MacArthur and Levins formalize a d/w niche-overlap threshold model
Researchers report size-ratio patterns near 1.3 across many taxa as apparent confirmation
Simberloff and Boecklen show many of these patterns fail a randomized null-model test

questions.explanation: Hutchinson's empirical observation came first, MacArthur and Levins gave it theoretical backing, subsequent researchers reported confirming ratios, and Simberloff and Boecklen's null-model critique later showed much of that confirming literature did not hold up statistically.

lessons.label: Modern Coexistence Theory

sections.heading: Two numbers instead of one story
sections.body: Peter Chesson's 2000 Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics paper 'Mechanisms of Maintenance of Species Diversity' reorganized decades of scattered coexistence mechanisms — niche partitioning, resource ratios, storage effects — into one unified accounting framework built on two quantities. Stabilizing niche differences measure how much more a species limits itself relative to how much it limits its competitors; formally, they capture the tendency of intraspecific competition to exceed interspecific competition, the same idea buried inside the Lotka-Volterra alpha coefficients but now generalized to any mechanism (resource partitioning, natural enemies, temporal or spatial variation). Average fitness differences measure which species would simply outcompete the other in the absence of any niche difference — differences in intrinsic growth rate, competitive ability, or resource requirements that favor one species regardless of niche overlap. Chesson's central claim: coexistence is possible if and only if stabilizing niche differences are large enough to overcome the average fitness difference between the two species.

sections.heading: The mutual-invasibility test
sections.body: The framework's operational core is the mutual-invasibility criterion, inherited from earlier invasion-analysis work but formalized by Chesson: a pair of species coexists stably if each one, reduced experimentally or observationally to very low density while its competitor sits at its own equilibrium, has a positive per-capita growth rate. If species A can invade a resident population of species B, and species B can likewise invade a resident population of A, low-density rescue works in both directions and the pair persists together. If only one direction works, that species excludes the other. Practically, ecologists estimate this by growing each species alone to measure its intrinsic performance, then introducing rare individuals into an established stand of the other and tracking whether that rare population grows or shrinks.

sections.heading: Why 'different niches' alone proves nothing
sections.body: The framework's sharpest teaching point is that niche difference is necessary but not sufficient. A textbook-strong niche difference can still fail to produce coexistence if the average fitness difference is large enough to swamp it — imagine two plant species partitioning soil depth almost perfectly (strong stabilization) but one photosynthesizing at twice the rate of the other (large fitness inequality): the faster species can still win. Conversely, species with nearly identical niches can coexist a long time if their fitness difference is close to zero, since neither has enough advantage to drive the other out quickly. This is why Chesson's framework displaced simpler 'they use different resources, so they coexist' reasoning: it requires measuring, not just describing, both quantities.

lessons.workedExample: Two annual plant competitors are grown in three plot types: A alone, B alone, and A rare within an established B stand (and the reverse). From the monoculture plots, researchers estimate each species' fitness parameters (germination rate, competitive response to crowding). From the invasion plots, they measure whether rare A grows in a B-dominated plot and vice versa. Suppose rare A's per-capita growth is +0.15 per year (positive, can invade) but rare B's is -0.05 per year (negative, cannot invade) — this is not coexistence but slow-motion exclusion of B, even if the two species clearly used somewhat different rooting depths. The niche difference reduced competition, and might make B's decline much slower than the Lotka-Volterra baseline predicts, but it was not large enough to overcome A's fitness advantage.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on modern coexistence theory to catch students who describe a niche difference and stop, treating description as explanation. A weak answer says 'they use different resources, so they coexist.' A strong answer names the two required quantities, explains that coexistence needs stabilizing niche differences to exceed the average fitness difference, and — ideally — describes how the mutual-invasibility test would actually be run for their own study system (grow each species alone, then introduce it rare into the other's established population, and track whether it grows).

questions.prompt: Under Chesson's modern coexistence theory, two species coexist stably when:

options.text: They occupy visibly different habitats
Stabilizing niche differences are large enough to overcome the average fitness difference between them
Their population sizes happen to be equal at the study's end
Neither species can grow when rare

explanations.a: Visible habitat difference alone does not guarantee coexistence; it must be shown to sufficiently offset any fitness inequality.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the framework's central inequality: niche stabilization must exceed the fitness gap for both species to persist together.
explanations.c: Equal population sizes at one point in time say nothing about long-run dynamics or whether each species can recover from low density.
explanations.d: The opposite is required: coexistence needs each species to be able to grow when rare (positive invasion growth rate for both).

questions.prompt: The mutual-invasibility criterion tests coexistence by:

options.text: Checking whether both species have identical carrying capacities
Checking whether each species, introduced at low density into its established competitor's population, has a positive growth rate
Measuring whether the two species ever physically touch
Comparing the two species' geographic range sizes

explanations.a: Equal carrying capacities are neither necessary nor sufficient for coexistence in this framework.
explanations.b: Correct — coexistence requires that each species can increase from rarity against an established competitor; this is tested in both directions.
explanations.c: Physical contact is irrelevant to the invasion-growth-rate criterion.
explanations.d: Range size is not part of the mutual-invasibility test, which is about per-capita growth rate at low density.

questions.prompt: Why is 'these species use different niches' not by itself a sufficient explanation for observed coexistence?

options.text: Niche difference is never real; it is always an experimental artifact
A large enough average fitness difference between the species can still drive exclusion despite substantial niche difference
Niche differences only matter for plants, not animals
Coexistence theory does not use the concept of niche at all

explanations.a: Niche differences can be real and measurable; the issue is that they are not automatically sufficient for coexistence.
explanations.b: Correct — the framework's key insight is that niche difference is necessary but not sufficient; it must exceed the competing species' fitness inequality.
explanations.c: The framework applies generally across taxa, not only plants.
explanations.d: Niche difference (as stabilizing difference) is one of the two central quantities in the framework, not an excluded concept.

questions.prompt: Match each Chesson framework term to what it captures.

right.text: How much more a species limits itself compared to its competitor
Which species would win in the absence of any niche difference
The operational test: can each species grow when rare against the other's established population

questions.explanation: Stabilizing niche differences capture self-limitation relative to competitor-limitation; average fitness differences capture inherent competitive inequality apart from niche overlap; mutual invasibility is the testable prediction that follows when stabilization exceeds fitness inequality.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of an experimental test of modern coexistence theory for two competing plant species.

items.text: Grow each species alone to estimate its intrinsic performance parameters
Establish each species at its own equilibrium in separate resident plots
Introduce the other species at low density into each resident plot
Measure the invader's per-capita growth rate in both directions to test mutual invasibility

questions.explanation: Estimating baseline performance from monocultures comes first, then establishing resident populations, then the low-density invasion trials in both directions, then comparing invasion growth rates to determine whether coexistence is predicted.

lessons.label: Fluctuation-Dependent Coexistence

sections.heading: Hutchinson's paradox: too many species, too few resources
sections.body: In his 1961 paper 'The Paradox of the Plankton,' G. Evelyn Hutchinson pointed out that open-water phytoplankton communities routinely hold dozens of species competing for a tiny handful of limiting resources (light, nitrogen, phosphorus, silicate) in an environment with no obvious spatial structure to partition — exactly the setup where competitive exclusion should whittle diversity down hard. His proposed resolution was that the environment never sits still long enough for exclusion to finish: constant physical and seasonal disturbance keeps resetting the competitive race before any one species wins, so a non-equilibrium, fluctuating environment can itself sustain diversity that a stable one could not. That insight opened an entire branch of coexistence theory built on fluctuations as a mechanism, not just noise to average away.

sections.heading: The storage effect: three ingredients, not just 'variability helps'
sections.body: Robert Warner and Peter Chesson formalized this in 1985 as the storage effect, showing fluctuations promote coexistence only when three specific ingredients are all present together. First, species-specific environmental responses: different species must do relatively better in different years or patches (species A thrives in wet years, species B in dry ones), so no single competitor dominates every condition. Second, covariance between environment and competition: the very years that are good for a species must also be years of intensified competition, which caps how much advantage that good year actually delivers — otherwise a lucky species would simply run away with the population. Third, buffered population growth: a life-history feature — a long-lived adult stage, a dormant seed bank, a resting egg bank — that lets a species survive bad years without dying out, effectively 'storing' the gains from its good years until the next one arrives. Remove any one ingredient and the mechanism collapses back toward ordinary exclusion.

sections.heading: A second fluctuation mechanism, and where it was actually measured
sections.body: A related but distinct mechanism, relative nonlinearity of competition, lets species coexist when they differ in how their growth rate curves bend (convex versus concave) in response to fluctuating resource or competitor levels, so each species' fitness responds differently to variance itself, not just to the mean. The storage effect's most convincing field quantification came from D. Lawrence Venable's decades-long study of Sonoran Desert winter annual plants at Tumamoc Hill, Arizona, where dozens of species germinate from a persistent soil seed bank in response to variable winter rainfall. Angert, Huxman, Chesson, and Venable's 2009 PNAS paper used this long-term demographic dataset — germination fractions, seed survival, per-capita growth rates species by species across many recorded years — to directly calculate the strength of the storage effect from field data for the first time, finding it a substantial stabilizing force among the desert annuals, closely tied to each species' low, bet-hedging germination fraction acting as the buffering seed bank.

lessons.workedExample: Two Sonoran Desert winter annuals differ in which rainfall years favor them: species X germinates heavily and grows well in wet years, species Y tolerates dry years better. In any single wet year, X's population would surge, but wet years also trigger dense germination from the seed bank, intensifying competition for space and soil moisture right when X is trying to capitalize — the environment-competition covariance that caps X's runaway advantage. Meanwhile only a fraction of each species' seeds germinate each year (the rest stay dormant in the seed bank), so a string of bad years for Y does not eliminate Y's ungerminated seed reserve. Angert et al.'s 2009 analysis quantified exactly this dynamic across the real Tumamoc Hill annual community, converting a qualitative story into a measured stabilizing contribution to coexistence.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe the storage effect because 'a fluctuating environment lets species coexist' is a claim students make constantly and rarely explain mechanistically. A weak answer stops at 'the environment varies, so species coexist.' A strong answer names all three required ingredients — species-specific environmental response, environment-competition covariance, and a buffering life-history stage — and can point to a real buffering mechanism in their own study system (a seed bank, a long-lived adult stage, diapausing eggs), showing they understand that variability alone does nothing without a way to bank the gains from good times.

questions.prompt: What puzzle did Hutchinson's 1961 'Paradox of the Plankton' identify?

options.text: Why phytoplankton communities have so few species despite abundant resources
Why many phytoplankton species coexist on very few limiting resources, seemingly violating competitive exclusion
Why plankton cannot photosynthesize in deep water
Why phytoplankton reproduce asexually

explanations.a: The paradox is the opposite: too many coexisting species relative to the few limiting resources available.
explanations.b: Correct — dozens of phytoplankton species persist on a handful of shared resources, which competitive exclusion theory suggests should not be stable.
explanations.c: Photosynthesis depth limits are a real constraint but not the subject of Hutchinson's paradox.
explanations.d: Reproductive mode is unrelated to the paradox, which concerns species diversity versus resource number.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three required ingredients of the storage effect?

options.text: Species-specific responses to environmental variation
Covariance between environment and competition
Buffered population growth via a long-lived or dormant life stage
Identical resource requirements across all competing species

explanations.a: This is one of the three required ingredients — different species must respond differently to environmental conditions.
explanations.b: This is one of the three required ingredients — good years for a species must also be years of intensified competition.
explanations.c: This is one of the three required ingredients — a buffering life stage lets species survive bad years without extinction.
explanations.d: Correct — identical resource requirements would work against coexistence, not enable it; the storage effect requires species-specific, not identical, responses.

questions.prompt: In Venable's Sonoran Desert winter annuals, what life-history trait provides the 'buffering' required by the storage effect?

options.text: A persistent soil seed bank with partial, variable germination each year
Extremely fast maturation within a single week
Migration to wetter regions during drought years
Perennial root systems that never die back

explanations.a: Correct — only a fraction of seeds germinate each year, leaving a dormant reserve in the soil that survives bad years and buffers population growth, exactly the storage-effect requirement.
explanations.b: Fast maturation is a feature of desert annuals generally but is not the buffering mechanism the storage effect requires.
explanations.c: These are annual plants with a seed bank, not migratory organisms.
explanations.d: Winter annuals are not perennials; their persistence mechanism is the dormant seed bank, not a perennial root system.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher(s)/paper to its contribution to fluctuation-dependent coexistence theory.
