right.text: Identified the paradox of high plankton diversity on few resources
Formalized the three-ingredient storage effect model
First field quantification of the storage effect using desert annual demographic data

questions.explanation: Hutchinson posed the motivating puzzle in open-water plankton; Warner and Chesson gave it a formal three-part mechanism; Angert, Huxman, Chesson, and Venable later measured that mechanism's real magnitude in a long-term Sonoran Desert annual plant dataset.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps of the storage effect operating in a fluctuating environment, from a good year for a species to its long-term persistence.

items.text: An environmental condition arrives that specifically favors species X over its competitors
Species X's strong response also triggers intensified competition, capping its population surge
A subsequent unfavorable period arrives that favors a different competitor
Species X's buffered life stage (seed bank, long-lived adults) carries it through the unfavorable period without extinction

questions.explanation: The storage effect requires the sequence of a species-specific good period, capped by covarying competition, followed by an unfavorable period that the buffering life stage allows the species to survive, so it can capitalize on its next good period.

lessons.label: Intransitivity, Priority Effects, and Alternative Community States

sections.heading: Rock-paper-scissors competition: coexistence without niche difference
sections.body: Every mechanism so far assumed competition is hierarchical: rank species by competitive ability and the top-ranked one wins. Intransitive competition breaks that ranking into a cycle, A beats B, B beats C, but C beats A, so no species is unconditionally dominant. Barry Sinervo and Curt Lively's 1996 Nature paper documented exactly this among male side-blotched lizards (Uta stansburiana): orange-throated males are aggressive and out-compete blue-throated mate-guarders for territory; blue males successfully guard mates against yellow-throated 'sneaker' males, who mimic females to slip past mate-guarding; yet sneaker yellows out-reproduce orange males, who cannot defend against covert sneaking across such large territories. The three morphs cycle in frequency roughly every four to five years, a rock-paper-scissors loop maintaining all three strategies without any of them driving the others extinct. Benjamin Kerr, Margaret Riley, Marcus Feldman, and Brendan Bohannan's 2002 Nature study built the same logic into bacteria: a colicin-producing E. coli strain (C) kills a sensitive strain (S), S outgrows a colicin-resistant strain (R) because R pays no toxin cost but grows slightly slower than S, and R resists C's toxin and outcompetes C. Crucially, Kerr et al. showed this three-way loop only sustains all three strains when dispersal is spatially limited (a petri dish); in well-mixed liquid culture, two of the three strains go extinct — intransitivity permits coexistence without any niche difference, but only where local interactions let the cycle keep chasing itself around rather than collapsing to whichever strain currently dominates everywhere at once.

sections.heading: Priority effects: who arrives first can decide who wins
sections.body: Separately, community assembly can be history-dependent even without a competitive cycle. James Drake's laboratory pond-community assembly experiments in the late 1980s and 1990s showed that introducing the same regional species pool in different orders produced different, persistent final communities, evidence that early colonizers can lock in an advantage (via early resource capture, or by changing the environment) that later arrivals cannot overcome even though they could win if they had arrived first. Tadashi Fukami and colleagues demonstrated the mechanism concretely in flower nectar: yeast and bacterial species that colonize nectar first alter its sugar concentration and pH, reshaping the environment for whichever microbe arrives second; a separate line of work (Herrera and Pozo 2010) found some nectar-colonizing yeasts raise nectar temperature enough to be measurable. Robert Alford and Henry Wilbur's 1985 Ecology study on Bufo americanus and Rana sylvatica tadpoles found that hatching order shifted competitive outcomes between the two species in experimental ponds, a priority effect in a system many students could replicate.

sections.heading: Alternative stable states demand a high evidence bar
sections.body: Priority effects raise the further, stronger claim of alternative stable states: the idea that identical environmental conditions can support two (or more) persistently different community configurations, and which one you get depends on history rather than the current environment. This claim requires more than showing two different communities exist under similar conditions — that could simply reflect an unmeasured environmental difference between sites. The rigorous bar is demonstrating hysteresis: experimentally push a system from state A toward the conditions favoring state B, then relax the perturbation back to the original conditions, and show the community stays in state B rather than snapping back to A. Without that return-trajectory test, an observed pattern of two distinct communities is only suggestive, not proof, of true alternative stable states.

lessons.workedExample: A pond ecology project finds two nearby ponds with similar depth and nutrient levels: one dominated by clear water and submerged plants, the other turbid and dominated by phytoplankton. A student claims 'alternative stable states.' To actually test that claim rather than assume it, they would need to experimentally reduce phytoplankton in the turbid pond (e.g., via a biomanipulation like temporarily removing planktivorous fish) enough to trigger a switch toward plant dominance, then let the manipulation lapse — and show the pond stays clear rather than reverting to turbid. If it snaps back to turbid the moment fish are restored, the two ponds more likely reflect a real underlying difference (nutrient load, fish community) rather than two stable states of one shared underlying system.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push hardest on 'alternative stable states' claims because the phrase gets used loosely for what is often just two different environments. A weak answer points at two visibly different communities and calls it alternative stable states. A strong answer either demonstrates hysteresis with a perturb-and-release experiment, or explicitly says the evidence only supports a priority effect (or an unmeasured environmental gradient) and stops short of the stronger claim — showing they know the difference between 'these look different' and 'this system has two stable configurations under identical conditions.'

questions.prompt: In Sinervo and Lively's side-blotched lizard system, which mating strategy relationship makes it intransitive rather than hierarchical?

options.text: Orange beats blue, blue beats yellow, and yellow beats orange, forming a cycle
Orange always beats both blue and yellow
All three morphs are functionally identical
Yellow always beats both orange and blue

explanations.a: Correct — the cyclic relationship (orange beats blue, blue beats yellow, yellow beats orange) means no morph is universally dominant, the defining feature of intransitive competition.
explanations.b: A strict hierarchy where orange dominates both would be transitive, not the rock-paper-scissors pattern documented in this system.
explanations.c: The three morphs have measurably different competitive outcomes against each other; they are not functionally identical.
explanations.d: Yellow beats orange in this cycle but loses to blue, so it is not universally dominant either.

questions.prompt: What did Kerr et al.'s 2002 E. coli experiment show about spatial structure and intransitive competition?

options.text: All three bacterial strains coexisted equally well in both spatially structured and well-mixed conditions
The three-strain rock-paper-scissors loop maintained all strains only under limited local dispersal; well-mixed culture led to extinction of two strains
Spatial structure had no effect on the outcome
Only the colicin-producing strain could ever survive, regardless of conditions

explanations.a: The two conditions produced different outcomes; spatial structure was essential to maintaining all three strains.
explanations.b: Correct — on the spatially structured agar plate all three strains persisted in a rock-paper-scissors pattern, while in well-mixed liquid culture two strains went extinct.
explanations.c: Spatial structure was the pivotal variable distinguishing coexistence from collapse to fewer strains.
explanations.d: The colicin producer did not universally win; the outcome depended on dispersal structure, and different strains dominated under different conditions.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum rigorous evidence needed to claim 'alternative stable states' rather than a priority effect or hidden environmental difference?

options.text: Observing two different communities in two different locations
Demonstrating hysteresis: pushing the system toward the other state and showing it persists there after the perturbation is removed
Showing that one community has more species than the other
Citing that the two communities have been stable for many years

explanations.a: Two different communities in different places could simply reflect different environmental conditions, not alternative states of the same system.
explanations.b: Correct — the rigorous test is a perturb-and-release experiment showing the system remains in the new state rather than reverting, which rules out a simple environmental-gradient explanation.
explanations.c: Species richness differences alone say nothing about whether the states are alternative stable configurations of the same environment.
explanations.d: Long-term stability alone does not distinguish two persistently different environments from two true alternative states of one environment.

questions.prompt: Match each study/system to the phenomenon it demonstrates.

left.text: Kerr et al. colicin-producing E. coli

right.text: Intransitive rock-paper-scissors competition maintaining three male mating morphs
Intransitive loop requiring spatial structure to sustain all competitors
Priority effect via environment modification by early colonizers
Priority effect via hatching-order shift in competitive outcome

questions.explanation: The lizard and bacterial systems both demonstrate intransitive (rock-paper-scissors) competition, with the bacterial case additionally showing dispersal-dependence; the nectar microbe and tadpole systems both demonstrate priority effects, one through environmental modification and one through order-dependent competitive outcomes.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a rigorous experimental test for alternative stable states in a shallow pond system.

items.text: Identify two ponds with similar environmental conditions but different community states (clear vs. turbid)
Experimentally perturb the turbid pond (e.g., temporarily remove planktivorous fish) to push it toward the clear-water state
Confirm the pond shifts to the clear-water state under the perturbation
Remove the perturbation and observe whether the pond remains clear (hysteresis) or reverts to turbid

questions.explanation: A rigorous alternative-stable-states test starts from an observed pattern, actively perturbs the system toward the other state, confirms the shift, and then critically tests whether the new state persists after the perturbation ends — persistence (hysteresis) is what distinguishes true alternative stable states from a temporary, perturbation-dependent change.

lessons.label: Primary Succession and the Chronosequence Method

sections.heading: Bare rock to forest: the Glacier Bay sequence
sections.body: Primary succession builds a community on substrate with no prior soil or biological legacy — bare rock, fresh lava, glacial till. The classic case is Glacier Bay, Alaska, where the ice front has retreated roughly 100 km since the mid-1700s, leaving a natural time series of exposed land from decades to over two centuries old. William S. Cooper began permanent plots there in 1916 and published the sequence in 1923: pioneer mosses and the nitrogen-fixing shrub Dryas drummondii colonize bare till first, followed by nitrogen-fixing alder (Alnus) thickets, then Sitka spruce, and eventually western hemlock forest after roughly 150 years. Robert Crocker and James Major returned in 1955 with soil chemistry and showed why the sequence runs in that order: Dryas and alder fix atmospheric nitrogen via root-nodule bacteria, driving soil nitrogen from near zero to build-up rates of tens of kg/ha/year under alder, while soil pH drops from about 8.0 on fresh till to about 5.0 under mature spruce-hemlock as organic acids accumulate. The plants are literally engineering the soil their successors need.

sections.heading: Krakatau and Mount St. Helens: two different starting lines
sections.body: Krakatau's 1883 eruption sterilized the island completely; the first plants recorded in 1886 were a few ferns and grasses arriving as wind-blown spores and seeds, with forest cover documented within about 40 years — a case of true primary succession from a lifeless substrate. Mount St. Helens (1980) looks superficially similar but is often reclassified as secondary succession in disturbed patches because so much biological legacy survived: buried rhizomes of fireweed and other plants, gophers and small mammals under snowpack, and pocket gopher burrowing that redistributed surviving soil organisms sped recovery dramatically compared to sterile substrate nearby. The contrast matters for judging any recovering-landscape claim — what survived the disturbance often predicts recovery speed better than distance to a seed source.

sections.heading: The chronosequence shortcut, and its catch
sections.body: No one can watch one plot for 200 years, so ecologists substitute space for time: a chronosequence treats sites of different known ages (here, distance from the retreating ice front) as stand-ins for stages of one time series. Edward Johnson and Kiyoko Miyanishi's 2008 critique names the trap: sites of different ages usually differ in more than age alone — parent material, drainage, and disturbance history can all vary across the sequence, so a pattern that looks like temporal change might really be a spatial artifact. A chronosequence is a reasonable working hypothesis, not a proven trajectory, unless the sites are checked for comparable starting conditions.

lessons.workedExample: A team samples four Glacier Bay sites at estimated ages of 20, 60, 120, and 200 years since deglaciation and finds soil nitrogen and canopy height both rising with age — the standard chronosequence story. But the 120-year site sits on a steeper slope with different bedrock than the others. Before concluding that succession alone drives the pattern, a careful analyst checks whether slope or bedrock could explain the outlier independently of time, and looks for supporting evidence such as Crocker and Major's actual repeated soil measurements rather than trusting one snapshot across sites.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe chronosequence work because it is the single most common design flaw in student succession projects — comparing different-aged patches and calling the difference "succession over time" without ruling out that the patches simply started out different. A strong answer names Johnson and Miyanishi's critique directly and explains what independent evidence (repeated measurement, matched parent material, known disturbance history) would strengthen the space-for-time inference. A weak answer treats the chronosequence as if it were a literal time-lapse.

questions.prompt: What made Dryas and alder critical early colonizers in the Glacier Bay chronosequence documented by Crocker and Major (1955)?

options.text: They tolerate the low soil pH left by retreating ice
They fix atmospheric nitrogen, building up soil nitrogen that later species need
They produce shade that cools the soil for spruce seedlings
They are wind-pollinated and disperse fastest

explanations.a: Fresh till starts near pH 8, not low; pH falls later as organic matter accumulates under the plants, not before them.
explanations.b: Correct — Dryas and alder host nitrogen-fixing root bacteria, and Crocker and Major measured the resulting rise in soil nitrogen as the key resource shift enabling spruce and hemlock to establish later.
explanations.c: Shading becomes important in later inhibition-stage dynamics, not as the mechanism explaining these particular pioneer species.
explanations.d: Dispersal ability explains arrival, not why these species specifically enable the species that follow them.

questions.prompt: Johnson and Miyanishi's 2008 critique of the chronosequence method centers on which problem?

options.text: Chronosequences can never include more than three sites
Sites of different ages may differ in factors besides age, confounding the space-for-time substitution
Soil pH cannot be measured accurately in the field
Nitrogen-fixing plants are too rare to sample reliably

explanations.a: The critique is about validity of inference, not about a hard limit on sample size.
explanations.b: Correct — differences in parent material, drainage, or disturbance history across sites of different age can produce patterns that mimic succession without any temporal process occurring.
explanations.c: Their argument is about site comparability, not measurement precision.
explanations.d: The critique applies to chronosequences generally, not specifically to nitrogen-fixer abundance.

questions.prompt: Match each site to the feature that defines its succession case.

right.text: Sterilized island recolonized from wind-blown spores and seeds
Retreating ice front providing a natural age gradient of exposed till
Surviving rhizomes and burrowing animals sped recovery, blurring primary/secondary succession

questions.explanation: Glacier Bay's retreating ice created the classic chronosequence Cooper and later Crocker and Major studied; Krakatau's 1883 eruption left bare, lifeless substrate recolonized purely by dispersal; Mount St. Helens retained biological legacies (buried rhizomes, surviving burrowers) that accelerated recovery in many patches.

questions.prompt: Order the Glacier Bay successional stages from earliest to latest, per Cooper (1923) and Crocker and Major (1955).

items.text: Pioneer mosses and Dryas colonize bare till
Nitrogen-fixing alder thickets dominate
Sitka spruce establishes
Western hemlock forest with acidified soil

questions.explanation: The documented sequence runs moss/Dryas, then alder (further building soil nitrogen), then spruce, then hemlock forest roughly 150 years after deglaciation, with soil pH dropping from about 8 to about 5 across the sequence.

lessons.label: Mechanisms of Succession

sections.heading: Three ways early species affect the next arrivals
sections.body: Joseph Connell and Ralph Slatyer's 1977 paper gave succession its most-used framework by asking a mechanistic question: how do early-occupying species affect who colonizes next? Facilitation means early species change the environment in ways that make it more suitable for later species — Glacier Bay's nitrogen-fixing Dryas and alder enabling spruce is a textbook case. Tolerance means early species neither help nor hinder later arrivals; later species simply grow slowly and eventually outcompete earlier ones regardless of what the earlier ones did to the site. Inhibition means early species actively resist replacement — established individuals monopolize space, light, or nutrients and can only be replaced when they die or are damaged, not out-competed while alive. The three models make different, testable predictions: under facilitation, removing early species should delay or prevent later species from establishing; under inhibition, removing early species should speed up the arrival of later ones; under tolerance, removal should have little effect on the eventual outcome.

sections.heading: Egler's alternative: composition set from day one
sections.body: Frank Egler's 1954 initial floristic composition model rejected the idea that later species must wait for earlier ones to arrive or exit at all. Instead, most of the species that will ever occupy a site are present from the very start as seeds, seedlings, or root fragments; succession then proceeds simply because fast-growing early species (annual weeds, grasses) mature and set seed quickly while slower long-lived species (shrubs, trees) take longer to grow large enough to dominate visually. What looks like sequential replacement is really differential growth rates among species that were co-present all along — the composition was fixed early, only the visible dominance shifts. This matters for restoration: if Egler's model holds, seeding the desired late-stage species at the outset can shortcut decades of waiting.

sections.heading: Testing the models and the realistic mix
sections.body: Removal experiments discriminate the models directly: field studies on rocky intertidal shores and in old-field succession have physically cleared early colonizers from replicate plots and tracked whether later species arrive faster, slower, or unchanged relative to controls. Real successions rarely fit one pure model throughout — facilitation typically dominates early, when nitrogen-fixers or shade-tolerant nurse plants improve harsh conditions, while inhibition often takes over later, when dense canopies, thick litter, or allelopathic chemical suppression (as documented in some Mediterranean shrublands) block new establishment until a gap opens. A single successional sequence can therefore show facilitation in its first decades and inhibition for the rest of its trajectory.

lessons.workedExample: A restoration ecologist studies an abandoned agricultural field colonized first by annual weeds, then perennial grasses, then shrubs. To test which Connell-Slatyer mechanism dominates, they set up plots where they hand-pull the annual weeds as soon as they appear versus untouched controls. If perennial grasses establish faster in the weeded plots, that is evidence for inhibition (weeds were suppressing grasses). If grasses establish at the same rate regardless, that supports tolerance. If grasses actually establish slower or fail in weeded plots, that points to facilitation — the weeds were doing something useful, like shading bare soil and reducing evaporation.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on succession mechanism because "succession happens" is a description, not an explanation, and only a removal or manipulation design can distinguish facilitation from inhibition from tolerance — observation alone cannot. A strong answer proposes or cites a specific removal experiment and states what result each of the three models predicts before the data are collected. A weak answer describes the sequence of species observed without ever explaining why one replaced the next.

questions.prompt: Under Connell and Slatyer's inhibition model, what happens if you experimentally remove established early-successional individuals?

options.text: Later species establish faster than in untouched controls
Later species establish more slowly than in untouched controls
There is no measurable effect on later species
Early species instantly regrow and exclude all later species permanently

explanations.a: Correct — under inhibition, established individuals actively hold space/resources against later species while alive, so removing them opens space and speeds up replacement relative to controls.
explanations.b: This would be the opposite of the inhibition prediction; slower establishment after removal is closer to what facilitation predicts.
explanations.c: No effect from removal is the tolerance prediction, not inhibition.
explanations.d: Inhibition describes resistance by living individuals, not instant regrowth after removal.

questions.prompt: Egler's 1954 initial floristic composition model differs from Connell and Slatyer's models chiefly by proposing that:

options.text: Later species physically cannot arrive until earlier species have modified the soil
Most species present across the whole sequence are already there from the start, and succession is mainly a matter of differing growth rates
Succession never has a predictable endpoint
Only wind-dispersed species can participate in succession

explanations.a: That description matches facilitation, which Egler's model was proposed as an alternative to, not a restatement of.
explanations.b: Correct — in Egler's model the eventual species pool is largely set by initial colonization, and the sequence we observe reflects fast-maturing versus slow-growing species reaching dominance at different times, not sequential arrival.
explanations.c: Egler's model still allows a predictable trajectory driven by growth-rate differences; it does not claim succession is unpredictable.
explanations.d: The model makes no dispersal-mode restriction; it concerns timing of establishment versus dominance.

questions.prompt: Match each Connell-Slatyer model to its defining prediction about early species' effect on later species.

right.text: Early species make conditions more suitable for later ones; removal delays later species
Early species neither help nor hinder; later species eventually win on their own growth traits regardless
Early species resist replacement while alive; removal speeds later species' arrival

questions.explanation: Facilitation predicts removal experiments delay later colonizers because a beneficial modification is lost; tolerance predicts removal has little effect because later species were going to win by growing slowly but persistently regardless; inhibition predicts removal speeds up later colonizers because a resource-monopolizing resident is gone.

questions.prompt: Order the typical dominant mechanism across a long successional sequence, from earliest phase to latest phase, as described for real-world successions like Glacier Bay.

items.text: Nitrogen-fixers and nurse plants ease harsh early conditions (facilitation-dominant)
Mixed establishment as conditions moderate
Dense canopies and litter suppress new establishment until a gap opens (inhibition-dominant)

questions.explanation: Real sequences commonly begin with facilitation easing harsh abiotic conditions for later species, then shift toward inhibition as established vegetation becomes dense enough to monopolize light, space, and nutrients against new colonizers.

lessons.label: Disturbance Regimes and the Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis

sections.heading: Describing a disturbance regime
sections.body: A disturbance is any discrete event that removes organisms and opens space or resources — a storm, fire, landslide, or predation outbreak. Ecologists characterize a site's disturbance regime with four properties: frequency (how often disturbances occur), intensity (how much damage each event causes), extent (spatial area affected), and return interval (average time between successive events at a given point). The same disturbance type can produce very different regimes: a reef hit by frequent, mild wave stress has a different regime than one hit rarely by a catastrophic hurricane, even if total long-run damage is similar.

sections.heading: Connell's 1978 intermediate disturbance hypothesis
sections.body: Joseph Connell's 1978 paper, drawing on coral reefs and tropical rainforests, proposed that species diversity peaks at intermediate levels of disturbance frequency or intensity rather than at either extreme. The logic: at very low disturbance, competitively dominant species exclude others over time (as in classical competitive exclusion), driving diversity down; at very high disturbance, only the fastest-colonizing, most disturbance-tolerant species persist, again driving diversity down; at intermediate disturbance, competitive exclusion is repeatedly interrupted before it completes, allowing both early-successional and late-successional species to coexist in a shifting mosaic of patches at different recovery stages. Michael Huston's dynamic equilibrium model (1979) reframed this as a balance between disturbance frequency and each community's competitive-exclusion rate — the diversity peak shifts depending on how fast the dominant competitor would otherwise take over, so "intermediate" is relative to the system, not a fixed disturbance level.

sections.heading: The live controversy: should IDH be abandoned?
sections.body: Jeremy Fox's 2013 paper, provocatively titled "The intermediate disturbance hypothesis should be abandoned," argued two things: first, that the verbal logic linking competition theory to a hump-shaped diversity curve does not actually follow from standard competition models when examined formally — a peak at intermediate disturbance is not a robust theoretical prediction. Second, that empirical support is weak: reviews of field and experimental datasets find hump-shaped patterns in only a minority of cases, with monotonic or flat relationships at least as common. David Sheil and David Burslem published a 2013 response directly to Fox defending IDH's continued usefulness, arguing that Fox's theoretical critique targets an oversimplified version of the hypothesis and that mixed empirical support is normal for a broadly-scoped ecological hypothesis rather than grounds for discarding it outright. The dispute remains active, and both sides agree the original verbal hypothesis needs sharper, more mechanistic restatement — they disagree on whether that restatement rescues IDH or replaces it.

lessons.workedExample: A student surveys coral cover across a reef gradient exposed to different storm-wave intensities: sheltered lagoon (low disturbance), mid-reef flat (moderate wave action), and exposed fore-reef (frequent heavy surge). If species richness peaks on the mid-reef flat, that is consistent with IDH — competitive dominants have not excluded others, but conditions are not so harsh that only a few tolerant species survive. A rigorous write-up must also report the alternative: Fox (2013) found many real disturbance gradients are flat or monotonic, so the student should test whether a straight decline or incline fits the data just as well as a hump before claiming IDH support, rather than assuming the hump a priori.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this topic specifically because it is a hypothesis actively disputed among working ecologists, and a student who presents IDH as settled fact reveals they read only the textbook summary. A strong answer states Connell's original logic, then names Fox's 2013 theoretical and empirical objections and the Sheil/Burslem rebuttal, and takes a position on which is more convincing for their own data. A weak answer recites "diversity peaks at intermediate disturbance" without acknowledging it is contested.

questions.prompt: According to Connell's 1978 intermediate disturbance hypothesis, why does diversity decline at very LOW disturbance frequency?

options.text: Competitively dominant species have time to exclude other species
Only fast-colonizing weedy species can survive
Nutrient levels become too low without periodic disturbance
Predators go locally extinct

explanations.a: Correct — with disturbance rare, competitive exclusion has time to run to completion, so the strongest competitors dominate and diversity falls.
explanations.b: That describes the high-disturbance end of the curve, where only tolerant, fast colonizers persist, not the low-disturbance end.
explanations.c: IDH's logic centers on competitive exclusion timing, not on nutrient depletion.
explanations.d: The hypothesis is framed around competition and colonization dynamics among the disturbed species, not predator persistence.

questions.prompt: What is the core claim of Fox's 2013 paper regarding the intermediate disturbance hypothesis?

options.text: Disturbance never affects species diversity in any system
The hump-shaped prediction does not follow rigorously from competition theory, and empirical support is weak
IDH is correct but only applies to coral reefs, not rainforests
Higher disturbance always increases diversity

explanations.a: Fox's critique is specifically about the intermediate-disturbance hump prediction, not a claim that disturbance is irrelevant to diversity generally.
explanations.b: Correct — Fox argued the verbal logic behind IDH does not hold up under formal competition models, and that a review of real datasets finds hump-shaped patterns in only a minority of cases.
explanations.c: Connell's original paper drew on both reefs and rainforests; Fox's critique is not restricted to one system type.
explanations.d: This overstates and misstates Fox's argument, which is about weak/mixed support for a hump shape, not a claim that more disturbance is always better.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher/paper to their contribution to the disturbance-diversity debate.

right.text: Proposed the original intermediate disturbance hypothesis using reef and rainforest data
Reframed diversity peak as a balance between disturbance frequency and competitive-exclusion rate
Argued IDH should be abandoned on theoretical and empirical grounds
Rebutted that critique, defending IDH's continued value

questions.explanation: Connell originated IDH from reef/rainforest observations; Huston's dynamic equilibrium model made the peak's position dependent on each system's competitive-exclusion rate; Fox argued in 2013 the hump does not follow rigorously from competition theory and lacks strong empirical support; Sheil and Burslem published a 2013 response directly to Fox defending IDH's continued usefulness.

questions.prompt: Order these four properties as they would typically be assessed when characterizing a site's disturbance regime, from most basic (how often) to most integrative (long-run average spacing).

items.text: Frequency — how often disturbances occur
Intensity — how much damage each event causes
Extent — spatial area affected
Return interval — average time between events at a point

questions.explanation: The four descriptors of a disturbance regime are frequency, intensity, extent, and return interval; return interval is the most integrative because it summarizes the long-run average spacing implied by frequency at a given location.

lessons.label: Metacommunities: Communities Connected by Dispersal

sections.heading: A community is never fully isolated
sections.body: A metacommunity is a set of local communities linked by the dispersal of multiple interacting species — the pond down the road is not ecologically independent of the pond you are sampling if organisms move between them. Mathew Leibold and colleagues' influential 2004 synthesis organized how ecologists think about this linkage into four paradigms, distinguished mainly by two axes: how strong dispersal is between patches, and how much the patches differ environmentally. Patch dynamics assumes identical patches where species trade off colonization versus competitive ability, so species persist regionally through a shifting mosaic of local extinction and recolonization even though no single patch holds all species long-term. Species sorting assumes patches differ environmentally and dispersal is moderate — just enough to let each species reach the patches that suit it, so local composition tracks local environmental conditions closely, the same logic as niche-based coexistence but applied across a landscape.

sections.heading: Mass effects and the neutral paradigm
sections.body: Mass effects (source-sink dynamics) occurs when dispersal is strong enough to override local environmental filtering: a species can maintain a population in a patch where it would otherwise go locally extinct, because immigrants from a nearby source patch continuously rescue it. This is the classic source-sink pattern — a source population produces a surplus of dispersers, some of which persist in sink habitats only through continued immigration, not because the sink itself supports positive growth. The neutral paradigm, built on Stephen Hubbell's 2001 unified neutral theory, goes further and assumes all species are demographically equivalent per capita — differences in who lives where arise purely from stochastic birth, death, and dispersal, not from any niche difference at all. The four paradigms are not mutually exclusive descriptions of reality; they are idealized end-members that let researchers ask which forces (environment vs. dispersal vs. chance) dominate a given system.

sections.heading: Testing it: variation partitioning
sections.body: The standard empirical test is variation partitioning: community composition data (species abundances across sites) are decomposed via constrained ordination into variance explained by measured environmental variables, variance explained by spatial variables (distance or spatial eigenvectors representing dispersal limitation), a shared fraction, and unexplained residual variance. A pattern dominated by the environmental fraction supports species sorting; a pattern dominated by the pure spatial fraction supports dispersal limitation or mass effects. The well-known criticisms: spatial variables often absorb variance from environmental factors that were never measured (spatial autocorrelation in unmeasured soil or climate variables masquerades as a "dispersal" signal), and total explained variance in real metacommunity datasets is frequently low — commonly under 30% — leaving most compositional variation unattributed to either fraction, which limits how strongly any single paradigm can be declared the winner.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher samples zooplankton across 20 ponds, measuring pH, nutrient levels, and pairwise distances between ponds. Variation partitioning finds 25% of compositional variance explained purely by environment, 10% purely by spatial position, 8% shared, and 57% unexplained. The environment-dominant fractions suggest species sorting is the stronger force here, but the researcher must flag that the spatial fraction could still be hiding an unmeasured environmental gradient (say, canopy cover correlated with pond location) rather than true dispersal limitation, and that more than half the variance remains unaccounted for by either predictor set.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe metacommunity framing because it forces a student to think beyond a single site and ask what role connectivity plays — a question most single-site projects never address. A strong answer identifies which of the four paradigms best fits their system and why (dispersal strength, environmental heterogeneity), and if they ran variation partitioning, names the confound of spatial variables absorbing unmeasured environmental variation. A weak answer treats each sampled site as ecologically sealed off from its neighbors.

questions.prompt: Match each metacommunity paradigm from Leibold et al. (2004) to its defining assumption.

right.text: Identical patches; species persist regionally via colonization-competition trade-offs
Patches differ environmentally; moderate dispersal lets composition track local conditions
Strong dispersal rescues populations in patches where they could not persist alone (source-sink)
Species are demographically equivalent; composition arises from stochastic birth, death, dispersal

questions.explanation: Patch dynamics assumes identical patches with colonization-competition trade-offs; species sorting assumes environmental heterogeneity with dispersal just strong enough to sort species into suitable patches; mass effects involves strong dispersal producing source-sink rescue; the neutral paradigm, following Hubbell (2001), assumes no per-capita fitness differences among species.

questions.prompt: In a sink population maintained by mass effects, what keeps the population from going locally extinct?

options.text: Local birth rates exceed local death rates
Continued immigration from a nearby source population
The species evolves rapid local adaptation
Competitors are entirely absent from the sink

explanations.a: By definition a sink has negative local growth on its own; if births exceeded deaths locally it would not be a sink.
explanations.b: Correct — sink populations persist only because immigrants from a source patch continually replace individuals lost to negative local growth.
explanations.c: Mass effects describes an ecological/demographic process, not local evolutionary adaptation.
explanations.d: Competitor absence is not part of the source-sink definition; sinks can have competitors present.

questions.prompt: A criticism commonly raised against variation partitioning as a test of metacommunity structure is that:

options.text: It can only be applied to fewer than five sites
Spatial variables can absorb variance from unmeasured environmental factors, and explained variance is often low
It always shows dispersal limitation regardless of the data
It cannot be computed for zooplankton or other aquatic organisms

explanations.a: Variation partitioning is typically applied to multi-site datasets and has no such small-sample restriction as its defining flaw.
explanations.b: Correct — spatially structured but unmeasured environmental variables can inflate the "pure spatial" fraction, and real datasets frequently leave the majority of compositional variance unexplained by either fraction.
explanations.c: The method's result depends on the data; it does not have a built-in bias toward any one paradigm.
explanations.d: The method is taxon-general and has been applied widely to aquatic communities including zooplankton.

questions.prompt: Order these four metacommunity paradigms from weakest to strongest role of dispersal relative to local environmental filtering, as framed by Leibold et al. (2004).

items.text: Species sorting (moderate dispersal, strong environmental filtering)
Patch dynamics (dispersal enables regional persistence via trade-offs)
Mass effects (strong dispersal overrides local filtering)
Neutral (dispersal and chance dominate; no environmental filtering)

questions.explanation: Species sorting keeps environmental filtering dominant with just enough dispersal to sort species appropriately; patch dynamics relies more on dispersal-driven colonization-competition trade-offs; mass effects has dispersal strong enough to sustain sink populations against local filtering; the neutral paradigm removes environmental filtering from the picture entirely, leaving dispersal and demographic stochasticity as the only drivers.

lessons.label: Resilience, Regime Shifts, and Hysteresis

sections.heading: Two meanings of resilience
sections.body: C.S. Holling's 1973 paper split "resilience" into two distinct properties that are easy to conflate. Engineering resilience is how fast a system returns to its prior state after a small perturbation — the speed of recovery near a stable point, like a ball rolling back to the bottom of a bowl after a light tap. Ecological resilience is instead the size of the disturbance a system can absorb before it flips into a fundamentally different, alternative stable state — the width of the bowl, not the speed of the roll back. A system can have fast engineering resilience (it snaps back quickly from small shocks) while having low ecological resilience (a moderately larger shock still tips it into collapse). Holling argued ecological resilience, not recovery speed, is what actually matters for long-term persistence under real-world variability and shocks.

sections.heading: Shallow lakes: a textbook regime shift with hysteresis
sections.body: Marten Scheffer's shallow-lake model, developed through the 1990s, is the canonical illustration. Under low nutrient loading, lakes sit in a clear-water state dominated by submerged aquatic plants that stabilize sediment and outcompete algae. As nutrient loading rises, the lake can abruptly flip to a turbid, algae-dominated state once a threshold is crossed — plants die from light limitation, sediment resuspends, and algae dominate. The critical twist is hysteresis: simply reducing nutrients back below the original tipping threshold does NOT restore the clear state, because the turbid state has its own separate stability created by different feedbacks (resuspended sediment blocking light, fish community shifts favoring algae-grazers' predators). Nutrients typically must be cut far below the original forward threshold — sometimes requiring active intervention like fish removal (biomanipulation) — before the lake flips back to clear water. The system's history, not just its current state, determines which community persists.

sections.heading: Caribbean reefs and early-warning signals
sections.body: A field-scale regime shift occurred on Caribbean coral reefs after 1983, when a disease epidemic killed roughly 90–95% of the long-spined sea urchin Diadema antillarum across the region — removing the dominant grazer that had kept fast-growing macroalgae in check. Combined with prior overfishing of herbivorous fish, many reefs flipped from coral-dominated to macroalgae-dominated states that have persisted for decades in many locations, another documented case of hysteresis where coral cover has not simply rebounded as urchin populations partially recovered. This motivated the search for early-warning indicators that a system is approaching a tipping point before it flips: critical slowing down predicts that as a system nears a threshold, its recovery rate from small perturbations slows, which should show up statistically as rising variance and rising autocorrelation in monitored time series (e.g., chlorophyll or algae cover measurements). The idea is theoretically well-supported and confirmed in controlled lab and mesocosm systems, but there is active, unresolved dispute about whether these signals are reliably detectable in noisy, irregularly sampled real-world field data before a shift actually happens, rather than only being visible in hindsight.

lessons.workedExample: A monitoring program tracks a shallow lake's chlorophyll-a concentration monthly for 15 years as agricultural nutrient runoff slowly rises. In the final three years before the lake visibly turns turbid, the variance of monthly chlorophyll readings around the trend roughly triples, and month-to-month autocorrelation rises from about 0.3 to about 0.7 — both consistent with critical slowing down. A rigorous report would flag that these are proposed early-warning signals with real controversy attached: with only one lake and irregular sampling gaps in years 6 and 11, the signal could partly reflect sampling artifacts rather than a genuine approach to a tipping point, and cross-system replication would be needed to claim a general early-warning method.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe hysteresis and resilience because they cut against the intuitive assumption that removing a stressor simply reverses its effect. A strong answer explains WHY the reverse threshold differs from the forward threshold — a distinct feedback loop stabilizes the new state — rather than just asserting that recovery is "harder." On early-warning signals, a strong answer also volunteers that the field-data reliability of critical slowing down is disputed, not settled; a weak answer treats rising variance as a foolproof alarm.

questions.prompt: Holling's 1973 distinction between engineering resilience and ecological resilience is best summarized as:

options.text: Engineering resilience is speed of return to a state; ecological resilience is the size of disturbance a system can absorb before flipping states
Engineering resilience applies only to human-built structures; ecological resilience applies only to living systems
The two terms are synonyms Holling used interchangeably
Ecological resilience measures species richness; engineering resilience measures biomass

explanations.a: Correct — engineering resilience is about recovery rate near a stable point, while ecological resilience is about the magnitude of disturbance tolerable before the system shifts to an alternative stable state.
explanations.b: Both terms as Holling defined them apply to ecological systems; "engineering" describes the type of resilience (recovery speed), not the domain of application.
explanations.c: Holling's whole point was that conflating the two terms leads to poor management decisions; he deliberately distinguished them.
explanations.d: Neither term is defined in terms of richness or biomass directly; both concern system stability dynamics.

questions.prompt: In Scheffer's shallow-lake model, why does reducing nutrient loading back below the original tipping threshold often fail to restore the clear-water state?

options.text: Aquatic plants are extinct globally and cannot recolonize
The turbid state is stabilized by its own separate feedbacks, requiring nutrients to drop further (hysteresis) before flipping back
Nutrient reduction has no effect on algae under any circumstances
Lakes only flip states once and can never return to a prior state under any conditions

explanations.a: Plants are not globally extinct; the barrier to recolonization is the altered light and sediment environment, not species loss at a global scale.
explanations.b: Correct — the turbid state's feedbacks (resuspended sediment, altered fish communities) create a separate zone of stability, so the backward threshold sits below the forward one; this gap is hysteresis.
explanations.c: Nutrient reduction does matter — it is necessary, just often not sufficient alone at the original threshold level.
explanations.d: Reversal is possible with sufficiently low nutrients or active intervention like biomanipulation; it is difficult, not permanently impossible.

questions.prompt: What event around 1983 contributed to the Caribbean's coral-to-macroalgae regime shift?

options.text: A hurricane destroyed all reef structure directly
A disease epidemic killed roughly 90-95% of the grazing sea urchin Diadema antillarum
Ocean acidification dissolved coral skeletons within a single year
A new predator was introduced that ate all herbivorous fish

explanations.a: The 1983 event was a disease die-off, not a physical storm-damage event, though storms have separately affected Caribbean reefs.
explanations.b: Correct — the Diadema antillarum die-off removed the dominant algae-grazer, and combined with existing overfishing of herbivorous fish, allowed macroalgae to overtake many reefs.
explanations.c: Acidification is a slower, chronic global stressor, not the specific 1983 trigger event.
explanations.d: The mechanism was a grazer die-off from disease, not a new predator reducing herbivorous fish.

questions.prompt: Order the reasoning steps behind using critical slowing down as an early-warning indicator of an approaching regime shift.

items.text: As a system nears a tipping point, its recovery rate from small perturbations slows
Slower recovery causes fluctuations to persist longer, raising variance and autocorrelation in monitored data
Rising variance/autocorrelation is proposed as a statistical signal detectable before the actual shift
Field application is disputed because real data are noisy and irregularly sampled

questions.explanation: The theoretical chain runs: slowing recovery near a threshold produces longer-persisting fluctuations, which shows up as rising variance and autocorrelation, proposed as an early-warning signal — but whether this signal is reliably detectable in real, noisy field time series remains actively disputed.

lessons.label: Communities Under Directional Change

sections.heading: Reorganization, not synchronized shift
sections.body: Under a directional pressure like climate warming, a community does not move as an intact block — each species tracks the cues and constraints relevant to it, so the community reshuffles into new combinations. This individualistic response traces back to Henry Gleason's 1926 argument that plant communities are not superorganisms but loose associations of species independently responding to environment, and it explains why paleoecologists studying pollen records (notably Williams and Jackson's 2007 synthesis) keep finding no-analog communities in the past — species combinations with no equivalent existing anywhere on the modern landscape, because each species' range shifted at its own pace and in its own direction as ice-age climate changed. The same logic applies going forward: as species shift ranges individualistically under current warming, novel combinations with no modern analog are expected to keep forming rather than today's communities simply relocating intact.

sections.heading: Phenological mismatch: pied flycatchers arriving too late
sections.body: Christiaan Both and Marcel Visser's research on Dutch pied flycatchers (Ficedula hypoleuca) is the classic case of a timing-driven mismatch. Their 2001 Nature paper showed flycatchers, which winter in Africa and time spring arrival using photoperiod and conditions along the migration route, could not advance their arrival date as fast as local caterpillar food peaks were shifting earlier under warming — caterpillar peak date is set by local temperature and advanced faster than the birds' arrival. A 2006 follow-up across multiple European populations linked this mismatch directly to population trend: sites where the gap between arrival and the caterpillar peak had widened the most showed the steepest population declines, because chicks hatched too late relative to peak food availability suffered lower survival. The mechanism matters for judging any phenology claim: a shifting date alone is not evidence of harm — it is the growing GAP between the interacting species' shifted dates that predicts the demographic cost.

sections.heading: Thermophilization and why richness counts can mislead
sections.body: Thermophilization describes a community's average thermal affinity rising over time as warm-adapted species become relatively more abundant and cold-adapted species relatively less abundant — even before any local extinction occurs. Ecologists quantify this with the community temperature index (CTI), the abundance-weighted mean of each species' thermal preference (typically its range-wide mean temperature), tracked in repeated surveys; rising CTI in European breeding-bird and forest-plant communities has been documented over recent decades. This is exactly why counting species lost understates reorganization: a site can retain its full species list and even its species richness number while its relative abundances quietly shift toward warm-adapted species and away from cold-adapted ones — richness is blind to that turnover in composition, so a stable species count can mask a community that has already substantially reorganized.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher resurveys a montane bird community after 25 years and finds the same 30 species present both times — richness unchanged, so a naive read says "no change." But computing the community temperature index from each survey's abundance data shows CTI rose by roughly 0.8°C, meaning warm-adapted species like blackcaps became proportionally more common while cold-adapted species like willow warblers became proportionally rarer, without either going locally extinct. Reporting only the species list would miss the reorganization entirely; reporting CTI reveals a community actively tracking warming through internal abundance shifts, the same mechanism behind Bertrand et al.'s documented thermophilization in French forest plant communities.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this topic because "no species were lost, so nothing changed" is a common and specifically wrong conclusion that a strong project should preempt. A strong answer distinguishes richness (a count) from composition (relative abundances) and can explain a mechanism — phenological mismatch, individualistic range shifts, or thermophilization — that reorganizes a community while its species list stays flat. A weak answer treats an unchanged species count as proof of ecological stability.

questions.prompt: In Both and Visser's pied flycatcher research, what specifically predicted population decline across European sites?

options.text: How early the birds arrived in absolute terms
The size of the gap between arrival date and the local caterpillar food peak
Total African wintering-ground rainfall
The number of eggs laid per clutch

explanations.a: Absolute arrival date alone was not the predictor; sites could have similarly early arrival but differ in decline depending on how the caterpillar peak had shifted.
explanations.b: Correct — the 2006 multi-population follow-up found that sites with the widest mismatch between flycatcher arrival and the local caterpillar peak showed the steepest population declines, because late-hatched chicks missed peak food availability.
explanations.c: Wintering-ground conditions affect survival and departure timing broadly, but the specific predictor identified for population decline was the mismatch gap, not rainfall totals.
explanations.d: Clutch size is a life-history trait, not the variable shown to predict decline across the mismatch study.

questions.prompt: Why do paleoecologists find "no-analog communities" in pollen records from past climate transitions?

options.text: Because species went extinct and left gaps in the fossil record
Because each species shifted its range individualistically, producing combinations with no modern equivalent
Because pollen cannot be identified to species level
Because communities always shift as intact, unchanged blocks

explanations.a: No-analog communities are about novel co-occurrence, not primarily about extinction gaps in the record.
explanations.b: Correct — following Gleason's individualistic concept, species respond to changing climate independently and at different rates, so past assemblages sometimes combined species that never co-occur in any modern community.
explanations.c: Pollen identification limits exist but are not the reason no-analog combinations are found; the pattern reflects genuine novel co-occurrence.
explanations.d: The individualistic response is the opposite of intact-block movement — that assumption is exactly what no-analog evidence argues against.

questions.prompt: The community temperature index (CTI) is best described as:

options.text: The number of thermally-tolerant species present at a site
The abundance-weighted average thermal preference of the species in a community
The maximum recorded temperature at a survey site
A count of species that have gone locally extinct due to heat

explanations.a: CTI is not a species count of any kind; it is a weighted average across the whole community's composition.
explanations.b: Correct — CTI weights each species' typical thermal preference by its relative abundance in the community, so it rises (thermophilization) as warm-adapted species become proportionally more common, even without local extinction.
explanations.c: CTI is a biological composition metric derived from survey data, not a direct climate/temperature measurement.
explanations.d: CTI can rise even with zero local extinctions, purely from abundance shifts among species that are all still present.

questions.prompt: Order the logical steps explaining why a community's species richness can stay flat while it substantially reorganizes under warming.

items.text: Species respond individualistically to warming rather than as an intact unit
Warm-adapted species become proportionally more abundant; cold-adapted species become proportionally less abundant
No species is locally extirpated, so the raw species count (richness) is unchanged
Community temperature index rises, revealing reorganization that a richness count alone would miss

questions.explanation: Because species shift individualistically, relative abundances reshuffle toward warm-adapted species before any local extinction occurs; richness stays flat since the same species list remains present, but the abundance-weighted CTI rises, exposing compositional reorganization that a simple species count cannot detect.

units.label: Community Ecology in Practice: Case Studies and Projects

lessons.label: Designing a Community-Ecology Science-Fair Study

sections.heading: Pick a gradient or a contrast, not a vague comparison
sections.body: Real community-ecology projects are built on a defined axis, not on "comparing two random places." Three axes recur because they reliably produce measurable compositional turnover: urban-to-rural gradients (McKinney's 2002 review found urbanization consistently filters out habitat specialists and favors a small set of generalists), canopy-gap versus closed-forest contrasts (Runkle's 1981 work on gap-phase dynamics showed gap size predicts which tree and herb species can establish), and upstream-downstream gradients in streams, where the River Continuum Concept (Vannote et al. 1980) predicts a predictable shift in invertebrate feeding groups as channel width and organic-matter source change. Choosing one of these gives you a testable prediction before you collect a single sample.

sections.heading: Replicate at the level you want to conclude about
sections.body: The single most common student error is pseudoreplication: treating five quadrats inside one urban park as five independent "urban" data points. Hurlbert's 1984 paper on pseudoreplication in field ecology is explicit that if your claim is about urban versus rural sites, your unit of replication is the site, and subsamples within a site only describe within-site variance, not between-condition variance. A design with one urban park and one rural field, however many quadrats each, has an effective sample size of n=1 per condition — no statistical test can rescue that.

sections.heading: How many independent sites do you actually need?
sections.body: For a multivariate compositional test like PERMANOVA, power depends less on total species richness and more on between-site variability (dispersion) within each group. As a rule of thumb, fewer than four replicate sites per condition gives a permutation test almost no power to detect anything but an enormous effect; six to ten sites per group is a realistic student-project target, and pilot data (even two quick sites) can reveal whether your groups are so noisy that more replication is needed before the design is worth running. Once you know how many sites you need, choose their locations by interspersing them across the study area rather than clustering all "urban" sites in one part of town and all "rural" sites in another. Clustered sites confound your gradient variable with unmeasured spatial covariates — soil type, elevation, or local weather that just happens to track geography — so an apparent compositional difference could reflect proximity rather than the gradient itself. Interspersed replicates, picked from a map before visiting, let you rule that out.

sections.heading: Permits, ethics, and a paper trail a judge can check
sections.body: Field collection on public land usually needs a scientific-collecting permit; know before you sample whether your target site requires one. Keep GPS coordinates, dated photo-vouchers, and, for anything preserved, a specimen label with site, date, and collector — this is what lets a judge or a future researcher verify your identifications. Collect the minimum needed for identification and never over-harvest a small or visibly rare population.

lessons.workedExample: A student wants to test whether leaf-litter ant assemblages differ along an urbanization gradient in their city. They select nine sites spanning downtown plazas, suburban parks, and rural forest edges (three replicate sites per zone, chosen from a map before visiting so site choice isn't biased by which ants they happen to see). At each site they run three pitfall traps for 48 hours, but average those three traps into one site-level composition vector before analysis — so their real sample size for the compositional test is nine sites, not twenty-seven traps. They log GPS coordinates and photograph each trap location for their permit records.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "how many independent sites did you have?" because it is the fastest way to catch pseudoreplication, and a project that pooled quadrats or traps within one location as if they were independent evidence of a between-condition effect has an inflated, invalid p-value no matter how sophisticated its statistics look. A strong answer names the actual number of independent sites per condition and explains why subsamples were averaged up to the site level first. A weak answer quotes a large total sample size ("I had 60 data points") without being able to say how many independent locations that number came from.

questions.prompt: A student compares plant diversity in one urban lot and one rural field, taking ten quadrats in each. What is their effective sample size for testing an urban-versus-rural effect?

options.text: n = 20, since there are twenty quadrats total
n = 10 per group, one per quadrat
n = 1 per group, since there is only one independent site per condition
n = 2, one for each condition, regardless of how many quadrats

explanations.a: Twenty quadrats are not twenty independent replicates of the urban-versus-rural contrast; they are twenty subsamples of just two locations.
explanations.b: Ten quadrats within one site describe within-site variation, not independent evidence for the urban-versus-rural comparison itself.
explanations.c: Correct — with one urban site and one rural site, the unit of replication for the between-condition claim is the site, giving n=1 per group; this is Hurlbert's classic pseudoreplication problem.
explanations.d: n=2 total ignores that the claim is about urban versus rural as groups, and each group still only has one independent site behind it.

questions.prompt: Match each classic gradient design to the study or concept that grounds it.

right.text: McKinney 2002 review: urbanization filters out specialists, favors generalists
Runkle 1981: gap size predicts which species establish
Vannote et al. 1980 River Continuum Concept

questions.explanation: McKinney's urbanization synthesis, Runkle's gap-phase forest dynamics, and Vannote's River Continuum Concept are the named bases for these three canonical gradient designs.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of setting up a defensible community-ecology field design, from first to last.

items.text: Define the gradient or contrast and the prediction it implies
Choose enough independent replicate sites per condition
Secure any needed collecting permit and plan voucher records
Collect subsamples at each site and average them to one site-level value
Run the compositional analysis across sites

questions.explanation: The prediction and design come first, then adequate independent replication, then legal/ethical clearance, then within-site data collection reduced to site-level values, and only then the analysis.

questions.prompt: Why does PERMANOVA power depend more on between-site dispersion than on raw species richness?

options.text: Because richness has no effect on any statistical test
Because a permutation test's ability to detect a group difference is limited by how much sites within a group already vary from each other
Because PERMANOVA only works with presence-absence data
Because dispersion is fixed by the number of species observed

explanations.a: Richness can matter for other measures, but the question is specifically about what limits power in a permutation-based compositional test.
explanations.b: Correct — if sites within a group are highly variable, a real between-group difference is harder to distinguish from noise, so high within-group dispersion is what actually erodes power, independent of total richness.
explanations.c: PERMANOVA works on any dissimilarity matrix, including abundance-based ones like Bray-Curtis, not just presence-absence.
explanations.d: Dispersion is a property of how sites vary from each other, not a fixed consequence of species counts.

lessons.label: Case Study: The Microbiome as a Community

sections.heading: Colonization order and priority effects in the infant gut
sections.body: The infant gut is a real-time natural experiment in community assembly. Dominguez-Bello et al. (2010) showed that delivery mode sets the founding community: vaginally-born infants are first colonized by Lactobacillus-dominated taxa resembling the mother's vaginal flora, while C-section infants are first colonized by skin-associated taxa like Staphylococcus. La Rosa et al. (2014), tracking preterm infants longitudinally, found gut assembly follows a fairly reproducible successional sequence keyed to postmenstrual age rather than random arrival order — but early differences from delivery mode can still leave a detectable signature months later, a textbook priority effect: who arrives first constrains who can establish afterward.

sections.heading: Dispersal versus selection above and below ground
sections.body: Plant-associated microbiomes split the same assembly forces differently. Leaf-surface (phyllosphere) communities are shaped heavily by dispersal — windblown and rain-splashed cells arriving from the surrounding air and neighboring plants — so nearby leaves often converge in composition regardless of host genotype. Root (rhizosphere) communities are shaped more by selection: root exudates recruit a subset of the surrounding soil pool based on chemistry, so genetically different plant lines in identical soil can host measurably different root microbiomes. Nemergut et al. (2013) formalized this by mapping microbial assembly onto the same four processes (selection, dispersal, drift, diversification) that Vellend used for macroscopic communities.

sections.heading: From sequences to a site-by-taxon matrix, and its trap
sections.body: 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing (or shotgun metagenomics for finer resolution) turns a sample into read counts per taxon, assembled into the same site-by-taxon matrix used for any community dataset. A first trap sits upstream of the analysis, in the wet lab: which primer pair amplifies which stretch of the 16S gene (commonly a single variable region like V4, or a wider span like V3-V4) is a methodological choice, not a neutral default, because different primer sets bind unevenly to different taxa and can systematically over- or under-detect entire phyla — so two studies using different primers on the same community can report different composition even with identical samples. A second trap is that sequencing yields relative, not absolute, abundances: reads per sample are compositional, forced to sum to a fixed total, so if one taxon blooms, every other taxon's proportion must fall even if its true abundance didn't change (Aitchison 1982's compositional-data problem). Ecologists disagree on rarefying (subsampling every sample to equal depth) versus not — McMurdie and Holmes (2014) argued rarefying discards real data and called it "inadmissible," while others defend it as the simplest fix for uneven sequencing depth. "Dysbiosis," a term for a supposedly disrupted microbiome, remains contested because no consensus threshold separates a disrupted community from ordinary healthy variation (Olesen and Alm 2016).

lessons.workedExample: A student sequences gut microbiomes from ten C-section and ten vaginally-delivered infant stool samples at one month. Raw 16S counts show C-section infants with a higher relative proportion of Staphylococcus. Before concluding anything, they check sequencing depth per sample — one C-section sample has half the reads of the others — so they either rarefy all samples to the lowest depth or use a compositional (CLR) transform rather than comparing raw proportions directly. They also resist calling the C-section profile "dysbiotic," since it falls within the range reported for healthy infants at that age in the literature, and instead report it descriptively as a compositional difference tied to delivery mode.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe microbiome projects on the compositionality trap because it is the easiest way to produce a spurious result: a taxon can appear to "decrease" in relative abundance purely because another taxon bloomed, with no real change in its own population. A strong answer explains that percentages or relative reads are compositional and describes a specific fix (rarefaction, CLR transform, or reporting absolute qPCR-calibrated counts) rather than just reporting raw percentages. A weak answer treats a shift in relative abundance as proof a taxon's actual abundance changed, or throws around "dysbiosis" as if it were a defined, measurable state rather than a contested label.

questions.prompt: Why are 16S sequencing read counts described as "compositional" data?

options.text: Because they are always normally distributed
Because the proportions of taxa in a sample are constrained to sum to a fixed total, so one taxon rising forces others' proportions down
Because they can only be collected from soil, not from animals
Because they measure DNA quality rather than taxon identity

explanations.a: Read-count distributions are typically skewed, not normal; that is unrelated to why they're called compositional.
explanations.b: Correct — because total reads per sample are fixed, taxon proportions are relative to each other, so a real increase in one taxon mechanically deflates the reported proportions of others even if their true abundance didn't change.
explanations.c: Compositionality applies to any relative-abundance sequencing dataset, plant, animal, or soil.
explanations.d: Read counts reflect relative taxon abundance in the sample, not a direct measure of DNA quality.

questions.prompt: Match each microbiome finding or debate to its source.

left.text: Delivery mode sets the founding gut community
Mapped microbial assembly onto selection, dispersal, drift, diversification

right.text: Dominguez-Bello et al. 2010
McMurdie and Holmes 2014
Nemergut et al. 2013

questions.explanation: Dominguez-Bello linked delivery mode to founding gut taxa, McMurdie and Holmes challenged rarefaction, and Nemergut et al. applied the four community-assembly processes to microbes.

questions.prompt: Why is "dysbiosis" considered a contested term among microbiome researchers?

options.text: Because no consensus threshold distinguishes a disrupted community from normal healthy variation
Because it refers only to viral, not bacterial, communities
Because it was disproven by shotgun metagenomics
Because it can only be diagnosed with a blood test

explanations.a: Correct — Olesen and Alm (2016) and others note the term is used loosely across studies without an agreed quantitative definition, so what counts as "dysbiotic" varies by paper.
explanations.b: Dysbiosis is discussed broadly across bacterial, fungal, and viral community contexts, not restricted to viruses.
explanations.c: Shotgun metagenomics is a sequencing method, not evidence against the concept; the criticism is about definitional looseness, not disproof.
explanations.d: Dysbiosis claims are typically based on sequencing-derived community composition, not blood tests.

questions.prompt: Root (rhizosphere) microbiomes tend to be shaped more strongly by which assembly process than leaf-surface (phyllosphere) microbiomes are?

options.text: Selection, via root exudate chemistry recruiting specific taxa
Random genetic drift alone
Speciation occurring within the sample
Wind-driven dispersal from distant sites

explanations.a: Correct — root exudates chemically filter which soil taxa can establish, giving genetically distinct plants measurably different root microbiomes even in identical soil, a selection-dominated pattern.
explanations.b: Drift plays a role in any community but isn't the process distinguishing rhizosphere from phyllosphere assembly in this contrast.
explanations.c: Speciation operates on much longer timescales and isn't the relevant assembly force in a single growing season.
explanations.d: Dispersal is the dominant force for phyllosphere (leaf-surface) communities, the opposite of what the question asks about roots.

lessons.label: Case Study: Invasion and Biotic Resistance

sections.heading: Elton's hypothesis: diverse communities resist invasion
sections.body: In his 1958 book The Ecology of Invasions by Animals and Plants, Charles Elton proposed that species-rich communities are harder to invade than species-poor ones, because a full set of competitors and predators already occupies the available niche space, leaving few openings for a newcomer. This biotic-resistance hypothesis became a foundational, testable prediction: more diversity should mean fewer successful invasions. Simberloff and Von Holle (1999) later named a contrasting mechanism, invasional meltdown, where an already-established invader makes a community easier, not harder, for further invaders to enter — for example an invasive plant that recruits an invasive pollinator or soil mutualist, or an invasive predator that removes a native check on a second invader. The two ideas aren't mutually exclusive: a community can resist invasion up to a point and then, once one invader gains a foothold, start facilitating the next.

sections.heading: The invasion paradox: two scales, two opposite answers
sections.body: Small, controlled experiments have generally supported Elton. In Tilman-style plots and related manipulations (e.g., Knops et al. 1999, Naeem et al. 2000), plots seeded with more resident plant species consistently received fewer successful invaders, matching biotic resistance. But large-scale observational surveys across landscapes (Stohlgren et al. 1999 among others) found the opposite: regions and sites with higher native plant diversity also tended to have more invasive species, a positive diversity-invasibility relationship. This contradiction, seemingly the same question yielding opposite answers depending on scale, became known as the invasion paradox.

sections.heading: Fridley et al. 2007: resolving it through scale-dependent covariates
sections.body: Fridley, Stachowicz, and colleagues (Ecology, 2007) reconciled the paradox by pointing to extrinsic covariation: at small experimental scales, diversity itself directly limits open niche space (biotic resistance dominates), but at large landscape scales, both native diversity and invader success are independently driven by the same underlying factors — resource availability, disturbance regime, propagule pressure, and climate favorability. A resource-rich, disturbed, well-connected site tends to support both more native species and more invaders simultaneously, producing a positive correlation that has nothing to do with diversity itself causing invasibility.

sections.heading: Real invaders, community-level consequences
sections.body: Concrete cases show invasion reshapes whole communities, not just species lists. The zebra mussel (Dreissena polymorpha), introduced to the Great Lakes around 1988 via ballast water, filters phytoplankton so efficiently it restructured plankton and benthic communities across the basin.
