questions.explanation: A comparative test starts with a hypothesis, then data collection including a phylogeny, then converts raw species values into phylogenetically independent contrasts, and only then tests for a statistically valid correlation.

lessons.label: Scope: What Behavioral Ecology Is and Is Not

sections.heading: Four fields that all study "aggression" and mean different things
sections.body: Behavioral ecology shares its subject matter with several neighboring fields, and confusing them is a fast way to misjudge or misdesign a project. Comparative psychology studies learning and cognition in lab-controlled settings — a rat pressing a lever in a Skinner box to earn food is a comparative-psychology aggression proxy if the question is about frustration-induced responding; the focus is proximate (mechanism, learning rules) and the setting is deliberately artificial to isolate variables. Evolutionary psychology asks how the human mind's cognitive architecture was shaped by ancestral selection pressures, often inferring an adaptation (e.g., a proposed evolved jealousy response tied to paternity uncertainty) from present-day human behavior rather than measuring fitness directly, and its subject is specifically Homo sapiens. Animal welfare science studies aggression as a marker of stress or compromised well-being — a hen pecking cage-mates under crowding is scored for what it reveals about the birds' affective state and living conditions, not what it reveals about adaptive value. Behavioral ecology alone asks the survival-value question about aggression in a naturalistic context: does winning fights predict this individual's actual territory quality, mating access, or offspring survival, measured in or close to the animal's real environment.

sections.heading: What a legitimate behavioral-ecology fair project looks like
sections.body: A project sits in this field's lane when it studies wild or semi-naturalistic organisms (a schoolyard bird population, a local ant colony, even a well-designed seminatural enclosure) rather than a fully artificial lab apparatus; frames its question in terms of fitness and environment (does this behavior correlate with a resource, a mate, survival, or a measurable proxy for one of those) rather than pure mechanism or learning; and is observation-first, building an ethogram and collecting baseline behavioral data before imposing any manipulation, so the study captures behavior as it actually happens rather than behavior forced into an artificial task.

sections.heading: A constraint that shapes what's feasible: vertebrate rules
sections.body: Science fairs under ISEF (International Science and Engineering Fair) rules impose real limits on vertebrate behavioral work: projects involving vertebrate animals require prior Scientific Review Committee approval, generally prohibit pain, distress, or invasive procedures, and require that any manipulation minimize stress — rules that push most feasible student behavioral-ecology projects toward observational designs on wild or captive-but-unmanipulated vertebrates, or toward invertebrates (ants, isopods, Drosophila) where welfare rules are lighter and manipulative experiments are more accessible.

lessons.workedExample: Four researchers each watch the same species — a captive cichlid fish flaring its gill covers at a mirror image. A comparative psychologist asks whether the fish habituates to the reflection over repeated trials (a learning-mechanism question). An evolutionary psychologist has no natural application here, since the field's subject is human cognition specifically. A welfare scientist asks whether chronic mirror-induced aggression display raises cortisol and indicates the tank setup is stressing the fish. A behavioral ecologist asks whether, in the wild population this species comes from, males that flare and win more real territorial contests hold better spawning sites and sire more offspring — the only one of the four questions that connects the display to fitness in something like the animal's natural context.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask "what field is this, really?" because students often borrow methods across these fields without noticing the mismatch — running a psychology-style operant task but calling the conclusion an adaptive/evolutionary claim. A weak answer can't say what makes their project behavioral ecology specifically, versus psychology or welfare science. A strong answer explicitly frames the question around fitness and a naturalistic or semi-naturalistic setting ("I'm testing whether foraging success predicts something like survival or condition, in a population close to its natural context") and, if vertebrates were involved, can describe what oversight or approval the project needed before data collection began.

questions.prompt: Match each research question about "aggression" to the field that would ask it.

left.text: Does winning more territorial fights predict a male's mating success and offspring survival in the wild?
Does repeated exposure to a mirror image cause a fish's aggressive display to habituate?
Does chronic aggressive interaction under crowding raise stress hormones and indicate poor housing conditions?
Did an evolved jealousy response shaped by ancestral mating competition explain a human behavior pattern?

right.text: Behavioral ecology
Comparative psychology
Animal welfare science
Evolutionary psychology

questions.explanation: Behavioral ecology asks about naturalistic fitness consequences; comparative psychology asks about learning mechanisms; welfare science asks about affective/stress state; evolutionary psychology asks about human mind adaptations.

questions.prompt: Which feature most reliably distinguishes a behavioral-ecology project from a comparative-psychology project studying the same species?

options.text: Behavioral ecology never uses any form of controlled observation
Behavioral ecology frames the question around fitness/environment in a naturalistic context, rather than mechanism/learning in a controlled lab task
Comparative psychology only studies invertebrates
Behavioral ecology only studies mammals

explanations.a: Behavioral ecology uses systematic, often carefully controlled observation (e.g., ethograms); the distinction is not about rigor but about question type and setting.
explanations.b: Correct — the defining split is fitness-and-naturalistic-context (behavioral ecology) versus mechanism-and-controlled-task (comparative psychology).
explanations.c: Comparative psychology studies a wide range of taxa, including many vertebrates (rats, pigeons, primates); this option is factually wrong.
explanations.d: Behavioral ecology studies organisms across the tree of life, not only mammals; this option is factually wrong.

questions.prompt: Under ISEF-style science fair rules, a student proposing to induce mild stress in a vertebrate species (e.g., a captive fish) to study behavioral responses would need to do what before starting?

options.text: Nothing extra — vertebrate behavioral manipulations have no special review requirement
Obtain prior Scientific Review Committee approval, and design the study to avoid pain, distress, and invasive procedures
Switch the study to a human subject instead, which has fewer restrictions
Only vertebrate studies performed outdoors require any approval

explanations.a: Vertebrate work under ISEF rules specifically requires prior review; this option is incorrect.
explanations.b: Correct — ISEF rules require Scientific Review Committee approval for vertebrate animal projects and generally prohibit pain, distress, or invasive procedures.
explanations.c: Human-subject research carries its own separate, generally stricter review requirements (informed consent, IRB-equivalent processes), not fewer restrictions.
explanations.d: The approval requirement applies to vertebrate work regardless of indoor/outdoor setting; location is not the deciding factor.

questions.prompt: A student wants a strong behavioral-ecology fair project. Which design best fits the field's scope, given typical ISEF constraints on vertebrates?

options.text: An operant lever-press task on a lab mouse measuring learning speed
An observation-first ethogram study of foraging behavior in a wild ant colony, related to colony food-return rate
A survey asking human participants to self-report jealousy in relationships
A stress-hormone assay on a crowded vertebrate population with no fitness measure attached

explanations.a: This is a comparative-psychology design (learning mechanism, controlled lab task), not a behavioral-ecology one.
explanations.b: Correct — a naturalistic organism, an observation-first ethogram, and a link to a fitness-relevant outcome (food return, a colony-level proxy for fitness) fits squarely within behavioral ecology's scope, and invertebrates avoid the heavier vertebrate review burden.
explanations.c: This is an evolutionary-psychology-style design focused on human self-report, not naturalistic animal fitness data.
explanations.d: This is closer to an animal-welfare-science design (stress state) and also raises the vertebrate review requirements without even including a fitness measure.

lessons.label: Optimal Diet: The Prey-Choice Model

sections.heading: Ranking prey by profitability, not abundance
sections.body: The contingency (prey-choice) model, formalized by Robert MacArthur and Eric Pianka in 1966 and later refined by Eric Charnov, treats a forager as an economic agent choosing among prey types encountered while searching. Each prey type i has an energy value E_i and a handling time h_i (pursuit, subdual, chewing) once found. Its profitability is E_i/h_i, energy per unit time actually spent handling it. The model ranks prey from most to least profitable and asks a sharp question: given the best items are already worth eating, when should a forager bother with a lower-ranked one?

sections.heading: The inclusion rule and the zero-one rule
sections.body: A prey type should be added to the diet only if its profitability exceeds the intake rate the forager already achieves by searching for and eating only higher-ranked types. That comparison rate depends on how often the forager encounters those better items while searching (search rate and their density), not on how common the candidate item itself is. This yields the model's most surprising, testable claim, the zero-one rule: a prey type should be either always attacked on encounter or never attacked, with no in-between. Counterintuitively, whether a low-ranked item enters the diet hinges on the encounter rate with superior prey, not with the item itself — so a forager can ignore an item at any density if better items are common enough.

sections.heading: Krebs et al. 1977 and the mismatch with real diets
sections.body: John Krebs, Julian Erichsen, Michael Webber, and Charnov tested the model in 1977 by presenting great tits (Parus major) with mealworm pieces of two handling-time classes on a conveyor belt, letting the birds encounter items in a controlled, randomized sequence and manipulating the encounter rate with the profitable type. Birds broadly followed the qualitative predictions: they became more selective, dropping the poorer type, as the encounter rate with the better type rose, and selectivity tracked the profitable type's abundance rather than the poor type's, as predicted. But the fit was not exact — subjects, including Krebs's tits and foragers in many later field studies, routinely show partial preferences, eating the lower-ranked item some fraction of the time rather than obeying a strict zero-one switch. Proposed explanations include recognition and discrimination costs (distinguishing prey types isn't free or perfectly accurate), the value of sampling to track a changing environment, missing nutrient or toxin constraints the pure energy-maximizing model ignores, and simple errors near the decision threshold where the two options are nearly equal in value.

lessons.workedExample: A shorebird searches mudflat prey. Large worms: E=8 J, h=2 s, profitability=4 J/s, encountered at 0.5/s while searching. Small worms: E=3 J, h=1 s, profitability=3 J/s. If the bird eats only large worms, its overall intake rate is (0.5 encounters/s x 8 J)/(1 s search + 0.5 x 2 s handling) = 4 J/(2 s) = 2 J/s. Since the small worm's profitability (3 J/s) exceeds this 2 J/s baseline, the model predicts it should be included even though it is individually less profitable than the large worm — and, per the zero-one rule, included every time it is encountered, never just sometimes.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about diet breadth to see if the student understands that inclusion depends on the encounter rate with better prey, not on the candidate prey's own abundance — the model's least intuitive claim. A weak answer says 'the bird eats what's common'; a strong answer says 'the bird adds the worm because pursuing only the top-ranked item wasn't yielding enough energy per second, and that threshold moves only if the top item's availability changes.' An even stronger answer volunteers that real animals show partial preferences the strict model doesn't predict, and can name a plausible reason (discrimination error, sampling, nutrient needs) — showing they grasp the model as a testable idealization, not a description of literal behavior.

questions.prompt: In the prey-choice model, a prey item's profitability is defined as:

options.text: Its energy content divided by its handling time
Its encounter rate divided by its energy content
Its energy content divided by the total search time
Its abundance in the environment

explanations.a: Correct — profitability E/h measures energy gained per unit of handling time, which is what determines a prey type's rank.
explanations.b: This inverts the ratio and swaps in encounter rate, which affects whether an item is included, not its profitability rank.
explanations.c: Search time is part of computing the overall diet intake rate, not an individual item's profitability.
explanations.d: Abundance affects encounter rate, but profitability is about energy per handling time, independent of how common the item is.

questions.prompt: According to the model, whether a lower-ranked prey type should be included in the diet depends primarily on:

options.text: The lower-ranked item's own encounter rate
The encounter rate with higher-ranked, more profitable prey
The forager's total gut capacity
The time of day the item is encountered

explanations.a: This is the counterintuitive trap — the item's own abundance does not determine whether it is included.
explanations.b: Correct — inclusion is decided by comparing the candidate's profitability to the intake rate from pursuing only better-ranked prey, which depends on how often those better items are encountered.
explanations.c: Gut capacity is not part of the classic energy-rate-maximizing contingency model.
explanations.d: Time of day is not a variable in this model.

questions.prompt: Krebs et al. (1977) tested the model using great tits and mealworm pieces presented on:

options.text: A conveyor belt with controlled encounter sequences
Free-ranging forest transects
Seed trays filled with sand
An artificial patch with a removable lid

explanations.a: Correct — the conveyor belt let experimenters control the sequence and rate at which prey types of different handling times appeared.
explanations.b: Free-ranging transects would not allow the precise control over encounter rate the test required.
explanations.c: Sand-filled seed trays are the giving-up-density method used in predation-risk foraging studies, a different paradigm.
explanations.d: Lidded patches describe Cowie's 1977 patch-travel-time experiment, not the prey-choice conveyor-belt test.

questions.prompt: A key documented mismatch between the model's zero-one rule and real foraging behavior is that animals often show:

options.text: Complete refusal of all low-ranked prey regardless of conditions
Partial preferences, eating a lower-ranked item only some of the time
Random prey choice unrelated to profitability
Perfect adherence to the strict zero-one switch

explanations.a: Complete refusal would actually be consistent with the zero-one rule's 'never' outcome.
explanations.b: Correct — real foragers frequently eat a lower-ranked item some fraction of encounters rather than switching sharply between always and never, a well-documented deviation.
explanations.c: Choice still correlates with rank order in most tests; it is not random.
explanations.d: Perfect adherence is what the idealized model predicts, but it is the deviation from this that is the notable empirical finding.

lessons.label: The Marginal Value Theorem and Patch Use

sections.heading: Depleting patches and the leaving decision
sections.body: Prey-choice theory assumes food is met one item at a time while searching continuously. Many real foragers instead work patches, clumps of food (a berry bush, a rotting log, a shoal) where intake starts fast and slows as the patch is depleted or the forager's target items get wary. Eric Charnov's 1976 marginal value theorem (MVT) asks: given that travelling between patches costs time and yields nothing, when should a forager abandon a depleting patch for a fresh one? The answer is elegantly simple: leave when the patch's current instantaneous intake rate (the marginal rate) drops to the average rate achievable across the whole habitat, including travel time.

sections.heading: The graphical solution: a tangent line from travel time
sections.body: Charnov solved this graphically. Plot cumulative energy gained in a patch against time spent in it; because of depletion this gain curve rises steeply at first then flattens (decelerating, concave). Place travel time T on the x-axis to the left of the origin. Draw the straight line from that point (-T, 0) that is tangent to the gain curve. The tangent's point of contact marks the optimal patch residence time, because the tangent's slope equals the marginal intake rate at that instant, and that slope is also the maximum achievable long-run average rate over the whole travel-plus-foraging cycle. Any earlier departure wastes a patch still yielding above the habitat average; any later departure drags down the average by the diminishing tail. The key prediction falls straight out of the geometry: longer travel time between patches shifts the tangent point rightward, so foragers should stay longer in patches when patches are farther apart.

sections.heading: Testing it: Cowie 1977 and giving-up time as a leaving rule
sections.body: Richard Cowie tested MVT in 1977 with great tits foraging for mealworm pieces hidden in sawdust-filled plastic cups mounted in an artificial 'tree' inside an aviary. Cowie manipulated travel time by fitting cardboard lids of different weights over the cups, forcing birds to spend more or less effort and time getting into each cup before it counted as reaching a new patch. As predicted, birds given longer effective travel times stayed longer per patch and left with less food still un-harvested (a lower giving-up density) than birds with cheap access. Because the instantaneous intake rate itself is hard to observe directly, foraging ecologists commonly use giving-up time, the time since the last prey capture, as an operational proxy for the leaving rule: if capture rate has fallen enough that the forager hasn't found anything in a stretch of time consistent with the marginal threshold, it moves on.

lessons.workedExample: A tit forages patches with gain curve G(t) = 12(1 - e^(-t/4)) joules after t seconds in-patch (fast initial gain, flattening quickly), and travel time between patches is T = 4 s. Numerically stepping through: at t=2s, G=12(1-e^-0.5)=4.7 J, marginal rate (slope) ≈12/4 x e^-0.5≈1.82 J/s; at t=6s, G=12(1-e^-1.5)=9.3 J, marginal rate≈0.67 J/s. The habitat's long-run average rate for a given residence time t is G(t)/(T+t). Trying t=6s: 9.3/(4+6)=0.93 J/s, well above the marginal rate at that point (0.67 J/s) — the patch has already been overstayed. Solving the tangency condition G'(t*)=G(t*)/(T+t*) exactly gives e^(-t*/4)=4/(8+t*), whose root is t*≈4.6s, so the bird should have left around t≈4.6s, not lingered to t=6s; if T doubled to 8s, redoing the ratio shows the best t shifts later, confirming longer travel means longer patch stays.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges use MVT to test whether a student can connect a graph to a mechanism rather than reciting 'leave when it's not worth it anymore.' A weak answer stops at 'animals leave depleted patches.' A strong answer states the actual decision rule (leave when marginal intake rate equals the habitat-wide average, tangent from -T), derives the travel-time prediction from the geometry rather than asserting it, and can name Cowie's lid-weight manipulation as the operational test — showing they understand giving-up time as a measurable stand-in for an intake rate that can't be watched directly.

questions.prompt: The marginal value theorem predicts a forager should leave a depleting patch when:

options.text: The patch is completely empty
The instantaneous intake rate in the patch drops to the habitat-wide average rate
A fixed amount of time has elapsed regardless of intake
The forager has eaten exactly half of the patch's initial food

explanations.a: Waiting for a patch to be fully empty would waste time better spent traveling to a fresh patch once the rate drops below average.
explanations.b: Correct — this is the core MVT rule: leave when the current marginal rate equals the long-run average rate achievable across the whole habitat including travel.
explanations.c: A fixed time rule ignores how travel time and patch quality shift the optimal residence time.
explanations.d: There is no fixed depletion fraction; the optimal point depends on the shape of the gain curve and travel time, not a percentage.

questions.prompt: In Charnov's graphical solution, the optimal patch residence time is found where:

options.text: A line from (-T, 0) is tangent to the cumulative gain curve
The gain curve crosses the x-axis
The gain curve reaches its maximum possible value
A vertical line through the origin intersects the curve

explanations.a: Correct — the tangent from the travel-time point on the negative x-axis to the concave gain curve marks the point where marginal rate equals the best achievable long-run average.
explanations.b: The gain curve, being cumulative energy, does not cross the x-axis after foraging begins.
explanations.c: The curve's maximum (full depletion) is not the optimum; leaving earlier, before full depletion, maximizes the long-run rate.
explanations.d: A vertical line through the origin ignores travel time entirely, which is central to the solution.

questions.prompt: Cowie's 1977 great tit experiment manipulated travel time using:

options.text: Cardboard lids of varying weight on sawdust-filled cups
A conveyor belt delivering prey at fixed intervals
Seed trays buried at different depths in sand
Playback of predator calls near the patches

explanations.a: Correct — lids of different weights on the cup patches forced more or less effort/time to access each patch, simulating different travel times.
explanations.b: The conveyor belt is the apparatus from Krebs et al.'s prey-choice experiment, not Cowie's patch study.
explanations.c: Sand-buried seed trays describe giving-up density predation-risk assays, a different technique.
explanations.d: Predator playback tests risk effects on foraging, not Cowie's travel-time manipulation.

questions.prompt: Order these events in applying the marginal value theorem to a foraging bout, from start to the leaving decision.

items.text: Forager enters a fresh patch after traveling time T
Intake rate is high as food is easy to find
Depletion causes the marginal intake rate to decline
Marginal rate falls to the habitat-wide average rate
Forager departs for the next patch

questions.explanation: A forager arrives after paying travel cost, initially harvests quickly, experiences declining returns as the patch depletes, and departs exactly when the marginal rate matches the best long-run average — leaving any earlier or later would lower overall intake.

lessons.label: Central-Place Foraging and Load Size

sections.heading: Foraging with a fixed home to return to
sections.body: The marginal value theorem assumes gains are consumed on the spot. Many foragers instead must haul food back to a fixed location, a nest, burrow, hive, or lodge, before it counts, provisioning young or caching for winter. Gordon Orians and N. E. Pearson extended patch theory to this case in the late 1970s with the central-place foraging model. Because every trip pays a fixed round-trip travel cost regardless of load size, the model treats travel time exactly as MVT treats it, except now the 'patch' gain curve is the accumulation of items into a load, and the payoff of a trip must be averaged over the full round-trip time, not just the time in the patch.

sections.heading: The load-size prediction
sections.body: Applying the same marginal logic as MVT, a central-place forager should keep adding items to its load only while doing so raises the rate of delivery per unit of total trip time (travel out, load, travel back); it should depart once further loading yields diminishing returns relative to that round-trip average. Because travel time scales with distance, the model makes a clean, testable prediction: foragers exploiting more distant patches should carry larger loads back to the central place than foragers working nearby patches, since a longer unavoidable travel cost is best amortized over more food per trip rather than more frequent, smaller trips. Formally, if L(n) is the energy value of a load of n items and T is the fixed round-trip travel time, the forager maximizes the delivery rate L(n)/(T+t(n)), where t(n) is time spent loading; this is the same tangent-line construction as MVT, but with T playing the role of travel time and L(n) playing the role of the patch gain curve.

sections.heading: Testing it: Kacelnik's starlings and cutting beavers
sections.body: Alex Kacelnik tested the model in 1984 with European starlings (Sturnus vulgaris) trained to collect leatherjackets (cranefly larvae) from a feeding tray and fly them back to a nestbox at experimentally varied distances. Load size (number of larvae carried per trip) rose with distance in close quantitative agreement with the energy-maximizing prediction, though birds tended to slightly undershoot the very largest predicted loads at the farthest distances, plausibly because carrying capacity or handling constraints (larvae held crosswise in the bill) cap how much a beak can hold. Outside the lab, the same logic shows up in plant-eating central-place foragers: beavers (Castor canadensis) cutting trees for food and lodge material consistently select larger-diameter trees at greater distances from the water's edge, since a long overland haul is best justified by a bigger single load rather than repeated small trips through a habitat where beavers are also exposed and vulnerable away from water.

lessons.workedExample: A starling's nestbox sits 50 m from a feeding tray versus a second box at 200 m. Round-trip travel time scales with distance; suppose flight speed gives 10 s round trip per 50 m of distance, so travel costs are 10 s and 40 s respectively. Each additional larva costs roughly 2 s to pick up and adds a fixed energy value, so loading time rises linearly with load size while travel cost is fixed per trip. Dividing total energy delivered by total trip time (travel + loading) and maximizing that ratio shows the optimal load is larger at 200 m than at 50 m, because the fixed 40 s travel cost is better amortized across more larvae; Kacelnik's actual starlings showed almost exactly this scaling, load size increasing with distance.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing central-place foraging wants to know if the student sees why distance, not local abundance, drives load size — a specific instance of amortizing a fixed cost. A weak answer says 'animals farther away carry more because they're greedier' or 'to save trips' without the mechanism. A strong answer explains that round-trip travel time is a sunk cost independent of load, so maximizing delivery rate per total trip time pushes the optimal load upward as travel time rises, and can cite Kacelnik's starlings or the beaver tree-size pattern as a real test, including that starlings slightly undershot the extreme prediction, which shows they understand the model is being fit to data, not just quoted.

questions.prompt: The central-place foraging model's key departure from the basic marginal value theorem is that:

options.text: Gains must be averaged over a full round trip, including a fixed travel cost, before the animal can use the food
There is no patch depletion in central-place foraging
Travel time is irrelevant to the optimal decision
The forager never returns to the same patch twice

explanations.a: Correct — because food must be carried back before it counts, the payoff of a foraging trip is the load size divided by total round-trip time, not just time spent gathering.
explanations.b: Patches can still deplete; the model layers a return-trip requirement on top of, not instead of, patch dynamics.
explanations.c: Travel time is central to the model — it is precisely what drives the load-size prediction.
explanations.d: Foragers can and do revisit the same patch on repeated trips; that's not what distinguishes the model.

questions.prompt: The central-place foraging model predicts that, as distance from the central place increases, optimal load size should:

options.text: Decrease, since farther patches are riskier
Increase, to better amortize the fixed round-trip travel cost
Stay constant regardless of distance
Drop to zero beyond a threshold distance

explanations.a: Risk can matter in some systems, but the model's core prediction is about amortizing travel cost, not risk avoidance.
explanations.b: Correct — a longer fixed travel cost is best offset by carrying more food per trip, so load size should rise with distance.
explanations.c: Constant load size ignores the travel-cost amortization logic that is the model's central prediction.
explanations.d: The model doesn't predict abandonment at a threshold distance; it predicts a scaling of load size with distance.

questions.prompt: Match each central-place foraging study to its key finding.

right.text: Larger prey loads carried on trips to more distant nestboxes, closely matching energy-maximizing predictions
Larger-diameter trees selected at greater distances from water

questions.explanation: Kacelnik's starlings carrying leatherjackets to nestboxes at varied distances showed load size scaling with distance as predicted; beavers, a plant-eating central-place forager, show the analogous pattern by cutting bigger trees farther from the water's edge.

questions.prompt: In Kacelnik's starling experiment, actual load sizes at the farthest distances tended to:

options.text: Exceed the model's prediction due to hoarding behavior
Slightly undershoot the largest predicted loads, plausibly due to bill-carrying constraints
Match the prediction exactly at every distance with no deviation
Show no relationship to distance at all

explanations.a: There is no evidence of hoarding causing loads to exceed prediction in this experiment.
explanations.b: Correct — birds tended to carry slightly fewer larvae than the pure energy-maximizing prediction at the largest distances, likely because the bill can only physically hold so many larvae crosswise.
explanations.c: The fit was close but not exact, particularly diverging at the extremes, which is itself an informative result about physical constraints.
explanations.d: Load size did scale with distance; this option contradicts the study's central finding.

lessons.label: Foraging Under Predation Risk

sections.heading: The eating-versus-being-eaten trade-off
sections.body: Every foraging model so far maximizes energy intake as if food were the only thing at stake. Real foragers also risk being eaten while they eat, and time spent scanning for predators is time not spent harvesting. Joel Brown formalized this trade-off in 1988 with the giving-up density (GUD): the density of food remaining in a patch when a forager quits harvesting it. Because a forager should stop once the harvest rate falls to a quitting-harvest-rate threshold that reflects not just metabolic cost and competing opportunities but also the perceived predation cost of staying, a higher GUD (more food left behind, abandoned sooner) signals the forager judged that patch riskier. Brown operationalized this with seed trays mixed into a known volume of sand: seeds are progressively harder to find as density drops, so the sand slows depletion enough to measure a stable giving-up point, and comparing GUDs across microhabitats (open versus covered, moonlit versus dark, near versus far from cover) gives a field-measurable index of perceived risk without ever seeing a predator.

sections.heading: Vigilance, group size, and two competing explanations
sections.body: A forager can also manage risk directly through vigilance, pausing to scan instead of feeding. A robust empirical pattern is the group-size effect: individual vigilance (time spent scanning per individual) declines as group size increases, even though total group vigilance may rise. Two explanations compete. The many-eyes hypothesis (Pulliam, 1973) argues that with more individuals scanning collectively, each one can safely scan less often because the group's aggregate detection probability stays high; predators are spotted sooner by someone, so any one animal can afford to look away more. The dilution effect argues instead that an individual's own probability of being the one caught falls simply because there are more bodies in the group among which risk is spread, independent of who is watching. Both predict lower individual vigilance in bigger groups, so distinguishing them requires manipulating detection versus number separately, which is why field tests remain an active area of behavioral ecology rather than a settled question.

sections.heading: The landscape of fear
sections.body: John Laundré and colleagues extended these ideas from single patches to whole landscapes with the landscape-of-fear concept, mapping how perceived predation risk varies spatially and drives habitat use even where direct kills are rare. Their work on wolves reintroduced to Yellowstone showed elk shifting habitat use away from risky, low-visibility areas (dense conifer, riparian corridors) regardless of whether wolves were actually present there, illustrating that the fear of predation, not just realized predation, can restructure an ecosystem's plant communities through altered browsing pressure — a risk effect that in some systems appears to rival direct killing in shaping prey populations and vegetation.

lessons.workedExample: A field ecologist sets seed trays with 5 g of millet mixed into 1 L of sand at two microhabitat types: under shrub cover and in open grass, replicated across 20 stations each, checked after one night. Trays under cover average a GUD of 1.2 g remaining; open trays average 3.4 g remaining. Because open habitat offers less concealment from aerial predators, rodents foraging there quit harvesting sooner, at a higher remaining seed density, even though the food itself is identical, demonstrating that GUD tracks perceived predation risk rather than food quality or abundance.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe giving-up density because it's a clean, field-deployable way to measure something invisible, an animal's perceived fear, and a project either uses it correctly or reveals it doesn't understand what GUD indexes. A weak answer treats a high GUD as 'the animal wasn't hungry.' A strong answer explains that GUD reflects the quitting-harvest-rate threshold, which rises with perceived predation cost, so comparing GUDs across microhabitats isolates risk perception while holding food constant, and can also distinguish many-eyes from dilution as competing (not identical) explanations for the group-size vigilance effect rather than treating them as synonyms.

questions.prompt: Giving-up density (GUD), as developed by Brown (1988), measures:

options.text: The density of food remaining in a patch when a forager stops harvesting it
The total number of predators in a habitat
The forager's body mass at the end of a foraging bout
The number of seeds a forager can carry in one trip

explanations.a: Correct — GUD is the food density left behind when the forager judges the harvest rate no longer worth the combined metabolic, opportunity, and predation costs of staying.
explanations.b: GUD is an indirect behavioral index of perceived risk, not a direct predator count.
explanations.c: Body mass is not what a seed-tray assay measures.
explanations.d: This describes central-place load size, a different concept from GUD.

questions.prompt: A higher GUD in a risky microhabitat compared to a safe one indicates that the forager:

options.text: Found more food overall in the risky habitat
Quit harvesting sooner, leaving more food behind, consistent with a higher perceived predation cost
Was less hungry when foraging in the risky habitat
Ignored predation risk entirely

explanations.a: GUD measures what's left, not what was found; a higher GUD means less was harvested before quitting.
explanations.b: Correct — a higher GUD means the forager abandoned the patch at a higher remaining food density, indicating it perceived a higher cost (often predation risk) to continued foraging there.
explanations.c: Hunger state is a possible confound to control for, not what a properly designed risk comparison is measuring.
explanations.d: A raised GUD in risky habitat is itself evidence the forager is responding to risk, not ignoring it.

questions.prompt: Match each explanation for reduced individual vigilance in larger groups to its core logic.

right.text: More individuals collectively scanning means a predator is detected sooner, so any one animal can safely scan less
An individual's own chance of being the one caught falls simply because risk is spread across more bodies

questions.explanation: Many-eyes (Pulliam 1973) is about detection efficiency scaling with group size; dilution is about risk-sharing among more individuals independent of who is watching. Both predict lower individual vigilance in larger groups, which is why they are hard to tell apart without careful manipulation.

questions.prompt: Laundré's landscape-of-fear work on Yellowstone wolves and elk showed that:

options.text: Elk avoided risky habitat only in years when wolves actually killed elk there
Elk shifted away from low-visibility, risky habitat based on perceived risk, independent of whether wolves were actually present
Wolves had no measurable effect on elk habitat use
Elk vegetation browsing was unaffected by wolf reintroduction

explanations.a: The point of the landscape-of-fear concept is that avoidance tracks perceived risk, not only confirmed kills.
explanations.b: Correct — elk avoided dense, low-visibility habitat based on the risk it posed, whether or not a wolf was actually there at the time, showing fear itself restructures habitat use.
explanations.c: Wolf reintroduction was associated with measurable shifts in elk habitat use and browsing patterns in this body of work.
explanations.d: Altered browsing pressure from shifted elk habitat use is the mechanism by which this risk effect propagates to vegetation.

lessons.label: Risk-Sensitive Foraging and State-Dependence

sections.heading: Why variance matters, not just the mean
sections.body: Every model so far assumes a forager should maximize the mean rate of energy gain. But two food options can have identical average payoffs and differ sharply in variance: a constant-reward option (say, always 3 units) versus a variable one (0 or 6 units with equal chance, averaging 3). Which a forager should prefer depends on its physiological state, not just the arithmetic mean, because an animal that starves before the average has time to pay off gets no benefit from a favorable long-run mean. This is risk-sensitive foraging theory, and its central empirical finding is the energy-budget rule.

sections.heading: Caraco's juncos and the energy-budget rule
sections.body: Thomas Caraco, with Sean Martindale and Thomas Whittam, ran a now-classic series of experiments starting in 1980 on yellow-eyed juncos (Junco phaeonotus) choosing between a fixed-reward and a variable-reward feeding option. When birds were well-fed and their expected energy budget for the period was positive (they could meet their needs on the constant option alone), they consistently preferred the constant, lower-variance option, showing risk aversion, the same logic behind why a person with adequate savings avoids a coin-flip bet with equal expected value. When food was withheld or temperatures dropped so that the constant option alone would not cover the day's energy needs, putting the birds in a negative energy budget, the same individuals switched to preferring the variable option, showing risk-proneness (risk-seeking) — because only the variable option's chance of a large payoff offered any possibility of surviving the shortfall, even though its guaranteed-failure branch was worse. The rule, budget positive favors safety, budget negative favors a gamble, has since been replicated across many taxa and is one of the most robust findings in foraging behavioral ecology.

sections.heading: State-dependence and daily-routine models
sections.body: The energy-budget rule is a special case of a broader idea: state-dependent decision theory, developed extensively by John McNamara and Alasdair Houston, which treats an animal's current state, chiefly its fat reserves and the time remaining until a deadline like nightfall or migration, as a variable the optimal decision must be computed against, not held constant. Daily-routine models solve, for every possible combination of reserve level and time-of-day, which foraging option (safe patch, risky patch, or resting) maximizes survival probability to the next morning. Because the optimal choice depends on state, two individuals facing an identical external environment (same patches, same predators, same weather) can rationally make opposite decisions if one entered the day with more stored fat than the other — a low-reserve individual near a winter evening deadline may accept a risk it would refuse at midday when reserves are ample and time remains to recover from a bad outcome.

lessons.workedExample: A junco needs 30 J to survive the night. Option A (constant) reliably delivers 25 J over the remaining foraging window. Option B (variable) delivers 60 J with probability 0.5 and 0 J with probability 0.5, also averaging 30 J across many trials. If the bird's current reserves plus Option A guarantee survival (positive budget), Option A wins with certainty while B risks total failure half the time despite equal or higher mean, so risk-aversion favors A. If reserves are low enough that even Option A's 25 J falls short of the 30 J needed, only Option B's 0.5 chance of 60 J offers any path to survival, so the same bird should now choose B, illustrating Caraco's energy-budget rule directly.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge raises risk-sensitive foraging to test whether a student can move past 'animals maximize average food' to a more sophisticated claim: that variance itself is a decision variable, and its value flips sign depending on whether the animal is above or below its survival requirement. A weak answer says 'sometimes animals gamble.' A strong answer names the energy-budget rule explicitly, states both directions (risk-averse when budget positive, risk-prone when negative), and explains state-dependence as the reason two animals in identical conditions can rationally disagree — because the deadline-and-reserves calculation, not the environment, differs between them.

questions.prompt: According to Caraco's energy-budget rule, a forager with a positive expected energy budget (needs are met by the safe option) should:

options.text: Prefer the constant, low-variance option (risk-averse)
Prefer the variable, high-variance option (risk-prone)
Show no preference between options
Switch preference randomly from trial to trial

explanations.a: Correct — when the safe option already meets survival needs, a forager gains nothing from variance and avoids the risk of the variable option's low-payoff branch.
explanations.b: Risk-proneness is predicted when the budget is negative, not positive.
explanations.c: Caraco's juncos showed a clear, consistent, state-dependent preference, not indifference.
explanations.d: The preference tracked energy state systematically, not randomly.

questions.prompt: When a forager's energy budget is negative (the safe option alone won't meet survival needs), risk-sensitive theory predicts it should:

options.text: Stop foraging entirely to conserve energy
Prefer the variable option, since only its chance of a large payoff offers a path to survival
Prefer the constant option even more strongly than when the budget is positive
Split effort equally between all available options regardless of variance

explanations.a: Stopping foraging guarantees failure to meet the deficit; it is not the predicted response.
explanations.b: Correct — with a guaranteed shortfall from the safe option, only the variable option's upside gives any chance of meeting the energy requirement, so the forager should become risk-prone.
explanations.c: This is the opposite of the predicted flip; positive budgets favor the constant option, not negative ones.
explanations.d: The rule predicts a state-dependent preference reversal, not equal effort across options.

questions.prompt: In state-dependent decision models (McNamara and Houston), the key insight is that the optimal foraging decision depends on:

options.text: Only the external environment, since all individuals should behave identically
The individual's own state, such as fat reserves and time remaining until a deadline, in addition to the environment
Only the individual's genetic identity, regardless of physiological condition
Group size alone

explanations.a: This is precisely what state-dependent models reject — identical environments can produce different optimal decisions depending on state.
explanations.b: Correct — reserves and time-to-deadline are treated as decision variables, so the same environment can yield different optimal choices for individuals in different states.
explanations.c: Genetic identity is not the variable these models track; physiological state is.
explanations.d: Group size is relevant to vigilance and predation-risk models, not the core variable in daily-routine state models.

questions.prompt: Two juncos face identical patches, predators, and weather, but one has much lower fat reserves near a winter evening deadline. State-dependent theory predicts:

options.text: Both should make the identical foraging choice since the environment is identical
The low-reserve bird may rationally accept a risk the higher-reserve bird refuses
The high-reserve bird should always take more risks to build up extra reserves
Reserve level is irrelevant once the deadline is fixed

explanations.a: This ignores state-dependence, the model's central claim, that identical environments can yield different optimal decisions.
explanations.b: Correct — the low-reserve bird facing a possible shortfall before the deadline may rationally gamble, while the well-provisioned bird has no such incentive.
explanations.c: A well-provisioned bird has less need to gamble, so extra risk-taking is not predicted for it.
explanations.d: Reserve level relative to the deadline requirement is exactly what drives the decision in these models.

lessons.label: Habitat Selection, Territoriality, and the Ideal Free Distribution

sections.heading: The ideal free distribution and input matching
sections.body: Stephen Fretwell and Henry Lucas proposed the ideal free distribution (IFD) in 1970 to predict how competitors should distribute themselves across habitat patches that differ in resource supply rate. The model assumes individuals are 'ideal' (they know the quality of every patch) and 'free' (they can move to any patch without cost or restriction), and that per-capita intake at a patch falls as more competitors pile in. At equilibrium no individual can improve its intake by switching patches, which forces a specific quantitative prediction called input matching: the number of competitors at each patch should be proportional to that patch's resource input rate, so a patch receiving twice the food supply of another should end up with roughly twice the competitors.

sections.heading: Testing it, and where the 'ideal' and 'free' assumptions break
sections.body: David Harper tested input matching directly in 1982 by throwing bread pellets to captive mallards (Anas platyrhynchos) at two feeding stations simultaneously, one delivering pellets at twice the rate of the other. Ducks distributed themselves closely tracking the 2:1 supply ratio, a striking confirmation of the basic model. But real animals are rarely fully ideal or fully free: competitive asymmetries mean some individuals control disproportionate shares of a patch's resources regardless of headcount, which Fretwell extended as the ideal despotic distribution, where dominant individuals monopolize the best patches and subordinates are pushed to poorer ones even though the population's overall distribution no longer matches input ratios. A further complication is the ecological trap: when a habitat's outward cues (structure, visual quality) no longer reliably signal its actual quality, for instance a field that looks safe but sits next to a road or has been invaded by a novel predator, animals can be drawn to settle in poor habitat by cues evolution tuned to a different, safer past, undermining the 'ideal' assumption that individuals can accurately assess quality.

sections.heading: Territoriality as an economic decision
sections.body: Jerram Brown's 1964 concept of economic defendability reframed territoriality itself as a cost-benefit decision rather than a fixed trait: an animal should defend an area only when the resource gain from exclusive access exceeds the energetic and risk costs of defending it (patrolling, displaying, fighting). When resources are too sparse to be worth defending, or so abundant that exclusion is pointless, non-territorial behavior should be favored instead, meaning the same species can shift in and out of territoriality as conditions change. Frank Gill and Larry Wolf demonstrated this directly in 1975 with golden-winged sunbirds in Kenya, showing that individuals defended nectar-rich flower territories when the energetic value of exclusive access exceeded defense costs, but abandoned defense when nectar became either too scarce (not worth defending) or artificially superabundant (defense costs exceeded any marginal benefit of exclusivity), switching territoriality on and off within the same population based purely on the economics of the moment.

lessons.workedExample: Two ponds receive food inputs of 40 items/min and 20 items/min. Under pure input matching, if 30 ducks are foraging across both, the IFD predicts roughly 20 ducks at the high-input pond and 10 at the low-input pond (the 2:1 ratio preserved). Harper's actual mallard trials, throwing bread at a 2:1 rate between two real feeding stations, produced duck counts tracking that ratio closely once ducks had time to sample and redistribute, though initial settlement before full sampling deviated further from the prediction, illustrating that IFD is an equilibrium outcome, not an instantaneous one.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about habitat distribution or territoriality to see whether a student treats these as economic equilibria with testable numeric predictions, not vague 'animals go where resources are' statements. A weak answer says 'ducks go to more food.' A strong answer states the input-matching ratio explicitly, names Harper's bread-throwing test, and can explain at least one reason real distributions deviate from ideal predictions, dominance hierarchies producing an ideal despotic distribution, or a habitat cue mismatch producing an ecological trap. On territoriality, a strong answer states Brown's economic-defendability logic and cites Gill and Wolf's sunbirds switching territorial behavior on and off as nectar availability changed, rather than treating territoriality as a fixed species trait.

questions.prompt: The ideal free distribution's input-matching prediction states that, at equilibrium, the number of competitors at a patch should be:

options.text: Equal across all patches regardless of resource supply
Proportional to that patch's resource input rate
Inversely proportional to patch size
Determined solely by which patch was discovered first

explanations.a: Equal distribution regardless of supply is what would happen without competition for resources shaping settlement, which contradicts the model.
explanations.b: Correct — because per-capita intake equalizes across patches at equilibrium, competitor numbers must track resource input rates, e.g. a 2:1 supply ratio yields roughly a 2:1 competitor ratio.
explanations.c: Patch size is not the variable the classic IFD model predicts distribution from; resource input rate is.
explanations.d: Discovery order might affect transient dynamics but not the predicted equilibrium under ideal, free assumptions.

questions.prompt: Harper's 1982 test of the ideal free distribution used:

options.text: Bread pellets thrown at two rates to two mallard feeding stations
Sawdust cups with hidden mealworms
A conveyor belt of prey items
Nectar concentration manipulated in artificial flowers

explanations.a: Correct — Harper threw bread at two different rates to two mallard stations and found duck numbers tracked the supply ratio, confirming input matching.
explanations.b: Sawdust cups describe Cowie's patch-travel-time MVT test, a different study.
explanations.c: The conveyor belt describes Krebs et al.'s prey-choice test.
explanations.d: Artificial nectar flowers relate to sunbird territoriality studies, not Harper's IFD test.

questions.prompt: An ideal despotic distribution differs from an ideal free distribution because it accounts for:

options.text: Dominant individuals monopolizing disproportionate shares of the best patches
Resources that never deplete
Animals that cannot move between patches at all
A complete absence of competition

explanations.a: Correct — despotic distributions incorporate competitive asymmetry, where dominants control more resources per capita than subordinates, breaking the simple input-matching ratio.
explanations.b: Non-depleting resources are not what distinguishes the despotic variant; competitive dominance is.
explanations.c: Both IFD and its despotic variant generally assume free movement; the despotic version differs in resource control, not mobility.
explanations.d: Despotic distributions specifically model unequal competition, the opposite of no competition.

questions.prompt: An ecological trap occurs when:

options.text: A habitat's outward cues no longer reliably signal its actual quality, drawing animals into poor habitat
A predator physically blocks access to a high-quality patch
Two competitors of equal dominance fight to a draw over a patch
A patch's resource input rate exceeds what any single forager can consume

explanations.a: Correct — an ecological trap arises when cues an animal evolved to trust for assessing quality become decoupled from actual habitat quality, undermining the 'ideal' (accurate assessment) assumption of IFD.
explanations.b: Physical blockage is an access-cost issue, not a cue-quality mismatch, and doesn't define an ecological trap.
explanations.c: A dominance standoff is a despotic-distribution dynamic, not a trap based on misleading cues.
explanations.d: Superabundant resources relate to territoriality economics, not the cue-mismatch definition of an ecological trap.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or pair to their contribution on territoriality and habitat distribution.

right.text: Proposed the ideal free distribution and input matching
Framed territoriality as economically defendable only when benefits exceed defense costs
Showed sunbirds switching nectar-territory defense on and off as resource economics changed

questions.explanation: Fretwell and Lucas built the foundational IFD model; Brown supplied the economic-defendability logic for when territoriality should evolve at all; Gill and Wolf provided a direct field test showing golden-winged sunbirds turning territorial defense on and off as nectar supply made it economically worthwhile or not.

lessons.label: Sampling Rules: Altmann's Framework

sections.heading: The paper that made field ethology a science
sections.body: Before 1974, most primate field studies recorded behavior however the observer happened to notice it: whatever animal was doing something conspicuous, whenever it did it. Jeanne Altmann's 1974 paper in the journal Behaviour, "Observational Study of Behavior: Sampling Methods," surveyed this literature and showed that this default approach — ad libitum sampling — is not a neutral baseline but a specific, biased sampling rule. Because the observer's attention is the instrument, ad lib data systematically overrepresents large, close, active, or otherwise conspicuous individuals, and overrepresents brief, dramatic acts (a fight, a mount) over long, quiet states (resting, low-intensity foraging). Altmann's contribution was to name several alternative rules explicitly, so a reader could judge exactly what bias a given dataset carries.

sections.heading: Five named rules
sections.body: Focal-animal sampling designates one individual per session and records its behavior — continuously or at set intervals — for a fixed period, regardless of what anyone else is doing; this gives an unbiased picture of one animal's time budget. Scan (instantaneous) sampling sweeps the whole visible group at fixed intervals and records each individual's state at that instant, trading fine-grained continuity for a group-wide snapshot. Behavior sampling (Altmann also called it "all occurrences of some behaviors") tracks the whole group but restricts recording to one or a few pre-defined, easily detected behaviors — every copulation, every predator alarm — whenever and to whomever they occur. Sequence sampling records the order of behavioral events, useful for interaction structure. Ad libitum, the default Altmann critiqued, remains legitimate only for pilot work or genuinely novel, unpredictable events. Altmann's 1974 paper (Behaviour 49(3-4):227-267) also formalized two further named rules: one-zero sampling, which records only whether a behavior occurred at all within an interval rather than how often or how long, and sociometric-matrix sampling, which tracks which individuals interact with which.

sections.heading: Matching rule to research question
sections.body: The choice is dictated by what quantity the question actually needs. A time budget — what fraction of the day a troop spends feeding versus resting — needs scan or focal sampling, because both give a denominator (total observation time or total scans) against which a duration or proportion is meaningful. A rare, brief social event such as a copulation or an aggressive coalition needs behavior sampling: focal sampling on one animal would miss most such events entirely, since any single individual is rarely the one involved at any given moment, while behavior sampling scans the whole group continuously for that one signal.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher studying a 25-animal baboon troop wants two numbers: the percentage of daylight hours spent grooming (a time budget) and the rate of copulations per estrous female per day (a rare event). For the time budget, she uses scan sampling every 10 minutes, sweeping all visible animals and recording each one's current activity state. For copulations, scan sampling would badly undercount — a mount can last seconds — so she instead uses behavior sampling: continuous group-wide monitoring restricted to that one conspicuous, discrete behavior, logging every occurrence with its time and the identities involved, regardless of what else is happening.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks "why did you sample behavior the way you did?" because the answer reveals whether the student understands that observation method determines what bias is baked into the data. A weak answer is "we watched the animals and wrote down what they did" — undisclosed ad libitum sampling, which overweights conspicuous animals and acts and cannot support a quantitative claim like a time budget. A strong answer names the specific rule ("scan sampling at fixed intervals for the time budget, behavior sampling for the rare aggressive events") and explains why that rule fits the specific quantity being estimated.

questions.prompt: Altmann's 1974 paper identified which sampling rule as the pre-existing default in the literature, and criticized it as the most bias-prone?

options.text: Ad libitum sampling
Focal-animal sampling
Scan sampling
Behavior sampling

explanations.a: Correct — ad libitum sampling (recording whatever is most noticeable, whenever) was the unstated default in most pre-1974 studies Altmann reviewed, and it systematically overrepresents conspicuous animals and dramatic acts.
explanations.b: Focal-animal sampling is a deliberate, unbiased-per-individual rule Altmann recommended as an alternative, not the biased default she critiqued.
explanations.c: Scan sampling is a systematic group-wide rule Altmann formalized; it was not the pre-existing biased default.
explanations.d: Behavior sampling targets specific pre-defined behaviors systematically; it is not the undisclosed default Altmann criticized.

questions.prompt: Match each research need to the sampling rule best suited to it.

left.text: Estimating a group's overall time budget (% feeding, resting)
Recording rare copulations across an entire troop
Getting one individual's complete, continuous activity record
Noting a genuinely unpredicted, never-before-seen behavior

right.text: Scan (instantaneous) sampling
Behavior sampling (all occurrences)
Focal-animal sampling
Ad libitum sampling

questions.explanation: Scan sampling gives a group-wide snapshot suited to time budgets; behavior sampling tracks the whole group for one rare, conspicuous act; focal sampling gives one individual's full continuous record; ad libitum remains legitimate for capturing unpredictable, never-anticipated events.

questions.prompt: What specific bias does undisclosed ad libitum sampling introduce into a dataset?

options.text: It underrepresents conspicuous individuals and overrepresents quiet, hidden ones
It overrepresents conspicuous individuals and dramatic, brief acts, at the expense of quiet or subtle states
It has no systematic bias because the observer records everything seen
It only biases duration estimates, never frequency estimates

explanations.a: This is backwards — conspicuous animals and acts are more likely to catch an observer's eye, not less.
explanations.b: Correct — because attention is the instrument, animals that are large, close, or active, and behaviors that are brief and dramatic, are systematically overrepresented relative to quiet, long-lasting states.
explanations.c: The bias is systematic, not random noise, precisely because human attention is not evenly distributed across animals and behaviors.
explanations.d: The bias distorts both which behaviors get recorded at all (frequency) and how much attention quiet states receive (duration), not just one of the two.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of running a scan-sampling protocol on a visible group.

items.text: Define the behavior state categories in advance
Set a fixed scan interval (e.g., every 10 minutes)
At each interval, sweep across all visible individuals
Record each individual's instantaneous state at that moment
Wait until the next interval and repeat

questions.explanation: Categories and interval must be fixed before data collection begins; then each scan sweeps the group, logs each animal's state at that instant, and the cycle repeats at the next fixed interval, producing a systematic group-wide time series rather than an opportunistic one.

lessons.label: Recording Rules and Interval Choice

sections.heading: Continuous recording versus instantaneous point sampling
sections.body: Once you've picked a sampling rule (focal, scan, and so on), you still need a recording rule for how the observer captures time. Continuous recording logs the exact start and stop time of every occurrence of a target behavior, giving true frequency (events per unit time) and true duration (total and per-bout time). It is the gold standard but is labor-intensive: a single observer can usually continuous-record only one individual, or a handful of easily distinguished behaviors, at once. Instantaneous point sampling instead checks the subject's state only at fixed-interval ticks (say, every 30 seconds) and records whichever state is occurring at that instant. Summed across many ticks, the proportion of "on" ticks approximates the proportion of time in that state — but only if the interval is short relative to the behavior's typical bout length; a coarse interval will simply miss short bouts entirely, undercounting frequency and distorting duration estimates.

sections.heading: One-zero sampling and why Altmann flagged it
sections.body: One-zero sampling, common in 1960s-70s zoo and lab ethology, scores each fixed interval as a simple 1 (behavior occurred at all during the interval) or 0 (it did not), regardless of how many times it occurred or for how long. Altmann's 1974 critique showed this is neither a frequency measure nor a duration measure but an unpredictable hybrid of both: if a behavior occurs in short bouts many times within one interval, one-zero scores it identically to a single long bout filling the whole interval, so it systematically overestimates the proportion of time spent in a state relative to true continuous data, while simultaneously undercounting how often the behavior actually started. Because of this confound, one-zero sampling is now recommended only when continuous recording is genuinely infeasible, and results should be reported explicitly as a one-zero index, not converted into implied durations.

sections.heading: Choosing and reporting an interval from pilot data
sections.body: A defensible instantaneous-sampling interval is not guessed; it comes from a short pilot session using continuous recording to build a bout-duration distribution for the target behavior. A common rule of thumb sets the interval at roughly one-fifth to one-half of the mean bout duration, so most bouts span at least one full tick and are not systematically skipped. The chosen rule, interval, and its pilot justification belong in the methods section verbatim — "instantaneous point sampling at 15-second intervals, set at one-fifth the 75-second mean vigilance-bout duration measured in a 2-hour pilot" — so another researcher could reproduce the exact protocol rather than guess at what "checking periodically" meant.

lessons.workedExample: A pilot continuous-recording session on captive meerkats measures a mean vigilance-bout duration of 8 seconds and a mean feeding-bout duration of 90 seconds. A 30-second scan interval, chosen for convenience, would badly undersample vigilance: most 8-second bouts start and end between ticks and are simply invisible to the sampler, while feeding — much longer than the interval — is captured reasonably well. The fix is behavior-specific: keep the 30-second (or coarser) instantaneous interval for feeding, but switch to continuous recording, or a much shorter ~2-second interval, for vigilance.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks "how did you choose your sampling interval?" because an arbitrary interval silently discards data from short behaviors without the student realizing it. A weak answer is "we checked every five minutes because that seemed reasonable." A strong answer cites a pilot bout-duration measurement and a stated rule — interval set to roughly one-fifth of mean bout length — and can say which behaviors in the study were too brief for the chosen interval and had to be handled differently (continuous recording or a shorter tick).

questions.prompt: What does one-zero sampling systematically bias when a behavior occurs in several short bouts within one interval?

options.text: It has no bias since it just records presence or absence
It underestimates the proportion of time spent in the state
It overestimates the proportion of time in the state while undercounting how often bouts actually began
It perfectly reproduces true continuous-recording duration

explanations.a: One-zero scoring conflates frequency and duration into a single ambiguous number, which is exactly the systematic bias Altmann identified.
explanations.b: It biases toward overestimating time in state, not underestimating it, because any occurrence — however brief — scores the whole interval as "1".
explanations.c: Correct — a single tick scored as 1 whether the behavior happened once briefly or filled the whole interval, so short, frequent bouts inflate the apparent proportion of time in that state and collapse multiple distinct bout-starts into one scored interval.
explanations.d: One-zero sampling is precisely the method Altmann showed diverges from true continuous-recording duration and frequency.

questions.prompt: A defensible instantaneous-sampling interval should be chosen how?

options.text: As long as possible, to minimize the number of observations needed
Arbitrarily, since any fixed interval gives comparable results
Based on pilot continuous-recording data on the target behavior's bout-duration distribution, short relative to mean bout length
Matched to the observer's convenience, e.g., once per coffee break

explanations.a: A long interval relative to bout length causes short bouts to be systematically missed, undermining the estimate.
explanations.b: Interval choice is not arbitrary — too coarse an interval relative to bout length produces biased results, as shown in the meerkat vigilance example.
explanations.c: Correct — pilot continuous data reveals the true bout-duration distribution, and setting the interval as a fraction (roughly one-fifth to one-half) of the mean bout length keeps most bouts detectable.
explanations.d: Observer convenience has nothing to do with whether the interval captures the behavior's true temporal structure.

questions.prompt: Match each recording rule to what it directly and reliably measures.

left.text: Instantaneous point sampling (interval short relative to bout length)

right.text: Exact frequency and exact duration of every occurrence
Approximate proportion of time in a state
An ambiguous hybrid index conflating frequency and duration

questions.explanation: Continuous recording captures exact timing of every occurrence; instantaneous sampling with an appropriately short interval approximates proportion of time in state; one-zero sampling produces neither a clean frequency nor a clean duration measure, only a confounded presence/absence index.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for choosing and reporting a sampling interval.

items.text: Run a short pilot session using continuous recording
Compute the bout-duration distribution for the target behavior
Set the interval to roughly one-fifth to one-half of mean bout length
Collect the full dataset using the chosen instantaneous interval
Report the exact rule and interval, with its pilot justification, in the methods

questions.explanation: The interval must be derived from real bout-duration data collected before the main study, then applied consistently, and finally reported explicitly so the protocol is reproducible by another researcher.

lessons.label: Observer Reliability and Bias Control

sections.heading: Quantifying agreement, not just claiming it
sections.body: Raw percent agreement between two observers is misleading because it doesn't account for agreement expected by chance alone — if a behavior occurs 90% of the time, two observers guessing "present" with that same 90% probability would agree by chance alone 82% of the time (0.9² + 0.1²). Cohen's kappa (1960) corrects for this by comparing observed agreement to chance-expected agreement for categorical scoring (e.g., which of five behavior states an animal is in). The conventional benchmark scale, from Landis and Koch (1977), reads kappa above roughly 0.6 as "substantial" agreement and above roughly 0.8 as "almost perfect" agreement; values below that call the coding scheme or training into question before any real data collection begins. For continuous measures — bout duration, time spent in a state — the analogous statistic is the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), which captures how much of the total variance in the measurement is between true subjects versus between observers.

sections.heading: A double-scoring protocol that runs all season
sections.body: Reliability should not be checked once during training and then assumed to hold. A practical protocol randomly selects 10-20% of sessions (or a matched percentage of recorded video) throughout the field season for independent double-scoring by a second observer, blind to the first observer's codes, with kappa or ICC recomputed periodically rather than only at the start. Intra-observer reliability matters too: the same observer re-scores a subset of their own earlier video weeks later, checking whether their own criteria have stayed stable.

sections.heading: Expectancy, drift, and habituation
sections.body: Observer expectancy bias is the tendency to unconsciously score data in the direction the observer expects or hopes for. The canonical illustration is Clever Hans, a horse whose owner believed could do arithmetic; psychologist Oskar Pfungst's 1907 investigation showed the horse was actually reading unconscious postural and facial cues from the questioner, who unknowingly relaxed at the correct tap count — the horse was answering the human, not the math. In behavioral fieldwork the fix is blind scoring: coding video or field notes without knowing which treatment or hypothesis-relevant group the subject belongs to. Observer drift is a related but separate problem — criteria for scoring a borderline behavior can gradually shift over a multi-month season even without any expectancy bias, which periodic mid-season double-scoring is designed to catch. Finally, a habituation period — days to weeks, depending on species and prior human contact — must pass between an observer's arrival and the start of data collection, so that the behavior recorded reflects the animal's normal repertoire rather than a disturbance response to being watched.

lessons.workedExample: Two observers independently score aggression categories (chase, bite, display, none) in captive fish from the same video clips for 15% of all trials. Cohen's kappa on the four-category codes comes out to 0.74, in the "substantial" range, while the ICC on the continuous duration of chasing bouts is 0.88. A closer look shows most of the disagreement came from one observer who knew which tank held the manipulated (treatment) fish and was slightly more likely to code ambiguous approaches as "display" in that tank — a small expectancy effect. Switching to coded, treatment-blind video filenames for all future scoring removed the discrepancy in a follow-up spot-check.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks "how do you know your results aren't just one observer's impression?" because unreliable, unblinded scoring can manufacture an effect that isn't real. A weak answer is "I was very careful and consistent." A strong answer reports an actual kappa or ICC value from double-scored sessions, states the double-scoring rate (e.g., 15% of trials), explains that scoring was blind to treatment identity, and names the habituation period observed before data collection began.

questions.prompt: Why is Cohen's kappa preferred over raw percent agreement between two observers?

options.text: Kappa is always a larger, more flattering number
Kappa corrects for the level of agreement expected by chance alone
Percent agreement cannot be computed for categorical data
Kappa requires no second observer

explanations.a: Kappa is typically lower than raw percent agreement, not higher, precisely because it subtracts out chance agreement.
explanations.b: Correct — raw percent agreement can look high purely because a category is common and both observers guess it often; kappa compares observed agreement to what chance alone would produce.
explanations.c: Percent agreement can be computed for categorical data; the issue is that it is uncorrected for chance, not that it's impossible to calculate.
explanations.d: Kappa, like percent agreement, requires two independent observers scoring the same material to compare.

questions.prompt: The Clever Hans case, investigated by Oskar Pfungst in 1907, is the classic illustration of which bias in observational research?

options.text: Observer drift over a long field season
One-zero sampling's conflation of frequency and duration
Expectancy effects, where unconscious cues from the observer/questioner shape the apparent result
Trigger lag in motion-triggered recording devices

explanations.a: Drift is a gradual change in an observer's own scoring criteria over time, unrelated to Hans reading cues from his questioner in real time.
explanations.b: One-zero sampling is a recording-rule issue with duration/frequency confounds, not an expectancy-bias case.
explanations.c: Correct — Hans appeared to solve arithmetic but was actually detecting subtle, unconscious postural cues from the human asking the question, who unknowingly relaxed at the correct answer; this is the founding example of expectancy/cueing bias in behavioral study.
explanations.d: Trigger lag is a hardware property of camera traps, unrelated to Pfungst's investigation of a horse and its questioner.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its definition in observer-reliability practice.

right.text: Chance-corrected agreement statistic for categorical codes
Reliability statistic for continuous measures such as bout duration
Gradual, unintentional change in an observer's own scoring criteria over a season
Time animals are given to acclimate to observer presence before data collection begins

questions.explanation: Kappa handles categorical agreement, ICC handles continuous-measure agreement, drift describes a slow unintentional shift in one observer's own criteria, and the habituation period is the pre-data-collection window that lets animals resume normal behavior around the observer.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a sound observer-reliability protocol across a field season.

items.text: Train all observers together on shared scoring criteria
Run a pilot double-scoring session to calibrate before real data collection
Allow a habituation period so animals resume normal behavior
Collect data, randomly double-scoring 10-20% of sessions blind to treatment
Periodically recompute kappa/ICC across the season to catch drift
