questions.explanation: Shared training and pilot calibration come first, then a habituation period lets subjects settle before real data collection starts, after which ongoing blind double-scoring and periodic reliability checks catch drift that a single upfront check would miss.

lessons.label: Field Experiments in Behavior

sections.heading: Manipulating a wild system without leaving it
sections.body: Pure observation can only reveal correlation, so behavioral ecologists manipulate one variable in situ while keeping the rest of the system natural. Playback experiments broadcast a recorded stimulus — a rival's territorial song, a predator's alarm call — through a speaker and measure the focal animal's response, testing what information content the animal extracts from the signal. Decoys and taxidermy mounts test responses to visual stimuli the same way. Giving-up density (GUD) trays, introduced by Joel Brown in 1988, bury a fixed mass of food in sand or substrate and measure how much food is left when a forager quits, using the giving-up density itself as a bioassay of perceived predation risk or missed-opportunity cost. Supplemental feeding tests whether food limits reproduction or behavior; translocation and removal experiments (moving or excluding a territory holder) test how quickly and by whom a vacated resource is contested.

sections.heading: The pseudoreplication trap in playback design
sections.body: Stuart Hurlbert's 1984 paper named pseudoreplication as treating non-independent samples as if they were independent replicates. Donald Kroodsma's critiques (Auk, 1986, and Animal Behaviour, 1989) applied this specifically to a generation of bird-song playback studies that used a single recorded exemplar per treatment — one "aggressive" song and one "neutral" song, each played repeatedly to dozens of subjects — and then treated the many subjects as independent replicates of the treatment. Statistically, the true unit of replication is the exemplar, not the subject: any observed difference could simply be a quirk of that one recording rather than a general property of the treatment category. The fix is straightforward — use multiple independent exemplars per treatment (recordings from several different individuals), randomize which exemplar and which treatment order each subject receives, and analyze exemplar as a factor, not just subject.

sections.heading: What counts as a real control
sections.body: A control must isolate the specific variable under test, not just the presence of any stimulus. For playback, a silent trial (speaker present, nothing played) controls for the disturbance of setting up equipment near the animal, while a heterospecific or non-signal sound controls for a generic startle response to any noise, isolating the response specific to the conspecific signal's content. For a GUD array, an empty tray (same handling, no food reward) controls for disturbance from tray placement itself. Because habitat quality, predator density, and food availability vary between sites, a between-site comparison confounds the treatment with whatever the sites differed on anyway; a paired, within-site design — placing control and treatment trays or triggering control and treatment playbacks at the same location, ideally in randomized order — removes that site-level confound entirely.

lessons.workedExample: Kotler and Brown's classic GUD studies on Negev Desert gerbils placed paired seed trays side by side at the same site — one in open microhabitat, one under bush cover — both refilled nightly with an identical weighed seed-sand mixture, and weighed the remaining seed each morning. Because both trays sat at the same site experiencing the same overall predator density and productivity, the difference in giving-up density between open and covered trays isolates the effect of microhabitat-specific predation risk on foraging effort, rather than confounding it with which site happened to have more predators overall.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks "what was your control, and what exactly does it isolate?" because naming a control without explaining what confound it removes suggests the design wasn't really thought through. A weak answer is "we had a group we didn't play anything to." A strong answer specifies the confound each control removes — a silent trial isolates signal content from generic disturbance, an empty tray isolates food reward from handling — and, for playback, explains why multiple independent song exemplars per treatment were used rather than one recording repeated on every subject.

questions.prompt: What is the specific statistical flaw Kroodsma identified in early bird-song playback studies that used one recorded exemplar per treatment played to many subjects?

options.text: Pseudoreplication: the exemplar, not the subject, is the true unit of replication
Sample sizes were too large to analyze
The birds habituated to the sound too quickly to respond
The recordings were not loud enough to trigger a response

explanations.a: Correct — treating many subjects exposed to the same single recording as independent replicates of a treatment (Hurlbert's 1984 pseudoreplication) means any observed effect could just reflect a quirk of that one exemplar, not the treatment category in general.
explanations.b: The problem is about the level at which independence is claimed, not about sample size being too large.
explanations.c: Habituation speed is a real design concern in playback work but is not the specific flaw Kroodsma's pseudoreplication critique targets.
explanations.d: Signal amplitude is a calibration issue, unrelated to the statistical non-independence Kroodsma flagged.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended fix for the single-exemplar pseudoreplication problem in playback experiments?

options.text: Play the single best recording even louder
Use multiple independent exemplars per treatment, drawn from different individuals, and randomize order
Abandon playback experiments entirely in favor of observation only
Use the same exemplar but test twice as many subjects

explanations.a: Amplitude has nothing to do with whether the exemplar itself is representative of the treatment category.
explanations.b: Correct — using several independent recordings per treatment and analyzing exemplar as a factor restores true replication at the level the treatment claim is being made about.
explanations.c: Playback remains a valid and widely used method; the fix is a better design, not abandoning the method.
explanations.d: More subjects exposed to the same single exemplar does not fix pseudoreplication — it still tests one recording's properties, just with more subjects hearing it.

questions.prompt: Match each field manipulation to its appropriate control.

right.text: Silent trial or a heterospecific/non-signal sound
Empty tray with identical handling but no food reward
Same site and time with no decoy present

questions.explanation: Each control isolates the specific stimulus content (signal, food reward, or visual predator cue) from the general disturbance of the experimental setup itself.

questions.prompt: Why does a paired, within-site design generally beat a between-site comparison for a field manipulation?

options.text: It requires fewer total trials to run
It removes site-level confounds like differing predator density or productivity that a between-site design would mix up with the treatment effect
It eliminates the need for any control condition
It guarantees a statistically significant result

explanations.a: Trial count depends on the specific design, not inherently on whether it is paired within-site or between-site.
explanations.b: Correct — sites differ in baseline predator density, food availability, and habitat quality, so comparing treatment at one site to control at another confounds the treatment with whatever the sites differed on; pairing both conditions at the same site controls for that.
explanations.c: A control condition is still required within a paired design; pairing does not replace the need for one.
explanations.d: No design guarantees significance; pairing improves internal validity by removing a specific confound, not the outcome of a statistical test.

lessons.label: Instruments: Cameras, Loggers, and Recorders

sections.heading: Camera traps: zone, lag, and effort
sections.body: Motion- or heat-triggered camera traps let researchers sample animals without a human present, but three technical properties shape what the resulting data mean. The detection zone is the cone-shaped area where the passive infrared sensor actually triggers, which is narrower than the camera's visible field of view, so an animal can appear in a photo without ever having tripped the sensor, or trip the sensor just outside the frame. Trigger lag is the delay between detection and the shutter firing, which can cause fast-moving animals to be missed or only partially captured. Because deployment length varies by camera and by study, effort is standardized as camera-trap-nights — one camera active for one night equals one unit — making detection rates comparable across arrays and studies of different duration or camera number.

sections.heading: Defining an independent detection
sections.body: A single animal lingering in front of a camera, or walking back and forth, can trigger dozens of photos that are really one event, so studies define an independence interval — commonly 30 minutes, following conventions like O'Brien et al. (2003) and widely used in camera-trap reviews such as Rovero and Zimmermann's — after which a new photo of the same species (or same identifiable individual) at that station counts as a new, independent detection. Without a stated interval, raw photo counts wildly inflate apparent abundance for whichever species happens to sit still longest.

sections.heading: Bio-loggers, acoustic recorders, and RFID, and their trade-offs
sections.body: GPS tags record location fixes at a programmed interval, trading fix frequency against battery life and onboard memory. Tri-axial accelerometers record acceleration along three axes at high frequency, and when paired with machine-learning classifiers trained on ground-truthed behavior, the resulting acceleration signatures can distinguish behavioral states — resting, walking, foraging, flying — without any direct observation at all, a technique used from cheetah sprints to seabird foraging dives. A widely cited rule of thumb, often called the 5% rule (sometimes stated as 3-5% of body mass), caps total tag-plus-harness mass to limit its effect on the animal's movement energetics, though it is a rough guideline, not a guarantee that a tag under that threshold has zero effect — some species and life stages are far more sensitive than others. Autonomous acoustic recording units (ARUs), such as Wildlife Acoustics Song Meters, log audio on a schedule over days to weeks, later processed by automated species-identification software (e.g., BirdNET) to enable passive acoustic monitoring with no observer physically present. RFID or PIT-tag antennas at feeders or nest-box entrances automatically log every visit by a tagged individual, yielding continuous individual-level attendance records no direct-observation protocol could match. Every one of these devices can itself change the behavior it measures — a camera's infrared glow, a collar's drag, or an antenna's hum near a feeder — so device effects belong in the discussion of any study that uses them.

lessons.workedExample: A study tagging 20-gram songbirds with miniature GPS loggers must keep total tag-plus-harness mass under roughly 1 gram to respect the 5% body-mass guideline. Separately, a 15-station camera-trap array run for 30 days accumulates 450 camera-trap-nights of effort; raw triggers show 900 total photos of one resident deer revisiting a single station, but applying a 30-minute independence interval collapses those into a much smaller number of true independent detection events — the number that actually belongs in a relative-abundance index, since reporting raw photo counts would make that one deer look like far more animal activity than actually occurred.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks how effort and detections were standardized because raw device output (photo counts, GPS fixes) is not directly comparable across studies or even across stations in the same study. A weak answer reports "we got 900 photos of deer" with no denominator. A strong answer reports camera-trap-nights as the effort unit, states the independence interval used to define a detection event, and — for a tagged or collared species — acknowledges the tag-mass guideline followed and any suspected device effect on the animal's behavior.

questions.prompt: Camera-trap survey effort is conventionally standardized using which unit?

options.text: Total number of raw photos captured
Camera-trap-nights (one camera active for one night = one unit)
Total memory card capacity used
Number of species detected, regardless of effort

explanations.a: Raw photo counts conflate effort with detection rate and with how long any one animal lingered; they are not an effort unit.
explanations.b: Correct — camera-trap-nights standardizes deployment duration across cameras and studies, giving a consistent denominator for computing detection rates.
explanations.c: Memory card capacity is a hardware limit, unrelated to standardizing sampling effort across sites or studies.
explanations.d: Species richness is an outcome measure, not a measure of the sampling effort that produced it.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a defined independence interval (e.g., 30 minutes) in camera-trap analysis?

options.text: To set how long the camera's battery lasts
To distinguish separate, independent detection events from repeated photos of one animal lingering at the station
To determine the size of the detection zone
To decide how often the memory card must be swapped

explanations.a: Battery life is a hardware property unrelated to how detections are counted from the resulting photos.
explanations.b: Correct — without a stated interval, one animal that lingers or repeatedly walks past the camera would inflate the apparent detection count for that species relative to species that pass through quickly.
explanations.c: Detection zone is a property of the sensor's field of triggering, set by the device and its placement, not by the independence interval.
explanations.d: Memory card swapping is a logistical concern unrelated to defining what counts as one detection event in the data.

questions.prompt: The widely cited tag-mass guideline for bio-loggers limits total tag mass to roughly what fraction of the animal's body mass?

options.text: There is no widely cited guideline

explanations.a: Correct — the commonly cited rule of thumb caps tag-plus-harness mass at roughly 3-5% of body mass to limit effects on movement energetics, though it remains a rough guideline rather than a guarantee against device effects.
explanations.b: A tag at 25-30% of body mass would be expected to substantially impair movement in most tagged species; this far exceeds the conventional guideline.
explanations.c: 50% of body mass is far beyond any accepted tagging guideline and would be considered a serious welfare concern.
explanations.d: A widely cited guideline does exist, commonly referenced as the 3-5% (or "5%") rule.

questions.prompt: Match each instrument to what it primarily enables.

right.text: Presence/relative abundance via motion-triggered detection
Fine-scale behavioral-state classification from movement signatures
Passive species detection from recorded audio, no observer present
Automatic logging of individual visits at a fixed point

questions.explanation: Camera traps give presence/relative-abundance data from motion triggers, accelerometers classify behavioral states from acceleration signatures, ARUs passively detect species from audio without an observer, and RFID/PIT antennas automatically log individually identified visits at a fixed station.

lessons.label: Marking and Identifying Individuals

sections.heading: Why identity is the gateway to real questions
sections.body: A dataset of anonymous sightings can describe a population's average behavior, but it cannot answer whether a given individual behaves consistently over time (repeatability, the statistical basis of "animal personality" as framed by Sih et al. in 2004), whether that individual survived and reproduced (mark-recapture demography), or how it is related to others (pedigree-based quantitative genetics and kin-selection tests). Long-running studies such as the banded great tit population at Wytham Woods, running since the 1940s, and marked red deer on the Isle of Rum, are only possible because every animal carries a durable, individually unique identifier that links each new observation back to a known history. Without stable individual identity, every sighting is a fresh anonymous data point, and none of these repeated-measures questions can be asked at all.

sections.heading: Artificial marks — and the fact that marks are not neutral
sections.body: Bird banding with unique color-combination leg bands dates to the early 20th century and remains a core method; insects are marked with numbered tags or paint dots, and honeybee queens use an internationally agreed color-by-year code (white, yellow, red, green, blue, cycling through years ending in 1/6, 2/7, 3/8, 4/9, and 5/0) so any beekeeper can read a queen's approximate age at a glance. Mammals are marked with ear tags or freeze brands. Crucially, a mark can become part of the experiment rather than a neutral label: Nancy Burley's 1982 zebra finch experiments found that leg-band color itself shifted mate preference, with red-banded males rated more attractive and green- or pink-banded males less attractive than unbanded controls, independent of any real quality difference. A researcher who ignores this risks confounding a mark's own color with the behavior it was meant to merely track.

sections.heading: Natural marks and honest reporting of the unmarked
sections.body: Photo-identification exploits naturally occurring, stable variation instead of an applied mark: individually distinct humpback whale fluke pigmentation patterns (pioneered by Katona and Whitehead), unique spot patterns on whale sharks, whisker-spot arrangements on lions, and wing-wear or nick patterns in bees and dragonflies. These avoid handling stress and the mark-effect risk entirely but demand careful, often double-reviewed, photo-matching protocols. Sexing and ageing from plumage, tooth wear, size, or molt stage let a study stratify data without needing full individual identity. When a population genuinely cannot be marked or reliably re-identified, honest practice reports the data as "observations" or "sightings" rather than as counts of distinct "individuals," since the same unmarked animal could easily be recounted.

lessons.workedExample: A 3-year study of chipmunk boldness bands each captured animal with a unique three-color leg-band combination (e.g., red-blue-yellow) recorded at first capture, letting the same individual's open-field boldness score be compared year over year — exactly what a repeatability estimate requires. A parallel leopard study instead relies entirely on each cat's unique rosette pattern from camera-trap photos, avoiding capture altogether, but requires two independent reviewers to confirm a match before an individual is logged, precisely because photo-ID errors (splitting one animal into two, or merging two into one) would corrupt the same repeated-measures logic the marking is meant to enable.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks "how do you know these are 30 different individuals and not fewer animals sighted repeatedly?" because an unjustified assumption of distinctness silently converts pseudo-replicated sightings into inflated sample size. A weak answer assumes every sighting is a new individual. A strong answer names the specific identification method used (band combination, natural photo-ID feature), acknowledges that a chosen artificial mark can itself bias behavior (citing evidence like Burley's band-color effect), and, for any unmarked cases, explicitly downgrades those data points to "observations" rather than counting them as individuals.

questions.prompt: Nancy Burley's 1982 zebra finch leg-band experiments demonstrated what important caveat about marking animals?

options.text: Leg bands have no measurable effect on any aspect of behavior
Band color itself can shift mate preference and attractiveness, making the mark a potential confound
Zebra finches cannot be marked with leg bands at all
Only wing marks, never leg bands, affect mate choice

explanations.a: The study specifically found band color did have a measurable effect, contradicting this option.
explanations.b: Correct — red-banded males were rated more attractive and green/pink-banded males less attractive than unbanded birds, showing the mark itself can bias the very behavior (mate choice) a study might be trying to measure.
explanations.c: Zebra finches were successfully banded in the study; the finding was about the mark's effect, not feasibility.
explanations.d: The finding concerned leg-band color specifically, not a claim that only wing marks matter.

questions.prompt: What does stable individual identification make possible that a series of anonymous sightings cannot support?

options.text: Estimating repeatability of behavior, mark-recapture survival, and pedigree-based analyses
Determining the total species richness at a site
Measuring ambient temperature during observation
Calculating a sampling interval from pilot bout-duration data

explanations.a: Correct — linking repeated observations to the same known individual over time is what allows repeatability, survival/mark-recapture, and kinship/pedigree questions to be answered at all.
explanations.b: Species richness can be estimated from anonymous species-level sightings without individual identity.
explanations.c: Temperature measurement is unrelated to whether individuals are identifiable.
explanations.d: Sampling-interval choice depends on bout-duration data, not on whether individuals are individually marked.

questions.prompt: Match each marking approach to its example.

left.text: Applied artificial mark on a vertebrate

right.text: Humpback whale fluke pigmentation pattern
Unique color leg-band combination
Honeybee queen color-by-year paint code

questions.explanation: Fluke pigmentation is a naturally occurring, stable pattern used for photo-ID; leg bands are an applied artificial mark on birds/mammals; and the internationally agreed queen-marking color code is the standard insect-marking convention in beekeeping.

questions.prompt: When a population truly cannot be marked or reliably re-identified, what is the honest way to report the data?

options.text: Report every count as a distinct individual, since re-sighting is unlikely
Report the data as observations or sightings, not as counts of individuals
Exclude the population from the study entirely
Estimate individual identity using body size alone

explanations.a: Assuming every sighting is a new individual risks inflating the apparent sample size with recounted animals.
explanations.b: Correct — labeling the data as observations/sightings rather than individuals is honest about the uncertainty and avoids overstating how many distinct animals were actually studied.
explanations.c: Exclusion is unnecessary; the data remain useful for many purposes (e.g., presence, activity patterns) as long as they are honestly labeled as sightings rather than individuals.
explanations.d: Body size alone is rarely a reliable individual identifier and would introduce its own matching errors without solving the underlying problem.

lessons.label: Ethics, Permits, and Welfare

sections.heading: The governing frameworks
sections.body: The Association for the Study of Animal Behaviour (ASAB) and the Animal Behavior Society (ABS) jointly publish annually updated "Guidelines for the Treatment of Animals in Behavioural Research and Teaching" in the journals Animal Behaviour and Animal Behavior, covering justification of animal numbers and procedures, housing and field-disturbance standards, and reporting expectations. In the United States, any institutionally affiliated research on live vertebrates — university, and for many programs, high-school science-fair research done under institutional mentorship — requires prior review by an Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) before any animal contact begins, not as a formality filed afterward. Russell and Burch's 1959 framework of the 3Rs — Replacement (use a non-animal alternative if one answers the question), Reduction (use the minimum number of animals needed for valid results), and Refinement (minimize pain, distress, and disturbance in the procedures used) — underlies how such review bodies evaluate a proposed protocol.

sections.heading: What actually governs a science-fair entry
sections.body: For an ISEF-affiliated science-fair project specifically, the binding rules are Society for Science's International Rules, particularly the Vertebrate Animal (VA) rules. Any project involving live vertebrates requires pre-approval before experimentation begins — approval sought or granted after data collection already started disqualifies the project regardless of how sound the science later turns out to be. Projects beyond simple observation typically require a Designated Supervisor or Qualified Scientist overseeing the work, and protocols that would cause pain, distress, or death without strong scientific and veterinary justification are prohibited outright. Purely observational field studies of unrestrained wild vertebrates — no capture, no handling, no manipulation that could cause distress — generally qualify for a lower review tier than studies involving capture, marking, or playback intense enough to provoke a strong flight or alarm response, which push the project into full VA review.

sections.heading: Field-specific welfare practice
sections.body: Practical welfare rules in the field include time limits on nest or den visits, staying outside a species' flush distance, and avoiding especially vulnerable windows such as early incubation when disturbance risks nest abandonment. Pre-set stopping rules — for example, ending a playback trial immediately if the focal animal flees rather than simply increasing vigilance, or capping total stimulus exposure per individual per day — convert vague good intentions into an enforceable protocol decided before data collection, not improvised in the moment. Capturing, marking, or collecting protected or invasive species requires the relevant state or federal wildlife permits in addition to institutional review. Finally, because manipulation always risks introducing its own artifacts and disturbance, a well-designed, purely observational study is frequently both the more ethical and the scientifically stronger choice — it sidesteps manipulation-driven confounds while still answering a real behavioral question.

lessons.workedExample: A student proposes testing whether a recorded hawk alarm call changes chipmunk vigilance behavior. Because the design involves only observing free-ranging wild vertebrates' response to an acoustic stimulus, with no capture or handling, it can typically proceed under a lower review tier once pre-approved, provided it caps trials per individual per day, sets playback volume to match natural call levels, and includes an explicit stopping rule — for instance, ending a trial immediately if the animal flees the area rather than merely raising its head — rather than continuing to collect data on a visibly stressed subject.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks "was this approved before you started, and what would have made you stop a trial?" because ethics treated as paperwork filed after data collection is not real ethical review. A weak answer describes getting a signature after the fact or has no answer for what would trigger stopping a trial. A strong answer states that approval was obtained before experimentation began, names a concrete stopping rule tied to a specific observable sign of distress, and explains why the chosen design (e.g., no capture, playback volume matched to natural levels) kept risk to the animals low in the first place.

questions.prompt: Russell and Burch's 1959 "3Rs" framework stands for which three principles?

options.text: Replacement, Reduction, Refinement
Recording, Reliability, Reporting
Randomization, Replication, Regulation
Repeatability, Reversibility, Restraint

explanations.a: Correct — Replacement (use a non-animal alternative where possible), Reduction (minimize animal numbers to what valid results require), and Refinement (minimize pain and distress in procedures used) are the three principles.
explanations.b: These are observer-reliability concepts from a different topic (recording rules), not the 3Rs of animal-research ethics.
explanations.c: Randomization and replication are experimental-design concepts, not the specific ethics framework Russell and Burch proposed.
explanations.d: These terms are not the standard 3Rs; Replacement, Reduction, and Refinement is the established framework.

questions.prompt: Under ISEF Vertebrate Animal (VA) rules, when must a project involving live vertebrates be approved?

options.text: Before experimentation begins
Any time before the science fair judging round
After preliminary data collection, once feasibility is confirmed
Approval is optional if the study is observational

explanations.a: Correct — prior approval before any experimentation with live vertebrates begins is required; approval obtained afterward does not satisfy the rule, regardless of the study's scientific merit.
explanations.b: Approval must precede experimentation, not merely precede the judging round after data has already been collected.
explanations.c: Starting data collection before approval violates the rule even if the study later proves feasible and well-designed.
explanations.d: Even purely observational vertebrate studies require some level of prior review under the VA rules, though the review tier may be lighter.

questions.prompt: Which type of vertebrate behavior project typically qualifies for a lower review tier under VA rules?

options.text: A study involving trapping and physically restraining animals for repeated marking
A purely observational field study of unrestrained wild vertebrates with no capture or manipulation
A study administering an experimental substance to test its behavioral effect
A study involving surgical implantation of a tracking device

explanations.a: Capture and restraint substantially raise the risk of distress and push a project into full VA review, not a lower tier.
explanations.b: Correct — observation-only designs with no capture, handling, or manipulation that could cause distress generally qualify for a lighter review tier than manipulative or invasive designs.
explanations.c: Administering a substance is an invasive manipulation requiring full review and strong justification, not a lower-tier study.
explanations.d: Surgical implantation is an invasive procedure requiring the highest level of review and veterinary oversight.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of running an ethically sound field behavior study on wild vertebrates.

items.text: Define a concrete distress-based stopping rule for any trial
Submit the protocol for IACUC/VA prior approval before any animal contact
Allow a habituation or pilot period once approved
Collect data, enforcing the stopping rule in real time
Report compliance and any deviations in the final write-up

questions.explanation: The stopping rule must be defined before the protocol is submitted, approval must precede any animal contact, a habituation/pilot period follows approval, data collection then proceeds under the enforced stopping rule, and compliance is documented afterward.

lessons.label: From Raw Records to Rates and Time Budgets

sections.heading: Counts are not data until you divide
sections.body: A scored ethogram — timestamped events and states — is not yet analyzable. It has to be converted into three summary numbers: frequency (events per unit observation time, e.g. pecks/hour), duration (total or mean time spent in a state), and proportion of time budget (duration in a state divided by total observation time for that subject). The trap is the denominator problem: if focal A was watched for 20 minutes and shows 8 foraging bouts while focal B was watched 45 minutes and shows 12, the raw counts say B forages more. Divide by effort and the ranking flips — A is 24 bouts/hour, B is 16/hour. Any comparison across individuals, sessions, or treatments that skips this division is comparing observation effort, not behavior. Altmann's 1974 focal-animal and scan-sampling framework built time budgets exactly this way, as proportions of sampled time, precisely so unequal watch lengths would not bias the result.

sections.heading: Where does one bout end and the next begin?
sections.body: Duration measures also need a rule for grouping successive short acts into a single 'bout' rather than counting each pause as a new event. Picking an arbitrary gap (e.g. 'more than 10 seconds apart = new bout') is unfalsifiable — a different analyst picks a different number and gets a different answer. Fagen and Young (1978), refined by Sibly, Nott and Fletcher (1990), gave a data-driven fix: log-survivorship analysis. Take every inter-act gap, and for each gap length t plot the log of the number of gaps still 'surviving' (≥ t) against t. If gaps came from one random process, the plot is a straight line (a single exponential). Real behavior usually shows two slopes: a steep initial drop (short within-bout pauses) followed by a shallower tail (long between-bout intervals). The breakpoint between the two slopes is the bout criterion interval (BCI) — the defensible, data-derived cutoff, rather than a guessed number.

sections.heading: Building the time budget
sections.body: Once bouts are defined, three linked numbers describe the behavior: frequency (bouts per hour), mean bout length (total duration ÷ number of bouts), and proportion of time (total duration ÷ total observation time). These three are related — proportion of time equals frequency multiplied by mean bout length — so a treatment that halves bout frequency but doubles mean length can leave the time budget unchanged even though the underlying pattern changed completely, which is exactly the kind of result a good analysis should be able to detect and explain rather than average away.

lessons.workedExample: A student observes vigilance in ground squirrels: Squirrel 1 watched 15 min, 6 vigilance bouts, total vigilant time 90 s. Squirrel 2 watched 40 min, 10 bouts, total vigilant time 300 s. Raw duration says Squirrel 2 is more vigilant (300 s > 90 s). Converting to rate: Squirrel 1 = 24 bouts/hour, mean bout 15 s, proportion of time = 10%. Squirrel 2 = 15 bouts/hour, mean bout 30 s, proportion of time = 12.5%. Squirrel 2 is still slightly more vigilant by proportion, but the frequency comparison reverses — Squirrel 1 actually scans more often, just in shorter bursts — a distinction the raw totals hid entirely.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe this because dividing by observation effort is the single most common place a student behavioral project silently breaks. A weak answer reports raw counts or total durations and treats unequal watch times as a footnote. A strong answer states the observation time for every subject up front, reports frequency and proportion of time (not just one), and can explain — ideally with a log-survivorship plot or at least a stated bout-gap rule — why acts were grouped into bouts the way they were, rather than picking a round-number cutoff because it looked reasonable.

questions.prompt: Focal A is watched 10 minutes and shows 4 chase events; Focal B is watched 30 minutes and shows 9 chase events. Which statement is correct?

options.text: B chases more often, since 9 > 4
A chases more often per unit time, since 24/hr > 18/hr
They chase equally often since both are 'a few' events
The comparison is impossible without duration data

explanations.a: Comparing raw counts ignores that B was watched three times as long as A — this is the denominator problem the lesson warns against.
explanations.b: Correct — dividing by observation time gives A = 24 events/hour and B = 18 events/hour, reversing the raw-count impression.
explanations.c: The rates are not equal; 24/hr is meaningfully higher than 18/hr.
explanations.d: Frequency (events per time) can be computed from counts and observation time alone; duration of each event is not required for a rate.

questions.prompt: In a log-survivorship plot of inter-act gap lengths, what does the breakpoint between the steep initial slope and the shallower tail represent?

options.text: A recording error that should be discarded
The bout criterion interval (BCI), separating within-bout pauses from between-bout intervals
The mean total observation time per subject
The point where the animal stopped performing the behavior entirely

explanations.a: The break is an expected feature of two-process data, not an artifact to throw out.
explanations.b: Correct — Fagen and Young (1978) used exactly this break as a data-derived bout criterion interval instead of an arbitrary gap cutoff.
explanations.c: Observation time is a separate quantity tracked per subject, unrelated to the shape of the gap-length distribution.
explanations.d: The plot describes gap lengths across the whole session, not a single stopping point.

questions.prompt: Match each time-budget quantity to its definition.

right.text: Bouts per unit observation time
Total duration in the state ÷ number of bouts
Total duration in the state ÷ total observation time

questions.explanation: Frequency normalizes bout counts by watch time; mean bout length normalizes total duration by number of bouts; proportion of time normalizes total duration by total observation time. Proportion of time equals frequency times mean bout length.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a defensible bout-length analysis, from raw records to a stated bout criterion.

items.text: Score every act with a timestamp during observation
Compute the gap length between every pair of successive acts
Plot log(number of gaps surviving ≥ t) against t
Identify the breakpoint between the steep and shallow slopes
Use that breakpoint as the bout criterion interval to group acts into bouts

questions.explanation: Log-survivorship analysis starts from raw timestamps, derives gap lengths, plots their survivorship on a log scale, reads off the slope break, and only then uses that break as the grouping rule — the criterion is derived from the data, not assumed before looking at it.

lessons.label: Preference and Selection Indices

sections.heading: Use versus availability, not use alone
sections.body: An animal eating mostly beetles tells you nothing about preference until you know what was on offer. Selection indices compare the proportion of a resource used, r, against the proportion available, p. Ivlev's electivity index (Ivlev 1961), E = (r − p)/(r + p), is the classic form: it ranges from −1 (total avoidance) to +1 (total preference), with 0 meaning use matches availability exactly. Its weakness is nonlinearity — E compresses as p gets small, so equal-sized preferences at different availabilities are not directly comparable. Jacobs (1974) proposed D = (r − p)/(r + p − 2rp), which behaves more linearly across the full range of p and is now the more commonly recommended electivity statistic for that reason.

sections.heading: Manly's alpha and testing the whole diet or habitat set at once
sections.body: Both E and D compare one resource type at a time. Manly's alpha (from Manly, Miller and Cook 1972, later generalized by Chesson 1978) instead standardizes selection across every resource category simultaneously: alpha_i is proportional to (r_i / p_i), rescaled so all alpha values across categories sum to 1. This makes alpha directly interpretable as 'if the animal chose randomly among what's left, category i would get this share' — useful when a forager is choosing among many prey types or habitat patches at once rather than just one focal resource against everything else. For a single categorical test — does observed habitat use differ from availability at all — a chi-square goodness-of-fit test compares observed counts in each category to expected counts (available proportion × total observations); a significant result says selection is non-random without saying which categories drive it.

sections.heading: Compositional analysis, and the honest limit of all of these
sections.body: Habitat proportions are compositional data — they sum to 1, so categories are not statistically independent, which inflates false positives in naive chi-square or ANOVA tests run category-by-category. Aebischer, Robertson and Kenward (1993) introduced compositional analysis: log-ratio transform the proportions, then test used versus available compositions with a MANOVA-style approach that respects the unit-sum constraint and treats each animal as one independent replicate. But every one of these methods shares an unavoidable weak point: 'availability' is not a measured fact, it is a decision the investigator makes — the whole study area? the home range? only patches within reach in one night? Redefining the available area can flip the same use data from 'strong preference' to 'no selection' to 'avoidance' without a single new observation, which is why a competent write-up always states, explicitly, how availability was defined and defends that choice.

lessons.workedExample: A student tracks deer habitat use: forest is used 60% of fixes, grassland 20%, edge 20%. If 'available' is the entire 10 km2 study area — forest 30%, grassland 50%, edge 20% — Ivlev's E for forest = (0.6−0.3)/(0.6+0.3) = +0.33 (preference), and for grassland = (0.2−0.5)/(0.7) = −0.43 (avoidance). Now redefine availability as only the deer's 2 km2 home range, where forest happens to cover 55% and grassland 25%: forest's E drops to (0.6−0.55)/(1.15) ≈ +0.04 (essentially neutral) and grassland's E becomes (0.2−0.25)/(0.45) ≈ −0.11 (mild, not strong, avoidance). Identical use data, two defensible availability definitions, two very different preference stories.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on selection indices because the arithmetic is easy to get right while the underlying claim is easy to get wrong. A weak answer reports a preference index and stops. A strong answer states exactly what was treated as 'available' and why (whole landscape vs. home range vs. accessible patches), acknowledges that a different reasonable choice could shift or reverse the result, and — if comparing multiple habitat categories at once — knows that testing them one at a time with repeated chi-square tests overstates significance because the categories are not independent, which is precisely what compositional analysis exists to fix.

questions.prompt: A resource is used at proportion r = 0.4 and available at proportion p = 0.4. What does Ivlev's electivity index E equal, and what does that mean?

options.text: E = 0.8; strong preference
E = 0; use matches availability, no evidence of selection
E = -0.4; avoidance
E cannot be computed when r equals p

explanations.a: E = (r-p)/(r+p) = 0/0.8 = 0, not 0.8; this option miscalculates the formula.
explanations.b: Correct — when use exactly equals availability, the numerator (r-p) is zero, giving E = 0, the reference point for 'no selection'.
explanations.c: E is 0, not negative; avoidance requires r < p.
explanations.d: E is well-defined whenever r+p is not zero; r = p simply gives the neutral value.

questions.prompt: Why did Jacobs (1974) propose D = (r-p)/(r+p-2rp) as an alternative to Ivlev's E?

options.text: D is easier to compute by hand
D behaves more linearly across the range of availability p, making preferences of equal strength more comparable at different p
D removes the need to know availability at all
D applies only to plant resources, unlike E

explanations.a: D is not simpler arithmetically than E — both are ratio formulas of similar complexity.
explanations.b: Correct — Ivlev's E compresses nonlinearly as p shrinks, so the same underlying preference strength yields different E values at different availabilities; Jacobs' D corrects this.
explanations.c: D still requires both r and p as inputs, exactly like E.
explanations.d: Both indices are general-purpose and apply to any resource-use comparison, not just plants.

questions.prompt: Why is testing habitat categories one at a time with separate chi-square tests problematic when the categories are proportions that sum to 1?

options.text: Chi-square tests cannot be used on proportions under any circumstances
The categories are not statistically independent, so repeated per-category tests inflate the false-positive rate
Proportions summing to 1 always indicate perfect selection
Chi-square requires availability data that compositional data lacks

explanations.a: Chi-square goodness-of-fit is a standard tool for count/proportion data; the issue is non-independence across categories, not the test itself.
explanations.b: Correct — because the proportions are constrained to sum to 1, an increase in one category's use mechanically implies a decrease elsewhere, violating the independence assumption behind treating each category test separately; this is exactly what compositional analysis (Aebischer et al. 1993) was built to address.
explanations.c: Summing to 1 is a mathematical property of any proportion breakdown, unrelated to whether selection occurred.
explanations.d: Compositional data still includes availability; the problem is statistical non-independence, not missing data.

questions.prompt: Match each method to what it is best suited for.

right.text: Simple one-resource-at-a-time electivity, historically first but nonlinear
Standardized selection ratio across many resource categories at once
Testing full used-vs-available composition while respecting the unit-sum constraint

questions.explanation: Ivlev's E handles one category against the rest; Manly's alpha rescales selection ratios across all categories to sum to 1; compositional analysis (Aebischer, Robertson & Kenward 1993) log-ratio transforms the full composition so categories are tested without violating independence assumptions.

lessons.label: Non-independence, Pseudoreplication, and Repeatability

sections.heading: Hurlbert's pseudoreplication, applied to behavior
sections.body: Stuart Hurlbert's 1984 paper in Ecological Monographs (54: 187–211) named a problem that still trips up behavioral projects: treating non-independent measurements as if each one were an independent replicate, then running inferential statistics on the inflated sample size. Hurlbert reviewed published field experiments across ecology and found pseudoreplication was widespread among studies that used inferential statistics. In a behavior context the trap looks like: watching one bird 30 times and analyzing 30 data points as though 30 different birds were sampled, or playing the same three song recordings to 90 subjects and treating the responses as 90 independent tests of 'how animals respond to song' rather than 3 tests of specific exemplars replicated across subjects. Both the individual and the stimulus can be the non-independent unit.

sections.heading: The fix: random effects, not bigger n
sections.body: The statistical fix is a mixed-effects model: fit individual identity (and, for playback work, stimulus exemplar identity) as a random effect, with the fixed effect of interest (treatment, sex, condition) estimated on top of it. This keeps every repeated measurement in the analysis — nothing is thrown away — while correctly crediting the true number of independent units (animals, or exemplars) rather than the inflated number of measurements. A model with 10 fish measured 5 times each has an effective replication closer to 10 than 50, and a mixed model with fish ID as a random intercept produces standard errors and p-values that reflect that reality instead of overstating confidence.

sections.heading: Repeatability as the intraclass correlation, and its ceiling on other correlations
sections.body: Repeated measures on the same individuals also answer a question in their own right: how consistent is an individual's behavior over time? Repeatability, R, is the intraclass correlation coefficient — the proportion of total variance in a trait that lies between individuals rather than within them, R = variance-among-individuals / (variance-among-individuals + variance-within-individuals), estimable from a one-way ANOVA (Lessells and Boag 1987) or more flexibly from a mixed model (Nakagawa and Schielzeth 2010). Bell, Hankison and Laskowski's 2009 meta-analysis in Animal Behaviour, pooling hundreds of estimates across taxa, put the average behavioral repeatability at about 0.37 — meaning a typical behavior is roughly two-thirds within-individual noise or plasticity and only about a third stable individual difference. This matters beyond description: repeatability sets a hard statistical ceiling on how strongly any single behavior can correlate with another variable, such as fitness — the maximum possible correlation is bounded by the square root of R. With R ≈ 0.37, no honest single-behavior-fitness correlation can exceed roughly 0.6, however large the sample.

lessons.workedExample: A team measures boldness (latency to emerge from a shelter) in 12 sticklebacks, testing each fish 4 times, for 48 total trials. Treating all 48 as independent and running a simple correlation between latency and body size gives an artificially small p-value because each fish's 4 trials are correlated with each other (pseudoreplication). Instead, the team fits a mixed model with fish ID as a random intercept and body size as a fixed effect, and separately computes repeatability from a one-way ANOVA on the same data: mean square among fish = 210, mean square within fish = 60, mean group size n = 4, giving among-fish variance = (210-60)/4 = 37.5, so R = 37.5/(37.5+60) ≈ 0.38 — close to Bell et al.'s cross-taxa average, and a signal that roughly 38% of the variation in boldness is a stable individual trait worth relating to fitness.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'how many times did you measure each animal, and how did you handle the repeats?' because it is the fastest way to tell whether a student understands their own sample size. A weak answer says '30 trials' when that means one animal tested 30 times, and runs a t-test as if n=30. A strong answer states the true number of independent units (animals or stimulus exemplars), explains that repeated measures were handled with a random effect for individual (and exemplar, for playback designs) rather than pooled as independent, and — if repeatability is part of the claim — reports R as a number, not just 'the behavior was fairly consistent,' and recognizes that a modest R legitimately caps how strong any behavior-fitness correlation can be.

questions.prompt: A researcher plays the same 3 recorded songs to 60 birds and analyzes the 60 responses as 60 independent replicates of 'response to song.' What is the pseudoreplication here?

options.text: There is none; 60 birds is a large, valid sample
The stimulus (song exemplar) is pseudoreplicated — there are really only 3 independent stimulus replicates, reused across birds
Birds cannot be used as subjects in playback experiments
60 is too small a sample regardless of design

explanations.a: 60 independent birds does not fix the problem if all of them heard from a pool of only 3 songs — the songs, not just the birds, need independent replication.
explanations.b: Correct — inferences about 'response to song' generalize only as far as the number of independent song exemplars used; treating 60 trials of 3 songs as 60 independent tests of song overstates the true replication, exactly the pattern Hurlbert (1984) flagged.
explanations.c: Birds are a standard, valid subject for playback work; the issue is stimulus replication, not the taxon.
explanations.d: Sample size of 60 subjects is not inherently too small; the flaw is which unit is truly independent, not the raw count.

questions.prompt: What is the standard statistical fix for repeated measurements on the same individuals, without discarding any data?

options.text: Average all repeats into one value per individual before any modeling
Fit a mixed-effects model with individual identity as a random effect
Randomly delete repeats until each individual has exactly one measurement
Ignore the repetition; more data points always improve a model

explanations.a: Averaging discards within-individual variation entirely and cannot separate individual consistency from measurement noise, unlike a mixed model.
explanations.b: Correct — a random intercept (or slope) for individual identity keeps every measurement while correctly attributing shared variance to the individual rather than treating repeats as independent.
explanations.c: Deleting data to force independence throws away real information the mixed-model approach preserves.
explanations.d: Treating repeated, non-independent measurements as independent inflates the effective sample size and understates uncertainty — this is the pseudoreplication problem itself.

questions.prompt: Bell, Hankison and Laskowski (2009) found average behavioral repeatability across taxa to be about R = 0.37. What does this value most directly imply?

options.text: 37% of individuals show no behavior at all
On average, about 37% of total variance in a behavior lies between individuals, and about 63% is within-individual variation
Behavior is unmeasurable and repeatability estimates should be discarded
Every behavior in every species has exactly this repeatability

explanations.a: R describes a variance partition, not the fraction of individuals displaying a behavior.
explanations.b: Correct — R is the intraclass correlation, so R ≈ 0.37 means roughly a third of total variance is stable between-individual differences and the rest is within-individual plasticity or noise.
explanations.c: A moderate R is a usable, informative estimate, not a reason to discard the method.
explanations.d: 0.37 is a cross-taxa, cross-behavior average from a meta-analysis; individual behaviors and species vary considerably around it.

questions.prompt: Match each term to what it describes in a repeated-measures behavioral analysis.

right.text: Treating non-independent repeated measures as independent replicates
Model term that credits shared variance to the individual, correcting the effective sample size
Proportion of total variance that lies between individuals rather than within them

questions.explanation: Pseudoreplication (Hurlbert 1984) is the error of inflating replication by ignoring non-independence; a random effect for individual identity is the mixed-model fix; repeatability is the intraclass correlation that quantifies how much of a behavior's variance is a stable individual trait.

lessons.label: Sequences, Transitions, and Social Networks

sections.heading: Behavior as structure: transition matrices
sections.body: Some questions are not about how often a behavior occurs but about what predictably follows what. First-order Markov transition analysis (Slater 1973; Lehner 1979) tallies, for every behavior, how often each other behavior immediately follows it, producing an observed transition matrix. Compared against an expected matrix — built from each behavior's overall frequency under the assumption that sequence is random — a chi-square test asks whether the sequence has real structure. If display A is followed by display B far more than B's baseline frequency predicts, that transition is a genuine behavioral link, not coincidence; courtship sequences and agonistic escalation ladders are classic cases where specific, non-random transition chains (not just individual act frequencies) carry the biological signal. A kinematic (flow) diagram turns the matrix into a directed graph — each behavior a node, each transition an arrow whose thickness scales with probability — making dominant pathways through a behavioral repertoire visible at a glance rather than buried in a table.

sections.heading: Latency as response strength
sections.body: When the question is how strongly a stimulus provokes a response rather than what sequence follows, latency — the time from stimulus onset to first response — is the standard metric. Shorter latency generally indicates a stronger or more salient stimulus (a predator model that triggers an alarm call in 2 seconds is read as more threatening than one that takes 20), and latency pairs naturally with the sequence tools above: a fast first response can also be scored for what it transitions into.

sections.heading: From individual sequences to social structure
sections.body: The same 'who follows whom' logic scales up to groups. Association data — records of which individuals were observed together — are typically converted into a half-weight index (Cairns and Schwager 1987): HWI = x / (x + yAB + 0.5(yA + yB)), where x is the number of sampling periods both A and B were seen together, yAB is periods both were seen but apart, and yA, yB are periods only one of the pair was seen. HWI corrects for the fact that one member of a pair being harder to detect should not, by itself, make the pair look less associated. A matrix of pairwise HWIs becomes a social network: degree (number of distinct associates) identifies gregarious versus solitary individuals, and centrality measures (e.g., betweenness) flag individuals who bridge otherwise separate subgroups — often the ones whose removal would matter most to group cohesion. Because raw association counts are heavily shaped by how often each individual was simply sampled, testing whether a network is more structured than chance requires a permutation-based null model that shuffles observed associations while respecting real sampling constraints — group size and each individual's own sampling frequency — rather than a naive full shuffle that would create impossible group compositions (Bejder et al. 1998; Whitehead's SOCPROG framework).

lessons.workedExample: A student records 800 behavioral transitions in captive chimpanzees. Overall, grooming makes up 15% of all acts. If sequence were random, grooming should follow 'approach' about 15% of the time; observed data show grooming follows approach in 42% of cases (84 of 200 approach-initiated transitions). A chi-square goodness-of-fit test comparing the observed 42% to the 15% random expectation is significant (p < 0.001), showing approach reliably predicts grooming rather than the two co-occurring by chance. Separately, the student builds a 12-individual association matrix using HWI from 40 sampling scans; one adult female has HWI > 0.3 with individuals from three otherwise non-overlapping subgroups and the highest betweenness centrality in the network — a likely social 'broker' whose removal, in a permutation test against 1000 group-structure-respecting shuffles, produces a significantly less connected network than observed.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe sequence and network claims because 'X often happens near Y' is a much weaker claim than 'X predicts Y transitions,' and only the second survives a chi-square test against the random-sequence baseline. A weak answer reports raw transition counts or association counts and calls a busy-looking flow diagram or network graph 'proof' of structure. A strong answer states the expected-under-random baseline it compared against, reports the test statistic, and — for network claims specifically — explains why a null model has to preserve real sampling structure (group size, individual detectability) rather than shuffling associations freely, since a naive shuffle can manufacture apparent structure or destroy real structure by creating group compositions that could never have been observed.

questions.prompt: Grooming makes up 15% of all recorded acts overall, but observed data show it follows 'approach' 42% of the time. What does a chi-square test comparing 42% to the 15% baseline assess?

options.text: Whether grooming occurs more often than approach in absolute terms
Whether the approach-to-grooming transition happens more often than expected if the sequence of acts were random
Whether grooming causes approach behavior
Whether the animals were sampled for a sufficient duration

explanations.a: The test compares a specific transition rate to a random-sequence baseline, not the raw frequencies of the two acts against each other.
explanations.b: Correct — the expected rate under random sequencing is grooming's overall frequency (15%); a significant excess at 42% shows non-random sequential structure, i.e. approach predicts grooming.
explanations.c: A significant transition test shows statistical association in sequence, not a causal mechanism — causation would need a manipulative experiment.
explanations.d: Sampling duration affects statistical power but is a separate question from what the chi-square test itself measures.

questions.prompt: Why does the half-weight index (HWI) include the term 0.5(yA + yB) rather than simply counting joint sightings over total sightings?

options.text: It arbitrarily halves the score to make indices easier to compare across studies
It corrects for cases where only one member of a pair was detected, so imperfect detection of one partner does not automatically deflate the pair's apparent association
It only applies to species with fewer than two sexes
It converts the index from a proportion into a raw count

explanations.a: The 0.5 weighting is a specific correction for one-sided detection, not an arbitrary rescaling.
explanations.b: Correct — Cairns and Schwager (1987) designed HWI so that periods when only A or only B was seen (not both, and not confirmed apart) are down-weighted rather than counted as full evidence of non-association, since the missing partner may simply have been undetected.
explanations.c: HWI is a general pairwise association measure with no dependency on number of sexes.
explanations.d: HWI remains a bounded ratio (0 to 1), not a raw count.

questions.prompt: Why is a naive full-shuffle permutation test inappropriate for testing whether an association network is more structured than chance?

options.text: Permutation tests can never be used on network data
A full shuffle can create group compositions that violate real sampling constraints (like group size or individual detectability), manufacturing or masking structure that isn't real
Permutation tests require normally distributed data, which association counts never have
Shuffling always increases the apparent number of associates per individual

explanations.a: Permutation tests are the standard tool here; the issue is how the shuffle is constrained, not whether to use one at all.
explanations.b: Correct — data-stream permutation methods (Bejder et al. 1998; Whitehead's SOCPROG) preserve each individual's sampling frequency and realistic group sizes when shuffling, so the null distribution reflects a plausible random world rather than an impossible one.
explanations.c: Permutation tests are nonparametric and specifically avoid distributional assumptions like normality.
explanations.d: A shuffle's effect on apparent degree depends on the specific data and constraints used, not a fixed direction.

questions.prompt: Match each social-network term to what it identifies.

right.text: Number of distinct associates an individual has
How often an individual lies on the shortest path connecting other pairs, flagging bridging individuals
Pairwise association strength corrected for imperfect co-detection

questions.explanation: Degree counts an individual's direct associates; betweenness centrality identifies individuals who connect otherwise separate parts of the network; the half-weight index quantifies pairwise association strength while correcting for cases where only one partner was detected.

lessons.label: Space and Direction

sections.heading: Two ways to draw a home range, and why they disagree
sections.body: The oldest home-range estimator, the minimum convex polygon (MCP; Mohr 1947), draws the smallest convex shape enclosing a chosen percentage (typically 95%, to drop extreme outliers) of an animal's location fixes. It is simple and easy to communicate, but it has a real flaw: because it must be convex, it includes any unused area between far-apart points — a fox that uses two separate patches on either side of a road gets an MCP that also 'contains' the road and everything between, wildly overestimating true range. Kernel density estimation (KDE), introduced for home-range work by Worton (1989), instead builds a smooth utilization distribution — a probability surface of where the animal is likely to be — from which you can draw a 95% isopleth (the overall home range) and, separately, a 50% isopleth (the core area of concentrated use). KDE can show two disconnected high-use patches exactly like the fox's, something a single convex polygon structurally cannot do.

sections.heading: The choice that quietly controls the KDE answer
sections.body: KDE's result is highly sensitive to bandwidth (h), the smoothing parameter controlling how far each point's influence spreads. Too large a bandwidth oversmooths, inflating the range and blurring real gaps between patches; too small undersmooths, fragmenting one continuous range into disconnected islands around each fix. Silverman's reference bandwidth (h_ref) is a simple rule-of-thumb default; least-squares cross-validation (LSCV) instead picks h by minimizing prediction error on the data itself, and is generally preferred when it converges, though it can behave poorly with clustered, non-independent fixes — a reminder that reporting a home-range area without stating the bandwidth method is reporting a number that depends on an unstated, arbitrary choice. Overlap between two animals' ranges, whether measured as simple polygon-area overlap or the more informative utilization-distribution overlap index (which weights by how intensively each part of the shared area is used, not just whether it's shared), is the standard way to quantify territoriality or shared space use.

sections.heading: Direction is not a number line: circular statistics
sections.body: Compass bearings and orientations wrap around: 359° and 1° are almost the same direction, but an ordinary arithmetic mean would place their average near 180° — exactly backwards. Circular statistics fix this by treating each bearing as a unit vector and averaging the vector components: the mean direction is the angle of the summed vector (atan2 of summed sine and cosine components), and the mean vector length, r (0 to 1), measures concentration — r near 1 means bearings cluster tightly around one direction, r near 0 means they are scattered or uniform. The Rayleigh test uses r and sample size n to test the null hypothesis that bearings are uniformly distributed around the full circle (no preferred direction); a significant Rayleigh test (formalized for circular data by Batschelet 1981 and Fisher 1993) is the standard evidence that an animal's departure headings, body orientations, or other directional data reflect a real preferred direction rather than chance.

lessons.workedExample: A fox is tracked with 60 GPS fixes across two seasons. The 95% MCP gives a home range of 4.1 km2, drawn as one solid convex shape that includes a stretch of pasture the fox never actually crosses. A 95% KDE isopleth (bandwidth chosen by LSCV) gives 2.6 km2, correctly split into two lobes connected only by a narrow travel corridor, and its 50% core-area contour reveals two separate high-use patches — a den site and a foraging field — that the single MCP blob could never reveal. Separately, 20 fledgling birds are released and their initial flight bearings recorded: the vector mean bearing is 214° (southwest) with r = 0.79; a Rayleigh test on n=20, r=0.79 is significant (p < 0.001), meaning the birds are not dispersing randomly but show a real preferred departure direction.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe home-range and orientation methods because both have a wrong-by-default naive version that looks plausible on a poster. A weak answer draws an MCP and reports its area with no mention of outlier handling or bandwidth choice, or worse, averages compass bearings with ordinary arithmetic (which silently breaks near 0°/360°). A strong answer names which estimator was used and why (MCP for a quick, comparable-to-older-literature number; KDE with a stated bandwidth method for a realistic, possibly multi-core range), and for directional data, reports the mean vector length r alongside the mean bearing and a Rayleigh test — showing they know direction needs a fundamentally different average than a ruler measurement does.

questions.prompt: Why can a 95% minimum convex polygon badly overestimate the true area used by an animal with two separate high-use patches?

options.text: MCP always uses 100% of points regardless of the percentage requested
MCP must be convex, so it includes all unused space between the two patches
MCP can only be computed for animals with a single core area
MCP ignores the outermost 5% of points, shrinking the estimate

explanations.a: The percentage (e.g., 95%) controls how many outlier points are dropped before drawing the polygon; it does not force use of 100% of points.
explanations.b: Correct — because a convex polygon cannot have an indentation, any straight line between two far-apart used patches sweeps in the unused space between them, inflating the area.
explanations.c: MCP can be computed for any point set; the flaw is that its shape assumption misrepresents multi-patch use, not that it fails to run.
explanations.d: Dropping outliers with a 95% MCP reduces area relative to a 100% MCP, but the core overestimation problem — convexity forcing inclusion of unused space — remains regardless.

questions.prompt: What does the KDE bandwidth (h) control, and what happens if it is set too large?

options.text: It controls sample size; too large a value discards real GPS fixes
It controls how far each point's influence spreads on the utilization distribution; too large a value oversmooths, inflating the range and blurring real gaps
It controls the confidence level of the isopleth; too large a value produces a 50% contour instead of 95%
It has no effect on the resulting home-range area

explanations.a: Bandwidth is a smoothing parameter applied to the existing fixes; it does not add or remove data points.
explanations.b: Correct — h sets the spread of each fix's kernel; oversmoothing with too large an h merges genuinely separate patches and inflates the estimated range.
explanations.c: The isopleth percentage (95% vs 50%) is a separate, user-chosen contour level applied after the utilization distribution is built; it is not set by bandwidth.
explanations.d: KDE results are highly sensitive to bandwidth choice, which is exactly why the lesson stresses reporting the method used to select it.

questions.prompt: 20 birds have departure bearings averaging to a vector mean of 214° with r = 0.79. What does r = 0.79 indicate?

options.text: 79% of the birds departed exactly at 214°
The bearings are tightly clustered around the mean direction, close to maximal concentration
There is a 79% chance the birds departed at 214° by coincidence
The sample size was 79% larger than needed

explanations.a: r describes vector concentration across the whole sample, not the fraction of birds hitting one exact bearing.
explanations.b: Correct — r ranges from 0 (uniform/scattered) to 1 (all bearings identical); 0.79 indicates strong clustering around the mean direction, consistent with a real preferred heading.
explanations.c: r is not a probability value; the Rayleigh test (using both r and n) is what produces a p-value for testing non-uniformity.
explanations.d: r is unrelated to sample size adequacy; it purely measures angular concentration.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for testing whether a set of compass bearings shows a significant preferred direction.

items.text: Record each individual's bearing as an angle (0-360 degrees)
Convert each bearing to a unit vector (sine and cosine components)
Sum the vector components and compute the mean vector angle and length r
Run a Rayleigh test using r and sample size n against the null of a uniform circular distribution

questions.explanation: Circular statistics require converting raw bearings to vector components before averaging, because an ordinary arithmetic mean is invalid on a wrapped scale; only after computing the vector mean and r can a Rayleigh test formally assess whether the directional preference is statistically significant.

lessons.label: Honest Interpretation and Judge Q&A

sections.heading: Just-so stories: naming a function is not demonstrating one
sections.body: In 1979, Stephen Jay Gould and Richard Lewontin published 'The Spandrels of San Marco and the Panglossian Paradigm' in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B, attacking what they called the adaptationist habit of inventing a plausible adaptive story for any trait and treating the story's plausibility as evidence — borrowing the term 'just-so story' from Kipling to mock explanations that are neat, satisfying, and untested. Their point was not that adaptation is rare; it is that a trait's current function has to be demonstrated, not assumed, because every trait also has a history (it may be a byproduct of another adaptation, a developmental constraint, or genetic drift) that a tidy adaptive narrative skips past. The demonstrated version of an adaptive claim looks like Marion Petrie's peacock work: rather than just asserting that long trains signal quality, Petrie and Halliday (1994) experimentally shortened some males' trains and showed their mating success dropped relative to controls — a manipulation that tests the causal claim, not just a correlation consistent with it.

sections.heading: Morgan's Canon: don't reach for the fancier explanation
sections.body: Anthropomorphic language — 'the bird decided,' 'the fish wanted to' — is not harmless color; it smuggles in an unsupported claim about mechanism, implying deliberation or understanding the data cannot support. C. Lloyd Morgan's 1894 canon states the corrective principle plainly: an action should never be interpreted as the outcome of a higher psychological faculty if it can be explained by a faculty lower on the psychological scale — a crow that drops nuts on roads to crack them is more parsimoniously explained by reinforcement learning from trial and error than by an inferred understanding of physics, unless a study specifically rules the simpler account out.

sections.heading: Reporting honestly under judge pressure
sections.body: Two habits separate a defensible interpretation from an overclaimed one. First, report effect sizes with confidence intervals (e.g., 'a 12-percentage-point difference, 95% CI 4–20') rather than a bare 'p < 0.05,' since a p-value alone says nothing about how large or precise an effect is. Second, come prepared with the confounds you could not control and a ranked list of alternative explanations for your own result — a judge's 'what else could explain this?' is not a trick question, it is the single most predictable question at a science fair, and a ranked answer (most to least likely, with reasons) reads as scientific honesty rather than a weakness in the project.

lessons.workedExample: A student observes captive crows dropping walnuts onto a paved area rather than dirt and writes: 'the crows decided pavement was better and understood it would crack the shell faster.' A judge asks what else could explain the pattern. A weak response repeats the original claim. A strong response offers a ranked alternative list: (1) simple reinforcement learning — drops on pavement cracked nuts more often early on, increasing future pavement drops, no understanding of physics required (Morgan's Canon); (2) pavement areas may simply have been more visually salient or closer to perch sites, a confound in site choice never controlled; (3) only after ruling out (1) and (2) with, say, a controlled choice test between equally-accessible pavement and dirt patches would 'crows selectively choose the surface that cracks nuts' become a demonstrated claim rather than a plausible story — mirroring exactly the gap Gould and Lewontin identified between narrative and evidence.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges lean on 'what else could explain this?' because it is the fastest test of whether a student can hold their own conclusion at arm's length. A weak answer treats the question as an attack and defends the original interpretation harder. A strong answer treats it as expected, and has a ranked list ready — the most likely alternative first, with the specific reason it wasn't or couldn't be ruled out — plus reports the actual effect size and its uncertainty rather than hiding behind a p-value, and avoids intention-implying language ('decided,' 'understood,' 'wanted') for anything not experimentally demonstrated.

questions.prompt: What was the core criticism Gould and Lewontin (1979) made of 'just-so story' adaptationism?

options.text: That natural selection does not exist
That plausible adaptive narratives were often treated as evidence of function without being tested
That all traits are non-adaptive byproducts
That peacocks do not have long trains

explanations.a: Gould and Lewontin accepted natural selection as real; their target was a sloppy method of inferring function, not selection itself.
explanations.b: Correct — their 1979 Royal Society paper argued that a satisfying adaptive story is not the same as demonstrated evidence for a trait's current function, since traits can also arise as byproducts, from constraint, or from drift.
explanations.c: They argued some traits are byproducts, not that all traits are — the paper is a call for testing, not a blanket claim of non-adaptation.
explanations.d: The peacock train example belongs to Petrie's later experimental work, not to Gould and Lewontin's claim.

questions.prompt: What did Petrie and Halliday's (1994) train-shortening experiment demonstrate that a purely observational correlation between train length and mating success could not?

options.text: That train length has no relationship to mating success
A causal link — experimentally reducing train length reduced mating success relative to controls
That peacocks choose mates based on plumage color, not length
That train length is entirely genetic with no environmental influence

explanations.a: The manipulation found the opposite — shortened trains reduced mating success, indicating a real relationship.
explanations.b: Correct — manipulating the trait directly and comparing to controls tests causation, moving the claim from 'consistent with a story' to 'demonstrated function,' which a correlation alone cannot do.
explanations.c: The experiment manipulated train length specifically, not plumage color.
explanations.d: The experiment addressed mating consequences of train length, not its heritability or developmental origin.
