questions.prompt: Morgan's Canon (1894) states that a behavior should be explained by which psychological faculty when multiple explanations are possible?

options.text: The highest faculty consistent with the observation
The lowest faculty on the psychological scale that can still account for the observation
Whichever faculty makes the animal seem most intelligent
It does not address faculties, only physical mechanisms

explanations.a: This is the opposite of Morgan's Canon, which explicitly warns against defaulting to higher faculties.
explanations.b: Correct — Morgan's Canon is a parsimony principle: never invoke a higher faculty (like understanding or intention) if a lower one (like simple learning) can explain the behavior.
explanations.c: The canon is about explanatory economy, not about flattering the animal's apparent intelligence.
explanations.d: The canon is specifically about the level of psychological faculty invoked in explanation, not physical mechanism per se.

questions.prompt: Match each interpretive habit to the problem it addresses.

left.text: Reporting effect size with a confidence interval
Giving a ranked list of alternative explanations

right.text: Avoids hiding the magnitude and precision of a result behind a bare p-value
Answers 'what else could explain this?' with prioritized, reasoned alternatives instead of defensiveness
Prevents attributing behavior to an unsupported higher cognitive process when a simpler one explains it

questions.explanation: Confidence intervals communicate effect magnitude and uncertainty beyond a bare p-value; a ranked alternatives list turns the judge's hardest question into a demonstration of rigor; Morgan's Canon guards against anthropomorphic overinterpretation by defaulting to the simplest sufficient explanation.

lessons.label: The Founding Ethologists and the Move to the Field

sections.heading: Three men, one Nobel, and a new way of watching animals
sections.body: In 1973 the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Karl von Frisch, Konrad Lorenz, and Nikolaas Tinbergen "for their discoveries concerning organization and elicitation of individual and social behaviour patterns" — the first (and still only) Nobel awarded for behavior itself. Von Frisch spent decades decoding the honeybee waggle dance, showing in work published through the 1940s and summarized in his 1967 book that the angle of the dance relative to gravity encodes direction to a food source relative to the sun, and the duration of the waggle run encodes distance. Lorenz worked on greylag geese in the 1930s, describing imprinting: goslings follow the first moving object they see during a brief sensitive window after hatching, a discovery that became the centerpiece of his theory that behavior is organized around fixed, innate "instincts" triggered by specific releasing stimuli.

sections.heading: Tinbergen: taking the question outdoors
sections.body: Tinbergen's contribution was methodological as much as empirical. His digger wasp studies (Philanthus triangulum, published from the 1930s onward) showed females memorizing a ring of landmarks around their nest burrow before foraging; when Tinbergen displaced the ring of pinecones while the wasp was away, she searched at the new, wrong center — proof the wasp used relative landmark position, not any single object, to relocate home. With Perdeck, his 1950 herring gull chick work used cardboard dummy bills to show chicks peck preferentially at a red spot near the tip of an adult's lower mandible, isolating the releasing stimulus from the parent's whole appearance. Tinbergen insisted any behavior needed answers to four questions — causation, development, function, and evolutionary history — a framework still taught as "Tinbergen's four questions."

sections.heading: The instinct fight and the rebrand into behavioral ecology
sections.body: Lorenz's innate-instinct model drew a sharp counterattack from developmental psychologist Daniel Lehrman, whose 1953 paper "A Critique of Konrad Lorenz's Theory of Instinctive Behavior" argued that labeling behavior "innate" hid rather than explained its developmental origins, since even fixed-looking behaviors depend on experience and physiological state during development. That fight over nature versus development never fully resolved, but the field moved past it by changing the question: instead of asking what triggers a behavior, John Krebs and Nick Davies's 1978 textbook Behavioural Ecology: An Evolutionary Approach asked what a behavior is worth in fitness currency, launching behavioral ecology as the study of behavior as an economic, cost-benefit adaptation shaped by natural selection.

lessons.workedExample: Tinbergen's 1938 pinecone-ring experiment on Philanthus triangulum: while a female wasp foraged, he arranged 20 pinecones in a circle around her nest entrance, let her learn the array, then — while she was away — shifted the entire ring a meter to one side, leaving the actual burrow uncovered in its original spot. Returning wasps searched the center of the shifted ring, not the true burrow, showing they encode the nest's position relative to the whole landmark configuration rather than fixating on any single cue. This is a clean field-experimental design: one manipulated variable (landmark position), a directly observable outcome (search location), and a result that rules out competing explanations (single-object cues, olfactory tracking) in one move.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about the founding ethologists to test whether a student can distinguish description from experiment. Lorenz's imprinting and von Frisch's dance decoding are largely descriptive natural history, powerful but not manipulative; Tinbergen's landmark-displacement and dummy-bill studies are true experiments with a manipulated variable and a controlled comparison. A strong answer names Tinbergen's four questions and can say which one a given project addresses (causation vs. function vs. development vs. evolutionary history); a weak answer treats 'ethology' as a synonym for 'watching animals' without naming what made the 1930s–50s work rigorous enough to reshape the field.

questions.prompt: In Tinbergen's pinecone-displacement experiment with digger wasps, what did shifting the landmark ring while the wasp was away demonstrate?

options.text: Wasps navigate using magnetic field detection
Wasps encode nest location relative to the whole array of surrounding landmarks, not a single fixed cue
Wasps cannot relocate their nests without visual cues at all
Wasps use scent trails laid down during the outbound flight

explanations.a: The experiment manipulated visual landmarks, not magnetic cues, and returning wasps followed the shifted visual array, ruling out a purely magnetic explanation.
explanations.b: Correct — when the whole ring of pinecones moved, wasps searched the new center, showing they use the relative configuration of landmarks, not any single object or absolute location.
explanations.c: Wasps clearly used cues to search at all — the point is which cue (relative configuration vs. a fixed spot) they relied on, not whether they used any cue.
explanations.d: A scent-trail explanation would predict wasps searching at the true burrow location regardless of landmark position, which is not what happened.

questions.prompt: Daniel Lehrman's 1953 critique of Lorenz's instinct theory argued primarily that:

options.text: Imprinting does not actually occur in geese
Calling a behavior 'innate' can obscure rather than explain its developmental origins
Honeybees do not really communicate location through dance
Tinbergen's landmark experiments were poorly controlled

explanations.a: Lehrman did not dispute that imprinting occurs; his target was the theoretical framing of instinct, not this specific phenomenon.
explanations.b: Correct — Lehrman argued that even behaviors that look fixed and automatic depend on developmental and physiological history, so 'innate' as an explanation can mask the actual causal story.
explanations.c: Von Frisch's dance-language findings were not Lehrman's target; his critique addressed Lorenz's instinct concept specifically.
explanations.d: Lehrman's critique was aimed at Lorenz's theoretical framework, not at Tinbergen's experimental methods.

questions.prompt: What shift did Krebs and Davies's 1978 textbook Behavioural Ecology represent relative to classical ethology?

options.text: A return to purely descriptive natural history
A move from asking what triggers a behavior to asking what a behavior costs and yields in fitness terms
A rejection of Tinbergen's four-questions framework entirely
A focus exclusively on laboratory rather than field studies

explanations.a: The shift was toward more quantitative, hypothesis-driven analysis, not back toward description.
explanations.b: Correct — behavioral ecology reframed behavior as an economic decision shaped by natural selection, asking about costs, benefits, and fitness payoffs rather than releasing stimuli.
explanations.c: Tinbergen's four questions (causation, development, function, evolutionary history) remained foundational; behavioral ecology mainly sharpened the functional question.
explanations.d: Behavioral ecology strongly emphasized field studies of animals under natural conditions, continuing rather than abandoning Tinbergen's field tradition.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher to their landmark contribution.

right.text: Decoded the honeybee waggle dance
Described imprinting in greylag geese
Digger wasp landmark-displacement and gull dummy-bill experiments
Published the 1953 critique of instinct theory

questions.explanation: Von Frisch decoded the bee dance's direction/distance code; Lorenz described goose imprinting and built the instinct framework; Tinbergen ran the wasp and gull field experiments and posed the four questions; Lehrman challenged the instinct concept on developmental grounds.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the historical sequence in which they occurred.

items.text: Lorenz describes imprinting in greylag geese
Tinbergen and Perdeck publish the herring gull dummy-bill studies
Lehrman publishes his critique of Lorenz's instinct theory
Von Frisch, Lorenz, and Tinbergen share the Nobel Prize
Krebs and Davies publish Behavioural Ecology: An Evolutionary Approach

questions.explanation: Lorenz's imprinting work dates to the 1930s, the gull dummy-bill studies to 1950, Lehrman's critique to 1953, the shared Nobel Prize to 1973, and the Krebs and Davies textbook to 1978.

lessons.label: Hamilton, Kin Selection, and the Group-Selection War

sections.heading: Hamilton's rule and the arithmetic of helping relatives
sections.body: William D. Hamilton's 1964 two-part paper "The Genetical Evolution of Social Behaviour" in the Journal of Theoretical Biology solved a problem that had troubled Darwin: why would an animal ever sacrifice its own reproduction to help another? Hamilton's answer, now called Hamilton's rule, is rb > c — a gene for helping spreads whenever the benefit (b) to the recipient, discounted by their genetic relatedness (r) to the helper, exceeds the cost (c) to the helper. A full sibling has r = 0.5, a cousin r = 0.125; helping a full sibling raise two extra offspring (b = 2) at a cost of one of your own (c = 1) satisfies 0.5 × 2 = 1, which is not greater than c — but helping raise three would (0.5 × 3 = 1.5 > 1). Because the helper's genes ride along in relatives' offspring, selection can favor apparent altruism as long as the inclusive-fitness math works out, not just direct offspring count.

sections.heading: Field tests: squirrels and tits
sections.body: Paul Sherman's 1977 Science paper on Belding's ground squirrels tested Hamilton's rule directly. Females are philopatric (stay near their birthplace, surrounded by kin) while males disperse; Sherman found females gave alarm calls at predators significantly more often than males, and specifically more often when close kin were nearby — costly behavior (the caller draws predator attention) that pays off only when it protects relatives. Ben Hatchwell's long-term work on long-tailed tits (Aegithalos caudatus) found a parallel pattern in cooperative breeding: after their own nest fails, tits that become helpers overwhelmingly redirect their effort to relatives' nests when relatives are available nearby, choosing kin over unrelated pairs even when both are accessible.

sections.heading: The 2010 attack and the 137-author rebuttal
sections.body: In 2010, Martin Nowak, Corina Tarnita, and E. O. Wilson published "The Evolution of Eusociality" in Nature, arguing that inclusive-fitness theory is only a special-case approximation of standard natural selection, not generally applicable, and that eusociality is better explained by direct group-level selection models without invoking relatedness as the driving force. The paper provoked an unusually large response: a 2011 Nature rebuttal, "Inclusive Fitness Theory and Eusociality," led by Patrick Abbot and carrying 137 co-authors, argued Nowak et al. had misrepresented both the mathematics (inclusive fitness and their alternative model are provably equivalent under general conditions) and the empirical record of relatedness-driven cooperation. The dispute is not fully settled: proponents on both sides agree the frameworks are mathematically interconvertible in many cases, but disagree sharply on which one generates better predictions and which better explains why eusociality evolved disproportionately in haplodiploid lineages like ants, bees, and wasps.

lessons.workedExample: Applying Hamilton's rule to a Belding's ground squirrel alarm call: suppose calling costs the caller a 10% increase in predation risk this season, translating to c = 0.1 expected offspring lost, while the call saves on average 1 offspring-equivalent among nearby kin (b = 1). If the nearest kin are full sisters (r = 0.5), rb = 0.5 × 1 = 0.5, comfortably exceeding c = 0.1, so calling is favored. If instead the nearest animals are unrelated migrants (r ≈ 0), rb = 0, so the same call is a pure fitness loss and selection should suppress it — exactly the pattern Sherman found: males, who disperse away from kin, called far less than philopatric, kin-surrounded females.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge presses on kin selection to see whether a student can do the arithmetic rather than just cite 'selfish gene' as a slogan. A strong answer plugs in actual relatedness coefficients (0.5 for siblings, 0.25 for half-sibs or grandparents, 0.125 for cousins) and shows why rb > c predicts who helps whom, then can name a real test like Sherman's squirrels. A weak answer treats kin selection as meaning animals help their species or their group, which is precisely the group-selection confusion Hamilton's math was built to correct — and a judge who catches that conflation will ask a direct follow-up.

questions.prompt: Under Hamilton's rule rb > c, a squirrel considering an alarm call that costs c = 0.2 offspring-equivalents will be favored by selection if it helps a relative with r = 0.25 (a half-sibling) gain how many offspring-equivalents at minimum?

options.text: Just over 0.05
Just over 0.8
Exactly 0.2
Just over 1.25

explanations.a: This reverses the inequality; solving rb > c for b requires b > c / r, not b > c × r.
explanations.b: Correct — rb > c means 0.25 × b > 0.2, so b > 0.8; the benefit to the half-sibling must exceed 0.8 offspring-equivalents for the call to be favored.
explanations.c: Setting b equal to c ignores relatedness entirely, treating the half-sibling as if it shared 100% of genes with the caller.
explanations.d: This overshoots the threshold; b need only exceed 0.8, not 1.25, for the inequality to hold.

questions.prompt: What was the central mathematical claim of Nowak, Tarnita, and Wilson's 2010 Nature paper?

options.text: Relatedness has no effect whatsoever on cooperative behavior in any species
Inclusive fitness theory is only a special-case approximation, not a generally applicable framework, compared to standard natural-selection models
Belding's ground squirrels do not actually give alarm calls
Haplodiploidy is irrelevant to the evolution of eusociality

explanations.a: The paper did not deny relatedness effects outright; it argued inclusive-fitness math is a limited special case, not that relatedness is irrelevant.
explanations.b: Correct — Nowak, Tarnita, and Wilson argued standard natural-selection models are more general and that inclusive fitness only applies validly under restrictive conditions.
explanations.c: The paper did not dispute Sherman's empirical alarm-call data; its target was the theoretical framework used to explain such data.
explanations.d: The paper actually engaged closely with haplodiploid eusocial insects as its central case study, not dismissed their relevance.

questions.prompt: The 2011 Nature rebuttal to Nowak, Tarnita, and Wilson, led by Patrick Abbot, was notable for which feature?

options.text: It was written by a single author working alone over a decade
It had 137 co-authors and argued the original paper misrepresented both the math and the empirical literature
It conceded that group selection fully replaces kin selection
It was published in a minor journal with little readership

explanations.a: The rebuttal was a large collective response, not a solo effort — its scale was itself part of the story.
explanations.b: Correct — the rebuttal carried 137 co-authors and argued Nowak et al. had misunderstood the mathematics and misrepresented decades of empirical support for inclusive fitness.
explanations.c: The rebuttal defended inclusive fitness theory rather than conceding to the alternative group-level framework.
explanations.d: It was published in Nature, the same high-profile journal as the original paper.

questions.prompt: Match each study or figure to what it demonstrated or argued.

right.text: Formalized rb > c as the condition for altruism to spread
Showed philopatric female squirrels give more kin-directed alarm calls than dispersing males
Showed failed breeders redirect helping effort toward relatives' nests
Argued inclusive fitness is not generally applicable and proposed a group-level alternative

questions.explanation: Hamilton derived the rb > c rule; Sherman found kin-biased alarm-calling in ground squirrels; Hatchwell found kin-biased helping in long-tailed tits; Nowak, Tarnita, and Wilson challenged inclusive fitness as a general framework.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the kin-selection debate chronologically.

items.text: Hamilton publishes 'The Genetical Evolution of Social Behaviour'
Sherman publishes the Belding's ground squirrel alarm-call study
Nowak, Tarnita, and Wilson publish 'The Evolution of Eusociality'
Abbot and 136 co-authors publish the Nature rebuttal

questions.explanation: Hamilton's foundational papers appeared in 1964, Sherman's squirrel data in 1977, the Nowak/Tarnita/Wilson challenge in 2010, and the 137-author rebuttal in 2011.

lessons.label: Reciprocity, Cooperation, and Its Critics

sections.heading: Trivers's reciprocal altruism and the tit-for-tat solution
sections.body: Robert Trivers's 1971 paper "The Evolution of Reciprocal Altruism" in the Quarterly Review of Biology proposed that unrelated individuals could evolve to help each other if the interaction repeats: I pay a small cost to help you today, you pay a small cost to help me later, and both of us gain more than we spent — provided cheaters (who take help but never repay) can be detected and punished. The problem was formalized as a game: political scientist Robert Axelrod ran computer tournaments of the iterated Prisoner's Dilemma and, with Hamilton, published the results in Science in 1981 ("The Evolution of Cooperation"). The simplest strategy submitted, tit-for-tat (cooperate first, then copy your partner's last move) by Anatol Rapoport, won repeatedly against far more complex programs, because it was nice (never defects first), retaliatory (punishes defection immediately), forgiving (returns to cooperation once the partner does), and clear (easy for a partner to read and exploit-proof against).

sections.heading: Vampire bats: the textbook empirical case
sections.body: Gerald Wilkinson's 1984 Nature paper on the common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus) supplied the field's clearest real-world match to reciprocal altruism. Vampire bats can starve within about 60 hours without a blood meal, but hunts fail often; Wilkinson found roost-mates that had fed successfully would regurgitate blood to share with a hungry roost-mate, and repaid partners preferentially — a bat that had previously received a donation was far more likely to be fed by that same donor later, even correcting for kinship. Because bats can recognize individuals and track past exchanges over long roosting associations, the case satisfied the theory's hard requirements: repeated interaction, individual recognition, and the ability to track debts.

sections.heading: Clutton-Brock's challenge: is reciprocity actually common?
sections.body: Tim Clutton-Brock's influential 2009 Nature review "Cooperation Between Non-Kin in Animal Societies" argued that true, contingent reciprocity — the tit-for-tat mechanism, where an individual's future help is conditional on a partner's past behavior — is in fact rare outside a handful of well-documented cases like vampire bats and some primate grooming/coalition systems. Clutton-Brock's alternative explanations for most apparent animal 'cooperation': byproduct mutualism (both partners benefit simultaneously from a shared act, no accounting needed, as in group hunting), kin-biased helping disguised as reciprocity, and enforcement through punishment or policing rather than voluntary reciprocation. Since then, partner choice — preferentially associating with and rewarding better cooperators, letting competition for good partners do the enforcing — has gained ground as a more empirically supported alternative mechanism than strict tit-for-tat accounting.

lessons.workedExample: Wilkinson's vampire bat colonies were tracked over multiple years at a site in Costa Rica. He staged 'starvation' by preventing individual bats from foraging one night, then recorded whether roost-mates donated blood. Statistically, the best predictor of whether bat A fed a hungry bat B was not simply relatedness but B's own history of having fed A in the past — an association that held up even after controlling for kinship using genetic data. This is the signature test of reciprocity versus kin selection: if helping tracks 'who helped me' independent of 'who is my relative,' Trivers's mechanism, not Hamilton's, is doing the explanatory work.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about reciprocity to see if a student can tell apart three mechanisms that look identical from the outside — kin selection, reciprocal altruism, and byproduct mutualism — because they predict different data. A strong answer says what evidence would distinguish them: reciprocity requires showing debt-tracking independent of relatedness (as Wilkinson did), while byproduct mutualism requires showing the 'helper' benefits immediately regardless of the partner's future behavior. A weak answer calls any observed helping between unrelated animals 'reciprocal altruism' without checking whether the interaction is even repeated or individuals can recognize each other — exactly the overreach Clutton-Brock's 2009 critique targeted.

questions.prompt: In Axelrod's iterated Prisoner's Dilemma tournaments — later interpreted with Hamilton in their 1981 Science paper — why did tit-for-tat outperform more complex strategies?

options.text: It always defected regardless of the opponent's move
It cooperated first, then simply copied the partner's previous move — nice, retaliatory, forgiving, and easy to read
It used a random mix of cooperation and defection to confuse opponents
It required memory of the entire game history rather than just the last move

explanations.a: Always-defect strategies scored poorly against other cooperative strategies over repeated rounds, since they triggered permanent retaliation.
explanations.b: Correct — tit-for-tat's simplicity (start nice, mirror the last move) made it robust: it never exploited first but punished defection immediately and forgave once cooperation resumed.
explanations.c: A random strategy was actually tested and performed worse, since it was neither reliably exploitable-proof nor consistently cooperative.
explanations.d: Tit-for-tat only needs the single most recent move, which is part of why it is so simple and robust, not a strategy requiring full history.

questions.prompt: What made Wilkinson's 1984 vampire bat data a strong test of reciprocal altruism rather than kin selection?

options.text: Only closely related bats ever shared blood
Feeding a hungry bat was best predicted by whether that bat had previously fed the donor, even after controlling for relatedness
Bats shared blood randomly regardless of any prior interaction
Blood-sharing only occurred once per bat's lifetime

explanations.a: If sharing tracked only relatedness, that would support kin selection instead — the actual finding was that past reciprocal history predicted sharing independent of kinship.
explanations.b: Correct — the key result was that donation history, not just genetic relatedness, predicted who fed whom, isolating reciprocity as an active mechanism.
explanations.c: Sharing was systematically patterned by prior donation history, not random.
explanations.d: Bats formed long-term roost associations with repeated feeding events over years, which is required for reciprocity to function at all.

questions.prompt: Clutton-Brock's 2009 review argued that most apparent cooperation between non-kin animals is better explained by which alternative(s) rather than strict contingent reciprocity?

options.text: Byproduct mutualism, disguised kin-biased helping, and enforcement through punishment or policing
Random chance with no underlying mechanism at all
Universal group selection acting on entire populations
Pure genetic drift unrelated to any fitness benefit

explanations.a: Correct — Clutton-Brock argued that byproduct mutualism, kin bias mistaken for reciprocity, and enforced cooperation account for most cases previously labeled reciprocal altruism.
explanations.b: Clutton-Brock proposed specific alternative mechanisms with fitness consequences, not the absence of mechanism.
explanations.c: Group selection was not the alternative Clutton-Brock proposed; his critique operated within individual-level selection thinking.
explanations.d: Genetic drift is a non-selective process and was not part of Clutton-Brock's argument about cooperative behavior.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or study to their contribution to the reciprocity debate.

right.text: Proposed reciprocal altruism as a mechanism for cooperation between non-kin
Published the tournament results showing tit-for-tat's success, with their evolutionary interpretation
Documented debt-tracked blood-sharing in vampire bats
Argued true reciprocity is rare and most cooperation has other causes

questions.explanation: Trivers proposed the theory, Axelrod and Hamilton formalized and tested it via tournament, Wilkinson supplied the strongest field data, and Clutton-Brock later challenged how common the mechanism really is.

questions.prompt: Order these publications chronologically.

items.text: Trivers, 'The Evolution of Reciprocal Altruism'
Axelrod and Hamilton, 'The Evolution of Cooperation'
Wilkinson's vampire bat blood-sharing study
Clutton-Brock's 'Cooperation Between Non-Kin in Animal Societies'

questions.explanation: Trivers's theory paper appeared in 1971, the Axelrod-Hamilton tournament results in 1981, Wilkinson's bat study in 1984, and Clutton-Brock's critical review in 2009.

lessons.label: Sexual Selection: Widowbirds, Handicaps, and the Beauty Debate

sections.heading: Andersson's scissors: manipulating the tail itself
sections.body: Male long-tailed widowbirds (Euplectes progne) grow tails up to half a meter long, far beyond anything needed for flight, and hold territories that attract multiple females. Malte Andersson's 1982 Nature study cut the tails of some males down to about 14 cm and glued the cut sections onto other males, elongating them to roughly 75 cm, while control groups had tails cut and reglued to their own original length or left untouched. Over the following weeks, males with experimentally elongated tails acquired significantly more new nests (more mates) than shortened or control males — strong evidence that females were choosing mates based on tail length itself, not on some other quality merely correlated with a naturally long tail, because the manipulation randomized tail length independent of the male's own condition.

sections.heading: Zahavi's handicap and Grafen's proof
sections.body: Amotz Zahavi proposed in 1975 that costly, seemingly wasteful ornaments could be honest signals precisely because they are costly: only a genuinely high-quality male can afford to grow a tail that impairs flight and still survive, so the handicap itself guarantees the signal cannot be faked by low-quality males. The idea was widely doubted as mathematically unworkable until Alan Grafen's 1990 paper "Biological Signals as Handicaps" built a formal evolutionarily stable strategy model showing that under the right cost structure — where the marginal cost of signaling is lower for higher-quality individuals — handicap signaling is a stable, non-bluffable equilibrium. Grafen's model turned Zahavi's verbal argument into rigorous theory and made the handicap principle a mainstream explanation alongside older ideas.

sections.heading: Fisherian runaway versus 'beauty happens'
sections.body: A separate, still-unresolved question is why female preference exists at all. R. A. Fisher's 1930 runaway model proposed that if a preference and a trait become genetically linked, preference and ornament can escalate together with no reference to survival value, purely because sons inheriting the trait are more attractive to daughters inheriting the preference — a self-reinforcing loop capped only by natural-selection costs. Richard Prum's 2017 book The Evolution of Beauty revived and sharpened a pure-Fisherian, 'arbitrary' position, arguing many ornaments (his flagship case is bird-of-paradise plumage) evolve through female aesthetic preference alone with no honest information about male quality at all — genuine 'beauty happens.' This sits against the good-genes and sensory-bias adaptationist camp, which holds ornaments typically do track real quality (as handicap theory requires) or exploit pre-existing perceptual biases. The dispute is not resolved because both camps predict elaborate ornaments and strong preferences; what would settle it is whether ornament expression reliably correlates with independently measured survival or offspring quality across many systems, and that correlation is inconsistent across taxa.

lessons.workedExample: In Andersson's experiment, 36 male widowbirds were assigned to four groups: tail-shortened, tail-elongated, control-cut (tail cut then reglued to original length, controlling for handling stress), and unmanipulated control. Elongated males (tails artificially lengthened to about 75-cm total) increased their nest counts substantially relative to their pre-manipulation baseline, while shortened males' nest counts dropped; the two control groups showed no significant change. Because males were randomly assigned to treatment, any difference in mating success can be attributed to tail length itself rather than to which individual males happened to already be high quality — the manipulation, not just a correlation between natural tail length and mating success, is what makes this the field's textbook demonstration of female choice.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes sexual selection to check whether a student understands why manipulation experiments like Andersson's are more convincing than a simple correlation between tail length and mate number. A strong answer explains that correlational data alone cannot separate 'females prefer long tails' from 'high-quality males happen to grow long tails and also win independently' — only randomizing tail length breaks that confound. A weak answer cites Andersson's result as if it were an observational survey, or conflates the handicap principle (why costly signals are honest) with Fisherian runaway (why any arbitrary preference can escalate) as though they were the same claim rather than competing explanations for the same pattern.

questions.prompt: Why was cutting and gluing widowbird tails, rather than just measuring naturally long- versus short-tailed males, essential to Andersson's conclusion?

options.text: It made the experiment easier to publish in a high-profile journal
It randomized tail length independent of a male's other qualities, isolating tail length as the cause of mating success
It allowed the birds to be individually marked for identification
It reduced the cost of the study compared to observational fieldwork

explanations.a: Publication considerations are not the scientific reason for the design; the design choice was about causal inference.
explanations.b: Correct — without manipulation, naturally long-tailed males might simply be higher quality in other ways, confounding the interpretation; randomized manipulation breaks that link.
explanations.c: Marking for identification is a separate, minor logistical matter and not the core reason for the surgical manipulation.
explanations.d: The manipulation was scientifically, not economically, motivated, and manipulative field experiments are typically more resource-intensive than simple observation.

questions.prompt: What did Grafen's 1990 model contribute to Zahavi's 1975 handicap principle?

options.text: It disproved the handicap principle mathematically
It showed, using a formal ESS model, that costly honest signaling can be a stable equilibrium when signal cost scales inversely with quality
It replaced the handicap principle with Fisherian runaway entirely
It showed handicaps only work in species without female choice

explanations.a: Grafen's model supported rather than disproved the handicap principle, resolving earlier doubts about its mathematical soundness.
explanations.b: Correct — Grafen formalized the condition (quality-dependent marginal signaling cost) under which costly signals remain honest and non-bluffable at evolutionary equilibrium.
explanations.c: Grafen's model addressed handicap signaling specifically; it did not replace or merge with the separate Fisherian runaway mechanism.
explanations.d: The handicap principle is specifically about signals used in mate choice, so it presupposes rather than excludes female choice.

questions.prompt: What is the core difference between Fisherian runaway and Prum's 'beauty happens' view versus the good-genes/handicap camp?

options.text: Fisherian/arbitrary models require preference and trait to be genetically linked and predict no necessary link to honest quality information; good-genes models predict ornaments reliably track real quality
There is no actual difference between the two camps
Good-genes models deny that female preference exists at all
Fisherian models require ornaments to be costly while good-genes models require them to be cost-free

explanations.a: Correct — the arbitrary/Fisherian camp holds ornaments can be pure aesthetic products of preference-trait coevolution with no honest information, while good-genes/handicap models predict the ornament tracks real underlying quality.
explanations.b: The two camps make different, empirically distinguishable predictions about whether ornament expression correlates with quality, so the difference is substantive, not semantic.
explanations.c: Good-genes models assume female preference exists; they diverge on why preference exists and what it tracks, not on whether it exists.
explanations.d: Cost is central to the handicap principle specifically, but the Fisherian/arbitrary framework does not require ornaments to be cost-free either — cost is not the axis that separates the two camps.

questions.prompt: Match each person to their contribution to sexual selection theory.

right.text: Ran the widowbird tail-manipulation field experiment
Proposed the handicap principle verbally in 1975
Formalized the handicap principle with an ESS model in 1990
Argued for arbitrary, non-informative 'beauty happens' preference evolution

questions.explanation: Andersson supplied the field experiment, Zahavi the original handicap idea, Grafen its mathematical proof, and Prum the modern arbitrary-preference revival.

questions.prompt: Order these ideas and studies chronologically.

items.text: Fisher proposes the runaway selection model
Zahavi proposes the handicap principle
Andersson publishes the widowbird tail-manipulation experiment
Grafen publishes the formal ESS proof of the handicap principle
Prum publishes The Evolution of Beauty

questions.explanation: Fisher's model dates to 1930, Zahavi's handicap idea to 1975, Andersson's field experiment to 1982, Grafen's formal proof to 1990, and Prum's book to 2017.

lessons.label: Testing Optimality: Triumphs and the Spandrels Backlash

sections.heading: Great tits and optimal diet
sections.body: John Krebs, Jeremy Erichsen, Michael Webber, and Eric Charnov's 1977 Animal Behaviour paper "Optimal Prey Selection in the Great Tit (Parus major)" tested optimal-foraging theory's clean prediction: when profitable prey are abundant, foragers should ignore less profitable prey entirely rather than take a random mix, and the decision to include low-value prey should depend only on the encounter rate with high-value prey, not on the low-value prey's own abundance. Presenting captive great tits with two sizes of mealworm pieces on a moving belt at controlled encounter rates, Krebs's team found birds did switch to strict specialization on the larger piece as its encounter rate rose, matching the zero-one rule the model predicted — a striking, quantitatively precise fit between an economic model and real behavior.

sections.heading: Wagtails and wasps: real economics in the field
sections.body: Nick Davies and Alasdair Houston's 1981 study of pied wagtails (Motacilla alba) defending riverbank feeding territories along the River Cam found owners tolerated a subordinate 'satellite' bird sharing the territory only when prey were abundant enough that the marginal cost of an intruder was low, and evicted satellites when food grew scarce — territory defense tracked a real cost-benefit currency (energy intake versus energy spent chasing) rather than fixed aggression. Jane Brockmann, Alan Grafen, and Richard Dawkins's 1979 analysis of the digger wasp Sphex ichneumoneus found females either dig a fresh burrow or enter and usurp an existing one, and modeled the choice as an evolutionarily stable mixed strategy: because usurping succeeds often enough to be worthwhile but not so often that everyone should usurp, natural selection maintains both tactics in the same population in stable proportion — one of the first field-tested examples of a mixed ESS.

sections.heading: Gould and Lewontin's spandrels, and the modern defense
sections.body: Stephen Jay Gould and Richard Lewontin's 1979 paper "The Spandrels of San Marco and the Panglossian Paradigm," published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B, attacked what they called the adaptationist programme: the habit of assuming every trait is a discrete adaptation optimized by selection and inventing a plausible story to explain it, named after the spandrels (the triangular spaces between arches and a dome) of Venice's San Marco basilica, which are architectural byproducts of the arch design, not features designed for their own sake, yet could be mistaken for intentional design if studied in isolation. The standard defense from behavioral ecologists is that optimality models were never claimed to be automatically true — they are explicit, falsifiable hypotheses about a currency (like net energy intake) and constraints, and a poor fit is itself informative, revealing a missing constraint or wrong currency rather than a failure of the approach. In response to Gould and Lewontin, the field increasingly pre-registers which currency and constraints a model assumes before comparing predictions to data, treating mismatches as diagnostic rather than embarrassing.

lessons.workedExample: In the Krebs great tit study, when the encounter rate with large mealworm pieces was low, birds accepted both large and small pieces as they were encountered — a generalist strategy. As the experimenters increased the density of large pieces on the belt (without changing the density of small pieces), the model predicted a sharp threshold beyond which birds should reject every small piece encountered, regardless of how often small pieces appeared. The observed data matched this zero-one threshold closely rather than showing a gradual, proportional shift toward large-piece preference — the kind of precise, non-intuitive quantitative prediction (a threshold, not a gradient) that makes optimal foraging theory a genuine test rather than a post-hoc story.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge raises Gould and Lewontin's spandrels critique to test whether a student treats optimality models as certainties or as testable hypotheses. A strong answer says a model's currency and constraints were specified in advance, that a mismatch between prediction and data would have been informative rather than fatal, and can point to an actual quantitative fit (like the great tit zero-one threshold) as evidence the approach earns its keep empirically rather than by storytelling. A weak answer either dismisses adaptationism entirely by citing 'spandrels' as a gotcha, or defends every observed trait as necessarily optimal without acknowledging that behavioral ecologists themselves built the falsification standard the spandrels critique demanded.

questions.prompt: What did the great tit optimal foraging experiments find as the encounter rate with profitable prey increased?

options.text: Birds gradually increased their preference for large prey in rough proportion to encounter rate
Birds showed a sharp threshold, switching to strict specialization on large prey and rejecting small prey entirely, matching the model's zero-one prediction
Birds ignored prey size entirely and foraged randomly
Birds abandoned foraging altogether when large prey became abundant

explanations.a: A gradual, proportional shift is what a naive intuition might predict, but it is not what the zero-one model predicted or what was observed.
explanations.b: Correct — the model predicted and the data showed a threshold effect: complete specialization on large prey once its encounter rate passed a critical point, independent of small prey's own abundance.
explanations.c: Birds showed clear prey-size-dependent selectivity that tracked encounter rates, not random foraging.
explanations.d: Birds continued foraging; the change was in prey selectivity, not foraging effort overall.

questions.prompt: In Brockmann, Grafen, and Dawkins's digger wasp study, why did both digging and burrow-entering ('usurping') persist as strategies in the same population?

options.text: Because usurping always failed and was maintained only by mutation
Because the two tactics form a stable mixed evolutionarily stable strategy, with usurping successful often enough to persist but not so often that it should replace digging entirely
Because wasps chose randomly with no fitness consequences either way
Because only male wasps dig and only female wasps usurp

explanations.a: If usurping always failed, selection would eliminate it; its persistence implies it succeeds often enough to be a viable alternative.
explanations.b: Correct — the analysis showed a mixed ESS in which the relative payoff of each tactic depends on its frequency in the population, keeping both stable at an equilibrium proportion.
explanations.c: The whole point of the ESS analysis was that the choice has real fitness consequences that balance at equilibrium, not that it is fitness-neutral.
explanations.d: The dig-versus-enter choice was a strategic option available within one sex (females), not a sex-linked division of labor.

questions.prompt: Gould and Lewontin's 'spandrels' metaphor was meant to illustrate what risk in evolutionary reasoning?

options.text: That architectural byproducts of one design choice can be mistaken for independently selected adaptations if studied without considering how they arose
That all traits are necessarily non-adaptive byproducts
That optimality models can never be tested empirically
That natural selection does not operate on behavior

explanations.a: Correct — spandrels are structural byproducts of arch geometry, not designed features, illustrating how a trait can look adaptive without being independently selected for its current use.
explanations.b: Gould and Lewontin did not claim all traits are non-adaptive; they warned against assuming every trait must be an adaptation without evidence.
explanations.c: Their critique was aimed at unfalsifiable storytelling, not at the possibility of rigorous testing itself — indeed it pushed the field toward more rigorous tests.
explanations.d: The critique concerned methodology (how adaptationist claims are justified), not a denial that selection acts on behavior.

questions.prompt: Match each study to its system and finding.

right.text: Great tits show a zero-one threshold in prey selectivity
Pied wagtails tolerate satellites only when food is abundant
Digger wasps maintain a stable mix of digging and burrow-entering
Critiqued unfalsifiable adaptationist storytelling using an architectural metaphor

questions.explanation: Krebs's team tested great tit diet choice, Davies and Houston tested wagtail territory economics, Brockmann's team tested wasp nesting ESS, and Gould and Lewontin critiqued the broader adaptationist method.

questions.prompt: Order these publications chronologically.

items.text: Krebs, Erichsen, Webber & Charnov's great tit optimal diet paper
Gould & Lewontin's 'Spandrels of San Marco'
Davies & Houston's pied wagtail territory economics paper

questions.explanation: The great tit optimal diet paper appeared in 1977, the spandrels critique in 1979, and the pied wagtail territory economics study in 1981.

lessons.label: The Sociobiology Controversy and Its Human Aftermath

sections.heading: Wilson's 1975 synthesis and its final chapter
sections.body: E. O. Wilson's 1975 book Sociobiology: The New Synthesis spent 26 chapters systematically applying the new tools of kin selection, reciprocal altruism, and optimality reasoning to social behavior across the animal kingdom — ants (Wilson's own specialty), fish, birds, and primates — largely uncontroversially. The firestorm was over Chapter 27, "Man," which extended the same adaptive, fitness-based reasoning to human behavior: aggression, sex roles, and social structure treated as potentially shaped by natural selection like any other species' traits. Within months, the Sociobiology Study Group, a Boston-area collective including Wilson's own Harvard colleagues Stephen Jay Gould and Richard Lewontin, published a widely read open letter in the New York Review of Books, "Against 'Sociobiology'" (1975), charging that extending adaptationist explanations to humans risked providing pseudo-scientific justification for existing inequalities, racism, and sexism by framing them as biologically natural rather than socially constructed.

sections.heading: Two divergent successors: HBE and evolutionary psychology
sections.body: The controversy did not kill the project of studying human behavior evolutionarily; it split into two research programs with different methods. Human behavioral ecology (HBE) kept behavioral ecology's core method — measure actual fitness-relevant outcomes in living populations and test optimality or game-theoretic predictions against them — applied to humans. Kristen Hawkes and Nicholas Blurton Jones's long-term work with the Hadza of Tanzania quantified foraging returns (calories per hour) for different resources and ages, testing whether foraging choices track caloric optimization or other currencies like status or provisioning of specific kin; Kim Hill and Hillard Kaplan's parallel work with the Ache of Paraguay measured hunting returns and mortality data to test predictions about food sharing and parental investment directly against demographic records.

sections.heading: Evolutionary psychology's different bet
sections.body: Evolutionary psychology, developed prominently by Leda Cosmides and John Tooby from the 1980s onward, took a different route: rather than measuring current fitness outcomes, it infers psychological "modules" — specialized cognitive mechanisms, like cheater-detection reasoning or kin-recognition systems — argued to have been shaped by selection pressures in the Pleistocene environment of evolutionary adaptedness, testable via laboratory reasoning tasks rather than field fitness data. Behavioral ecologists have generally kept their distance from this approach and retained the wild-organism framing (fitness measured in real populations under real ecological constraints) precisely because Pleistocene psychological adaptations are difficult to test directly against data, whereas a Hadza forager's actual caloric return rate is a number you can go out and measure this season.

lessons.workedExample: Hawkes and Blurton Jones found that older Hadza women, well past their own reproductive years, maintained very high foraging returns digging tubers and continued provisioning grandchildren — a pattern used to test the 'grandmother hypothesis,' that menopause and extended female post-reproductive lifespan can be favored by selection if older women's continued foraging effort raises the survival of grandchildren more than continued childbearing would raise their own direct fitness. This is a genuinely testable HBE claim: it predicts measurable caloric contributions from grandmothers and measurable survival differences for grandchildren with and without an active foraging grandmother, and both have been checked against real Hadza demographic and foraging-return data rather than inferred from a hypothesized ancestral module.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge raises the sociobiology controversy to see whether a student can separate the real methodological content from the politics, and correctly place a project within HBE versus evolutionary psychology if it touches human behavior at all. A strong answer explains HBE's requirement of measurable, present-day fitness-relevant data (calories, offspring survival) as its safeguard against just-so storytelling, and can name a specific study like Hawkes's Hadza work. A weak answer either treats 'sociobiology' as a slur without knowing what the 1975 book actually argued, or cites an evolutionary-psychology claim about ancestral minds as though it carries the same evidentiary weight as a measured foraging-return dataset.

questions.prompt: Which specific part of Wilson's 1975 Sociobiology triggered the major public controversy?

options.text: The chapters on ant social behavior, which Wilson had studied his whole career
Chapter 27, which extended adaptive, fitness-based reasoning to human behavior
The book's bibliography and citation format
Its chapters on fish schooling behavior

explanations.a: The ant chapters, reflecting Wilson's own specialty, were the least controversial part of the book.
explanations.b: Correct — Chapter 27, 'Man,' applied the same evolutionary-fitness framework used for other species to human behavior, which is what drew the political and scientific backlash.
explanations.c: Citation format was not a substantive point of controversy; the objection was to the book's central argument.
explanations.d: The fish behavior chapters were not the focus of the public dispute.

questions.prompt: What was the central objection raised in the Sociobiology Study Group's 1975 letter 'Against Sociobiology'?

options.text: That kin selection math was numerically incorrect
That extending adaptationist reasoning to humans risked providing pseudo-scientific justification for existing social inequalities
That Wilson had fabricated his ant behavior data
That optimal foraging theory could not be tested empirically

explanations.a: The critique was not a mathematical objection to kin-selection theory itself; it targeted the human application of adaptationist reasoning.
explanations.b: Correct — the letter's central concern was social and political: that framing human inequalities as evolutionarily natural could lend them false scientific legitimacy.
explanations.c: No data-fabrication allegation was part of this critique; it was a conceptual and political objection.
explanations.d: The letter was about the human-behavior extension in Chapter 27, not about testability of optimal foraging theory in other species.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes human behavioral ecology from evolutionary psychology as approaches to human behavior?

options.text: HBE measures present-day fitness-relevant outcomes in living populations; evolutionary psychology infers psychological modules shaped by inferred Pleistocene selection pressures
HBE studies only non-human animals and never humans
Evolutionary psychology relies on demographic mortality data from living foraging populations
The two approaches are functionally identical in method

explanations.a: Correct — HBE's method is to test optimality/fitness predictions against measurable outcomes today, while evolutionary psychology infers ancestral cognitive adaptations tested via lab tasks rather than current fitness data.
explanations.b: HBE specifically applies behavioral-ecology methods to human populations, such as the Hadza and Ache studies.
explanations.c: Reliance on demographic and foraging-return data from living populations is characteristic of HBE, not evolutionary psychology.
explanations.d: The two fields differ substantially in method and evidence standards, which is precisely why behavioral ecologists distinguish themselves from evolutionary psychologists.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher or group to their role in this history.

right.text: Wrote Sociobiology: The New Synthesis, including the controversial Chapter 27
Published the 1975 NYRB letter attacking the human application of sociobiology
Studied Hadza foraging returns to test the grandmother hypothesis
Developed evolutionary psychology's module-based approach

questions.explanation: Wilson wrote the original book, the Sociobiology Study Group publicly attacked its human chapter, Hawkes and Blurton Jones did HBE fieldwork among the Hadza, and Cosmides and Tooby founded evolutionary psychology.

questions.prompt: Order these developments chronologically.

items.text: Wilson publishes Sociobiology: The New Synthesis
The Sociobiology Study Group publishes 'Against Sociobiology' in the New York Review of Books
Cosmides and Tooby begin developing evolutionary psychology's modular framework

questions.explanation: Wilson's book appeared in 1975, the Sociobiology Study Group's rebuttal followed within the same year, and evolutionary psychology as a distinct research program developed from the 1980s onward.

lessons.label: Replication, Bias, and the Credibility Debate

sections.heading: The decline effect and publication bias
sections.body: Behavioral ecology went through its own reliability reckoning starting in the early 2000s. Michael Jennions and Anders Møller's 2002 meta-analysis in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, "Relationships Fade with Time," pooled effect sizes across many published ecology and evolution studies and found a systematic pattern now called the decline effect: the very first published study on a relationship tends to report a substantially larger effect than later studies of the same relationship, with average effect sizes shrinking as more data accumulate. The leading explanation is publication bias — journals and researchers favor striking, statistically significant first results, so early estimates are inflated by which findings got published at all, and later, better-powered or more numerous studies regress toward the true, smaller effect.

sections.heading: A field figure at the center of a data-integrity case
sections.body: The decline-effect finding gained a sharper edge because one of its own co-authors became central to a data-integrity scandal. Anders Møller, a prominent proponent of fluctuating-asymmetry research (the idea that random deviations from bodily symmetry signal poor developmental quality and predict mate choice), retracted a 1998 Oikos paper on herbivore-induced fluctuating asymmetry in oak leaves after the laboratory technician who had measured the asymmetry alleged the underlying data had been fabricated (note that this is a separate body of work from his widely cited barn-swallow tail-asymmetry research). The Danish Committees on Scientific Dishonesty investigated and in the early 2000s found Møller guilty of scientific dishonesty, a verdict he publicly contested; further retractions of his earlier work followed in subsequent years. The case became a cautionary reference point in behavioral ecology precisely because fluctuating-asymmetry research had been an active, widely cited subfield built substantially on results later shown to be unreliable.

sections.heading: Low power, inflated effects, and the fix
sections.body: A parallel problem is chronic low statistical power: many classic behavior studies used small sample sizes (a few dozen animals, sometimes fewer) because behavioral data are expensive and slow to collect, and small-sample studies systematically overestimate true effect sizes when only significant results get published — a dynamic that fueled overconfidence during the 2000s–2010s boom in animal-personality and "behavioral syndrome" research, where correlations between boldness, aggression, and other traits were often reported from small, unreplicated samples. The field's response has converged on several concrete practices: preregistering hypotheses and analysis plans before data collection (locking in what counts as confirmatory versus exploratory), open data and code policies so re-analysis is possible, and coordinated multi-lab or "many-analysts" replication projects that test the same hypothesis across independent research groups and often independent analytical approaches to separate a real effect from a fluke of one lab's methods.

lessons.workedExample: Suppose a 2005 study with 24 birds reports a strong, statistically significant correlation (r = 0.55) between boldness and aggression, and it becomes a widely cited example of a behavioral syndrome. A 2020 multi-lab replication pools 600 birds across eight labs using a preregistered protocol and finds r = 0.12, still detectable with the larger sample but far smaller. This is the decline effect in miniature: the small original study, published partly because its large effect cleared the significance bar, overestimated the true relationship, and the properly powered, preregistered replication revealed the more modest reality — exactly the pattern Jennions and Møller documented at meta-analytic scale.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks whether a famous finding has been replicated to test whether a student treats published results as settled fact or as claims with a track record worth checking. A strong answer names the decline effect directly, explains that early, small, significant-result-only studies tend to overstate effects, and can describe what a preregistered or multi-lab replication would add. A weak answer either assumes any published, cited study is automatically reliable, or overcorrects into assuming all older behavioral findings are worthless — the accurate position is that effect sizes should be trusted in proportion to sample size, preregistration, and independent replication, not publication date or citation count alone.

questions.prompt: What did Jennions and Møller's 2002 meta-analysis find regarding effect sizes in ecology and evolution research over time?

options.text: Effect sizes stayed constant regardless of how many studies accumulated
The first published study on a relationship tends to report a larger effect than later studies, a pattern called the decline effect
Later studies always report larger effects than the original study
Effect sizes are unrelated to publication bias

explanations.a: The meta-analysis specifically found systematic change over time, not stability.
explanations.b: Correct — this decline effect describes the tendency of initial, often small and significance-selected studies to overstate true effect sizes relative to accumulated later evidence.
explanations.c: The pattern runs the opposite direction: effect sizes tend to shrink, not grow, as more studies accumulate.
explanations.d: Publication bias (favoring large, significant early results) is the leading proposed explanation for the decline effect, not an unrelated factor.

questions.prompt: What made the Anders Møller data-integrity case particularly significant for behavioral ecology's credibility?

options.text: It involved a researcher unconnected to any influential subfield in the discipline
A co-author of decline-effect research was himself found guilty of fabricating data underlying an active, widely cited subfield (fluctuating asymmetry)
It showed that no behavioral ecology data has ever been questioned before or since
It concerned a subfield with no connection to mate choice or signaling research

explanations.a: Møller was a prominent, influential figure in fluctuating-asymmetry research specifically, which is what made the case so significant.
explanations.b: Correct — the case was notable both because Møller co-authored the decline-effect meta-analysis and because the misconduct finding concerned data underlying an active area of behavioral ecology.
explanations.c: The case is precisely an example of behavioral ecology data being investigated and questioned, not evidence that scrutiny never occurs.
explanations.d: Fluctuating asymmetry research was closely tied to signaling and mate-choice theory, making the case directly relevant to that literature.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a concrete practice the field has adopted in response to low power and inflated effect sizes?

options.text: Preregistering hypotheses and analysis plans, sharing open data and code, and running multi-lab replication projects
Publishing only studies with the largest reported effect sizes
Reducing sample sizes to speed up publication
Abandoning statistical significance testing altogether with no replacement standard

explanations.a: Correct — preregistration, open data/code, and coordinated multi-lab or many-analysts replication are the field's main concrete responses to the credibility problems described.
explanations.b: Favoring the largest effect sizes is the bias that caused the problem, not a solution to it.
explanations.c: Smaller samples worsen, rather than fix, low statistical power.
explanations.d: The response has been to add rigor (preregistration, replication) around significance testing, not to discard evidentiary standards without replacement.

questions.prompt: Match each term or practice to its definition.

right.text: Effect sizes shrinking as more studies accumulate after an inflated first result
Locking in hypotheses and analysis plans before data collection
Small sample sizes that inflate published effect sizes when only significant results are reported
Independent research groups testing the same hypothesis to separate real effects from single-lab artifacts

questions.explanation: Each term names a distinct piece of the credibility problem or its fix: the decline effect is the symptom, low power and publication bias are contributing causes, and preregistration and multi-lab replication are the field's structural responses.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a proper replication check a student should apply when evaluating whether a famous behavioral finding still holds.

items.text: Identify the original study's sample size and whether the result was statistically significant
Check whether independent labs or later, larger studies have tested the same relationship
Compare the effect size of the original study to the effect size found in later or pooled studies
Judge confidence in the finding based on convergence across independent, adequately powered replications, not on the original study's fame alone

questions.explanation: A sound replication check starts by assessing the original study's power, looks for independent follow-up work, compares effect sizes across studies to detect a decline effect, and finally bases confidence on convergent, well-powered evidence rather than a single famous result.

lessons.label: Mating Systems and the Environment

sections.heading: Emlen and Oring: mating systems are set by the environment, not the species
sections.body: In a 1977 Science paper, Stephen Emlen and Lewis Oring argued that a species' mating system is not a fixed trait but an outcome of ecology acting on individuals competing to monopolize mates. They defined the environmental potential for polygamy as the degree to which either resources critical to females (food, nest sites) or females themselves can be economically defended and monopolized by one sex, usually males. When receptive females or key resources are clumped in space or time, one male can guard many mates; when they are dispersed, he cannot, and monogamy or scramble competition results. Emlen and Oring also introduced the operational sex ratio (OSR) — the ratio of sexually active males to sexually receptive females at a given moment — as the proximate driver of competition intensity: a male-skewed OSR (common because females are often unavailable while pregnant, incubating, or lactating) intensifies male-male competition and favors polygyny.

sections.heading: The polygyny threshold: when sharing a good territory beats monopolizing a poor one
sections.body: Jared Verner and Mary Willson (1966) and Gordon Orians (1969) formalized why females sometimes choose to become a second mate on a rich male's territory rather than the sole mate of a male on a poor one. Plot female fitness against territory quality separately for monogamous and already-mated (polygynous) settlement: both lines rise with quality, but the polygyny line sits below the monogamy line because she shares male help and resources. The polygyny threshold is the point on the male-quality axis where the polygyny curve for a superior territory crosses the monogamy curve for an inferior one — beyond that point, a female does better as mate two on the good territory than as mate one on the bad one. Red-winged blackbirds, where territory quality (marsh vegetation, food) varies enormously and females tolerate co-wives on the best territories, are the model system.

sections.heading: Lek evolution: males defend nothing but display space
sections.body: Leks are aggregations of males displaying with no resources or parental care on offer, seen in sage grouse, birds-of-paradise, and some ungulates. Three (non-exclusive) models explain why males cluster despite no monopolizable resource. The hotspot model: males settle where female traffic naturally concentrates (near feeding or travel corridors), so clustering is a byproduct of female movement. The hotshot model: subordinate males settle near a few highly attractive 'hotshot' males to intercept females drawn to them. The female-preference (or predation-dilution) model: females themselves prefer clustered males, either because comparison-shopping lowers search costs or because a group dilutes each male's predation risk, so male clustering is directly selected by female choice.

lessons.workedExample: A field team studies red-winged blackbirds (Agelaius phoeniceus) across a marsh with patchy vegetation. Territory A has dense cattails, abundant insect prey, and low nest-predation; Territory B is sparse and exposed. A female settling as the sole mate on B raises 2.1 fledglings per season; a female settling as second mate on A, splitting the male's vigilance and provisioning with a co-wife, still raises 3.4 fledglings because A's resource base is that much richer. Since 3.4 > 2.1, A has crossed the polygyny threshold and females should prefer it even shared. Verner and Orians's model predicts exactly this: once between-territory quality variance is large enough, female fitness curves for monogamous settlement on poor sites and polygynous settlement on rich sites cross, and settlement pattern should track that crossing point rather than simple site quality.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks 'why does this species have this mating system?' to test whether a student treats mating system as an adaptive response to measurable ecology rather than a fixed label. A weak answer says 'males are polygynous because they're bigger' or cites the species as if the system were taxonomically fixed. A strong answer names the resource-distribution or OSR driver, and for a lek species, commits to one candidate mechanism (hotspot, hotshot, or female preference) and states what data would distinguish it — e.g., mapping whether male clusters track female travel routes (hotspot) versus mapping mating skew toward specific central males (hotshot).

questions.prompt: According to Emlen and Oring (1977), what primarily determines the environmental potential for polygamy?

options.text: The absolute population density of the species
Whether resources or mates can be economically monopolized in space and time
The average lifespan of females
The phylogenetic relatedness of the species to known polygynous taxa

explanations.a: Density alone does not determine monopolizability; a dense but evenly dispersed resource can still be impossible for one individual to defend.
explanations.b: Correct — Emlen and Oring's central claim is that polygamy potential tracks how economically defensible mates or resources are, which depends on their spatial and temporal clumping.
explanations.c: Lifespan affects reproductive rate but is not the mechanism Emlen and Oring identified as driving monopolization potential.
explanations.d: Mating systems are labile within lineages and respond to current ecology, not simply inherited from relatives.

questions.prompt: In the Verner-Willson-Orians polygyny threshold model, a female should accept becoming a second mate when:

options.text: Her fitness as a co-mate on a high-quality territory exceeds her fitness as sole mate on a low-quality territory
The operational sex ratio is exactly 1:1
No males are defending any territory at all
She has already mated once before in her life

explanations.a: Correct — this is the defining crossover condition of the polygyny threshold: shared access to a superior territory outweighs sole access to an inferior one.
explanations.b: A balanced OSR is unrelated to the threshold logic, which concerns territory-quality variance, not sex ratio.
explanations.c: The model assumes males are defending territories of varying quality; without territories there is nothing to compare.
explanations.d: Prior mating history is not a variable in the Verner-Willson-Orians model.

questions.prompt: Match each lek-evolution model to its core mechanism.

right.text: Males cluster near paths of naturally high female traffic
Subordinate males settle near a few highly attractive males
Females actively prefer clustered males, driving male aggregation

questions.explanation: Hotspot clustering follows female movement patterns, hotshot clustering follows a few top-quality males, and the female-preference model treats clustering itself as a female-selected trait, e.g. via reduced search costs or diluted predation risk.

questions.prompt: A male-skewed operational sex ratio (OSR) at a given moment tends to:

options.text: Reduce competition among males for mates
Intensify male-male competition, favoring polygynous or scramble mating
Force the species into strict lifelong monogamy
Have no measurable effect on mating behavior

explanations.a: A male-skewed OSR means more males compete for fewer available females, increasing rather than reducing competition.
explanations.b: Correct — with many sexually active males per receptive female, competition for access intensifies, which Emlen and Oring identified as a proximate driver of polygyny/scramble systems.
explanations.c: OSR skew makes monopolization harder to avoid, not a guarantee of monogamy; it usually pushes systems away from strict pair-bonding.
explanations.d: OSR is central to Emlen and Oring's framework precisely because it does predict shifts in competitive intensity and mating system.

lessons.label: Mate Choice and Honest Signalling

sections.heading: Condition-dependent color: house finches and the carotenoid honesty mechanism
sections.body: Ornaments stay honest when they are costly to produce or maintain in a way that only high-quality individuals can afford. Geoffrey Hill's work on house finches (Haemorhous mexicanus) through the 1990s showed male plumage redness is a textbook case: finches cannot synthesize carotenoid pigments themselves, so feather color directly tracks how much carotenoid-rich food a male ate during molt, and males carrying heavier parasite loads (coccidian infections) convert dietary carotenoids into color less efficiently, producing duller, more yellow-orange plumage. Hill showed experimentally that females strongly prefer redder males and that redness predicted male provisioning ability and offspring survival, making color an honest, physiologically-enforced index of foraging skill and health rather than an arbitrary preference.

sections.heading: Fluctuating asymmetry: a claim that shrank under scrutiny
sections.body: In the 1990s, fluctuating asymmetry (FA) — small random deviations from bilateral symmetry, thought to reflect an individual's inability to buffer development against stress — was proposed as a universal signal of genetic quality, with symmetric individuals reported as more attractive across many taxa. Later meta-analyses, including work by A. R. Palmer in the late 1990s, found the original effect sizes were inflated, likely by publication bias favoring positive results and small original sample sizes. FA is now treated cautiously: a real but weak and inconsistent signal in some systems, not the general law of attraction it was once presented as — a useful case study in how a striking early result can outrun its evidence.

sections.heading: MHC-based choice, backup signals, and copied preferences
sections.body: Choice is not only about visible ornaments. Claus Wedekind's 1995 'sweaty T-shirt' study found women rated the body odor of men with dissimilar major histocompatibility complex (MHC) genotypes as more pleasant, suggesting olfactory cues support MHC-disassortative mating that boosts offspring immune diversity; three-spined sticklebacks show a related but distinct pattern, with females using odor cues to select mates that give offspring an optimal, intermediate number of MHC alleles rather than simply the most dissimilar genotype (Reusch et al. 2001). Because no single cue perfectly indexes quality, many species assess multiple signals; the backup-signal hypothesis holds redundant signals as insurance against noise in any one channel, while the multiple-messages hypothesis holds each signal encodes a different quality (color for parasite load, song rate for foraging condition). Costly signals split into handicaps (the cost itself proves quality, as in Zahavi's principle) versus indices (cost is mechanistically inseparable from the trait, like body-size-limited call frequency). Finally, mate choice is sometimes socially transmitted: mate-choice copying, first demonstrated in guppies by Lee Dugatkin (1992), shows females preferring males they observed being chosen by other females, independent of the male's own traits.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher supplements the diet of half a captive house finch population with extra carotenoids (via colored food dye studies mimicking Hill's design) while leaving the rest on a standard diet, then scores plumage redness and runs female choice trials. Supplemented males grow significantly redder feathers and win significantly more female choice trials, confirming color is causally, not just correlationally, tied to resource access. A parallel FA study on the same population, measuring wing-length asymmetry, finds a weak and non-significant relationship with mating success — consistent with the modern, deflated view of FA rather than the strong 1990s claims, and a good example of why a single well-controlled diet manipulation is more convincing evidence of honesty than a correlational symmetry measurement.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing signal honesty wants to know whether a student understands WHY a trait can't be faked, not just that 'females prefer bright colors.' A weak answer states the preference without a mechanism. A strong answer identifies the enforcement mechanism — resource limitation, parasite interference, or a physiological cost — and, crucially, is willing to say when the honesty claim is shaky, citing the FA literature's decline as evidence they know the field self-corrects rather than treating every classic finding as settled fact.

questions.prompt: Why is carotenoid-based redness in house finches considered an honest signal?

options.text: Because females have no other way to assess males
Because finches cannot synthesize carotenoids themselves, so color depends on diet quality and is reduced by parasite load
Because redness is entirely genetically fixed at hatching
Because all male finches display identical coloration

explanations.a: Females use multiple cues in many species; lack of alternatives isn't why this signal is honest.
explanations.b: Correct — redness is constrained by dietary carotenoid intake and degraded by parasitic infection, making it hard for a low-quality male to fake.
explanations.c: If color were fixed at hatching regardless of condition, it could not honestly signal current foraging or health status; Hill's diet manipulations show it is condition-dependent.
explanations.d: Color varies substantially among males, which is exactly what allows it to function as an informative signal.

questions.prompt: What happened to the fluctuating asymmetry (FA)-attractiveness literature after its peak in the 1990s?

options.text: It was fully confirmed by every subsequent large-scale study
Meta-analyses found the original effect sizes were likely inflated, and the signal is now viewed as weak and inconsistent
It was renamed and remains the strongest known honest signal across all taxa
FA research was shown to apply only to plants, not animals

explanations.a: The opposite occurred — later, larger analyses failed to replicate the strength of early claims.
explanations.b: Correct — publication bias and small original samples inflated early FA-attractiveness effect sizes; later meta-analyses found much weaker, inconsistent support.
explanations.c: FA is now considered one of the weaker and more contested signal candidates, not the strongest.
explanations.d: FA research addressed animal (and some human) mate choice specifically, not plants.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher/study to its finding.

right.text: Women preferred body odor of MHC-dissimilar men in a T-shirt-rating study
