Female sticklebacks used odor cues to select for an optimal number of MHC alleles
Female guppies copied other females' mate choices

questions.explanation: Wedekind's human 'sweaty T-shirt' study supports MHC-disassortative mate choice via odor, while Reusch's stickleback study shows females use odor to select for an optimal number of MHC alleles in offspring; Dugatkin's guppy experiments established mate-choice copying as socially transmitted preference.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a Zahavian 'handicap' signal from an 'index' signal?

options.text: A handicap's cost is what proves quality; an index's cost is mechanistically inseparable from the trait itself
Handicaps are always visual while indices are always acoustic
Indices are learned behaviors while handicaps are always innate
There is no meaningful difference between the two

explanations.a: Correct — a handicap (like an elaborate tail) is costly and that cost enforces honesty; an index (like a body-size-limited call frequency) can't be faked because the physical link between trait and quality is direct, not just costly.
explanations.b: Modality (visual vs. acoustic) is not what defines the handicap/index distinction; both types occur across sensory channels.
explanations.c: Learned versus innate is a separate axis from the cost-based handicap/index distinction.
explanations.d: The distinction is meaningful and central to signal-honesty theory.

questions.prompt: The 'backup-signal' hypothesis for why animals use multiple signals proposes that:

options.text: Each additional signal is redundant insurance against noise or error in perceiving any single signal
Each signal encodes a completely different, non-overlapping quality
Multiple signals evolve only by genetic drift with no function
Animals use only one signal at a time, never multiple

explanations.a: Correct — the backup-signal hypothesis treats redundant signals as insurance against transmission or perception failure in any one channel.
explanations.b: That description matches the competing 'multiple-messages' hypothesis, not the backup-signal hypothesis.
explanations.c: Both hypotheses propose functional roles for multiple signals, not driftonly explanations.
explanations.d: Many species (birds, lizards, insects) demonstrably combine visual, acoustic, and chemical signals simultaneously.

lessons.label: Sexual Conflict, Sperm Competition, and Extra-Pair Paternity

sections.heading: Sperm competition and paternity assurance
sections.body: When a female mates with more than one male within a fertile period, the sperm of rival males compete inside her reproductive tract, a process Geoff Parker formalized as sperm competition theory in 1970. Last-male sperm precedence — where the most recent mate fertilizes a disproportionate share of eggs, well documented in insects and some birds — creates strong selection on males to mate last or to displace rival sperm. Two behavioral responses follow directly: mate guarding, where a male stays close to his mate to physically block rival access during her fertile window, and frequent copulation, where a male repeatedly re-mates with his own partner to dilute or overwhelm any sperm a rival deposited. Both behaviors are paternity-assurance tactics, and their intensity tracks paternity risk — males guard hardest when rival males are locally abundant or when the female has recently been near other males.

sections.heading: Sexually antagonistic coevolution: an arms race between the sexes
sections.body: Because male and female fitness optima over mating rate and mating control often diverge, traits in one sex that increase its fitness can directly reduce the other's, producing a coevolutionary arms race. Water striders (Gerris) are a well-studied case: Göran Arnqvist and Locke Rowe's work through the 1990s-2000s documented males evolving grasping genital structures to force mating and females evolving resisting abdominal spines and behaviors to shake males off, with populations under stronger sexual conflict showing exaggerated versions of both traits in lockstep. In Drosophila melanogaster, Tracey Chapman and colleagues (1995) showed that seminal fluid accessory-gland proteins transferred during mating, while boosting a male's own paternity share, measurably shorten female lifespan when females re-mate repeatedly — a male-benefit, female-cost trait maintained despite its toll on the female.

sections.heading: Infanticide as sexual conflict, and the DNA revolution that broke 'monogamy'
sections.body: Sarah Blaffer Hrdy's studies of Hanuman langurs in the 1970s proposed sexually selected infanticide: incoming males that take over a troop kill unweaned infants sired by the ousted male, which shortens the females' lactational infertility and lets the new male sire his own offspring sooner — a male reproductive strategy directly opposed to female and offspring interests. The clearest overturn of a long-standing assumption came from DNA fingerprinting, developed by Alec Jeffreys in 1984 and applied to birds starting in the late 1980s. Ornithologists had assumed social pair-bonds meant genetic monogamy; DNA paternity testing instead revealed extra-pair paternity (EPP) is widespread. A landmark synthesis by Simon Griffith, Ian Owens, and Katherine Thuman (2002) found extra-pair young average roughly 11% of offspring across socially monogamous passerine species, but with huge variance — reed buntings (Emberiza schoeniclus) exceed 50%, as shown by Dixon and colleagues (1994), meaning most broods contain young sired outside the social pair bond.

lessons.workedExample: A team studies a population of socially monogamous reed buntings and genotypes every nestling and both social parents using microsatellite markers. In a sample of 40 nests, 24 contain at least one extra-pair young, and across all nestlings, 55% were not sired by the social father — consistent with Dixon et al.'s (1994) published figures for this species. The team also notes males in this population mate-guard intensively during the female's fertile period, exactly as sperm competition theory predicts: guarding is a male countermeasure to a real, high, measured paternity risk, and the persistence of such high EPP despite guarding shows female control over extra-pair copulations is also strong, illustrating sexual conflict as an ongoing tug-of-war rather than a one-sided male tactic.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about extra-pair paternity to test whether a student understands that 'monogamy' is a social, not genetic, category, and can explain why the two diverge. A weak answer says birds 'cheat' without a fitness framework. A strong answer explains the asymmetry in stakes — a female extra-pair copulation directly gains genetic diversity or 'good genes' for offspring at some risk of losing male care, while a male gains an extra paternity share at near-zero cost — and cites a real EPP-rate figure (the ~11% cross-species average or the >50% reed bunting extreme) rather than a vague 'sometimes it happens.'

questions.prompt: According to Griffith, Owens, and Thuman's (2002) synthesis, what is the approximate average rate of extra-pair young across socially monogamous passerine species?

options.text: About 0%, confirming genetic monogamy is the norm
About 11%, with wide variation across species
About 90%, meaning almost no social pairs are genetically monogamous
Exactly 50% in every species studied

explanations.a: DNA fingerprinting overturned the assumption of strict genetic monogamy in socially monogamous birds; the average is well above zero.
explanations.b: Correct — the cross-species average is roughly 11%, though individual species range from near 0% to over 50%.
explanations.c: 90% is far above the documented average, though a few species-specific figures approach or exceed 50%, not 90%, at the high end.
explanations.d: The rate varies enormously by species (e.g., reed buntings exceed 50%) rather than being a fixed 50% constant.

questions.prompt: Why do males frequently re-mate with their own partners under sperm competition theory?

options.text: To dilute or numerically overwhelm sperm that a rival male may have deposited, given last-male sperm precedence
Because repeated mating has no effect on paternity share
To reduce the female's overall fertility
Because females require exactly one mating to become fertile

explanations.a: Correct — with last-male sperm precedence common, frequent copulation raises a male's relative share of sperm present at fertilization, functioning as a paternity-assurance tactic.
explanations.b: Sperm competition theory specifically predicts mating frequency affects paternity share, which is why the behavior is selected for.
explanations.c: The goal is paternity assurance for the guarding male, not reducing female fertility.
explanations.d: Repeated mating as a tactic implies fertility is not capped at one mating; multiple matings change the paternity outcome.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher (or research team) to their contribution.

right.text: Formalized sperm competition theory
Documented coevolving grasping/resisting morphology in water striders
Showed Drosophila seminal proteins reduce female lifespan
Proposed sexually selected infanticide in langurs

questions.explanation: Parker built the formal theory of sperm competition; Arnqvist and Rowe documented the water-strider genital arms race; Chapman's team showed male-benefit, female-cost seminal proteins in fruit flies; Hrdy proposed that infanticide by incoming male langurs is a male reproductive strategy.

questions.prompt: Order these events in the history of understanding avian mating systems.

items.text: Ornithologists assume social pair-bonds equal genetic monogamy
Alec Jeffreys develops DNA fingerprinting (1984)
Researchers apply DNA paternity testing to wild bird populations
Griffith, Owens, and Thuman (2002) synthesize cross-species EPP rates

questions.explanation: The pre-DNA assumption of genetic monogamy came first; Jeffreys's 1984 DNA fingerprinting technique made paternity testing possible; researchers then applied it to birds starting in the late 1980s, revealing widespread extra-pair paternity; and the 2002 synthesis quantified the pattern across many species.

lessons.label: Parental Care, Family Conflict, and Brood Parasitism

sections.heading: Trivers's parent-offspring conflict: relatedness asymmetry drives disagreement
sections.body: Robert Trivers's 1974 paper argued that because a parent is equally related (r = 0.5) to all its offspring but an offspring is related to itself by r = 1 and to its siblings by only r = 0.5, parent and offspring should disagree over how long investment continues. From the parent's-eye view, weaning or fledging should happen once the marginal fitness gain to the current offspring drops below the gain the parent could get investing in future offspring instead. From the offspring's-eye view, because it values its own survival twice as much as a full sibling's, it should demand investment past that point — favoring itself even at some cost to future siblings. The conflict is not over whether care should happen, but over exactly when it should stop, and it predicts an evolutionary tug-of-war rather than either party simply getting its optimum.

sections.heading: Begging, scramble, and honest signalling within the brood
sections.body: Nestling begging — loud, conspicuous calling and gaping — is the clearest observable expression of this conflict. H. Charles J. Godfray's 1991 model treated begging as a costly, honest signal of hunger: because intense begging carries real costs (energy expenditure, predator attraction), only genuinely hungry chicks should beg at the highest intensity, letting parents allocate food efficiently based on an honest cue. But begging also functions as sibling scramble competition, where the loudest or most central chick simply out-competes siblings for a fixed food delivery regardless of true relative need, especially in species where parents deliver food to whichever nestling is most conspicuous rather than assessing all chicks. Both mechanisms can operate simultaneously, and separating them experimentally (e.g., testing whether begging tracks true hunger versus just settling within-brood contests) remains an active research question.

sections.heading: Clutch size, biparental negotiation, and the cuckoo arms race
sections.body: David Lack's 1947 clutch-size hypothesis proposed that natural selection favors the clutch size that maximizes the number of surviving offspring, not the largest physically possible clutch — because each additional egg divides finite parental provisioning, and above the optimum, survival per chick drops faster than brood size rises. This was tested directly with brood-size manipulation experiments, adding or removing eggs/chicks from nests and tracking fledging success, which repeatedly confirmed manipulated broods above the natural optimum fledge fewer, lower-condition young. Where two parents share care, each faces a temptation to reduce its own effort if the partner compensates, so biparental care functions as a continuous negotiation, formalized in game-theoretic models where each parent's optimal effort depends on the other's. The starkest interspecific version of the conflict is brood parasitism: cuckoos (Cuculus canorus) lay mimetic eggs in host nests, hosts evolve egg-rejection based on pattern and color discrimination, and Nicholas Davies and Michael Brooke's model-egg experiments (late 1980s-1990s) placed artificial eggs of varying mimicry into host nests and showed rejection rates tracked how closely the model matched the host's own eggs — direct experimental proof of an ongoing coevolutionary arms race.

lessons.workedExample: A researcher manipulates great tit (Parus major) clutches to create three groups: reduced (natural minus 2 eggs), natural, and enlarged (natural plus 2 eggs). Fledging success per chick is highest in the reduced group, declines modestly in the natural group, and drops sharply in the enlarged group, while total fledglings produced peaks near the natural clutch size and falls in the enlarged group as starvation and reduced body condition set in — reproducing the classic Lack-hypothesis pattern. In a parallel reed warbler population parasitized by cuckoos, Davies-and-Brooke-style model-egg trials show hosts reject 90% of poorly mimetic model eggs but under 20% of high-mimicry models, demonstrating discrimination is graded by mimicry accuracy rather than all-or-nothing, exactly the signature of an active arms race rather than a settled one-sided outcome.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probing parent-offspring conflict wants to see whether a student can state the relatedness asymmetry (r=1 to self vs r=0.5 to siblings) that generates the disagreement, not just describe begging as 'cute chick behavior.' A weak answer treats begging as simple communication of hunger with no cost or conflict framing. A strong answer distinguishes the honest-signal and scramble-competition explanations for begging, and for clutch size, correctly states that Lack's optimum is NOT the maximum physically possible clutch — a common student error — citing a brood-manipulation result as evidence.

questions.prompt: Why does Trivers's (1974) parent-offspring conflict theory predict disagreement over the timing of weaning?

options.text: Because offspring value themselves (r=1) more than they value a full sibling (r=0.5), while a parent is equally related to both
Because parents and offspring have no genetic relationship at all
Because offspring cannot survive without indefinite parental care
Because only offspring benefit from any investment, never parents

explanations.a: Correct — the relatedness asymmetry (offspring r=1 to self, r=0.5 to siblings; parent r=0.5 to all offspring) means offspring favor themselves more strongly than a parent should, producing conflict over the investment cutoff.
explanations.b: Parents and offspring are highly related (r=0.5); the conflict arises despite, not because of, absent relatedness.
explanations.c: The theory concerns an economic tradeoff over timing, not an absolute inability to survive without care.
explanations.d: Parental investment carries a real cost to the parent's future reproduction, which is exactly why parents have an interest in limiting it.

questions.prompt: David Lack's clutch-size hypothesis predicts that the evolutionarily favored clutch size is:

options.text: The largest clutch size physically possible for the species
The clutch size that maximizes the number of offspring that survive to independence
Always exactly one offspring per breeding attempt
Determined solely by egg size, independent of parental provisioning

explanations.a: This is the common misconception Lack's hypothesis directly refutes: maximum possible clutch size overwhelms parental provisioning and reduces survival.
explanations.b: Correct — Lack argued selection favors the clutch size maximizing surviving offspring, not the raw egg count, because provisioning capacity is finite.
explanations.c: Optimal clutch size varies by species and food availability; it is not fixed at one.
explanations.d: Provisioning capacity is central to the hypothesis — larger clutches divide finite parental food delivery among more chicks.

questions.prompt: In Godfray's (1991) model, why can nestling begging function as an honest signal of hunger?

options.text: Because begging is completely costless and any chick can do it freely
Because begging carries real costs (energy, predator attraction), so only genuinely hungry chicks should beg most intensely
Because parents cannot hear or perceive begging calls
Because begging always equalizes food among all chicks regardless of hunger

explanations.a: A costless signal is exactly what honesty theory says CANNOT stay reliable — costlessness invites overstatement by low-need individuals.
explanations.b: Correct — cost is what enforces honesty: only chicks with enough true need to justify the energetic and predation-risk cost should beg at the highest intensity.
explanations.c: Parents responding to begging calls is the entire premise of begging functioning as a signal.
explanations.d: Scramble-competition dynamics can produce unequal outcomes; begging does not guarantee equalized food regardless of hunger.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of Davies and Brooke's model-egg experimental approach to testing host egg rejection.

items.text: Note that cuckoos lay eggs mimicking the host species' own egg pattern and color
Create artificial model eggs varying in how closely they mimic the host's real eggs
Place model eggs into host nests
Measure rejection rate as a function of mimicry accuracy

questions.explanation: The experiment begins from the observed natural phenomenon of egg mimicry, then manipulates mimicry accuracy in artificial eggs, places them into real nests, and measures how rejection scales with how closely the model matches the host's own eggs — the design that reveals graded discrimination consistent with an active coevolutionary arms race.

lessons.label: Cooperation, Kinship, and Dominance Structure

sections.heading: Hamilton's rule and the haplodiploidy hypothesis
sections.body: William Hamilton's 1964 rule states an altruistic act should be favored by selection when rB > C, where r is the genetic relatedness between actor and recipient, B is the fitness benefit to the recipient, and C is the fitness cost to the actor. Applied numerically: a helper related to a beneficiary by r=0.5 (a full sibling) should help whenever the benefit delivered is more than twice the cost paid (since 0.5B > C requires B > 2C). Hamilton also proposed haplodiploidy — the sex-determination system in Hymenoptera (ants, bees, wasps) where females develop from fertilized (diploid) eggs and males from unfertilized (haploid) eggs — could help explain eusociality, because full sisters share r=0.75 with each other (versus the usual 0.5), giving females unusually high relatedness to their sisters and a genetic incentive to help raise them rather than reproduce directly. This 3/4-relatedness argument has since been heavily qualified: eusociality also requires multiple additional preconditions (a defensible nest, overlapping generations, a monogamous ancestral mating system so the 3/4 figure actually holds), and eusociality has evolved in some diploid species (naked mole-rats) where the 3/4 relatedness boost is absent entirely, showing haplodiploidy is neither necessary nor sufficient on its own.

sections.heading: Cooperative breeding: meerkats and Florida scrub-jays
sections.body: Cooperative breeding, where non-breeding helpers assist a dominant pair in raising young, has been studied intensively in meerkats (Suricata suricatta) by Tim Clutton-Brock's Kalahari Meerkat Project. Helpers perform sentinel duty (standing guard against predators while the group forages, at real personal cost in feeding time) and allolactation (subordinate females that have never bred can lactate and nurse the dominant female's pups). Because meerkat groups are typically extended family units, these costly helping behaviors deliver indirect fitness benefits consistent with Hamilton's rule. Florida scrub-jays (Aphelocoma coerulescens), studied long-term by Glen Woolfenden and John Fitzpatrick, show a different driver: habitat saturation. Suitable scrub habitat is fully occupied, so young jays often cannot find an open territory to breed on their own and instead delay dispersal, staying on the natal territory as helpers-at-the-nest until a breeding vacancy or territory opens up nearby — cooperation driven as much by ecological constraint as by kin-selected benefit.

sections.heading: Scoring dominance hierarchies and the dear-enemy effect
sections.body: Beyond kin cooperation, many social groups organize around linear dominance hierarchies, and quantifying them requires standardized metrics. David's score sums an individual's proportion of wins against each opponent, weighted by that opponent's own success, producing a continuous rank measure from a win/loss matrix. Han de Vries's h' (normalized Landau's index) measures how strongly linear (transitive, non-circular) a hierarchy is, ranging from 0 (no linearity) to 1 (perfectly linear), and is the standard test for whether a group's dominance relationships form a true pecking order rather than an unstable triangle of relationships. Separately, winner and loser effects describe how a recent win increases the probability of winning the next contest (and a recent loss increases the probability of losing the next one), independent of underlying fighting ability, meaning hierarchy position can be partly self-reinforcing. In territorial species, the dear-enemy effect (documented by Edward Temeles and others) describes reduced aggression toward known, established neighbors compared to unfamiliar intruders, because a settled neighbor is a smaller ongoing threat to the territory than a stranger testing new ground.

lessons.workedExample: A meerkat group of 12 includes a dominant breeding pair and 10 non-breeding helpers, most closely related to the pups by r=0.5 (siblings) or r=0.25 (half-sibs/aunts). A sentinel helper's shift costs it roughly 15% of its normal foraging intake that hour (C), but its vigilance calls cut pup predation risk enough to save on average 0.6 additional pups per season across the group (B, shared across kin). Using Hamilton's rule with r=0.5, the helper needs 0.5B > C; converting to comparable fitness units, the model shows the indirect benefit comfortably exceeds the direct foraging cost, so sentinel behavior is predicted to persist — consistent with Clutton-Brock's long-term Kalahari field data showing helpers with more close kin in the group perform more sentinel bouts than helpers in groups with fewer relatives.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about Hamilton's rule to see whether a student can actually apply rB > C with real numbers, not just recite it as a slogan. A weak answer says 'kin selection means animals help relatives.' A strong answer plugs in an actual relatedness coefficient (0.5 for siblings, 0.25 for half-sibs or cousins-once-removed-equivalent, 0.75 for haplodiploid full sisters) and shows the inequality being satisfied or violated for a specific case, and — for eusociality specifically — knows to qualify the haplodiploidy hypothesis rather than presenting it as a settled, sufficient explanation.

questions.prompt: Under Hamilton's rule (rB > C), a helper related to a beneficiary by r = 0.5 should help when:

options.text: The benefit to the recipient is more than twice the cost to the helper
The benefit equals exactly the cost
The cost is greater than the benefit, regardless of relatedness
Relatedness is irrelevant to the decision

explanations.a: Correct — solving 0.5B > C gives B > 2C, so the benefit must exceed twice the cost for helping to be favored at r=0.5.
explanations.b: If B equals C exactly, then 0.5B = 0.5C < C, meaning the rule is NOT satisfied and helping is not favored.
explanations.c: The rule can still favor helping even when C is substantial, as long as B is large enough relative to r; cost alone doesn't decide it.
explanations.d: Relatedness (r) is the multiplier on benefit in Hamilton's rule; it is central, not irrelevant.

questions.prompt: What is the key qualification modern biologists add to the haplodiploidy hypothesis for eusociality?

options.text: Haplodiploidy is neither necessary nor sufficient alone — eusociality also requires factors like a defensible nest and ancestral monogamy, and occurs in diploid species too
Haplodiploidy has been fully disproven and plays no role whatsoever
Haplodiploidy is the only possible explanation and applies to all eusocial species without exception
Haplodiploidy only matters for solitary, non-social insect species

explanations.a: Correct — the 3/4-relatedness advantage requires ancestral monogamy to actually hold, additional ecological preconditions are needed, and diploid eusocial species (naked mole-rats) show haplodiploidy isn't required.
explanations.b: Haplodiploidy still plausibly contributes in some lineages; it's qualified, not entirely discarded.
explanations.c: Naked mole-rats are diploid and eusocial, directly contradicting haplodiploidy as the sole universal explanation.
explanations.d: Haplodiploidy is specifically relevant to social, not solitary, insect species — it concerns relatedness among cooperating individuals.

questions.prompt: Match each cooperative-breeding system to its primary documented driver.

right.text: Kin-selected benefit within extended family groups
Habitat saturation limiting available breeding territories

questions.explanation: Clutton-Brock's meerkat work emphasizes kin-selected helping within close-knit family groups, while Woolfenden and Fitzpatrick's scrub-jay work emphasizes ecological constraint — full habitat occupancy leaving no open territories for young jays to disperse to and breed independently.

questions.prompt: What does de Vries's h' (normalized Landau's index) measure in a dominance hierarchy?

options.text: The total number of individuals in the group
How strongly linear/transitive the hierarchy is, from 0 (not linear) to 1 (perfectly linear)
The average lifespan of dominant individuals
The genetic relatedness between top-ranked individuals

explanations.a: Group size is not what h' quantifies; h' is a structural measure of the win/loss relationships themselves.
explanations.b: Correct — h' tests whether dominance relations form a consistent, transitive pecking order versus unstable, circular (rock-paper-scissors-like) relationships.
explanations.c: Lifespan is unrelated to what h' measures; it is purely about hierarchy structure from contest outcomes.
explanations.d: Relatedness is a separate concept from dominance linearity; h' is computed from win/loss records, not pedigree.

questions.prompt: The 'dear-enemy effect' predicts that a territory holder will show:

options.text: More aggression toward familiar, established neighbors than toward unfamiliar intruders
Less aggression toward familiar, established neighbors than toward unfamiliar intruders
Identical aggression toward all individuals regardless of familiarity
No aggression toward any conspecific under any circumstance

explanations.a: This reverses the effect; established neighbors, being known and already settled, provoke less aggression, not more.
explanations.b: Correct — a familiar neighbor with its own established territory poses less of an ongoing threat than an unfamiliar intruder who might be testing for a new territory to take, so aggression toward neighbors is reduced.
explanations.c: The whole point of the effect is a difference in response based on familiarity/relationship history.
explanations.d: Territory holders still respond aggressively to unfamiliar intruders; the effect concerns a relative reduction toward known neighbors specifically.

lessons.label: Communication, Deception, and Noise

sections.heading: Sensory drive and functionally referential alarm calls
sections.body: John Endler's sensory drive hypothesis (developed through the 1980s-90s) argues signal design coevolves with the sensory environment: signals are shaped by what the receiver's sensory system can detect against the local background, not by conspicuousness in the abstract. His guppy (Poecilia reticulata) work showed male orange-and-black spot coloration is tuned to ambient light conditions in each stream — in clear, well-lit pools guppies evolve brighter, more saturated colors that stand out, while in tannin-stained, dim streams color intensity is muted, tracking what actually transmits well through that specific light environment, balanced against predation risk from visually-hunting fish. Signal content can also be highly specific: Robert Seyfarth and Dorothy Cheney's 1980 playback experiments on vervet monkeys (Chlorocebus pygerythrus) in Amboseli established functionally referential alarm calls — vervets give acoustically distinct calls for leopards, eagles, and snakes, and playback of a recorded call alone (with no predator present) reliably triggered the predator-appropriate escape response (climbing trees for leopard calls, looking up and hiding in bushes for eagle calls, looking down at the ground for snake calls), proving the calls function almost like predator-specific words rather than generic distress noise.

sections.heading: Deceptive signals and eavesdropping
sections.body: Not all signals are honest. Fiddler crabs (Uca species) that lose their large signaling claw regenerate a lighter, weaker, but visually similar replacement claw; Patricia Backwell and colleagues' studies showed these regenerated claws can be less effective in actual fights yet still succeed in male-male threat displays and female mate attraction, functioning as a partial bluff that exploits the difficulty of assessing true claw strength from appearance alone. Fork-tailed drongos (Dicrurus adsimilis) in the Kalahari, studied by Tom Flower (2011), give false alarm calls — including mimicking other species' alarm calls — to startle other animals like pied babblers or meerkats into dropping food, then steal it; drongos vary their call type to avoid habituation, a genuine case of tactical deception maintained by the payoff of stolen food outweighing any cost of occasionally being ignored. Communication is also not limited to the intended sender-receiver pair: eavesdropping, where a third party (predator, competitor, or rival) intercepts a signal meant for someone else, and audience effects, where a signaler changes its behavior because it detects it is being watched by an eavesdropper, both show that signals exist in a networked, not strictly private, social environment.

sections.heading: Anthropogenic noise and the urban great tit
sections.body: Human-generated noise is now a documented selective pressure on animal signals. Hans Slabbekoorn and Margriet Peet (2003) compared great tit (Parus major) song across territories within the city of Leiden and found birds in noisier urban territories sing at significantly higher minimum frequencies than birds in quieter territories nearby, an adjustment that shifts song out of the low-frequency band dominated by traffic noise, preserving the signal's audibility to potential mates and rivals. Follow-up work across many bird species (and independently in some anurans and marine mammals) has found similar shifts toward higher pitch and, in some cases, increased amplitude (the Lombard effect) in noisy environments, showing urban noise adaptation is a broad, repeated pattern rather than a single-species anomaly — and raising open questions about whether such shifts carry hidden costs, since frequency and amplitude in birdsong are often linked to body size or condition signalling that gets altered as a side effect.

lessons.workedExample: A team records great tit song at 20 territories across a mix of urban intersections and quiet park interiors in the same city, matching Slabbekoorn and Peet's original design. Urban-intersection males sing with a minimum frequency averaging roughly 3.8 kHz versus about 3.4 kHz for park males — a shift that moves the song above the dominant 1-3 kHz energy band of road traffic noise. Separately, the team runs a vervet-style playback: broadcasting a recorded eagle alarm call to a group with no eagle present reliably produces individuals looking up and diving for cover, while a leopard call recorded from the same group instead sends them climbing into trees, confirming call-specific rather than generic responses just as Seyfarth and Cheney found in Amboseli.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about functionally referential calls or urban noise adaptation to test whether a student can connect a signal's DESIGN to the specific selective pressure that shaped it, rather than describing communication in generic terms. A weak answer says 'animals communicate to warn each other' or 'city birds sing louder.' A strong answer names the actual mechanism — Endler's sensory-drive tuning to ambient light, or Slabbekoorn's frequency shift specifically escaping the traffic noise band — and can distinguish honest referential signalling (vervet calls) from tactical deception (drongo false alarms, fiddler crab bluff claws), since conflating the two is a common error.

questions.prompt: In Seyfarth and Cheney's (1980) vervet monkey playback experiments, what result established the calls as 'functionally referential'?

options.text: Monkeys ignored all playback calls equally
A recorded call alone, with no predator present, triggered the predator-specific escape response matching that call type
All alarm calls produced the exact same generic response regardless of predator type
Only visual cues, never acoustic calls, triggered any escape response

explanations.a: Vervets responded strongly and specifically to playback, not by ignoring it; that specificity is the key finding.
explanations.b: Correct — playback alone (no real predator) still triggered the correct predator-specific escape behavior, showing the call itself carries specific referential information.
explanations.c: The critical finding was that responses DIFFERED by call type (climbing for leopard calls, looking up for eagle calls, looking down for snake calls) — a generic response would not support functional reference.
explanations.d: The experiments used only acoustic playback with no predator visible, directly showing calls alone are sufficient to trigger specific responses.

questions.prompt: What did Slabbekoorn and Peet (2003) find about great tit song in noisy urban territories?

options.text: Urban birds sing at significantly lower minimum frequencies than rural birds
Urban birds sing at significantly higher minimum frequencies, shifting out of the low-frequency traffic noise band
Noise has no measurable effect on great tit song
Urban birds stop singing entirely in noisy areas

explanations.a: The shift is upward, not downward — lower frequencies overlap more with traffic noise, which is what urban birds avoid.
explanations.b: Correct — higher minimum frequency moves the song's energy out of the low-frequency band where traffic noise concentrates, preserving signal audibility.
explanations.c: Slabbekoorn and Peet found a clear, measurable effect within a single city, with noisier territories linked to higher minimum song frequency.
explanations.d: Birds continued singing but with an adjusted frequency; they did not stop signalling altogether.

questions.prompt: Match each example to whether it illustrates honest referential signalling or tactical deception.

left.text: Fork-tailed drongo false alarm calls to steal food
Fiddler crab display with a regenerated (weaker) claw

right.text: Honest, functionally referential signal
Tactical deception exploiting another species' response
Bluff signal exploiting the difficulty of assessing true strength

questions.explanation: Vervet alarm calls reliably and honestly reference specific predator types; drongo false alarms deceive other species into abandoning food; and fiddler crabs with regenerated claws bluff apparent fighting strength that the visual signal cannot fully verify.

questions.prompt: Under Endler's sensory drive hypothesis, guppy color signals in dim, tannin-stained streams tend to be:

options.text: Identical in intensity to guppies in clear, well-lit pools
More muted/less saturated, tuned to what transmits well in that specific light environment
Entirely absent, since no color signal can function in any dim environment
Randomly variable with no relationship to the local light environment

explanations.a: Sensory drive predicts signal design tracks the local sensory/light environment, so intensity should differ, not stay identical, across habitats.
explanations.b: Correct — Endler's work found color intensity is tuned to ambient light conditions, muted in dim streams and brighter in well-lit pools, balanced against predation risk.
explanations.c: Guppies still signal in dim streams; the signal is adjusted (muted), not eliminated.
explanations.d: The core finding is a systematic, non-random relationship between light environment and signal design.

questions.prompt: An 'audience effect' occurs when:

options.text: A signaler changes its behavior because it detects it is being observed by a third party
A receiver ignores all signals directed at it
Two signalers of the same species never interact
A signal has absolutely no cost to produce

explanations.a: Correct — an audience effect is a change in signalling behavior triggered specifically by the presence of an observing third party (an eavesdropper), showing signals are shaped by a broader social network than just sender and intended receiver.
explanations.b: Ignoring signals describes receiver non-response, not the audience-effect concept, which is about the signaler's behavioral change.
explanations.c: Audience effects concern interactions being watched by an extra party, not an absence of interaction.
explanations.d: Signal cost is a separate concept (relevant to honesty theory) unrelated to the definition of an audience effect.

units.label: Applied Behavioral Ecology and Fair Projects

lessons.label: Behavior-Based Conservation and Evolutionary Traps

sections.heading: When a reliable cue turns lethal
sections.body: Schlaepfer, Runge, and Sherman formalized the modern concept of the "ecological trap" (a term first used by Dwernychuk and Boag in 1972) in an influential 2002 review, describing a specific failure mode: a cue that reliably predicted high fitness for millions of years becomes decoupled from fitness because the environment changed faster than the cue-response could evolve, yet animals keep using it. Sea turtle hatchlings are the textbook case. Emerging from the nest at night, they orient toward the brightest, lowest horizon — for their entire evolutionary history, moonlight and starlight scattering off open water. Beachfront streetlights and hotel lighting are brighter than that horizon, so hatchlings crawl inland instead, into dune vegetation, storm drains, roads, and waiting ghost crabs. Researchers tracking Florida nesting beaches have reported hundreds of thousands of hatchlings disoriented by artificial light in a single season, which is why Florida coastal counties began mandating shielded, amber or low-pressure-sodium fixtures on nesting beaches starting in the 1980s.

sections.heading: Polarized light and the Allee effect
sections.body: A second trap runs on a different sense entirely. Mayflies and caddisflies find water by polarotaxis: detecting the strong horizontal polarization that reflects off a smooth surface. Asphalt roads, black plastic sheeting, dark car hoods, and solar panels polarize light just as strongly, and Gábor Horváth's research group documented Ephemera danica mayflies abandoning a nearby creek to lay doomed egg batches on an adjacent Hungarian road — a "polarized light pollution" trap strong enough to pull insects from real water at a distance. That is a sensory trap, not a density problem. A separate failure mode is the Allee effect: per-capita growth rate falls at low population density because mates get harder to find. Component Allee effects from mate limitation are argued to have compounded the passenger pigeon's collapse, since the species depended on massive colonial aggregations to breed, and they still depress reintroduction success in species that need a quorum of conspecifics to pair up.

sections.heading: Trap-happy bias and designing interventions around it
sections.body: Monitoring itself carries behavioral bias. Since the 1950s, mark-recapture ecologists have documented individuals that become trap-happy (returning for bait, deflating apparent abundance) or trap-shy after one capture (avoiding the trap thereafter, deflating apparent survival); modern capture-recapture models, following Otis et al.'s 1978 heterogeneity framework, explicitly estimate individual capture probability to correct for it. On the intervention side, conservationists now train behavior deliberately. Captive-bred black-footed ferrets given controlled exposure to a live badger before release survived substantially longer in the wild than untrained, cage-reared ferrets in Miller and Biggins's trials. Soft release — an on-site acclimation pen with supplemental food before the animal is free to leave — reduces post-release dispersal and predation versus a hard release straight from a transport crate. These fixes still fail often: head-started turtles and hatchery salmon released without real predator experience, and reintroduced ferret populations that crashed from plague and low genetic diversity despite predator training, show behavior modification helps but is rarely sufficient alone.

lessons.workedExample: The magnitude — hundreds of thousands of Florida sea turtle hatchlings a year encountering disorienting artificial light — is not just a headline number; it is how the intervention gets evaluated. Beach patrols count disoriented hatchling tracks each morning (circles, U-turns toward dune vegetation and roads instead of a straight line to the surf) as a direct behavioral audit. When a county adopts a lighting ordinance requiring shielded, amber, low-glare fixtures on beachfront properties, biologists compare disorientation-event counts on regulated versus unregulated stretches of the same beach the following nesting season — a natural experiment where the outcome measure is the hatchlings' own crawl path, not a survey or a model.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge asks about traps to see whether a student understands that maladaptive behavior does not require a mutant or a broken instinct — it can be a perfectly intact, historically reliable instinct meeting an environment that changed too fast for evolution to track. A weak answer says light "confuses" turtles. A strong answer names the mechanism (hatchlings orient to the brightest low horizon, and artificial light now out-competes the ocean's reflected light), gives a magnitude (hundreds of thousands of hatchlings a year in Florida), and can distinguish this sensory-cue failure from a density-driven failure like the Allee effect — because conflating the two leads to the wrong fix.

questions.prompt: What defines an evolutionary (ecological) trap, as Schlaepfer, Runge, and Sherman framed it in 2002?

options.text: A cue that never had any relationship to fitness
A cue that once reliably predicted high fitness but has become decoupled from fitness by rapid environmental change, while animals keep responding to it
Any human structure that kills wildlife by direct collision
A genetic mutation that produces maladaptive behavior

explanations.a: Traps specifically involve cues that WERE reliable — that history is what makes the mismatch dangerous rather than simply neutral.
explanations.b: Correct — the defining feature is a formerly-honest cue-fitness link broken by a faster-than-evolutionary-timescale change, with the behavioral response still intact.
explanations.c: Direct collision (e.g., window strikes) is a hazard but not necessarily a trap; a trap specifically involves a misleading behavioral cue, not just physical harm.
explanations.d: Traps are typically about an intact, unmutated instinct meeting a novel stimulus, not a genetic defect in the behavior itself.

questions.prompt: Match each case to the mechanism or intervention involved.

right.text: Drawn inland by artificial beachfront lighting brighter than the ocean horizon
Drawn to lay eggs on asphalt or solar panels by polarized light mimicking water
Improved post-release survival via controlled exposure to a live badger
Biased by trap-happy or trap-shy individual variation in capture probability

questions.explanation: Turtles misread artificial light as the sea horizon; aquatic insects misread polarized reflections as water; ferret survival improved with predator-avoidance training; and mark-recapture estimates are distorted by consistent individual differences in willingness to re-enter a trap.

questions.prompt: An Allee effect specifically describes a population in which:

options.text: Per-capita growth rate declines as density increases, due to competition for food
Per-capita growth rate declines at low density, often because mates or cooperators become hard to find
Growth rate is constant and independent of density
Growth rate increases indefinitely regardless of density

explanations.a: That describes ordinary negative density dependence (competition), which is the opposite pattern from an Allee effect.
explanations.b: Correct — an Allee effect is a decline in per-capita growth at LOW density, commonly from mate limitation, which is why small or sparse populations can spiral toward extinction even without further external pressure.
explanations.c: Density-independent growth would show no relationship between density and per-capita growth rate at all.
explanations.d: Unlimited growth ignores both resource limits and the specific low-density mechanism an Allee effect describes.

questions.prompt: Order the typical steps of a soft release protocol for a reintroduced animal, from first to last.

items.text: Animal is held in an on-site acclimation pen at the release location
Supplemental food is provided while the animal becomes familiar with its surroundings
Supplemental feeding is gradually reduced
The pen is opened and the animal leaves on its own schedule

questions.explanation: Soft release starts with confinement at the actual release site so the animal can orient to real local cues, adds supplemental food to bridge the gap while it learns the area, tapers that support, and finally lets the animal choose when to disperse — which reduces the panic dispersal and starvation risk of a hard release.

lessons.label: Animal Personality and Behavioral Syndromes in the Wild

sections.heading: Consistent differences, not noise around a mean
sections.body: For decades, individual variation around a species' average behavior was treated as measurement noise to be averaged away. Animal personality research argues the opposite: some of that variation is a consistent, repeatable trait of the individual, and ignoring it hides real ecology. Réale, Reader, Sol, McDougall, and Dingemanse's influential 2007 Biological Reviews framework organized the field around five commonly scored axes — shyness-boldness (response to risk), exploration-avoidance (response to novelty), general activity, aggressiveness, and sociability. The flagship axis is bold-shy: bold individuals approach novel objects and predators faster and take more risks; shy individuals hang back. When two or more of these axes correlate within individuals — bold animals also being more aggressive and more active, for instance — Sih, Bell, and Johnson's 2004 review termed the correlated package a behavioral syndrome, extending the concept from single traits to a suite that constrains how an individual can respond across different contexts.

sections.heading: Repeatability as the entry ticket
sections.body: A behavior only counts as personality if it is repeatable: consistent within an individual across time or context, relative to variation across the population. Bell, Hankison, and Laskowski's 2009 Animal Behaviour meta-analysis of hundreds of studies found repeatability moderate on average — a little over a third of behavioral variance sits at the individual level rather than being reshuffled trial to trial — which sets an upper bound on how strongly the trait can respond to selection. Réale and colleagues extended this in 2010 with the pace-of-life syndrome: bold, aggressive, highly active individuals tend to run a fast physiological program — higher metabolic rate, faster growth, earlier reproduction, shorter lifespan — while shy individuals run slow, tying behavioral type directly to life-history strategy rather than treating personality as a behavior-only phenomenon.

sections.heading: Applied stakes, and where the field overreached
sections.body: Personality has measurable ecological consequences. Bold, exploratory cane toads (Rhinella marina) are disproportionately the ones found at the Australian invasion front; because they disperse farthest and their offspring inherit both the dispersal tendency and the boldness, Phillips and Shine's spatial-sorting mechanism has helped the invasion front's advance rate roughly quintuple since toads were introduced in 1935. Personality also biases who survives harvest and reintroduction: hook-vulnerable, bold fish are selectively removed by angling, and bold translocated individuals sometimes locate resources faster but also take more predation risk, making translocation outcomes personality-dependent rather than uniform. The field's early enthusiasm drew a sharp correction: Carter, Feeney, Marshall, Cowlishaw, and Heinsohn's 2013 Biological Reviews critique argued many studies measured one context-specific response and labeled it "personality" without demonstrating real cross-context consistency, inflating how universal and stable these traits actually are.

lessons.workedExample: Cane toads were introduced to Queensland in 1935 to control cane beetles; today the invasion front moves roughly fivefold faster than it did in the first decades after release. The mechanism is spatial sorting: the boldest, most exploratory toads disperse farthest each generation, arrive at the range edge, and breed with other bold dispersers there, so front-line offspring inherit both longer legs and bolder personalities. Common-garden breeding experiments (raising front and core toads' offspring under identical conditions) confirmed the difference is heritable, not just environmental conditioning — meaning personality variation, filtered by dispersal distance alone, is accelerating a biological invasion across an entire continent.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe personality because it is easy to state as a slogan ("animals have personalities too") and hard to demonstrate rigorously. A weak answer describes one bold individual anecdotally. A strong answer states the operational requirement — the behavior must be repeatable across time or context relative to population variation, not just observed once — and can explain why that matters: without demonstrated repeatability, a single bold response is indistinguishable from noise, and claiming a "syndrome" requires showing multiple traits actually correlate within individuals, which is exactly the standard the 2013 Carter et al. critique found much of the early literature had skipped.

questions.prompt: What minimum evidence is required before a behavior can be called part of an animal's "personality"?

options.text: It was observed once in a striking way
It is repeatable — consistent within the individual across time or context, relative to variation across the population
It differs from the behavior of a closely related species
It can be described using human personality vocabulary like "friendly" or "grumpy"

explanations.a: A single observation cannot distinguish a stable trait from a one-off response to that day's conditions.
explanations.b: Correct — repeatability (consistency within individuals relative to population variance) is the formal entry requirement the field uses before calling a behavior a personality trait.
explanations.c: Cross-species comparison says nothing about whether the behavior is consistent within a given individual.
explanations.d: Using human-like labels is just descriptive shorthand; it does not establish repeatability.

questions.prompt: Match each researcher/team to their key contribution to animal personality research.

right.text: Proposed the five-axis framework: boldness, exploration, activity, aggressiveness, sociability
Defined "behavioral syndrome" as a suite of correlated traits across contexts
Meta-analyzed repeatability of behavior across many taxa and studies
Critiqued the field for often measuring one context-specific response, not proven cross-context consistency

questions.explanation: Réale et al. 2007 supplied the standard five-axis vocabulary; Sih, Bell & Johnson 2004 formalized the behavioral-syndrome concept; Bell, Hankison & Laskowski 2009 quantified how repeatable behavior actually is across the literature; and Carter et al. 2013 pushed back on overclaiming.

questions.prompt: In the pace-of-life syndrome framework, a bold, highly active individual is predicted to also show:

options.text: Slower metabolic rate, slower growth, and a longer lifespan
Higher metabolic rate, faster growth, earlier reproduction, and a shorter lifespan
No relationship at all between behavior and physiology
Random variation in metabolic rate unrelated to boldness

explanations.a: That is the "slow" pace-of-life profile predicted for shy individuals, the opposite pairing.
explanations.b: Correct — the pace-of-life syndrome links bold, active behavioral types to a fast physiological and life-history program: higher metabolism, faster growth, earlier breeding, shorter life.
explanations.c: The whole point of the framework is that behavior and physiology are coupled, not independent.
explanations.d: The pace-of-life syndrome specifically predicts a systematic, not random, covariation.

questions.prompt: Why did cane toad boldness accelerate the species' invasion speed across Australia roughly fivefold since 1935?

options.text: Bold toads reproduce faster regardless of location
Bold, exploratory toads disperse farthest, concentrate at the range edge, and their offspring inherit both dispersal ability and boldness — spatial sorting
Toads at the invasion front were a genetically distinct species
Bold toads only appeared after pesticide use began

explanations.a: The mechanism is about where bold individuals end up (the range edge), not a blanket reproductive advantage everywhere.
explanations.b: Correct — spatial sorting concentrates the boldest, farthest-dispersing individuals at the invasion front, and because the trait is heritable, front-line populations become progressively bolder and faster-dispersing each generation.
explanations.c: Front and core populations are the same species; common-garden experiments showed the difference is a heritable trait distribution shift, not speciation.
explanations.d: The acceleration is explained by evolutionary spatial sorting during range expansion, not a pesticide-related cause.

lessons.label: Urban Behavior and Human-Wildlife Conflict

sections.heading: Cities select for boldness
sections.body: Flight-initiation distance (FID) — how close a threat can approach before an animal flees — is the standard behavioral proxy for boldness in the field. Anders Pape Møller's comparative work across many European bird species found urban populations consistently have shorter FIDs than rural conspecifics of the same species, tolerating much closer human approach before fleeing. Two mechanisms combine to produce this: individual habituation, where repeated harmless encounters with people teach an animal that humans are not a threat, and a filtering effect, where only individuals bold enough to tolerate constant human activity settle and breed successfully in cities in the first place, so urban populations are progressively enriched for boldness across generations. The same pattern shows up in urban coyotes, foxes, and raccoons, which forage closer to buildings and people, and at shorter distances, than their rural counterparts.

sections.heading: Food conditioning and why it ends in lethal control
sections.body: Boldness becomes dangerous once it is reinforced with food. Bears that get even one meal from an unsecured cooler or dumpster rapidly learn to associate human spaces with easy calories, a process wildlife agencies call food conditioning; the same dynamic drives aggressive begging in temple macaques in Bali and India. The park-service slogan "a fed bear is a dead bear" reflects a hard behavioral reality: food-conditioned bears habitually return to human areas even after being trapped and relocated, escalate toward property damage or injury, and are usually euthanized rather than re-released, because relocation rarely un-teaches an association that strong. This is why attractant management — bear-proof trash cans and food-storage lockers, electric fencing around beehives and chicken coops — is treated as the highest-leverage intervention: it prevents the conditioning from ever starting.

sections.heading: Fear of the human super predator, and building around behavior
sections.body: Justin Suraci and colleagues' 2019 Ecology Letters playback experiment in California's Santa Cruz Mountains broadcast recorded human voices versus a non-threatening control sound (tree frog calls) at paired camera-and-speaker stations. Medium-sized carnivores such as bobcats became more nocturnal and cautious around the human-voice speakers, evidence that fear of humans functions as a landscape-scale "super predator" effect capable of reshaping mesopredator activity independent of any actual encounter. Practical mitigation now leans on exactly this kind of behavioral lever: aversive conditioning with rubber bullets or trained Karelian bear dogs to re-teach wariness, and wildlife crossing structures engineered around known species preferences. Along Banff National Park's Trans-Canada Highway, Tony Clevenger's monitoring of 44 crossing structures recorded over 200,000 uses by 11 large-mammal species; grizzly bears and wolves favor high, wide overpasses while black bears and cougars favor long, narrow underpasses, and fencing paired with crossings cut collisions by 80% overall.

lessons.workedExample: At Suraci's paired stations in the Santa Cruz Mountains, sites broadcasting human voice recordings on a loop showed bobcats and other medium carnivores shifting activity later into the night and spending less time in the open, compared to matched sites playing tree frog calls as a control. Because the only difference between treatments was the sound, not any real human presence, the result isolates fear of the acoustic cue itself — the same logic wildlife managers now borrow deliberately, using human-voice or air-horn deterrents to hold bears and cougars back from campgrounds without a single physical encounter, trading a costly lethal-removal decision for a much cheaper behavioral one.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes urban wildlife behavior to see whether a student can trace a full causal chain rather than stopping at "animals get used to people." A weak answer says bold animals are "more adapted to cities." A strong answer names the two mechanisms driving reduced FID (habituation plus differential settlement of bold individuals), explains specifically why food conditioning — not proximity alone — is what forces lethal control, and can describe a real behavior-based mitigation (aversive conditioning, attractant management, or a species-specific crossing structure) rather than a vague call for "more education."

questions.prompt: Flight-initiation distance (FID) measures:

options.text: The top running speed of an animal fleeing a predator
How close an approaching threat can get before the animal flees
The distance an animal travels once it has fled
How far an animal ranges from its den or nest each day

explanations.a: FID is about the threshold distance that triggers flight, not the speed of the flight itself.
explanations.b: Correct — FID is the approach distance at which an animal breaks and flees, and it is the standard field proxy for boldness: shorter FID means the animal tolerates closer approach.
explanations.c: The distance fled afterward is a different measure, sometimes recorded separately as flee distance.
explanations.d: Home range size is unrelated to FID; an animal can have a small range and still a large or small FID.

questions.prompt: In Suraci et al.'s 2019 human-voice playback experiment, what happened at speakers broadcasting human voices compared to the tree-frog control?

options.text: Medium-sized carnivores like bobcats became more nocturnal and cautious
All wildlife activity was unaffected by either sound
Large carnivores approached the speakers more closely to investigate
Only bird species responded to the playback

explanations.a: Correct — mesopredators such as bobcats shifted activity later into the night and became warier at human-voice sites, consistent with fear of humans acting as a landscape-scale super-predator effect.
explanations.b: The whole point of the paired design was that the two sound treatments produced measurably different responses.
explanations.c: The documented pattern was avoidance and increased caution, not attraction or investigation.
explanations.d: The study tracked mammalian carnivores using camera traps and collars, not primarily birds.

questions.prompt: Match each species group to the Banff crossing-structure design it prefers.

right.text: High, wide, short overpasses
Long, low, narrow underpasses

questions.explanation: Clevenger's Banff monitoring found grizzly bears and wolves preferentially use open, high, wide overpasses, while black bears and cougars preferentially use long, narrow, low underpasses — which is why effective crossing networks mix both structure types rather than relying on one design.

questions.prompt: Why do wildlife agencies usually euthanize food-conditioned bears rather than relocate them?

options.text: Relocation is illegal under federal law in all cases
Food conditioning is a strong, persistent learned association, so relocated bears typically resume seeking human food and return or reoffend elsewhere
Food-conditioned bears cannot survive being moved to a new territory
Relocated bears always lose their fear of natural predators

explanations.a: Relocation is legal and used routinely for non-food-conditioned bears; the policy issue is behavioral, not legal.
explanations.b: Correct — once a bear has strongly learned that humans mean food, moving it to a new location does not erase that learned association, so it tends to re-offend, which is the behavioral logic behind the "a fed bear is a dead bear" policy.
explanations.c: Survival after relocation is not the primary reason; the concern is the persistence of the learned food-seeking behavior itself.
explanations.d: This describes an unrelated and unsupported claim about predator fear, not the actual mechanism driving the euthanasia decision.

lessons.label: Learning, Social Information, and Animal Culture

sections.heading: Behavior that spreads without genes
sections.body: Social learning — acquiring a behavior by observing or interacting with others rather than discovering it alone — lets a population share information on a timescale far faster than genetic evolution allows, and when a socially learned behavior persists and varies between populations of the same species, biologists call it a tradition or culture. The classic long-run case is blue tits and great tits prising the foil or cardboard tops off doorstep milk bottles to drink the cream. First recorded in 1921 in Swaythling, near Southampton, the behavior had been documented across most of Britain by 1947, a spread James Fisher and R. A. Hinde mapped from hundreds of reports in their 1949 paper. For decades it was unclear whether that spread reflected true social transmission or many birds independently reinventing the same trick — a distinction that matters enormously and that only careful experimental design can resolve.

sections.heading: Proving conformity experimentally
sections.body: Lucy Aplin and colleagues settled that question for a related case in 2015. Working across eight wild great tit subpopulations in Wytham Woods, England, they trained seed birds in each subpopulation to solve a two-option puzzle box — a sliding door that opened equally well left or right, an arbitrary choice with no functional advantage either way. The seeded solution spread through each subpopulation and persisted for months, and critically, birds conformed to whichever option was locally dominant even after individually discovering that the other option also worked, evidence of genuine conformist transmission rather than convergent private discovery. Network-based diffusion analysis (NBDA), a statistical method that compares how well a behavior's spread pattern fits a social-network model versus an independent-invention model, is what lets researchers distinguish the two possibilities rigorously in the wild.

sections.heading: Strategic copying, and what's lost when a tradition dies
sections.body: Animals don't copy indiscriminately. Two strategies dominate the social-learning-strategies literature: copy-when-uncertain, leaning on social information specifically when your own information is unreliable or the situation is novel, and copy-the-successful, weighting imitation toward individuals with demonstrated high payoffs. Both appear in humpback whales, whose evolving songs and the lobtail feeding technique — a tail-slap before bubble-net feeding that Jenny Allen and colleagues' 2013 Science study, using 27 years of Gulf of Maine sighting data and NBDA, found spread through the population via social transmission, contingent on local sand-lance prey availability, not independent invention. The conservation stakes are concrete: Jesmer et al.'s 2018 Science study found translocated bighorn sheep and moose are not born knowing how to migrate — they must learn to track the spring green-up ("green-wave surfing") through experience, and it took nearly 40 years for reintroduced bighorn herds to reach 80% migratory, and roughly 90 years for moose. A lost migratory tradition is lost knowledge, not just lost individuals.

lessons.workedExample: In Aplin's Wytham Woods experiment, two great tits per subpopulation were captured, trained on one door direction, and released; automated RFID feeders then logged every bird's choices for months. The result that mattered wasn't just that the trained solution spread — it was that individuals who had personally tried and succeeded with the non-local option still switched to match their neighbors' locally dominant choice, the behavioral signature of conformity rather than pure copying-of-what-works. Because the two door options were engineered to be functionally identical, any consistent local majority could only be explained by social influence, not by one option being objectively better.
lessons.judgeFraming: A judge probes cultural transmission because "the behavior spread through the population" is easy to say and easy to get wrong — spread can look identical whether it's true social learning or many individuals independently stumbling onto the same solution. A weak answer just asserts social learning happened. A strong answer names the tool that actually distinguishes the two hypotheses (network-based diffusion analysis, comparing observed spread against a social-network-weighted model) and can explain why an arbitrary, functionally-equivalent behavior — like Aplin's two-option puzzle box — is a stronger test case than a behavior where one option is simply better.

questions.prompt: What did Aplin et al. (2015) mean by demonstrating "conformist transmission" in great tits?

options.text: Birds always chose whichever door option was objectively faster to open
Birds adopted the locally dominant solution even after personally discovering that the alternative solution also worked
Birds never learned from each other and solved the puzzle independently
Only juvenile birds were capable of learning the puzzle solution

explanations.a: The two door options were engineered to be functionally equivalent, so there was no objectively faster choice to gravitate toward.
explanations.b: Correct — the signature of conformity is switching to match the local majority even when an individual's own experience says the minority option works fine, which is exactly what Aplin's birds did.
explanations.c: The whole finding was the opposite: the seeded solution spread through the population well beyond the originally trained individuals.
explanations.d: The study tracked the whole subpopulation via RFID-tagged feeders, not juveniles specifically.

questions.prompt: What statistical approach lets researchers distinguish true social transmission of a behavior from many individuals independently inventing the same behavior?

options.text: Network-based diffusion analysis (NBDA), comparing the observed spread pattern to a social-network-weighted model
Simply counting how many individuals show the behavior
Measuring the average body size of individuals showing the behavior
Comparing behavior rates between captive and wild populations only

explanations.a: Correct — NBDA tests whether the timing and pattern of a behavior's spread fits a model where social connections predict acquisition better than a model of independent, asocial discovery; both Aplin (2015) and Allen (2013) used this method.
explanations.b: A raw count can't distinguish social spread from independent reinvention; both would eventually produce a similar count.
explanations.c: Body size is unrelated to distinguishing the transmission mechanism.
explanations.d: A captive-versus-wild comparison addresses a different question and isn't the tool used to test transmission pathway.

questions.prompt: Match each social learning strategy to its description.

right.text: Rely more on social information specifically when personal information is unreliable or the situation is novel
Weight imitation toward individuals who have demonstrated high success or payoff

questions.explanation: Copy-when-uncertain is a context-dependent rule that switches on social reliance when personal knowledge is weak; copy-the-successful is a content-biased rule that targets whom to copy based on demonstrated success, rather than copying indiscriminately.

questions.prompt: According to Jesmer et al. (2018), roughly how long did it take translocated bighorn sheep herds to reach 80% migratory, and moose to become migratory, in newly colonized habitat?

options.text: About 2 years for sheep, 5 years for moose
About 40 years for sheep, roughly 90 years for moose
Both species were migratory immediately upon release, with no learning period
About 40 years for moose, roughly 90 years for sheep

explanations.a: The actual timescales were far longer — on the order of decades, not single years — reflecting a genuinely slow, generational learning process.
explanations.b: Correct — it took nearly 40 years for reintroduced bighorn sheep herds to reach 80% migratory and roughly 90 years for moose, showing migration is learned and culturally transmitted, not innate.
explanations.c: The central finding was the opposite: translocated populations were initially largely non-migratory and only gained migratory behavior gradually.
explanations.d: The timescales are swapped; bighorn sheep reached the 80% migratory threshold faster (about 40 years) than moose (about 90 years).

questions.prompt: Order the historical events in the blue tit milk-bottle-opening story.

items.text: Tits first observed prising open milk bottle tops in Swaythling, near Southampton (1921)
The behavior is documented spreading to most districts of Britain
Fisher and Hinde compile over 400 sighting reports into their landmark 1949 paper
The behavior declines as home milk delivery and bottle materials change

questions.explanation: The behavior was first recorded in 1921, spread widely across Britain over the following decades, was formally documented and mapped by Fisher and Hinde in 1949, and eventually declined once the ecological opportunity itself (doorstep glass milk bottles) disappeared with changing dairy practices.

lessons.label: Collective Behavior and Movement

sections.heading: Group patterns from purely local rules
sections.body: A fish school wheeling in unison or a starling flock pulsing overhead has no leader and no bird holding a map of the whole group, yet the pattern looks coordinated. Iain Couzin and colleagues' 2002 model showed why: give each individual three concentric zones around itself — a short-range zone of repulsion (move away from anyone too close, avoiding collision), a medium-range zone of orientation (align direction with neighbors at that range), and a longer-range zone of attraction (move toward neighbors farther out, avoiding isolation) — and simulate nothing more than those three local rules. Depending on how large the orientation zone is relative to the others, the same simple rule set generates qualitatively different emergent group states: a loosely packed stationary swarm, a rotating torus or mill where individuals circle a common center, or a polarized group all moving in one direction, with no individual ever told which state to produce.

sections.heading: Topological, not metric, neighbors
sections.body: Couzin's model assumed interaction zones defined by fixed physical distance. Michele Ballerini and colleagues tested that assumption directly in 2008 by photographing real starling flocks of up to several thousand birds over Rome with synchronized cameras and reconstructing every individual's three-dimensional position. Each bird, they found, interacts with roughly six to seven nearest neighbors regardless of how far away those neighbors actually are — a topological rule, not a metric one. This matters functionally: a flock under predator attack can compress or stretch by a large factor in density, and a fixed-distance rule would then either fragment the group (neighbors falling outside a too-small metric radius) or make it unresponsive (too many neighbors inside a too-large one); a fixed neighbor-count rule keeps cohesion and responsiveness constant across those density swings.

sections.heading: Quorums, many wrongs, and measuring it yourself
sections.body: Groups don't just move together — they decide together. Ashley Ward, David Sumpter, and Couzin's 2008 work on fish shoals found individuals use a quorum response: a disproportionate, threshold-triggered commitment once enough neighbors have already committed to a direction, which filters out noise from a misinformed minority far better than simple averaging would. Thomas Seeley documented an analogous quorum in honeybee swarms choosing a new nest site — competing scout groups recruit via waggle dances, and a site's scouts cross-inhibit rivals with a stop signal once their numbers cross a threshold, helping resolve near-ties fast. Group movement is also more accurate than solitary movement: Simons formalized the many-wrongs principle in 2004, showing that when each individual's navigational error is independent, averaging those errors across a group converges on the true direction — demonstrated in homing pigeons, where pairs navigate more accurately than lone birds. None of this required exotic equipment to discover; multi-camera photogrammetry and, increasingly, cheap consumer drones now put flock- and shoal-scale 3D tracking within reach of a well-planned student project.

lessons.workedExample: Ballerini's team filmed starling flocks over Rome's Termini train station using multiple synchronized still cameras positioned at different angles, then used stereo-photogrammetry to reconstruct the exact 3D position of every visible bird in a single frame — flocks sometimes numbering in the low thousands. For each bird they calculated how strongly its movement correlated with each neighbor, ranked by both distance and rank order. The correlation dropped off sharply after the sixth or seventh nearest neighbor no matter how spread out or packed the flock was at that moment, which is the direct evidence for a topological rather than metric interaction rule — a finding that would have been invisible without reconstructing full 3D positions rather than just watching flock shape from the ground.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe collective behavior because "they move as a group" explains nothing on its own — the interesting science is which local rule produces which global pattern, and how you would actually test that rule against real animals rather than assume it. A weak answer describes the flock shape. A strong answer names a specific rule (zones of repulsion/orientation/attraction, or a quorum threshold) and cites the empirical test that distinguished it from a plausible alternative — Ballerini's topological-versus-metric result is the sharpest example, because it shows the naive assumption (fixed distance) was simply wrong once someone reconstructed real 3D flock data.

questions.prompt: In Couzin et al.'s (2002) model, what does the zone of repulsion govern, and why does it take priority over the other zones?

options.text: Long-range attraction to the group's center of mass; it has the lowest priority
Collision avoidance at very short range; it overrides the other rules to prevent individuals from colliding
Velocity alignment with nearby neighbors at a medium range
Choosing which direction the whole group will travel

explanations.a: That describes the zone of attraction, which is the longest-range and lowest-priority rule, the opposite of repulsion.
explanations.b: Correct — the zone of repulsion operates at the shortest range and takes precedence over orientation and attraction specifically to prevent individuals from colliding with their closest neighbors.
explanations.c: Alignment is governed by the separate, medium-range zone of orientation, not the repulsion zone.
explanations.d: No single zone "chooses" group direction; direction is an emergent outcome of all three local rules acting together across many individuals.
