explanations.b: Both techniques can be applied to water, soil, or other environmental samples; the sample type is not the distinguishing factor.
explanations.c: It is metabarcoding that critically depends on a reference database to assign sequences to species; qPCR is designed around one known target sequence.
explanations.d: They are distinct laboratory approaches with different targets, costs, and outputs.

questions.prompt: In the Asian carp eDNA controversy in the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, what was the core scientific dispute?

options.text: Whether eDNA sampling was too expensive to continue
Whether positive eDNA detections above the electric barrier reflected live fish present, or contamination/transported DNA, since intensive netting largely failed to find live carp
Whether Asian carp eDNA could be detected at all with any method
Whether the electric barrier itself was releasing contaminant DNA

explanations.a: Cost was not the central dispute; the disagreement was about what a positive result actually proved.
explanations.b: Correct — DNA from bighead and silver carp was repeatedly detected above the barrier starting around 2009-2010, but follow-up netting and electrofishing largely did not find live fish, raising the unresolved question of whether the DNA indicated live presence, contamination, or transported material.
explanations.c: The DNA was in fact detected; the dispute was about interpreting a positive result, not detection failure.
explanations.d: The controversy centered on the source of the DNA signal in the water, not on the barrier as a DNA source itself.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of a defensible eDNA water-sampling workflow, from field to result.

items.text: Collect water sample and a field blank (clean water processed identically)
Filter the sample to concentrate DNA on a membrane
Extract DNA and run qPCR or metabarcoding, including lab negative controls
Check field and lab controls for contamination before interpreting any positive result

questions.explanation: A field blank is collected alongside the real sample, both are filtered, DNA is extracted and amplified with lab negative controls included, and only after confirming both control types are clean is a positive detection interpretable as a real signal rather than contamination.

lessons.label: Remote Sensing and Landscape Metrics

sections.heading: Free imagery students can actually use
sections.body: Satellite imagery that used to require institutional budgets is now free and downloadable: Landsat (USGS/NASA, continuous archive back to 1972, current sensors at 30 m resolution), Sentinel-2 (European Space Agency, 10 m resolution in key bands, launched 2015), and in the U.S. the National Agriculture Imagery Program (NAIP, roughly 0.6-1 m resolution, flown in growing-season cycles). Coarser Landsat trades detail for the longest continuous historical record of any civilian satellite program, useful for tracking decades of change; Sentinel-2's finer resolution and 5-day revisit suit shorter, more detailed studies; NAIP's near-photographic resolution is unmatched for fine-scale U.S. land-cover work but lacks Landsat's global reach and multi-decade depth. From these bands, the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) — the normalized ratio of near-infrared to red reflectance — gives a cheap, well-validated proxy for vegetation greenness and density, and classifying pixels into land-cover categories (forest, cropland, water, built) is the basic building block for any landscape-scale monitoring project.

sections.heading: The Hansen forest-change product and its caveat
sections.body: Matthew Hansen and colleagues at the University of Maryland published "High-Resolution Global Maps of 21st-Century Forest Cover Change" in Science in 2013, using the full global Landsat archive at 30 m resolution to map annual tree-cover loss and gain worldwide; the product powers the widely used Global Forest Watch platform. Its critical caveat, which a careful student must state: the algorithm measures tree cover, not forest in the ecological or legal sense, so it counts the harvest of a planted timber or oil-palm plantation as "loss" identically to old-growth deforestation, even though the plantation may simply regrow on a normal rotation cycle. Reading a Global Forest Watch alert as evidence of permanent deforestation without checking land-use context can therefore overstate real forest loss in plantation-heavy regions.

sections.heading: Quantifying pattern with landscape metrics
sections.body: Beyond classifying cover, landscape ecology quantifies spatial pattern itself using metrics computed in software like FRAGSTATS (developed by Kevin McGarigal) or the R package landscapemetrics: patch density (number of discrete habitat patches per unit area), edge density (total edge length relative to area, a proxy for fragmentation and edge effects), mean patch size, and indices like contagion and proximity that capture how clumped versus scattered patches of a class are. Every one of these metrics is sensitive to two analyst choices that must be reported alongside any result: pixel resolution (coarser pixels merge small patches and shrink apparent edge, systematically changing patch counts) and the minimum mapping unit (the smallest area counted as a distinct patch, which directly sets how much fine-scale fragmentation the analysis can even see).

lessons.workedExample: A student compares forest fragmentation around a nature reserve using two different data sources: 30 m Landsat and 10 m Sentinel-2, both classified into forest/non-forest for the same year. Patch density computed from Sentinel-2 comes out roughly 2.5 times higher than from Landsat, and mean patch size is smaller, purely because the finer pixels resolve small forest fragments that Landsat's coarser grid merges into surrounding land cover. The student reports both results side by side rather than picking one, explicitly noting that the apparent fragmentation difference is a resolution artifact, not a real ecological difference between years or sites.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe remote sensing because a pretty NDVI map or a Global Forest Watch screenshot is easy to present as a finished analysis when it is really a set of choices in disguise. A weak answer treats a downloaded forest-loss layer as ground truth. A strong answer names the sensor and its resolution, states the minimum mapping unit used, and can explain why the Hansen product's "loss" pixel might just be a plantation harvest rather than permanent deforestation. A student who says "our patch density would look different at a coarser resolution" is showing they understand that landscape metrics measure the interaction between real pattern and the resolution used to see it, not pattern alone.

questions.prompt: Match each imagery source to its defining characteristic.

right.text: 30 m resolution, longest continuous historical satellite record (since 1972)
10 m resolution in key bands, 5-day revisit, ESA program
Roughly 0.6-1 m resolution, U.S.-only, growing-season aerial flights

questions.explanation: Landsat trades resolution for the longest historical depth; Sentinel-2 offers finer resolution and frequent revisits; NAIP offers near-photographic detail but only within the U.S. and only during growing seasons.

questions.prompt: What is the key caveat of the Hansen et al. (2013) global forest-change product behind Global Forest Watch?

options.text: It only covers tropical countries
It measures tree cover loss, not forest loss specifically, so it counts plantation harvest cycles as loss identically to permanent deforestation
It has no publicly available data
It only detects change over a 1 m resolution grid

explanations.a: The product is global, based on the full worldwide Landsat archive, not limited to the tropics.
explanations.b: Correct — because the underlying algorithm detects tree canopy cover change rather than forest as an ecological or legal category, a harvested timber or oil-palm plantation registers as "loss" the same as old-growth clearing, which can overstate net deforestation in plantation-heavy landscapes.
explanations.c: The product is specifically known for being freely and publicly available through Global Forest Watch, which is central to its impact.
explanations.d: The underlying Landsat data used is 30 m resolution, not 1 m.

questions.prompt: Two teams compute patch density for the same landscape using different pixel resolutions (10 m vs. 30 m). What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: The results will be identical, since patch density is resolution-independent
The finer 10 m data will likely show higher patch density and smaller mean patch size, since it resolves small fragments the coarser grid merges
The coarser 30 m data will always show more patches
Patch density cannot be computed without field verification

explanations.a: Landscape metrics including patch density are well documented to be sensitive to pixel resolution; they are not resolution-independent.
explanations.b: Correct — finer pixels can distinguish small, separate patches that coarser pixels blur together into one larger patch or absorb into the surrounding matrix, so higher resolution typically yields more, smaller detected patches.
explanations.c: Coarser data tends to merge small patches together, reducing rather than increasing the counted number of patches.
explanations.d: Patch density is a computable metric directly from classified imagery; field verification improves classification accuracy but is not required to compute the metric itself.

questions.prompt: What does NDVI (Normalized Difference Vegetation Index) approximate?

options.text: Soil moisture content directly
Vegetation greenness/density, based on the ratio of near-infrared to red reflectance
Precise species identity of vegetation
Atmospheric temperature

explanations.a: Soil moisture requires other indices or sensors; NDVI is not a direct moisture measure, though it can correlate indirectly through vegetation stress.
explanations.b: Correct — healthy, dense vegetation strongly reflects near-infrared and absorbs red light, so the normalized ratio of these two bands gives a widely validated proxy for vegetation greenness and density.
explanations.c: NDVI cannot distinguish species; it only reflects overall vegetation vigor and density at the pixel level.
explanations.d: NDVI is derived from reflected light in specific bands, not thermal/temperature data.

lessons.label: Tracking Movement and Space Use

sections.heading: Choosing a tag: VHF, GPS, satellite, and light-level
sections.body: Tracking technology trades location accuracy, fix frequency, and battery life against each other, and no single tag wins on all three. VHF (very-high-frequency) radio collars are cheap and long-lived but require a researcher with a directional antenna to manually triangulate location, so fix rate is limited by field labor. GPS collars log a precise location automatically at set intervals, but each fix drains battery, forcing a direct trade-off between fix frequency and deployment duration. Argos satellite tags (Doppler-shift-based, flying on NOAA polar-orbiting satellites since the 1970s) and the newer ICARUS system (International Cooperation for Animal Research Using Space, hosted on the International Space Station since 2020) transmit location without the animal needing to be recaptured, ideal for animals that migrate beyond field-crew range, but Argos accuracy is coarser than GPS. Light-level geolocators are the lightest and cheapest option (as small as ~0.5-1 g), estimating position from sunrise/sunset timing rather than direct fixes, at the cost of poor accuracy — often on the order of 100-200 km — making them suited only to coarse migratory-route questions, typically on small birds too light for any heavier tag.

sections.heading: Weight limits and fix-rate bias
sections.body: A widely cited field rule of thumb caps tag mass at roughly 3-5 percent of the animal's body mass (closer to 3 percent for flying or energetically constrained species, where drag and lift matter, and toward 5 percent for larger terrestrial mammals), based on studies showing heavier tags measurably alter behavior, energy expenditure, or survival. Even a well-chosen GPS collar does not get a clean fix every time it tries: dense canopy, deep canyons, or an animal curled up can block the satellite signal, and studies have repeatedly shown fix-rate bias — successful fixes are non-random with respect to habitat, so a naive analysis of only the successful fixes over-represents open habitat and under-represents dense cover, biasing any downstream home-range or habitat-selection estimate unless the missing fixes are accounted for.

sections.heading: From points to home ranges, and the permitting gate
sections.body: Turning a cloud of location points into a home-range estimate has evolved through three main methods. The minimum convex polygon (MCP) simply draws the smallest convex shape enclosing all points — simple and comparable across old studies, but sensitive to outliers and prone to including large unused areas. Kernel density estimation (KDE) instead builds a smooth probability surface of use, better reflecting concentrated activity, but classic KDE assumes each point is statistically independent, which GPS data rarely are since consecutive fixes are close together in time and space (autocorrelated). Autocorrelated kernel density estimation (AKDE), developed by Chris Fleming, Justin Calabrese, and colleagues (implemented in the ctmm R package, key papers from 2015 onward), explicitly models that temporal autocorrelation instead of ignoring it, producing home-range estimates with honest, often substantially wider confidence intervals than KDE gives. Most published telemetry studies collar a strikingly small number of animals per population — often fewer than 10-20 — which limits how confidently a home-range or movement finding generalizes, and any project involving capture and tagging requires IACUC-equivalent animal-welfare approval and wildlife-agency permits before a single animal is handled, a gate that applies regardless of a project's educational intent.

lessons.workedExample: A study collars 8 foxes with GPS units set to fix every 2 hours, but canopy cover in the forested third of the study area causes 35% of attempted fixes there to fail, compared to only 8% failure in open fields. A naive MCP built from only the successful fixes would visually suggest the foxes prefer open habitat, when the truth is partly an artifact of fix-rate bias: the animals may be using forest just as much, but the collar simply logs fewer points there. Switching to AKDE and explicitly modeling the missing-fix pattern by habitat corrects the apparent home range and reveals forest use closer to what field observations (scat, tracks) already suggested.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe tracking studies because home-range maps look authoritative while hiding several silent biases. A weak answer presents an MCP or KDE map as simply "where the animal lives." A strong answer names the tag type and fix interval, states the weight-to-body-mass ratio to show the tag was not a welfare risk, and — critically — can explain fix-rate bias: that missing GPS fixes are not random with respect to habitat, so raw successful-fix maps can systematically misrepresent habitat use unless corrected. A student who mentions IACUC-equivalent approval for a capture-based project, unprompted, signals they understand tracking is not just data collection but a regulated intervention on a live animal.

questions.prompt: Match each tracking technology to its defining trade-off.

right.text: Cheap and long-lived, but requires manual field triangulation for each fix
Precise automatic fixes, but fix frequency directly trades off against battery life
No recapture needed for data, but coarser location accuracy than GPS
Extremely light and cheap, but only ~100-200 km position accuracy from sunrise/sunset timing

questions.explanation: Each tag type trades accuracy, automation, weight, and battery life differently: VHF needs field labor, GPS trades fix rate for battery, satellite tags avoid recapture at coarser accuracy, and geolocators are lightest but least precise.

questions.prompt: Why does fix-rate bias matter for home-range estimation from GPS collar data?

options.text: It doesn't matter, since missing fixes are random
Missing fixes are often non-random with respect to habitat (e.g., dense canopy blocks signal), so analyzing only successful fixes can systematically misrepresent true habitat use
Fix-rate bias only affects VHF collars, not GPS
It only matters for animals that migrate internationally

explanations.a: The core problem with fix-rate bias is precisely that missing fixes are NOT random; they correlate with habitat features like canopy cover.
explanations.b: Correct — because dense cover or terrain can block satellite signal, successful fixes over-represent open habitat, biasing home-range or habitat-selection estimates unless the missing-fix pattern is explicitly accounted for.
explanations.c: Fix-rate bias is specifically a GPS satellite-signal issue; VHF tracking has its own separate limitations (field-labor-limited fix rate) but not this particular bias.
explanations.d: Fix-rate bias arises from local signal obstruction (canopy, terrain) and applies to any GPS-tracked animal, not only migratory or international cases.

questions.prompt: What does autocorrelated kernel density estimation (AKDE) address that classic kernel density estimation (KDE) does not?

options.text: AKDE removes the need for any GPS data at all
AKDE explicitly models the temporal autocorrelation between closely spaced GPS fixes, which classic KDE assumes away
AKDE only works for animals with fewer than 3 location points
AKDE and KDE are mathematically identical methods

explanations.a: AKDE, like KDE, is built directly from a series of location fixes such as GPS data; it does not eliminate the need for tracking data.
explanations.b: Correct — classic KDE assumes each point is statistically independent, which consecutive GPS fixes rarely are; AKDE (Fleming, Calabrese, and colleagues, via the ctmm package) models that autocorrelation directly, yielding more honest, often wider confidence intervals.
explanations.c: AKDE is designed for realistic telemetry datasets with many autocorrelated points, not tiny point sets.
explanations.d: They differ specifically in how they treat the independence assumption between successive location points.

questions.prompt: A commonly cited rule of thumb caps tracking-tag mass at roughly what percentage of an animal's body mass?

options.text: 20-25 percent
3-5 percent
50 percent
There is no widely cited guideline

explanations.a: A tag at 20-25 percent of body mass would be expected to substantially impair behavior and survival; this far exceeds accepted guidelines.
explanations.b: Correct — the commonly cited rule of thumb is roughly 3-5 percent of body mass, tighter (closer to 3 percent) for flying or energetically constrained species and looser (closer to 5 percent) for larger terrestrial mammals.
explanations.c: 50 percent is wildly outside any accepted animal-welfare guideline for tracking devices.
explanations.d: The 3-5 percent body-mass rule is a widely referenced guideline in wildlife telemetry literature, grounded in studies of tag effects on behavior and survival.

lessons.label: What a Population Trend Number Really Means

sections.heading: An index is not a headcount
sections.body: The Living Planet Index (LPI), maintained by WWF and the Zoological Society of London, is the source of the oft-quoted claim that vertebrate populations fell 68% between 1970 and 2016 (Living Planet Report 2020). It is built from roughly 20,811 population time series covering 4,392 vertebrate species, weighted by realm (terrestrial, freshwater, marine) and taxonomic group so that heavily monitored groups like temperate birds do not swamp poorly monitored ones like tropical amphibians. Each series is smoothed and gaps between survey years are interpolated using a generalized additive model fit in log10 space, then converted into year-over-year ratios. The index is the geometric mean of those ratios across all populations — a rate-of-change average, not a sum of animals counted. To see why that distinction matters, consider two populations: one goes from 100 to 200 individuals (a ratio of 2.0) and another goes from 100 to 50 (a ratio of 0.5). An arithmetic mean of those ratios is 1.25, suggesting net growth; a geometric mean is exactly 1.0, showing the gain and loss perfectly offset — because a halving and a doubling are equal and opposite on a proportional scale, not on a linear one. The LPI uses the geometric mean precisely because proportional change, not absolute change, is what is comparable across species of wildly different population sizes.

sections.heading: Why the headline number is not the typical population
sections.body: Leung et al. (2020, Nature, 'Clustered versus catastrophic global vertebrate declines') re-analyzed the same underlying LPI data and found the 1970–2016 decline is driven by a small cluster of extreme crashes — on the order of 1% of populations, concentrated in about 16 systems such as Latin American reptiles/amphibians/mammals, Indo-Malayan freshwater birds and amphibians, Arctic mammals, and fish worldwide. Strip those clusters out and the remaining populations show no clear mean trend — closer to stable. This happens because a geometric mean of ratios is dominated by proportional collapses: a population falling from 1,000 to 10 individuals contributes a ratio of 0.01, and in log space that single series can outweigh dozens of gently fluctuating ones. The headline percentage is real, but it describes the aggregate, not 'the typical population,' and it does not mean 99% of monitored species are crashing.

sections.heading: Reporting a trend honestly
sections.body: A defensible trend claim fits a log-linear model — regressing log(abundance) on year, so the slope is a constant per-year rate of change — and reports that slope with a confidence interval, not a single bare percentage. State how missing years were imputed, since GAM interpolation assumes a smooth trajectory between real counts and can mask real crashes or recoveries. Distinguish 'the median population in this dataset changed by X%' from 'the mean-weighted index changed by Y%' — they can point in different directions, and conflating them is the most common misuse of the LPI in student and even journalistic writing.

lessons.workedExample: A dataset has 20 amphibian populations tracked 2000–2020. Nineteen fluctuate mildly and end within 10% of their start. One, in a wetland drained for agriculture, collapses from 4,000 to 40 individuals (a ratio of 0.01). The median population's trend is roughly flat. But the geometric mean of all 20 ratios — the LPI-style statistic — is pulled sharply downward by that one log-scale outlier, potentially yielding an aggregate 'decline' of roughly 20-28% even though 19 of 20 sites look stable. A student reporting only 'amphibians declined 35% at my sites' has reproduced the LPI's own headline-vs-median gap without realizing it.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask about aggregate trend statistics because the LPI's 68%/73% figures are the most-cited numbers in popular conservation writing, and repeating them uncritically is a tell that a student never opened the methodology. A strong answer explains that the index is a geometric mean sensitive to a minority of extreme proportional declines (citing Leung et al. 2020) and reports their own data's median alongside any mean-based statistic. A weak answer treats 'X% decline' as if it describes every population in the sample, or cannot explain why a geometric mean behaves differently from an arithmetic one.

questions.prompt: The Living Planet Index aggregates population time series using which statistic?

options.text: The arithmetic mean of raw population counts
The geometric mean of year-over-year rates of change
The median of final population sizes
A simple sum of all counted individuals

explanations.a: Raw counts across species (birds, fish, amphibians) are not comparable units, so the index never sums or averages them directly.
explanations.b: Correct — each population's series is converted to year-over-year ratios in log space, and those ratios are combined with a geometric mean, weighted by realm and taxon.
explanations.c: The median of final sizes would ignore trajectory entirely and is not how the LPI is calculated.
explanations.d: Summing individuals across unrelated species (e.g., elephants and minnows) produces a meaningless number, which is exactly why an index of relative change is used instead.

questions.prompt: According to Leung et al. (2020), what mainly drives the LPI's large aggregate decline figure?

options.text: A broad, roughly uniform decline spread evenly across almost all monitored populations
A small cluster of populations with extreme proportional collapses concentrated in specific systems
Sampling more species in 2016 than in 1970
A change in which countries reported data to WWF

explanations.a: Leung et al. found the opposite: most populations showed no clear mean trend once the extreme-decline clusters were removed.
explanations.b: Correct — around 1% of populations, clustered in about 16 systems (e.g., Latin American reptiles/amphibians/mammals, Indo-Malayan freshwater taxa, Arctic mammals, global fish), account for most of the aggregate decline.
explanations.c: Changing sample composition is a real methodological concern for indices generally, but it is not the mechanism Leung et al. identified for this pattern.
explanations.d: Reporting-country changes are not the explanation given in the paper; the effect is about which populations, not which countries, dominate the statistic.

questions.prompt: Why can one population crashing from 1,000 to 10 individuals dominate a geometric-mean index even among dozens of stable populations?

options.text: Because the geometric mean is computed in log space, where a 99% proportional loss is a very large negative value relative to small fluctuations in stable populations
Because the LPI weights larger-bodied animals more heavily
Because population crashes are always measured with more precision than stable counts
Because the index drops all populations that do not decline before averaging

explanations.a: Correct — ratios are log-transformed before averaging, so a proportional collapse (a ratio near 0) contributes a disproportionately large negative log value compared to populations only fluctuating a few percent.
explanations.b: The LPI weights by realm and taxonomic group, not by body size.
explanations.c: Measurement precision is unrelated to why proportional collapses dominate a geometric mean; the effect is purely mathematical.
explanations.d: The index does not discard stable populations; all monitored populations are included in the geometric mean.

questions.prompt: Match each step in building the LPI to what it accomplishes.

left.text: Weighting by realm and taxonomic group
Taking the geometric mean across populations

right.text: Fills gaps between survey years with an assumed smooth trajectory
Puts unlike species on a comparable relative-change scale
Prevents heavily monitored groups from swamping poorly monitored ones
Aggregates rates of change without letting raw scale dominate, but stays sensitive to proportional collapses

questions.explanation: Each processing step solves a specific problem: interpolation handles missing years, ratios make species comparable, realm/taxon weighting prevents sampling bias, and the geometric mean aggregates relative change — while remaining vulnerable to domination by extreme proportional declines.

questions.prompt: A student's project reports 'our fish site declined 40%' based only on the index-style aggregate across five monitored plots. What is the strongest way to make this claim more honest?

options.text: Round the number to 50% so it sounds more dramatic and grant-worthy
Report the median plot's trend alongside the aggregate, and give the log-linear slope with a confidence interval instead of a single bare percentage
Drop the plot with the smallest population so the number looks cleaner
Report the number without describing how gaps in the survey years were filled in

explanations.a: Inflating a number for dramatic effect is not a scientific improvement and misrepresents the data.
explanations.b: Correct — pairing the aggregate with the median trend shows whether a few outliers are driving the number, and a fitted slope with uncertainty is more defensible than one raw percent.
explanations.c: Discarding a real data point to make the result look tidier is a form of selective reporting, not honest analysis.
explanations.d: Omitting how missing years were interpolated hides an assumption that can materially change the reported trend; it should be stated, not left out.

lessons.label: Counterfactuals: Compared to What?

sections.heading: Protected areas are not placed at random
sections.body: The question 'did this protected area work?' seems to invite a simple before-after comparison: measure deforestation inside the reserve before and after it was designated. That comparison is biased, because reserves are not assigned by lottery. Governments tend to protect land that is steep, remote, poor soil, or far from roads — land nobody was going to clear anyway. A naive before-after (or protected-vs-unprotected) comparison then credits the protection policy for deforestation that would never have happened. This is the core problem of impact evaluation: every causal claim about an intervention needs a credible counterfactual, an estimate of what would have happened without it, and simple observed comparisons rarely supply one.

sections.heading: Andam et al. (2008): matching collapses the naive estimate
sections.body: Andam, Ferraro, Pfaff, Sánchez-Azofeifa, and Robalino (PNAS, 2008) tested this directly on Costa Rica's protected-area network. A naive comparison of protected versus unprotected land overstated avoided deforestation, because protected parcels were systematically steeper, higher-elevation, farther from roads and markets, and on poorer soils than unprotected parcels — all factors that independently suppress deforestation. The team used statistical matching: for each protected pixel, they found unprotected pixels with near-identical slope, elevation, road distance, and soil quality, then compared deforestation rates only within matched pairs. Once matched, the estimated effect of protection on avoided deforestation shrank substantially from the naive figure — roughly an order of magnitude smaller, dropping from a naive estimate on the order of several percentage points of avoided deforestation per year to well under one percentage point per year once matched. Protection still mattered, but far less than the raw comparison implied, because most of the raw difference was really the land's own inaccessibility doing the work.

sections.heading: Other designs that manufacture a counterfactual
sections.body: Matching is one of several standard tools. BACI (Before-After-Control-Impact) designs pair a treatment site with a similar untreated control site and track both before and after the intervention, so a shared regional shock (drought, a market crash) does not get misread as the treatment's effect. Difference-in-differences compares the change over time in a treated group to the change over time in a control group, isolating the treatment's effect from any parallel trend both groups shared. Regression discontinuity exploits a sharp boundary — comparing land just inside a reserve edge to land just outside it — on the logic that plots meters apart on either side of an arbitrary line are otherwise nearly identical, so any jump in outcomes at the line is attributable to protection status itself.

lessons.workedExample: A team claims a new marine reserve cut fishing pressure 60% by comparing catch-per-boat inside the reserve after closure to catch-per-boat inside the same area before closure. But the surrounding fishery also crashed regionally that year from a fuel-price spike that idled boats everywhere. A BACI redesign compares the reserve to a similar unprotected reef nearby, both before and after closure: if catch fell 60% inside the reserve but also fell 45% at the unprotected control reef over the same period, the reserve's own causal effect is closer to a 15-percentage-point difference-in-differences, not 60%.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges push on 'compared to what?' because it is the single fastest way to separate a real impact evaluation from a before-after anecdote, and conservation projects are especially prone to this error since sites are chosen for convenience or existing protection, not at random. A strong answer names the specific comparison group used, states what confounders it controls for (as in Andam et al.'s slope/elevation/road/soil matching), and can explain why the naive estimate was biased in a specific direction. A weak answer reports a before-after difference and calls it 'the effect' without ever naming a control.

questions.prompt: Why does a naive before-after comparison overstate the effect of many protected areas on avoided deforestation?

options.text: Protected areas are randomly assigned, so any difference must be caused by protection
Protected land tends to be systematically less accessible and less agriculturally valuable than unprotected land, so it would have seen less deforestation anyway
Satellite imagery cannot detect deforestation inside reserve boundaries
Deforestation rates are constant everywhere regardless of land quality

explanations.a: The opposite is true — protected areas are not randomly assigned, which is exactly why a naive comparison is biased.
explanations.b: Correct — Andam et al. (2008) showed protected Costa Rican land was systematically steeper, higher, farther from roads, and on poorer soil, all of which independently reduce deforestation pressure regardless of legal status.
explanations.c: Satellite-based deforestation detection works fine inside reserves; the bias is about site selection, not measurement technology.
explanations.d: Deforestation rates vary strongly with slope, access, and soil, which is precisely the confound driving the naive estimate's bias.

questions.prompt: What did statistical matching on slope, elevation, road distance, and soil do to Andam et al.'s (2008) estimate of Costa Rica's protected-area effect?

options.text: It increased the estimated effect beyond the naive comparison
It substantially reduced the estimated effect compared to the naive comparison, though protection still had a measurable impact
It had no effect on the estimate
It proved protected areas caused more deforestation than unprotected land

explanations.a: Matching removed confounds that were inflating the naive estimate, so the effect shrank rather than grew.
explanations.b: Correct — after matching on observable confounders, the estimated avoided deforestation dropped well below the naive figure, but protection still showed a real, smaller, positive effect.
explanations.c: The whole point of the paper is that matching changed the estimate substantially; it was not a null result.
explanations.d: Matching still found protection reduced deforestation relative to matched unprotected land, just by less than the naive comparison suggested.

questions.prompt: Match each impact-evaluation design to the logic it relies on.

right.text: Pairs treated units with untreated units that share observable confounding characteristics
Tracks a treated site and a similar untreated site both before and after, so shared regional shocks cancel out
Compares the change over time in treated vs. control groups to isolate the treatment's effect from a shared trend
Compares units just inside and just outside a sharp treatment boundary, which are otherwise nearly identical

questions.explanation: Each design manufactures a counterfactual differently: matching pairs on confounders, BACI adds a control site across time, difference-in-differences isolates a trend, and regression discontinuity exploits a sharp assignment boundary.

questions.prompt: A regional fuel-price spike idles fishing boats everywhere the same year a marine reserve closes to fishing. Which design best isolates the reserve's own effect from the fuel-price shock?

options.text: Comparing catch inside the reserve before versus after closure only
A BACI or difference-in-differences design comparing the reserve to a similar unprotected control site, both before and after closure
Reporting the raw percent drop in catch inside the reserve as the effect of protection
Averaging catch across all years since the reserve was created

explanations.a: A before-after comparison inside the reserve alone cannot separate the reserve's effect from the region-wide fuel shock, since both hit the same year.
explanations.b: Correct — comparing changes in the reserve to changes at a similar unprotected control site nets out the shared regional shock, leaving an estimate closer to the reserve's true effect.
explanations.c: The raw drop conflates the reserve's effect with the fuel-price shock's effect on the whole regional fishery.
explanations.d: Averaging across years does not separate a shared external shock from the treatment's effect; it can even smear the shock across the whole time series.

lessons.label: Power, Type II Error, and the Cost of Missing a Decline

sections.heading: Two ways to be wrong, and conservation cares more about one
sections.body: A statistical test can fail in two directions: a Type I error declares a decline that is not real (a false alarm), and a Type II error fails to detect a decline that is real (a miss). Standard hypothesis testing is built to control Type I error tightly (conventionally at 5%), but says nothing by default about Type II error — and in conservation, a missed decline is usually the costlier mistake, because a stock can be quietly extirpated while surveys keep reporting 'no significant trend.' Statistical power is 1 minus the Type II error rate: the probability a test correctly detects a real decline of a given size, given the sampling design actually used.

sections.heading: Taylor et al. (2007): power was catastrophically low
sections.body: Taylor, Martinez, Gerrodette, Barlow, and Hrovat (Marine Mammal Science, 2007) computed power to detect a 'precipitous decline' — defined by the U.S. Marine Mammal Protection Act as a 50% drop in abundance over 15 years, the threshold for listing a stock as depleted — using the actual survey frequency and precision on record for 127 U.S. marine mammal stocks. They found 70% of those stocks had survey programs too imprecise to reliably detect a 50% decline over 15 years. Specific cases were stark: Atlantic spotted dolphins in the western North Atlantic had roughly 11% power to detect that decline, and Pacific white-sided dolphins off the U.S. West Coast had roughly 15% power. A coin flip would have done nearly as well. The mechanism is straightforward: power depends on effect size, the year-to-year variance (coefficient of variation) of abundance estimates, and the number of surveys — and cetacean surveys are typically infrequent, expensive, and noisy (CVs often 20-50%), so the sampling design was never built to catch a real decline of that size.

sections.heading: Reporting non-significance honestly, and the precautionary shift
sections.body: 'Not statistically significant' means the data could not rule out no-change at the chosen confidence level; it does not mean the population is stable, and treating it that way is a Type II error hiding in plain sight. Honest reporting states the estimated power alongside the result — a non-significant trend from a test with 11% power to detect the decline of concern is nearly uninformative, while the same non-significant result from a test with 90% power is meaningful evidence of stability. This gap motivates the precautionary principle in conservation policy: when monitoring cannot reliably detect a decline of concern, the burden of proof should shift toward managers demonstrating a stock is not declining, rather than requiring conservationists to prove that it is.

lessons.workedExample: A stock is surveyed every 5 years with an abundance estimate CV of 30%. A biologist wants to detect a 50% decline over 15 years (three survey intervals) at the standard 5% significance level. Plugging that effect size, CV, and sample size into a power calculation yields power well under 50% — meaning even if the stock truly halved, the survey program would more likely than not report 'no significant decline.' A manager who takes that non-significant result as proof of a healthy stock, rather than as a low-power test that could not have caught the decline even if it happened, has committed exactly the error Taylor et al. warned about.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe power because 'the difference was not statistically significant' is the single most misused phrase in student conservation projects — it is routinely presented as evidence of no effect when it is really an admission the test could not see one. A strong answer states or estimates the power of their own test, names the sample size and variance driving it, and explicitly separates 'we found no evidence of decline' from 'we have evidence of no decline.' A weak answer reports a p-value above 0.05 and concludes the population is fine.

questions.prompt: In conservation monitoring, why is a Type II error (failing to detect a real decline) often considered more costly than a Type I error (a false alarm)?

options.text: Type II errors are impossible to make in ecological studies
A missed real decline can let a stock continue crashing undetected until intervention is too late or impossible
Type I errors never occur once significance is set at 5%
Type II errors only affect the researcher's reputation, not the species

explanations.a: Type II errors are common, especially when statistical power is low, as Taylor et al. (2007) demonstrated for marine mammal stocks.
explanations.b: Correct — a false 'no decline' result can delay or prevent management action while a real decline continues, which is why conservation statistics often weight Type II error heavily.
explanations.c: Setting significance at 5% only caps the Type I error rate; Type I errors can still occur roughly 5% of the time by design.
explanations.d: A missed decline has direct consequences for the species (delayed protection), not just for how the researcher is perceived.

questions.prompt: Taylor et al. (2007) found that what fraction of the 127 U.S. marine mammal stocks they examined had survey programs too imprecise to reliably detect a 50% decline over 15 years?

options.text: About 10%
About 30%
About 70%
Essentially 0%; nearly all had adequate power

explanations.a: 10% substantially understates the scale of the problem the paper reported.
explanations.b: 30% is roughly the inverse of the actual finding — 30% had adequate precision, not 70%.
explanations.c: Correct — roughly 70% of the 127 stocks studied lacked the survey precision needed to reliably detect a precipitous (50% over 15 years) decline.
explanations.d: The paper's central, widely cited finding is the opposite: power was inadequate for the large majority of stocks examined, with some (like Atlantic spotted dolphins) as low as ~11%.

questions.prompt: Which factor does NOT directly determine the statistical power of a trend test?

options.text: The size of the effect (decline) you are trying to detect
The precision (coefficient of variation) of each abundance estimate
The number of independent surveys conducted
The species' common name

explanations.a: Effect size is a core input to any power calculation — larger declines are easier to detect at fixed sample size and precision.
explanations.b: Precision (CV) of the abundance estimates directly sets how much noise a real signal must overcome, and lower CV raises power.
explanations.c: More independent surveys reduce the standard error of the estimated trend, which raises power.
explanations.d: Correct — a species' name has no statistical bearing on power; only effect size, measurement precision, sample size, and significance threshold do.

questions.prompt: A study reports 'the population trend was not statistically significant (p = 0.31), so the population is stable.' What is the most accurate criticism of this statement?

options.text: p = 0.31 actually proves the population is declining
Nothing is wrong; non-significance is equivalent to proof of stability
A non-significant result only means the data could not rule out no-change at the chosen threshold; without reporting power, it cannot be read as evidence the population is actually stable
The p-value should have been compared to 0.10 instead of 0.05

explanations.a: A p-value above the significance threshold does not indicate a decline; it indicates the test failed to reject no-change, which is a different claim entirely.
explanations.b: This is the exact error the lesson addresses — non-significance without reported power can just as easily reflect low power to detect a real decline as it can reflect true stability.
explanations.c: Correct — the statement conflates 'failed to detect a decline' with 'detected no decline is present.' Reporting the test's power against a decline of concern is required to interpret the non-significant result honestly.
explanations.d: Changing the significance threshold does not resolve the underlying conflation between non-significance and proof of stability; it only shifts where that same conflation would occur.

lessons.label: The Evidence Gap and Why Interventions Go Untested

sections.heading: Most conservation actions are chosen from habit, not evidence
sections.body: William Sutherland and colleagues built the Conservation Evidence project at Cambridge to do something surprisingly rare in the field: systematically catalog conservation interventions (planting hedgerows for farmland birds, building bat gantries over roads, translocating a threatened amphibian) alongside every published test of whether each one actually works. The project exposed how thin the evidence base is. In analyses of the database, roughly 32% of catalogued interventions for amphibians and 25% for birds had no associated tests at all, or only reviews with no primary studies behind them — meaning practitioners choosing that action have no evaluated evidence to draw on, only precedent and intuition. Globally, the density of studies is so low that for a typical location there is, on average, fewer than one relevant study within 2,000 km.

sections.heading: 'Evidence complacency' and why the gap persists
sections.body: Sutherland and Wordley named this pattern evidence complacency in a 2017 Nature Ecology & Evolution paper: a culture in which decisions are made without seeking or using available evidence, and where the impact of actions is rarely tested afterward even when they could be. Their example is a bat gantry — an overhead crossing meant to guide bats safely over roads — which UK studies found ineffective at actually reducing bat road mortality, yet gantries kept being built into new road projects because the *idea* was already institutionally normal. Publication bias compounds the gap: studies showing an intervention worked are more likely to be written up and published than studies showing it did nothing, so even the tests that do exist skew optimistic, and failed or null interventions are underrepresented in what a practitioner can find.

sections.heading: Fixing this with systematic review and reporting standards
sections.body: The response is Evidence-Based Conservation: instead of one convenient study, a systematic review exhaustively searches all available literature (published and unpublished, or 'grey' literature) using a pre-registered protocol, appraises study quality, and synthesizes the results, so a single flashy but unreplicated finding cannot dominate practice. The Collaboration for Environmental Evidence (CEE) publishes formal guidelines (currently version 5.0) that set the standard for how such reviews should be planned, searched, and reported, and runs an open-access journal, Environmental Evidence, so protocols and results are checkable rather than buried. A science-fair project that cites a single supportive paper for its chosen intervention has not done what a systematic review does; citing the Conservation Evidence rating (or its absence) for that action is a meaningfully stronger evidentiary basis.

lessons.workedExample: A student proposes installing nest boxes to help a declining local bird species, citing one paper showing nest boxes worked well for a different species in a different country. Checking the Conservation Evidence database for the actual target species and region reveals the action falls into the roughly 25%+ of bird interventions with no local test at all — the supportive citation is real but not transferable evidence. A stronger project either finds a systematic review covering the same species/habitat combination, or explicitly frames its own field trial as adding a data point to a genuinely under-tested action, rather than presenting nest boxes as a proven solution.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'has this actually been tested for your species, in a place like yours?' because most students cite one convenient success story rather than checking whether the action is broadly evaluated or sits in the untested minority. A strong answer distinguishes 'an action that worked once, somewhere' from 'an action supported by a systematic review across many sites,' and can say honestly if their chosen intervention is one of the many still under-evidenced. A weak answer treats any single positive citation as settling the question.

questions.prompt: In analyses of the Conservation Evidence database, roughly what share of catalogued interventions for amphibians had no associated primary studies (untested or reviews only)?

options.text: Roughly 32%
Roughly 2%
Essentially 0%; nearly all interventions are tested
100%; no amphibian intervention has ever been tested

explanations.a: Correct — about 32% of catalogued amphibian interventions had no primary tests, only reviews, or nothing at all in the database.
explanations.b: 2% dramatically understates the gap the database analyses actually found.
explanations.c: The database's central finding is the opposite: a substantial share of common interventions lack primary evidence.
explanations.d: Some amphibian interventions do have tests; the gap is large but not total.

questions.prompt: What does Sutherland and Wordley's term 'evidence complacency' describe?

options.text: A shortage of funding for conservation biology as a field
A culture where decisions are made and repeated without seeking or using available evidence, and impacts go untested even when testing is feasible
The tendency of journals to reject all conservation manuscripts
A statistical bias in how the Living Planet Index is calculated

explanations.a: Funding shortages are a related but distinct issue; evidence complacency is specifically about not seeking or using evidence that may already exist or be feasible to gather.
explanations.b: Correct — the term describes persistence of practice by habit, precedent, and intuition rather than by consulting or generating tested evidence, illustrated by bat gantries that kept being built despite evidence they did not work.
explanations.c: The term is not about journal rejection rates.
explanations.d: This concept is unrelated to the LPI's mathematical construction; it concerns decision-making culture in conservation practice, not index statistics.

questions.prompt: Why does publication bias make the existing conservation literature look more favorable to interventions than it should?

options.text: Because journals require every published study to report a positive result before accepting it
Because studies showing an intervention worked are more likely to be written up and published than studies showing it had no effect, skewing the visible evidence toward success
Because negative results are scientifically impossible to obtain
Because the Conservation Evidence database only accepts positive findings

explanations.a: Journals do not have a formal positive-result requirement, but informal incentives still favor publishing and pursuing 'it worked' findings over null results.
explanations.b: Correct — this asymmetry in what gets written up and published means the surviving literature systematically over-represents successful interventions relative to how often they actually succeed.
explanations.c: Null results are entirely obtainable; the issue is that they are less likely to be published, not impossible to produce.
explanations.d: Conservation Evidence deliberately includes null and negative findings; that is part of what makes it useful against publication bias, not a source of it.

questions.prompt: Order these steps as they occur in conducting a formal systematic review under Collaboration for Environmental Evidence (CEE) guidelines.

items.text: Register a pre-specified protocol defining the question and search strategy
Exhaustively search published and unpublished ('grey') literature
Appraise the quality and risk of bias of each study found
Synthesize results across studies and publish the review openly

questions.explanation: CEE-standard systematic reviews begin with a registered protocol (to prevent cherry-picking questions after seeing results), then search broadly across both published and grey literature, then critically appraise each study's quality, and finally synthesize and publish the findings openly.

lessons.label: Declaring Extinction, and the Cost of Being Wrong

sections.heading: From a 50-year rule to exhaustive surveys
sections.body: Older conservation practice often used an informal '50-year rule': if no confirmed sighting had occurred in 50 years despite reasonable search effort, a species could be presumed extinct. The IUCN Red List replaced that shortcut with a stricter standard: a species is listed Extinct (EX) only when there is no reasonable doubt the last individual has died, which in practice requires that exhaustive surveys in known and expected habitat, at appropriate times (season, time of day), throughout its historic range, have failed to record an individual over a time frame appropriate to the species' life cycle. This shifts the burden from a fixed clock to demonstrated search effort — a species surveyed thoroughly for five years can be declared extinct sooner than one that simply has not been reported in fifty.

sections.heading: Turning silence into a number: Solow's optimal linear estimation
sections.body: Even 'exhaustive' surveys leave uncertainty, so statisticians built models that use the pattern of a sighting record's own decline to estimate an extinction date. Solow's optimal linear estimation (OLE) treats the gaps between the last several confirmed sightings as data: if sightings were frequent and then abruptly stopped, that pattern is itself evidence, and OLE produces a confidence interval for when extinction likely occurred, extending beyond the last confirmed record. Turvey and colleagues applied this logic to the Yangtze river dolphin (baiji) after a intensive six-week, multi-team 2006 survey of the entire Yangtze found no baiji; sighting-based estimation methods were consistent with functional extinction around that period, and the dolphin was subsequently declared possibly extinct — the first cetacean extinction attributable to human activity.

sections.heading: The ivory-billed woodpecker: a case study in evidentiary standards
sections.body: The opposite risk — declaring extinction too soon, called the Romeo error (after the Shakespeare character who acts fatally on a false report of death) — is illustrated by the ivory-billed woodpecker. Long presumed extinct in the US, a 2004 Arkansas sighting led a Cornell-based team to publish 'Ivory-billed Woodpecker Persists in Continental North America' in Science (Fitzpatrick et al., 2005), citing eyewitness reports, foraging sign, and a four-second video. Ornithologists David Sibley, Louis Bevier, Michael Patten, and Chris Elphick published a formal comment in Science the following year arguing the video showed a Pileated Woodpecker — its wings show a black trailing edge in flight, unlike the ivory-bill's white one — reigniting the dispute rather than resolving it. No unambiguous photograph has settled the case since. The episode is now a standard teaching example of how thin a single video or witness record is as extinction (or rediscovery) evidence, and of 'Lazarus species' — organisms like the coelacanth, rediscovered in 1938 after presumed Cretaceous extinction — that show declaring extinction from absence of evidence is itself a fallible, revisable claim.

lessons.workedExample: A small freshwater fish has not been recorded since 2010 despite three short surveys in 2015, 2018, and 2022, none targeting its known spawning season. Under the old 50-year rule, nothing could be concluded for decades. Under the IUCN exhaustive-survey standard, the species cannot yet be declared extinct either, because the surveys were not exhaustive (wrong season, short duration, incomplete range coverage) — the correct classification is 'Possibly Extinct' or 'Critically Endangered,' not Extinct, until a survey matched to its biology and full range comes back empty. Declaring it extinct now, then finding one in 2027, would be a Romeo error with real cost: habitat protections and funding for the species would likely have already been withdrawn.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges probe extinction claims because 'presumed extinct' sounds definitive but is usually a probabilistic judgment resting on search effort, not certainty. A strong answer explains what would count as an adequately exhaustive survey for their specific organism (season, habitat, range coverage) and can name the Romeo-error cost of declaring too soon versus the cost of declaring too late. A weak answer treats 'no one has seen it in years' as automatically equivalent to extinct, without addressing whether anyone actually looked properly.

questions.prompt: What does the modern IUCN standard require before listing a species as Extinct (EX), in place of the older informal 50-year rule?

options.text: Simply that 50 calendar years have passed since the last sighting, regardless of search effort
Exhaustive surveys of known and expected habitat, at appropriate times, across the species' historic range, that fail to record an individual over a timeframe appropriate to its life cycle
A unanimous vote among all national wildlife agencies
A single confirmed absence during one field season

explanations.a: This describes the older, cruder 50-year rule the IUCN standard was designed to replace.
explanations.b: Correct — the modern standard ties the extinction call to demonstrated, adequately timed and located search effort rather than to a fixed number of years.
explanations.c: No such voting mechanism exists in the IUCN Red List assessment process.
explanations.d: A single season's absence is far short of the exhaustive, range-wide, appropriately timed search the standard requires.

questions.prompt: What does Solow's optimal linear estimation (OLE) method use to estimate an extinction date?

options.text: The genetic diversity of museum specimens
The pattern and spacing of the last several confirmed sighting dates in the historical record
Satellite measurements of habitat loss alone
A fixed 50-year waiting period after the last sighting

explanations.a: Genetic diversity is unrelated to OLE, which is a sighting-record statistical method.
explanations.b: Correct — OLE treats the gaps between the last several sightings as informative data, producing a confidence interval for the true extinction date, as applied to the baiji's 2006 survey record.
explanations.c: Habitat-loss data can motivate concern but is not the input OLE itself uses; OLE is specifically a sighting-record method.
explanations.d: OLE replaces exactly this kind of fixed waiting period with a statistically derived estimate.

questions.prompt: The 2006 Yangtze survey and subsequent analysis of the baiji (Yangtze river dolphin) led researchers to conclude what?

options.text: The population had rebounded significantly
The species was likely functionally extinct, the first cetacean extinction attributable to human activity
The species had never actually existed
Sightings were too frequent to draw any conclusion

explanations.a: The intensive six-week 2006 survey found no baiji at all, the opposite of a rebound.
explanations.b: Correct — the survey and sighting-based extinction estimation were consistent with the baiji's functional extinction around that period, making it the first cetacean extinction widely attributed to human causes.
explanations.c: The baiji was a well-documented, historically confirmed species; the finding concerned its extinction, not its existence.
explanations.d: Sightings had become rare and sparse by the 2000s, which is precisely what made a statistical extinction-date estimate necessary.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its correct description from the ivory-billed woodpecker and related extinction-evidence cases.

right.text: Declaring a species extinct prematurely, prompting real-world consequences based on a false report of its death
A species rediscovered after being presumed extinct, such as the coelacanth in 1938
The Science paper claiming continued persistence of the ivory-billed woodpecker in Arkansas based on video and eyewitness evidence
The published comment arguing the video evidence actually showed a Pileated Woodpecker, not an ivory-bill

questions.explanation: The Romeo error names the cost of premature extinction declarations; Lazarus species are later rediscovered after presumed extinction; Fitzpatrick et al. (2005, Science) made the persistence claim; Sibley et al. (2006, Science) disputed the video evidence behind it.

lessons.label: Confounds Judges Will Find in a Conservation Study

sections.heading: Pseudoreplication: one site is not forty quadrats
sections.body: Stuart Hurlbert's 1984 paper 'Pseudoreplication and the Design of Ecological Field Experiments' (Ecological Monographs) named the single most common design flaw he found scanning 176 published ecological studies: treating non-independent samples as if they were independent replicates. Surveying one protected reserve and one unprotected control site, then counting 40 quadrats inside each and running a t-test on 40-vs-40, gives an n of 1-vs-1 for the actual treatment (reserve status), not 40-vs-40 — the quadrats within a site share the same weather, soil, management history, and are not independent draws of 'what protection does.' Hurlbert found this error in roughly a quarter of the studies he reviewed and nearly half of those that used inferential statistics at all. The fix is interspersion: multiple, physically separate reserves and controls, so the true treatment-level replicate count matches what the statistics claim.

sections.heading: Scale mismatch and the 'rock and ice' confound
sections.body: A second failure mode is scale mismatch: measuring an outcome at a grain finer or coarser than the process that actually drives it, so noise (or an unrelated pattern) swamps the real effect. Bird territory counts at the scale of individual trees say little about a landscape-level fragmentation effect, and vice versa. Layered onto this is the classic 'rock and ice' confound named in the protected-area literature: reserves are disproportionately sited on land that is steep, high-elevation, remote, and agriculturally poor — the same bias Andam et al. (2008) quantified for Costa Rica — so a comparison group of 'unprotected land' is systematically more productive and more accessible than the reserves, not a fair counterfactual. A student comparing biodiversity inside a mountain reserve to biodiversity in nearby farmland is comparing rock-and-ice to fertile valley, not testing protection.

sections.heading: Detection confounds: it's not there, or you just didn't see it
sections.body: A count of zero individuals means either the species is absent or it was present but not detected — observer skill, time of day, season, and weather all change detection probability independently of true abundance. An observer who is more experienced at the treatment site, or who surveys the reserve in calm morning weather and the control site during midday wind, will find systematically different counts even with identical true populations. The fix is to design detection confounds out directly: use paired plots surveyed by the same observer(s) under matched conditions, randomize which site is visited first and by whom, and where possible use repeat-visit occupancy methods that estimate detection probability separately from true occupancy, rather than assuming every zero count means true absence.

lessons.workedExample: A student compares insect diversity in one protected wetland (8 pitfall traps) to one unprotected wetland (8 pitfall traps), runs a t-test treating the 16 traps as independent, and reports p < 0.05 for higher diversity in the reserve. A judge asks how many reserves and how many controls were sampled: the honest answer is one and one. The traps are pseudoreplicates — they share a single site's soil, hydrology, and edge effects — so the true treatment sample size is n=1 vs n=1, for which no valid p-value exists. A defensible redesign samples pitfall traps across at least 4-5 physically separate reserves and 4-5 separate unprotected wetlands, matched on elevation and accessibility, with trap-checking randomized across sites and observers.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'how many independent sites did you actually sample?' because pseudoreplication is the single fastest way to expose a p-value that does not mean what it claims, and it is extremely common in student reserve-vs-control projects that sample many subplots inside just one site per condition. A strong answer distinguishes the number of subsamples from the number of independent treatment-level replicates, names what makes the comparison groups non-equivalent beyond the treatment itself (the rock-and-ice confound), and describes how observer or timing differences were controlled. A weak answer reports a large subsample size as if it were the true replicate count and never mentions who did the surveying or when.

questions.prompt: A student samples 40 quadrats inside one protected reserve and 40 inside one unprotected site, then runs a t-test treating it as n=40 vs n=40. What is the actual treatment-level sample size, and what is this error called?

options.text: n=40 vs n=40; this is a correctly replicated design
n=1 vs n=1; this is pseudoreplication, as described by Hurlbert (1984)
n=80 vs n=80; combining both sites doubles the valid sample size
n=0 vs n=0; quadrat data can never be analyzed statistically

explanations.a: The quadrats within each single site are not independent of one another (shared soil, hydrology, management), so treating them as 40 independent replicates overstates the real sample size.
explanations.b: Correct — since there is only one reserve and one control site, the true treatment-level replication is n=1 vs n=1; the 40 quadrats are subsamples, not independent replicates, which is exactly the pseudoreplication Hurlbert (1984) documented in roughly a quarter of the studies he reviewed.
explanations.c: Combining both groups' counts does not create additional independent treatment-level replicates; it still reflects only two sites total.
explanations.d: Quadrat data can be analyzed, but only at the level of true independent replicates (sites), or with statistical methods that explicitly model non-independence.

questions.prompt: What is the 'rock and ice' confound in protected-area comparisons?

options.text: Protected reserves are disproportionately sited on steep, remote, low-productivity land, making them systematically different from typical unprotected comparison land for reasons unrelated to protection itself
Rocky terrain makes wildlife surveys physically impossible
Ice cover prevents any conservation research from occurring at high latitudes
Protected areas and unprotected areas are always geologically identical

explanations.a: Correct — because reserves tend to be placed on land nobody wanted to develop anyway (steep, remote, poor soil), a naive comparison to unprotected (often more fertile, accessible) land confounds site quality with protection status.
explanations.b: The confound is about systematic site-selection bias, not about physical survey difficulty on rocky ground.
explanations.c: The name is metaphorical for low-productivity, hard-to-access terrain generally, not a literal claim about polar research.
explanations.d: The entire point of the confound is that protected and unprotected land are systematically different, not identical, in the characteristics that independently drive the outcome being measured.

questions.prompt: Two sites have identical true bird populations, but the reserve is surveyed at dawn in calm weather by an experienced birder, while the control site is surveyed at midday in wind by a novice. The reserve shows a higher count. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The reserve genuinely supports more birds because it is protected
A detection confound — differences in observer skill, time of day, and weather changed detection probability, not true abundance
Birds can sense legal protection status and congregate accordingly
The result is unaffected by survey conditions since bird counts are always exact

explanations.a: The scenario stipulates identical true populations, so a genuine protection effect cannot explain the count difference; something else in the design must be responsible.
explanations.b: Correct — dawn calm conditions and an experienced observer both raise detection probability independent of true abundance, so the count gap reflects a detection confound rather than a real ecological difference.
explanations.c: This is not a mechanism in wildlife biology; the explanation must be methodological, not behavioral.
explanations.d: Bird counts are estimates limited by detectability, which is exactly why conditions like time of day, weather, and observer experience matter.

questions.prompt: Order these design steps to remove pseudoreplication and detection confounds from a reserve-vs-control comparison.

items.text: Select multiple physically separate reserve and control sites, matched on elevation, access, and soil
Randomize which sites and plots are visited first and by which observer
Survey paired plots under matched time-of-day and weather conditions
Analyze treatment effects using site as the unit of replication, not subplots within a single site

questions.explanation: A sound design first secures true independent replicates by choosing multiple matched sites, then randomizes visit order and observer assignment to prevent systematic detection bias, standardizes survey conditions across paired plots, and finally analyzes the data at the level of the true independent replicate (site), not the pseudoreplicated subsample.

lessons.label: From Game Management to a Field: The Historical Arc

sections.heading: Two founding camps: wise use versus preservation
sections.body: George Perkins Marsh's Man and Nature (1864) is usually credited as the first work to argue, with evidence, that human land use causes lasting ecological damage — he traced Mediterranean deforestation to soil erosion and river siltation and warned the United States was repeating it. That warning split into two rival philosophies. Gifford Pinchot, first chief of the U.S. Forest Service, pushed utilitarian 'wise use': manage nature for sustained human benefit. John Muir, Sierra Club founder, pushed preservation: some land should be protected untouched. Their fight came to a head over Hetch Hetchy, a valley in Yosemite that San Francisco wanted to dam for water. Congress passed the Raker Act in 1913 approving the dam; Muir, devastated, died the following year. Alongside them, George Bird Grinnell founded the first Audubon Society (1886) and, with Theodore Roosevelt, the Boone and Crockett Club (1887), building the institutional base for game and habitat protection.

sections.heading: Leopold: from managing game to an ethic
sections.body: Aldo Leopold's Game Management (1933) was the field's first textbook — it treated wildlife populations as manipulable through habitat, predator control, and harvest, effectively founding wildlife management as an applied science. Leopold's thinking then moved past management-for-yield. A Sand County Almanac, published posthumously in 1949 (he died fighting a grass fire in 1948), articulated the 'land ethic': extending the community concept from people to soils, waters, plants, and animals, judging an action right when it preserves the integrity, stability, and beauty of that community.

sections.heading: Silent Spring and the machinery that followed
sections.body: Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962) shifted conservation from a naturalist's concern to a public mobilization: she documented how DDT bioaccumulated up food chains and thinned raptor eggshells, and the backlash helped create the EPA (1970) and a U.S. DDT ban (1972). Law and institutions then codified what counted as a legitimate research question. The Endangered Species Act (1973) made extinction risk a regulatory category requiring formal science (listing, critical habitat, recovery plans). CITES, signed in 1973 and in force by 1975, regulated international wildlife trade. Michael Soulé and Bruce Wilcox's edited volume Conservation Biology: An Evolutionary-Ecological Perspective (1980) named and framed a new 'crisis discipline' — one that must act under uncertainty because the cost of waiting for certainty is extinction. The Society for Conservation Biology, founded in 1985, and its journal (1987), gave that discipline a home, turning conservation from a management craft into a mission-driven science with its own peer review.

lessons.workedExample: A student asks 'when did protecting nature become science instead of just ethics?' Point to the sequence: Marsh (1864) supplied the evidence that land use causes damage; Leopold's Game Management (1933) supplied testable techniques (predator control, habitat manipulation, harvest quotas); Soulé and Wilcox (1980) supplied the disciplinary claim that conservation is a distinct, mission-driven science justified by the urgency of extinction, not just applied wildlife biology. A strong project traces its own research question back along this chain — e.g., a habitat-restoration study sits downstream of Leopold's management tradition, while an extinction-risk model sits downstream of the 1980 crisis-discipline framing.
lessons.judgeFraming: Judges ask 'where does this field's science come from?' to see whether a student understands conservation biology as a discipline shaped by specific historical fights, not a timeless umbrella term for 'caring about nature.' A weak answer says 'people have always wanted to protect animals.' A strong answer names the Pinchot-Muir split as the origin of a real tension still present in the field (use versus preservation), and can explain why Soulé and Wilcox needed to argue, in 1980, that conservation deserved to be its own science — because before that it was scattered across wildlife management, forestry, and natural history with no shared journal or theory.

questions.prompt: The Hetch Hetchy dam fight is remembered as the defining clash between which two conservation philosophies?

options.text: Gifford Pinchot's utilitarian 'wise use' versus John Muir's preservationism
Aldo Leopold's land ethic versus Rachel Carson's public-health framing
Michael Soulé's crisis discipline versus island biogeography theory
George Perkins Marsh's erosion warnings versus CITES trade regulation

explanations.a: Correct — Pinchot argued for damming Hetch Hetchy to serve San Francisco's water needs (wise use), while Muir fought to preserve the valley untouched; the Raker Act (1913) sided with Pinchot's camp.
explanations.b: Leopold and Carson were not on opposite sides of Hetch Hetchy; both wrote decades later and were not direct antagonists in that dispute.
explanations.c: Soulé's crisis-discipline framing (1980) postdates Hetch Hetchy by nearly seven decades and concerns disciplinary identity, not a specific dam fight.
explanations.d: Marsh's 1864 work predates the dispute and CITES (1975) is a trade treaty, not a party to the Hetch Hetchy fight.

questions.prompt: What did Aldo Leopold's 'land ethic,' articulated in A Sand County Almanac (1949), add beyond his earlier Game Management (1933)?

options.text: The first statistical method for estimating population size
A moral extension of 'community' to soils, waters, plants, and animals, not just a management technique
The legal basis for the Endangered Species Act
The first captive-breeding protocol for endangered mammals

explanations.a: Statistical population estimation is a separate methodological tradition, not what the land ethic contributed.
explanations.b: Correct — Game Management treated wildlife as a resource to manipulate; the land ethic reframed the whole biotic community as deserving moral standing, judging actions by whether they preserve its integrity and stability.
explanations.c: The ESA (1973) came after Leopold's death and was driven by a separate legislative and scientific process, not directly by the land ethic.
explanations.d: Captive breeding as a formal recovery tool developed later, through 20th-century zoo and wildlife-agency programs, not from Leopold's writing.

questions.prompt: Put these milestones in chronological order.

items.text: Marsh's Man and Nature published
Leopold's Game Management published
Silent Spring published
Soulé and Wilcox's Conservation Biology published
Society for Conservation Biology founded

questions.explanation: Marsh (1864) came first, then Leopold's management textbook (1933), then Carson's public mobilization (1962), then Soulé and Wilcox's disciplinary manifesto (1980), and finally the professional society that institutionalized the field (1985).

questions.prompt: Match each law or treaty to what it actually regulates.

right.text: Domestic listing, critical habitat, and recovery planning for at-risk species
International trade in wildlife and wildlife products
Use of a specific agricultural pesticide, following eggshell-thinning evidence
Approval to dam Hetch Hetchy valley for San Francisco's water supply

questions.explanation: The ESA governs domestic listing and recovery; CITES governs cross-border trade; the DDT ban addressed a specific chemical's ecological harm; the Raker Act authorized the dam that ended the Hetch Hetchy fight in Pinchot's favor.

lessons.label: SLOSS: The Debate That Built Reserve Design

sections.heading: Diamond's geometric rules
sections.body: In 1975, Jared Diamond published 'The Island Dilemma' in Biological Conservation, translating MacArthur and Wilson's equilibrium theory of island biogeography (1967) into practical reserve-design rules for conservationists.
